Now we will return again to the Amlicites, for they also had a mark set upon them; yea, they set the mark upon themselves, yea, even a mark of red upon their foreheads.

provenance.other: “In their foreheads” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, all in Revelation, and “receive his mark” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 14:9. A mark set on a forehead outside Revelation occurs only at Ezekiel 9:4, which is adjudicated at 3:7. The Book of Mormon's 'a mark of red upon their foreheads' matches no KJV verse; the shared element is the forehead and the marking, not a run of words.
provenance.significance: Revelation is the KJV's one place where a mark is something people take rather than something God sets, and that is exactly the distinction Alma 3:13 stops to make: 'they also had a mark set upon them; yea, they set the mark upon themselves.' The Lamanites' mark is Genesis 4:15's, imposed; the Amlicites' is Revelation 13:16's, received. Revelation 13:16 also happens to enumerate its recipients as 'both small and great, rich and poor, free and bond' — the formula Alma 1:30 used for a church that made no distinctions — and Revelation 14:9-11 attaches the mark to worship of the beast, which is what 3:18 calls 'open rebellion against God'. The chapter's theology of the curse turns on the difference between the two kinds of mark, and it has a KJV verse for each.

links.note: 'They set the mark upon themselves, yea, even a mark of red upon their foreheads.' No run is reproduced and the phrase 'in their foreheads' is spread over five verses of one book, so the row is not carried by rarity. It is carried by the distinction the verse itself draws — a mark taken rather than given — for which the KJV has exactly one model. Offered under CONVENTIONS §0a.
links.whyNot: Foreheads are the obvious place to put a visible faction-mark and a writer needs no source for it. Nothing else in Alma 3 is apocalyptic, there is no beast and no worship, and the red of the Amlicite mark has no counterpart in Revelation.
links.text: And he causeth all, both small and great, rich and poor, free and bond, to receive a mark in their right hand, or in their foreheads:

pericopes.text: Thus the word of God is fulfilled, for these are the words which he saith to Nephi: Behold, the Lamanites have I cursed; and I will set a mark upon them, that they and their seed may be separated from thee and thy seed, from this time henceforth and forever, except they repent of their wickedness and turn to me, that I may have mercy upon them.

provenance.other: “Be separated” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 25:23 and Exodus 33:16; “shall be separated” occurs in exactly one, Genesis 25:23; “manner of people” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. mediation-check.py against Romans 9:12, the New Testament's quotation of the oracle, returns one decisive point for Genesis: Paul quotes only 'the elder shall serve the younger', and it is the clause about two peoples being separated — the half Romans omits — that the Book of Mormon has.
provenance.significance: Genesis 25:23 is the KJV's founding oracle of two peoples divided before birth, and Alma 3:14 is its Nephite reissue: 'that they and their seed may be separated from thee and thy seed, from this time henceforth and forever.' The mediation result is the finding. Romans 9 uses this oracle to argue that election precedes works — 'the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil' — and quotes exactly the half about the elder serving the younger. Alma 3 takes the other half, the separation, and attaches to it something neither Genesis nor Romans has: a condition. 'Except they repent of their wickedness and turn to me, that I may have mercy upon them.' The oracle that Paul made unconditional is made conditional here, and the chapter then spends 3:18-19 insisting that the cursed bring the curse on themselves. Whatever else Alma 3 is doing with descent, it is not doing Romans 9's thing with it.

links.note: 'That they and their seed may be separated from thee and thy seed, from this time henceforth and forever.' Two KJV singletons and a two-verse phrase, all from the one verse in the Bible where two peoples are separated by divine decree before they have done anything. The formula 'from this time henceforth and forever' is the Book of Mormon's own — the KJV writes 'from this time forth and for evermore' (Psalm 113:2, 115:18) — and is recorded as a departure. The mediation test was run and is decisive for the Old Testament form.
links.text: And the LORD said unto her, Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.

provenance.other: “Except they repent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 2:22, 'except they repent of their deeds'. Alma 3:14 has 'except they repent of their wickedness' — five consecutive words of the singleton with the final noun changed.
provenance.significance: Revelation 2:20-23 is the letter to Thyatira, and its subject is a woman who teaches the servants of God to commit fornication, her space to repent already given and refused, and her children killed with death. The two things it shares with Alma 3 beyond the phrase are the terms of the sentence: a curse that runs to the seed, and a door left open on condition of repentance. Revelation 2:23 ends 'I will give unto every one of you according to your works' — the singleton form of the phrase Alma 3:26 uses thirteen verses later in Revelation 20's form, 'according to their works'. The catalogue records the coincidence without building on it.
provenance.alternative: The clause as ordinary conditional English, requiring no source.

links.note: 'Except they repent of their wickedness and turn to me.' A five-word run of a KJV singleton, inside a verse whose principal source is Genesis 25:23. Filed as an echo rather than an allusion because nothing else in Alma 3 is Thyatiran and the clause is the kind of thing a writer of scriptural English produces unprompted — but the run is exact and the string exists once in the Bible.
links.whyNot: A conditional clause built from four of the commonest words in religious English plus 'except'. The KJV's single occurrence may say more about how rarely it uses 'except' with a plural subject than about dependence, and Revelation 2 contributes nothing else to the chapter.
links.text: Behold, I will cast her into a bed, and them that commit adultery with her into great tribulation, except they repent of their deeds.

pericopes.text: And again: I will set a mark upon him that mingleth his seed with thy brethren, that they may be cursed also.
And again: I will set a mark upon him that fighteth against thee and thy seed.

And again I say, He that departeth from thee, shall no more be called thy seed; and I will bless thee, &c. and whomsoever shall be called thy seed, henceforth and forever: and these were the promises of the Lord unto Nephi, and to his seed.

Now the Amlicites knew not that they were fulfilling the words of God, when they began to mark themselves in their foreheads; nevertheless they had come out in open rebellion against God; therefore it was expedient that the curse should fall upon them.—
Now I would that ye should see that they brought upon themselves the curse; and even so doth every man that is cursed, bring upon himself his own condemnation.

Now it came to pass that not many days after the battle which was fought in the land of Zarahemla, by the Lamanites and the Amlicites, that there was another army of the Lamanites came in upon the people of Nephi, in the same place where the first army met the Amlicites.
And it came to pass that there was an army sent to drive them out of their land.—
Now Alma himself being afflicted with a wound, did not go up to battle at this time against the Lamanites;
but he sent up a numerous army against them; and they went up and slew many of the Lamanites, and drove the remainder of them out of the borders of their land;
and then they returned again, and began to establish peace in the land, being troubled no more for a time with their enemies.
Now all these things were done, yea, all these wars and contentions was commenced and ended, in the fifth year of the reign of the Judges;

and in one year was thousands and tens of thousands of souls sent to the eternal world, that they might reap their rewards according to their works, whether they were good or whether they were bad, to reap eternal happiness or eternal misery, according to the spirit which he listed to obey, whether it be a good spirit or a bad one;

provenance.route: Revelation 20:12-13, with Galatians 6:7-8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “According to their works” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — 2 Corinthians 11:15, Revelation 20:12 and 20:13 — and the two in Revelation are the last judgment. “Life everlasting” occurs in exactly four, of which Galatians 6:8 is the one paired with reaping. “Whether it be good or bad” occurs in exactly five, of which 2 Corinthians 5:10 is the only judgment verse; the other four are Levitical valuation.
provenance.significance: Revelation 20:13 is the KJV's one verse in which the sea gives up its dead to be judged, and twenty-three verses earlier this chapter left bones in the depths of the sea (3:3). Alma 3:26 then judges the same battle's dead 'according to their works, whether they were good or whether they were bad' — Revelation 20's formula with 2 Corinthians 5:10's qualification attached, the latter spoken of the judgment seat of Christ, which is the office Alma occupies in Zarahemla. The reaping is Paul's: Galatians 6:7-8 is the KJV's one place where what a man reaps depends on which of two spirits he sowed to, corruption from the flesh and 'life everlasting' from the Spirit, and Alma 3:26 has 'eternal happiness or eternal misery, according to the spirit which he listed to obey'. Three sources, one sentence, and the arithmetic is what makes it a war chapter's ending: thousands and tens of thousands sent to the eternal world in one year.

links.note: 'That they might reap their rewards according to their works, whether they were good or whether they were bad, to reap eternal happiness or eternal misery.' A composite. Revelation 20:12-13 supplies the judgment formula and the dead the chapter has already put in the sea; Galatians 6:7-8 supplies the reaping and the two spirits; 2 Corinthians 5:10 supplies the good-or-bad. None is reproduced as a clause, and the row is filed at moderate on the cumulation rather than on any one contact.
links.whyNot: Judgment-by-works language is among the KJV's most widely distributed and the Book of Mormon has its own settled version of it from 2 Nephi 9:15 onward. 'According to their works' is the only rare element, and it is three verses rather than one.
links.text: And the sea gave up the dead which were in it; and death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them: and they were judged every man according to their works.

pericopes.text: for every man receiveth wages of him who he listeth to obey, and this according to the words of the spirit of prophecy; therefore let it be according to the truth. And thus endeth the fifth year of the reign of the Judges.

provenance.other: “To whom ye obey” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 6:16, and “servants to obey” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. “The wages of sin” occurs in exactly one, Romans 6:23. Alma 3:27 fuses them: 'every man receiveth wages of him who he listeth to obey.' The verb 'listeth' is not Paul's — it occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 3:8 and James 3:4, both of wind — and it is the Book of Mormon's own substitution for Paul's 'yield yourselves'.
provenance.significance: Romans 6:16 makes obedience a transfer of ownership: 'to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are.' Romans 6:23 prices it: 'the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life.' Alma 3:27 puts the two together and thereby changes one thing — Paul is careful that only one side pays wages, since eternal life is a gift and not earned, and the Book of Mormon has both sides paying. Whether that is a flattening of Paul or a deliberate answer to him is the interesting question, and the chapter's context argues for deliberate: 3:19 has just insisted that 'every man that is cursed, bring upon himself his own condemnation', which is the whole point of making the wage symmetrical. The substituted verb does the same work. 'Listeth' is the KJV's word for wind blowing where it will, and putting it where Paul had 'yield yourselves' turns a submission into a choice.

links.note: 'For every man receiveth wages of him who he listeth to obey.' Three KJV singletons from two adjacent verses of one chapter, recombined. The row is high on the rarity and on the fusion being demonstrably of Romans 6 rather than of any single verse; the substituted 'listeth' is recorded as a departure rather than as evidence. This is the first use of Romans 6:16/6:23 in Alma; the same pairing recurs at Alma 5:42.
links.text: Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?

pericopes.text: Now it came to pass in the sixth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, there was no contentions nor wars in the land of Zarahemla;

and the people being afflicted, yea, greatly afflicted for the loss of their brethren, and also for the loss of their flocks and herds, and also for the loss of their fields of grain, which was trodden under foot and destroyed by the Lamanites,

and so great was their afflictions, that every soul had cause to mourn; and they believed that it was the judgments of God sent upon them, because of their wickedness and their abominations; therefore they were awakened to a remembrance of their duty.

And they began to establish the church more fully; yea, and many were baptized in the waters of Sidon, and were joined to the church of God; yea, they were baptized by the hand of Alma, who had been consecrated the high priest over the people of the church, by the hand of his father Alma.

And it came to pass in the seventh year of the reign of the Judges, there was about three thousand five hundred souls that united themselves to the church of God, and were baptized. And thus ended the seventh year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi; and there was continual peace in all that time.

And it came to pass in the eighth year of the reign of the Judges, that the people of the church began to wax proud, because of their exceeding riches, and their fine silks, and their fine twined linen, and because of their many flocks and herds, and their gold, and their silver, and all manner of precious things, which they had obtained by their industry; and in all these things were they lifted up in the pride of their eyes, for they began to wear very costly apparel.

links.text: Thus wast thou decked with gold and silver; and thy raiment was of fine linen, and silk, and broidered work; thou didst eat fine flour, and honey, and oil: and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and thou didst prosper into a kingdom.

provenance.other: “silk” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Proverbs 31:22, Ezekiel 16:10, Ezekiel 16:13 and Revelation 18:12 — and only two of them set it beside fine linen and beside gold and silver: Ezekiel 16:13 and Revelation 18:12. “fine twined linen” occurs in exactly twenty KJV verses, every one of them in Exodus and every one of them describing the tabernacle's hangings or the high priest's ephod. “costly apparel” occurs in no KJV verse at all; the nearest thing to it is 1 Timothy 2:9's “costly array”, in a list that likewise runs gold and pearls before the clothing.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 16 is the KJV's set piece on a people decked in gold and silver, fine linen and silk, who then 'trust in thine own beauty' (16:15) — and the same chapter itemizes the resulting sin at 16:49 as 'pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness ... neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.' Alma 4 works through that itemization in Ezekiel's own order: the finery at 4:6, the pride at 4:6 and 4:8, and the hand not strengthened at 4:12, where the needy have backs turned on them. Recover the context and the chapter is not merely denouncing luxury; it is running Ezekiel's indictment of Jerusalem against a church. The second borrowing cuts the other way: 'fine twined linen' is, in the KJV, sanctuary cloth and nothing else — the veil, the court hangings, the ephod — so the fabric Exodus reserves for the holy place and the high priest's vestment is here being worn as costly apparel by the congregation of a church whose high priest is Alma, who at 4:20 will confine himself wholly to the high priesthood.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 18:12's merchandise of Babylon has the same four commodities and is the likelier source if the writer is reaching for a picture of doomed commerce rather than of a decked bride.

links.note: 'Their exceeding riches, and their fine silks, and their fine twined linen, and ... their gold, and their silver, and all manner of precious things ... they began to wear very costly apparel.' The commodity list is Ezekiel 16:13's, which is the KJV's one verse pairing silk with fine linen under gold and silver. The chapter's argument is a reversal of Alma 1: at 1:32 costly apparel and the pride of the eyes belonged to those outside the church, and here the same wardrobe and the same phrase have moved inside it, 'even to exceed the pride of those who did not belong' (4:9). Adjudicated at Alma 1:29 and 1:32 as the book's first use; the row is given here because the transfer of the wardrobe is the point being made.

pericopes.text: Now this was the cause of much affliction to Alma, yea, and to many of the people which Alma had consecrated to be teachers, and priests, and elders, over the church; yea, many of them were sorely grieved for the wickedness which they saw had begun to be among their people.

For they saw and beheld with great sorrow, that the people of the church began to be lifted up in the pride of their eyes, and to set their hearts upon riches and upon the vain things of the world; that they began to be scornful, one towards another, and they began to persecute those that did not believe according to their own will and pleasure.

links.text: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.

provenance.other: “set not your heart upon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon's own form, 'set their hearts upon riches', occurs in no KJV verse; what it has done is turn the psalm's prohibition into a report that it was disobeyed.
provenance.significance: Alma 4:8 makes two charges in one clause — that the people were lifted up in the pride of their eyes, and that they set their hearts upon riches and upon the vain things of the world — and Psalm 62 makes exactly those two in consecutive verses. Verse 9 weighs the proud: 'men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity.' Verse 10 forbids the riches: 'become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.' Vanity, riches and the setting of the heart are all three in the psalm's two verses and all three in Alma's one, which is more than the shared idiom by itself would give. The metalepsis is that the psalm is a psalm of trust — 'my soul, wait thou only upon God' — so the sin Alma names is, in its source, a failure of waiting.

links.note: 'To set their hearts upon riches and upon the vain things of the world.' Psalm 62:10 is the only KJV verse that puts the heart, the setting, and riches into one prohibition, and the surrounding words supply Alma's other term as well: the psalmist's 'become not vain' and 'lighter than vanity' stand behind 'the vain things of the world'. Below any quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion; the evidence is the coincidence of three elements, not the length of a run.

pericopes.text: And thus in this eighth year of the reign of the Judges, there began to be great contentions among the people of the church; yea, there was envyings, and strife, and malice, and persecutions, and pride, even to exceed the pride of those who did not belong to the church of God.

links.text: For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men?

provenance.other: “envying and strife” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — 1 Corinthians 3:3, James 3:14 and James 3:16 — and only the first of them is addressed to a congregation about its own divisions. The plural 'envyings' of the Book of Mormon's wording is the form at 2 Corinthians 12:20 and Galatians 5:21, both of them Pauline vice lists.
provenance.significance: The verse that supplies the pair also supplies the diagnosis Alma 4 is reaching for and does not state: 'ye are yet carnal ... and walk as men.' Paul's charge at Corinth is not that the church has sinners in it but that its members behave like people who are not in it — which is precisely Alma 4:9's sting, that the pride within the church came 'even to exceed the pride of those who did not belong to the church of God.' The same three-verse cluster, at 1 Corinthians 3:3-4, is also one of only three KJV settings for “not carnal”; the third is 2 Corinthians 10:4, which stands behind this chapter's other Pauline reach, at 4:19.

links.note: 'There was envyings, and strife, and malice, and persecutions, and pride.' The head of the list is the KJV pair, and the setting is Paul's: divisions inside a congregation. Alma 1:32 had put envyings and strife outside the church, among those who did not belong to it; four chapters later the identical vocabulary describes the church itself, which is the reversal the whole chapter is built on. Recorded here rather than at Alma 1:32 because the second use is the argument.

pericopes.text: And thus ended the eighth year of the reign of the Judges; and the wickedness of the church was a great stumbling block to those who did not belong to the church; and thus the church began to fail in its progress.

links.text: But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.

provenance.other: “stumblingblock” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses. Nine of them are a stumblingblock laid by God, by an idol, or by an enemy; only 1 Corinthians 8:9 and Romans 14:13 have it laid inadvertently by the strong in the path of somebody weaker, which is the sense Alma 4:10 needs. The 1830 text prints 'stumbling block' as two words and 1920 hyphenated it — a change toward the KJV's own 'stumbling-block' at Ezekiel 3:20 (CONVENTIONS §8), though the sense is not Ezekiel's.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 8 is an argument that a believer's own liberty, exercised without regard for who is watching, destroys the weaker brother: 'shall not the conscience of him which is weak be emboldened' (8:10). Alma 4:10-11 is the same mechanism at the scale of a whole church — its wickedness a stumbling block to those outside it, its example leading unbelievers 'on from one piece of iniquity to another'. Read against Paul, the striking thing is what the Book of Mormon has changed: Paul's stumblingblock is a permitted thing done carelessly, Alma's is sin outright, and the transposition makes the borrowed figure heavier than its source. 1 Corinthians 10:32, 'Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God', is the same argument's summary and the machine's highest-ranked candidate three times over in this chapter.

links.note: 'The wickedness of the church was a great stumbling block to those who did not belong to the church.' The KJV word is used eleven times, but in only two of them does an insider's conduct become the obstacle for an outsider, and both are Paul on the Corinthian and Roman congregations. The next verse's 'example of the church began to lead those who were unbelievers, on from one piece of iniquity to another' repeats 1 Corinthians 8:10's emboldened conscience without repeating its words, which is why the row sits here and carries 8:10 as a composite rather than as a second link.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass in the commencement of the ninth year, Alma seeing the wickedness of the church, and seeing also that the example of the church began to lead those who were unbelievers, on from one piece of iniquity to another, thus bringing on the destruction of the people;

yea, seeing great inequality among the people, some lifting themselves up with their pride, despising others, turning their backs upon the needy, and the naked, and those which were hungry, and those which were athirst, and those which were sick and afflicted.

links.text: And he spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others:

provenance.other: “despised others” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “shall be abased” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 23:12, Luke 14:11 and Luke 18:14 — of which only Luke 18:14 stands in the same parable as the singleton.
provenance.significance: The two halves of Alma 4:12-13 are the two men of the parable. Luke 18:9 gives the first exactly — 'certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others' — and Luke 18:14 gives the antithesis on which the Book of Mormon's sentence is hinged, 'every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted': some lifting themselves up with their pride, despising others; while others were abasing themselves. What the borrowing does with its source is worth noticing. In Luke the exalting and the abasing are two individuals at prayer and the reversal is eschatological, God's to perform. In Alma they are two parties in a congregation and the abasing is voluntary and present, something the humble do to themselves in the same clause that has them succouring the poor. The parable has been converted from a warning about prayer into a description of a class division, and the borrowed verb changed voice on the way.

links.note: 'Some lifting themselves up with their pride, despising others' — against Luke 18:9's 'trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others', the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase. The next verse's 'abasing themselves' completes the pair from Luke 18:14. Two words and a structure, well below any quotation threshold; the case rests on the singleton and on the fact that the source supplies both sides of Alma's antithesis in the right order.

links.text: Then shall they also answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, or athirst, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister unto thee?

provenance.other: “athirst” occurs in exactly five KJV verses; three are literal thirst or the invitation of Revelation, and only Matthew 25:44 places the word in a roll of the destitute beside the naked and the sick. The Book of Mormon's list — needy, naked, hungry, athirst, sick — has four of the six members of that roll, in a scrambled but recognisable order.
provenance.significance: Matthew 25 states the list twice, and Alma 4:12 has taken it from the wrong mouth. At 25:35-36 the sheep are told what they did: 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink.' The word 'athirst' belongs only to the second statement, 25:44, which is the goats' protest — 'when saw we thee an hungred, or athirst, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister unto thee?' So the vocabulary in which Alma describes people turning their backs on the needy is the vocabulary of those who are told, at the judgment, that they turned their backs; and the very next verse, 4:13, supplies the sheep's side of the same list, imparting substance and feeding the hungry. The two verses are the two halves of Matthew 25, and the sorting has already happened before the chapter says a word about judgment.

links.note: 'Turning their backs upon the needy, and the naked, and those which were hungry, and those which were athirst, and those which were sick and afflicted.' The distinctive word is 'athirst', which in this sense the KJV uses once, in the goats' answer at Matthew 25:44. Alma 1:27 has the same roll on its positive side ('the poor, and the needy, and the sick, and the afflicted') and is the book's first use; the reason to write the row here rather than only cross-reference it is that Alma 4:12 adds 'athirst' and the turned backs, which is what pins the wording to the second of Matthew's two lists rather than the first.

pericopes.text: Now this was a great cause for lamentations among the people, while others were abasing themselves, succoring those who stood in need of their succor, such as imparting their substance to the poor and the needy; feeding the hungry; and suffering all manner of afflictions, for Christ’s sake, which should come according to the spirit of prophecy,

links.text: Have I committed an offence in abasing myself that ye might be exalted, because I have preached to you the gospel of God freely?

provenance.other: “abasing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The finite forms are commoner — “shall be abased” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — so the participle is the only distinctive part of the contact.
provenance.significance: The KJV's single 'abasing' sits in the one Pauline sentence about a minister who lowered himself so that his hearers might be raised, and did it by preaching 'the gospel of God freely' — without charge. That is the practice this book has already made its test of a true teacher at Alma 1:26, and it is what Alma himself does at 4:18-20 when he keeps the priesthood and hands the judgment seat away. So the word arrives already attached to the chapter's own solution to the problem it is describing: against a church whose members are lifted up, the answer offered is a ministry that abases itself and takes nothing for it.

links.note: 'While others were abasing themselves, succoring those who stood in need of their succor.' The participle is a KJV singleton at 2 Corinthians 11:7, which is worth recording even though the primary source of the exalt/abase antithesis in these two verses is Luke 18:14 (linked at 4:12). The interest is that the one place the KJV inflects the verb this way is a passage about self-lowering ministry supported by nobody, which is where this chapter ends up six verses later.
links.whyNot: A single participle, and English inflection could produce it from Luke 18:14's 'abased' without any contact with 2 Corinthians at all. The senses also differ: Paul abases himself in the conduct of a mission, whereas Alma 4:13's humble abase themselves in devotion and almsgiving. Withdraw the row if the Lukan link at 4:12 is thought to account for the vocabulary on its own.

pericopes.text: looking forward to that day, thus retaining a remission of their sins; being filled with great joy, because of the resurrection of the dead, according to the will, and power, and deliverance of Jesus Christ from the bands of death.

links.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,

provenance.other: “resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Alma 4:14 does not have the phrase entire; it has 'the resurrection of the dead' and 'deliverance of Jesus Christ from the bands of death' split across a clause boundary, with 'deliverance' standing where the KJV has 'resurrection' and 'the bands of death' where it has 'the dead'.
provenance.significance: If the contact is real it is a substitution rather than a borrowing, and the substituted words are the argument: Peter's resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead becomes a deliverance of Jesus Christ from the bands of death, which converts an event into a rescue and makes Christ the one delivered rather than only the one raised. The surrounding matter agrees: 1 Peter 1:3-8 has the hope that looks forward, the inheritance reserved, and a joy the believer has now in something not yet seen, all of which Alma 4:14 states in a single sentence — looking forward to that day, retaining a remission of sins, filled with great joy.

links.note: 'Because of the resurrection of the dead, according to the will, and power, and deliverance of Jesus Christ from the bands of death.' The n-gram stream sees only 'Jesus Christ from the'; what makes it worth a row is that the KJV joins those words to a resurrection exactly once, and that the joy-in-hope frame of 1 Peter 1:3-8 matches the rest of the verse. 'Bands of death' is in no KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own idiom, used heavily in the next chapter.
links.whyNot: Split agreement across a clause boundary with the head noun replaced, which is weak evidence on its own; 'the resurrection of the dead' occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses and is Pauline boilerplate, and 'Jesus Christ' beside it may be no more than the two commonest words in the register meeting by chance.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that Alma, having seen the afflictions of the humble followers of God, and the persecutions which was heaped upon them by the remainder of his people, and seeing all their inequality, he began to be very sorrowful; nevertheless the spirit of the Lord did not fail him.

And he selected a wise man which was among the elders of the church, and gave him power according to the voice of the people, that he might have power to enact laws according to the laws which had been given, and to put them in force, according to the wickedness and the crimes of the people.
Now this man’s name was Nephihah, and he was appointed Chief Judge; and he sat in the judgment seat, to judge and to govern the people.
Now Alma did not grant unto him the office of being High Priest over the church, but he retained the office of High Priest unto himself; but he delivered the judgment seat unto Nephihah:

and this he did, that he himself might go forth among his people, or among the people of Nephi, that he might preach the word of God unto them, to stir them up in remembrance of their duty, and that he might pull down, by the word of God, all the pride and craftiness, and all the contentions which was among his people, seeing no way that he might reclaim them, save it were in bearing down in pure testimony against them.

links.text: See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.

provenance.other: “pull down” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Jeremiah 1:10, Jeremiah 18:7 and Luke 12:18 — and “pulling down” occurs in exactly one, 2 Corinthians 10:4. tools/mediation-check.py was run on the pair and returns one decisive point: the Book of Mormon has Jeremiah's infinitive 'pull down', not Paul's gerund 'pulling down'. The wording is therefore Jeremiah's even though the argument is Paul's.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 1:10 is a commission: a man set over nations and kingdoms 'to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant' — and set over them holding no office in any of them, which is exactly the position Alma has just put himself in by delivering the judgment seat to Nephihah and keeping only the word. What Alma pulls down is not a kingdom but 'all the pride and craftiness, and all the contentions', and the instrument is named twice in the verse: 'by the word of God'. That is where 2 Corinthians 10:4 presses, and it should be recorded even though the diff went the other way — 'the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds' is the doctrine of Alma 4:18-20 in one sentence, that the judgment seat was the carnal weapon and was laid down on purpose.
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 10:4, on the argument rather than the wording; note that 1 Corinthians 3:3, the source at 4:9, is one of only three KJV settings for “not carnal” and 2 Corinthians 10:4 is another, so the chapter touches both ends of that small set.

links.note: 'That he might pull down, by the word of God, all the pride and craftiness, and all the contentions which was among his people.' Two candidates compete and they pull opposite ways: Jeremiah 1:10 has the verb form, 2 Corinthians 10:4 has the situation. mediation-check.py decides the wording for Jeremiah on the single point where the two diverge, and the row is filed accordingly with the Pauline reading kept as the alternative. 'Craftiness' is not decisive either way — it occurs in five KJV verses, two of them Pauline.

pericopes.text: And thus in the commencement of the ninth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, Alma delivered up the judgment seat to Nephihah, and confined himself wholly to the high priesthood of the holy order of God, to the testimony of the word, according to the spirit of revelation and prophecy.
Now it came to pass that Alma began to deliver the word of God unto the people, first in the land of Zarahemla, and from thence throughout all the land.
And these are the words which he spake to the people in the Church which was established in the city of Zarahemla, according to his own record, saying:

I, Alma, having been consecrated by my father Alma, to be a High Priest over the Church of God, he having power and authority from God to do these things, behold, I say unto you, that he began to establish a Church in the land which was in the borders of Nephi; yea, the land which was called the land of Mormon; yea, and he did baptize his brethren in the waters of Mormon.
And behold, I say unto you, they were delivered out of the hands of the people of king Noah, by the mercy and power of God.

And behold, after that, they were brought into bondage by the hands of the Lamanites, in the wilderness; yea, I say unto you, they were in captivity, and again the Lord did deliver them out of bondage by the power of his word; and we were brought into this land and here we began to establish the Church of God throughout this land, also.

And now behold, I say unto you, my brethren, you that belong to this Church, have you sufficiently retained in remembrance the captivity of your fathers? Yea, and have you sufficiently retained in remembrance his mercy and long-suffering towards them? And moreover, have ye sufficiently retained in remembrance that he hath delivered their souls from hell?

Behold, he changed their hearts; yea, he awaked them out of a deep sleep, and they awoke unto God. Behold, they were in the midst of darkness; nevertheless, their souls were illuminated by the light of the everlasting word; yea, they were encircled about by the bands of death, and the chains of hell, and an everlasting destruction did await them.

links.text: Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.

provenance.other: “arise from the dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:14; “awake out of sleep” occurs in exactly one, Romans 13:11. Both are Pauline and both belong to the same small figure — sleep, waking, and light — which the KJV has nowhere else in this combination. “deep sleep” by itself occurs in exactly ten KJV verses and is no help.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:7 puts four things in one sentence and Ephesians 5 puts the same four in four verses: sleep, waking, darkness, light. 'Ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord' (5:8); 'Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light' (5:14). What the Book of Mormon adds is the object of the waking — 'they awoke unto God' — and the source of the light, 'the light of the everlasting word', which turns Paul's baptismal summons into a report of a conversion that has already happened. The metalepsis is in what Ephesians 5:14 is: a fragment the KJV marks as a citation ('Wherefore he saith'), a hymn quoted inside the epistle. Alma 5:7 is therefore quoting a quotation, and the awakening it describes is the one the church sings about itself.

links.note: 'He awaked them out of a deep sleep, and they awoke unto God. Behold, they were in the midst of darkness; nevertheless, their souls were illuminated by the light of the everlasting word.' Ephesians 5:14 is the KJV's one verse joining sleep to rising and to Christ giving light, and Romans 13:11-12 — 'to awake out of sleep ... the night is far spent, the day is at hand; let us therefore cast off the works of darkness' — supplies the waking verb and the darkness. Neither is reproduced as a clause; the case is the co-occurrence of the whole figure with two KJV singletons inside it.

pericopes.text: And now I ask of you my brethren, were they destroyed? Behold, I say unto you, nay, they were not.

And again I ask, was the bands of death broken, and the chains of hell which encircled them about, were they loosed? I say unto you, yea, they were loosed, and their souls did expand, and they did sing redeeming love. And I say unto you, that they are saved.

And now I ask of you on what conditions are they saved? Yea, what grounds had they to hope for salvation? What is the cause of their being loosed from the bands of death? Yea, and also, the chains of hell?

Behold, I can tell you: did not my father Alma believe in the words which was delivered by the mouth of Abinadi? And was he not a holy prophet? Did he not speak the word of God, and my father Alma believe them?
And according to his faith there was a mighty change wrought in his heart. Behold I say unto you, that this is all true.—

And behold, he preached the word unto your fathers, and a mighty change was also wrought in their hearts; and they humbled themselves, and put their trust in the true and living God. And behold, they were faithful until the end; therefore they were saved.
And now behold, I ask of you, my brethren of the Church, have ye spiritually been born of God? Have ye received his image in your countenances? Have ye experienced this mighty change in your hearts?

Do ye exercise faith in the redemption of him who created you? Do you look forward with an eye of faith, and view this mortal body raised in immortality, and this corruption raised in incorruption, to stand before God, to be judged according to the deeds which hath been done in the mortal body?

links.text: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

provenance.other: “this mortal must put on immortality” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “put on incorruption” occurs in exactly two, 1 Corinthians 15:53 and 15:54, which are the same sentence stated and then restated. No other KJV passage pairs mortal with immortality and corruption with incorruption.
provenance.significance: Two changes are worth recording. Paul's order is corruption first and mortality second; Alma's is mortality first and corruption second, so the Book of Mormon reverses the couplet while keeping both halves. And Paul's verb is 'put on' — a garment metaphor that governs the whole of 1 Corinthians 15:53-54 — where Alma 5:15 has 'raised'. That matters here because the garment metaphor is not lost, it is moved: six verses later, at 5:21-24, this sermon's whole argument turns on garments washed white and garments stained, and Paul's clothing of the resurrection body is where the KJV keeps that image. The chapter takes the doctrine in one verse and the metaphor in another.
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 5:10's 'the things done in his body' stands behind the second half of Alma 5:15, 'judged according to the deeds which hath been done in the mortal body'; that link is adjudicated at 2 Nephi 9:15.

links.note: 'View this mortal body raised in immortality, and this corruption raised in incorruption.' Against 1 Corinthians 15:53: 'For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.' Both antitheses, both demonstratives, and the KJV's abstract nouns; only the verb and the order of the pair are changed. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations, and catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because the two clauses are reproduced as clauses.

pericopes.text: I say unto you, can you imagine to yourselves that ye hear the voice of the Lord, saying unto you, in that day, Come unto me ye blessed, for behold, your works have been the works of righteousness upon the face of the earth?

links.text: Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world:

provenance.other: “come ye blessed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has 'Come unto me ye blessed', which splices Matthew 25:34's greeting onto Matthew 11:28's invitation, a phrase this same sermon uses twice at 5:34 and 5:35.
provenance.significance: This is the second of three places where Alma's preaching runs on Matthew 25, and the three are in the parable's own order: the neglected at Alma 4:12 (the goats' list, Matthew 25:44), the welcome at 5:16 (Matthew 25:34), and the inheritance at the right hand at 5:58 (Matthew 25:33-34). Recovering the context sharpens Alma's question rather than merely sourcing it. In Matthew the sentence is spoken by the King to people who did not know they had served him — 'when saw we thee an hungred?' — whereas Alma asks his hearers to imagine hearing it said of works they can already name, 'your works have been the works of righteousness upon the face of the earth'. The next verse then withdraws the imagining as a possible lie. Matthew's sheep are surprised; Alma's audience is invited to audit itself in advance, which is a use of the parable the parable does not make.

links.note: 'Can you imagine to yourselves that ye hear the voice of the Lord, saying unto you, in that day, Come unto me ye blessed.' The greeting is the KJV's only 'come, ye blessed', at Matthew 25:34, with 'unto me' carried over from the other great invitation. Alma 4:12 has already borrowed from the far side of the same parable and 5:58 will borrow the right hand, so the row also fixes the recurrence.

pericopes.text: Or do ye imagine to yourselves that ye can lie unto the Lord in that day, and say, Lord, Our works have been righteous works upon the face of the earth, and that he will save you?

Or otherwise, can ye imagine yourselves brought before the tribunal of God, with your souls filled with guilt and remorse; having a remembrance of all your guilt; yea, a perfect remembrance of all your wickedness; yea, a remembrance that ye have set at defiance the commandments of God?
I say unto you, can ye look up to God at that day with a pure heart and clean hands? I say unto you, can you look up, having the image of God engraven upon your countenances?

links.text: He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.

provenance.other: “clean hands” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 24:4 and Job 17:9, and “a pure heart” in exactly four; the two are joined in one clause only at Psalm 24:4. Alma 5:19 inverts the order to 'a pure heart and clean hands'.
provenance.significance: Psalm 24 is an entrance liturgy: 'Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?' — and the answer is the man with clean hands and a pure heart. Alma 5:19 asks the same question about the same qualification and moves it to the judgment: 'can ye look up to God at that day with a pure heart and clean hands?' The gate the psalm guards is a temple gate in this life and Alma has made it the last one. The transposition is exact enough to be deliberate: both are entrance examinations, both turn on the same two possessions, and both are put as a question rather than a rule.

links.note: 'Can ye look up to God at that day with a pure heart and clean hands?' The pair is Psalm 24:4's and is joined nowhere else in the KJV. Note what the sermon does with it four verses on: the psalm's clean hands become garments washed white at 5:21-24, so the same test is put twice, once in the psalm's terms and once in Revelation's.

links.text: But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away:

provenance.other: “engraven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 3:7, and that verse also carries 'countenance' — the two words Alma 5:19 puts together. Alma 5:14's 'received his image in your countenances' supplies the third term, and 'image' is the governing noun of the same Pauline passage at 3:18.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 3 is the KJV's one place where engraving, a shining countenance, and being changed into an image belong to a single argument: the law was 'written and engraven in stones' and left Moses' face too bright to look at, whereas those who behold the Lord 'are changed into the same image from glory to glory'. Alma 5:14 and 5:19 ask a congregation whether that change has happened to their faces — 'have ye received his image in your countenances ... can you look up, having the image of God engraven upon your countenances?' Paul's contrast is between what is engraven in stone and what is written in the heart; Alma's question moves the engraving onto the face, which is the one surface Paul's argument leaves it off.
provenance.alternative: The image language may be Genesis 1:26-27's and the engraving simply a metaphor of permanence, in which case there is no contact with 2 Corinthians at all.

links.note: 'Can you look up, having the image of God engraven upon your countenances?' The interest is a lexical accident worth recording: the KJV inflects 'engrave' this way exactly once, and that once is in the passage where the glory of Moses' countenance is being argued against the changing of believers into an image. Two verses of Alma 5 supply all three of that passage's nouns.
links.whyNot: No clause is shared and the words arrive in different grammatical roles — Paul engraves a law in stones, Alma engraves an image on faces. 'Engraven' may simply be the natural KJV-register participle for a writer who has already used 'engraven' vocabulary of the plates elsewhere in the corpus, in which case the singleton is an artifact of English morphology rather than evidence of contact. Withdraw if a reader thinks 'image' and 'countenance' are independently available from Genesis 1:26.

pericopes.text: I say unto you, can ye think of being saved when you have yielded yourselves to become subjects to the Devil?

I say unto you, ye will know at that day, that ye cannot be saved: for there can no man be saved except his garments are washed white; yea, his garments must be purified until they are cleansed from all stain, through the blood of him of whom it hath been spoken by our fathers which should come to redeem his people from their sins.

links.text: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

provenance.other: “washed their robes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Revelation 7:14 is also the only KJV verse in which a garment is made white by blood, which is the paradox Alma 5:21 and 5:27 both state and neither explains.
provenance.significance: The image is impossible on its face — blood whitens nothing — and Revelation supplies the only warrant in the KJV for using it, so the borrowing is not decorative. What Alma does with it is to run it both ways at once: at 5:21 and 5:27 garments are made white through the blood of Christ, and at 5:22 garments are 'stained with blood' as the evidence that will testify the wearer a murderer. The same fluid cleanses and convicts within two verses, and the sermon relies on the reader hearing Revelation 7:14 under the first use to feel the second. Revelation 3:5 then supplies the next move: the one who overcomes is clothed in white raiment and his name is not blotted out of the book of life — which is exactly where this sermon goes at 5:57-58.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 1:5, 'washed us from our sins in his own blood', has the washing without the garments and may be the proximate phrase.

links.note: 'There can no man be saved except his garments are washed white; yea, his garments must be purified until they are cleansed from all stain, through the blood of him ... which should come to redeem his people from their sins.' The KJV washes robes once, at Revelation 7:14, and makes them white in blood once, in the same clause. Alma 5:24's 'whose garments are cleansed, and are spotless, pure and white' repeats it, as does 5:27; adjudicated here at first use.

links.text: And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.

provenance.other: “his people from their sins” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has the clause entire with one verb changed, 'redeem' for 'save'; “redeem his people” occurs in no KJV verse at all. The formula is used three times in two chapters — Alma 5:21, 5:27 and 6:8 — and adjudicated here at first use.
provenance.significance: Matthew 1:21 is not a statement about atonement, it is an etymology: 'thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.' The clause exists in the KJV to explain a name. That is what makes its arrival in Alma 5 worth recording, because the sermon's central demand, eleven verses later, is precisely about a name — 'in his own name he doth call you, which is the name of Christ ... if ye will not hearken unto the voice of the good shepherd, to the name by which ye are called' (5:38). Alma 5:21 supplies the definition of the name and 5:38 asks whether the hearers answer to it. The substitution of 'redeem' for 'save' is the Book of Mormon's own and shifts the clause from naming to purchase, which is also the direction 5:27's blood and 5:42's wages are moving.

links.note: 'Through the blood of him of whom it hath been spoken by our fathers which should come to redeem his people from their sins.' Five words reproduced exactly from the KJV's one verse that has them, with the governing verb replaced. The machine ranked Matthew 1:21 at both 5:21 and 5:27 and was right, which is worth saying because it was right for the usual wrong reason — the run is long — and the evidence that makes it a link is that the run is unique.

pericopes.text: And now I ask of you, my brethren, how will any of you feel, if ye shall stand before the bar of God, having your garments stained with blood, and all manner of filthiness? Behold, what will these things testify against you?
Behold, will they not testify that ye are murderers, yea, and also that ye are guilty of all manner of wickedness?

Behold, my brethren, do ye suppose that such an one can have a place to sit down in the Kingdom of God, with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob, and also all the holy prophets, whose garments are cleansed, and are spotless, pure and white?

links.text: There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out.

provenance.route: Luke 13:28-29, with Matthew 8:11-12 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sit down in the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 13:29; “children of the kingdom” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 8:12 and Matthew 13:38. The saying exists in two Gospel forms and Alma 5:24-25 has elements only one of them supplies: Luke names 'all the prophets' beside the patriarchs and says 'kingdom of God', which is Alma's wording, while Matthew names the patriarchs without prophets and says 'kingdom of heaven'. A third element comes from neither Gospel: “with Abraham with Isaac and with Jacob”, with the preposition repeated before each name, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 2:24 — 'God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.' Matthew 8:11 and Luke 13:28 both read 'with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob'. Alma 5:24 has the Exodus form of the list inside the Gospel form of the saying.
provenance.significance: The two verses take the two halves of one saying and keep them in the saying's own order. Luke 13:28-29 gives the seating — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, with those who are thrust out watching — and Alma 5:24 reproduces the list with 'all the holy prophets' in Luke's slot. Matthew 8:12 then gives the sentence Alma 5:25 needs and Luke does not have: 'the children of the kingdom shall be cast out.' Alma turns that phrase inside out. In Matthew the children of the kingdom are the ones expelled from it; in Alma they are expelled and reassigned — 'they are the children of the kingdom of the Devil' — so the paradox Matthew leaves standing, that the kingdom's own children lose it, is resolved by giving them another kingdom to be children of. The patriarch formula itself is worth the extra line. The repeated preposition is the Pentateuch's covenant idiom and its one KJV instance, Exodus 2:24, is the verse where God remembers the covenant and the exodus begins — so the list Alma uses to describe who sits down in the kingdom is worded as the list of those to whom a promise was made, not as the list of dinner guests the Gospels give.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 8:11 alone, if 'all the holy prophets' is thought to be the Book of Mormon's own addition rather than Luke's contribution; the phrase is a standing formula elsewhere in the corpus.

links.note: 'Do ye suppose that such an one can have a place to sit down in the Kingdom of God, with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob, and also all the holy prophets ... they shall be cast out, for they are the children of the kingdom of the Devil.' The seating is Luke's — his is the only KJV verse with 'sit down in the kingdom', and only he puts the prophets in the list — and the casting out and the children of the kingdom are Matthew's. A composite of the two synoptic forms rather than either one, which is itself the finding.

pericopes.text: I say unto you, nay, except ye make our creator a liar from the beginning, or suppose that he is a liar from the beginning; or also, ye cannot suppose that such an one can have place in the kingdom of heaven, but they shall be cast out, for they are the children of the kingdom of the Devil.
And now behold, I say unto you, my brethren, if ye have experienced a change of heart, and if ye have felt to sing the song of redeeming love, I would ask, can ye feel so now?

Have ye walked, keeping yourselves blameless before God? Could ye say, if ye were called to die at this time, within yourselves, that ye have been sufficiently humble? That your garments have been cleansed and made white, through the blood of Christ, which will come to redeem his people from their sins?

Behold, are ye stripped of pride? I say unto you, if ye are not, ye are not prepared to meet God. Behold, ye must prepare quickly, for the kingdom of Heaven is soon at hand, and such an one hath not eternal life.

links.text: Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.

provenance.other: “prepare to meet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon's form is the passive of it — 'ye are not prepared to meet God' — repeated at 5:29 and 5:31 as a refrain.
provenance.significance: Amos 4:12 is the end of a chapter of withheld judgments: five times God says 'yet have ye not returned unto me', and then, because the warnings failed, 'prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.' It is not an invitation. It is the sentence that follows the exhausting of invitations, and what Israel is being told to prepare for is the meeting itself, on the far side of repentance's last refusal. Alma 5 is built the same way — three times over, at 5:28, 5:29 and 5:31, a hearer is told he is not prepared and that he must prepare quickly — and the borrowed line brings its own deadline with it. The chapter's other refrain, the axe already laid at the root (5:52), is the New Testament version of the same threat, so the sermon is bracketed by the two KJV passages in which the time for warning has just run out.

links.note: 'Are ye stripped of pride? I say unto you, if ye are not, ye are not prepared to meet God.' The KJV says 'prepare to meet thy God' once, in Amos, and the Book of Mormon has turned the imperative into a diagnosis: not 'prepare' but 'ye are not prepared', which is why the sentence can be repeated as a test at 5:29 and 5:31. 'Stripped of pride' and 'stripped of envy' are the Book of Mormon's own; the KJV never strips a person of an abstraction.

pericopes.text: Behold, I say, is there one among you who is not stripped of envy? I say unto you, that such an one is not prepared, and I would that he should prepare quickly, for the hour is close at hand, and he knoweth not when the time shall come: for such an one is not found guiltless.
And again I say unto you, is there one among you that doth make a mock of his brother, or that heapeth upon him persecutions?
Wo unto such an one, for he is not prepared, and the time is at hand that he must repent, or he cannot be saved;
yea, even wo unto all ye workers of iniquity; repent, repent, for the Lord God hath spoken it.
Behold, he sendeth an invitation unto all men; for the arms of mercy is extended towards them, and he saith, Repent, and I will receive you;
yea, he saith, Come unto me and ye shall partake of the fruit of the tree of life; yea, ye shall eat and drink of the bread and the waters of life freely;

links.text: And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.

provenance.other: “water of life” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Revelation 21:6, 22:1 and 22:17 — and all three are in the last two chapters of Revelation; “bread of life” occurs in exactly two, John 6:35 and 6:48. The Book of Mormon's clause fuses three of Revelation's: the tree of life whose fruit is given to him that overcometh (2:7 and 22:14), the water of life taken 'freely' (22:17, and 21:6 to him that is athirst), and the invitation 'Come'. 'Bread of life' is not Revelation's but John 6:35's; the KJV never puts bread and the water of life in one clause, which is the Book of Mormon's own splice.
provenance.significance: Revelation 22:17 is the last invitation in the Bible and it is issued by the Spirit and the bride — that is, by the church — to whoever will come. Alma 5:33-34 has God issue it himself, 'he sendeth an invitation unto all men', and the sermon ends at 5:62 by making Alma the one who repeats it to those outside the church: 'unto those which do not belong to the church, I speak by way of invitation.' The borrowing therefore carries its speaker with it. The chapter's closing move is to put the preacher in the position Revelation gives the bride, and the fruit of the tree of life is what he offers, which in Revelation 2:7 and 22:14 is reserved for those who overcome and keep the commandments.

links.note: 'Come unto me and ye shall partake of the fruit of the tree of life; yea, ye shall eat and drink of the bread and the waters of life freely.' Three of Revelation's images in one sentence, with 'freely' — the word that makes the invitation unconditional — carried over from 22:17 and 21:6. Isaiah 55:1's 'come ye to the waters ... without money and without price' is the Old Testament behind Revelation and may be independently in view; the presence of the tree of life and of 'freely' points at Revelation.

pericopes.text: yea, come unto me and bring forth works of righteousness, and ye shall not be hewn down and cast into the fire:
for behold, the time is at hand that whosoever bringeth forth not good fruit, or whosoever doeth not the works of righteousness, the same hath cause to wail and mourn.

O ye workers of iniquity; ye that are puffed up in the vain things of the world; ye that have professed to have known the ways of righteousness; nevertheless ye have gone astray, as sheep having no shepherd, notwithstanding a shepherd hath called after you, and art still calling after you, but ye will not hearken unto his voice.

links.text: But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.

provenance.route: Matthew 9:36, with Isaiah 53:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “as sheep having no shepherd” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The related figures are worded differently — Numbers 27:17 and 1 Kings 22:17 have 'as sheep which have no shepherd', Mark 6:34 'as sheep not having a shepherd' — so the Book of Mormon has Matthew's exact participle and word order. 'Gone astray' is Isaiah 53:6's, 'All we like sheep have gone astray'.
provenance.significance: The sentence welds the two halves of the KJV's sheep language and reverses the moral of each. Matthew 9:36's shepherdless crowd moves Jesus to compassion — they are not blamed, they have no shepherd. Isaiah 53:6's straying sheep are blamed, and the verse ends by laying their iniquity on another. Alma 5:37 makes them one accusation and adds the fact that removes the excuse: 'notwithstanding a shepherd hath called after you, and art still calling after you, but ye will not hearken unto his voice.' These sheep have a shepherd. The borrowed phrase is used precisely against itself, and the next two verses name the shepherd from John 10.

links.note: 'Ye have gone astray, as sheep having no shepherd.' Matthew 9:36 is the KJV's only instance of the phrase in this exact form, and Isaiah 53:6 supplies the verb. The point of the row is the qualification that follows in the same verse, which cancels the condition the borrowed clause describes.

pericopes.text: Behold, I say unto you, that the good shepherd doth call you; yea, and in his own name he doth call you, which is the name of Christ; and if ye will not hearken unto the voice of the good shepherd, to the name by which ye are called, behold, ye are not the sheep of the good shepherd.

links.text: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.

provenance.other: “the good shepherd” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 10:11 and John 10:14, and nowhere else in the Bible. “one fold” occurs in exactly one, John 10:16. The Book of Mormon uses 'the good shepherd' five times in this chapter alone.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:38-39 does not merely borrow the title; it reproduces the chapter's structure. John 10 runs on the sheep knowing the shepherd's voice (10:3-4), on the good shepherd naming himself (10:11, 10:14), and on there being one fold (10:16) — and Alma asks, in order, whether his hearers hearken to the voice, tells them the good shepherd calls 'in his own name ... which is the name of Christ', and then asks the question John's 'one fold' makes unanswerable: 'if ye are not the sheep of the good shepherd, of what fold are ye?' John leaves one fold and no alternative; Alma supplies the alternative — 'the Devil is your shepherd, and ye are of his fold' — which is a completion of John's figure that John does not offer and that John 10:12's hireling and wolf make possible. The wolf returns at 5:59-60.

links.note: 'The good shepherd doth call you; yea, and in his own name he doth call you, which is the name of Christ.' The title exists in the KJV only at John 10:11 and 10:14. What the sermon adds is the second fold: because John allows only one, Alma's question 'of what fold are ye?' has a single available answer and he gives it. Adjudicated at 5:38; the shepherd runs through 5:39, 5:41, 5:57 and 5:60.

pericopes.text: And now if ye are not the sheep of the good shepherd, of what fold are ye? Behold, I say unto you, that the Devil is your shepherd, and ye are of his fold; and now who can deny this? Behold, I say unto you, whosoever denieth this, is a liar and a child of the Devil;

links.text: Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son.

provenance.route: 1 John 2:22 with Acts 13:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “is a liar” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, three of them in 1 John; only 1 John 2:22 attaches the charge to denying — 'Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ?' “child of the devil” in the singular occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:10, Paul's rebuke of Elymas; 1 John 3:10 has the plural.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:39 fuses the two. 'Whosoever denieth this, is a liar and a child of the Devil' takes the denier-is-a-liar of 1 John 2:22 and the singular epithet of Acts 13:10, and lands where 1 John 3:10 already stands: 'In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil.' What is denied has changed, and instructively. In 1 John the lie is denying that Jesus is the Christ; in Alma it is denying Alma's own inference — that a man who is not the good shepherd's sheep must be the Devil's. The borrowed apparatus of antichrist is thereby attached to a conclusion the sermon has just reached rather than to a creed, which is the strongest rhetorical move in the chapter and the one most worth flagging to a reader.

links.note: 'Whosoever denieth this, is a liar and a child of the Devil.' The two components have precise KJV homes — the denier-liar of 1 John 2:22 and the singular 'child of the devil' of Acts 13:10 — and are joined nowhere in the Bible. Moderate rather than high because both are short and the vocabulary of liars and devils is available generally; the pairing, and the fact that each half is rare, is the evidence.

pericopes.text: for I say unto you, that whatsoever is good, cometh from God, and whatsoever is evil, cometh from the Devil;

therefore, if a man bringeth forth good works, he hearkeneth unto the voice of the good shepherd, and he doth follow him; but whosoever bringeth forth evil works, the same becometh a child of the Devil: for he hearkeneth unto his voice, and doth follow him.
And whosoever doeth this must receive his wages of him; therefore, for his wages he receiveth death, as to things pertaining unto righteousness, being dead unto all good works.—

links.text: For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

provenance.other: “wages of sin” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Wages' by itself occurs in exactly seventeen and is everywhere else a labourer's pay; Romans 6:23 is the only KJV verse in which wages are what sin pays and what is paid is death.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:41-42 has the whole of Romans 6:16-23 compressed: whom you obey you follow, whom you follow you serve, and the servant is paid. Paul's argument turns on the clause Alma 5:42 reproduces almost as a technical term — 'as to things pertaining unto righteousness' answers Romans 6:20's 'when ye were the servants of sin, ye were free from righteousness'. The metalepsis is in what Romans 6:23 goes on to say and Alma 5:42 withholds: 'but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.' Paul's sentence has two halves and its force is the asymmetry between them — sin pays a wage, God gives a gift. Alma quotes the first half at the man who has chosen the Devil and lets the second half stand unspoken; it has already been offered, at 5:33-34, to anyone who will come.

links.note: 'Whosoever doeth this must receive his wages of him; therefore, for his wages he receiveth death, as to things pertaining unto righteousness, being dead unto all good works.' The KJV pays a wage for sin exactly once. The Book of Mormon keeps Paul's transaction and his righteousness clause and drops his contrast, which is the interpretive fact worth recording.

pericopes.text: And now my brethren, I would that ye should hear me, for I speak in the energy of my soul; for behold, I have spoken unto you plain, that ye cannot err, or have spoken according to the commandments of God.

For I am called to speak after this manner, according to the holy order of God, which is in Christ Jesus; yea, I am commanded to stand and testify unto this people the things which have been spoken by our fathers, concerning the things which is to come.

And this is not all. Do ye suppose that I know not of these things myself? Behold, I testify unto you, that I do know that these things whereof I have spoken, are true. And how do ye suppose that I know of their surety?

Behold, I say unto you, they are made known unto me by the holy spirit of God. Behold, I have fasted and prayed many days, that I might know these things of myself. And now I do know of myself that they are true; for the Lord God hath made them manifest unto me by his holy spirit; and this is the spirit of revelation which is in me.

And moreover, I say unto you, that as it has thus been revealed unto me, that the words which have been spoken by our fathers, are true, even so according to the spirit of prophecy, which is in me, which is also by the manifestation of the spirit of God,

I say unto you, that I know of myself that whatsoever I shall say unto you concerning that which is to come, is true; and I say unto you, that I know that Jesus Christ shall come; yea, the Son of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace, and mercy, and truth. And behold, it is he that cometh to take away the sins of the world; yea, the sins of every man which steadfastly believeth on his name.

links.text: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

provenance.route: John 1:14 and 1:29 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “only begotten of the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “full of grace and truth” occurs in exactly one — the same verse, John 1:14, where they stand in the same order and adjacent. The Book of Mormon inserts one word into the second: 'full of grace, and mercy, and truth'.
provenance.significance: The inserted 'mercy' is the whole interest of the row. John 1:14's pair is fixed KJV vocabulary and is repeated at 1:17, and the triad grace-mercy-truth exists in the KJV only in epistolary greetings (1 Timothy 1:2, 2 Timothy 1:2, 2 John 1:3), never of the incarnate Word. Behind those greetings stands Exodus 34:6's 'abundant in goodness and truth', the formula John is widely taken to be rewriting. So the Book of Mormon's version reads as John 1:14 with a term restored from the Old Testament formula John compressed. The verse then adds John 1:29 — 'it is he that cometh to take away the sins of the world' against 'the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' — with the singular sin pluralised and the Lamb dropped, so that the second borrowing is de-Johannine in exactly the way the first is not.
provenance.alternative: If the triad is taken from an epistolary greeting rather than from John, the source is 2 John 1:3 or 1 Timothy 1:2; but neither has 'the only begotten of the Father' beside it, and that phrase is a KJV singleton.

links.note: 'The Son of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace, and mercy, and truth. And behold, it is he that cometh to take away the sins of the world.' Two KJV singletons from one verse, in order, with one word interpolated — this is a quotation on any definition, though it is below Skousen's threshold and is not one of his 36. Frederick's monograph is an argument about the Gospel of John in the Book of Mormon and his discussion of John 1:12-14 falls in the same passage of his book as this verse; the catalogue's index of him records that co-occurrence and nothing stronger, and no claim about what he identifies is made here.

pericopes.text: And now I say unto you, that this is the order after which I am called; yea, to preach unto my beloved brethren; yea, and every one that dwelleth in the land; yea, to preach unto all, both old and young, both bond and free; yea, I say unto you, the aged, and also the middle aged, and the rising generation; yea, to cry unto them that they must repent and be born again;

yea, thus saith the spirit, Repent all ye ends of the earth, for the Kingdom of Heaven is soon at hand; yea, the Son of God cometh in his glory, in his might, majesty, power and dominion. Yea, my beloved brethren, I say unto you, that the spirit saith, Behold the glory of the King of all the earth; and also the King of Heaven shall very soon shine forth among all the children of men;

links.text: To the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever. Amen.

provenance.route: Jude 1:25 and Psalm 47:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “majesty dominion and power” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jude 1:25, where the full series is 'glory and majesty, dominion and power' — four nouns that Alma 5:50 has in 'his glory, in his might, majesty, power and dominion', with 'might' added and the last two reversed. “King of all the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 47:7.
provenance.significance: Both borrowings are doxological and both are moved. Jude's four nouns are the closing ascription of an epistle, said to God; Alma 5:50 makes them the equipage of an arrival — 'the Son of God cometh in his glory, in his might, majesty, power and dominion'. Psalm 47:7's title belongs to a psalm of enthronement sung after a victory, and Alma applies it to a king who has not yet appeared: 'Behold the glory of the King of all the earth; and also the King of Heaven shall very soon shine forth.' A doxology for what God is has become a description of what is about to happen, which is the tense the whole sermon is written in.

links.note: 'The Son of God cometh in his glory, in his might, majesty, power and dominion ... Behold the glory of the King of all the earth.' Two KJV singletons in one verse, neither reproduced as a clause: Jude's four-noun ascription with a fifth interpolated, and Psalm 47:7's royal title. Recorded as an echo because the agreement is a vocabulary set rather than a construction; the case is that both sets are unique in the KJV and both are in the same sentence.
links.whyNot: Doxological nouns cluster in the KJV and a writer working in that register could reassemble them without a source; 1 Peter 5:11, Revelation 1:6 and Revelation 5:13 all have overlapping series. The claim rests on Jude 1:25 being the only verse with these three in sequence, and on the coincidence with the Psalm 47 title in the same breath.

pericopes.text: and also the spirit saith unto me, yea, crieth unto me with a mighty voice, saying, Go forth and say unto this people, repent, for except ye repent ye can in no wise inherit the Kingdom of Heaven.

And again I say unto you, the spirit saith, Behold, the axe is laid at the root of the tree; therefore every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit, shall be hewn down and cast into the fire; yea, a fire which cannot be consumed; even an unquenchable fire. Behold, and remember, the holy one hath spoken it.

links.text: And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.
