provenance.other: “the axe is laid” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9, which are the same sentence in the two Gospels; “hewn down and cast into the fire” occurs in exactly three, those two and Matthew 7:19. tools/mediation-check.py was run on Matthew 3:10 against Luke 3:9 and reported no decisive divergence, because the two differ only in the position of 'therefore', which its matcher ignores as a common word. The judgment is therefore made by eye, on two points. First, word order: Matthew 3:10 reads 'therefore every tree which', Luke 3:9 'every tree therefore which', and the Book of Mormon reads 'therefore every tree that' — Matthew's order, though the relative pronoun is neither Gospel's here but Matthew 7:19's, whose sentence is 'Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire' and which the machine ranked above both Baptist verses. Second, and decisively, the same verse ends 'even an unquenchable fire': “unquenchable fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:12, while Luke 3:17 has the inverted “fire unquenchable”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse of its own. The chapter's repeated 'kingdom of Heaven' (5:28, 5:50, 5:51) points the same way, since Luke never uses the phrase.
provenance.significance: John the Baptist's preaching is the armature of the entire sermon, not a single citation. Matthew 3:2's 'Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand' is Alma 5:28, 5:50 and 5:51; Matthew 3:8's 'fruits meet for repentance' is Alma 5:54's 'works which is meet for repentance'; Matthew 3:10's axe and burning are Alma 5:35, 5:36, 5:52 and 5:56; Matthew 3:12's unquenchable fire closes 5:52. The metalepsis is in who is being addressed. In Matthew, John says all of it to Pharisees and Sadducees who have come out to his baptism — insiders presenting themselves for a rite — and warns them not to plead descent from Abraham. Alma 5 is preached to the members of a church, is preoccupied from 5:24 with whether they may sit down with Abraham, and ends at 5:62 by inviting the outsiders to be baptized. The sermon has been built on the one New Testament passage where the baptizer's threat falls on the people already inside.

links.note: 'Behold, the axe is laid at the root of the tree; therefore every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit, shall be hewn down and cast into the fire; yea, a fire which cannot be consumed; even an unquenchable fire.' A near-verbatim reproduction of Matthew 3:10 with Matthew 3:12's closing phrase appended. Attributed within the sermon to the Spirit — 'the spirit saith' — and closed with 'the holy one hath spoken it', which is worth noting: the Book of Mormon assigns the Baptist's words to their speaker's source rather than to the Baptist.

pericopes.text: And now my beloved brethren, I say unto you, can ye withstand these sayings; yea, can ye lay aside these things, and trample the holy one under your feet; yea, can ye be puffed up in the pride of your hearts; yea, will ye still persist in the wearing of costly apparel, and setting your hearts upon the vain things of the world, upon your riches;

links.text: Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?

provenance.other: “trodden under foot the Son of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Trodden under foot' by itself occurs in five and was set aside as common vocabulary at Alma 4:2; what makes this instance different is that the object is a person, which the KJV has only here.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 10:29 is the KJV's severest sentence about apostasy, and every element of it is already in this sermon. It asks what punishment is due to one who 'hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing' — trampling, blood, sanctification, holiness. Alma 5:53-54 has the trampling of the holy one, and one verse later the hearers' brethren 'have been sanctified by the holy spirit'; the blood of the covenant is the blood that has been washing garments since 5:21. And Hebrews 10:26's premise — 'if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth' — is the situation of Alma 5 exactly: a church, having known, persisting. The borrowing brings the harshest available frame to bear on people who are still being invited to repent.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 7:6's swine that 'trample them under their feet' is the other KJV trampling of something holy, and 'the holy' is its object there too ('give not that which is holy unto the dogs'); it is arguably nearer in wording and further in argument.

links.note: 'Can ye lay aside these things, and trample the holy one under your feet.' The KJV tramples a divine person once, at Hebrews 10:29, and the surrounding verses supply the blood, the sanctifying and the wilful sin that the rest of Alma 5:53-54 is made of. Moderate rather than high because the Book of Mormon's verb is 'trample' and the KJV's is 'trodden'; Matthew 7:6 has 'trample' with a holy object and is kept as the alternative.

pericopes.text: yea, will ye persist in supposing that ye are better one than another; yea, will ye persist in the persecutions of your brethren, who humble themselves, and do walk after the holy order of God, wherewith they have been brought into this Church, having been sanctified by the holy spirit; and they do bring forth works which is meet for repentance;
yea, and will you persist in turning your backs upon the poor, and the needy, and in withholding your substance from them?
And finally, all ye that will persist in your wickedness, I say unto you, that these are they which shall be hewn down and cast into the fire, except they speedily repent.

And now I say unto you, all you that are desirous to follow the voice of the good shepherd, come ye out from the wicked, and be ye separate, and touch not their unclean things; and behold, their names shall be blotted out, that the names of the wicked shall not be numbered among the names of the righteous, that the word of God may be fulfilled, which saith, The names of the wicked shall not be mingled with the names of my people.

links.text: Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you.

provenance.route: Isaiah 52:11 → 2 Corinthians 6:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Isaiah 52:11 in the KJV reads 'Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing; go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD.'
provenance.other: “be ye separate” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “touch not the unclean” occurs in exactly one — both 2 Corinthians 6:17, and neither is in Isaiah. tools/mediation-check.py was run on Alma 5:57 against Isaiah 52:11 and 2 Corinthians 6:17 and returns one decisive point, for Paul: the Book of Mormon has 'among them, and be ye separate' where Isaiah has 'thence'. Paul's negative is 'touch not the unclean thing' and Isaiah's is 'touch no unclean thing'; Alma 5:57 has 'touch not their unclean things', which is Paul's construction with the noun made plural and possessive.
provenance.significance: This is the clearest mediation result in the chapter and it is worth stating plainly: where the Book of Mormon quotes an Old Testament verse that the New Testament also quotes, this verse follows the New Testament's wording, including the clause Paul added and Isaiah does not contain. Recovering Paul's context then does real work. 2 Corinthians 6:17 is the centre of a paragraph about being unequally yoked with unbelievers, addressed to a congregation and demanding separation inside a mixed community — not the exodus from Babylon that Isaiah 52:11 describes. Alma 5:57 needs exactly Paul's situation and not Isaiah's: his hearers are not in exile among foreigners, they are a church with wicked members in it, and the separation he commands is a purging of a name-list, not a journey. The verse that follows in Paul, 'I will receive you', is also already in this sermon, at 5:33.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 52:11 is the ultimate source and is quoted elsewhere in the Book of Mormon (3 Nephi 20:41); the mediation call here is about which English wording Alma 5:57 has, not about which text is older.

links.note: 'Come ye out from the wicked, and be ye separate, and touch not their unclean things.' Against 2 Corinthians 6:17: 'Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing.' Three clauses in order, with 'from among them' replaced by 'from the wicked' — which is the only substantive change and is a gloss, naming who 'them' are. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his 36; catalogued as a quotation on the reproduction of the clauses.

links.text: Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous.

provenance.other: “blotted out of the book” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “written with the righteous” occurs in exactly one — the same verse, Psalm 69:28, and in that order. 'Book of life' by itself occurs in exactly eight KJV verses, six of them in Revelation, so the book is common property and the pairing of the blotting with the not-being-written-among-the-righteous is not.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:57-58 has all three of Psalm 69:28's moves and keeps them in the psalm's sequence: the names blotted out, the names of the wicked not numbered among the names of the righteous, and then the names of the righteous written in the book of life. The KJV's one verse that does the same work is the psalmist's imprecation against his persecutors. What the Book of Mormon changes is the agent and the mood. In the psalm the blotting is asked of God against enemies; in Alma it is an administrative consequence of a separation the hearers perform themselves — 'come ye out from the wicked ... and behold, their names shall be blotted out'. A curse has become a church register. Revelation 3:5's promise, that the overcomer's name will not be blotted out of the book of life, is the New Testament form and is the verse that supplies the white raiment this sermon has been using since 5:21; both halves of Revelation 3:5 are in Alma 5, which is worth recording even though the wording here is the psalm's.

links.note: 'Their names shall be blotted out, that the names of the wicked shall not be numbered among the names of the righteous ... For the names of the righteous shall be written in the Book of Life.' Two KJV singletons from one verse, in order. Alma 5:57 then attributes the sentence to scripture — 'that the word of God may be fulfilled, which saith, The names of the wicked shall not be mingled with the names of my people' — and the words quoted are in no KJV verse; the nearest thing the KJV has to the citation being claimed is Psalm 69:28, which is the link.

pericopes.text: For the names of the righteous shall be written in the Book of Life; and unto them will I grant an inheritance at my right hand. And now my brethren, what have ye to say against this? I say unto you, if ye speak against it, it matters not, for the word of God must be fulfilled.

For what shepherd is there among you having many sheep, doth not watch over them, that the wolves enter not and devour his flock? And behold, if a wolf enter his flock, doth he not drive him out? Yea, and at the last, if he can, he will destroy him.

And now I say unto you, that the good shepherd doth call after you; and if you will hearken unto his voice, he will bring you into his fold, and ye are his sheep; and he commandeth you that ye suffer no ravenous wolf to enter among you, that ye may not be destroyed.

links.text: For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.

provenance.other: “enter in among you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is the KJV's only wolves entering a flock: 'after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.' “ravening wolves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:15, which is the adjective behind the Book of Mormon's 'ravenous wolf'. John 10:12's wolf catches and scatters but does not enter.
provenance.significance: Acts 20 is Paul's farewell to the elders of Ephesus, and the verse before the wolves is the one that makes the borrowing pointed: 'Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God.' It is a charge to pastors about what will happen when the pastor leaves. Alma 5:59-60 turns it into a charge to the flock itself — 'he commandeth you that ye suffer no ravenous wolf to enter among you' — so the duty of the overseer is devolved onto the congregation, which is precisely the move Alma 4:18-20 made when he kept the priesthood and asked the people to be watched over by a word rather than an office. The chapter's shepherd language began at 5:38 with John 10 and ends here with Acts 20, and between them the shepherd has stopped being only Christ.

links.note: 'He commandeth you that ye suffer no ravenous wolf to enter among you, that ye may not be destroyed.' Acts 20:29 is the KJV's only verse with wolves entering in among a flock and the only verse with the phrase 'enter in among you'; Matthew 7:15 supplies 'ravening', which the Book of Mormon has as 'ravenous'. The previous verse's rhetorical question — 'what shepherd is there among you having many sheep, doth not watch over them, that the wolves enter not and devour his flock?' — states the same figure first and is covered by this row.

pericopes.text: And now I, Alma, do command you in the language of him who hath commanded me, that ye observe to do the words which I have spoken unto you.

I speak by way of command unto you that belong to the church; and unto those which do not belong to the church, I speak by way of invitation, saying, Come and be baptized unto repentance, that ye also may be partakers of the fruit of the tree of life.

And now it came to pass that after Alma had made an end of speaking unto the people of the church, which was established in the city of Zarahemla, he ordained priests and elders, by laying on his hands according to the order of God, to preside and watch over the church.

links.text: And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.

provenance.other: “ordained them elders” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “prayed with fasting” occurs in exactly one — the same verse, Acts 14:23, and consecutively within it. “laying on of hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 6:2, where it stands in a list of first principles beside baptisms, resurrection and judgment; 1 Timothy 4:14 has 'the laying on of the hands of the presbytery'. Alma 6:1's 'to preside and watch over the church' has no KJV phrase behind it, though “watch for your souls” occurs in exactly one verse, Hebrews 13:17, where it is what those who have the rule over a congregation do and must give account for.
provenance.significance: One KJV verse describes the founding of a church in the two acts this chapter is made of, and it does them in this chapter's order: elders ordained, then prayer with fasting. Alma 6:1 ordains, Alma 6:6 commands the church to 'gather themselves together oft, and join in fasting and mighty prayer', and between them 6:2-4 receives the penitent and rejects the impenitent. What the Book of Mormon changes is who fasts. In Acts 14:23 the apostles pray and fast over the elders they have just appointed and commend them to the Lord; in Alma 6:6 the whole church fasts, and it fasts not for its own officers but 'in behalf of the welfare of the souls of those who knew not God'. The apparatus of ordination is borrowed and then turned outward, which is the same movement the previous chapter made when it ended by addressing those who do not belong to the church.
provenance.alternative: Acts 13:2-3, where fasting, prayer and the laying on of hands occur together in that order, is the nearer parallel for 6:1 alone; it lacks the elders.

links.note: 'He ordained priests and elders, by laying on his hands according to the order of God, to preside and watch over the church.' Acts 14:23 is the KJV's only ordaining of elders and its only praying with fasting, and both of its halves are used in this eight-verse chapter. No clause is reproduced — the evidence is that two rare phrases from one verse organise two ends of one narrative — so the row is an allusion and not a quotation.

links.text: And it shall be, when the officers have made an end of speaking unto the people that they shall make captains of the armies to lead the people.

provenance.other: “made an end of speaking unto the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The shorter formula “made an end of speaking” occurs in exactly nine and is standard KJV narrative furniture, so the weight of this row rests entirely on the two words that extend it, 'unto the people'.
provenance.significance: The eight-word run is the longest in the chapter and its source has a shape worth noticing: in Deuteronomy 20:9 the end of the speech is the cue for appointing officers — 'when the officers have made an end of speaking unto the people, that they shall make captains of the armies to lead the people' — and Alma 6:1 makes an end of speaking unto the people and immediately ordains priests and elders. Speech, then appointment, in both. The setting is a muster for war in one and the organising of a church in the other, and that distance is what keeps this an echo; but the sequence is the same and the KJV joins these particular words nowhere else.

links.note: 'After Alma had made an end of speaking unto the people of the church ... he ordained priests and elders.' A singleton run, but a formulaic one: 'made an end of speaking' is available from nine KJV verses and the additional 'unto the people' is the commonest possible continuation. Recorded because the source verse independently supplies the very sequence Alma 6:1 executes, which is more than the string by itself would predict.
links.whyNot: The phrase is narrative boilerplate at its core and the two extending words are not distinctive. Deuteronomy 20 is a law of war and shares no vocabulary with Alma 6 beyond the run; a reader who thinks the sequence speech-then-appointment is simply what happens next in any such account should decline the row, and it would then fall to the standing formulaic exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that whomsoever did not belong to the church who repented of their sins, was baptized unto repentance, and was received into the church.

links.text: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:

provenance.other: “baptize you with water unto repentance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and 'unto repentance' as the thing baptism is for occurs in the KJV only there. Mark 1:4 and Luke 3:3 have 'the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins', which is a different construction.
provenance.significance: This is where Alma 5's borrowed sermon becomes an event. The whole of the preceding chapter is built on Matthew 3:2-12 — the axe at the root, the fruit, the unquenchable fire, the kingdom at hand, the works meet for repentance — and Matthew 3:11 is the one verse of that passage the sermon does not use, because it is the verse about what John does rather than what he says. Alma 6:2 supplies it: the outsiders repent and are 'baptized unto repentance'. The narrative has completed the chapter John the Baptist's preaching left unfinished, and it has done it in the Baptist's own words, which is why the row belongs at this verse and not among Alma 5's recurrences.
provenance.alternative: 'Baptized unto repentance' is a standing Book of Mormon formula (2 Nephi 31:11, Mosiah 26:22 and elsewhere) and may reach Alma 6:2 through the corpus rather than directly from Matthew.

links.note: 'Whomsoever did not belong to the church who repented of their sins, was baptized unto repentance, and was received into the church.' The phrase is Matthew 3:11's and the KJV has it nowhere else. Its force here is positional: it closes the Matthew 3 material that runs through Alma 5, and it does so at the point where the sermon's outsiders are actually baptized.

pericopes.text: And it also came to pass that whomsoever did belong to the church, that did not repent of their wickedness, and humble themselves before God; I mean those which were lifted up in the pride of their hearts; the same were rejected, and their names were blotted out, that their names were not numbered among those of the righteous;
and thus they began to establish the order of the church in the city of Zarahemla.
Now I would that ye should understand that the word of God was liberal unto all; that no one was deprived of the privilege of assembling themselves together to hear the word of God;

links.text: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.

provenance.other: “to all men liberally” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The adverb itself is nearly as rare: “liberally” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, James 1:5 and Deuteronomy 15:14, and the adjective 'liberal' in four, of which Isaiah 32:8's 'the liberal deviseth liberal things' is the only one with an abstract subject. Alma 6:5's construction — a thing, not a person, being 'liberal unto all' — is in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: James 1:5 is about a giver who does not discriminate and does not upbraid: God 'giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not.' Alma 6:5 transfers the adverb from the giver to the gift — 'the word of God was liberal unto all' — and then states the corollary James leaves implicit, that 'no one was deprived of the privilege of assembling themselves together to hear the word of God.' That is the sentence the chapter needs, because the three verses before it have just described a congregation rejecting members and blotting out names, and 6:5 is the qualification: the exclusion was from the church roll, not from the preaching. The borrowed word is doing the work of insisting that a disciplined church is not a closed one, and James's second clause, that God does not upbraid the asker, sits behind it unstated.

links.note: 'The word of God was liberal unto all; that no one was deprived of the privilege of assembling themselves together to hear the word of God.' The adverb is very rare in the KJV and its one relevant occurrence is James 1:5's 'giveth to all men liberally'. The Book of Mormon has moved it from the giving to the thing given, which is the change worth recording; the theological point of the verse is entirely in that move.

pericopes.text: nevertheless the children of God were commanded that they should gather themselves together oft, and join in fasting and mighty prayer, in behalf of the welfare of the souls of those who knew not God.

And now it came to pass that when Alma had made these regulations, he departed from them, yea, from the church which was in the city of Zarahemla, and went over upon the east of the river Sidon, into the valley of Gideon, there having been a city built which was called the city of Gideon, which was in the valley that was called Gideon, being called after the man which was slain by the hand of Nehor with the sword.

And Alma went and began to declare the word of God unto the church which was established in the valley of Gideon, according to the revelation of the truth of the word which had been spoken by his fathers, and according to the spirit of prophecy which was in him, according to the testimony of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, which should come for to redeem his people from their sins, and the holy order by which he was called. And thus it is written. Amen.

links.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

provenance.other: “spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 19:10. “testimony of Jesus” occurs in exactly four, all of them in Revelation, and Revelation 19:10 is one of them — because 19:10's closing sentence is the equation of the two: 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.' Alma 6:8 has both phrases, in that order, in consecutive clauses.
provenance.significance: The two terms are joined in the KJV by a definition and in Alma 6:8 by a pair of parallel prepositional phrases: 'according to the spirit of prophecy which was in him, according to the testimony of Jesus Christ, the Son of God'. What Revelation 19:10 asserts as an identity, Alma 6:8 lays out as two authorities for one act of preaching — and thereby says the same thing without arguing it, since the two 'according to' clauses govern the same verb. Recovering the context adds the sharper point. Revelation 19:10 is spoken by an angel refusing worship: 'See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant.' The sentence exists to deny that the one who brings the testimony is himself to be venerated, which is a serviceable thing to have echoing under a chapter in which a high priest has just laid down the judgment seat (4:20) and gone out with nothing but the word. The narrator's 'thus it is written. Amen.' closes the account on the borrowed formula.

links.note: 'According to the spirit of prophecy which was in him, according to the testimony of Jesus Christ.' Two phrases whose KJV homes are one verse and one book: 'spirit of prophecy' occurs once in the Bible, and all four occurrences of 'testimony of Jesus' are in Revelation. Alma 4:20 and 5:47 use 'the spirit of prophecy' earlier without the testimony beside it; here the pair arrives together and in Revelation's order, which is what makes this the place to adjudicate it.

links.text: She saith unto him, Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world.

provenance.route: John 11:27, spliced with Matthew 1:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the Son of God which should come” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “should come into the world”, the continuation John gives it, occurs in exactly two, John 6:14 and John 11:27. The Book of Mormon breaks off at exactly the point where the two Johannine verses would diverge and completes the sentence from elsewhere: 'which should come for to redeem his people from their sins' is Matthew 1:21's clause, adjudicated at Alma 5:21 and used a third time here.
provenance.significance: The seam is the finding. Alma 6:8 runs Martha's confession — 'thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come' — up to its last three words and then substitutes the angel's explanation of the name Jesus for John's 'into the world'. Two of the New Testament's set-piece confessions are welded at the joint, and the weld is legible because each half is a KJV singleton. What the substitution does is characteristic of this book: John's clause locates Christ in space and time, Matthew's states what he is for, and the Book of Mormon consistently prefers the second. The same operation produced Alma 5:21's 'redeem' for Matthew's 'save'.
provenance.alternative: Mark 1:1's 'Jesus Christ, the Son of God' and Acts 8:37's 'I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God' are the other confessional formulae in play; neither has 'which should come'. The project's index of Frederick records both of those verses as occurring near Alma 6:8 in his book — that is a co-occurrence in our extraction, not a source he proposes, and no claim is made here about what he identifies.

links.note: 'The testimony of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, which should come for to redeem his people from their sins.' Seven words reproduced from John 11:27, which is the KJV's only verse with them, followed by five reproduced from Matthew 1:21, which is the KJV's only verse with those. The n-gram stream ranked both and was right about both; what it could not see is that they are consecutive and that the join falls exactly where John's sentence would have ended differently.

pericopes.text: Behold my beloved brethren, seeing that I have been permitted to come unto you, therefore I attempt to address you in my language; yea, by my own mouth, seeing that it is the first time that I have spoken unto you by the words of my mouth, I having been wholly confined to the judgment seat, having had much business that I could not come unto you;

and even I could not have come now at this time, were it not that the judgment seat hath been given to another, to reign in my stead; and the Lord in much mercy hath granted that I should come unto you.

And behold, I have come, having great hopes and much desire that I should find that ye had humbled yourselves before God, and that ye had continued in the supplicating of his grace, that I should find that ye were blameless before him; that I should find that ye were not in the awful dilemma that our brethren were in at Zarahemla;
but blessed be the name of God that he hath given me to know, yea, hath given unto me the exceeding great joy of knowing that they are established again in the way of his righteousness.

And I trust, according to the spirit of God which is in me, that I shall also have joy over you; nevertheless I do not desire that my joy over you, should come by the cause of so much afflictions and sorrow which I have had for the brethren at Zarahemla: for behold, my joy cometh over them after wading through much afflictions and sorrow.

But behold, I trust that ye are not in a state of so much unbelief as were your brethren; I trust that ye are not lifted up in the pride of your hearts; yea, I trust that ye have not set your hearts upon riches, and the vain things of the world; yea, I trust that you do not worship idols, but that ye do worship the true and the living God; and that ye look forward for the remission of your sins with an everlasting faith which is to come.

links.text: For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God;

provenance.other: 'The living and true God' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 1:9. Alma inverts the pair to 'the true and the living God'; the constituent phrases 'the living God' (28 verses) and 'the true God' (5) are each common, but their conjunction is not.
provenance.significance: The rarity is not in the words but in the movement. Paul's one use of the phrase is the hinge of a sentence about converts who 'turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God', and Alma 7:6 makes the same turn in the same order: 'ye do not worship idols, but ye do worship the true and the living God.' Idols first, the living and true God second, the verb of service or worship governing both. What Paul reports of the Thessalonians as an accomplished conversion, Alma expresses as a hope about Gideon — the congregation he has come to test. Recover Paul's next clause and the hope acquires its object: those who turned 'to wait for his Son from heaven', which is precisely what Alma spends verses 7 through 13 telling Gideon to do.

links.note: 'Ye do not worship idols, but that ye do worship the true and the living God; and that ye look forward for the remission of your sins with an everlasting faith which is to come.' The KJV's single occurrence of 'the living and true God' sits in its single verse about turning from idols to that God and waiting for his Son, and Alma reproduces all three moves — idols renounced, the living and true God worshipped, the coming Son awaited — with the adjective pair reversed. Reversal of a fixed pair is the ordinary signature of quotation from memory rather than from a page. Well under Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages.

pericopes.text: For behold, I say unto you, there be many things to come; and behold, there is one thing which is of more importance than they all: for behold, the time is not far distant, that the Redeemer liveth and cometh among his people.

Behold, I do not say that he will come among us at the time of his dwelling in his mortal tabernacle; for behold, the spirit hath not said unto me that this should be the case. Now as to this thing I do not know; but this much I do know, that the Lord God hath power to do all things which is according to his word.

But behold, the spirit hath said this much unto me, saying: Cry unto this people, saying, Repent ye, and prepare the way of the Lord, and walk in his paths, which are straight: for behold, the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand, and the Son of God cometh upon the face of the earth.

links.text: For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

provenance.other: 'Prepare ye the way of the Lord' occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Isaiah 40:3 and its three Gospel citations. 'Make his paths straight' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all of them Gospel: Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4. 'The kingdom of heaven is at hand' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all of them Matthew: 3:2, 4:17, 10:7.
provenance.significance: mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Matthew against Isaiah: the Book of Mormon has 'his paths', which the Gospels supply and Isaiah does not, and it lacks Isaiah's 'in the desert a highway for our God'. So Alma is not preaching from Isaiah 40; he is preaching from the Gospel's reading of Isaiah 40. The second half of the composite settles which Gospel. 'Repent ye ... for the kingdom of heaven is at hand' is Matthew 3:2, the verse immediately before the citation, and 'kingdom of heaven' for 'kingdom of God' is Matthew's idiom exclusively. What the Spirit tells Alma to cry to this people is therefore John the Baptist's sentence and its Matthean frame, in Matthew's order: repentance, the kingdom, then the way of the Lord. The suppressed correspondence is who is speaking. Alma is a chief judge who has laid down the judgment seat to preach, addressing a people about a Redeemer not yet come; the words he is given are the forerunner's.

links.note: 'Cry unto this people, saying, Repent ye, and prepare the way of the Lord, and walk in his paths, which are straight: for behold, the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.' Two Matthean units, 3:2 and 3:3, in Matthew's sequence. The machine proposed Luke 17:21 and Matthew 26:45 here on 'behold the kingdom of' and 'at hand and the son of', and both are artifacts of connective word order: neither has 'prepare the way of the Lord' anywhere near it. The mediation is decisive — 'his paths' is the Gospels' addition to Isaiah, and the Book of Mormon has it.

pericopes.text: And behold, he shall be born of Mary, at Jerusalem, which is the land of our forefathers, she being a Virgin, a precious and chosen vessel, who shall be overshadowed, and conceive by the power of the Holy Ghost, and bring forth a son, yea, even the Son of God;

links.text: And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS.

provenance.other: 'The power of the Highest shall overshadow' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:35; the verb 'overshadow' in that sense occurs nowhere else in the KJV of the annunciation's kind. 'Conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:31.
provenance.significance: Alma has Gabriel's two verses in Gabriel's order but compressed into one clause and re-voiced in the third person: overshadowed, conceive, bring forth a son. The one word that carries the whole is 'overshadowed', which is a passive with no stated agent in Alma and a stated agent in Luke — 'the power of the Highest'. Alma then supplies the agent from the other half of Luke 1:35, 'the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee', writing 'conceive by the power of the Holy Ghost'. That fusion is the finding: Luke keeps the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest as two parallel members of a Hebrew couplet, and Alma collapses them into a single agent. A reader who recovers Luke's context gets a distinction the Book of Mormon has already resolved.

links.note: 'She being a Virgin, a precious and chosen vessel, who shall be overshadowed, and conceive by the power of the Holy Ghost, and bring forth a son, yea, even the Son of God.' Two KJV singletons from adjacent verses of the annunciation, in sequence, with Luke's couplet of agents fused into one. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Matthew 1:18 and Luke 1:35 at this verse; the wording is Luke's throughout and Matthew 1:18 contributes nothing verbally, so the link sits on Luke and Matthew is registered as an exclusion. 'Precious and chosen vessel' is not KJV: 'chosen vessel' is Acts 9:15, of Paul, and the collocation with 'precious' is the Book of Mormon's own.

pericopes.text: and he shall go forth, suffering pains, and afflictions, and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith, He will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people;

links.text: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.

provenance.other: 'Bare our sicknesses' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and 'took our infirmities' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both of them Matthew 8:17. Isaiah 53:4 in the KJV reads 'borne our griefs' and 'carried our sorrows' — neither 'sicknesses' nor 'infirmities' appears anywhere in the Isaiah verse. The citation frame is separately rare: 'that the word might be fulfilled' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 15:25, and 'might be fulfilled which saith' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 19:24.
provenance.significance: This is the cleanest mediation case in the chapter and one of the cleanest in the book. Alma marks the sentence as a citation — 'this that the word might be fulfilled which saith' — and then gives, as the word to be fulfilled, a phrase that exists in the KJV only in Matthew's Greek-derived rendering of Isaiah, not in the KJV's Isaiah. mediation-check.py returns two decisive points: the Book of Mormon has Matthew's citation frame and Matthew's 'sicknesses', and neither of Isaiah's 'griefs' nor 'sorrows'. The metalepsis is severe once recovered. Matthew 8:17 is not a passion text at all: Matthew attaches it to an evening of healings at Peter's house, reading Isaiah's suffering servant as a healer of bodies. Alma 7:11-12 does exactly the same thing — it takes the atonement out of the register of guilt and into the register of pain, sickness, and infirmity, and it does so by quoting the one KJV verse where that reading of Isaiah 53 has already been made. Alma's Christ is Matthew's Christ of the sickbed before he is Isaiah's man of sorrows. One further consequence of the frame. Both Johannine formulas Alma has spliced introduce quotations of Scripture being fulfilled by something done TO Jesus — hatred without a cause, soldiers casting lots for his coat. Alma's frame introduces a quotation about what Jesus will take upon himself. The borrowed grammar of passion-fulfilment has been turned to describe an act.

links.note: "This that the word might be fulfilled which saith, He will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people." The quoted word is Matthew 8:17, not Isaiah 53:4: 'sicknesses' is Matthew's, and Isaiah's KJV has 'griefs' and 'sorrows'. The frame around it is not Matthew's, and is itself a finding — Alma's 'that the word might be fulfilled which saith' splices the KJV's one occurrence of 'that the word might be fulfilled' (John 15:25) to its one occurrence of 'might be fulfilled which saith' (John 19:24), joined at the shared word 'fulfilled'. So the sentence quotes Matthew inside a frame welded out of two verses of John. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Isaiah 53:4 and Matthew 8:17 together here; the mediation test decides between them, and it decides for Matthew.

pericopes.text: and he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which binds his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to suffer his people according to their infirmities.

links.text: For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted.

provenance.other: 'Succour them that are tempted' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 2:18, which is also the KJV's only verse pairing 'suffered' with 'succour'. 'The feeling of our infirmities' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 4:15.
provenance.significance: The 1830 reading is the evidence. Alma 7:12 in the first edition ends 'that he may know according to the flesh how to suffer his people according to their infirmities' — 'suffer', not 'succor'; the 1920 edition emended it, and every modern reader has the emended word. The emendation is almost certainly right as sense, and it is exactly what makes the borrowing visible, because Hebrews 2:18 is the one KJV verse in which both words stand in one sentence and in this relation: he suffered, therefore he can succour. The 1830 text has taken the wrong half of that sentence — or has preserved a scribal collision between the two — and either way it shows a compositor's eye on Hebrews 2:18 rather than on a general idea of sympathy. Verse 11's 'temptations of every kind' is Hebrews 2:18's 'tempted' twice over, and 'their infirmities' is Hebrews 4:15's. So the argument Alma is making — that Christ takes on flesh in order to know experientially how to help — is the argument of Hebrews 2-4, made in its vocabulary.

links.note: 'He will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy … that he may know according to the flesh how to suffer his people according to their infirmities.' The 1830 'suffer' where 1920 reads 'succor' is what identifies the source: Hebrews 2:18 is the only KJV verse in which suffering and succouring are the two halves of one clause, and Alma has both words within two verses. 'Bowels may be filled with mercy' is not Hebrews but Colossians 3:12's KJV singleton 'bowels of mercies', filed here as a secondary observation rather than a link because a single common noun is doing all the work. See 7:11 for the 'infirmities' half, which is Matthew 8:17's.

pericopes.text: Now the spirit knoweth all things; nevertheless the Son of God suffereth according to the flesh, that he might take upon him the sins of his people, that he might blot out their transgressions, according to the power of his deliverance; and now behold, this is the testimony which is in me.

Now I say unto you, that ye must repent, and be born again: for the spirit saith, If ye are not born again, ye cannot inherit the Kingdom of Heaven; therefore come and be baptized unto repentance, that ye may be washed from your sins, that ye may have faith on the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sins of the world, which is mighty to save and to cleanse from all unrighteousness;

links.text: The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.

provenance.other: 'Which taketh away the sin of the world' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:29. 'Mighty to save' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 63:1. 'Cleanse us from all unrighteousness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 1:9. 'Ye must be born again' is John 3:7; 'born again' occurs in exactly three KJV verses.
provenance.significance: One sentence of Alma 7:14 strings three KJV singletons from three different books: 'the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sins of the world, which is mighty to save and to cleanse from all unrighteousness.' John supplies the Lamb, Isaiah 63 supplies 'mighty to save', 1 John supplies the cleansing. What holds them together is that all three are answers to the question of who can deal with sin, and the middle one is the odd member: Isaiah 63:1 is the Edom oracle, the figure coming from Bozrah with dyed garments, and the dye in the next verses turns out to be blood from a winepress of wrath. Alma has taken the KJV's one self-description of a redeemer as 'mighty to save' and set it between the Lamb and the cleansing, so that a phrase whose home context is the treading of enemies is made to serve the washing of sinners. Note also that the 1830 has 'which taketh away' where 1920 reads 'who' — the first edition preserves John's relative pronoun exactly and the modernization erases it.

links.note: 'That ye may have faith on the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sins of the world, which is mighty to save and to cleanse from all unrighteousness.' John 1:29 verbatim but for the plural 'sins', in the 1830's KJV pronoun 'which' that 1920 changed to 'who'; then two further KJV singletons in the same breath. The verse opens with 'ye must repent, and be born again … ye cannot inherit the Kingdom of Heaven', which fuses John 3:7's 'ye must be born again' with John 3:3's 'cannot see the kingdom of God' recast in Paul's 'inherit' (1 Corinthians 15:50) and Matthew's 'kingdom of heaven'. The machine found John 1:29 and 1 Corinthians 15:50; Isaiah 63:1 and 1 John 1:9 were invisible to it.

pericopes.text: yea, I say unto you, Come and fear not, and lay aside every sin, which easily doth beset you, which doth bind you down to destruction; yea, come and go forth, and shew unto your God that ye are willing to repent of your sins, and enter into a covenant with him to keep his commandments, and witness it unto him this day, by going into the waters of baptism;

links.text: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,

provenance.other: 'Lay aside every weight' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and 'easily beset' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both of them Hebrews 12:1; 'beset' in any form occurs in only a handful of KJV verses and nowhere else with 'easily'.
provenance.significance: Alma has collapsed Hebrews' two objects into one. The KJV distinguishes the weight from the sin — 'lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us' — and Alma writes 'lay aside every sin, which easily doth beset you', taking the adjective of the first object and the relative clause of the second and welding them onto a single noun. The transposition 'easily doth' for 'doth so easily' is the kind of small dislocation that quotation from memory produces and copying does not. Recover the context and the borrowing gains an argument Alma does not state: Hebrews 12:1 is about running a race in view of a cloud of witnesses, and Alma's next clause turns the laying aside into a public act — 'come and go forth, and shew unto your God that ye are willing to repent … and witness it unto him this day, by going into the waters of baptism.' Hebrews' witnesses watch the runner; Alma's convert is himself the witness.

links.note: 'Lay aside every sin, which easily doth beset you, which doth bind you down to destruction.' Two KJV singletons from one verse of Hebrews, fused onto a single noun. The machine ranked Nehemiah 9:8 at this verse on 'a covenant with him to', which is connective; the actual borrowing was invisible to it. The 1830 'shew' later in the verse, modernized to 'show' in 1920, is a further KJV spelling the first edition preserves.

pericopes.text: and whosoever doeth this, and keepeth the commandments of God from thenceforth, the same will remember that I say unto him, yea, he will remember that I have said unto him, he shall have eternal life, according to the testimony of the Holy Spirit, which testifieth in me.

And now my beloved brethren, do you believe these things? Behold, I say unto you, yea, I know that you believe them; and the way that I know that ye believe them, is by the manifestation of the spirit which is in me. And now because your faith is strong concerning that, yea, concerning the things which I have spoken, great is my joy.

links.text: But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.

provenance.other: 'The manifestation of the Spirit' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 12:7. The noun 'manifestation' occurs in exactly two KJV verses in all, the other being Romans 8:19.
provenance.significance: Alma uses the phrase to answer an epistemological question he has just put to himself: he knows Gideon believes, and 'the way that I know that ye believe them, is by the manifestation of the spirit which is in me.' Paul's one use of the phrase is the premise of his argument that gifts are distributed severally to each — the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal — which is to say that the phrase's home context is about the Spirit's presence in other people, and Alma has turned it into an instrument for reading other people. Recover Paul's chapter and the discerning of spirits turns out to be one of the nine gifts he goes on to list, four verses later; Alma is claiming that gift without naming it.

links.note: 'The way that I know that ye believe them, is by the manifestation of the spirit which is in me.' A four-word KJV singleton, and the noun itself is nearly a KJV hapax. Recorded at moderate rather than high because 'manifestation of the Spirit' had become ordinary revivalist English long before 1830 and could reach the page without Paul in view; the count is what keeps the row.
links.whyNot: The phrase is a commonplace of nineteenth-century American religious speech, so KJV rarity may not indicate KJV dependence here. Nothing else of 1 Corinthians 12 is present in the verse.

pericopes.text: For as I said unto you from the beginning, that I had much desire that ye was not in the state of dilemma like your brethren, even so I have found that my desires have been gratified.
For I perceive that ye are in the paths of righteousness; I perceive that ye are in the path which leads to the kingdom of God; yea, I perceive that ye are making his paths straight;

links.text: He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.

provenance.other: 'The paths of righteousness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 23:3. Proverbs 8:20 has 'in the way of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of judgment'; Proverbs 2:20 has 'the paths of the righteous'. Neither has Alma's phrase.
provenance.significance: The verse runs three 'I perceive' clauses in ascending order — the paths of righteousness, the path which leads to the kingdom of God, the making of his paths straight — and the first and third are borrowed from opposite ends of the canon. The third returns to Matthew 3:3, adjudicated at 7:9, so Alma's picture of Gideon's congregation is framed by the psalm at one end and the forerunner at the other: a people the Lord leads in the paths of righteousness are the people preparing his way. The middle clause, which is the only one that names the destination, is the one with no biblical wording at all.

links.note: 'I perceive that ye are in the paths of righteousness … yea, I perceive that ye are making his paths straight.' A KJV singleton, but a short and proverbial one, and 'paths of righteousness' is the sort of phrase a preacher could reach for without Psalm 23 in view — hence moderate rather than high. What raises it above passing is the third clause of the same sentence, which is unmistakably Matthew 3:3 and shows Alma still working the vocabulary of paths he took up at 7:9.
links.whyNot: Three words, in a construction common to devotional English of every period. The link rests on the KJV count and on the company it keeps in the verse, not on volume.

pericopes.text: I perceive that it hath been made known unto you by the testimony of his word, that he cannot walk in crooked paths; neither doth he vary from that which he hath said; neither hath he a shadow of turning from the right to the left, or from that which is right to that which is wrong; therefore, his course is one eternal round.

links.text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.

provenance.other: 'Shadow of turning' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and 'no variableness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both of them James 1:17; the phrase 'shadow of turning' occurs nowhere else in the KJV in any form.
provenance.significance: Alma reproduces James's pair in James's order and in James's syntax — a negated first member, then 'neither' and the second: 'neither doth he vary from that which he hath said; neither hath he a shadow of turning.' James's 'no variableness' becomes a verb, 'doth not vary', and the second member is verbatim. What Alma does with it is the interesting part. James's immutability is about the reliability of gifts descending from the Father of lights; Alma's is forensic, about a God whose word can be relied on because he cannot walk in crooked paths — the argument of the whole address, that the testimony Alma has borne will hold. He then closes the verse with 'his course is one eternal round', which is not KJV and is the Book of Mormon's own figure. So a KJV singleton about light is being made to do the work of a proof of divine consistency.

links.note: 'Neither doth he vary from that which he hath said; neither hath he a shadow of turning from the right to the left.' The one KJV verse that has both 'variableness' and 'shadow of turning' supplies both, in order and in the same negated-pair construction. Nothing in the dossier reached this verse at all; the machine returned no candidates for 7:20.

pericopes.text: And he doth not dwell in unholy temples; neither can filthiness, or any thing which is unclean be received into the kingdom of God; therefore I say unto you, the time shall come, yea, and it shall be at the last day, that he which is filthy, shall remain in his filthiness.

links.text: He that is unjust, let him be unjust still: and he which is filthy, let him be filthy still: and he that is righteous, let him be righteous still: and he that is holy, let him be holy still.

provenance.other: 'He which is filthy' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 22:11. The KJV's other constructions use 'he that is'; the relative 'which' with 'filthy' occurs only here, and the 1830 preserves it where 1920 reads 'who'.
provenance.significance: Alma's clause is Revelation 22:11 turned from an imperative into a prediction. John writes a jussive — let him be filthy still — spoken from the very end of the canon, after which nothing changes; Alma writes 'the time shall come, yea, and it shall be at the last day, that he which is filthy, shall remain in his filthiness', which supplies the date John leaves implicit and converts the permission into a fate. The 1830's 'which' rather than 'who' is what makes the borrowing legible: it is John's relative pronoun in John's collocation, and the 1920 modernization removes the only word that distinguishes the phrase from ordinary English.

links.note: 'The time shall come, yea, and it shall be at the last day, that he which is filthy, shall remain in his filthiness.' A five-word KJV singleton reproduced exactly in the first edition, from the KJV's one verse about the irrevocability of moral state at the end. The 1830 'which' → 1920 'who' change is flagged in the dossier and matters: the modernized text no longer matches Revelation. No machine candidate reached this verse.

links.text: Howbeit the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands; as saith the prophet,

provenance.other: 'Dwelleth not in temples made with hands' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 7:48 and Acts 17:24. 'Unholy' occurs in four KJV verses (Leviticus 10:10, 1 Timothy 1:9, 2 Timothy 3:2, Hebrews 10:29) and in none of them with 'temple'.
provenance.significance: Both KJV verses deny that God dwells in temples of any kind; Alma denies only that he dwells in unholy ones, which reverses the point while keeping the sentence shape. That reversal is why this is an echo and not an allusion — the wording is close enough to notice and the doctrine is opposite, and a catalogue that recorded only the resemblance would misreport it. The one thing that keeps it above the exclusion line is the setting. Stephen's speech in Acts 7 is a prophet's last address to a people who will kill him, and Alma 7 is the address immediately preceding Alma's own rejection at Ammonihah in chapter 8.

links.note: 'And he doth not dwell in unholy temples.' A negated dwelling-in-temples sentence in the shape of Acts 7:48 / 17:24, with the qualifier that undoes it: Luke's God dwells in no temples made with hands, Alma's God dwells in holy ones and not unholy ones. Recorded at moderate on the strength of the construction, not the doctrine. 'Unholy temples' is not a KJV phrase.
links.whyNot: The shared material is a common verb and a common noun in a negated clause; the sense is contrary to both KJV verses, and the Book of Mormon's own body-as-temple idiom (compare 1 Corinthians 3:16-17, also not verbally present) would account for the sentence without any borrowing at all.

pericopes.text: And now my beloved brethren, I have said these things unto you, that I might awaken you to a sense of your duty to God, that ye may walk blameless before him; that ye may walk after the holy order of God, after which ye have been received.

links.text: But because I have said these things unto you, sorrow hath filled your heart.

provenance.other: 'I have said these things unto you' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 16:6. The Johannine farewell discourse uses several near variants — 'these things have I spoken unto you' at John 15:11, 16:1, 16:4, 16:25, 16:33 — but this exact word order occurs once.
provenance.significance: Seven words in sequence, and the only KJV verse that has them belongs to a farewell address. Alma 7 is also a farewell: he has laid down the judgment seat, he speaks to Gideon 'by my own mouth' for the first and, as chapter 8 shows, the last extended time before Ammonihah, and he ends the chapter with a blessing on houses, lands, flocks and herds. What Jesus says the words produce is sorrow; what Alma says they are for is 'that I might awaken you to a sense of your duty to God'. That is the interesting divergence and the reason to record the row rather than pass it over as boilerplate.

links.note: 'I have said these things unto you, that I might awaken you to a sense of your duty to God.' A seven-word KJV singleton, but composed entirely of function words and one weak verb, so the count overstates the distinctiveness — the same sentence could be written by anyone. Recorded at moderate because the run is exact and long and because both settings are valedictory. Flagged as the chapter's weakest accepted row.
links.whyNot: Every word is common; only the order is rare, and rare orderings of common words are the failure mode the n-gram stream is worst at. If this row is wrong it is wrong in the direction the pilot warned about at Job 42:7.

pericopes.text: And now I would that ye should be humble, and be submissive, and gentle; easy to be entreated; full of patience and long suffering; being temperate in all things; being diligent in keeping the commandments of God at all times; asking for whatsoever things ye stand in need, both spiritual and temporal; always returning thanks unto God for whatsoever things ye do receive,

links.text: But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.

provenance.other: 'Easy to be intreated' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 3:17 (the 1830 spells it 'entreated'). 'Temperate in all things' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 9:25. 'Full of patience' occurs in no KJV verse; 'full of mercy' is James 3:17's own continuation.
provenance.significance: Alma's virtue list reproduces three consecutive members of James's — gentle, easy to be entreated, full of — in James's order, and then substitutes: James has 'full of mercy and good fruits', Alma has 'full of patience and long suffering'. The substitution is not random. Mercy is what Alma has just said Christ's bowels are filled with at 7:12; having given mercy to the Redeemer he gives patience to the congregation, and the slot in James's sentence is preserved while its filler moves. The next item, 'temperate in all things', leaves James for Paul and for another KJV singleton, from the one verse about an athlete training for a corruptible crown — which sets the whole list under the figure of a contest, as Hebrews 12:1 did at 7:15.

links.note: 'Be humble, and be submissive, and gentle; easy to be entreated; full of patience and long suffering; being temperate in all things.' Two KJV singletons in one clause, the first three items in James's own sequence. The 1830 spells 'entreated' where the KJV has 'intreated', so this is one of the rare places the first edition is the modernized form; 1920 also joins 'long suffering' into 'long-suffering'. No machine candidate reached this verse.

pericopes.text: and see that ye have faith, hope, and charity, and then ye will always abound in good works;

links.text: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.

provenance.other: The triad 'faith, hope, charity' in this order occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:13. 'Charity' as the third member is what makes the count decisive: the KJV's 'charity' is a translation choice, and modern versions read 'love', so a modern Bible cannot produce this triad in these words at all.
provenance.significance: The triad is Paul's and the KJV's third word is the tell. Where a reader of a modern version finds faith, hope and love, Alma has faith, hope and charity, which is the King James lexical decision specifically. What Alma adds is a consequence Paul does not draw: 'and then ye will always abound in good works'. Paul ends his sentence by ranking the three; Alma ends his by making them productive, which is the emphasis of James — whose verse he has just quoted in the line before — rather than of 1 Corinthians 13. The two verses together, James 3:17 and 1 Corinthians 13:13, put a Pauline triad to a Jamesian use.

links.note: 'And see that ye have faith, hope, and charity, and then ye will always abound in good works.' The KJV's one occurrence of the triad in this order, with 'charity' — the King James word, not a modern version's. 'Abound in good works' occurs in no KJV verse; 2 Corinthians 9:8's 'abound to every good work' is the nearest and is not close enough to catalogue.

pericopes.text: and may the Lord bless you, and keep your garments spotless, that ye may at last be brought to sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the Holy Prophets, which have been ever since the world began, having your garments spotless, even as their garments are spotless in the kingdom of Heaven, to go no more out.

links.text: And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.

provenance.other: 'Sit down with Abraham' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 8:11, and it is the only KJV verse joining the patriarchal triad to 'the kingdom of heaven'. 'Which have been since the world began' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:70; Acts 3:21's 'since the world began' lacks the relative clause.
provenance.significance: Both singletons come from the same fourteen verses of Luke and Matthew that Alma has been quoting all chapter, and one of them is the chapter's own bookend. Matthew 8:11 stands seven verses before Matthew 8:17, which Alma quoted at 7:11 — the two ends of a single Matthean passage, used at the two ends of a single address. The metalepsis is in what Matthew 8:11 is for. It is the saying about the centurion, in which the many who sit down with the patriarchs come from the east and west and 'the children of the kingdom shall be cast out'. Alma is promising a congregation of Nephites, on the far side of the world from Jerusalem, a seat at that table; the verse he promises it in is the KJV's one verse about outsiders taking the insiders' places.
provenance.alternative: Luke 13:28-29 has the same saying with the patriarchs and the four quarters, but reads 'sit down in the kingdom of God' and lacks 'sit down with Abraham'; the Book of Mormon has Matthew's form on both points.

links.note: 'That ye may at last be brought to sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the Holy Prophets, which have been ever since the world began … in the kingdom of Heaven, to go no more out.' Two KJV singletons in one sentence, from Matthew's centurion saying and from the Benedictus. The 1830 'which have been' preserves Luke's relative where 1920 reads 'who'. Luke 13:28-29's parallel form is ruled out on 'kingdom of heaven' and on 'sit down with'.

pericopes.text: And now my beloved brethren, I have spoken these words unto you, according to the spirit which testifieth in me; and my soul doth exceedingly rejoice, because of the exceeding diligence and heed which ye have given unto my word.

And now, may the peace of God rest upon you, and upon your houses and lands, and upon your flocks and herds, and all that you possess; your women and your children, according to your faith and good works, from this time forth and forever. And thus I have spoken. Amen.

And now it came to pass that Alma returned from the land of Gideon, after having taught the people of Gideon many things which cannot be written, having established the order of the church, according as he had before done in the land of Zarahemla; yea, he returned to his own house at Zarahemla, to rest himself from the labors which he had performed.
And thus ended the ninth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.

And it came to pass in the commencement of the tenth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, that Alma departed from thence, and took his journey over into the land of Melek, on the west of the river Sidon, on the west, by the borders of the wilderness;
and he began to teach the people in the land of Melek, according to the holy order of God by which he had been called; and he began to teach the people throughout all the land of Melek.
And it came to pass that the people came to him throughout all the borders of the land which was by the wilderness side. And it came to pass that they were baptized throughout all the land,
so that when he had finished his work at Melek, he departed thence, and travelled three days’ journey on the north of the land of Melek; and he came to a city which was called Ammonihah.

Now it was the custom of the people of Nephi, to call their lands, and their cities, and their villages, yea, even all their small villages, after the name of him who first possessed them; and thus it was with the land of Ammonihah.
And it came to pass that when Alma had came to the city of Ammonihah, he began to preach the word of God unto them.
Now satan had got great hold upon the hearts of the people of the city of Ammonihah; therefore they would not hearken unto the words of Alma.

Nevertheless Alma labored much in the spirit, wrestling with God in mighty prayer, that he would pour out his spirit upon the people which was in the city; that he would also grant that he might baptize them unto repentance;

links.text: For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.

provenance.other: The verb 'wrestle' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 6:12. The preterite 'wrestled' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Genesis 30:8, 32:24 and 32:25, all of Jacob or of Rachel; 'wrestlings' occurs in exactly one, Genesis 30:8. The Book of Mormon's participle 'wrestling' occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.significance: Two sources, and the reason to name both is that Alma's sentence takes something incompatible from each. Ephesians supplies the register: the KJV uses the verb 'wrestle' exactly once, of a contest waged not against flesh and blood but in the spirit against powers — and Alma 8:9-10 sets the wrestling immediately after the statement that 'Satan had got great hold upon the hearts of the people', and says Alma 'labored much IN THE SPIRIT, wrestling'. Genesis supplies the preposition: Paul's wrestling is against, Alma's is 'with God', which is Jacob's at Peniel and no one else's. So the combatant is Paul's and the opponent is Jacob's, and what results is a sentence in which a prophet grapples with God about a city held by Satan. The Jacob half then pays: four verses later an angel appears to Alma and blesses him, which is how the night at Peniel ends and not how Ephesians 6 ends.

links.note: 'Alma labored much in the spirit, wrestling with God in mighty prayer.' The KJV has the verb once, at Ephesians 6:12, in the spirit and against powers; it has the past tense three times, all of Jacob, and always 'with'. Alma has the tense and preposition of Genesis and the arena of Ephesians. Recorded at moderate because a single verb is carrying the link and because 'wrestling with God in prayer' had long been ordinary evangelical English by 1830 — though that idiom is itself downstream of these same verses.
links.whyNot: One word of verbal contact, in a phrase already naturalized in nineteenth-century revival speech. No machine candidate reached this verse and nothing else of either source is present.

pericopes.text: nevertheless, they hardened their hearts, saying unto him, Behold, we know that thou art Alma; and we know that thou art High Priest over the church which thou hast established in many parts of the land, according to your tradition; and we are not of thy church, and we do not believe in such foolish traditions.

And now we know that because we are not of thy church, we know that thou hast no power over us; and thou hast delivered up the judgment seat unto Nephihah; therefore thou art not the Chief Judge over us.

Now when the people had said this, and had withstood all his words, and reviled him, and spit upon him, and caused that he should be cast out of their city, he departed thence and took his journey towards the city which was called Aaron.

links.text: And cast him out of the city, and stoned him: and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man’s feet, whose name was Saul.

provenance.route: Acts 7:57-58 with the passion predictions → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Cast him out of the city' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:58. 'Spit upon' occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Leviticus 15:8, Matthew 27:30, Mark 10:34 and Mark 15:19 — that is, once of ritual uncleanness and three times of Jesus. 'Reviled' occurs in exactly five KJV verses, three of them of Jesus at the cross.
provenance.significance: Alma 8:13 gives four things done to the prophet in order: they withstood his words, reviled him, spit upon him, and cast him out of their city. Every one of the last three is a KJV verb of the passion, and the last is the KJV's single occurrence of its phrase, in the verse where Stephen is put outside Jerusalem to be killed. What the sequence does is place Alma in a line the reader is expected to complete: reviled and spat upon is what happens to Jesus, cast out of the city is what happens to Stephen, and the one thing Alma 8 withholds is the stoning that follows in Acts 7:58 and the death that follows in Mark 10:34. He is thrown out and walks away weighed down with sorrow. The metalepsis is in the withheld clause — the reader who recovers Acts 7:58 finds the stones and the young man named Saul, and neither arrives; Alma is instead sent back, and it is the city that will be destroyed.

links.note: 'They had withstood all his words, and reviled him, and spit upon him, and caused that he should be cast out of their city.' Three KJV passion verbs in sequence, closing on the KJV's only occurrence of 'cast him out of the city', which is Stephen's martyrdom. The machine ranked Daniel 3:11 here on 'that he should be cast', which is the fiery furnace and shares only the passive construction. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his passages.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that while he was journeying thither, being weighed down with sorrow, wading through much tribulation and anguish of soul, because of the wickedness of the people which was in the city of Ammonihah. And it came to pass that while Alma was thus weighed down with sorrow, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared unto him, saying,

Blessed art thou, Alma; therefore lift up thy head and rejoice, for thou hast great cause to rejoice: for thou hast been faithful in keeping the commandments of God from the time which thou received thy first message from him. Behold, I am he that delivered it unto you;

links.text: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.

provenance.other: 'Thou hast been faithful' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 25:21, Matthew 25:23 and Luke 19:17. Two of the three are the parable of the talents; the third is Luke's parable of the pounds, which reads 'faithful in a very little'.
provenance.significance: Taken alone this is a four-word commendation formula and would not carry much. What carries it is that Alma 8 goes back to Matthew 25 a second time, eleven verses later and in the angel's own idiom: at 8:26 Alma blesses Amulek in the words of Matthew 25:35, the sheep who fed the hungry stranger. So the chapter opens its supernatural frame with the lord's word to the faithful servant and closes it with the Son of Man's word to the sheep — the two halves of one Matthean discourse, used at the two ends of one episode, on the two men the episode is about. Alma is the servant found faithful; Amulek is the stranger's host. That distribution is the finding, and neither half is visible without the other.

links.note: 'Blessed art thou, Alma; therefore lift up thy head and rejoice … for thou hast been faithful in keeping the commandments of God.' Matthew's commendation of the faithful servant, with 'in' from Luke 19:17's variant rather than Matthew's 'over'. Moderate on its own evidence; what raises it is Alma 8:26's use of Matthew 25:35 for Amulek, which makes this chapter a two-point sampling of a single chapter of Matthew. The machine proposed Luke 19:17 here, which is the same formula in the parallel parable, and the choice between them is not decidable on four words.
links.whyNot: Four common words in a formula the KJV itself uses three times, and the preposition Alma has is Luke's rather than Matthew's. If the Matthew 25:35 row at 8:26 were withdrawn, this row should be withdrawn with it.

pericopes.text: and behold, I am sent to command thee that thou return to the city of Ammonihah, and preach again unto the people of the city; yea, preach unto them.—Yea, say unto them, except they repent, the Lord God will destroy them.

links.text: Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee.

provenance.other: 'Three days' journey' occurs in exactly seven KJV verses; the one that attaches it to a city rather than to a march is Jonah 3:3, 'Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days' journey', a KJV singleton for 'an exceeding great city'. 'The second time, saying' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Jeremiah 1:13, Jeremiah 13:3 and Jonah 3:1. Alma 8 has no phrase of Jonah verbatim, which is why this is figural and kjvSpecific is 'uncertain'.
provenance.significance: The shape is Jonah's and the tell is the measurement. Alma 8:6 has him travel 'three days' journey' and arrive at a city; the KJV's one use of that distance as the measure of a city is Nineveh's. Thereafter the sequence runs point for point: a prophet sent to a great wicked city, who leaves it — Jonah by ship, Alma cast out and 'about to set my back towards this land forever' (8:24) — and is then commissioned a second time in the same words as the first, with the destruction now named. Jonah 3:1's 'the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time' is answered at Alma 8:29, 'And the word came to Alma, saying, Go'; Jonah 3:4's 'Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown' is answered at 8:16, 'except they repent, the Lord God will destroy them.' Alma even arrives, like Jonah, sick of the errand and 'weighed down with sorrow'. The suppressed correspondence is the ending. Jonah's book exists to record that Nineveh repented and was spared, and that the prophet was angry about it. Ammonihah does not repent, and is destroyed in Alma 16. The type-scene is set up so that its one available outcome is the one Jonah did not get, and the reader who knows Jonah is told, by the shape alone and before any of it happens, that this city is being given its second chance.
provenance.alternative: Jonah 1:2's 'Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it' is the first commission and equally close; the second is preferred because Alma 8:16 is explicitly a re-sending.

links.note: 'I am sent to command thee that thou return to the city of Ammonihah, and preach again unto the people of the city … except they repent, the Lord God will destroy them.' No wording of Jonah is reproduced, so this is catalogued on narrative form: the prophet sent to a great city, rejected, re-commissioned in the same terms, and given a threat of destruction to deliver. What keeps it from being a bare thematic association is Alma 8:6, where the city is reached at 'three days' journey' — the KJV's measure of Nineveh, and of no other city. The machine proposed 2 Samuel 15:34 here on 'thou return to the', which is Hushai being sent back to Absalom, and has nothing else. Compare the Jonah link already made at 1 Nephi 2:13, where 'that great city' is the borrowed phrase; there the epithet is taken and here the plot is, and Alma is a different hand.

pericopes.text: For behold, they do study at this time that they may destroy the liberty of thy people, (for thus saith the Lord,) which is contrary to the statutes, and judgments, and commandments which he hath given unto his people.

Now it came to pass that after Alma had received his message from the angel of the Lord, he returned speedily to the land of Ammonihah. And it came to pass that he entered the city by another way, yea, by the way which was on the south of the city Ammonihah.

links.text: So he went another way, and returned not by the way that he came to Bethel.

provenance.other: 'Another way' occurs in exactly four KJV verses: 1 Kings 13:10, 1 Kings 18:6, Matthew 2:12 and James 2:25. 'Come home with me, and eat bread' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 13:15; 'did eat bread in his house' occurs in exactly one, 1 Kings 13:19. Both belong to the same episode as the first.
