provenance.significance: 1 Kings 13 is the KJV's one story built entirely out of these elements: a man of God sent against a city to prophesy, forbidden to eat bread there, who leaves by 'another way'; who is then met by a local prophet saying 'Come home with me, and eat bread'; who goes back with him and 'did eat bread in his house'. Alma 8 runs the same five moves in the same order — sent against Ammonihah, hungry, entering 'by another way', met by Amulek offering food and lodging, eating bread in his house and being filled. The reversal is the whole point and it is exact. In 1 Kings the eating is the disobedience: the man of God had been charged 'Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest', and returning to eat is what a lion kills him for on the road. In Alma the eating is the obedience — he entered by another way because an angel had sent him back, and the man who feeds him is the man the angel had prepared and is about to become his fellow-witness. Where 1 Kings 13 makes hospitality the trap that destroys the prophet, Alma 8 makes it the means by which the mission is saved. That inversion is the argument for reading the borrowing as deliberate rather than accidental: an accident would not have gotten the sequence right and the moral backwards.

links.note: 'He returned speedily to the land of Ammonihah … and he entered the city by another way.' The verbal contact is one four-verse phrase; the case rests on sequence, and on the fact that the two KJV singletons of the same episode ('Come home with me, and eat bread'; 'did eat bread in his house') are matched by Alma 8:20-22 in order. Recorded at moderate for that reason — the wording will not carry it alone, and the register at 8:21 notes that 'bread and meat', a KJV singleton at Genesis 45:23, is not a contributor here. No machine candidate reached 8:18 at all.
links.whyNot: One shared phrase and a narrative shape. A prophet arriving hungry and being fed is a common enough scene in the KJV (compare 1 Kings 17:10-16, Judges 6:19) that the ordering could be coincidence; the inversion of the moral is what argues against coincidence, and inversion is not evidence a sceptic has to accept.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that as he entered the city, he was an hungered, and he saith to a man, Will ye give to an humble servant of God something to eat?

And the man saith unto him, I am a Nephite, and I know that thou art a Holy Prophet of God, for thou art the man which an angel saith in a vision, Thou shalt receive; therefore go with me into my house, and I will impart unto thee of my food; and I know that thou will be a blessing unto me and my house.
And it came to pass that the man received him into his house; and the man was called Amulek; and he brought forth bread and meat, and sat before Alma.
And it came to pass that Alma ate bread and was filled; and he blessed Amulek and his house, and he gave thanks unto God.
And after he had eat and was filled, he saith unto Amulek, I am Alma, and am the High Priest over the church of God throughout the land.

And behold, I have been called to preach the word of God among all this people, according to the spirit of revelation and prophecy; and I was in this land, and they would not reccive me, but they cast me out, and I was about to set my back towards this land forever.
But behold, I have been commanded that I should turn again and prophesy unto this people, yea, and to testify against them concerning their iniquities.
And now Amulek, because thou hast fed me and took me in, thou art blessed: for I was an hungered, for I had fasted many days.

links.text: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:

provenance.other: 'Took me in' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:35, and 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same. 'He was afterward an hungred' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 4:2, the only KJV verse joining fasting to subsequent hunger.
provenance.significance: Alma's sentence to Amulek reproduces two of Matthew 25:35's three clauses and its verdict: hungry and fed, taken in, therefore blessed. The one word that fixes the source is 'took me in', which the KJV uses in this sense once. What follows from recovering the context is the chapter's severest claim. Matthew 25:35 is spoken by the Son of Man on the throne of judgment to the sheep at his right hand, and it is glossed four verses later — 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.' So when Alma tells Amulek 'because thou hast fed me and took me in, thou art blessed', he is speaking the words of the judge about himself, and the blessing is the judge's own 'Come, ye blessed of my Father' of 25:34. The other half of the parable is what the chapter has already narrated: Ammonihah refused the hungry prophet and cast him out, which is Matthew 25:42's 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat.' Alma 16 destroys the city. The parable's two verdicts are distributed across one chapter and its sequel, the sheep in Amulek's house and the goats in the city outside it. Note also that Alma's reason for hunger — 'for I had fasted many days' — is Matthew 4:2's, the only KJV verse where a fast is the cause of hunger, and there the fast precedes a confrontation with Satan; Alma 8:9 had said that Satan 'had got great hold upon the hearts of the people'.

links.note: 'Because thou hast fed me and took me in, thou art blessed: for I was an hungered, for I had fasted many days.' Two clauses of Matthew 25:35, including its one-verse phrase 'took me in', with the parable's verdict attached; and the hunger explained in Matthew 4:2's terms. The 1830 'an hungered' modernizes the KJV's 'an hungred' but preserves the archaic construction, which no version after the KJV has. No machine candidate reached this verse or 8:19.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Alma tarried many days with Amulek, before he began to preach unto the people.
And it came to pass that the people did wax more gross in their iniquities.

And the word came to Alma, saying, Go; and also say unto my servant Amulek, Go forth and prophesy unto this people, saying: Repent ye, for thus saith the Lord: Except ye repent, I will visit this people in mine anger; yea, and I will not turn my fierce anger away.
And it came to pass that Alma went forth, and also Amulek, among the peopeople, to declare the words of God unto them; and they were filled with the Holy Ghost;

and they had power given unto them, insomuch that they could not be confined in dungeons; neither were it possible that any man could slay them; nevertheless they did not exercise their power until they were bound in bands and cast into prison. Now this was done that the Lord might show forth his power in them.

links.text: But all this was done, that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples forsook him, and fled.

provenance.other: 'This was done, that' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 1:22, 21:4 and 26:56 — all narratorial purpose clauses, and all Matthew's. 'Twelve legions of angels' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 26:53. 'Shew my power in thee' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 9:17.
provenance.significance: The borrowing is a whole argument, not a phrase. Matthew 26:53-56 is the KJV's one passage in which a man declares that overwhelming power is available to him, declines to use it, submits to arrest, and has a narrator explain the restraint in a purpose clause beginning 'all this was done, that'. Alma 8:31 does each of those four things in order: power such that no dungeon could hold them and no man could slay them, 'nevertheless they did not exercise their power', bound and cast into prison, 'Now this was done that the Lord might show forth his power in them.' The formula is Matthew's — three KJV verses have it and all three are his. The divergence is in what the purpose clause names, and it is the interesting part: Matthew's restraint is for the fulfilment of scripture, Alma's is for a demonstration of power, so the very capacity that was renounced is the thing the renunciation exists to display. The Pauline singleton behind that second half is Romans 9:17's 'that I might shew my power in thee', spoken of Pharaoh — of a man hardened, in a narrative of hardened hearts, which is what Alma 8:11 has just said of Ammonihah.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 1:22 and 21:4 have the same formula in the same author; 26:56 is preferred because only there is the clause explaining a deliberate non-use of power at an arrest.

links.note: 'They had power given unto them, insomuch that they could not be confined in dungeons … nevertheless they did not exercise their power until they were bound in bands and cast into prison. Now this was done that the Lord might show forth his power in them.' A four-word narratorial formula the KJV uses three times, all in Matthew, deployed at the one point of Alma 8 that matches its Matthean setting. The 1830 reads 'show' where the KJV would have 'shew', which is a point against KJV-specific orthography here and is recorded as such; the formula itself is unaffected. The machine did rank Matthew 26:56 at this verse, on the same run.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they went forth and began to preach and to prophesy unto the people, according to the spirit and power which the Lord had given them.

And again: I Alma, having been commanded of God that I should take Amulek and go forth and preach again unto this people, or the people which was in the city of Ammonihah.—And it came to pass as I began to preach unto them, they began to contend with me, saying:
Who art thou? Suppose ye that we shall believe the testimony of one man, although he should preach unto us that the earth should pass away?

links.text: It is also written in your law, that the testimony of two men is true.

provenance.other: 'The testimony of two men' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:17. Deuteronomy 19:15, the law John is citing, uses neither 'testimony' nor 'men': 'at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.' The Book of Mormon's noun is John's.
provenance.significance: The objection at Ammonihah is a legal one and it is stated in the KJV's terms: 'Suppose ye that we shall believe the testimony of one man?' The KJV's one verse about the testimony of two men is the verse in which Jesus answers exactly this objection, raised against him in exactly this form — the Pharisees at John 8:13 have just said 'Thou bearest record of thyself; thy record is not true.' Alma's opponents have made the Pharisees' argument. What the Book of Mormon then does with it is the finding: it concedes the point and satisfies it. Amulek has already been commanded to go forth with Alma at 8:29, and at Alma 10:12 the narrative says outright that the people were astonished 'that there was more than one witness who testified'. The law of witnesses is raised as an objection and answered by supplying the second witness, which is the same move John 8:18 makes with the Father. Note that 'testimony' is John's word and not the law's, so the Book of Mormon has the objection in its Gospel form rather than its Deuteronomic one.

links.note: 'Suppose ye that we shall believe the testimony of one man?' No clause is reproduced, so this is an echo rather than an allusion; what identifies it is that the KJV puts this rule in the form 'the testimony of two men' exactly once, and does so where the rule is being used against a solitary preacher. Compare also the crowd's opening question at 9:2, 'Who art thou?', which is John 1:19's question to John the Baptist — the figure whose cry Alma will quote at 9:25 and 9:28.
links.whyNot: The shared material is one noun and a numeral, and a hostile crowd demanding corroboration is a scene that could be written without any source. The row rests on the KJV count and on the answering move at Alma 10:12.

pericopes.text: Now they understood not the words which they spake, for they knew not that the earth should pass away.
And they sayeth also, We will not believe thy words, if thou shouldst prophesy that this great city should be destroyed in one day.
Now they knew not that God could do such marvellous works, for they were a hard hearted and a stiffnecked people.
And they sayeth, Who is God, that sendeth no more authority than one man among this people, to declare unto them the truth of such great and marvellous things?
And they stood forth to lay their hands on me; but behold, they did not. And I stood with boldness to declare unto them, yea, I did boldly testify unto them, saying:
Behold, O ye wicked and perverse generation, how have ye forgotten the tradition of your fathers; yea, how soon ye have forgotten the commandments of God.
Do ye not remember that our father Lehi was brought out of Jerusalem by the hand of God? Do ye not remember that they were all led by him through the wilderness?
And have ye forgotten so soon how many times he delivered our fathers out of the hands of their enemies, and preserved them from being destroyed, even by the hands of their own brethren?

Yea, and if it had not been for his matchless power, and his mercy, and his long suffering towards us, we should unavoidably have been cut off from the face of the earth, long before this period of time, and perhaps been consigned to a state of endless misery and wo.

Behold, now I say unto you, that he commandeth you to repent; and except ye repent, ye can in no wise inherit the kingdom of God. But behold, this is not all: he hath commanded you to repent, or he will utterly destroy you from off the face of the earth; yea, he will visit you in his anger, and in his fierce anger he will not turn away.

links.text: And that the whole land thereof is brimstone, and salt, and burning, that it is not sown, nor beareth, nor any grass groweth therein, like the overthrow of Sodom, and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath:

provenance.other: 'In his anger, and in his' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 29:23. 'Fierce anger' alone occurs in twenty KJV verses and points nowhere, which is why the excluded row at Alma 8:29 was declined and this one is not.
provenance.significance: The doubled prepositional phrase is the KJV's only instance, and its verse is the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah — which is what makes it worth recording here rather than filing with the generic anger-of-the-Lord diction. Three verses later Alma tells Ammonihah it will be 'more tolerable' for the Lamanites in the day of judgment, which is Matthew 10:15's saying about the land of Sodom and Gomorrha. So a Sodom formula and a Sodom saying arrive within four verses of each other, from opposite testaments, at a city that is destroyed in a single day in Alma 16. Deuteronomy 29:23 is also the verse the KJV uses to describe what a land looks like afterwards — brimstone and salt, not sown, no grass — which is very close to what Alma 16:10 will report of Ammonihah's site.

links.note: 'He will visit you in his anger, and in his fierce anger he will not turn away.' The one KJV verse with the doubled phrase is the Sodom overthrow, and the chapter reaches Sodom again at 9:15 by a different route. Moderate: the shared words are function words, and prophetic anger-diction is common stock — the count and the thematic convergence are the argument. The machine ranked this verse's candidate correctly, which is unusual.
links.whyNot: The run is 'in his anger, and in his', which is five function words and a common noun; the singleton status is an artifact of how few KJV verses double the preposition at all. Nothing else of Deuteronomy 29 appears.

pericopes.text: Behold, do ye not remember the words which he spake unto Lehi, saying, That inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land? And again it is said, That inasmuch as ye will not keep my commandments, ye shall be cut off from the presence of the Lord.

Now I would that ye should remember, that inasmuch as the Lamanites have not kept the commandments of God, they have been cut off from the presence of the Lord. Now we see that the word of the Lord hath been verified in this thing, and the Lamanites have been cut off from his presence, from the beginning of their transgressions in the land.

Nevertheless I say unto you, that it shall be more tolerable for them in the day of judgment, than for you, if ye remain in your sins; yea, and even more tolerable for them in this life, than for you, except ye repent,

links.text: Verily I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city.

provenance.route: Matthew 10:15 with 11:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'More tolerable for' occurs in exactly five KJV verses (Matthew 10:15, 11:22, 11:24, Mark 6:11, Luke 10:14); 'in the day of judgment, than for' occurs in exactly three (Matthew 10:15, 11:24, Mark 6:11). Alma has the prepositional form of the three — 'in the day of judgment', not Matthew 11:22's and Luke 10:14's 'at the day' — and the pronoun of Matthew 11:22, 'than for you'.
provenance.significance: The saying is fused from two of its five KJV occurrences and the fusion is legible word by word: 'in the day of judgment' comes from the Matthew 10:15 / 11:24 / Mark 6:11 form and 'than for you' from Matthew 11:22, so Alma has neither verse whole. What decides which of them is the source rather than the supplement is the setting. Matthew 10:14-15 and its Marcan parallel are the sending of the Twelve: 'whosoever shall not receive you, nor hear your words, when ye depart out of that house or city, shake off the dust of your feet … It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city.' That is the situation of Alma 8 exactly — a preacher not received, reviled, and put out of a city — and Alma 9:15 is spoken on his return to the same city. The metalepsis is the fate. What the saying threatens is what Alma 16 delivers: Ammonihah is destroyed and its site left desolate, and the KJV's comparison-class for a city that will not hear a sent preacher is Sodom.
provenance.alternative: Luke 10:12 and 10:14 carry the same saying in the sending of the Seventy but read 'at the judgment' and 'at the day', neither of which the Book of Mormon has.

links.note: 'It shall be more tolerable for them in the day of judgment, than for you, if ye remain in your sins.' Eleven consecutive shared words at the machine's best match, and the two halves come from two different verses of the same saying: Matthew's 'in the day of judgment' and Matthew 11:22's 'than for you'. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages, though it is as close to a formal quotation as anything in Alma 9. Alma repeats the comparison at 9:23 in his own words ('far more tolerable for the Lamanites than for them'), which is the formula settling into his idiom rather than a second borrowing.

pericopes.text: for there are many promises which is extended to the Lamanites: for it is because of the traditions of their fathers that causeth them to remain in their state of ignorance; therefore the Lord will be merciful unto them, and prolong their existence in the land.

And at some period of time they will be brought to believe in his word, and to know of the incorrectness of the traditions of their fathers; and many of them will be saved, for the Lord will be merciful unto all who call on his name.

But behold, I say unto you, that if ye persist in your wickedness, that your days shall not be prolonged in the land, for the Lamanites shall be sent upon you; and if ye repent not, they shall come in a time when you know not, and ye shall be visited with utter destruction; and it shall be according to the fierce anger of the Lord;

links.text: And the wild beasts of the islands shall cry in their desolate houses, and dragons in their pleasant palaces: and her time is near to come, and her days shall not be prolonged.

provenance.other: 'Shall not be prolonged' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 13:22, the closing line of the oracle against Babylon. Alma 9:16 has used the same verb in the opposite direction four verses earlier — the Lord will 'prolong their existence in the land' for the Lamanites — and the KJV's only other sense of the verb with days is Deuteronomy's blessing formula 'that thy days may be prolonged'.
provenance.significance: Alma sets the two halves of the KJV's verb against each other and gives each to a different people. The Lamanites, whose ignorance is inherited, get the Deuteronomic promise: their existence in the land is prolonged. Ammonihah gets Isaiah 13:22, which is the KJV's one sentence saying that days shall NOT be prolonged, and says it of Babylon. Recover the three verses before it and the terms are supplied for everything else Alma 9 has said to this city: Isaiah 13:19 is 'Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah', which is the same comparison Alma made at 9:15 from Matthew, and Isaiah 13:20-22 is the desolate uninhabited site that Alma 16:10-11 will report of Ammonihah's ruin. The city that boasted at 9:4 that it could not be 'destroyed in one day' is answered with the oracle against the one city in scripture whose fall is the type of all such falls.

links.note: 'If ye persist in your wickedness, that your days shall not be prolonged in the land … ye shall be visited with utter destruction.' A KJV singleton, taken from the last line of the Babylon oracle and applied to a city that had just denied it could fall. The machine did rank Isaiah 13:22 here, on the same run. The contrast with 9:16's 'prolong their existence in the land' is within the same speech and is what makes the borrowing purposeful rather than incidental.

pericopes.text: for he will not suffer you that ye shall live in your iniquities, to destroy his people. I say unto you, Nay; he would rather suffer that the Lamanites might destroy all this people which is called the people of Nephi, if it were possible that they could fall into sins and transgransgressions, after having had so much light and so much knowledge given unto them of the Lord their God;

yea, after having been such a highly favored people of the Lord; yea, after having been favored above every other nation, kindred, tongue, or people; after having had all things made known unto them, according to their desires, and their faith, and prayers, of that which has been, and which is, and which is to come;

having been visited by the spirit of God; having conversed with angels, and having been spoken unto by the voice of the Lord; and having the spirit of prophecy, and the spirit of revelation, and also many gifts: the gift of speaking with tongues, and the gift of preaching, and the gift of the Holy Ghost, and the gift of translation;

yea, and after having been delivered of God out of the land of Jerusalem, by the hand of the Lord; having been saved from famine, and from sickness, and all manner of diseases of every kind; and they having been waxed strong in battle, that they might not be destroyed; having been brought out of bondage time after time, and having been kept and preserved until now; and they have been prospered until they are rich in all manner of things.

And now behold I say unto you, that if this people, who have received so many blessings from the hand of the Lord, should transgress, contrary to the light and knowledge which they do have; I say unto you, that if this be the case; that if they should fall into transgression, that it would be far more tolerable for the Lamanites than for them.

For behold, the promises of the Lord are extended to the Lamanites, but they are not unto you, if ye transgress: for hath not the Lord expressly promised and firmly decreed, that if ye will rebel against him, that ye shall utterly be destroyed from off the face of the earth?

And now for this cause, that ye may not be destroyed, the Lord hath sent his angel to visit many of his people, declaring unto them that they must go forth and cry mightily unto this people, saying, Repent ye, for the kingdom of Heaven is nigh at hand;

links.text: But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.

provenance.other: 'Cry mightily' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:8, in the king of Nineveh's decree. The Book of Mormon redirects the object: Jonah's Ninevites cry mightily unto God, Alma's messengers cry mightily unto the people.
provenance.significance: This is the Jonah frame of Alma 8 reappearing eleven verses later, and the redirection of the object is the argument. In Jonah the crying is the city's repentance — the king's decree that man and beast cry mightily unto God, which is the act Nineveh is spared for. In Alma 9:25 it is the messengers' preaching, addressed to the city and not to God, and the thing they cry is the demand for repentance rather than repentance itself. So the KJV's one phrase for a great city's successful repentance is placed in the mouths of the men sent to ask for one, at a city that will not give it. Ammonihah is offered the sentence Nineveh spoke and does not speak it.

links.note: 'The Lord hath sent his angel to visit many of his people, declaring unto them that they must go forth and cry mightily unto this people.' A KJV singleton with its object changed. On its own two words would be too little; it is written because the chapter it belongs to is already running the Jonah type-scene argued at Alma 8:16, and because this is the one moment where Jonah's actual vocabulary surfaces. The machine proposed Acts 12:11 here, on 'the Lord hath sent his angel', which is Peter's escape from Herod and is a three-verse formula (Daniel 3:28, 6:22, Acts 12:11) with no other contact.
links.whyNot: Two words. If the Jonah reading at 8:16 is declined, this row should go with it.

links.text: And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

provenance.route: Matthew 3:2 with Luke 21:31 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'The kingdom of heaven is at hand' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all Matthew's (3:2, 4:17, 10:7). 'Nigh at hand' occurs in exactly five (Joel 2:1, Luke 21:30, 21:31, John 11:55, 19:42), and the only one attaching it to a kingdom is Luke 21:31 — 'the kingdom of God is nigh at hand.' Neither testament has 'the kingdom of heaven is nigh at hand'.
provenance.significance: Alma 9:25 reads 'Repent ye, for the kingdom of Heaven is nigh at hand', which exists in no KJV verse because it is two verses welded together: Matthew supplies the kingdom of heaven and Luke supplies 'nigh'. The weld is worth noticing because Luke 21:31 is not the Baptist's preaching at all — it is the parable of the fig tree in the Olivet discourse, where the sign that the kingdom is nigh is the imminent destruction of Jerusalem. Alma's angel is announcing the same nearness to a city about to be destroyed, and the added adverb comes from the KJV's one apocalyptic use of the phrase. Alma had used the plain Matthean form at 7:9 in a congregation he approved of; at Ammonihah, and at 9:28's fuller 'prepare ye the way of the Lord', the same preaching returns with Luke's urgency attached.

links.note: 'Repent ye, for the kingdom of Heaven is nigh at hand.' Matthew's clause with one word of Luke's fused into it, producing a sentence in no KJV verse. See Alma 7:9 for the full argument on the Baptist's preaching, where the mediation test decides against Isaiah 40:3 and for the Gospel form; at 9:28 the same speech reaches 'prepare ye the way of the Lord', which is nearer to Matthew 3:3 than 7:9's version was, since it restores the 'ye'. The machine ranked Matthew 3:2 first here, its best call in the chapter.

pericopes.text: and not many days hence, the Son of God shall come in his glory; and his glory shall be the glory of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace, equity and truth, full of patience, mercy, and long suffering, quick to hear the cries of his people, and to answer their prayers.

links.text: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

provenance.other: 'The only begotten of the Father' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:14, and 'full of grace and truth' occurs in exactly one, the same. John's other formulations are 'his only begotten Son' (3:16) and 'the only begotten Son' (1:18, 3:18); the genitive with 'of the Father' is unique to the prologue. 'Shall come in his glory' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:31.
provenance.significance: Alma reproduces John 1:14's parenthesis almost entire — his glory, the glory of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth — and inserts one word into the KJV's fixed pair: 'full of grace, EQUITY and truth'. A third term dropped into a two-term formula is the most visible kind of alteration a borrower can make, and the term chosen is forensic. The clause that follows is the reason: 'full of patience, mercy, and long suffering, quick to hear the cries of his people', which is the Exodus 34:6 formula ('merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth') laid alongside John's. So the verse holds the two great KJV descriptions of divine character, the Sinai proclamation and the Johannine prologue, in one sentence, with equity added to join them. And the frame around all of it is Matthew's: 'the Son of God shall come in his glory' is the KJV's one occurrence of that clause, at Matthew 25:31, the opening of the sheep-and-goats judgment. That makes three separate uses of Matthew 25 in two chapters — the faithful servant at Alma 8:15, the hungry stranger at 8:26, the Son of Man on the throne here — and the third supplies the judge whose sentence the first two anticipate.

links.note: 'His glory shall be the glory of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace, equity and truth, full of patience, mercy, and long suffering.' Two KJV singletons from one verse of John's prologue, in John's order, with 'equity' inserted into 'full of grace and truth' and the Exodus 34:6 attribute-list appended. The machine scored John 1:14 at rarity 6.50 with a ten-word run, its highest score anywhere in these three chapters. Frederick's co-occurrence index (data/frederick-refs.json, from tools/parse-frederick.py) places Alma 9:26 within 1,500 characters of his discussion of John 1:14 and 1:16 — that index records proximity inside his argument about the Gospel of John, not a proposed source, and he offers no source list.
bibliography: Frederick 2016 — his index of co-occurrence (data/frederick-refs.json, from tools/parse-frederick.py) places Alma 9:26 within 1500 characters of his discussion of John 1:14 and John 1:16, alongside 2 John 1:3 and Exodus 34:6; that index records proximity in his argument about the Gospel of John, not a proposed source.

pericopes.text: And behold, he cometh to redeem those who will be baptized unto repentance, through faith on his name;

therefore prepare ye the way of the Lord, for the time is it hand that every man shall reap a reward of their works, according to that which they have been: if they have been righteous, they shall reap the salvation of their souls, according to the power and deliverance of Jesus Christ; and if they have been evil, they shall reap the damnation of their souls, according to the power and captivation of the Devil.—
Now behold, this is the voice of the angel, crying unto the people.

And now my beloved brethren, for ye are my brethren, and ye had ought to be beloved, and ye had ought to bring forth works which is mete for repentance, seeing that your hearts have been grossly hardened against the word of God, and seeing that ye are a lost and a fallen people.

links.text: But shewed first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the coasts of Judaea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance.

provenance.other: 'Works meet for repentance' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:20. 'Fruits meet for repentance' occurs in exactly one, Matthew 3:8. Luke 3:8 renders the Baptist's saying differently again, 'fruits worthy of repentance'. Alma 9:30 has 'works which is mete for repentance' — Paul's noun, not the Baptist's.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has both KJV forms of this phrase and puts each where it belongs. At Alma 13:13 it appears as 'bring forth fruit mete for repentance', which is Matthew 3:8's noun and Matthew 3:8's verb; here at 9:30 it is 'works', which is Acts 26:20's and belongs to Paul's account of his own preaching before Agrippa. That the two occurrences differ in exactly the one word that distinguishes their KJV sources is strong evidence that neither is a general memory of a floating phrase. What Acts 26:20 adds when recovered is the setting: Paul is on trial, defending a mission to people who tried to kill him, describing what he preached to them. Alma 9:30 is the last sentence before the crowd seeks to lay hands on him and cast him into prison.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 3:8's 'fruits meet for repentance' is equally rare and is the more familiar phrase, but its noun is 'fruits'; the Book of Mormon uses that form elsewhere and not here.

links.note: 'Ye had ought to bring forth works which is mete for repentance.' The KJV has this phrase twice, once with 'fruits' and once with 'works', and Alma 9:30 has the second. The verb, though, is the first's — 'bring forth' is Matthew 3:8's and not Acts 26:20's 'do' — so the sentence carries Matthew's imperative around Paul's noun. The 1830 spells 'mete', which the 1920 corrects to 'meet'; the first edition's spelling is a homophone error and does not affect the identification. No machine candidate reached this verse.

pericopes.text: Now it came to pass that when I, Alma, had spoken these words, behold, the people were wroth with me, because I said unto them that they was a hardhearted and a stiffnecked people;

links.text: When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth.

provenance.other: No phrase of Acts 7:54 is reproduced. The chapter's one hard verbal anchor to Acts 7 is at Alma 8:13, where 'cast him out of the city' is a KJV singleton at Acts 7:58. 'Stiffnecked people', which Alma 9:5 and 9:31 both use, occurs in exactly six KJV verses, all of them Exodus or Deuteronomy and none of them Acts — Acts 7:51's 'Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart' has the adjective without the noun.
provenance.significance: Alma 9 has the shape of Stephen's speech and it is worth saying so, provided the wording is not oversold. Stephen answers a charge by reciting the deliverances God worked for the fathers — the call out of a foreign land, the leading through the wilderness, the repeated rescues — and turns the recital on his hearers as an accusation that they have resisted what their fathers received. Alma 9:8-11 does exactly that with Lehi: brought out of Jerusalem by the hand of God, led through the wilderness, delivered out of the hands of their enemies many times, preserved by God's matchless power. Both speeches then close on the same word: Stephen calls his hearers stiffnecked, Alma reports at 9:31 that they were wroth 'because I said unto them that they was a hardhearted and a stiffnecked people'. And both end the same way, with the crowd enraged and laying hands on the speaker. The one difference is the one that matters: Acts 7:58 casts Stephen out of the city and stones him, and Alma 9:33 says 'the Lord did not suffer them that they should take me at that time.' The type-scene is set up and then interrupted — which is what the earlier half of it at Alma 8:13, where Alma is reviled, spat upon and cast out but not stoned, had already done.

links.note: 'The people were wroth with me, because I said unto them that they was a hardhearted and a stiffnecked people … and sought to lay their hands upon me, that they might cast me into prison.' Catalogued as figural: the verbal contact with Acts 7 in this chapter is nil, and 'stiffnecked people' is Exodus's phrase and not Luke's. The case is the shape — a recital of the fathers' deliverances turned into an indictment, ending in a crowd laying hands on the speaker — together with the KJV singleton at Alma 8:13 that puts Acts 7 in the chapter before. Recorded at moderate, and the whyNot names what would withdraw it.
links.whyNot: There is no shared wording at all, and a prophet rehearsing sacred history to a hostile audience is a form the Hebrew Bible supplies many times over (Joshua 24, Nehemiah 9, Psalm 78) without any need for Acts. If the Acts 7:58 link at Alma 8:13 were withdrawn, this row would have nothing left holding it and should be withdrawn too.

pericopes.text: and also because I said unto them that they were a lost and a fallen people, they was angry with me, and sought to lay their hands upon me, that they might cast me into prison;
but it came to pass that the Lord did not suffer them that they should take me at that time and cast me into prison.
And it came to pass that Amulek went and stood forth, and began to preach unto them also. And now the words of Amulek are not all written; nevertheless a part of his words are written in this book.
Now these are the words which Amulek preached unto the people which was in the land of Ammonihah, saying:

I am Amulek; I am the son of Giddonah, who was the son of Ishmael, who was a descendant of Aminadi: and it was that same Aminadi which interpreted the writing which was upon the wall of the temple, which was written by the finger of God.—

provenance.route: Daniel 5:5-28 + Exodus 31:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV contains exactly one episode of writing appearing on a wall and requiring an interpreter: Daniel 5. “With the finger of God” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Exodus 31:18, Deuteronomy 9:10 and Luke 11:20; the Book of Mormon reads “by the finger of God”.
provenance.significance: Amulek's credential is a great-grandfather who read writing on a temple wall, and the only such writing in the English Bible is MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN — a sentence of destruction on a city whose ruler has been weighed and found wanting, delivered in a hall where the vessels of the temple are being drunk from. Recover that and the genealogy stops being decorative: Amulek introduces himself to Ammonihah as the descendant of a man who once announced exactly the doom Amulek is about to announce, and by the end of the chapter he has announced it (10:22-23). The finger of God is the second half of the compound. In Exodus 31:18 and Deuteronomy 9:10 the phrase is used of the tables of the law, written on stone; in Daniel the writing on the plaister is written by the fingers of a man's hand. The Book of Mormon fuses them, so that the wall-writing carries the authority of Sinai — which is the point Amulek needs, since what he will shortly be accused of is speaking against the law.
provenance.alternative: Exodus 8:19's 'This is the finger of God' is the magicians' confession before Pharaoh, and Luke 11:20 makes the finger of God the agency of exorcism; neither supplies the participle 'written'.

links.note: 'That same Aminadi which interpreted the writing which was upon the wall of the temple, which was written by the finger of God.' No single phrase is long enough to carry the link alone — 'upon the wall' occurs in twelve KJV verses — but the scene is a KJV singleton at the level of event, and the second clause imports the Sinai formula. Daniel returns twice more in this chapter, at 'the holy ones of God' in 10:17 (Daniel 4:17) and 'stay his hand' in 10:23 (Daniel 4:35), both KJV singletons and both from the two Daniel chapters about a king's court under sentence. Three contacts with Daniel 4-5 in one discourse is the pattern, not the individual row.
links.text: In the same hour came forth fingers of a man’s hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king’s palace: and the king saw the part of the hand that wrote.

pericopes.text: And Aminadi was a descendant of Nephi, who was the son of Lehi, who came out of the land of Jerusalem, who was a descendant of Manasseh, who was the son of Joseph, which was sold into Egypt by the hands of his brethren.

provenance.other: “Sold into Egypt” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 45:4. Acts 7:9 has the same three words in a different order, 'sold Joseph into Egypt', and Genesis 37:28 says only that the brothers 'sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites'.
provenance.significance: mediation-check.py returns divergences in both directions here, because the two candidates share almost nothing but the three words at issue, and the tool is reading their non-overlap as evidence. The word order decides it: Alma 10:3 has 'sold into Egypt' contiguous, which is Genesis 45:4's sequence and not Acts 7:9's. What Alma adds — 'by the hands of his brethren' — is what Genesis 45:4 supplies from its setting rather than its wording, since the sentence is Joseph's own accusation spoken to those brothers.
provenance.alternative: Acts 7:9 attributes the sale to 'the patriarchs, moved with envy'; nothing of that phrasing survives here.

links.note: A genealogical formula, but the formula is quoting. The Book of Mormon's Joseph-of-Egypt material is dense enough elsewhere that a stock phrase here could be its own, so this is held at moderate: the case is the contiguous three-word run and its uniqueness, not the surrounding sentence.
links.text: And Joseph said unto his brethren, Come near to me, I pray you. And they came near. And he said, I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt.

pericopes.text: And behold, I am also a man of no small reputation among all those who know me; yea, and behold, I have many kindreds and friends, and I have also acquired much riches by the hand of my industry;

provenance.route: Acts (the 'no small' litotes) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The construction “no small” occurs in exactly five KJV verses and all five are in Acts: 12:18, 15:2, 19:23, 19:24, 27:20. It renders a Greek litotes that Luke is fond of and no other biblical writer uses in the KJV's English.
provenance.significance: This is not a borrowed phrase so much as a borrowed mannerism, and it is the entry point to what governs the whole chapter. Amulek introduces himself with a Lucan idiom; the men who come to trap him are 'lawyers', a word confined in the KJV to Luke; he perceives their thoughts in Luke's words (10:17); Satan is asked why he has taken hold of their hearts in the words of Acts 5:3 (10:25); their learning is described in the words used of Moses in Acts 7:22 (10:15); and the crowd finally calls him what Paul calls Elymas in Acts 13:10 (10:28). Alma 10 is a Luke-Acts chapter, and the litotes in its fourth verse is the first sign of it.
provenance.alternative: 'No small gain' at Acts 19:24 is the closest of the five to Amulek's own situation — a man of means whose income is threatened by preaching — and 10:32 says of his opponents that their object 'were to get gain'.

links.note: 'I am also a man of no small reputation among all those who know me.' Taken alone this would be an unremarkable English understatement and not worth a row. It earns one because the construction is a KJV property of exactly one book, and because that book supplies five further contacts in the same chapter. Held at moderate and taken openly as a risk: a nineteenth-century writer could reach 'no small reputation' without Acts.
links.whyNot: 'No small' was ordinary literary English by 1830 and needs no biblical source; the argument depends entirely on the density of Luke-Acts elsewhere in the chapter, which is evidence about the chapter and not about this verse.
links.text: For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen;

pericopes.text: nevertheless, after all this, I never have known much of the ways of the Lord, and his mysteries and marvellous power. I said I never had known much of these things; but behold, I mistake, for I have seen much of his mysteries and his marvellous power; yea, even in the preservation of the lives of this people;

nevertheless, I did harden my heart, for I was called many times, and I would not hear; therefore I knew concerning these things, yet I would not know; therefore I went on rebelling against God, in the wickedness of my heart, even until the fourth day of this seventh month, which is in the tenth year of the reign of our Judges.

provenance.other: “I would not hear” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Zechariah 7:13; the third-person 'would not hear' occurs in fourteen.
provenance.significance: Zechariah 7:13 is built on a reciprocity: 'as he cried, and they would not hear; so they cried, and I would not hear, saith the LORD of hosts.' The first-person form of the phrase is God's, and it is God's refusal that answers the people's. Amulek takes the divine half of the sentence and says it of himself — 'I was called many times, and I would not hear' — which puts his own past on the side of the verse where the LORD stands, and is precisely the confession the chapter needs him to make before he can accuse Ammonihah of the same thing at 10:25. The reciprocity is then completed at 10:22-23, where the Lord's answering refusal takes Jeremiah's form.

links.note: Three words, but the first-person form is a KJV singleton and its setting is the same one Amulek is describing: repeated prophetic calling met with refusal, and destruction following. Moderate rather than high because 'I would not hear' is a sentence anyone might write, and the machine stream, which ranked it, cannot tell a rare string from a rare thought.
links.text: Therefore it is come to pass, that as he cried, and they would not hear; so they cried, and I would not hear, saith the LORD of hosts:

pericopes.text: As I was a journeying to see a very near kindred, behold an angel of the Lord appeared unto me, and said, Amulek, return to thine own house, for thou shalt feed a prophet of the Lord; yea, a holy man, which art a chosen man of God; for he hath fasted many days because of the sins of this people, and he is an hungered, and thou shall receive him into thy house and feed him, and he shall bless thee and thy house; and the blessing of the Lord shall rest upon thee and thy house.

provenance.route: 2 Kings 4:8-17 (with 1 Kings 17:9-16) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “An holy man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Kings 4:9, where it is the Shunammite's word for Elisha; the fuller “holy man of God” likewise occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Alma 10:7 and 10:9 use it three times between them.
provenance.significance: The KJV has one scene in which a householder recognises a passing prophet as a holy man, makes room for him, feeds him, and is rewarded with a blessing on the house — 2 Kings 4:8-17, the Shunammite. It has a second, at Zarephath, where a stranger is commanded from heaven to sustain a hungry prophet and her house is provided for. Alma 10:7-11 is both at once, with the angel doing openly what the Shunammite works out for herself: 'thou shalt feed a prophet of the Lord; yea, a holy man'. What follows in 2 Kings 4 is a promised child, and in 1 Kings 17 a raised one; what follows in Alma is Amulek's house and kindred blessed (10:11) and, in chapter 14, burned. The type-scene is set up exactly and then broken, which is the reading the link makes available.
provenance.alternative: 'He hath fasted many days … and he is an hungered' takes its second half from Matthew 4:2, the only KJV verse that joins fasting to being 'an hungred' as consequence; 'an hungred' by itself occurs in nine.

links.note: Three uses of a KJV singleton in five verses, inside the one biblical scene that has the same shape. Held at high rather than certain because the phrase is short and the Book of Mormon has independent reason to call a prophet holy; the argument rests on the scene as much as the words, and 10:9's redundant repetition ('He is a holy man; wherefore I know he is a holy man') suggests the phrase is being handled as a formula received rather than a description composed.
links.text: And she said unto her husband, Behold now, I perceive that this is an holy man of God, which passeth by us continually.

provenance.other: “Return to thine own house” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 8:39; the shorter 'to thine own house' occurs in four.
provenance.significance: The angel's command to Amulek is five words of Luke verbatim, and Luke 8:39 is Jesus dismissing the healed Gerasene: 'Return to thine own house, and shew how great things God hath done unto thee.' The Book of Mormon has been to this episode before — 1 Nephi 7:11's 'how great things the Lord hath done for us' is the Markan form of the same sentence, Mark 5:19, and is invisible in editions after 1920, which changed 'how' to 'what'. So the first half of the dismissal was taken in 1 Nephi and the second half is taken here, from the other evangelist. What the borrowing does to Amulek is worth stating: the man sent home to testify in Luke is the man who has just been delivered from a legion of devils, and Amulek is sent home to feed a prophet — but he will be told, twenty-one verses later, that he is himself 'a child of the Devil' (10:28). The verse that commissions him is a verse about someone the devils have left.

links.note: A five-word KJV singleton reproduced exactly, in the mouth of an angel. The link is placed here rather than at 1 Nephi 7:11 because that row takes Mark's half of the saying and this one takes Luke's; the two together are the same Gospel scene entering the Book of Mormon twice, in different books and different hands.
links.text: Return to thine own house, and shew how great things God hath done unto thee. And he went his way, and published throughout the whole city how great things Jesus had done unto him.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I obeyed the voice of the angel, and returned towards my house. And as I was a going thither, I found the man which the angel said unto me, Thou shalt receive into thy house; and behold it was this same man which hath been speaking unto you concerning the things of God.—
And the angel said unto me, He is a holy man; wherefore I know he is a holy man, because it was said by an angel of God.

And again: I know that the things whereof he hath testified are true; for behold, I say unto you, that as the Lord liveth, even so he hath sent his angel to make these things manifest unto me; and this he hath done while this Alma hath dwelt at my house;

for behold, he hath blessed mine house, he hath blessed me, and my women, and my children, and my father, and my kinsfolks; yea, even all my kindred hath he blessed, and the blessing of the Lord hath rested upon us according to the words which he spake.

And now when Amulek had spoken these words, the people began to be astonished, seeing there was more than one witness which testified of the things whereof they were accused, and also of the things which was to come, according to the spirit of prophecy which was in them;

provenance.other: “At the mouth of two” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 17:6 and 19:15; both are the rule that a matter is established only by two witnesses, and the rule is quoted in the New Testament at Matthew 18:16 and 2 Corinthians 13:1.
provenance.significance: 'The people began to be astonished, seeing there was more than one witness.' The astonishment is legal, not devotional: what has changed is that Alma's testimony is now corroborated, and under Deuteronomy 19:15 a matter with two witnesses is established. That is why the next verse turns to lawyers — the crowd has just conceded the evidentiary point and the professionals move to attack the witnesses instead, which is what Mark 14:55 says the council did. The chapter is running a trial, and this verse is where the burden shifts.

links.note: No verbal contact worth counting; the link is to a rule rather than to a sentence, and it is recorded because the verse is unintelligible without it. Moderate, and kjvSpecific 'uncertain' accordingly — no English version's particular wording is in view.
links.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.

provenance.other: “Spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 19:10.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the phrase turns out to be a definition: 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.' Alma 10:12 says the two men testified 'according to the spirit of prophecy which was in them', and what they had been testifying to, from 9:26 onward, is the coming of the Son of God. The KJV's one use of the phrase supplies exactly the equation the chapter needs — that prophecy is testimony of Jesus — and it comes from the verse in which an angel refuses worship and redirects it, which is also what Amulek's angel does not have to do, because Amulek's account of him is an account of a messenger who commands and departs.
provenance.alternative: The machine proposed Romans 1:4's 'according to the spirit of holiness' for the shared four-word run; that phrase belongs to a christological formula about the resurrection and has nothing to do with witnesses.

links.note: Three words, one KJV verse, and the borrowing carries its source's definition with it. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold by a wide margin and not one of his passages; the case is the absolute rarity plus the fact that the phrase is doing in Alma 10:12 precisely what Revelation 19:10 says it means.
links.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

pericopes.text: nevertheless, there were some among them which thought to question them, that by their cunning devices they might catch them in their words, that they might find witness against them, that they might deliver them to the Judges, that they might be judged according to the law, and that they might be slain or cast into prison, according to the crime which they could make appear, or witness against them.

provenance.route: Mark 12:13 / Luke 20:20 / Matthew 5:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Catch him in his words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 12:13. “Deliver him unto the” occurs in exactly two, Psalm 41:2 and Luke 20:20; Luke 20:20's is the same entrapment scene. “Sought for witness against” occurs in exactly one, Mark 14:55.
provenance.significance: Four sentences of the Gospels' entrapment machinery are fused into one, in order. Men are sent 'that they might catch them in their words' — Mark 12:13, the Pharisees and Herodians sent to catch Jesus. 'That they might find witness against them' — Mark 14:55, the council seeking witness against Jesus to put him to death, and finding none. 'That they might deliver them to the Judges' — Luke 20:20, spies feigning themselves just men so that they might deliver him to the governor's authority. 'That they might be slain or cast into prison' — Matthew 5:25's chain, where the adversary delivers thee to the judge and the judge to the officer and thou art cast into prison. Recover all four and the verse says something the Book of Mormon does not say in its own voice: the trial of Alma and Amulek at Ammonihah is being narrated in the vocabulary of the trial of Jesus, and the reader who knows the source knows what the outcome will be four chapters before chapter 14 reaches it. The lawyers even feign the part Luke gives them: 10:24 has the crowd defend 'our wise Lawyers, which we have selected' as men who administer a law that 'is just'.
provenance.alternative: The n-gram stream's top proposal here was 1 Peter 4:6, on a seven-word run of 'that they might be judged according to'; that verse is about the dead hearing the gospel and shares only the passive construction.

links.note: Alma 10:13 has 'catch them in their words' where Mark has 'catch him in his words' — the pronouns are what the new setting requires, since two men are being trapped and not one. Held at high rather than certain because no single run exceeds five words and because the four sources are being combined rather than quoted; but each of the three named phrases is a KJV singleton or near-singleton, and all four come from the same handful of chapters.
links.text: And they send unto him certain of the Pharisees and of the Herodians, to catch him in his words.

pericopes.text: Now it was those men which sought to destroy them, which were Lawyers, which were hired or appointed by the people to administer the law at their times of trials, or at the trials of the crimes of the people, before the Judges.
Now these Lawyers were learned in all the arts and cunning of the people; and this was to enable them that they might be skilful in their profession.

provenance.other: “Learned in all the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:22.
provenance.significance: 'These Lawyers were learned in all the arts and cunning of the people.' The construction exists once in the English Bible, in Stephen's account of Moses — 'And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds' — and it is there a commendation, the education that equips a deliverer. Alma 10:15 keeps the frame and swaps the noun: not wisdom but 'arts and cunning', not Egypt but 'the people'. The swap is the argument. And the source is worth naming for a second reason: Acts 7 is the speech that gets Stephen killed by a council for speaking against the law and the holy place, which is the accusation the crowd brings against Amulek thirteen verses later ('he hath spoken against our law', 10:28) and the fate Ammonihah has in view.
provenance.alternative: Daniel 1:4's youths 'skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge' shares 'cunning' and the sense of trained expertise, but not the construction; and the KJV's 'cunning' there is the innocent one.

links.note: Four words and a substitution. The phrase is a KJV singleton, the substituted noun inverts its sense, and the chapter is already running on Luke-Acts. Note that 10:15's next clause, 'that they might be skilful in their profession', is the second half of Acts 7:22's own doublet ('mighty in words and in deeds') recast as professional competence.
links.text: And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they began to question Amulek, that thereby they might make him cross his words, or contradict the words which he should speak.

Now they knew not that Amulek could know of their designs. But it came to pass as they began to question him, he perceived their thoughts, and he saith unto them, O ye wicked and perverse generation; ye Lawyers and hypocrites; for ye are laying the foundations of the Devil; for ye are laying traps and snares to catch the holy ones of God;

provenance.route: Luke 5:22 / Luke 20:23 / Luke 11:45-52 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Perceived their thoughts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 5:22. “He perceived their” occurs in exactly one, Luke 20:23 — 'he perceived their craftiness'. 'Perverse generation' occurs in exactly two, Matthew 17:17 and Luke 9:41, both 'O faithless and perverse generation'; 'lawyers' occurs in five, all of them in Luke.
provenance.significance: Alma 10:16-17 stages Luke 20:20-23 twice over. Questioners approach to take hold of a man's words; the man perceives what is behind the question; he answers with a counter-question and an accusation. The Book of Mormon takes its verb from Luke 5:22, where Jesus perceives thoughts, and its situation from Luke 20:23, where he perceives craftiness — and then addresses the questioners as 'ye Lawyers and hypocrites', which is Luke 11 exactly, the one chapter of the Bible where woes are pronounced on lawyers as a class ('Woe unto you also, ye lawyers!', 11:46, 52). Amulek's opening vocative, 'O ye wicked and perverse generation', is the Gospel vocative with one adjective changed: the KJV's is 'O faithless and perverse generation', and swapping faithless for wicked converts a complaint about unbelief into a charge of guilt, which is what a trial needs.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 32:5's 'a perverse and crooked generation' and Philippians 2:15's 'crooked and perverse nation' are the other candidates for the vocative; neither has the initial 'O' or the direct address.

links.note: Two KJV singletons in one clause, both from Luke, both from the same kind of scene, and a Gospel vocative reproduced with a single substitution. The chapter's lawyers are Luke's lawyers — the word belongs to no other biblical book in the KJV — so the borrowing here is of a whole cast rather than a phrase.
links.text: But when Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answering said unto them, What reason ye in your hearts?

provenance.route: Joshua 23:13 + Daniel 4:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Traps” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 23:13, where it is paired with 'snares' — 'they shall be snares and traps unto you'. “Holy ones” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 4:17.
provenance.significance: 'Ye are laying traps and snares to catch the holy ones of God.' Both halves of the sentence are KJV singletons and they come from opposite ends of the canon. Joshua 23:13 is Joshua's farewell warning that unexpelled nations will become 'snares and traps unto you … until ye perish from off this good land which the LORD your God hath given you' — which is what Amulek says next, 'even to the utter destruction of this people' (10:18). The Book of Mormon has used this verse before, at 1 Nephi 2:24 and 2 Nephi 5:25, for its other image, the scourge; here it takes the traps and reverses the direction — in Joshua the trap is what a tolerated enemy becomes to Israel, and in Alma it is what Israel's own lawyers set for the prophets. Daniel 4:17's 'holy ones' are the heavenly watchers who decree a king's humbling, so the men being trapped are named with the word for the beings who pass sentence on a court.
provenance.alternative: 'Snares' alone occurs in fifteen KJV verses, most of them Psalms and Proverbs, and could not identify a source; the pairing with 'traps' is what makes Joshua 23:13 decisive.

links.note: Held at moderate rather than high because the two singletons are one word each and the sentence could be built from the general biblical stock of snare-imagery. The case is that both words are rare, that they arrive together, and that Joshua 23:13 supplies not only the pair but the destruction-from-off-the-land clause that Alma 10:18 completes.
links.text: Know for a certainty that the LORD your God will no more drive out any of these nations from before you; but they shall be snares and traps unto you, and scourges in your sides, and thorns in your eyes, until ye perish from off this good land which the LORD your God hath given you.

pericopes.text: ye are laying plans to pervert the ways of the righteous, and to bring down the wrath of God upon your heads, even to the utter destruction of this people;

provenance.other: “Pervert the ways” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 17:23. 'To pervert the' occurs in exactly two, Proverbs 17:23 and Acts 13:10 ('to pervert the right ways of the Lord').
provenance.significance: Proverbs 17:23 is a verse about judicial corruption specifically: 'A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment.' Alma 10:18 accuses the lawyers of 'laying plans to pervert the ways of the righteous', and Alma 10:32 supplies the gift out of the bosom — 'the object of these Lawyers were to get gain; and they got gain according to their employ.' The source and the charge fit each other so exactly that the substitution of 'the righteous' for 'judgment' reads as deliberate: the object of the perversion has moved from the process to the persons, which is what happens when a legal system is turned against witnesses. The chapter's other 'pervert' verse, Acts 13:10, is the one whose 'child of the devil' the crowd throws back at Amulek in 10:28, and whose 'pervert the right ways of the Lord' this catalogue has already adjudicated at 1 Nephi 13:27.

links.note: Four words from the KJV's only 'pervert the ways', and the source is the one proverb about bribed judges — in a chapter whose complaint is that judges and lawyers are paid by the case. The second half of the verse, 'to bring down the wrath of God upon your heads', has no single source; 'the wrath of God' is distributed across both testaments.
links.text: A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment.

pericopes.text: yea, well did Mosiah say, who was our last king, when he was about to deliver up the kingdom, having no one to confer it upon, causing that this people should be governed by their own voices; yea, well did he say, that if the time should come that the voice of this people should choose iniquity; that is, if the time should come that this people should fall into transgression, they would be ripe for destruction.

provenance.other: “Voice of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:7, where it is God's word to Samuel about Israel's demand for a king. 'The voice of the people' is the phrase 1 Samuel 8:7 puts in God's mouth when Israel demands a king, and it is adjudicated in this catalogue at Mosiah 7:9 and again at Mosiah 29:2.
provenance.significance: This is the clearest case of `OT-via-earlier-BoM` the catalogue has met so far, because the verse says so itself: 'yea, well did Mosiah say, who was our last king … yea, well did he say, that if the time should come that the voice of this people should choose iniquity … they would be ripe for destruction.' The proximate text is Mosiah 29:27, whose wording Amulek reproduces with one substitution ('this people' for 'the people'), and Mosiah 29 is itself the chapter that abolishes kingship using the phrase 1 Samuel 8 coined to describe its establishment. So the biblical source reaches Alma 10 at two removes, and the citation formula is explicit at the second. What Amulek adds is 'ripe for destruction', which is in no KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own idiom.
provenance.alternative: 1 Samuel 8:19's 'Nay; but we will have a king over us' stands behind Mosiah 29:5 in this catalogue; nothing of it is present here.

links.note: Recorded because a reader of Alma 10:19 should be sent to the biblical text under it, and because the mediation is the finding: the Book of Mormon is quoting itself quoting Samuel, and it names the intermediate step out loud. The 1830 reads 'our last king' where the 1920 reads 'the last king'; the possessive is Amulek claiming the Nephite constitution as his own, which is his defence at 10:26 — he has spoken 'in favor of your law, to your condemnation'.
links.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

pericopes.text: And now I say unto you, that well doth the Lord judge of your iniquities; well doth he cry unto this people, by the voice of his angels, Repent ye, repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.

provenance.other: “The kingdom of heaven is at hand” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 3:2, 4:17 and 10:7, and the imperative 'Repent ye' precedes it only at 3:2. Mark 1:15 has 'the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye', with the clauses reversed and the noun changed.
provenance.significance: The whole of John the Baptist's preaching, reproduced word for word and attributed to angels. The choice among the three candidates is decided by 'Repent ye': Matthew 4:17 has the bare 'Repent', Matthew 10:7 has no imperative at all, and Mark 1:15 has 'the kingdom of God'. Alma 10:20 reads 'Repent ye, repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand', which is Matthew 3:2's exact clause with the imperative doubled — and doubling it is the one thing the Book of Mormon adds, in a verse that has just twice said 'well doth he cry'. The metalepsis is in who is speaking. Matthew 3:2 belongs to the voice crying in the wilderness before a ministry begins; Alma 10:20 gives it to 'the voice of his angels' crying to a city about to be destroyed, so the sentence that in Matthew opens the gospel here closes a probation.
provenance.alternative: Mark 1:15 supplies 'repent ye' in the same sentence as a kingdom at hand, but its kingdom is God's, not heaven's.

links.note: Nine consecutive words of the KJV, from a verse identifiable by a single word of difference from its nearest neighbours. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six quotations, which is worth saying because the reproduction is otherwise complete. The 1830 capitalizes 'Kingdom of Heaven'.
links.text: And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

pericopes.text: Yea, well doth he cry, by the voice of his angels, that I will come down among my people, with equity and justice in my hands.

Yea, and I say unto you, that if it were not for the prayers of the righteous, which are now in the land, that ye would even now be visited with utter destruction; yet it would not be by flood, as were the people in the days of Noah, but it would be by famine, and by pestilence, and the sword.

provenance.route: Genesis 6-7 → KJV New Testament ('the days of Noah/Noe') → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Days of Noah” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 9:29 and 1 Peter 3:20. Genesis 9:29's is a lifespan ('all the days of Noah were nine hundred and fifty years'); 1 Peter 3:20's is the pre-flood generation, which is Alma's sense. The Gospels use the same typological formula but spell the name Noe (Matthew 24:37, Luke 17:26).
provenance.significance: Genesis never calls the flood generation 'the days of Noah'; that designation is a New Testament coinage, and it is always typological — the days of Noah are invoked to say what the days of a coming judgment will be like. Alma 10:22 uses it in exactly that way, as the measure against which a threatened destruction is calibrated, and it uses the one spelling of the name that belongs to the one New Testament verse outside the Gospels. So the flood reaches Alma 10 in the form the epistles gave it rather than in Genesis's own words, and mediation is recorded as OT-via-NT for that reason. mediation-check.py returns divergences in both directions between Genesis 7:23 and Matthew 24:38, which is a real result and not a bug: the verse has the Gospels' 'flood' and 'days that were before' and Genesis's 'earth', because it is summarising a story it is not quoting.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 54:9's 'the waters of Noah' is the other prophetic use, and it promises that the flood will not return — which is, oddly, the point Amulek is making, that this destruction 'would not be by flood'. Nothing of Isaiah's wording is present.

links.note: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 6:5-8 at this verse, and that is where the story is; the wording, such as it is, is the New Testament's. Held at moderate because two words are a thin basis, and recorded chiefly for the mediation finding. Amulek's clause 'it would not be by flood' presupposes Genesis 9:11's covenant without quoting it.
links.text: Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.

provenance.route: Jeremiah's triad (sword, famine, pestilence) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “By the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, five of them in Jeremiah and one in Ezekiel; the triad in some order runs through at least fifteen. It is Jeremiah's fixed formula for the destruction of Jerusalem and belongs to no other biblical writer in that form.
provenance.significance: The formula is not merely borrowed, it is inverted: Jeremiah's order is always sword-famine-pestilence and Alma's is 'by famine, and by pestilence, and the sword', twice (10:22, 10:23). Putting the sword last makes it the climax rather than the first stroke, which is what Ammonihah's end will actually be — not a siege but an army (Alma 16:2-3). And the setting is Jeremiah's exactly: a prophet in a doomed city telling its inhabitants which of three deaths awaits them, while the professionals of that city arrange his imprisonment. Jeremiah 38:2, one of the six, is spoken immediately before Jeremiah is let down into the dungeon; Alma 10:13 has already named prison as the lawyers' object.
provenance.alternative: Ezekiel 14:21's four sore judgments add 'the noisome beast' and are not in view.

links.note: No one occurrence of the triad can be singled out, which is why rarity is scored 3 and the source is given as Jeremiah 21:9 with the parallel verses composited rather than as a claim about one of them. The finding is the formula and its reversal. This is the Jerusalem-prophet register the Book of Mormon has used since 1 Nephi 1, redeployed for a Nephite city.
links.text: He that abideth in this city shall die by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence: but he that goeth out, and falleth to the Chaldeans that besiege you, he shall live, and his life shall be unto him for a prey.

pericopes.text: But it is by the prayers of the righteous that ye are spared; now therefore if ye will cast out the righteous from among you, then will not the Lord stay his hand, but in his fierce anger he will come out against you; then ye shall be smitten by famine, and by pestilence, and by the sword; and the time is soon at hand, except ye repent.

provenance.other: “Stay his hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 4:35, of God — 'none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?' “Except ye repent” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 13:3 and Luke 13:5, which are the same sentence twice.
provenance.significance: The collocation is a singleton and its one occurrence is about the same hand, but the grammar has been turned around: in Daniel nobody is able to stay God's hand, and in Alma God declines to stay it himself. That is not a misunderstanding — it is the same doctrine of unopposable judgment stated from the other side, and Daniel 4 is the chapter in which a king is warned, given twelve months, and then broken at the moment he congratulates himself. Ammonihah is given the same interval in the same terms: 'the time is soon at hand, except ye repent.' Luke 13:3-5 supplies that clause, and its context is Jesus refusing to concede that those killed by Pilate or by a falling tower were worse sinners than their neighbours — the exact refusal Amulek is making about the righteous whose prayers are keeping the city standing.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 5:25's 'his hand is stretched out still' is the more usual biblical image for judgment not withdrawn, and shares nothing verbal with this verse.

links.note: Held at moderate because the sense is reversed and the phrase is three ordinary words; recorded because those three words exist once in the English Bible and the source chapter is one of two the chapter has already drawn on (10:2, Daniel 5; 10:17, Daniel 4:17). Whether the reversal is a misreading of Daniel or a deliberate turn is not decidable from the text, and the catalogue does not decide it.
links.text: And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that the people were more angry with Amulek, and they cried out saying: This man doth revile against our laws, which are just, and our wise Lawyers, which we have selected.

But Amulek stretched forth his hand, and cried the mightier unto them, saying: O ye wicked and perverse generation; why hath Satan got such great hold upon your hearts? Why will ye yield yourselves unto him, that he may have power over you, to blind your eyes, that ye will not understand the words which are spoken, according to their truth?

provenance.route: Acts 5:3 (with Romans 6:16) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Why hath Satan” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:3. 'Yield yourselves' occurs in exactly three, 2 Chronicles 30:8, Romans 6:13 and Romans 6:16.
provenance.significance: Peter's question to Ananias — 'why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost' — is the KJV's only interrogation of that shape, and Amulek asks it of a crowd: 'why hath Satan got such great hold upon your hearts?' The substitution keeps the heart and changes the verb from filling to holding. Recover Acts 5 and the exchange that follows in Alma acquires its shape: Ananias's sin is a lie, Peter names it as Satan's work, and Ananias falls down dead. Three verses later the crowd of Ammonihah answers Amulek by saying 'this man is a child of the Devil, for he hath lied unto us' (10:28) — the same three terms, Satan, lying, and a verdict, turned back on the man who used them. Romans 6:16 supplies the second half of the verse and its logic: 'to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are'. Amulek asks why they will yield themselves to one who may 'have power over you', which is Paul's definition of what yielding does.
provenance.alternative: 2 Chronicles 30:8's 'yield yourselves unto the LORD' is the positive form of the same idiom and is not what Alma 10:25 describes.

links.note: A KJV singleton interrogative reproduced with its noun and its object intact, plus a Pauline construction that occurs three times in the Bible and twice in the one chapter that argues from it. The verse also opens with 'O ye wicked and perverse generation', which is 10:17's vocative repeated; that repetition is adjudicated at 10:17 and not again here.
links.text: But Peter said, Ananias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land?

provenance.route: Isaiah 6:10 → John 12:40 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Blinded their eyes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 12:40; Isaiah 6:10, which John is quoting, reads 'shut their eyes' instead and has no form of 'blind'.
provenance.significance: The mediation is decided by a single word and it decides in favour of John. Isaiah 6:10 tells the prophet to 'make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes'; John 12:40 renders the same passage 'He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart … nor understand with their heart'. Alma 10:25 has blinding and understanding together — 'to blind your eyes, that ye will not understand the words which are spoken' — which is John's pairing and not Isaiah's.
