The Book of Mormon has taken this pair before, at 1 Nephi 12:17 and 13:27, and the difference here is the agent: in John it is God who blinds, in the standard reading of Isaiah's commission it is the prophet, and in Alma 10:25 it is Satan, 'that he may have power over you, to blind your eyes'. Compare 2 Corinthians 4:4, where 'the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not' — the one New Testament verse that makes the blinder an adversary rather than God, and the reading Alma 10:25 has arrived at.
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 4:4 has the right agent but the wrong noun ('the minds'), and no form of 'eyes'.

links.note: Moderate rather than high: the shared material is one verb and one noun, and 'blind the eyes' is available to any writer. What holds the row up is that the KJV puts that exact participle-plus-noun in one verse only, that understanding is joined to it there as here, and that this Johannine pair is already an established Book of Mormon borrowing in an earlier book. Recorded as a fresh row rather than a recurrence because the agent has changed and the change is the argument.
links.text: He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.

pericopes.text: For behold, have I testified against your law? Ye do not understand; ye say that I have spoken against your law; but I have not; but I have spoken in favor of your law, to your condemnation.
And now behold, I say unto you, that the foundation of the destruction of this people is a beginning to be laid by the unrighteousness of your lawyers and your Judges.

And now it came to pass that when Amulek had spoken these words, the people cried out against him, saying, Now we know that this man is a child of the Devil, for he hath lied unto us; for he hath spoken against our law. And now he saith that he hath not spoken against it.

provenance.other: “Child of the devil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:10; the plural 'children of the devil' occurs in exactly one, 1 John 3:10. “We know that this man is a” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 9:24.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons in one accusation, and both of them belong to scenes of judicial hostility to a witness. The frame is John 9:24 — 'we know that this man is a sinner', said by the authorities to a man who will not retract his testimony — with the predicate replaced by Acts 13:10's, Paul's denunciation of Elymas the sorcerer. What makes the substitution more than clever is that Acts 13:10's sentence continues 'wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord', and Amulek has spent 10:18 accusing these same men of laying plans 'to pervert the ways of the righteous'. So the crowd answers a charge of perverting the ways by calling the accuser what Paul calls a man who perverts the ways, out of the same verse. This catalogue has already adjudicated the other half of Acts 13:10, the perverting clause, at 1 Nephi 13:27, where it is reproduced verbatim; here the Book of Mormon takes the vocative instead.
provenance.alternative: 1 John 3:10's plural is the general theological form and lacks the direct address.

links.note: The 1830 capitalizes 'Devil'. Held at high rather than certain because both singletons are short and because a hostile crowd calling a preacher a child of the devil is a thing that could be written without a source; what the row rests on is the two rare strings arriving in one sentence and the third contact with Acts 13:10 ten verses earlier.
links.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

pericopes.text: And again: he hath reviled against our Lawyers, and our Judges, &c.
And it came to pass that the Lawyers put it into their hearts that they should remember these things against him.

And it came to pass that there was one among them whose name was Zeezrom. Now he being the foremost to accuse Amulek and Alma, he being one of the most expert among them, having much business to do among the people.
Now the object of these Lawyers were to get gain; and they got gain according to their employ.

provenance.other: “Get gain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:13.
provenance.significance: The phrase is the Book of Mormon's standing term for corrupt religious and civil profit, adjudicated first at 2 Nephi 26:20, and its one biblical occurrence is the merchant's boast that James answers with 'ye know not what shall be on the morrow'. Alma 10:32 is the chapter's last sentence and it is a bare accountancy — 'the object of these Lawyers were to get gain; and they got gain according to their employ' — placed immediately after Zeezrom is introduced as the most expert of them. James 4:13-16 is about men who plan a year's trade without reference to God, and James 5:1-6 goes on to the wages kept back by fraud and the condemning and killing of the just, which is what Ammonihah's lawyers will do to the just in chapter 14. The 1830 reads 'were to get gain' where the 1920 reads 'was'; the plural verb keeps the object with the lawyers rather than with the profession.
provenance.alternative: Acts 19:24's 'no small gain' is the other candidate for a commercial-motive source and is the same Lucan idiom recorded at 10:4.

links.note: Two words, and a link across a book boundary rather than a recurrence entry, because Alma is a new book and a new hand and a reader shown nothing here would be told there is no borrowing. The argument was made at 2 Nephi 26:20; what is new is the application, which is not to priestcraft but to a paid legal profession.
links.text: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:

pericopes.text: Now it was in the law of Mosiah that every man which was a Judge of the law, or which was appointed to be Judges, should receive wages according to the time which they labored to judge those which were brought before them to be judged.

Now if a man oweth another, and he would not pay that which he did owe, he was complained of to the Judge; and the Judge executed authority, and sent forth officers that the man should be brought before him; and he judgeth the man according to the law and the evidences which are brought against him; and thus the man was compelled to pay that which he oweth, or be striped, or be cast out from among the people, as a thief and a robber.

provenance.other: “A thief and a robber” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:1.
provenance.significance: John 10:1's thief and robber is a figure: he is the man who does not come in by the door of the sheepfold, and the sentence is about false shepherds. Alma 11:2 flattens the figure into a legal category — a debtor who will not pay is 'cast out from among the people, as a thief and a robber' — and the flattening is characteristic of what this chapter does with the New Testament, which is to convert its sayings into Nephite statute. The verse's procedural frame comes from the other direction: complaint, judge, officers, compulsion to pay, prison or expulsion is Matthew 5:25-26 and its Lukan parallel at 12:58, the chain already used at Alma 10:13 for the prosecution of Alma and Amulek. So the law under which the two men will be tried is described in the words of the parable Jesus told about being tried.

links.note: Four words and a KJV singleton, in a verse that has no other business quoting the Gospel of John. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is a natural English pairing and because the sense has been narrowed from metaphor to charge sheet; the row is worth keeping because the narrowing is itself the observation.
links.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.

pericopes.text: And the Judge recieveth for his wages according to his time: a senine of gold for a day, or a senum of silver, which is equal to a senine of gold; and this is according to the law which was given.

Now these are the names of the different pieces of their gold, and of their silver, according to their value. And the names are given by the Nephites; for they did not reckon after the manner of the Jews which were at Jerusalem; neither did they measure after the manner of the Jews, but they altered their reckoning and their measure, according to the minds and the circumstances of the people, in every generation, until the reign of the Judges; they having been established by king Mosiah.
Now the reckoning is thus: A senine of gold, a seon of gold, a shum of gold, and a limnah of gold.
A senum of silver, an amnor of silver, an ezrom of silver, and an onti of silver.
A senum of silver was equal to a senine of gold; and either for a measure of barley, and also for a measure of every kind of grain.
Now the amount of a seon of gold, was twice the value of a senine;
and a shum of gold was twice the value of a seon;
and a limnah of gold was the value of them all;
and an amnor of silver was as great as two senums;
and an ezrom of silver was as great as four senums;
and an onti was as great as them all.
Now this is the value of the lesser numbers of their reckoning:
A shiblon is half of a senum: therefore a shiblon for half a measure of barley;
and a shiblum is a half of a shiblon;
and a leah is the half of a shiblum.
Now this is their number, according to their reckoning.
Now an antion of gold is equal to three shublons.

Now it was for the sole purpose for to get gain, because they recieved wages according to their employ; therefore they did stir up the people to riotings, and all manner of disturbances and wickedness, that they might have more employ; that they might get money according to the suits which was brought before them; therefore they did stir up the people against Alma and Amulek.

And this Zeezrom began to question Amulek, saying: Will ye answer me a few questions which I shall ask you? Now Zeezrom was a man which was expert in the devises of the Devil, that he might destroy that which was good; therefore he saith unto Amulek, Will ye aaswer the questions which I shall put unto you?

provenance.route: 2 Corinthians 2:11 (with Acts 26:3) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “His devices” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Daniel 11:24 and 2 Corinthians 2:11; only 2 Corinthians 2:11's are Satan's — 'we are not ignorant of his devices'. 'Expert' occurs in six KJV verses, five of them military; the sixth is Acts 26:3, 'expert in all customs and questions'.
provenance.significance: Zeezrom is introduced twice, at 10:31 as 'one of the most expert among them' and here as 'a man which was expert in the devises of the Devil' who opens with 'Will ye answer me a few questions which I shall ask you?' The KJV's one non-military expert is Paul's captatio to Agrippa, a man expert in questions, spoken at the start of a hearing; and the KJV's one Satanic 'devices' is Paul warning a congregation not to be outmanoeuvred. Both halves of Zeezrom's description are Pauline, and the second supplies the reason the questioning fails: Amulek is not ignorant of his devices either, which is exactly what 11:25 turns out to mean.
provenance.alternative: Ephesians 6:11's 'the wiles of the devil' is the other candidate and is closer in sense, but 'wiles' is not the Book of Mormon's word here; the 1830 spells it 'devises'.

links.note: Two words, and the row is held at moderate because 'devices of the devil' was a commonplace of nineteenth-century preaching that needs no particular verse behind it. What argues for the row is that the same sentence also carries the KJV's one civil use of 'expert', and that the chapter's other Zeezrom material (11:23, 11:25) is verifiably borrowed.
links.whyNot: 'The devices of the devil' is an English idiom of long standing and its presence proves nothing on its own; the case rests on the company it keeps in this chapter.
links.text: Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices.

pericopes.text: And Amulek saith unto him, Yea, if it be according to the spirit of the Lord, which is in me; for I shall say nothing which is contrary to the spirit of the Lord. And Zeezrom saith unto him, Behold, here is six onties of silver, and all these will I give thee if thou wilt deny the existence of a Supreme Being.

provenance.other: “All these things will I give thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 4:9, where the devil offers the kingdoms of the world; Luke 4:6 has 'All this power will I give thee'.
provenance.significance: Zeezrom lays down six onties of silver and says 'all these will I give thee if thou wilt deny the existence of a Supreme Being.' The construction is the devil's, from the third temptation, and it is preserved down to the conditional: offer, then 'if thou wilt', then the act demanded. What is demanded has been adjusted from worship of Satan to denial of God, which are the same transaction stated from opposite ends. Amulek's reply completes the identification by answering in the words Jesus used to the men who brought him a coin (11:23, Matthew 22:18), so the bribe scene runs the temptation and the tribute-money trap together — and Mark 12:15's version of the trap begins 'bring me a penny, that I may see it', which is what Zeezrom does with his silver.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 4:10's 'Get thee hence, Satan' is not taken up; Amulek's answering vocative is Matthew 23:15's 'child of hell', adjudicated at 11:23.

links.note: Six words, reproduced with the noun removed because the noun is now Nephite currency. The identification of the questioner with the tempter is not stated by the text and is the reading this link makes available; the text states only that Zeezrom was expert in the devices of the devil (11:21). Held at high on the singleton plus the exact conditional structure.
links.text: And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me.

pericopes.text: Now Amulek saith, O thou child of Hell, why tempt ye me? Knowest thou that the righteous yieldeth to no such temptations?

provenance.route: Matthew 23:15 + Matthew 22:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Child of hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 23:15. “Why tempt ye me” occurs in exactly three, Matthew 22:18, Mark 12:15 and Luke 20:23 — the same episode in all three, and Matthew's continues 'ye hypocrites'.
provenance.significance: Two sentences, both of them Jesus's, both from the confrontation with the Jerusalem authorities in the last week. 'O thou child of Hell' is the woe on the scribes and Pharisees who make a proselyte 'twofold more the child of hell than yourselves'; 'why tempt ye me' is the answer to the tribute-money trap. The Book of Mormon has been assembling this scene since Alma 10:13, which took its 'catch them in their words' from Mark 12:13 — the sending of the Pharisees and Herodians that produces the very question Matthew 22:18 answers. So chapter 10 borrows the sending and chapter 11 borrows the reply, in order, with the coin in between. Amulek's addition, 'knowest thou that the righteous yieldeth to no such temptations?', supplies from Matthew 4 what Matthew 22 leaves implicit: that a question with money behind it is a temptation and not an enquiry.
provenance.alternative: Luke 20:23's 'Why tempt ye me?' is the form already drawn on at Alma 10:17 for 'he perceived their craftiness'; Matthew 22:18 is preferred here because its 'ye hypocrites' answers Alma 10:17's 'ye Lawyers and hypocrites'.

links.note: A KJV singleton vocative and a three-verse interrogative, adjacent, both from the same week of the same Gospel narrative, in a scene the Book of Mormon has been building for a chapter and a half. The 1830 capitalizes 'Hell'. Held at high rather than certain because each phrase is short.
links.text: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.

pericopes.text: Believest thou that there is no God? I say unto you, nay: thou knowest that there is a God, but thou lovest that lucre more than him.

provenance.other: “Lucre” occurs in exactly six KJV verses. Five are the pastoral epistles' 'filthy lucre' as a disqualification for office; the sixth is 1 Samuel 8:3, where Samuel's sons 'turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment'.
provenance.significance: The split is the argument, and it is the same split this catalogue used at Mosiah 29:40. Of the six occurrences only one is about judges, and that one is the origin of Israel's demand for a king — the corrupt judiciary of 1 Samuel 8:3 is why 8:5 asks for a monarch. Alma 11 has just spent nineteen verses explaining that Nephite judges are paid by the case and 11:20 that their object is to stir up litigation; Amulek then tells Zeezrom he 'lovest that lucre more than him'. The verse under the accusation is the verse about judges who take bribes and pervert judgment — and Alma 10:18 has already accused these men of perverting the ways, out of the KJV's one 'pervert the ways of judgment' at Proverbs 17:23. Two different books of the Bible supply the same charge to the same chapter, and both are about bribed courts.
provenance.alternative: The pastoral epistles' 'filthy lucre' is the more familiar phrase and is what a nineteenth-century writer would most likely reach for; nothing of 'filthy' survives here.

links.note: One word. Recorded at moderate, and only because the distribution is informative: five of the six KJV occurrences are about ministers and the sixth is about judges, and the sixth is the one whose situation Alma 11 has constructed at length. Below any quotation threshold and offered as a reading rather than a demonstration.
links.text: And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment.

pericopes.text: And now thou hast lied before God unto me. Thou saidst unto me, Behold these six onties, which are of great worth, I will give unto thee, when thou had it in thy heart to retain them from me; and it was only thy desire that I should deny the true and living God, that thou mightest have cause to destroy me. And now behold, for this great evil thou shalt have thy reward.

provenance.other: “Lied unto men but unto God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:4. “Keep back part of the price” occurs in exactly one, Acts 5:3. Alma 10:25's 'why hath Satan' is the third KJV singleton from the same five verses.
provenance.significance: Alma 11:25 is the Ananias episode rewritten clause by clause. Acts 5:3-4: Satan has filled the heart; the sin is keeping back part of the price; the question is 'why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart?'; the verdict is 'thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God'; and Ananias falls down dead. Alma 11:25: 'thou hast lied before God unto me … when thou had it in thy heart to retain them from me … for this great evil thou shalt have thy reward.' Money offered and withheld, a lie whose real addressee is God, a heart that conceived it, and a sentence. The Book of Mormon reverses the direction of the fraud — Ananias withholds money he pretended to give the church, Zeezrom offers money he never meant to hand over — and keeps the theology of the lie exactly. That Alma 10:25 has already used Acts 5:3's 'why hath Satan' of this same crowd makes the pair a sustained borrowing rather than two coincidences: three KJV singletons out of one short passage, across two chapters, in the right order.
provenance.alternative: Acts 8:20's 'Thy money perish with thee' is the other Lucan money-and-the-Spirit rebuke; nothing of it is verbally present.

links.note: Not a quotation — no run exceeds four words — but an extended reproduction of a scene with three of its rarest strings intact. Subtype 'extended' records that the borrowing is of a passage rather than a phrase. The 1830's 'when thou had it in thy heart' is ungrammatical where the 1920 reads 'when thou hadst it'; the first edition's form is closer to nothing in the KJV and is simply the dictation's.
links.text: Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.

pericopes.text: And Zeezrom saith unto him, Thou sayest there is a true and a living God?
And Amulek saith, Yea, there is a true and a living God.

provenance.route: 1 Thessalonians 1:9 or Jeremiah 10:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Living and true God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 1:9. The Book of Mormon's order, 'true and living', occurs in no KJV verse. Jeremiah 10:10 has both adjectives but in separate clauses: 'the LORD is the true God, he is the living God'.
provenance.significance: Mediation is recorded as uncertain because the two candidates cannot be separated on the evidence and the Book of Mormon matches neither exactly. 1 Thessalonians 1:9 joins the adjectives and Alma reverses them; Jeremiah 10:10 has Alma's order but not Alma's construction. What is decidable is that the phrase is being used as a test of loyalty in all three: Paul's Thessalonians turned to it from idols, Jeremiah's verse stands in the middle of a polemic against wooden gods, and Zeezrom is being asked whether he will deny it for six onties of silver. Jeremiah 10:10's next clause — 'at his wrath the earth shall tremble' — is what happens to Zeezrom at 11:46.
provenance.alternative: 'The living God' alone is distributed across some thirty KJV verses and could not identify a source; the pairing with 'true' is what makes the row possible.

links.note: The phrase enters at 11:25, is repeated as a question at 11:26 and affirmed here, and this is the point at which the affirmation is made, so the row sits here. Moderate, and kjvSpecific 'uncertain' honestly: the wording is close to two verses and identical to neither, which is a different situation from the chapter's singletons.
links.text: For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God;

pericopes.text: Now Zeezrom saith, Is there more than one God?
And he answereth No.
Now Zeezrom saith unto him again: How knowest thou these things?
And he saith An angel hath made them known unto me.
And Zeezrom saith again: Who is he that shall come? Is it the Son of God?
And he said unto him, Yea.
And Zeezrom saith again: Shall he save his people in their sins? And Amulek answered and said unto him, I say unto you he shall not, for it is impossible for him to deny his word.

provenance.other: “Save his people from their sins” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 1:21, the angel's instruction to Joseph naming Jesus.
provenance.significance: The whole dispute of 11:34-37 is a preposition. Zeezrom asks 'Shall he save his people in their sins?' and Amulek answers that he shall not, 'for it is impossible for him to deny his word' — and the word he cannot deny is the one KJV sentence that says what Jesus's name means: he shall save his people FROM their sins. Recover Matthew 1:21 and Amulek's refusal stops being a doctrinal assertion and becomes an appeal to a text: the name itself forbids the answer Zeezrom wants, because a saviour who saved people in their sins would be misnamed. Zeezrom's trap depends on the reader not noticing the substituted preposition, which is why he can report Amulek to the crowd at 11:35 as having said 'he shall not save his people' with the qualifier dropped — and Amulek's answer at 11:36 is to put it back. That exchange is unintelligible without the KJV verse under it, and this is the strongest kind of evidence the catalogue collects: not a phrase reused but an argument that cannot be conducted without its source.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 130:8's 'he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities' is the Old Testament sentence behind Matthew's; it has none of Matthew's wording and would not support the wordplay.

links.note: Five words of a KJV singleton, altered by one preposition, and the alteration is what the passage is about. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations. Certain: no other explanation of 11:34-37 accounts for why the argument turns on 'in' versus 'from'.
links.text: And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.

pericopes.text: Now Zeezrom saith unto the people, See that ye remember these things; for he saith there is but one God; yet he saith that the Son of God shall come, but he shall not save his people, as though he had authority to command God.

provenance.other: 'There is but one God' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 8:6.
provenance.significance: Zeezrom's summary to the crowd — 'he saith there is but one God; yet he saith that the Son of God shall come' — is put in the words of the one Pauline verse that states monotheism and then immediately qualifies it with 'and one Lord Jesus Christ'. The qualification is precisely the move Zeezrom is trying to make sound like a contradiction, and Paul has already made it without contradiction. Whether the Book of Mormon intends that irony is not decidable; what the link does is put the reader in a position to see it, which is the whole use of Hays's metalepsis in a case where the borrowing is short.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 8:4's 'there is none other God but one' is the same argument in different words and shares nothing distinctive with Alma 11:35.

links.note: Five words. Recorded as an echo at moderate: the sentence is short enough that a writer arguing monotheism might produce it independently, and the rarity claim is doing all the work.
links.text: But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him.

pericopes.text: Now Amulek saith again unto him, Behold thou hast lied, for thou sayest that I spake as though I had authority to command God, because I said he shall not save his people in their sins.

And I say unto you again, that he cannot save them in their sins; for I cannot deny his word, and he hath said that no unclean thing can inherit the Kingdom of Heaven; therefore how can ye be saved, except ye inherit the Kingdom of Heaven?— Therefore ye cannot be saved in your sins.

provenance.route: Ephesians 5:5 (with 1 Corinthians 6:9-10) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Inherit the kingdom” occurs in exactly five KJV verses and in every one of them the kingdom is God's, or the Father's — the KJV never writes 'inherit the kingdom of heaven'. “Unclean person” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, and Ephesians 5:5 is the only one that denies such a person an inheritance.
provenance.significance: Amulek attributes the sentence to God — 'he hath said that no unclean thing can inherit the Kingdom of Heaven' — which makes it a quotation claim, and no KJV verse says it. What the KJV has is Ephesians 5:5, where 'no whoremonger, nor unclean person' has 'any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God', and 1 Corinthians 6:9-10, where a list of the unrighteous 'shall not inherit the kingdom of God'. The Book of Mormon compresses the list to 'no unclean thing' and swaps in Matthew's 'kingdom of heaven', a phrase confined in the KJV to that Gospel. The result is a sentence with two biblical parents and no biblical existence, offered as scripture — which is exactly the situation Alma 12:21 will create in the other direction when Antionah quotes Genesis 3 and is answered from it.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 21:27's 'there shall in no wise enter into it any thing that defileth' is closest to 'no unclean thing' as a formula about a thing rather than a person, and lacks the inheritance verb.

links.note: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Ephesians 5:5 at this verse. The catalogue agrees that Ephesians 5:5 is the nearest single source and records that the sentence Amulek quotes is a fusion rather than a citation; the substitution of 'kingdom of heaven' for the Pauline 'kingdom of God' is the part that makes the fusion visible. Moderate, because no distinctive string is reproduced.
links.text: For this ye know, that no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, hath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

pericopes.text: Now Zeezrom saith again unto him: Is the Son of God the very Eternal Father?
And Amulek saith unto him, Yea, he is the very Eternal Father of Heaven and of Earth, and all things which in them is; he is the beginning and the end, the first and the last;

provenance.other: “The beginning and the end, the first and the last” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 22:13, which is the last of the four Alpha-and-Omega sayings and the only one that stacks all three titles. 'All that in them is' occurs in exactly two, Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24.
provenance.significance: Ten consecutive words of the KJV's closing chapter, applied to the Son. Revelation 22:13 is Christ's own self-identification at the end of the canon, and taking it whole is how Amulek answers 'Is the Son of God the very Eternal Father?' — not with an argument but with a title deed. The verse's first half, 'the very Eternal Father of Heaven and of Earth, and all things which in them is', is the creation formula of Exodus 20:11 as the apostles pray it in Acts 4:24; so the answer to a question about the Son's identity is built out of the Sabbath commandment's account of who made the world plus Revelation's account of who ends it. Isaiah 44:6's 'I am the first, and I am the last' is the Old Testament source both New Testament passages are drawing on, and it too is spoken by the God who says 'beside me there is no God' — which is what Amulek said at 11:29.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 1:8, 1:11 and 21:6 each carry part of the formula; none has all four terms in Alma's order.

links.note: A ten-word verbatim run from a verse identifiable by that run alone, and one of the longest in Alma 10-12. Still below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six quotations, which should be said because the reproduction is otherwise complete and unbroken. Catalogued as a quotation on CONVENTIONS §2's rule that length does not decide the category by itself.
links.text: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.

pericopes.text: and he shall come into the world to redeem his people; and he shall take upon him the transgressions of those who believe on his name; and these are they that shall have eternal life, and salvation cometh to none else;

therefore the wicked remain as though there had been no redemption made, except it be the loosing of the bands of death; for behold, the day cometh that all shall rise from the dead and stand before God, and be judged according to their works.

provenance.other: “Stand before God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:12. “According to their works” occurs in exactly three, 2 Corinthians 11:15, Revelation 20:12 and Revelation 20:13; two of the three are in the same judgment scene as 'stand before God'.
provenance.significance: Two rare strings from one verse, in the same order and the same clause structure: 'all shall rise from the dead and stand before God, and be judged according to their works.' Revelation 20:12-13 is the great white throne — the dead, small and great, standing, the books opened, and each judged according to his works — and Alma 11:41-44 is a compressed version of it with one significant difference. In Revelation the resurrection is a sorting; in Alma it is universal first and the sorting comes after, which is the doctrinal point 11:41 exists to make, that 'the wicked remain as though there had been no redemption made, except it be the loosing of the bands of death'. The Book of Mormon takes Revelation's courtroom and inserts a general resurrection ahead of it.
provenance.alternative: Malachi 4:1's 'behold, the day cometh' supplies a six-word run at the head of the verse and was the machine's top proposal; it is a standard prophetic opener and its day burns as an oven, which is not this verse's subject.

links.note: The first half of the verse, 'as though there had been no redemption made', has no KJV source and is the Book of Mormon's own. The second half is Revelation 20:12's two rarest phrases in sequence. High rather than certain because neither string exceeds four words.
links.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

pericopes.text: Now there is a death which is called a temporal death; and the death of Christ shall loose the bands of this temporal death, that all shall be raised from this temporal death;

provenance.other: “Pains of death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:24 — 'having loosed the pains of death'. The Book of Mormon's 'bands of death' occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The verb decides it. Death in the KJV binds in several idioms — the sorrows of death, the snares of death, the cords of hell — but 'loose' is joined to death in exactly one verse, Peter at Pentecost saying God raised Jesus 'having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it'. Alma 11:41-42 uses 'loosing' twice with a noun of its own, 'the bands of death', and gives it the same agency: the death of Christ is what looses it. Acts 2:24 sits three verses before Acts 2:27's 'see corruption', which Alma 11:45 also has — so the whole of Amulek's resurrection doctrine is drawn from one paragraph of one Pentecost sermon.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 116:16's 'thou hast loosed my bonds' has the verb and a bond, but no death; 2 Samuel 22:6 and Psalm 18:5 have 'the snares of death' without the verb.

links.note: One word of the pair is the Book of Mormon's own, which is why this is moderate. The argument is the verb and the source paragraph, not the noun phrase — and the noun phrase's absence from the KJV is itself worth recording, since 'bands of death' is often assumed to be biblical.
links.text: Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it.

pericopes.text: the spirit and the body shall be re-united again, in its perfect form; both limb and joint shall be restored to its proper frame, even as we now are at this time; and we shall be brought to stand before God, knowing even as we know now, and have a bright recollection of all our guilt.

Now this restoration shall come to all, both old and young, both bond and free, both male and female, both the wicked and the righteous; and even there shall not so much as a hair of their heads be lost; but all things shall be restored to its perfect frame, as it is now, or in the body, and shall be brought and be arraigned before the bar of Christ the Son, and God the Father, and the Holy Spirit, which is one Eternal God, to be judged according to their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil.

provenance.route: Ecclesiastes 12:14 (frame from 2 Corinthians 5:10) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Whether it be good, or whether it be evil” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ecclesiastes 12:14 and Jeremiah 42:6. “Neither bond nor free” occurs in exactly one, Galatians 3:28, which is also the only verse joining that pair to 'neither male nor female'.
provenance.significance: mediation-check.py was run on this verse against 2 Corinthians 5:10 and returns divergences in both directions; the two that favour Paul are absences, and the one real word-level divergence is decisive the other way. Paul's clause ends 'whether it be good or bad'; Ecclesiastes 12:14's ends 'whether it be good, or whether it be evil', and Alma 11:44 has the doubled 'whether' and the word 'evil'. So the frame is Paul's — all appearing before a judgment seat of Christ, which Alma calls 'the bar of Christ' — and the closing clause is Ecclesiastes's, in the verse that closes Ecclesiastes. The merism that precedes it, 'both bond and free, both male and female', is Galatians 3:28's pair with its negatives removed: Paul abolishes the categories in Christ and Alma preserves them through the resurrection, which is the difference between a doctrine of union and a doctrine of restoration to 'perfect frame'.
provenance.alternative: Jeremiah 42:6 has the same doubled clause but is a promise of obedience, not a judgment.

links.note: A three-source verse where each source is identifiable and each contributes a different clause. The decisive evidence is one word, 'evil' against Paul's 'bad', which is what mediation-check.py was built to find. Note that the 1830 reads 'shall be restored to its perfect frame' with a singular pronoun for a plural antecedent throughout the verse; later editions did not regularize it here.
links.text: For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil.

provenance.other: “Hair of your head” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 21:18 — 'But there shall not an hair of your head perish.'
provenance.significance: 'There shall not so much as a hair of their heads be lost.' Luke 21:18 is a promise of preservation through persecution, made in the middle of the Olivet discourse to disciples who are told two verses earlier that 'some of you shall they cause to be put to death'. Alma 11:44 transposes the promise from history to resurrection: not that the faithful will survive but that the body will be reassembled entire. That transposition matters in this book, because Alma 14 is about to have the believers of Ammonihah burned alive while Alma and Amulek are made to watch, and the promise Luke attaches to martyrdom is the one Amulek has already given them in a form martyrdom cannot break.
provenance.alternative: Acts 27:34's 'there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you' and 1 Samuel 14:45's 'there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground' are the other biblical forms; both are about physical rescue and neither has Luke's possessive.

links.note: Held at moderate because the idiom is proverbial in English and appears in the KJV four times over; what argues for Luke 21:18 in particular is the possessive construction and the martyrological setting, which chapter 14 will make relevant.
links.text: But there shall not an hair of your head perish.

pericopes.text: Now behold I have spoken unto you concerning the death of the mortal body, and also concerning the resurrection of the mortal body. I say unto you, that this mortal body is raised to an immortal body; that is from death; even from the first death, unto life, that they can die no more; their spirits uniting with their bodies, never to be divided; thus the whole becoming spiritual and immortal, that they can no more see corruption.

provenance.other: “This mortal must put on immortality” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:53. “Raised in incorruption” occurs in exactly one, 1 Corinthians 15:42. 'See corruption' occurs in five, three of them the same Psalm quotation.
provenance.significance: 'This mortal body is raised to an immortal body … that they can no more see corruption.' Both halves come from 1 Corinthians 15, and from the two verses of it that the KJV makes unique: 15:42's sown-in-corruption-raised-in-incorruption and 15:53's mortal putting on immortality. What Alma adds is the anatomy — 'their spirits uniting with their bodies, never to be divided' — which Paul does not supply and which 11:43 has already spelled out down to limb and joint. The chapter's resurrection doctrine is thus Pauline in vocabulary and un-Pauline in interest: 1 Corinthians 15:44 distinguishes a natural body from a spiritual body, and Alma 11:43-45 insists instead that the raised body is the same body, 'even as we now are at this time'.
provenance.alternative: 'See corruption' cannot decide its own mediation. mediation-check.py on Psalm 16:10 against Acts 2:27 reports no decisive divergence, because the KJV renders the two verses identically except for the opening conjunction, which Alma does not reproduce. The phrase reaches Alma 11:45 either from the Psalm or from Peter's use of it, and the verse cannot say which; the surrounding 1 Corinthians 15 material is the reason mediation is recorded as direct-NT for the row as a whole.

links.note: Two KJV singletons from one chapter, paraphrased rather than quoted — 'this mortal body is raised to an immortal body' collapses 15:42 and 15:53 into a single clause. High rather than certain because the paraphrase leaves no long verbatim run; the case is that both source phrases are unique and adjacent in Paul.
links.text: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

pericopes.text: Now when Amulek had finished these words, the people began again to be astonished, and also Zeezrom began to tremble. And thus ended the words of Amulek, or this is all that I have written.

provenance.other: “Judgment to come” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 24:25, and it is the verse in which Felix trembles.
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly one scene in which a hearer of a discourse on the coming judgment trembles at it, and it has a detail that Alma 11 has already used: Acts 24:26 says Felix 'hoped also that money should have been given him of Paul', which is why he kept sending for him. Zeezrom's interrogation opened with six onties of silver (11:22) and closes with him beginning to tremble at a discourse on the resurrection and the bar of Christ. The sequence is the same and the order is the same — money first, then reasoning of judgment to come, then trembling — and Felix's response, 'Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee', is what Zeezrom conspicuously does not say, because Alma 12 has him ask again. That refusal to take Felix's exit is what makes Zeezrom's conversion possible, and it is only visible with the source in view.
provenance.alternative: Acts 16:29's jailer 'came trembling' after an earthquake, and Daniel 5:6's Belshazzar trembles at the writing on the wall; neither follows a discourse.

links.note: A KJV singleton phrase is not reproduced here — 'judgment to come' is Acts 24:25's, not Amulek's — so the link is to the scene and is typed as a type-scene rather than a verbal borrowing. What holds it at high is that the scene is unique in the KJV, that its three elements appear in Alma 11 in the same order, and that the money detail is peculiar enough to be doing more than coinciding.
links.text: And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee.

pericopes.text: Now Alma, seeing that the words of Amulek had silenced Zeezrom, for he beheld that Amulek had caught him in his lying and deceiving, to destroy him, and seeing that he began to tremble under a consciousness of his guilt, he opened his mouth and began to speak unto him, and to establish the words of Amulek, and to explain things beyond, or to unfold the Scriptures beyond that which Amulek had done.
Now the words that Alma spake unto Zeezrom, was heard by the people round about: for the multitude was great, and he spake on this wise:

Now Zeezrom, seeing that thou hast been taken in thy lying and craftiness, for thou hast not lied unto men only, but thou hast lied unto God. For behold, he knows all thy thoughts; and thou seest that thy thoughts are made known unto us by his spirit;

provenance.other: “Thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:4. Alma 12:3 reads 'thou hast not lied unto men only, but thou hast lied unto God' — the clause verbatim with one adverb inserted and the verb repeated.
provenance.significance: This is the third and fullest contact with Acts 5:1-5 in three chapters, and it is where the sentence itself arrives rather than the scene. Alma 10:25 took Acts 5:3's 'why hath Satan'; Alma 11:25 rebuilt the whole episode — money offered and withheld, a heart that conceived it, a lie whose real addressee is God; and Alma 12:3 now quotes Peter's verdict on Ananias almost word for word, in a different speaker's mouth, about the same man. Recover the source and the escalation is legible: Ananias falls down dead at Acts 5:5, and Zeezrom, hearing the sentence pronounced over him, 'began to tremble more exceedingly' (12:7) and then asks a question (12:8) — which is the one thing Ananias never gets to do. The Book of Mormon runs the Ananias scene twice and lets it end differently.
provenance.alternative: Acts 5:9's 'How is it that ye have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?' is the parallel verdict on Sapphira and is not in view.

links.note: Eleven words reproduced with one interpolation, from a KJV singleton. This is the clearest quotation in the three chapters and it is still below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six passages; catalogued as a quotation on CONVENTIONS §2, where length does not decide the category by itself. The link at 11:25 records the scene and this one records the sentence: CONVENTIONS §6a's rule is to put the link where the wording is, and the wording is here.
links.text: Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.

pericopes.text: and thou seest that we know that thy plan was a very subtle plan, as to the subtlety of the Devil, for to lie and to deceive this people, that thou mightest set them against us, to revile us and to cast us out.

provenance.route: 2 Corinthians 11:3 (with Genesis 3:1) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Subtilty” occurs in exactly six KJV verses and 'subtil' in exactly three; Genesis 3:1's serpent is 'more subtil than any beast of the field', and 2 Corinthians 11:3 is the one verse that reads that subtilty as an ongoing danger to a congregation — 'as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted'.
provenance.significance: Alma 12:4-6 calls Zeezrom's plan subtle 'as to the subtlety of the Devil' and then says the devil laid it 'to catch this people'; seventeen verses later the chapter is expounding Genesis 3. 2 Corinthians 11:3 is the hinge between those two halves and the only KJV verse that performs the same move — it takes the Eden serpent, identifies it with the adversary, and warns a specific congregation that the same subtilty is working on them now. Read Alma 12 with that verse in view and its structure stops looking like two subjects and starts looking like one: the deception of Ammonihah by a lawyer and the deception of Eve by a serpent are the same event twice, which is why Antionah's Genesis question at 12:21 is an answer to 12:4 and not a change of topic.
provenance.alternative: Acts 13:10's 'O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil' is the vocative the Book of Mormon has used at 2 Nephi 5:24 and Alma 10:28, and 2 Samuel 13:3's 'a very subtil man' is the only KJV 'very subtil'; neither reads Eden.

links.note: Held at moderate: no distinctive string is reproduced, and 'the subtlety of the devil' is available to any preacher. The row exists because the chapter's two halves are hard to relate without it and 2 Corinthians 11:3 relates them exactly. The 1830 spells 'subtlety' where the KJV spells 'subtilty'.
links.whyNot: The Genesis material at 12:21-26 is introduced by Antionah's question, not by Alma, so the chapter's Eden turn has an internal cause and does not require a mediating text.
links.text: But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.

pericopes.text: Now this was a plan of thine adversary, and he hath exercised his power in thee. Now I would that ye should remember that what I say unto thee, I say unto all.

And behold, I say unto you all, that this was a snare of the adversary, which he hath laid to catch this people, that he might bring you into subjection unto him, that he might encircle you about with his chains, that he might chain you down to everlasting destruction, according to the power of his captivity.

provenance.other: “Taken captive by him at his will” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 2:26; 'snare of the devil' occurs in exactly two, 1 Timothy 3:7 and 2 Timothy 2:26. “Chains of darkness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 2:4; the Book of Mormon's 'chains of Hell' occurs in none.
provenance.significance: One verse supplies three of Alma 12's controlling images and supplies them in its own order. 2 Timothy 2:26: a snare of the devil, out of which men must recover themselves, 'who are taken captive by him at his will'. Alma 12:6: 'this was a snare of the adversary, which he hath laid to catch this people, that he might bring you into subjection unto him'. Alma 12:11: 'they are taken captive by the Devil, and led by his will down to destruction'. Alma 12:17: 'according to the power and captivity of Satan; he having subjected them according to his will'. Snare, captivity, and the captor's will, three times across eleven verses, from a verse that has all three in eight words. The chains are the one element Paul does not supply; 'chains of hell' is not a KJV phrase, and its nearest sources are 2 Peter 2:4's chains of darkness and Jude 6's everlasting chains, both of which bind angels awaiting judgment rather than men.
provenance.alternative: 1 Timothy 3:7's snare of the devil is the same phrase in a different argument, about a bishop's reputation.

links.note: No single run is long, but the same eight-word KJV sentence is drawn on three times in one discourse and each time a different element of it surfaces. That is Hays's criterion of recurrence doing the work rather than volume. Held at high; certain would require a verbatim clause, and the Book of Mormon paraphrases throughout.
links.text: And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will.

pericopes.text: Now when Alma had spoken these words, Zeezrom began to tremble more exceedingly, for he was convinced more and more of the power of God; and he was also convinced that Alma and Amulek had a knowledge of him, for he was convinced that they knew the thoughts and intents of his heart: for power was given unto them that they might know of these things, according to the spirit of prophecy.

provenance.other: “The thoughts and intents of the heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 4:12. “Spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 19:10, adjudicated at Alma 10:12.
provenance.significance: Six words of a KJV singleton, and the singleton turns out to be the seam of the whole chapter. Hebrews 4:12 says the word of God is 'sharper than any twoedged sword … and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart'; Alma 12:7 says Alma and Amulek 'knew the thoughts and intents of his heart'. What makes this more than a borrowed phrase is where Hebrews 4:12 sits: it closes the argument that began at Hebrews 3:7 with 'harden not your hearts, as in the provocation' and ran through 'they shall not enter into my rest'. Alma 12 takes the end of that passage here and the beginning of it at 12:33-37, and hardening of the heart is its subject throughout the intervening verses (12:10, 12:11, 12:13). So the chapter is not quoting Hebrews twice; it is working through Hebrews 3:7-4:12 as a unit, from the far end backwards. Hebrews's discerning sword is also worth holding beside the flaming sword of Genesis 3:24 that Antionah will raise at 12:21 — two swords that keep men from something, one from the tree and one from the rest of God.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 2:10-11's 'the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God' is the other candidate for divine knowledge of a man's inward state and was the machine's proposal; it has neither noun.

links.note: A six-word KJV singleton reproduced exactly, with 'their' for 'the' as the new setting requires. Recorded at high; the strength of the row is less its own length than the fact that it identifies the source passage the rest of the chapter will quote at 12:33 and 12:35, which is where Hardy's apparatus also points.
links.text: For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

pericopes.text: And Zeezrom began to inquire of them diligently, that he might know more concerning the kingdom of God. And he saith unto Alma, What does this mean which Amulek hath spoken concerning the resurrection of the dead, that all shall rise from the dead, both the just and the unjust, and are brought to stand before God, to be judged according to their works?

And now Alma began to expound these things unto him, saying, It is given unto many to know the mysteries of God; nevertheless they are laid under a strict command, that they shall not impart only according to the portion of his word, which he doth grant unto the children of men, according to the heed and diligence which they give unto him;

provenance.other: “To know the mysteries” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 13:11 and Luke 8:10, which are the same saying; Matthew has 'the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven' and Luke 'of the kingdom of God'. 'The mysteries of God' as such is 1 Corinthians 4:1's phrase.
provenance.significance: Alma 12:9-11 is Matthew 13:11-12 expounded. Matthew: 'it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given. For whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance: but whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken away even that he hath.' Alma: it is given to many to know the mysteries of God; he that will not harden his heart is given 'the greater portion of the word, until … they know them in full'; he that will harden his heart is given 'the lesser portion of the word, until they know nothing concerning his mysteries.' The graduated economy — more to those who have, less to those who have not, until nothing — is Matthew's parable-theory verbatim in its logic, with one substitution that is the Book of Mormon's own doctrine: Matthew leaves the cause of the difference unstated and Alma names it as hardening the heart, which is the term he has taken from Hebrews 3 and will quote outright at 12:33. The two sources are being welded: Matthew supplies the mechanism, Hebrews supplies its cause.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 4:1's 'stewards of the mysteries of God' supplies Alma's noun phrase exactly but none of the graduated logic.

links.note: Five words shared with Matthew 13:11 and the whole of 13:12's argument reproduced without its wording. The 1830's 'that they shall not impart only according to the portion of his word' is the strict-command clause Matthew does not have; the 1920 keeps it. Held at high on the combination of a two-verse phrase and a reproduced argument.
links.text: He answered and said unto them, Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given.

pericopes.text: and therefore he that will harden his heart, the same receiveth the lesser portion of the word; and he that will not harden his heart, to him is given the greater portion of the word, until it is given unto him to know the mysteries of God, until they know them in full;

and he that will harden his heart, to him is given the lesser portion of the word, until they know nothing concerning his mysteries; and then they are taken captive by the Devil, and led by his will down to destruction. Now this is what is meant by the chains of Hell;
and Amulek hath spoken plainly concerning death, and being raised from this mortality to a state of immortality, and being brought before the bar of God, to be judged according to our works.
Then if our hearts have been hardened, yea, if we have hardened our hearts against the word, insomuch that it hath not been found in us, then will our state be awful, for then we shall be condemned:

for our words will condemn us, yea, all our work will condemn us; we shall not be found spotless; and our thoughts will also condemn us; and in this awful state, we shall not durst look up to our God; and we would fain be glad if we could command the rocks and the mountains to fall upon us, to hide us from his presence.

provenance.route: Hosea 10:8 → Revelation 6:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Hide us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 6:16. “Fall on us” occurs in exactly three, Hosea 10:8, Luke 23:30 and Revelation 6:16 — the same cry in three places. Only Revelation 6:16 adds rocks to the mountains, and only Revelation 6:16 asks to be hidden rather than covered.
provenance.significance: mediation-check.py was run on this verse against Hosea 10:8 and returns three decisive points for Revelation 6:16, on the two words that matter: Alma 12:14 has 'the rocks and the mountains' where Hosea and Luke have mountains and hills, and it has 'to hide us from his presence' where Hosea and Luke have 'Cover us'. So the Old Testament oracle reaches Alma 12 through John's use of it and not directly, which is what OT-via-NT records. The metalepsis is in who is speaking. In Hosea it is Israel under Assyrian judgment; in Luke it is the daughters of Jerusalem, told what they will say; in Revelation 6:15-16 it is 'the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains' hiding in the rocks from the wrath of the Lamb. Alma is addressing a city run by paid judges and expert lawyers, and the verse he reaches for is the one whose speakers are the powerful.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 2:19's 'they shall go into the holes of the rocks … for fear of the LORD' has rocks and hiding but no address to them, and Revelation 6:15 is quoting it.

links.note: 'We would fain be glad if we could command the rocks and the mountains to fall upon us, to hide us from his presence.' Not a quotation — the Book of Mormon supplies its own frame and its own verb — but the two elements that separate Revelation from its own sources are both present. High, on the mediation result rather than on run length.
links.text: And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb:

pericopes.text: But this cannot be; we must come forth and stand before him in his glory, and in his power, and in his might, majesty, and dominion, and acknowledge to their everlasting shame, that all his judgments are just; that he is just in all his works, and that he is merciful unto the children of men, and that he hath all power to save every man that believeth on his name, and bringeth forth fruit mete for repentance.

provenance.other: “Fruits meet for repentance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:8. The Book of Mormon's 1830 reading is 'fruit mete for repentance', which preserves the KJV's 'meet' under a variant spelling and makes the borrowing plainer than a modern text does. 'Majesty and dominion' occurs in no KJV verse; Jude 1:25's doxology has 'glory and majesty, dominion and power'.
provenance.significance: The second borrowing from John the Baptist's preaching in three chapters — Alma 10:20 has his 'Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand' from Matthew 3:2, and 12:15 has his demand for fruits from Matthew 3:8, six verses later in the same speech. Between them they take the Baptist's opening and his test, and both are given to Nephite preaching without attribution. Matthew 3:8's setting is worth recovering: it is addressed to Pharisees and Sadducees who have come to the baptism and are told not to plead descent from Abraham, 'for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham' — an argument from lineage refused, in a chapter whose speaker opened by reciting his own lineage back to Joseph (10:2-3).
provenance.alternative: Luke 3:8's 'fruits worthy of repentance' is the same demand in the parallel Gospel and does not have 'meet'.

links.note: Four words of a KJV singleton, with the 1830's spelling preserving the source word. The verse's first half, 'in his might, majesty, and dominion', is a doxological string with no single KJV source; Jude 1:25 has the nouns in a different order and is composited rather than claimed.
links.text: Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance:

pericopes.text: And now behold I say unto you, then cometh a death, even a second death, which is a spiritual death; then is a time that whosoever dieth in his sins, as to the temporal death, shall also die a spiritual death; yea, he shall die as to things pertaining unto righteousness;

then is the time when their torments shall be as a lake of fire and brimstone, whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever; and then is the time that they shall be chained down to an everlasting destruction, according to the power and captivity of Satan; he having subjected them according to his will.

provenance.other: “Ascendeth up for ever and ever” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:11, where it is the smoke of the torment of those who worship the beast. “Lake of fire and brimstone” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:10. “The second death” occurs in exactly four, all in Revelation, and 21:8 is the one that identifies it with the lake burning with fire and brimstone.
provenance.significance: Three KJV singletons and a four-verse phrase, all from one book, assembled into a single sentence: 'their torments shall be as a lake of fire and brimstone, whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever'. Revelation 14:11 supplies the ascending and the word 'torment'; Revelation 20:10 supplies the lake; Revelation 21:8 supplies the equation with the second death that Alma 12:16 has just made. What the Book of Mormon changes is the copula — Revelation's lake is a place and Alma's is a simile, 'their torments shall be AS a lake of fire and brimstone' — and that change is doctrinally load-bearing, since 12:16 has defined the second death as spiritual. The apparatus of Revelation is being kept and its literalism declined.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 19:3's 'her smoke rose up for ever and ever' is the other ascending-smoke verse and lacks 'ascendeth'.

links.note: The 1830's 'whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever' has the singular verb with a plural subject that the 1920 did not repair; the KJV's own 'ascendeth' governs the singular 'smoke', so the Book of Mormon has kept the source's verb and changed its subject. That is the sort of detail CONVENTIONS §8 asks to be flagged, and it is evidence of transcription rather than composition.
links.text: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

pericopes.text: Then I say unto you, they shall be as though there had been no redemption made; for they cannot be redeemed according to God’s justice; and they cannot die, seeing there is no more corruption.
Now it came to pass that when Alma had made an end of speaking these words, the people began to be more astonished;

provenance.other: “Made an end of speaking these words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 24:16. 'Made an end of speaking' without the object is common, in nine KJV verses; the four-word extension is what identifies the source.
provenance.significance: An eight-word verbatim run, and almost certainly not a borrowing from this verse in particular. The phrase is adjudicated in this catalogue at Jacob 3, and by Alma it has become the Book of Mormon's own narrative formula for closing a discourse — it appears in this exact form at Mosiah 8:19 and Alma 44:10 as well, and the shorter 'made an end of speaking' fifteen times. The row is written because Alma is a new book and a reader of Alma 12:19 shown nothing here would be told there is no contact, when in fact the sentence is a KJV singleton reproduced whole. What the catalogue claims is that the formula entered the text from 1 Samuel 24:16, not that this occurrence reaches for David and Saul.

links.note: Recorded across the book boundary under ADJUDICATING §4, with the argument left where it was made at Jacob 3:14. Moderate, and the confidence is about the formula's origin rather than about this verse's intention; context is scored 2 because 1 Samuel 24's scene has nothing to do with Alma 12's.
links.whyNot: A house formula by this point in the text; its recurrence proves the phrase was absorbed early, not that Alma 12:19 alludes to Saul weeping at the mouth of a cave.
links.text: And it came to pass, when David had made an end of speaking these words unto Saul, that Saul said, Is this thy voice, my son David? And Saul lifted up his voice, and wept.

pericopes.text: but there was one Antionah, who was a chief ruler among them, come forth and said unto him, What is this that thou hast said, that man should rise from the dead and be changed from this mortal to an immortal state, that the soul can never die?

What does this Scripture mean, which saith that God placed Cherubims and a flaming sword on the east of the garden of Eden, lest our first parents should enter and partake of the fruit of the tree of life, and live forever? And thus we see that there was no possible chance that they should live forever.

provenance.other: “Flaming sword” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:24, and “east of the garden of Eden” likewise occurs in exactly one, the same verse. The 1830 keeps the KJV's double plural 'Cherubims'.
provenance.significance: Antionah introduces it as a quotation — 'What does this Scripture mean, which saith …' — which makes this one of the few places in the Book of Mormon where a biblical verse is cited as a text to be construed rather than absorbed into the narration. What he then does with it is the argument: Genesis 3:22 gives God's reason for the expulsion ('lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever') and Antionah reads the two verses together to conclude 'there was no possible chance that they should live forever' — that is, that immortality was foreclosed, and Amulek's resurrection doctrine is therefore false. The trap is the same shape as Zeezrom's at 11:34: a real scripture, correctly quoted, made to prove a conclusion it does not carry. Alma's answer at 12:23-26 turns the same two verses around, arguing that the flaming sword is what makes redemption possible rather than what forecloses it.
provenance.alternative: Ezekiel 28:14-16's cherub in Eden is the other biblical Eden guardian and has no sword.

links.note: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 3:22-24 at this verse. Two KJV singletons and the source's own word order, presented by the text as a quotation of scripture. Certain, and one of the very few rows in these three chapters where attestation is scored at the top: this is not a link that needed finding.
links.text: So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.

pericopes.text: Now Alma saith unto him, This is the thing which I was about to explain. Now we see that Adam did fall by partaking of the forbidden fruit, according to the word of God; and thus we see, that by his fall, that all mankind became a lost and a fallen people.

provenance.other: 'Forbidden fruit' is not a KJV phrase; Genesis 3:6 has 'she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat', and the prohibition is at 2:17. The Book of Mormon's noun comes from English usage — Milton's, by way of two centuries of preaching — and not from the Authorized Version.
provenance.significance: This is the summary verse of Alma's answer and it carries almost no biblical wording, which is worth recording rather than dressing up. 'Adam did fall by partaking of the forbidden fruit … all mankind became a lost and a fallen people' is doctrine stated in the Book of Mormon's own vocabulary, using a phrase the KJV does not contain, about a narrative the KJV does. The verse is a reference to Genesis 3 rather than a borrowing from it, and CONVENTIONS §6a's instruction in that case is to say so and decide on our own evidence.
provenance.alternative: Romans 5:12-19's 'by one man sin entered into the world' is the standard New Testament formulation of this doctrine and the Book of Mormon does not use its wording either.

links.note: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 3:6-19 here, and the reference is right as a study edition's pointer: the reader of Alma 12:22 needs Genesis 3. As a claim about dependence it is thin, and the catalogue records it at moderate with the verbal case stated honestly as nearly absent. kjvSpecific is 'no': there is no wording to test, and 'forbidden fruit' is if anything evidence against a KJV route.
links.whyNot: No distinctive string is shared, and the one distinctive phrase Alma 12:22 does use is not in the KJV at all. The row rests on the chapter's explicit engagement with Genesis 3 at 12:21 and 12:23, not on this verse.
links.text: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.

pericopes.text: And now behold, I say unto you, that if it had been possible for Adam for to have partaken of the fruit of the tree of life at that time, that there would have been no death, and the word would have been void, making God a liar: for he said, If thou eat, thou shalt surely die.—

provenance.other: “Thou shalt surely die” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses; Genesis 2:17 is the first and the only one attached to eating. Alma 12:23 compresses 'in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die' to 'If thou eat, thou shalt surely die.'
provenance.significance: The quotation is introduced with 'for he said', so the text is claiming to cite, and the argument depends on the citation being exact enough to bind: if Adam had reached the tree of life, 'the word would have been void, making God a liar'. That is an argument about the reliability of a spoken sentence, and it needs the sentence. The counterpart is Genesis 3:4, where the serpent says 'Ye shall not surely die' — the KJV's one contradiction of this verse, and the first lie in scripture. Alma 12 has spent its first six verses on a liar whose plan was 'as to the subtlety of the Devil', and it now argues that the alternative to Adam's death would have made God the liar instead. Neither text says this. The pair says it.
provenance.alternative: Genesis 3:3's 'lest ye die' is Eve's looser report of the same prohibition and is not what Alma quotes.

links.note: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 2:17 here. Four words verbatim from a phrase the KJV uses ten times, with the identifying context supplied by the conditional 'if thou eat'. High rather than certain because the reproduced string is not itself rare; what makes the source unmistakable is that the verse names the speaker and the condition.
links.text: But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.

pericopes.text: And we see that death comes upon mankind, yea, the death which has been spoken of by Amulek, which is the temporal death; nevertheless there was a space granted unto man, in which he might repent; therefore this life became a probationary state; a time to prepare to meet God; a time to prepare for that endless state, which has been spoken of by us, which is after the resurrection of the dead.

Now if it had not been for the plan of redemption, which was laid from the foundation of the world, there could have been no resurrection of the dead; but there was a plan of redemption laid, which shall bring to pass the resurrection of the dead, of which has been spoken.

provenance.other: “From the foundation of the world” occurs in exactly six KJV verses. Only Revelation 13:8 attaches it to redemption — 'the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world' — and only Matthew 25:34 to a kingdom prepared.
provenance.significance: 'The plan of redemption, which was laid from the foundation of the world.' The phrase is common enough that it could not identify a source by itself, but the collocation with redemption is not: of the six occurrences, one joins the formula to the Lamb's death and the rest join it to election, to a kingdom, to secrets, or to the blood of the prophets. Alma 12:25 and 12:30 both use it of a plan of redemption 'prepared from the foundation of the world', which is the Revelation sense, and the Book of Mormon's contribution is the noun 'plan' — a word the KJV never uses in this connection at all.
provenance.alternative: Ephesians 1:4's 'chosen us in him before the foundation of the world' and 1 Peter 1:20's 'foreordained before the foundation of the world' both read 'before' rather than 'from', which is not Alma's preposition.

links.note: An echo, recorded at moderate. The preposition decides between the two families — 'from' is Revelation's and Matthew's, 'before' is Paul's and Peter's — and Alma has 'from'. That is a small finding but it is a real one, and it is the kind that a rarity count alone would have missed.
links.text: And all that dwell upon the earth shall worship him, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.

pericopes.text: And now behold, if it were possible that our first parents could have went forth and partaken of the tree of life, they would have been forever miserable, having no preparatory state; and thus the plan of redemption would have been frustrated, and the word of God would have been void, taking none effect.

provenance.other: “The word of God of none effect” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 7:13. 'Of none effect' alone occurs in exactly seven.
provenance.significance: 'The plan of redemption would have been frustrated, and the word of God would have been void, taking none effect.' Six of the seven KJV 'of none effect' verses are about vows, counsel, faith, a promise or a cross; the seventh joins the phrase to the word of God, and it is Jesus's charge that the scribes have made the word of God of none effect 'through your tradition'. Alma is arguing against a chief ruler who has just quoted scripture at him (12:21), and the phrase he reaches for is the one Jesus uses against professional interpreters who quote scripture to nullify it. Whether the writer heard that is not decidable; the reader who recovers Mark 7:13 hears it, and the charge fits Antionah exactly. Note also that 12:23 has already made the same point in different words — 'the word would have been void, making God a liar' — so the verse is a second attempt at a sentence, and the second attempt is the one that lands on the KJV's phrase.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 15:6's parallel reads 'the commandment of God of none effect', with the same charge and a different noun; Alma's noun is Mark's.

links.note: Five words of a KJV singleton. High rather than certain because 'of none effect' was ordinary legal English and the full phrase could be assembled without Mark; what argues for Mark 7:13 is the noun — 'the word of God' rather than 'the commandment' — and the polemical setting the two passages share.
links.text: Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.

pericopes.text: But behold, it was not so; but it was appointed unto man that they must die; and after death, they must come to judgment; even that same judgment of which we have spoken, which is the end.

provenance.other: “It is appointed unto men once to die” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:27, and the verse continues 'but after this the judgment'.
provenance.significance: 'It was appointed unto man that they must die; and after death, they must come to judgment; even that same judgment of which we have spoken, which is the end.' Both halves of Hebrews 9:27, in order, with 'once' dropped and the tense moved into the past because Alma is narrating the decree rather than stating the rule. The dropping of 'once' is not incidental in this chapter: 12:16 has just established a second death, and a source verse insisting that men die once would have been awkward. So the Book of Mormon takes the sentence and removes the one word that would have contradicted the doctrine it is building — which is the kind of small, deliberate-looking adjustment that a catalogue exists to notice and cannot interpret.
provenance.alternative: Ecclesiastes 12:14's judgment of every work is the Old Testament backing and is used at Alma 11:44; it has no appointment to die.

links.note: Nine words of a KJV singleton in sequence across two clauses. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his thirty-six, and catalogued as a quotation on the rarity and the completeness of the reproduction rather than on length. This is the chapter's third contact with Hebrews, after 4:12 at 12:7 and before 3:8-11 at 12:33-35.
links.text: And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:

pericopes.text: And after God had appointed that these things should come unto man, behold, then he saw that it was expedient that man should know concerning the things whereof he had appointed unto them;
therefore he sent angels to converse with them, which caused men to behold of his glory.

And they began from that time forth to call on his name; therefore God conversed with men, and made known unto them the plan of redemption, which had been prepared from the foundation of the world; and this he made known unto them, according to their faith and repentance, and their holy works;

wherefore he gave commandments unto men, they having first transgressed the first commandments as to things which were temporal, and becoming as Gods, knowing good from evil, placing themselves in a state to act, or being placed in a state to act, according to their wills and pleasures, whether to do evil or to do good;

provenance.other: “As gods, knowing good and evil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:5. Genesis 3:22 has the same idea in the singular — 'the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil'. Alma 12:31 reads 'becoming as Gods, knowing good from evil'.
provenance.significance: Five words of a KJV singleton, altered by one preposition: 'good and evil' becomes 'good from evil'. Genesis 3:5 is the serpent's promise, and Genesis 3:22 is God confirming that it came true; the Book of Mormon takes the serpent's phrasing, in the plural, and reports it as accomplished fact without comment on the speaker.
