The psalm forbids three things in order — trusting in oppression, growing vain by robbery, setting the heart on increasing riches — and Alma 17:14 reports a people who do all three, in reverse: 'their hearts were set upon riches, or upon gold, and silver, and precious stones; yet they sought to obtain these things by murdering and plundering, that they might not labor for them with their own hands'. The last clause is the psalm's implied contrast made explicit, since Psalm 62 sets the robber against the man whose expectation is from God alone. This is the kind of link the n-gram stream cannot see: the agreement is split across a clause boundary and reordered, and the machine proposed nothing on this verse but Revelation's merchandise list.
provenance.alternative: Proverbs 23:5, 'wilt thou set thine eyes upon that which is not?', is the other KJV verse about fixing the self on riches, but it is about wealth's disappearance and shares no robbery.

links.note: 'Their hearts were set upon riches, or upon gold, and silver, and precious stones; yet they sought to obtain these things by murdering and plundering.' Two KJV singletons out of one psalm verse, inverted from prohibition into description, with Revelation 18:12's singleton triad supplying the contents of the treasure. The machine ranked Revelation 18:12 here and it belongs — but as the list only; the sentence's argument is the psalm's.

pericopes.text: thus they were a very indolent people, many of whom did worship idols, and the curse of God had fell upon them because of the traditions of their fathers; notwithstanding, the promises of the Lord were extended unto them, on the conditions of repentance;

therefore this was the cause for which the sons of Mosiah had undertaken the work, that perhaps they might bring them unto repentance; that perhaps they might bring them to know of the plan of redemption;
therefore they separated themselves one from another, and went forth among them every man alone, according to the word and power of God, which was given unto him.

Now Ammon being the chief among them, or rather he did administer unto them; and he departed from them, after havgn blessed them according to their several stations, having imparted the word of God unto them, or administered unto them before his departure; and thus they took their several journeys throughout the land.
And Ammon went to the land of Ishmael, the land being called after the sons of Ishmael, which also became Lamanites.

And as Ammon entered the land of Ishmael, the Lamanites took him and bound him, as was their custom, to bind all the Nephites which fell into their hands, and carry them before the king; and thus it was left to the pleasure of the king to slay them, or to retain them in captivity, or to cast them into prison, or to cast them out of his land, according to his will and pleasure;
and thus Ammon was carried before the king which was over the land of Ishmael; and his name was Lamoni; and he was a descendant of Ishmael.
And the king inquired of Ammon if it were his desires to dwell in the land among the Lamanites, or among his people?
And Ammon said unto him, Yea, I desire to dwell among this people for a time; yea, and perhaps until the day I die.
And it came to pass that king Lamoni was much pleased with Ammon, and caused that his bands should be loosed; and he would that Ammon should take one of his daughters to wife.

But Ammon saith unto him, Nay, but I will be thy servant; therfore Ammon became a servant to king Lamoni. And it came to pass that he was set, among other servants, to watch the flocks of Lamoni, according to the custom of the Lamanites.

links.text: But if thou return to the city, and say unto Absalom, I will be thy servant, O king; as I have been thy father’s servant hitherto, so will I now also be thy servant: then mayest thou for me defeat the counsel of Ahithophel.

provenance.other: "I will be thy servant" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 2 Samuel 15:34. It is David's instruction to Hushai: go to the usurper, say this sentence, and from inside his household defeat the counsel of Ahithophel. Alma 17:25 has the sentence entire — 'Nay, but I will be thy servant' — spoken by a man who has just refused the king's daughter and is about to enter the king's service.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one offer of personal service to a king is a planted agent's cover story, and the Book of Mormon gives it to Ammon at the moment Ammon becomes exactly that. The reversal is precise. Hushai says it to a usurper in order to destroy him; Ammon says it to a legitimate king in order to convert him. Hushai declines nothing; Ammon declines a marriage that would have made him the king's kin, and takes the lower place instead, which is what puts him among the servants at the water of Sebus and gives the rest of the chapter its plot. Two more contacts with the same chapter of 2 Samuel follow at 17:29 and 17:31 — see the link there — so this is not one stray phrase but a sustained use of the Absalom narrative for a story about winning a court from within it.

links.note: 'But Ammon saith unto him, Nay, but I will be thy servant.' A five-word KJV singleton, and the machine did find it, at rarity 1.33 — low, because the words are individually common; the singleton count is what makes the case. Alma drops Hushai's vocative 'O king', which the situation supplies. The 1830 present-tense 'saith' for the narrative past, regularized to 'said' in 1920, is the first edition's habit and carries nothing.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after he had been in the service of the king three days, that as he was, with the Lamanitish servants, a going forth with their flocks, to the place of water, which was called the water of Sebus; (and all the Lamanites drive their flocks hither, that they might have water;)

therefore as Ammon and the servants of the king were driving forth their flocks to this place of water, behold, a certain number of the Lamanites who had been with their flocks to water, stood and scattered the flocks of Ammon, and the servants of the king, and they scattered them insomuch that they fled many ways.

Now the servants of the king began to murmur, saying: Now the king will slay us, as he has our brethren, because their flocks were scattered by the wickedness of these men. And they began to weep exceedingly, saying, Behold our flocks are scattered already.

Now they wept because of the fear of being slain. Now when Ammon saw this, his heart was swollen within him, with joy; for, said he, I will shew forth my power unto these my fellow servants, or the power which is in me, in restoring these flocks unto the king, that I may win the hearts of these my fellow servants, that I may lead them to believe in my words.

links.text: And on this manner did Absalom to all Israel that came to the king for judgment: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

provenance.other: "stole the hearts" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 2 Samuel 15:6, and the King James Bible has no other idiom for capturing a body of men's loyalty by personal manner. Alma 17:29 reads 'that I may win the hearts of these my fellow servants, that I may lead them to believe in my words'. Two verses later Ammon 'flattered them by his words' — and 'flattered' as a finite verb occurs in no KJV verse at all, though the KJV's fourteen instances of flattering speech (Psalm 12:2-3, Proverbs 2:16, 7:5, 7:21, 20:19, 26:28, 28:23, 29:5, 1 Thessalonians 2:5 and others) are without exception condemnations.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's third contact with 2 Samuel 15 and the one that shows what the first two were for. Absalom's method is set out in 15:2-6: he intercepts men who have a grievance against the king's administration, speaks to them personally, and so steals their hearts; then, at 15:34, David counters by planting Hushai with the words 'I will be thy servant'. Alma 17 gives Ammon both halves. He speaks Hushai's sentence at 17:25 to get inside the household, and he performs Absalom's manoeuvre at 17:29 on the king's own servants, who are at that moment in fear of the king and have precisely the grievance Absalom farmed. The single word changed is the verb. Absalom stole hearts; Ammon proposes to win them — and then the narrator, two verses later, says he flattered them, which is the KJV's word for what Absalom did and never for anything good. The Book of Mormon has taken the Bible's model of seduction into rebellion and made it the model of conversion, without quite laundering the vocabulary.

links.note: 'I will shew forth my power unto these my fellow servants … that I may win the hearts of these my fellow servants, that I may lead them to believe in my words.' The KJV's one heart-stealing sentence, with an honest verb in place of the dishonest one, applied to the same object — the men who serve a king and are disaffected from him. Offered under CONVENTIONS §0a: the shared string is short and the argument is cumulative across 17:25, 17:29 and 17:31 rather than resting on any single run. The machine found 17:25 and nothing here, which is what a split and reworded agreement looks like to a contiguous-window stream.

pericopes.text: Now these were the thoughts of Ammon, when he saw the afflictions of those which he termed to be his brethren.

And it came to pass that he flattered them by his words, saying: My brethren, be of good cheer and let us go in search of the flocks, and we will gather them together, and bring them back unto the place of water; and thus we will reserve the flocks unto the king, and he will not slay us.

And it came to pass that they went in search of the flocks, and they did follow Ammon, and they rushed forth with much swiftness, and did head the flocks of the king, and did gather them together again, to the place of water.

And those men again stood to scatter their flocks; but Ammon saith unto his brethren, Encircle the flocks round about, that they flee not; and I go and contend with these men which do scatter our flocks.
Therefore they did as Ammon commanded them, and he went forth and stood to contend with those which stood by the waters of Sebus; and they were not in number a very few;

therefore they did not fear Ammon, for they supposed that one of their men could slay him, according to their pleasure, for they knew not that the Lord had promised Mosiah that he would deliver his sons out of their hands; neither did they know any thing concerning the Lord; therefore they delighted in the destruction of their brethren; and for this cause they stood to scatter the flocks of the king.

But Ammon stood forth and began to cast stones at them with his sling; yea, with mighty power he did sling stones amongst them; and thus he slew a certain number of them, insomuch that they began to be astonished at his power; nevertheless they were angry because of the slain of their brethren, and they were determined that he should fall; therefore, seeing that they could not hit him with their stones, they came forth with clubs to slay him.

links.text: So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and smote the Philistine, and slew him; but there was no sword in the hand of David.

provenance.other: "with a sling" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 1 Samuel 17:50. "sling stones" occurs in exactly 2, Judges 20:16 — the seven hundred left-handed Benjamites who could sling at a hair's breadth 'and not miss' — and Zechariah 9:15. Alma 17:36 has both constructions in one sentence: 'began to cast stones at them with his sling; yea, with mighty power he did sling stones amongst them'.
provenance.significance: The sequence is 1 Samuel 17's, in 1 Samuel 17's order, and it is the order that carries the argument. Stones from a sling first; the enemy astonished; the champion killed and no one else — Alma 17:38 says in so many words that Ammon 'slew none save it were their leader', which is the whole point of David's combat, one death instead of a battle; and then a sword taken to the fallen body, David to sever a head at 17:51 and Ammon to sever arms at 17:37. Judges 20:16 supplies the marksmanship the story needs and the Book of Mormon inverts its detail: the Benjamite slingers cannot miss, and here it is the enemy who 'could not hit him with their stones'. What the Book of Mormon adds is the servants watching, which turns a duel into a demonstration — the reason Ammon gives at 17:29 for doing it at all.

links.note: 'Ammon stood forth and began to cast stones at them with his sling.' Catalogued as a conceptual allusion rather than a verbal one: the wording of the David combat is not reproduced, the sequence of it is, together with two rare sling constructions taken from the two KJV passages where slinging is done well. This is the chapter's most-noticed parallel and it is not ours; the Book of Mormon's own readers have read Ammon as David since the nineteenth century. Recorded at high because the sequence match is close and long, not because the verbal contact is.

pericopes.text: But behold, every man that lifted his club to smite Ammon, he smote off their arms with his sword; for he did withstand their blows by smiting their arms with the edge of his sword, insomuch that they began to be astonished, and began to flee before him; yea, and they were not few in number; and he caused them to flee by the strength of his arm.

links.text: And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest’s, and smote off his ear.

provenance.other: "smote off" occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses: Judges 5:26, where Jael smote off Sisera's head, and Matthew 26:51, where a disciple smote off the ear of the high priest's servant. Alma uses the phrase twice, at 17:37 and again at 17:39, and the 1830 reading at 17:39 is 'the arms which had been smote off' — the KJV's exact string, used as a participle. The 1920 edition corrected it to 'smitten off', which is better English and is no longer the King James phrase; and at 17:38 the 1830 'he smote off as many of their arms as was lifted against him' had no instrument, 1920 supplying 'with his sword'.
provenance.significance: The two KJV severings are a woman killing a sleeping general and a disciple defending his master in the garden, and the second is the one Jesus stops: put up thy sword. Ammon does it repeatedly, to men attacking a king's flocks, and the severed limbs are then carried in to the king 'for a testimony of the things which they had done' — the phrase Luke 9:5 gives the twelve for what they leave behind them in a town that will not hear. The Book of Mormon has assembled a missionary's credential out of the one sword-stroke the Gospels rebuke. The point is not that the writer intended the rebuke; it is that the King James Bible has almost no vocabulary for this act, and what little it has is attached to Gethsemane.

links.note: 'He smote off their arms with his sword; for he did withstand their blows by smiting their arms with the edge of his sword.' A two-verse KJV phrase, and the 1830 text has it in a form the modern edition no longer does — CONVENTIONS §8's case in reverse, where a later edition corrected the grammar and in doing so erased the borrowing. Catalogued at moderate: 'smote off' is short, and the direction of the correction is a better argument for the link than the phrase itself. The machine's candidate here, Psalm 89:43's 'the edge of his sword', is excluded at this verse.
links.whyNot: Two words, and they are the natural English for the action. A reader who thinks 'smote off' is simply what a KJV-formed writer would say when a limb comes away is not obliged to see Gethsemane behind it.

pericopes.text: Now six of them had fallen by the sling, but he slew none save it were their leader; and he smote off as many of their arms as was lifted against him, and they were not a few.

And when he had driven them afar off, he returned, and they watered their flocks and returned them to the pasture of the king, and then went in unto the king, bearing the arms which had been smote off by the sword of Ammon, of those who sought to slay him; and they were carried in unto the king, for a testimony of the things which they had done.
And it came to pass that king Lamoni caused that his servants should stand forth and testify to all the things which they had seen concerning the matter.

And when they had all testified to the things which they had seen, and he had learned of the faithfulness of Ammon in preserving his flocks, and also of his great power in contending against those who sought to slay him, he was astonished exceedingly, and saith, Surely, this is more than a man. Behold, is not this the Great Spirit which doth send such great punishments upon this people; because of their murders?

links.text: And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men.

provenance.other: "come down to us in the likeness of men" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Acts 14:11. Alma 18:4 has 'he hath come down at this time to preserve your lives', which shares 'come down' and nothing else; the case here is the shape of the scene, not the string.
provenance.significance: Acts 14 is the New Testament's one episode in which a crowd that has seen a missionary do something impossible concludes that a god has taken human form, and in which the missionary's first act is to deny it — 'Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you.' Alma 18 runs the same three beats in the same order: witnesses report what they saw (18:1-3), the king concludes 'Surely, this is more than a man … is not this the Great Spirit', and the missionary answers at 18:17, 'Behold, I am a man, and am thy servant.' Where Lystra ends with Paul barely restraining a sacrifice, Alma 18 turns the denial into the opening of a catechism: Ammon says he is a man and then, at 18:34, says what a man is — created after the image of God — which is the doctrine that makes the king's mistake intelligible rather than merely wrong.

links.note: 'Surely, this is more than a man. Behold, is not this the Great Spirit?' Catalogued as figural: the verbal contact with Acts 14:11 is a single phrase and the argument is the type-scene. The Book of Mormon's version is more theologically careful than the machine that found nothing here could register — Lamoni's servants at 18:3 say 'Whether he be the Great Spirit or a man, we know not', which is the Lystra crowd's question put as an open one.
links.whyNot: No run of KJV wording is reproduced. A reader may hold that a heathen king mistaking a wonder-worker for a god is a stock situation available to any nineteenth-century writer of missionary narrative, and that Acts 14 is one instance of it rather than the source.

pericopes.text: And they answered the king, and said, Whether he be the Great Spirit or a man, we know not; but this much we do know, that he cannot be slain by the enemies of the king; neither can they scatter the king’s flocks when he is with us, because of his expertness and great strength; therefore, we know that he is a friend to the king. And now, O king, we do not believe that a man hath such great power, for we know that he cannot be slain.

And now when the king heard these words, he said unto them, Now I know that it is the Great Spirit; and he hath come down at this time to preserve your lives, that I might not slay you as I did your brethren. Now this is the Great Spirit of which our fathers have spoken.

Now this was the tradition of Lamoni, which he had received from his father, that there was a Great Spirit. Notwithstanding they believed in a Great Spirit, they supposed that whatsoever they did, was right; nevertheless, Lamoni began to fear exceedingly, with fear lest he had done wrong in slaying his servants:
for he had slew many of them, because their brethren had scattered their flocks at the place of water; and thus because they had had their flocks scattered, they were slain.

Now it was the practice of the Lamanites, to stand by the waters of Sebus, to scatter the flocks of the people, that thereby they might drive away many that were scattered, unto their own land, it being a practice of plunder among them.
And it came to pass that king Lamoni inquired of his servants, saying: Where is this man that hath such great power?

And they saith unto him, Behold, he is feeding thy horses.—Now the king had commanded his servants previous to the time of the watering of their flocks, that they should prepare his horses and chariots, and conduct him forth to the land of Nephi: for there had been a great feast appointed at the land of Nephi, by the father of Lamoni, who was king over all the land.

Now when king Lamoni heard that Ammon was preparing his horses and his chariots, he was more astonished, because of the faithfulness of Ammon, saying: Surely, there has not been any servant among all my servants, that has been so faithful as this man; for even he doth remember all my commandments to execute them.
Now I surely know that this is the Great Spirit; and I would desire him that he come in unto me, but I durst not.

And it came to pass that when Ammon had made ready the horses and the chariots for the king and his servants, he went in unto the king, and he saw that the countenance of the king was changed; therefore he was about to return out of his presence;

links.text: Then the king’s countenance was changed, and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another.

provenance.other: "countenance was changed" occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Daniel 5:6 and Daniel 5:9, both of Belshazzar at the writing on the wall. "made a great feast" occurs in exactly 3 (Genesis 21:8, Esther 2:18, Daniel 5:1), and Alma 18:9 has just told us that 'there had been a great feast appointed at the land of Nephi' by the king's father, the king over all the land.
provenance.significance: This is where the chapter's frame declares itself. Daniel 5 opens with a king's great feast and turns on a king whose countenance is changed by something he cannot read, who then sends for a captive foreigner reputed to have the spirit of the gods, and offers him anything to interpret it. Alma 18 has the great feast at 18:9, the changed countenance at 18:12, the summons of the captive foreigner at 18:13, the offer of anything at 18:21, and the interpretation at 18:24-39. The Book of Mormon's alteration is that the thing the king cannot read is himself: what Ammon interprets is not a writing but the king's own thoughts, which is Daniel 2's problem transposed into Daniel 5's court — and Daniel 2:30's 'thoughts of thy heart' duly appears at Alma 18:20.

links.note: 'He saw that the countenance of the king was changed; therefore he was about to return out of his presence.' A two-verse KJV phrase belonging to one scene, and the scene is the one this chapter is built on. The machine proposed nothing at this verse; the Daniel frame is invisible to a contiguous n-gram stream because it is distributed across thirty verses and no single window is long.

pericopes.text: and one of the king’s servants said unto him, Rabbanah, which is, being interpreted, powerful, or great king, considering their kings to be powerful; and thus he said unto him, Rabbanah, the king desireth thee to stay;

links.text: Then Jesus turned, and saw them following, and saith unto them, What seek ye? They said unto him, Rabbi, (which is to say, being interpreted, Master,) where dwellest thou?

provenance.other: "which is being interpreted" occurs in exactly 5 KJV verses — Mark 5:41, Mark 15:22, Mark 15:34, John 1:41 and Acts 4:36 — and John 1:38 has the fuller 'which is to say, being interpreted'. In every one of them the formula glosses a Semitic word for a Greek reader. Alma 18:13's 'Rabbanah, which is, being interpreted, powerful, or great king' uses the KJV's gloss formula exactly, on a word built on the KJV's own 'Rabbi' (John 1:38) and 'Rabboni' (John 20:16, 'Rabboni; which is to say, Master').
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon here does the thing a translated record is supposed to do — carries a foreign word and glosses it — and it does it in the King James Bible's formula, on a word the King James Bible already glosses twice. The gloss even differs in the same way: John's Rabbi is rendered 'Master', a title of teaching, while Alma's Rabbanah is rendered 'powerful, or great king', with the narrator adding the reason, 'considering their kings to be powerful'. The second half of the verse thus does what no KJV gloss does, explaining not the word but the culture, and the effect is to mark the Lamanite title as the mistake it is: the servant addresses as a great king a man who has just refused to be one.

links.note: 'Rabbanah, which is, being interpreted, powerful, or great king.' Recorded for the formula and the coined word together. The Book of Mormon has one other transliterated-and-glossed term of this shape and no other place where the KJV's exact gloss formula appears; and John 20:16 supplies the rest of the scene, since Alma 18:14's next words are 'Ammon turned himself unto the king', where John has 'She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni'. 'Turned himself' occurs in five KJV verses and is not itself evidence.
links.whyNot: The gloss formula is the natural English for the operation and Joseph Smith's Bible supplied it; a reader may take Rabbanah as invented vocabulary given a KJV frame rather than as an allusion to any particular verse.

pericopes.text: therefore Ammon turned himself unto the king, and saith unto him, What wilt thou that I should do for thee, O king? And the king answered him not for the space of an hour, according to their time, for he knew not what he should say unto him.

links.text: Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was astonied for one hour, and his thoughts troubled him. The king spake, and said, Belteshazzar, let not the dream, or the interpretation thereof, trouble thee. Belteshazzar answered and said, My lord, the dream be to them that hate thee, and the interpretation thereof to thine enemies.

provenance.other: "for one hour" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Daniel 4:19 — 'was astonied for one hour, and his thoughts troubled him'. The Book of Mormon reads 'for the space of an hour, according to their time', which is not the KJV's string; "the space of an hour" occurs in no KJV verse. The claim here rests on the hour as a unit of stunned silence, which the King James Bible measures exactly once.
provenance.significance: The roles are exchanged, and the exchange is the point. In Daniel 4 it is the interpreter who is struck dumb for an hour, because he has understood the dream and it is terrible; the king has to prompt him to speak. In Alma 18 it is the king who cannot speak for an hour, 'for he knew not what he should say unto him', and the interpreter who has to prompt him — 'What desirest thou of me?' at 18:15. Daniel's hour is the silence of a man who knows; Lamoni's is the silence of a man who does not, and the chapter spends the next twenty verses supplying what he lacks. The 1830's added gloss 'according to their time' is the narrator's own, marking the hour as a foreign measure and so as a borrowed one.
provenance.alternative: The hour may be simply a round interval and no allusion at all; nothing else in Alma 18:14 is Daniel 4's.

links.note: 'And the king answered him not for the space of an hour, according to their time, for he knew not what he should say unto him.' Catalogued at moderate. The unit is the KJV's only hour of speechlessness and the surrounding chapter is demonstrably built on Daniel, which is why it is here at all; the wording is not reproduced, which is why it is not higher.

links.text: And Jesus answered and said unto him, What wilt thou that I should do unto thee? The blind man said unto him, Lord, that I might receive my sight.

provenance.route: Mark 10:51 + Mark 10:36 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: "What wilt thou that I should do" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Mark 10:51. Luke 18:41 has the same question with 'shall' for 'should'. Alma 18:14 reads 'What wilt thou that I should do for thee, O king?' — Mark's exact seven words, with 'for thee' in place of Mark's 'unto thee'; and 'for you' is precisely the preposition of Mark 10:36, 'What would ye that I should do for you', fifteen verses earlier in the same chapter.
provenance.significance: Mark 10 asks the question twice, and the two askings are the chapter's argument. At 10:36 it is put to James and John, who want the thrones on either side of Christ's glory, and the answer is a rebuke; at 10:51 it is put to blind Bartimaeus, who wants his sight, and the answer is a healing. Alma 18:14 fuses them — Mark 10:51's words with Mark 10:36's preposition — and puts the question to a man who is both: a king already on his throne, who is about to fall as if dead and rise seeing. Ammon asks it as a servant of the king, which reverses the direction of Mark entirely, since in both Marcan cases it is the master who asks and the suppliant who answers. Here the servant asks and the king cannot answer at all.

links.note: 'Therefore Ammon turned himself unto the king, and saith unto him, What wilt thou that I should do for thee, O king?' A seven-word KJV singleton with one preposition swapped for the one the same chapter uses. Catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the singleton rather than the length — well under Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six. The 1830 'saith' for the narrative past, regularized in 1920, is the first edition's habit throughout this chapter.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Ammon said unto him again, What desirest thou of me? But the king answered him not.

And it came to pass that Ammon, being filled with the spirit of God, therefore he perceived the thoughts of the king. And he saith unto him, Is it because that thou hast heard that I defended thy servants and thy flocks, and slew seven of their brethren with the sling, and with the sword, and smote off the arms of others, in order to defend thy flocks and thy servants; behold, is it this that causeth thy marvellings?
I say unto you, What is it, that thy marvellings are so great? Behold, I am a man, and am thy servant; therefore, whatsoever thou desirest which is right, that will I do.

Now when the king had heard these words, he marvelled again, for he beheld that Ammon could discern his thoughts; but notwithstanding this, king Lamoni did open his mouth, and said unto him, Who art thou? Art thou that Great Spirit, which knows all things?
Ammon answered and said unto him, I am not.

links.text: And they asked him, What then? Art thou Elias? And he saith, I am not. Art thou that prophet? And he answered, No.

provenance.other: Neither string is rare on its own — "Who art thou" occurs in exactly 18 KJV verses and "I am not" occurs in exactly 46 — but John 1:21 is the only KJV verse containing both, and John 1:19-21 is the only KJV passage in which the question 'Who art thou?' is answered with the words 'I am not'. Alma 18:18-19 is that exchange: 'Who art thou? Art thou that Great Spirit, which knows all things? Ammon answered and said unto him, I am not.'
provenance.significance: The forerunner's denial is the model, and it is the right model. John's three refusals — not the Christ, not Elias, not that prophet — clear the ground for the one he then points to; the questioners want to know who he is and he will only tell them who he is not. Ammon does the same and then does what John does next: having denied being the Great Spirit, he spends 18:24-39 identifying the God he is not, ending with 'the coming of Christ'. The chapter has given a missionary the Baptist's answer, and the answer works the same way — the denial is not modesty but the first move of the sermon.

links.note: 'Art thou that Great Spirit, which knows all things? Ammon answered and said unto him, I am not.' Three words, and they are three of the commonest in the King James Bible; the case is entirely structural, which is why it is at moderate. What makes it more than a coincidence of ordinary English is that the KJV joins this question to this answer exactly once, and the Book of Mormon joins them in the same order and to the same end.
links.whyNot: 'I am not' is not a borrowing in any ordinary sense. A reader may reasonably say that a man denying he is a god will say it in these words in any English, and that John 1 is a parallel rather than a source.

pericopes.text: And the king saith How knowest thou the thoughts of my heart? Thou mayest speak boldly, and tell me concerning these things; and also tell me by what power ye slew and smote off the arms of my brethren, that scattered my flocks.

links.text: But as for me, this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living, but for their sakes that shall make known the interpretation to the king, and that thou mightest know the thoughts of thy heart.

provenance.other: "thoughts of thy heart" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Daniel 2:30. The first-person form "the thoughts of my heart" occurs in exactly 1, Job 17:11, where it means a man's own broken purposes and not another's knowledge of them. Alma 18:20 reads 'How knowest thou the thoughts of my heart?' — Daniel's phrase turned into the king's question.
provenance.significance: Daniel 2:30 is the sentence in which the interpreter refuses the credit: the secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living. Alma 18 gives Lamoni the question that sentence answers, and gives Ammon the same refusal in his own idiom — 'Behold, I am a man' at 18:17, and at 18:35 'a portion of that Spirit dwelleth in me, which giveth me knowledge, and also power', which is Daniel's disclaimer with the source of the knowledge named. The whole exchange is the Daniel 2 audience run backwards: there the king demands that the wise man produce the thought, here the wise man produces it unasked and the king demands to know how. And the answer, in both books, is that the thought was never the interpreter's to see.

links.note: 'How knowest thou the thoughts of my heart?' A KJV singleton put in the mouth of the king it was originally spoken to. It arrives with the rest of the Daniel frame set at 18:12, and with the two verses at 18:16 and 18:18 in which Ammon 'perceived the thoughts of the king' and 'could discern his thoughts'. The Book of Mormon's own standing phrase for this, 'the thoughts and intents of the heart' from Hebrews 4:12, appears twelve verses later at 18:32 and is adjudicated elsewhere; it is a different phrase with a different source, and the distinction is worth keeping.

pericopes.text: And now if thou wilt tell me concerning these things, whatsoever thou desirest, I will give unto thee; and if it were needed, I would guard thee with my armies; but I know that thou art more powerful than all they; nevertheless, whatsoever thou desirest of me, I will grant it unto thee.

links.text: And I have heard of thee, that thou canst make interpretations, and dissolve doubts: now if thou canst read the writing, and make known to me the interpretation thereof, thou shalt be clothed with scarlet, and have a chain of gold about thy neck, and shalt be the third ruler in the kingdom.

provenance.other: The King James Bible has three scenes of a king offering an open-ended reward: Daniel 5:16-17, where the interpreter answers 'Let thy gifts be to thyself, and give thy rewards to another'; Mark 6:22-23, Herod's oath to the dancing girl, 'Ask of me whatsoever thou wilt, and I will give it thee … unto the half of my kingdom'; and Esther 5:3 and 5:6, 'What is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom'. No single one of the three is verbally reproduced at Alma 18:21; what is reproduced is the offer and the refusal that follows it.
provenance.significance: Alma 18:21 makes the offer twice in one verse — 'whatsoever thou desirest, I will give unto thee … whatsoever thou desirest of me, I will grant it unto thee' — and adds the one thing the biblical kings do not, an army: 'if it were needed, I would guard thee with my armies'. Ammon's answer at 18:22 is Daniel's answer in substance: he asks for nothing the king can give, only that the king hearken. In Daniel the refusal of the gifts is what proves the interpretation is not for sale; in Alma it is what turns the audience into a conversion. The one biblical parallel the chapter conspicuously does not take is Herod's, where the open promise is kept and a prophet's head is the price — and Alma 18 is a chapter in which a king's rash killing of servants (18:6) is what everyone in the room is afraid of.
provenance.alternative: Esther 5:3, if the emphasis is on a petitioner admitted to a king's presence and offered anything; but Esther's petitioner is inside the court and Ammon is a foreign captive, which is Daniel's position.

links.note: 'And now if thou wilt tell me concerning these things, whatsoever thou desirest, I will give unto thee.' Recorded as a conceptual allusion to Daniel 5:16-17 within the Daniel frame established at 18:12 and confirmed at 18:20; the wording belongs to no one of the three KJV reward-offers, and this row would not stand alone. What it adds to the frame is the refusal, which is the move that distinguishes Daniel from every courtier around him and Ammon from every servant around him.
links.whyNot: An open-ended royal offer is a folktale commonplace and the KJV has three of its own. Without the changed countenance at 18:12 and the thoughts of the heart at 18:20 there would be no reason to prefer Daniel 5 here, and a reader who declines the frame should decline this row with it.

pericopes.text: Now Ammon being wise, yet harmless, he saith unto Lamoni, Wilt thou hearken unto my words, if I tell thee by what power I do these things? and this is the thing that I desire of thee.

links.text: Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.

provenance.other: "wise as serpents and harmless as doves" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Matthew 10:16, and 'harmless' occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses altogether (Matthew 10:16, Philippians 2:15, Hebrews 7:26). Alma 18:22's 'Now Ammon being wise, yet harmless' strips the two similes and keeps the pair, in Matthew's order.
provenance.significance: Matthew 10:16 belongs to the missionary discourse — the sending out of the twelve as sheep among wolves — and it is the New Testament's one licence for cunning in a preacher. Alma 18:22 invokes it at the exact moment Ammon uses cunning: having been offered anything, he asks for the one thing that costs the king nothing and commits him to everything, 'Wilt thou hearken unto my words?' The 'yet' in 'wise, yet harmless' is the Book of Mormon's own gloss on Matthew's 'and', and it concedes what the verse is for: the two qualities are in tension, and the next verse says the king 'was caught with guile'.

links.note: 'Now Ammon being wise, yet harmless, he saith unto Lamoni, Wilt thou hearken unto my words, if I tell thee by what power I do these things?' A KJV singleton reduced to its two adjectives. Read with the verse that follows it — see the 2 Corinthians 12:16 link at 18:23 — this is the Book of Mormon assembling a defence of apostolic guile out of the two New Testament passages that offer one.

pericopes.text: And the king answered him, and said, Yea, I will believe all thy words; and thus he was caught with guile.

links.text: But be it so, I did not burden you: nevertheless, being crafty, I caught you with guile.

provenance.other: "caught you with guile" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:16, and "with guile" occurs in exactly 2, the other being Exodus 21:14, where a man kills his neighbour with guile and may be taken from the altar to die. Alma 18:23 reads 'and thus he was caught with guile'.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a piece of irony under duress. He is answering the charge that he was crafty with the Corinthians' money, and 'nevertheless, being crafty, I caught you with guile' is either his opponents' accusation quoted back at them or his own bitter concession — commentators have never agreed which, and that is the point of it. The Book of Mormon takes the disputed sentence, drops the irony, and applies it approvingly in the narrator's own voice to a conversion: the king believes, and thus he was caught with guile. Coming one verse after the wise-and-harmless of Matthew 10:16, the pair reads as a deliberate defence of the missionary's stratagem — and the only other KJV use of the phrase, at Exodus 21:14, is the law that denies sanctuary to a man who kills with guile, which is exactly the accusation the Lamanite court might have levelled at a Nephite who had killed seven of them the day before.

links.note: 'And the king answered him, and said, Yea, I will believe all thy words; and thus he was caught with guile.' Four words of a KJV singleton, reproduced exactly, in the passive. This is the chapter's most striking borrowing and the machine ranked nothing here — 'caught with guile' is four short common words, and the rarity lives in their combination, which is what a frequency-weighted n-gram stream is worst at seeing.

pericopes.text: And Ammon began to speak unto him with boldness, and said unto him, Believest thou that there is a God?

links.text: And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.

provenance.other: "with boldness" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Acts 4:31. The verbal form "speak boldly" occurs in exactly 2, Acts 18:26 and Ephesians 6:20 — and Ephesians 6:20's 'I am an ambassador in bonds: that therein I may speak boldly' is the wording Lamoni uses to Ammon at 18:20, 'Thou mayest speak boldly, and tell me concerning these things', to a man his people had bound at 17:20.
provenance.significance: Acts 4:31 makes boldness a consequence: they were filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake with boldness. Alma 18 has the same two clauses in the same order and eight verses apart — 'Ammon, being filled with the spirit of God' at 18:16, and 'Ammon began to speak unto him with boldness' at 18:24. The intervening verses are what the boldness is for. And the king has already given permission for it at 18:20, so that the missionary's boldness in Alma is licensed by the authority it is exercised on, which is the one thing Acts 4's boldness before the Sanhedrin conspicuously is not.

links.note: 'And Ammon began to speak unto him with boldness, and said unto him, Believest thou that there is a God?' Recorded as an echo: 'with boldness' is a KJV singleton but it is also a phrase any preacher's English supplies, and the argument is the pairing with 'filled with the spirit of God' at 18:16 rather than the two words themselves.
links.whyNot: Two common words. The link stands on the sequence filled-then-bold, which Acts 4:31 puts in one verse and Alma 18 spreads over eight; a reader may hold that the spread is too wide to be a borrowing.

pericopes.text: And he answered, and said unto him, I do not know what that meaneth.
And then Ammon saith, Believest thou that there is a Great Spirit?
And he saith, Yea.
And Ammon saith, this is God. And Ammon saith unto him again, Believest thou that this Great Spirit, which is God, created all things, which is in Heaven and in the Earth?
And he saith, Yea, I believe that he created all things which is in the earth; but I do not know the Heavens.
And Ammon saith unto him, The Heavens is a place where God dwells, and all his holy angels.
And king Lamoni saith, Is it above the earth?
And Ammon saith, Yea, and he looketh down upon all the children of men; and he knows all the thoughts and intents of the heart: for by his hand were they all created, from the beginning.
And king Lamoni saith, I believe all these things which thou hast spoken. Art thou sent from God?

Ammon saith unto him, I am a man; and man in the beginning, was created after the image of God; and I am called by his Holy Spirit to teach these things unto this people, that they may be brought to a knowledge of that which is just and true;

links.text: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

provenance.other: The Book of Mormon's preposition is not Genesis's. Genesis 1:27 has man created 'in his own image' and 'in the image of God'; Genesis 5:3 has Seth begotten 'after his image'; and "after the image of" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Colossians 3:10, 'the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him'. Alma 18:34 reads 'man in the beginning, was created after the image of God' — Genesis's doctrine with the Pauline preposition, and the same formula Mosiah 7:27 used.
provenance.significance: The substitution is small and it is consistent across the book, which is what makes it worth recording. Colossians 3:10 is not about the first creation but about the renewal of a convert — a new man renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him — and Alma 18:34 is spoken to a man about to be renewed, in the middle of a sentence about being 'called by his Holy Spirit to teach these things unto this people, that they may be brought to a knowledge of that which is just and true'. Knowledge is in both. The Book of Mormon's answer to 'Art thou sent from God?' is thus not simply Genesis 1 but Genesis 1 in the vocabulary Paul uses for conversion, which is what the whole chapter is engineering.
provenance.alternative: Genesis 9:6, 'for in the image of God made he man', which is the KJV's other statement of the doctrine and shares the preposition problem.

links.note: 'Ammon saith unto him, I am a man; and man in the beginning, was created after the image of God.' The chapter's doctrinal centre and the answer to Lamoni's mistake at 18:2: Ammon is not a god come down, and the reason a king could think so is that men are made in God's image. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 1:26-27 at this verse. The wording is Genesis's in substance and Colossians 3:10's in its preposition, and the same formula stands at Mosiah 7:27, where the argument for it was made; kjvSpecific is 'uncertain' because 'created after the image of God' is standard English theological diction independent of any one version.

pericopes.text: and a portion of that Spirit dwelleth in me, which giveth me knowledge, and also power, according to my faith and desires which is in God.

Now when Ammon had said these words, he began to the creation of the world, and also to the creation of Adam, and told him all the things concerning the fall of man, and rehearsed and laid before him the records and the Holy Scriptures of the people, and which had been spoken by the prophets, even down to the time that their father Lehi left Jerusalem;

and he also rehearsed unto them (for it was unto the king and to his servants,) all the journeyings of their fathers in the wilderness, and all their sufferings with hunger and thirst, and their travel, &c.;

and he also rehearsed unto them concerning the rebellions of Laman and Lemuel, and the sons of Ishmael, yea, all their rebellions did he relate unto them; and he expounded unto them all the records and Scriptures, from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem, down to the present time;

but this is not all, for he expounded unto them the plan of redemption, which was prepared from the foundation of the world; and he also made known unto them concerning the coming of Christ; and all the works of the Lord did he make known unto them.
And it came to pass that after he had said all these things, and expounded them to the king, that the king believed all his words.
And he began to cry unto the Lord, saying: O Lord, have mercy; according to thy abundant mercy which thou hast had upon the people of Nephi, have upon me and my people.

links.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,

provenance.other: "abundant mercy" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 1 Peter 1:3. The construction of Lamoni's prayer — 'have mercy … according to thy' — is Psalm 51:1's, 'Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness', which is the King James Bible's model penitential opening.
provenance.significance: The prayer of a man who has just been told the gospel for the first time is built out of the Bible's two great mercy formulas, and it changes one word in each. Psalm 51:1 supplies the shape and asks according to God's lovingkindness; 1 Peter 1:3 supplies 'abundant mercy', which in Peter is the ground of being begotten again unto a lively hope. Lamoni asks according to the abundant mercy 'which thou hast had upon the people of Nephi' — that is, he asks for mercy on the evidence of mercy already shown to someone else, which is a convert's argument and not a psalmist's. And what follows immediately is that he falls as if dead and rises two days later, which is the new birth 1 Peter 1:3 names, enacted.

links.note: 'O Lord, have mercy; according to thy abundant mercy which thou hast had upon the people of Nephi, have upon me and my people.' A KJV singleton in a KJV frame. The 1830 sentence is ungrammatical at its close — 'have upon me and my people', with the verb 'mercy' understood — and the modern text keeps it, which is the first edition's evidence that the phrase was assembled rather than composed.

pericopes.text: And now when he had said this, he fell unto the earth, as if he were dead.

links.text: And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead. And he laid his right hand upon me, saying unto me, Fear not; I am the first and the last:

provenance.other: "as dead" occurs in exactly 4 KJV verses (Isaiah 59:10, Matthew 28:4, Hebrews 11:12, Revelation 1:17) and "as one dead" in exactly 2 (Numbers 12:12, Mark 9:26). Of these only Revelation 1:17 has a living man collapsing at a disclosure of God and being raised from it. "fell unto the earth", the Book of Mormon's exact phrase, occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Revelation 6:13, where the subject is stars — see the exclusion at this verse.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible's collapses divide into the ones that are death (Matthew 28:4's keepers, Mark 9:26's boy, whom the bystanders pronounce dead) and the one that is a vision's cost. Revelation 1:17 is the second kind: John falls as dead at the sight of the Son of man and is raised by a hand and the words 'Fear not'. Alma 18:42-43 is neither quite — Lamoni falls and stays fallen for two days and two nights while his household mourns him, and what raises him is not a hand but the end of a private vision he reports in the next chapter. The Book of Mormon has taken the apocalyptic collapse and given it a funeral, which is what makes 19:1-13 possible.

links.note: 'And now when he had said this, he fell unto the earth, as if he were dead.' Recorded as an echo. The phrase is generic and the KJV's four candidates are all short; what points at Revelation 1:17 is the situation rather than the string, and a reader who wants a verbal source for this verse will not find one.
links.whyNot: Falling down as if dead needs no source. This row is at moderate because the type is distinctive in the KJV, not because the wording is.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that his servants took him and carried him in unto his wife, and laid him upon a bed; and he lay as if he were dead, for the space of two days and two nights; and his wife, and his sons, and his daughters mourned over him, after the manner of the Lamanites, greatly lamenting his loss.
And it came to pass that after two days and two nights, they were about to take his body and lay it in a sepulchre which they had made for the purpose of burying their dead.
Now the queen having heard of the fame of Ammon, therefore she sent and desired that he should come in unto her.
And it came to pass that Ammon did as he was commanded, and went in unto the queen, and desired to know what she would that he should do.
And she saith unto him, The servants of my husband have made it known unto me, that thou art a prophet of a Holy God, and that thou hast power to do many mighty works in his name;

links.text: And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

provenance.other: "many mighty works" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Matthew 13:58. The bare phrase 'mighty works' is common in the Synoptics; the quantified form is not, and Matthew 13:58 is the only place the KJV counts them.
provenance.significance: Matthew 13:58 is the KJV's one sentence about mighty works *not* done, and the reason it gives is unbelief — Jesus in his own country, among people who know his family. Alma 19 opens by putting that sentence into the mouth of a Lamanite queen about a Nephite stranger, and two verses later the narrator explains what has happened to her husband in exactly the countervailing term: 'the dark veil of unbelief being cast away from his mind' (19:6). The one KJV verse in which unbelief stops the works is thus the verse the chapter answers, and it is answered in a foreign court rather than a home town. Matthew's Nazareth asks 'is not this the carpenter's son?'; Lamoni's servants have asked whether Ammon is the Great Spirit or a man (18:3), and the queen has settled it as 'a prophet of a Holy God.'

links.note: 'That thou art a prophet of a Holy God, and that thou hast power to do many mighty works in his name.' A three-word KJV singleton, and the only quantified 'mighty works' in the Bible. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six; catalogued as an allusion on the rarity and on the direct contact with the chapter's own vocabulary of unbelief at 19:6. The queen's clause is the affirmative of Matthew's negative: where Matthew reports mighty works withheld for unbelief, she reports power to do them and asks for one.

pericopes.text: therefore, if this is the case, I would that ye should go in and see my husband, for he has been laid upon his bed for the space of two days and two nights; and some say that he is not dead, but others say that he is dead, and that he stinketh, and that he ought to be placed in the sepulchre; but as for myself, to me he doth not stink.

links.text: Jesus said, Take ye away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days.

provenance.other: "he stinketh" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, John 11:39. "two days and two nights" occurs in none — the KJV's countable interval before a raising is John's four days and the Synoptics' three days and three nights.
provenance.significance: This is where the chapter names its source, and it names it by contradiction. In John 11 the woman closest to the dead man is the one who raises the objection: the stone should stay, the body has turned, four days have passed. In Alma 19 the queen reports the objection as other people's — 'some say that he is not dead, but others say that he is dead, and that he stinketh' — and then refuses it in her own person: 'but as for myself, to me he doth not stink.' Martha's sentence is thus split in two and the queen is given the better half. The metalepsis is worth stating plainly: John's raising narrative is the one in which decay is admitted and overruled, and the Book of Mormon has taken the admission, put it in the crowd's mouth, and made the woman's private judgment the ground of the faith Ammon commends five verses later.

links.note: 'And that he stinketh, and that he ought to be placed in the sepulchre; but as for myself, to me he doth not stink.' A KJV singleton in the KJV's one four-day raising, and the verse that identifies which raising narrative this chapter is running. The 19:1 burial preparation, the sepulchre 'which they had made for the purpose of burying their dead', and the interval counted in days are all in place before the phrase arrives. What follows in the chapter confirms it: 'not dead, but sleepeth' at 19:8 (John 11:11) and 'Believest thou this?' at 19:9 (John 11:26, another singleton). The three occur in John's order.

pericopes.text: Now this was what Ammon desired, for he knew that king Lamoni was under the power of God; he knew that the dark veil of unbelief being cast away from his mind, and the light which did light up his mind, which was the light of the glory of God, which was a marvellous light of his goodness; yea, this light had infused such joy into his soul, the cloud of darkness having been dispelled, and the light of everlasting light was lit up in his soul; yea, he knew that this had overcame his natural frame, and he was carried away in God;
therefore, what the queen desired of him, was his only desire. Therefore he went in to see the king, according as the queen had desired him; and he saw the king, and he knew that he was not dead.
And he saith unto the queen, He is not dead, but he sleepeth in God, and on the morrow he shall rise again; therefore bury him not.

links.text: And when he was come in, he saith unto them, Why make ye this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth.

provenance.route: Mark 5:39 and John 11:11-23 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: "not dead, but sleepeth" occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — Matthew 9:24, Mark 5:39, Luke 8:52 — all three of Jairus's daughter. Only Mark and Luke add the entry into the house that Alma 19:7 has just narrated ('he went in to see the king'); Mark alone has 'when he was come in, he saith'. 'Shall rise again' occurs in 5 verses, of which John 11:23, 'Thy brother shall rise again', is the only one not about the third day of Christ's own passion.
provenance.significance: Two raisings are fused in a single sentence, and each supplies what the other lacks. From Jairus's daughter comes the diagnosis — the body is asleep, the mourners are wrong, and the physician says so on entering the house. From Lazarus comes the promise with a date on it: 'Thy brother shall rise again', which Martha at once postpones to the last day and Jesus at once brings forward. Ammon does the bringing forward himself — 'on the morrow he shall rise again' — and so removes the misunderstanding that John 11:24 is built on. The result is a raising narrative in which nobody is wrong except the crowd, and it is followed by the one instruction Jesus never has to give at either tomb: 'therefore bury him not.'

links.note: 'He is not dead, but he sleepeth in God, and on the morrow he shall rise again; therefore bury him not.' The four-word run belongs to one Gospel episode in three tellings, and 'shall rise again' pulls the other. 'He sleepeth in God' is not KJV and is the sentence's one theological addition — the Book of Mormon has already told the reader at 19:6 what the sleep is, a mind overcome by the light of the glory of God, which is neither Mark's death nor John's.

pericopes.text: And Ammon saith unto her, Believest thou this? And she said unto him, I have had no witness, save thy word, and the word of our servants; nevertheless, I believe that it shall be according as thou hast said.

links.text: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?

provenance.other: "Believest thou this" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, John 11:26. The answer follows John 11:27's shape as well: 'She saith unto him, Yea, Lord: I believe' becomes 'And she said unto him … nevertheless, I believe.' John 11:27 is already a source in this book, adjudicated at Alma 6:8 for 'the Son of God which should come'.
provenance.significance: The chapter has been running John 11 since 19:5, and here it takes the question the whole chapter of John turns on — the one Jesus puts to Martha before the tomb, on which the raising is conditioned. What the Book of Mormon changes is the ground of the answer. Martha answers a confession: 'I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God.' The queen answers an evidentiary complaint and then believes anyway — 'I have had no witness, save thy word, and the word of our servants; nevertheless, I believe.' Belief on testimony alone rather than on sight is John's own closing beatitude at 20:29, and it is what makes Ammon's next sentence possible: a woman outside the covenant people is told her faith exceeds anything inside it. Martha is never told that. She is inside.

links.note: 'And Ammon saith unto her, Believest thou this? And she said unto him, I have had no witness, save thy word … nevertheless, I believe.' Three words, and a KJV singleton, arriving fourth in a run of John 11 contacts (11:39 at 19:5; 11:11 and 11:23 at 19:8; 11:26-27 here) that occur in John's order. Catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the singleton and the sequence rather than the length — far below Skousen's threshold and not one of his thirty-six. Alma 15:6 has already staged a healing as a catechism on Matthew 9:28's 'Believe ye that I am able to do this?'; this is the same operation on a different singleton, and the two together are becoming a habit of the book's missionary narratives. The 1830 'saith' for the narrative past, regularized to 'said' in 1920, survives in Ammon's half of the exchange and not the queen's, which is the KJV's own asymmetry in John 11:26-27.

pericopes.text: And Ammon said unto her, Blessed art thou, because of thy exceeding faith; I say unto thee, woman, there has not been such great faith among all the people of the Nephites.

links.text: When Jesus heard it, he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.

provenance.other: "so great faith" occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Matthew 8:10 and Luke 7:9, in identical words — the same centurion in two Gospels. Nothing in Alma 19:10 discriminates between them, and the row is filed at Matthew 8:10 with Luke 7:9 named here rather than silently dropped. "O woman" and "great is thy faith" are each KJV singletons at Matthew 15:28, and 'speak the word only' is a singleton at Matthew 8:8.
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly two people whose faith is praised as exceeding Israel's, and both are Gentiles who ask for a household member to be healed at a distance: the centurion, and the woman of Canaan. Alma 19:9-10 is built out of both. From the centurion comes the structure — belief on the bare word ('I have had no witness, save thy word'; compare 'speak the word only'), and then the pronouncement measured against the covenant people, with 'the Nephites' standing where the KJV has 'Israel'. From the Canaanite woman comes the address: Ammon breaks his sentence to say 'I say unto thee, woman', which is Matthew 15:28's vocative and is not otherwise how this book speaks to anyone. What the substitution does is precise. 'No, not in Israel' is a rebuke of Israel; 'among all the people of the Nephites' is a rebuke of the Nephites, delivered by a Nephite in a Lamanite palace, in a chapter that ends with a Lamanite church.

links.note: 'Blessed art thou, because of thy exceeding faith; I say unto thee, woman, there has not been such great faith among all the people of the Nephites.' Two Gospel pericopes fused, and the fusion is legible because each contributes something the other has not: the comparative measure of faith against the covenant nation (Matthew 8:10 / Luke 7:9) and the vocative 'woman' with the praise of her faith (Matthew 15:28). 'Blessed art thou' is common in the KJV (5 verses) and carries no weight on its own; the row rests on the two-verse phrase and the singleton vocative.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that she watched over the bed of her husband, from that time, even until that time on the morrow which Ammon had appointed that he should rise.
And it came to pass that he arose, according to the words of Ammon; and as he arose, he stretched forth his hand unto the woman, and said, Blessed be the name of God, and blessed art thou:

links.text: Daniel answered and said, Blessed be the name of God for ever and ever: for wisdom and might are his:

provenance.other: "Blessed be the name of God" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Daniel 2:20. The far commoner formula is 'blessed be the name of the LORD' (Job 1:21, Psalm 113:2, and others); the substitution of 'God' for 'the LORD' is Daniel's alone.
provenance.significance: Alma 18 built the court scene out of Daniel — Belshazzar's changed countenance at Daniel 5:6, the offer of anything at 5:16, the thoughts of the heart at 2:30 — and this is the frame closing. Daniel 2:20 is the doxology Daniel speaks the moment the king's secret is revealed to him, before he goes in to the king; Alma 19:12 is the doxology the king himself speaks the moment he wakes. The Book of Mormon has moved the blessing from the interpreter to the interpreted, which is what the whole Ammon narrative is doing to the Daniel pattern: in Daniel the foreign king is never converted, he only acknowledges; here he rises, blesses God, and preaches (19:31).

links.note: 'And as he arose, he stretched forth his hand unto the woman, and said, Blessed be the name of God, and blessed art thou.' A six-word KJV singleton in the mouth of the risen king. 'Stretched forth his hand' is 7 KJV verses and carries nothing; the row is the doxology. Note where it stands in the chapter's economy — Lamoni's first act on waking is to bless God and then his wife, which is the inversion of 19:5, where the wife's private judgment against the crowd was all that stood between him and a sepulchre.

pericopes.text: for as sure as thou livest, behold, I have seen my Redeemer; and he shall come forth, and be born of a woman, and he shall redeem all mankind who believe on his name. Now when he had said these words, his heart was swollen within him, and he sunk again with joy; and the queen also sunk down, being overpowered by the spirit.

links.text: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:

provenance.other: "redeemer liveth" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Job 19:25, and 'my redeemer' in only 2 (Job 19:25 and Psalm 19:14). "born of a woman" occurs in 3, all of them Job — 14:1, 15:14, 25:4 — and in every one it means frail, short-lived and unclean; the KJV never uses it of Christ, whose incarnation at Galatians 4:4 is 'made of a woman'.
provenance.significance: Lamoni's confession is Job 19:25 with the verb moved. Job says 'I know that my redeemer liveth'; Lamoni says 'as sure as thou livest, behold, I have seen my Redeemer' — the living is transferred to the woman he is addressing, and what is predicated of the Redeemer is instead sight, which is Job's next verse and not his twenty-fifth ('yet in my flesh shall I see God … mine eyes shall behold'). The chapter has earned the transfer: Job speaks his confession out of a body eaten by worms, and Lamoni speaks his out of a body the court has just declared to stink. And the phrase the Book of Mormon then attaches to the Redeemer — 'born of a woman' — is the phrase Job uses three times for everything that makes a man perishable. Applied to the one who will 'redeem all mankind', it says that the Redeemer takes on precisely the condition Job's formula names.

links.note: 'For as sure as thou livest, behold, I have seen my Redeemer; and he shall come forth, and be born of a woman.' The verbal contact is distributed rather than continuous — 'liveth', 'my Redeemer', 'seen', 'born of a woman' — which is why the n-gram stream proposed nothing at this verse; a contiguous window cannot see it (CONVENTIONS §9). Two of the four elements are KJV singletons or near it, and all four come from one passage of Job apart from the shared 'born of a woman' formula, which is Job's as well. Recorded at 'high' rather than 'certain' because none of the four is a reproduced clause.

pericopes.text: Now Ammon seeing the spirit of the Lord poured out according to his prayers upon the Lamanites, his brethren, which had been the cause of so much mourning among the Nephites, or among all the people of God, because of their iniquities and their traditions; and Ammon fell upon his knees, and began to pour out his soul in prayer and thanksgiving to God, for what he had done for his brethren; and he was also overpowered with joy; and thus they all three had sunk to the earth.

Now when the servants of the king had seen that they had fallen, they also began to cry unto God, for the fear of the Lord had come upon them also: for it was they which had stood before the king, and testified unto him concerning the great power of Ammon.

And it came to pass that they did call on the name of the Lord in their might, even until they had all fallen to the earth, save it were one of the Lamanitish women, whose name was Abish, she having been converted unto the Lord for many years, on account of a remarkable vision of her father;

thus having been converted to the Lord, never had made it known; therefore when she saw that all the servants of Lamoni had fallen to the earth, and also her mistress, the queen, and the king, and Ammon lay prostrate upon the earth, she knew that it was the power of God; and supposing that this opportunity, by making known unto the people what had happened among them, that by beholding this scene, it would cause them to believe in the power of God, therefore she ran forth from house to house, making it known unto the people;

links.text: And she said unto her mistress, Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy.

provenance.other: "her mistress" occurs in 5 KJV verses; the collocation 'said unto her mistress' in exactly 1, 2 Kings 5:3. Alma 19:17 has 'her mistress, the queen', which is the Book of Mormon's only use of the word.
provenance.significance: The KJV has one servant woman who knows something about the true God that her foreign master's household does not, and whose telling of it sets the household's healing in motion: the little maid taken captive out of Israel who waits on Naaman's wife. She has no name, she speaks once, and the whole of 2 Kings 5 follows from her sentence. Abish is her counterpart with the terms reversed — a Lamanite, not an Israelite; converted in her own country by a vision of her father's, not carried off; silent for years rather than speaking once ('thus having been converted to the Lord, never had made it known'). And the outcome is reversed too. Naaman's healing converts one man who then asks for two mules' burden of earth to worship on; Abish's telling produces a church (19:35). Luke 4:27 makes Naaman the standing type of the outsider healed while Israel is passed over, which is the same argument Ammon has just made at 19:10 in the centurion's words — two independent KJV texts saying that faith outside the covenant people has outrun faith inside it, and the chapter uses both.

links.note: 'And also her mistress, the queen … therefore she ran forth from house to house, making it known unto the people.' Catalogued as figural: the verbal contact is 'her mistress' and the shape of the scene, not a run of words. It is written because the KJV's servant-woman-who-knows type has exactly one instance, because Alma 19 uses the one word that instance uses, and because the narrator goes out of his way at 19:16-17 to establish precisely the two facts 2 Kings 5:2-3 establishes about the maid — that she serves in the household and that she has knowledge of God the household lacks.
links.whyNot: A named servant with a private faith is a stock figure and needs no source, and 'her mistress' is the ordinary English for the relation. A reader may hold that Abish's function in the plot — to fetch a crowd — is generated by the narrative's own needs and that the resemblance to 2 Kings 5 is a resemblance between two stories that both require a servant to start them.

pericopes.text: and they began to assemble themselves together unto the house of the king. And there came a multitude, and to their astonishment, they beheld the king, and the queen, and their servants, prostrate upon the earth, and they all lay there as though they were dead; and they also saw Ammon, and behold, he was a Nephite.

And now the people began to murmur among themselves; some saying, That it was a great evil that had come upon them, or upon the king and his house, because he had suffered that the Nephite should remain in the land.
But others rebuked them, saying, The king hath brought this evil upon his house, because he slew his servants who had had their flocks scattered at the waters of Sebus;

and they were also rebuked by those men which had stood at the waters of Sebus, and scattered the flocks which belonged to the king, for they were angry with Ammon because of the number which he had slain of their brethren at the waters of Sebus, while defending the flocks of the king.

Now one of them, whose brother had been slain with the sword of Ammon, being exceeding angry with Ammon, drew his sword and went forth that he might let it fall upon Ammon, to slay him; and as he lifted the sword to smite him, behold, he fell dead.
Now we see that Ammon could not be slain, for the Lord had said unto Mosiah, his father, I will spare him, and it shall be unto him according to thy faith; therefore Mosiah trusted him unto the Lord.

And it came to pass that when the multitude beheld that the man had fell dead, who lifted the sword to slay Ammon, fear came upon them all, and they durst not put forth their hands to touch him, or any of those which had fallen; and they began to marvel again among themselves, what could be the cause of this great power, or what all these things could mean.

links.text: And great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things.

provenance.other: "fear came upon" occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — Job 4:14, Acts 2:43 and Acts 5:11 — and only the Acts pair follows a sudden death in an apostle's presence. 'Durst' occurs in 4 verses, of which Acts 5:13 is the one that describes a crowd afraid to approach. Acts 5 is already an established source in this book: the lie to the Holy Ghost stands behind Alma 10:25, 11:25 and 12:3.
provenance.significance: Acts 5:1-13 is the New Testament's one sequence in which a man drops dead in front of an apostle, fear falls on everyone who hears of it, and the people afterwards will not come near — 'of the rest durst no man join himself to them.' Alma 19:22-24 runs the same three beats: the Lamanite lifts his sword at Ammon and falls dead, 'fear came upon them all', and 'they durst not put forth their hands to touch him'. The moral direction is inverted, which is the interesting part. In Acts the dead are the liars inside the church and the fear disciplines the believers; here the dead man is an assailant from outside and the fear protects the missionary. Both texts then draw the same conclusion — that the untouchability is a fact about power and not about the man — and Alma 19:23 says so outright, in the language of an oath given to Mosiah rather than of a judgment: 'I will spare him, and it shall be unto him according to thy faith.'

links.note: 'Fear came upon them all, and they durst not put forth their hands to touch him.' Two of the three KJV verses with 'fear came upon' are in Acts, and the nearer of them stands eight verses from the only KJV crowd that 'durst' not approach a wonder-working preacher. Held at moderate: neither phrase is a singleton, and the sequence rather than any one string is the evidence. Note that 'put forth their hands' is a KJV singleton at Psalm 125:3, where it means to reach after iniquity — an unrelated sense, and not the source.
links.whyNot: The two contacts are three-verse and four-verse phrases, not singletons, and a crowd frightened by a sudden death is the natural thing for a narrator to write without a model. The row would be withdrawn if the Acts 5 language elsewhere in Alma turned out to be the book's own formula rather than a borrowing.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there was many among them, who said that Ammon was the Great Spirit, and others said he was sent by the Great Spirit;
but others rebuked them all, saying, That he was a monster, which hath been sent from the Nephites to torment us;

and there were some which said that Ammon was sent by the Great Spirit to afflict them, because of their iniquities, and that it was the Great Spirit that had always attended the Nephites, which had ever delivered them out of their hands; and they said that it was this Great Spirit which had destroyed so many of their brethren, the Lamanites;

and thus the contention began to be exceeding sharp among them. And while they were thus contending, the woman servant which had caused the multitude to be gathered together, came; and when she saw the contention which was among the multitude, she was exceeding sorrowful, even unto tears.

And it came to pass that she went and took the queen by the hand, that perhaps she might raise her from the ground; and as soon as she touched her hand, she arose and stood upon her feet, and cried with a loud voice, saying: O blessed Jesus, who has saved me from an awful hell! O blessed God, have mercy on this people.

links.text: And he gave her his hand, and lifted her up, and when he had called the saints and widows, presented her alive.

provenance.other: "gave her his hand" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Acts 9:41, and "by the hand, and lifted her up" in exactly 1, Mark 1:31. "took her by the hand" occurs in 3 verses (Matthew 9:25, Mark 1:31, Luke 8:54), all of raising or curing a woman. "stood upon her feet" occurs in none. Mark 1:31 has already been adjudicated in this book at Alma 15:6, for the hand-taking that cures Zeezrom's fever.
provenance.significance: In the KJV, raising a prostrate woman by the hand belongs to Christ and to Peter, and in Acts 9 it is done to Tabitha in a room full of widows, after which 'it was known throughout all Joppa; and many believed in the Lord.' Alma 19 gives the gesture to a woman — Abish takes the queen by the hand, and the queen then takes the king by the hand at 19:30, so the raising passes down a chain of three with no apostle in it at all. The Book of Mormon is careful about what this does and does not claim: 'that perhaps she might raise her from the ground' concedes that Abish does not know whether it will work, and the verse credits the rising to the touch rather than to a word of power. What follows is Tabitha's Joppa — knowledge spreading through the city, and many believing (19:31-35).

links.note: 'She went and took the queen by the hand, that perhaps she might raise her from the ground; and as soon as she touched her hand, she arose and stood upon her feet.' Catalogued at moderate. Taking a fallen person's hand needs no source, and the phrase the Book of Mormon uses is not exactly any of the three KJV forms; what carries the row is that the KJV's hand-raisings of women are a small and coherent set, that Alma 19:29-30 performs two of them in succession, and that the aftermath follows Acts 9:42. The 'perhaps' is not in any of them and is worth noticing — the one uncertain hand in the group is the one that belongs to a servant.
links.whyNot: No run of KJV wording is reproduced. A reader may take the gesture as the obvious way to get a fallen queen off the ground and decline the whole set.
