pericopes.text: And when she had said this, she clasped her hands, being filled with joy, speaking many words which were not understood; and when she had done this, she took the king, Lamoni, by the hand, and behold, he arose and stood upon his feet;

links.text: For he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries.

provenance.other: "no man understandeth" is a KJV singleton at 1 Corinthians 14:2. The Book of Mormon's 'speaking many words which were not understood' has the same predicate in the passive and no other shared word.
provenance.significance: Paul's chapter is the Bible's one sustained account of speech that nobody present can construe, and its whole argument is that such speech edifies no one until it is interpreted. Alma 19:30 gives the queen exactly that speech at exactly the moment the crowd outside is in contention over what has happened — and the narrative agrees with Paul: her unintelligible words change nothing, and what ends the contention is Lamoni's plain preaching in the next verse of 'the words which he had heard from the mouth of Ammon.' The chapter has already glossed one foreign word in the KJV's own formula at 18:13; here it declines to gloss, and the declining is the point.

links.note: 'She clasped her hands, being filled with joy, speaking many words which were not understood.' A single shared idea and one singleton predicate, so this is filed as an echo and not more. It is written because the Book of Mormon rarely reports unintelligible speech and because the sequence of 19:29-31 reproduces Paul's argument about it — ecstatic utterance, no effect, then intelligible preaching and conversion — without using Paul's vocabulary of tongues at all.
links.whyNot: The contact is one word, in a different voice, and a narrator describing joy that overflows language would write this sentence with no source in front of him. There is no 'tongue' or 'interpret' anywhere in the chapter to confirm that 1 Corinthians 14 is in view.

pericopes.text: and he immediately, seeing the contention among his people, went forth and began to rebuke them, and to teach them the words which he had heard from the mouth of Ammon; and as many as heard his words, believed, and were converted unto the Lord.
But there were many among them which would not hear his words; therefore they went their way.

And it came to pass that when Ammon arose, he also administered unto them, and also did all the servants of Lamoni; and they did all declare unto the people the self-same thing: that their hearts had been changed; that they had no more desire to do evil.
And behold, many did declare unto the people that they had seen angels, and had conversed with them; and thus they had told them things of God, and of his righteousness.
And it came to pass that there was many that did believe in their words; and as many as did believe, were baptized; and they became a righteous people, and they did establish a church among them:

and thus the work of the Lord did commence among the Lamanites; thus the Lord did begin to pour out his spirit upon them; and we see that his arm is extended to all people who will repent and believe on his name.

links.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

provenance.other: "believe on his name" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, John 1:12; so does the shorter 'on his name'. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase twice in this chapter, at 19:13 and again in the closing sentence here, and it has entered the book earlier at Alma 11:40.
provenance.significance: John 1:12 is the prologue's definition of who is admitted — not those born of blood or of the will of man, but as many as receive him — and the Book of Mormon puts its singleton at the end of the chapter in which a Lamanite court becomes a church. 'His arm is extended to all people who will repent and believe on his name' answers the prologue's next clause about birth and lineage with the argument this whole chapter has been making by narrative: the Lamanite queen's faith exceeded any among the Nephites (19:10), and the terms of admission are therefore not national.

links.note: 'We see that his arm is extended to all people who will repent and believe on his name.' A four-word KJV singleton closing the chapter. Frederick's monograph is an argument about the Gospel of John in the Book of Mormon and his discussion of John 1:12 falls in the same passage of his book as this verse; the catalogue's index of him records that co-occurrence and nothing stronger, and no claim about what he identifies is made here. The 'arm extended' half of the sentence is the book's own formula and is not Isaiah 5:25's 'his hand is stretched out still', which carries the opposite sense.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when they had established a church in that land, that king Lamoni desired that Ammon should go with him to the land of Nephi, that he might show him unto his father.

And it came to pass that the voice of the Lord came to Ammon, saying: Thou shalt not go up to the land of Nephi, for behold, the king will seek thy life; but thou shalt go to the land of Middoni; for behold, thy brother Aaron, and also Muloki and Ammah are in prison.
Now it came to pass that when Ammon had heard this, he saith unto Lamoni, Behold, my brother and brethren are in prison at Middoni, and I go that I may deliver them.

Now Lamoni saith unto Ammon, I know, in the strength of the Lord, thou canst do all things. But behold, I will go with thee to the land of Middoni; for the king of the land of Middoni, whose name is Antiomno, is a friend unto me; therefore I go to the land of Middoni; that I may flatter the king of the land; and he will cast thy brethren out of prison. Now Lamoni saith unto him, Who told thee that my brethren were in prison?

links.text: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.

provenance.route: Philippians 4:13 with Job 42:2 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: "can do all things" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Philippians 4:13. "I know that thou canst" occurs in exactly 1, Job 42:2, whose object is 'every thing' and not 'all things'. "canst do all things" occurs in none: the Book of Mormon's clause exists nowhere in the KJV and is made by putting Philippians' object into Job's second person.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons are fused here and each contributes the half the other cannot. Job 42:2 is Job's capitulation — 'I know that thou canst do every thing' — addressed to God out of the whirlwind, and it supplies the second-person confession. Philippians 4:13 is Paul's claim about himself, made in prison, and it supplies both 'all things' and the strength that is not the speaker's own. Lamoni's sentence therefore does something neither source does: it says to a man what Job says to God, on the ground Paul claims for himself, and it says it about a man who is on his way to open a prison. The composite is not a one-off. Ammon says the Philippians sentence in his own person at Alma 26:12 — 'in his strength I can do all things' — and Lamoni's line here is the same sentence in the second person, spoken about him by a Lamanite king before he has said it about himself.

links.note: 'I know, in the strength of the Lord, thou canst do all things.' The discrimination between the two sources is made by one word: the Book of Mormon has 'all things', which is Philippians', and not 'every thing', which is Job's, while keeping Job's 'I know that thou canst do'. Filed at Philippians 4:13 for that reason, with Job named in the composite. The machine proposed nothing at this verse — the agreement is split across a parenthetical clause, which a contiguous window cannot see (CONVENTIONS §9).

pericopes.text: And Ammon saith unto him, No one hath told me, save it be God: and he said unto me, Go and deliver thy brethren, for they are in prison in the land of Middoni.
Now when Lamoni had heard this, he caused that his servants should make ready his horses, and his chariots.
And he saith unto Ammon, Come, I will go with thee down to the land of Middoni, and there I will plead with the king, that he will cast thy brethren out of prison.
And it came to pass that as Ammon and Lamoni was a journeying thither, that they met the father of Lamoni, who was king over all the land.
And behold, the father of Lamoni saith unto him, Why did ye not come to the feast, on that great day when I made a feast unto my sons, and unto my people?
And he also saith, Whither art thou going with this Nephite, which is one of the children of a liar?
And it came to pass that Lamoni rehearst unto him whither he was going, for he feared to offend him.
And he also told him all the cause of his tarrying in his own kingdom, that he did not go unto his father, to the feast which he had prepared.

And now when Lamoni had rehearsed unto him all these things, behold, to his astonishment, his father was angry with him, and saith, Lamoni, thou art going to deliver these Nephites, which are sons of a liar. Behold, he robbed our fathers; and now his children are also come amongst us, that they may, by their cunning and their lyings, deceive us, that they again may rob us of our property.

Now the father of Lamoni commanded him that he should slay Ammon, with the sword. And he also commanded him that he should not go to the land of Middoni, but that he should return with him, to the land of Ishmael.

But Lamoni saith unto him, I will not slay Ammon, neither will I return to the land of Ishmael, but I go to the land of Middoni, that I may release the brethren of Ammon, for I know that they are just men, and holy prophets of the true God.
Now when his father heard these words, he was angry with him, and he drew his sword that he might smite him to the earth.

But Ammon stood forth and saith unto him, Behold, thou shalt not slay thy son; nevertheless, it were better that he should fall than thee: for behold, he hath repented of his sins; but if thou shouldst fall at this time, in thine anger, thy soul could not be saved.

And again: It is expedient that thou shouldst forbear; for if thou shouldst slay thy son, (he being and innocent man,) his blood would cry from the ground, to the Lord his God, for vengeance to come upon thee; and perhaps thou wouldst lose thy soul.

links.text: And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.

provenance.other: "blood crieth" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Genesis 4:10, and "from the ground" in 4, of which the other three are Ezekiel's temple measurements. mediation-check.py against Hebrews 12:24, the New Testament's one re-use of Abel's crying blood, returns one decisive point for Genesis 4:10: the Book of Mormon has 'crieth … from the ground' and not 'the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel'. The route is the Old Testament verse, not its epistle gloss.
provenance.significance: Genesis 4:10 is the Bible's first murder and the LORD's own question about it, and what Ammon does with it is transpose a fratricide into a filicide. Cain kills a brother and the blood cries from the ground; here a father is stopped one sentence short of killing a son, and the blood is warned in advance that it would cry. The transposition is exact in its terms — 'his blood would cry from the ground, to the Lord his God, for vengeance to come upon thee' keeps the crying, the ground, and the addressee of the cry, and supplies from Genesis 4:11-12 the consequence Ammon then names as the loss of a soul. What the Book of Mormon adds is the conditional. Genesis 4:10 is spoken after the fact and can only curse; Ammon speaks it before the fact, which turns the Bible's oldest sentence about blood into an argument for not shedding it, and it works: the king answers at 20:19 by conceding the premise, 'I know that if I should slay my son, that I should shed innocent blood.'

links.note: 'If thou shouldst slay thy son, (he being an innocent man,) his blood would cry from the ground, to the Lord his God, for vengeance to come upon thee.' A KJV singleton reproduced with only the tense changed. The 1830's parenthesis around 'he being and innocent man' — the compositor's 'and' for 'an' is a plain typographical slip, corrected later — sets the term the next verse then repeats as 'innocent blood', which is where the chapter's second source comes in.

pericopes.text: Now when Ammon had said these words unto him, he answered him, saying: I know that if I should slay my son, that I should shed innocent blood; for it is thou that hast sought to destroy him:

links.text: For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 19:4-6 and 20:30-33 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: "sin against innocent blood" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 1 Samuel 19:5; the Book of Mormon has the far commoner 'shed innocent blood' (7 verses), so the phrase itself is not the evidence and kjvSpecific is left uncertain. What is rare is the situation: 1 Samuel 19 and 20 hold the Bible's only sequence in which a king's son defends an outsider his father wants dead, argues that killing him would be innocent blood, and has a weapon turned on himself for it.
provenance.significance: Alma 20:14-20 is the Saul-and-Jonathan quarrel with the parts redistributed. Saul orders Jonathan to fetch David that he may be killed; Lamoni's father commands Lamoni to slay Ammon with the sword. Jonathan refuses and answers 'Wherefore shall he be slain? what hath he done?'; Lamoni refuses and answers that Ammon and his brethren 'are just men, and holy prophets of the true God'. Saul then casts a javelin at his own son; Lamoni's father draws his sword to smite his own son to the earth. In 1 Samuel the plea about innocent blood is the son's, made on the outsider's behalf; in Alma 20 the son cannot make it because the sword is now pointed at him, so the outsider makes it on the son's behalf — Ammon stands between them and argues that the king would be shedding his own son's innocent blood. And the outcome is the one 1 Samuel 19:6 records and 1 Samuel 20 revokes: 'Saul hearkened unto the voice of Jonathan: and Saul sware, As the LORD liveth, he shall not be slain.' Alma 20 makes the oath stick, and enlarges it — the king swears not only that no one will be slain but that his son may keep his kingdom, which is precisely what Saul was never willing to concede to Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:31, 'thou shalt not be established, nor thy kingdom').

links.note: 'I know that if I should slay my son, that I should shed innocent blood; for it is thou that hast sought to destroy him.' Catalogued as figural: the sequence is the evidence, not the string, since 'innocent blood' is spread across nineteen KJV verses. What makes it worth writing is that the Book of Mormon has already been reading the Davidic court narratives in this book — 2 Samuel 15:6 and 15:34 stand behind Alma 17 — and that the last clause here, 'it is thou that hast sought to destroy him', is the king conceding Jonathan's charge against Saul in Saul's own vocabulary of seeking a life (compare 20:2, 'the king will seek thy life').
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is one common phrase in a different construction. A father enraged at a son who has taken a stranger's part needs no biblical model, and a reader who declines the Saul frame loses nothing in the passage; the argument here rests entirely on the order of the beats and on this book's demonstrated habit of reading 1-2 Samuel.

pericopes.text: and he stretched forth his hand to slay Ammon. But Ammon withstood his blows, and also smote his arm that he could not use it.

links.text: And Abraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son.

provenance.other: "stretched forth his hand" occurs in exactly 7 KJV verses — Genesis 22:10, Exodus 10:22, Exodus 14:27, Isaiah 5:25, Ezekiel 10:7, Matthew 12:49, Matthew 14:31 — and "his hand to slay" occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses in that order, so the collocation is not itself a run; Genesis 22:10 is the only one of the seven in which the outstretched hand is raised to kill. It is also the only one in which the intended victim is the man's own son. The phrase on its own identifies nothing, which is why the machine ranked Matthew 12:49 here; the qualifier 'to slay' is what selects.
provenance.significance: The Akedah is the Bible's one scene of a father with his hand out to kill his son and a voice from outside stopping him, and Alma 20 stages it twice over in five verses. At 20:16 the father draws on the son; at 20:17 Ammon speaks the arresting line — 'thou shalt not slay thy son' — which is Genesis 22:12's 'Lay not thine hand upon the lad' in the Book of Mormon's own words; at 20:20 the hand goes out again and the KJV's phrase for it arrives. What the Book of Mormon changes is the ground of the arrest. In Genesis the hand is stayed because the father has proved that he fears God; here it is stayed because the son has repented and the father has not, so that Ammon's reason is the reverse of the angel's — 'it were better that he should fall than thee', since Lamoni is ready to die and his father is not. And where Genesis substitutes a ram, Alma 20 substitutes the outsider: the hand that goes out at 20:20 goes out at Ammon.

links.note: 'And he stretched forth his hand to slay Ammon.' Held at moderate. The five-word run is the KJV's commonest gesture and carries nothing by itself; the case is that the one KJV verse pairing it with slaying is a father over a son, and that the two verses on either side of this one are a father over a son. Against it, the hand at 20:20 is stretched at Ammon rather than at Lamoni, which is the point at which the Genesis 22 pattern breaks, and it breaks in the Book of Mormon's own direction — the missionary takes the blow the son was to receive.
links.whyNot: A reader may hold that 'stretched forth his hand' is simply how the KJV says a man reached out, that its use here for an attack is unremarkable, and that Alma 20:17's 'thou shalt not slay thy son' shares no word with Genesis 22:12. The row would be withdrawn if the Akedah left no other trace in this narrative; it is written because the surrounding verses supply father, son, raised hand and intervening voice in Genesis's order.

pericopes.text: Now when the king saw that Ammon could slay him, he began to plead with Ammon, that he would spare his life.
But Ammon raised his sword, and said unto him, Behold, I will smite thee, except thou wilt grant unto me that my brethren may be cast out of prison.
Now the king, fearing that he should lose his life, said, If thou wilt spare me, I will grant unto thee whatsoever thou wilt ask, even to the half of the kingdom.

links.text: And he sware unto her, Whatsoever thou shalt ask of me, I will give it thee, unto the half of my kingdom.

provenance.mt: Esther 5:3, 5:6 and 7:2 — 'even to the half of the kingdom' — is the Old Testament source of the formula, spoken three times by Ahasuerus to Esther at the banquet of wine.
provenance.route: Esther 5:3-7:2 → Mark 6:22-23 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: "half of my kingdom" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Mark 6:23; "half of the kingdom" in exactly 3, all Esther. "whatsoever thou wilt" occurs in exactly 2, Mark 6:22 and John 11:22. mediation-check.py run against Esther 5:6 and Mark 6:23 returns two decisive points for Mark — the Book of Mormon has 'Whatsoever thou shalt ask … I will give' rather than Esther's 'What is thy petition … and what is thy request', and it lacks Esther's closing 'it shall be performed'.
provenance.alternative: One datum runs the other way and is left standing rather than suppressed: the Book of Mormon reads 'the half of the kingdom' with Esther's definite article, not Mark's possessive 'my kingdom'. mediation-check.py cannot weigh it, since it discards single common words by design (ADJUDICATING §4), so it is recorded here. The judgment is that one article does not outweigh the syntax of the whole clause, but a reader who prefers Esther has that word to argue from.
provenance.significance: Mark 6:22-23 is Herod's oath at his own birthday feast, and it is the New Testament's one royal promise of half a kingdom — sworn to a dancing girl, and spent on the head of an imprisoned prophet. Alma 20:23 is the same oath under a raised sword, and it is spent the other way: what Ammon asks for with it is that prophets be let out of prison. The reversal is complete down to the machinery. Herod is 'exceeding sorry' but keeps his word 'for their sakes which sat with him'; Lamoni's father swears in fear of his life and then, at 20:26, goes past the terms of the oath of his own accord. Herod's feast kills John the Baptist; the feast in this narrative is the one Lamoni failed to attend (20:9), and the quarrel over his absence is what has brought the two kings face to face. What the Book of Mormon has done is take the Bible's most notorious half-kingdom promise, the one that costs a prophet his life, and make it the instrument by which three prophets are released.

links.note: 'I will grant unto thee whatsoever thou wilt ask, even to the half of the kingdom.' A KJV singleton and a two-verse phrase from the same two verses of Mark, with the Esther formula standing behind Mark. Filed as OT-via-NT on the mediation test rather than by default; the one word that resists it is recorded in provenance.alternative. Note that this is the second offer of anything a king has made Ammon in three chapters — Alma 18:21's is adjudicated to Daniel 5:16 — and the two are worded from different sources, which is an argument that the book is not running a single formula but reaching for a different royal-promise text each time.

pericopes.text: Now when Ammon saw that he had wrought upon the old king according to his desire, he saith unto him, If thou wilt grant that my brethren may be cast out of prison, and also that Lamoni may retain his kingdom, and that ye be not displeased with him, but grant that he may do according to his own desires, in whatsoever thing he thinketh, and then will I spare thee; otherwise I will smite thee to the earth.
Now when Ammon had said these words, the king began to rejoice because of his life.

And when he saw that Ammon had no desires to destroy him, and when he also saw the great love he had for his son Lamoni, he was astonished exceedingly, and saith, Because this is all that thou hast desired, that I would release thy brethren, and suffer that my son Lamoni should retain his kingdom, behold, I will grant unto you that my son may retain his kingdom from this time and forever; and I will govern him no more.

And I will also grant unto thee that thy brethren may be cast out of prison, and thou and thy brethren may come unto me, in my kingdom; for I shall greatly desire to see thee; for the king was greatly astonished at the words which he had spoken, and also at the words which had been spoken by his son Lamoni; therefore he was desirous to learn them.

And it came to pass that Ammon and Lamoni proceeded on their journey towards the land of Middoni. And it came to pass that Lamoni found favor in the eyes of the king of the land; therefore the brethren of Ammon was brought forth out of prison.

And when Ammon did meet them, he was exceeding sorrowful, for behold, they were naked, and their skins were worn exceedingly, because of being bound with strong cords. And they also had suffered hunger, thirst, and all kind of afflictions; nevertheless they were patient in all their sufferings.

And as it happened, it was their lot to have fallen into the hands of a more hardened and a more stiffnecked people; therefore they would not hearken unto their words, and they had cast them out, and had smote them, and had driven them from house to house, and from place to place, even until they had arriven to the land of Middoni; and there they were taken and cast into prison, and bound with strong cords, and kept in prison for many days; and were delivered by Lamoni and Ammon.

Now when Ammon and his brethren separated themselves in the borders of the land of the Lamanites, behold, Aaron took his journey towards the land which was called by the Lamanites, Jerusalem; calling it after the land of their fathers’ nativity; and it was away joining the borders of Mormon.—
Now the Lamanites, and the Amalekites, and the people of Amulon, had built a great city, which was called Jerusalem.

Now the Lamanites, of themselves, were sufficiently hardened, but the Amalekites, and the Amulonites, were still harder; therefore they did cause the Lamanites that they should harden their hearts, that they should wax stronger in wickedness, and their abominations.

links.text: For it was of the LORD to harden their hearts, that they should come against Israel in battle, that he might destroy them utterly, and that they might have no favour, but that he might destroy them, as the LORD commanded Moses.

provenance.other: "harden their hearts" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Joshua 11:20 — the third-person plural is unique, against the very common second-person 'harden not your hearts' and the Exodus narrative's 'I will harden Pharaoh's heart'. The shared run 'harden their hearts, that they should' is six words.
provenance.significance: The KJV says once, and only once, that a people's hearts were hardened so that they should do something, and it is the Canaanite kings marching into a war the LORD has already determined they will lose. The clause is one of the harder sentences in Joshua: the hardening is the LORD's, and its purpose is that 'he might destroy them utterly … and that they might have no favour.' Alma 21:3 keeps the syntax exactly and moves the agency off God: it is the Amalekites and the Amulonites, Nephite dissenters, who 'did cause the Lamanites that they should harden their hearts, that they should wax stronger in wickedness.' The theological substitution is the finding. Where Joshua has God harden a people toward their destruction, the Book of Mormon has apostates do it, which converts a predestinarian crux into a statement about who is responsible for a nation's ruin — and the narrative bears it out, since these are the cities the record will later report destroyed. Note also where the chapter ends: at 21:23 Aaron's counter-measure is Hebrews 3:13's daily exhortation, whose stated purpose is 'lest any of you be hardened.' The chapter opens on the KJV's one third-person hardening and closes on the KJV's one prescription against it.

links.note: 'They did cause the Lamanites that they should harden their hearts, that they should wax stronger in wickedness.' A six-word run containing a KJV singleton, with the purpose clause preserved and the agent changed. Hardness of heart is this book's constant vocabulary and most of its occurrences carry no source; this one does, because the plural possessive with a purpose clause after it exists in exactly one KJV verse.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Aaron came to the city of Jerusalem, and firstly began to preach to the Amalekites. And he began to preach to them in their synagogues, for they had built synagogues, after the order of the Nehors; for many of the Amalekites and the Amulonites were after the order of the Nehors.

Therefore, as Aaron entered into one of their synagogues to preach unto the people, and as he was speaking unto them, behold there arose an Amalekite, and began to contend with him, saying: What is that that thou hast testified? Hast thou seen an angel? Why do not angels appear unto us? Behold, are not this people as good as thy people?—

links.text: Then there arose certain of the synagogue, which is called the synagogue of the Libertines, and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia and of Asia, disputing with Stephen.

provenance.other: "there arose certain of the synagogue" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Acts 6:9; 'of the synagogue' alone occurs in 17 and is worthless. The Book of Mormon has 'behold there arose an Amalekite, and began to contend with him', which keeps the verb, the setting and the ensuing dispute but not the run; 'began to contend' occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Acts 6:9 is the New Testament's one sentence in which opposition to a preacher literally stands up inside a synagogue, and it is the beginning of the first Christian martyrdom. What Acts 6:10 then says is that the disputants 'were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake' — the objection fails on its merits and Stephen is killed anyway. Alma 21 gives the objector the better of the exchange in one respect and the worse in another: the Amalekite gets six sentences of argument, more direct speech than any opponent has been allowed since Zeezrom, and his questions are good ones, but Aaron answers by opening the scriptures and the synagogue simply refuses to hear (21:10). The Book of Mormon has substituted expulsion for stoning, and it will supply the prison two verses later.

links.note: 'As Aaron entered into one of their synagogues to preach unto the people … behold there arose an Amalekite, and began to contend with him.' Held at moderate: the shared elements are a verb, a setting and a dispute rather than a run of words, and a preacher heckled in a synagogue is the standing situation of Acts rather than of any one verse in it. It is written because Acts 6:9 is the only verse where the KJV puts 'there arose' and 'the synagogue' together, and because Aaron's opponents here — dissenters holding a rival priesthood 'after the order of the Nehors' — occupy the same structural place as Stephen's, freedmen of the diaspora contesting a fellow Jew.
links.whyNot: No clause is reproduced. Acts has at least four synagogue disputes (6:9, 9:29, 17:17, 18:19) and none of them is verbally closer than this; a reader may reasonably say the Book of Mormon is writing Acts's genre rather than any of its verses.

pericopes.text: Thou also sayest, Except we repent, we shall perish. How knowest thou the thought and intent of our heart? How knowest thou that we have cause to repent? How knowest thou that we are not a righteous people? Behold, we have built sanctuaries, and we do assemble ourselves together to worship God. We do believe that God will save all men.
Now Aaron said unto him, Believest thou that the Son of God shall come to redeem mankind from their sins?

And the man saith unto him, We do not believe that thou knowest any such thing. We do not believe in these foolish traditions. We do not believe that thou knowest of things to come, neither do we believe that thy fathers, and also that our fathers did know concerning the things which they spake, of that which is to come.

Now Aaron began to open the Scriptures unto them, concerning the coming of Christ, and also concerning the resurrection of the dead, and that there could be no redemption for mankind, save it were through the death and sufferings of Christ, and the atonement of his blood.

links.text: Opening and alleging, that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead; and that this Jesus, whom I preach unto you, is Christ.

provenance.other: "opening and alleging" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Acts 17:3, and "some mocked" in exactly 1, Acts 17:32; "departed from among them" occurs in exactly 1, Acts 17:33. "Resurrection of the dead" occurs in 11 and is not itself evidence. The Book of Mormon does not reproduce any of the three runs — its words are 'open the Scriptures', 'began to mock him', 'departed out of the synagogue' — so what is being claimed is the sequence, in which each of three consecutive Book of Mormon verses answers to a KJV verse that is unique in its wording.
provenance.significance: Acts 17:1-33 is the New Testament's fullest account of what a missionary does with a Bible in a synagogue and what happens to him afterwards, and Alma 21:9-11 runs it in order. Paul reasons out of the scriptures; Aaron opens the scriptures. Paul's argument is that Christ must needs have suffered and risen again from the dead; Aaron's is the coming of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and that there is no redemption 'save it were through the death and sufferings of Christ.' The hearers of the resurrection of the dead mock; Aaron's hearers are angry and 'began to mock him.' Paul departs from among them; Aaron 'departed out of the synagogue'. The Book of Mormon's one addition is the atonement of his blood, which Acts 17 does not name — and it is exactly the term the chapter's argument requires, because the Amalekite's position at 21:6 is that God will save all men and therefore that no blood is needed. Note also that the Areopagus is where Acts's mockery of the resurrection happens, not the Thessalonian synagogue; Alma 21 has compressed the chapter, putting the synagogue's refusal where Athens's mockery stood.

links.note: 'Now Aaron began to open the Scriptures unto them, concerning the coming of Christ, and also concerning the resurrection of the dead.' The case is cumulative rather than verbal: three consecutive verses of Alma 21 answer to Acts 17:3, 17:32 and 17:33, each of which is a KJV singleton in its own words, and they occur in Acts's order. 'Sufferings of Christ' at the end of the verse is a three-verse KJV phrase (2 Corinthians 1:5, 1 Peter 1:11, 1 Peter 5:1) and adds the noun Acts 17:3 has only as a verb. Not a quotation on any definition, and far below Skousen's threshold; catalogued as an extended allusion because the borrowing is of a passage's shape rather than of its sentences.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that as he began to expound these things unto them, they were angry with him, and began to mock him; and they would not hear the words which he spake;

therefore, when he saw that they would not hear his words, he departed out of the synagogue, and came over to a village which was called Ani-anti, and there he found Muloki a preaching the word unto them; and also Ammah, and his brethren. And they contended with many about the word.

And it came to pass that they saw that the people would harden their hearts; therefere they departed, and came over into the land of Middoni. And they did preach the word unto many, and few believed on the words which they taught.
Nevertheless, Aaron, and a certain number of his brethren, were taken and cast into prison, and the remainder of them fled out of the land of Middoni, unto the regions round about.
And those which were cast into prison suffered many things, and they were delivered by the hand of Lamoni and Ammon; and they were fed and clothed.

links.text: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.

provenance.other: No run is shared: 'fed and clothed' occurs in no KJV verse. What is shared is a set. Matthew 25:35-36 lists hunger, thirst, strangeness, nakedness, sickness and imprisonment, and Alma 20:29-21:14 supplies hunger, thirst, nakedness and imprisonment across two verses, then relieves them. Matthew 25:44's form of the same list is already adjudicated in this book at Alma 1:30, where the Book of Mormon has 'athirst' rather than 'thirsty' and so demonstrably has 25:44 in view; here the terms are those of 25:35-36, the sentence of blessing rather than of judgment.
provenance.significance: Alma 1:30 used the list to describe what the Nephite church did for the destitute; Alma 20:29-21:14 turns the missionaries themselves into the destitute and lets a Lamanite king perform the works on them. The reversal is the point of the whole Ammon narrative in miniature. In Matthew 25 the works are done to Christ in the person of the least, and the doers are surprised to learn it; here they are done to prophets by a converted heathen, and the record says only 'they were fed and clothed' — no commentary at all, in a book that comments on everything. That silence is what makes the row worth writing: the Book of Mormon states the works of mercy and leaves the reader to supply the sentence in Matthew that values them.

links.note: 'They were delivered by the hand of Lamoni and Ammon; and they were fed and clothed.' Catalogued as figural, with kjvSpecific 'no' — there is no wording to test. The evidence is that four items of a six-item KJV list occur across two adjacent verses of the Book of Mormon and are then answered by two of Matthew's verbs, and that this book has already shown at Alma 1:30 that it reads Matthew 25 as a list.
links.whyNot: Prisoners who are naked and hungry and then fed and clothed require no source; every element is what the situation dictates. A reader may hold that the resemblance to Matthew 25 is an artifact of both texts naming the same universal miseries, and nothing in Alma 21:14 would contradict him.

pericopes.text: And they went forth again to declare the word; and thus they were delivered for the first time out of prison; and thus they had suffered.

And they went forth whithersoever they were led by the spirit of the Lord, preaching the word of God in every synagogue of the Amalekites, or in every assembly of the Lamanites, where they could be admitted.

links.text: And when they were at Salamis, they preached the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews: and they had also John to their minister.

provenance.other: "preached the word of God in the synagogues" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Acts 13:5 — seven consecutive words, of which the Book of Mormon keeps 'the word of God in' and 'synagogue' with the number changed. "led by the spirit" occurs in exactly 2, Luke 4:1 and Romans 8:14.
provenance.significance: Acts 13:5 is the first sentence of the first missionary journey, and it establishes the method the rest of Acts follows: the synagogue first, wherever there is one. Alma 21:16 is the same sentence for the Lamanite mission, with one clause added that Acts never needs — 'or in every assembly of the Lamanites, where they could be admitted.' Acts's missionaries have a right of entry to a synagogue because they are Jews; Aaron and his brethren are foreigners preaching to a people whose houses of worship were built 'after the order of the Nehors' (21:4), and they go where they are let in. The qualification is the Book of Mormon writing its own situation into a borrowed formula, and it is the reason this mission's chapters are full of prisons where Acts 13's is full of proconsuls.

links.note: 'Preaching the word of God in every synagogue of the Amalekites, or in every assembly of the Lamanites, where they could be admitted.' A seven-word KJV singleton reproduced with the noun's number changed and its owners renamed. The machine ranked Acts 13:5 here, on 'word of god in' — one of the few places in these three chapters where the n-gram stream found the right verse. 'Whithersoever they were led by the spirit of the Lord' opening the same sentence is Romans 8:14's two-verse phrase and is recorded as a composite rather than argued.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lord began to bless them, insomuch that they brought many to the knowledge of the truth; yea, they did convince many of their sins, and of the tradition of their fathers, which were not correct.
And it came to pass that Ammon and Lamoni returned from the land of Middoni, to the land of Ishmael, which was the land of their inheritance.
And king Lamoni would not suffer that Ammon should serve him, or be his servant;
but he caused that there should be synagogues built in the land of Ishmael; and he caused that his people, or the people which was under his reign, should assemble themselves together.

And he did rejoice over them, and he did teach them many things. And he did also declare unto them that they were a people which was under him, and that they were a free people; that they were free from the oppressions of the king, his father; for that his father had granted unto him that he might reign over the people which were in the land of Ishmael, and in all the land round about.

And he also declared unto them that they might have the liberty of worshiping the Lord their God, according to their desires, in whatsoever place they were in, if it were in the land which was under the reign of king Lamoni.

And Ammon did preach unto the people of king Lamoni.—And it came to pass that he did teach them all things concerning things pertaining to righteousness. And he did exhort them daily, with all diligence; and they gave heed unto his word, and they were zealous for keeping the commandments of God.

links.text: But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.

provenance.other: "exhort one another daily" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Hebrews 3:13. Exhortation is common in the KJV and daily exhortation is not; Alma 21:23's 'he did exhort them daily, with all diligence' is the only place in this narrative where the adverb appears.
provenance.significance: Recover Hebrews 3:13's own sentence and the chapter closes on itself. The clause exists in the KJV for one reason — 'lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin' — and hardening is what Alma 21 has been about since its third verse, where the Amalekites cause the Lamanites to harden their hearts in Joshua 11:20's words. Aaron's mission fails among the hardened at 21:10-12; Ammon's succeeds among Lamoni's people at 21:20-23, and the difference the record reports is daily exhortation. Hebrews 3:13 sits inside the passage this book has already worked through in Alma 12 — Hebrews 3:7-4:12, from 'harden not your hearts, as in the provocation' to the discerning of the thoughts and intents of the heart — so the source is not new to the narrator, only newly used at its own subject.

links.note: 'And he did exhort them daily, with all diligence; and they gave heed unto his word.' A four-word KJV singleton with 'one another' dropped, since the exhorter here is one preacher rather than a congregation. 'Gave heed unto' is a two-verse phrase (Acts 3:5, Acts 8:6) and is not offered as evidence; the row is the daily exhortation and the hardening it is prescribed against.

pericopes.text: Now as Ammon was thus teaching the people of Lamoni continually, we will return to the account of Aaron and his brethren; for after he departed from the land of Middoni, he was led by the spirit to the land of Nephi; even to the house of the king which was over all the land, save it were the land of Ishmael; and he was the father of Lamoni.

And it came to pass that he went in unto him into the king’s palace, with his brethren, and bowed himself before the king, and said unto him, Behold, O king, we are the brethren of Ammon, whom thou hast delivered out of prison.

And now, O king, if thou wilt spare our lives, we will be thy servants. And the king saith unto them, Arise, for I will grant unto you your lives, and I will not suffer that ye shall be my servants; but I will insist that ye shall administer unto me; for I have been somewhat troubled in mind, because of the generosity, and the greatness of the words of thy brother Ammon; and I desire to know the cause why he has not come up out of Middoni, with thee.
And Aaron saith unto the king, Behold, the spirit of the Lord hath called him another way: he hath gone to the land of Ishmael, to teach the people of Lamoni.
Now the king saith unto them, What is this that ye have said concerning the spirit of the Lord? Behold, this is the thing which doth trouble me.
And also, what is this that Ammon said—if ye will repent ye shall be saved, and if ye will not repent, ye shall be cast off at the last day?

And Aaron answered him and said unto him, Believest thou that there is a God? And the king saith, I know that the Amalekites say that there is a God, and I have granted unto them that they should build sanctuaries, that they might assemble themselves together, to worship him. And if now thou sayest there is a God, behold, I will believe.
And now when Aaron heard this, his heart began to rejoice, and he saith, Behold, assuredly, as thou livest, O king, there is a God.
And the king saith, Is God that Great Spirit that brought our fathers out of the land of Jerusalem?

links.text: For the LORD our God, he it is that brought us up and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, and which did those great signs in our sight, and preserved us in all the way wherein we went, and among all the people through whom we passed:

provenance.other: “our fathers out of the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 24:17. The wider formula “brought thee out of the land of” occurs in four (Exodus 20:2, Deuteronomy 5:6, Deuteronomy 13:10, Psalm 81:10), and in every one of them the land is Egypt. The Book of Mormon substitutes Jerusalem, which is the one substitution the phrase cannot make in the KJV.
provenance.significance: The king is not asking a neutral question. He identifies God by the only formula the King James Bible has for identifying him — the deliverance of the fathers out of a land — and Joshua 24:17 is the verse where that formula is a people's answer at a covenant renewal, the reply to 'choose you this day whom ye will serve' and to Joshua's charge to put away 'the gods which your fathers served on the other side of the flood'. A Lamanite king who has just granted the Amalekites their sanctuaries is given the words of Israel renouncing its inherited gods, twelve verses before he does exactly that. The exchanged land is the point as well: Egypt is the house of bondage the fathers left, and for this book the land the fathers left is Jerusalem, so the creed arrives intact with one word moved.

links.note: 'Is God that Great Spirit that brought our fathers out of the land of Jerusalem?' The five-word run 'our fathers out of the land' is a KJV singleton, and the sentence around it is the standard KJV confession of God by his exodus — the preface to the Decalogue at Exodus 20:2, the people's creed at Joshua 24:17 — with Jerusalem where the KJV always has Egypt. Joshua 24 is preferred over Exodus 20 for the run itself ('our fathers', not 'thee') and for the setting: Joshua 24 is a confession made by a people choosing between the LORD and the gods of their fathers, which is the choice in front of this king. Note that the king reaches this creed unprompted; Aaron has said nothing about an exodus. The formula is presented as something the Lamanites already have, which is the chapter's premise about them.

pericopes.text: And Aaron said unto him, Yea, he is that Great Spirit, and he created all things, both in Heaven and in earth: believest thou this?—
And he saith Yea, I believe that the Great Spirit created all things, and I desire that ye should tell me concerning all these things, and I will believe thy words.

And it came to pass that when Aaron saw that the king would believe his words, he began from the creation of Adam, reading the Scriptures unto the king; how God created man after his own image, and that God gave him commandments, and that because of transgression, man had fallen.

links.text: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

provenance.other: The preposition is again not Genesis 1:27's. “created man in his own image” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 1:27; “after his image” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 5:3, of Adam begetting Seth. The 1830 reads 'after his own image', which is in no KJV verse at all — it is 1:27's possessive fitted to 5:3's preposition, the same fusion recorded at Alma 18:34 (where Colossians 3:10 supplies the parallel). 'Transgression' is likewise not Genesis's word for the fall; “Adam's transgression” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 5:14.
provenance.significance: What Aaron is described as doing is not quoting Genesis but reading it, and the summary tells us which Genesis he read: creation in the image, a commandment given, a transgression, a fall. That is the sequence of Genesis 1-3 as Romans 5 abstracts it, not as Genesis narrates it — Genesis 3 has a serpent, a woman, a tree and a curse, and Aaron's precis has none of them. The catalogue's interest is that a scene about a man reading scripture to a king reproduces the chapter divisions of a Pauline summary rather than the events of the text being read.
provenance.alternative: Genesis 9:6, 'for in the image of God made he man', the KJV's other statement of the doctrine.

links.note: 'He began from the creation of Adam, reading the Scriptures unto the king; how God created man after his own image, and that God gave him commandments, and that because of transgression, man had fallen.' Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 1:26-3 here, and the verse is a compressed recital of exactly that span: image (1:26-27), commandment (2:16-17), transgression and fall (3). The formula 'created after the image' was adjudicated at Mosiah 7:27 and used again at Alma 18:34, and the argument for its preposition is made there; what is new at 22:12 is that the image-clause is now one term of a four-term narrative summary rather than a standalone doctrine, and that the summary's connective term, 'transgression', is Paul's word for the fall and not Genesis's.

pericopes.text: And Aaron did expound unto him the Scriptures, from the creation of Adam, laying the fall of man before him, and their carnal state, and also the plan of redemption, which was prepared from the foundation of the world, through Christ, for all whosoever would believe on his name.

links.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

provenance.other: “believe on his name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:12. The near neighbours differ by a word that matters: 1 John 3:23 has 'believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ', John 2:23 'believed in his name'. “from the foundation of the world” occurs in six KJV verses and cannot on its own point to one of them; the collocation with 'prepared' is Matthew 25:34's, and that pairing was adjudicated at Alma 12:25 and 13:3.
provenance.significance: The clause that closes Aaron's precis of the plan of redemption is the clause that closes John's prologue, and John 1:12 is about what happens to those outside the covenant people — 'his own received him not, but as many as received him' — which is the situation of a Lamanite king being read the scriptures for the first time. The prologue's next verse is the one the king will quote back at 22:15 when he asks to be 'born of God'.

links.note: 'The plan of redemption, which was prepared from the foundation of the world, through Christ, for all whosoever would believe on his name.' Two KJV formulas are joined. The first, 'prepared from the foundation of the world', is Matthew 25:34's and has already been adjudicated in this book at 12:25 and 13:3; it is recorded here as a composite rather than argued again. The second is the finding: 'believe on his name' is John 1:12's alone, and it arrives two verses before the king asks to be 'born of God', which is John 1:13's phrase for the same people. Confidence is moderate because 'believe on his name' is by this point stock Book of Mormon diction and its first adoption is not in Alma; the argument here is for the pairing with the prologue, not for a fresh borrowing.

pericopes.text: And since man had fallen, he could not merit any thing of himself; but the sufferings and death of Christ atoneth for their sins, through faith and repentance, &c.; and that he breaketh the bands of death, that the grave shall have no victory, and that the sting of death should be swallowed up in the hopes of glory: and Aaron did expound all these things unto the king.

links.text: So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

provenance.mt: Isaiah 25:8, 'He will swallow up death in victory'; Hosea 13:14, 'O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction'.
provenance.route: Isaiah 25:8 + Hosea 13:14 → 1 Corinthians 15:54-55 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “swallowed up in victory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:54, and “sting of death” in exactly one, 1 Corinthians 15:56. Isaiah 25:8 has the swallowing and the victory but as an act God performs on death ('He will swallow up death in victory'), not as a state death is put into; Hosea 13:14, which supplies Paul's taunt, has neither 'sting' nor 'victory' in the KJV's Old Testament wording. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for 1 Corinthians 15:54 and none for Isaiah.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon does not quote Paul's sentences; it redistributes his nouns. Paul's taunt pairs death with sting and grave with victory — 'O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?' — and Alma 22:14 keeps that pairing exactly ('the grave shall have no victory ... the sting of death') while converting both rhetorical questions into flat statements and swapping the object of the swallowing: in Paul death is swallowed up in victory, here the sting of death is swallowed up in the hopes of glory. Recover Paul's context and the substitution reads as a deliberate softening for a catechumen. Paul's 'victory' is eschatological fact addressed to believers who already have the resurrection; 'the hopes of glory' is what a king who has not yet believed can be offered, and it is Colossians 1:27's phrase for Christ in the Gentiles. The chapter is teaching 1 Corinthians 15 to a man being told the plan for the first time, and it lowers the register accordingly.

links.note: 'He breaketh the bands of death, that the grave shall have no victory, and that the sting of death should be swallowed up in the hopes of glory.' Four of Paul's terms — grave, victory, sting, death, swallowed up — arrive together in one clause, and three of the phrases built from them are KJV singletons in 1 Corinthians 15. Hardy's apparatus cross-references 1 Corinthians 15:54-55 at this verse. Mediation is the interesting call and it is not close: Paul is quoting Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14, and every distinctive word the Book of Mormon has here is Paul's rather than the Old Testament's — 'sting' and 'grave' and 'victory' as a trio exist only in 1 Corinthians 15:55-56. Note that no clause is reproduced entire, so this falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his long quotations; what makes it certain is the density of singletons, not the length of any run. The 1830 reading 'atoneth' (1920 'atone') is the first edition's, and the '&c.' after 'through faith and repentance' is a compositor's abbreviation the later editions expand to 'and'.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after Aaron had expounded these things unto him, the king saith, What shall I do, that I may have this Eternal life of which thou hast spoken? Yea, what shall I do, that I may be born of God, having this wicked spirit rooted out of my breast, and receive his spirit, that I may be filled with joy, that I may not be cast off at the last day? Behold, saith he, I will give up all that I possess; yea, I will forsake my kingdom, that I may receive this great joy.

links.text: And, behold, one came and said unto him, Good Master, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?

provenance.other: “that I may have eternal life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 19:16 — Mark 10:17 and Luke 18:18 both read 'inherit' instead. “what shall I do that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 10:17. So the Book of Mormon's single question carries the interrogative of Mark's version and the verb of Matthew's, and Luke 18:18 supplies what neither of the others does: the questioner is 'a certain ruler'. “great possessions” occurs in three KJV verses, one of them Ecclesiastes 2:7 and the other two Matthew 19:22 and Mark 10:22, both of the same man.
provenance.significance: This is the rich young ruler, asked and answered the other way. In all three gospels a ruler asks what he must do for eternal life, is told to give up what he has, and goes away sorrowful because he had great possessions; here a ruler asks the same question in the same words and volunteers the answer before it is demanded of him — 'I will give up all that I possess; yea, I will forsake my kingdom.' The metalepsis is in what the source withholds. Matthew's man is offered perfection and declines it; Alma's king is offered nothing yet and offers everything, and the thing he offers is precisely the thing the gospel story says a man in his position cannot give. That the Book of Mormon should stage the reversal on a Lamanite rather than a Nephite is the whole burden of Alma 17-26.

links.note: 'What shall I do, that I may have this Eternal life of which thou hast spoken? ... I will give up all that I possess; yea, I will forsake my kingdom.' Two KJV singletons meet in one sentence: 'that I may have eternal life' is Matthew 19:16's alone (Mark and Luke read 'inherit'), and 'what shall I do that' is Mark 10:17's alone. The rest of the pericope follows: Luke's questioner is a ruler, and this one is a king; Matthew's and Mark's man has great possessions and will not part with them, and this one offers his kingdom unasked. The second half of the verse ('that I may be born of God') reaches instead for John 1:13, two verses past the phrase Aaron had used at 22:13, which is why John is recorded as a composite here rather than a separate link.

pericopes.text: But Aaron saith unto him, If thou desirest this thing, if thou wilt bow down before God, yea, if thou repent of all thy sins, and will bow down before God, and call on his name in faith, believing that ye shall recieve, then shalt thou recieve the hope which thou desirest.

links.text: And all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive.

provenance.other: “believing ye shall receive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 21:22. Mark 11:24 says the same thing in different words — 'believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them' — so the Book of Mormon's clause is Matthew's and not the synoptic commonplace.
provenance.significance: Matthew 21:22 is the promise attached to the withered fig tree, given to disciples who have just asked how the tree died so soon: the answer is that faith without doubting moves mountains and that whatsoever you ask believing, you receive. Aaron applies it to a man who has asked for something no mountain-moving is required for, and the condition he attaches — 'bow down before God ... repent of all thy sins ... call on his name in faith' — turns Matthew's promise about petition into a formula for conversion. The 1830's own spelling, 'recieve' twice, is the compositor's; the 1920 addition of 'wilt' before 'bow down' tidies a repetition the first edition left standing.

links.note: 'Call on his name in faith, believing that ye shall recieve, then shalt thou recieve the hope which thou desirest.' 'Believing, ye shall receive' is Matthew 21:22's alone in the KJV, and it arrives here as the operative clause of Aaron's instruction. What the Book of Mormon changes is the object: Matthew promises that you will receive the thing asked for, Aaron promises that you will receive 'the hope which thou desirest', which is a hope and not a thing. The machine streams did not propose this verse; the run is short and split by 'that ye shall'.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Aaron had said these words, the king did bow down before the Lord, upon his knees; yea, even he did prostrate himself upon the earth, and cried mightily, saying,

links.text: But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.

provenance.other: “cry mightily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:8, in the decree of the king of Nineveh. Revelation 18:2's 'cried mightily with a strong voice' is the only other KJV occurrence of the collocation in any inflection, and its speaker is an angel announcing a city's destruction rather than a man praying.
provenance.significance: This is the same KJV singleton that stands behind Alma 9:25, and it is here for the opposite reason. At 9:25 the argument was that the Book of Mormon had redirected Jonah's phrase away from its object — Nineveh cries mightily unto God, Alma's messengers cry mightily unto the people. At 22:17 the phrase goes home. The man crying mightily is a heathen king; he abases himself bodily, as the king of Nineveh rises from his throne and sits in ashes at Jonah 3:6; and ten verses later he 'sent a proclamation throughout all the land, amongst all his people', which is Jonah 3:7's decree proclaimed through Nineveh by the king and his nobles. The whole Ninevite sequence — king humbled, king decrees, city spared — runs through Alma 22-23, and the phrase that was pointed the wrong way at 9:25 is pointed the right way here.

links.note: 'The king did bow down before the Lord, upon his knees; yea, even he did prostrate himself upon the earth, and cried mightily.' 'Cry mightily' is Jonah 3:8's alone in the KJV, and the Book of Mormon has already used it once in this book, at 9:25. This is not that formula recurring. ADJUDICATING §4 distinguishes a narrator reusing his own phrase from a phrase returning to its source, and this is the second: 9:25 borrowed the words of a heathen king's decree and gave them to preachers addressing a city, and 22:17 gives them back to a heathen king, on his face, praying — with the proclamation through all his land following at 22:27 as it follows at Jonah 3:7. Judged as a fresh borrowing the verbal contact would be two words; judged as the completion of the Jonah frame Alma 8-9 opened, it is the chapter's structural argument.

pericopes.text: O God, Aaron hath told me that there is a God; and if there is a God, and if thou art God, wilt thou make thyself khown unto me, and I will give away all my sins to know thee, and that I may be raised from the dead, and be saved at the last day. And now when the king had said these words, he was struck as if he were dead.

links.text: Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,

provenance.other: There is no rare string here; the case is one of sequence. Philippians 3:8-11 runs: the loss of all things — 'that I may know him' — 'if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead'. Alma 22:18 runs: 'I will give away all my sins to know thee, and that I may be raised from the dead'. 'Raised from the dead' occurs in eight KJV verses and settles nothing on its own; the three steps in that order are what the link rests on.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Paul gives away all things to know Christ; the king gives away all his sins. Read Paul's context and the swap is pointed — what Paul counts as loss is his pedigree and his righteousness under the law, the assets of a man who had nothing to repent of, and the king has no such inventory to surrender. He is at 22:15 a rich young ruler who offers his kingdom, and at 22:18, three verses later, he has found that the thing actually asked of him is not the kingdom. The line is the most quoted sentence in the chapter and the reason is this compression: the Pauline renunciation with the object changed from possessions to sins.

links.note: 'I will give away all my sins to know thee, and that I may be raised from the dead, and be saved at the last day.' Philippians 3:8-11 is the only KJV passage that puts these three in this order — surrender everything, in order to know him, in order to attain the resurrection of the dead — and the king's prayer reproduces the sequence in one sentence. The verbal contact is thin, which is why this is moderate rather than high and why kjvSpecific is 'uncertain': 'know thee' and 'raised from the dead' are common English. What is not common is a prayer that makes knowledge of God the purpose of a renunciation and resurrection the purpose of the knowledge. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the reader who recovers Philippians 3 gets the king's inventory as the one Paul does not have.
links.whyNot: No phrase here is distinctive, and the sequence could be assembled from ordinary conversion diction without Philippians in view. A reader could reasonably decline the link and read the verse as the chapter's own composition out of the material of 22:15-16.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that his servants ran and told the queen all that had happened unto the king. And she came in unto the king; and when she saw him lay as if he were dead, and also Aaron and his brethren standing as though they had been the cause of his fall, she was angry with them, and commanded that her servants, or the servants of the king, should take them and slay them.

Now the servants had seen the cause of the king’s fall, therefore they durst not lay their hands on Aaron and his brethren; and they plead with the queen, saying, Why commandest thou that we should slay these men, when behold, one of them is mightier than us all? Therefore we shall fall before them.

Now when the queen saw the fear of the servants, she also began to fear exceedingly, lest there should some evil come upon her. And she commanded her servants that they should go and call the people, that they might slay Aaron and his brethren.

Now when Aaron saw the determination of the queen, and he also knowing the hardness of the hearts of the people, feared lest that a multitude should assemble themselves together, and there should be a great contention, and a disturbance among them; therefore he put forth his hand and raised the king from the earth, and said unto him, Stand: and he stood upon his feet, recieving his strength.

links.text: But Jesus took him by the hand, and lifted him up; and he arose.

provenance.other: “he was as one dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 9:26; “took him by the hand and lifted him up” occurs in exactly one, Mark 9:27. “received strength” occurs in two, Acts 3:7 and Hebrews 11:11, and only Acts 3:7 is a raising. “stand upright on thy feet” occurs in exactly one, Acts 14:10.
provenance.significance: Three KJV raisings are fused, and each contributes the element the others lack. Mark 9:26-27 supplies the frame: a body that onlookers take for a corpse, and a hand that lifts it. Acts 3:7 supplies the strength that returns to the feet. Acts 14:10 supplies the imperative 'Stand' — and Acts 14 is already the chapter this book has been working, since Alma 18:2 was adjudicated against Acts 14:11, where the crowd that sees a man stand upright cries that the gods are come down in the likeness of men. That is precisely the misunderstanding Aaron is racing to prevent at 22:22, and the verse he borrows from is the verse that produces it.

links.note: 'He put forth his hand and raised the king from the earth, and said unto him, Stand: and he stood upon his feet, recieving his strength.' The king has lain 'as if he were dead' since 22:18, which is Mark 9:26's situation and its KJV singleton; the raising is Mark 9:27's gesture; the word for what returns to his feet is Acts 3:7's. Alma 15:11 has already used the Acts 3 raising for Zeezrom and Alma 18:42 has already used Mark 9:26 for Lamoni, so the components are not new to the book — what is new is that they are combined, and that the combination is performed under threat, to disperse a mob rather than to heal a man. The 1830 spelling 'recieving' is the compositor's; 1920 corrects it and also deletes the 'and' before 'there should be a great contention'.

pericopes.text: Now this was done in the presence of the queen, and many of the servants. And when they saw it, they greatly marvelled, and began to fear. And the king stood forth and began to minister unto them. And he did minister unto them insomuch that his whole household were converted unto the Lord.
Now there was a multitude gathered together because of the commandment of the queen, and there began to be great murmurings among them, because of Aaron and his brethren.

links.text: And there was much murmuring among the people concerning him: for some said, He is a good man: others said, Nay; but he deceiveth the people.

provenance.other: “there was much murmuring” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 7:12, and it is the KJV's only instance of murmuring as the sound of a crowd divided over a teacher rather than of Israel complaining against Moses. The Book of Mormon's 'there began to be great murmurings among them' substitutes 'great' for 'much' and pluralizes the noun, which is why this is an echo and not an allusion.
provenance.significance: John 7 is the chapter where a crowd assembles about a teacher whose fate is undecided, splits over whether he is a good man or a deceiver, and is restrained because nobody dares lay hands on him. Alma 22:20-26 has the same three beats in the same order — the servants who 'durst not lay their hands on Aaron', the multitude gathered and murmuring, the crowd pacified — which is more than the shared phrase would carry on its own and is the reason the echo is worth recording.

links.note: 'There began to be great murmurings among them, because of Aaron and his brethren.' The KJV reserves 'murmuring' almost entirely for Israel in the wilderness; John 7:12 is the exception, and it is the exception that fits — a crowd gathered about preachers, divided about them, and not yet violent. The verbal contact is one substituted adjective away from exact and the link is recorded as an echo on that account. What raises it above the wording is the surrounding shape: at 22:20 the servants 'durst not lay their hands' on the brethren, which is John 7:30's and 7:44's refrain about the same crowd.

pericopes.text: But the king stood forth among them, and administered unto them. And it came to pass that they were pacified towards Aaron, and those which were with him.

And it came to pass that when the king saw that the people were pacified, he caused that Aaron and his brethren should stand forth in the midst of the multitude, and that they should preach the word unto them.

And it came to pass that the king sent a proclamation throughout all the land, amongst all hia people which was in all his land, which was in all the regions round about, which was bordering even to the sea, on the east, and on the west, and which was divided from the land of Zarahemla by a narrow strip of wilderness, which ran from the sea, east, even to the sea west, and round about on the borders of the sea shore, and the borders of the wilderness which was on the north, by the land of Zarahemla, through the borders of Manti, by the head of the river Sidon, running from the east towards the west; and thus were the Lamanites and the Nephites divided.

Now the more idle part of the Lamanites lived in the wilderness, and dwelt in tents; and they were spread through the wilderness, on the west, in the land of Nephi; yea, and also on the west of the land of Zarahemla, in the borders, by the seashore, and on the west, in the land of Nephi, in the place of their fathers’ first inheritance; and thus bordering along by the seashore.

And also there was many Lamanites on the east by the seashore, whither the Nephites had driven them. And thus the Nephites were nearly surrounded by the Lamanites; nevertheless the Nephites had taken possession of all the northern parts of the land, bordering on the wilderness, at the head of the river Sidon, from the east to the west, round about on the wilderness side; on the north, even until they came to the land which they called Bountiful.

And it bordered upon the land which they called Desolation; it being so far northward that it came into the land which had been peopled, and had been destroyed, of whose bones we have spoken, which was discovered by the people of Zarahemla; it being the place of their first landing.

And they came from there up into the south wilderness. Thus the land on the northward was called Desolation, and the land on the southward was called Bountiful; it being the wilderness which was filled with all manner of wild animals of every kind; a part of which had come from the land northward, for food.

And now it was only the distance of a day and a half’s journey for a Nephite, on the line Bountiful, and the land Desolation, from the East to the West sea; and thus the land of Nephi, and the land of Zarahemla, was nearly surrounded by water; there being a small neck of land between the land northward, and the land southward.

And it came to pass that the Nephites had inhabited the land Bountiful, even from the East unto the West sea, and thus the Nephites in their wisdom, with their guards and their armies, had hemmed in the Lamanites on the south, that thereby they should have no more possession on the north, that they might not overrun the land northward;

therefore the Lamanites could have no more possessions only in the land of Nephi, and the wilderness round about. Now this was wisdom in the Nephites; as the Lamanites were an enemy to them, they would not suffer their afflictions on every hand, and also that they might have a country whither they might flee, according to their desires.
And now I, after having said this, return again to the account of Ammon, and Aaron, Omner and Himni, and their brethren.

Behold, now it came to pass that the king of the Lamanites sent a proclamation among all his people, that they should not lay their hands on Ammon, or Aaron, or Omner, or Himni, nor neither of their brethren which should go forth preaching the word of God, in whatsoever place they should be, in any part of their land;

links.text: But before all these, they shall lay their hands on you, and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues, and into prisons, being brought before kings and rulers for my name’s sake.

provenance.other: “lay their hands on you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 21:12. The Book of Mormon has the phrase twice in two verses (23:1, 23:2) with the object changed from 'you' to the named missionaries, and it keeps Luke's third-person plural subject — the persecutors, not the prisoners.
provenance.significance: Luke 21:12 is Jesus telling his disciples what will be done to them: hands laid on them, delivered to synagogues, into prisons, brought before kings. Alma 23:1-2 is a king cancelling that list item by item, and the cancellation is issued from the one position in Luke's sentence that is not a victim's. The metalepsis is in the last clause of the source, 'for my name's sake': in Luke the king before whom the preacher is brought is the persecution's final stage, and here the king is the reason the preaching is safe. The Book of Mormon has taken the standard KJV catalogue of what happens to missionaries and made a royal decree out of its negation.

links.note: 'The king of the Lamanites sent a proclamation among all his people, that they should not lay their hands on Ammon, or Aaron, or Omner, or Himni, nor neither of their brethren which should go forth preaching the word of God.' 'Lay their hands on you' is Luke 21:12's alone in the KJV, and Luke 21:12 is the verse that assembles the whole apparatus this proclamation dismantles — hands, synagogues, prisons, kings. Mark 13:9 is the synoptic parallel and contributes the beating that Alma 23:2 also forbids. Note that the 1830's 'nor neither of their brethren' is a double negative the 1920 edition repairs to 'either'; the first edition's construction is not the KJV's here, and the borrowing is in the clause before it.

pericopes.text: yea, he sent a decree among them, that they should not lay their hands on them to bind them, or to cast them into prison; neither should they spit upon them, nor smite them, nor cast them out of their synagogues, nor scourge them; neither should they cast stones at them, but that they should have free access to their houses, and also their temples, and their sanctuaries;

links.text: But beware of men: for they will deliver you up to the councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues;

provenance.route: Matthew 10:17 (with John 16:2, Matthew 23:34) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Four of the decree's seven prohibitions are KJV singletons or near it. “scourge you in their synagogues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 10:17; “put you out of the synagogues” in exactly one, John 16:2; “in the synagogues ye shall be beaten” in exactly one, Mark 13:9. Spitting on a messenger is Mark 10:34's and Luke 18:32's; stoning one is Mark 12:4's, where the husbandmen 'cast stones' at the servant sent to them; binding and imprisoning is Acts 5:18, where the council 'laid their hands on the apostles, and put them in the common prison'. The pronoun is worth catching by eye: Matthew 23:34 has Jesus tell his hearers 'ye shall scourge in YOUR synagogues', and Matthew 10:17 tells the disciples 'they will scourge you in THEIR synagogues'. The Book of Mormon's 'nor cast them out of their synagogues' has Matthew 10:17's grammar, which is the correct one for a decree addressed to the persecutors about their own buildings.
provenance.significance: The list is not a list of things that might happen; it is the King James Bible's list, negated. Every item the decree forbids is an item the gospels promise will be done to a preacher, and they are assembled from the two discourses where Jesus tells his messengers what to expect (Matthew 10, Mark 13 / Luke 21) plus the passion predictions where the same is done to him. Recover those contexts and the decree reads as an answer to a prophecy: what Jesus says his messengers must endure, this king makes it illegal to do. The last item is the tell — 'but that they should have free access to their houses, and also their temples, and their sanctuaries' — because access to the synagogue is exactly what John 16:2 says will be withdrawn.

links.note: 'That they should not lay their hands on them to bind them, or to cast them into prison; neither should they spit upon them, nor smite them, nor cast them out of their synagogues, nor scourge them; neither should they cast stones at them.' Seven prohibitions, and each one names a specific KJV persecution rather than a general cruelty: scourging in synagogues (Matthew 10:17, a singleton), expulsion from synagogues (John 16:2, a singleton), beating in synagogues (Mark 13:9, a singleton), spitting and smiting (Mark 10:34), stoning a sent servant (Mark 12:4), binding and imprisonment (Acts 5:18). Matthew 10:17 is given as the source because it holds the two elements the Book of Mormon keeps together, the scourging and the synagogue, and because its pronoun is the one the Book of Mormon uses. No clause is reproduced entire and this falls well below Skousen's threshold for a quotation; what makes the case is that a seven-item list should be drawn item by item from one narrow band of the KJV.
