pericopes.text: and thus they might go forth and preach the word according to their desires, for the king had been converted unto the Lord, and all his household; therefore he sent this proclamation throughout the land unto his people, that the word of God might have no obstruction, but that it might go forth throughout all the land, that his people might be convinced concerning the wicked traditions of their fathers, and that they might be convinced that they were all brethren, and that they had not ought to murder, nor to plunder, nor to steal, nor to commit adultery, nor to commit any manner of wickedness.

links.text: He saith unto him, Which? Jesus said, Thou shalt do no murder, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness,

provenance.mt: Exodus 20:13-15, 'Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal.'
provenance.route: Exodus 20:13-15 → Matthew 19:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The whole decision rests on one word. “do no murder” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 19:18; every other KJV form of the sixth commandment — Exodus 20:13, Deuteronomy 5:17, Mark 10:19, Luke 18:20, Romans 13:9, James 2:11 — reads 'kill'. Alma 23:3 reads 'murder', and it reads it first in the list, which is Matthew 19:18's order and not Mark 10:19's or Exodus's. tools/mediation-check.py returns Matthew 19:18 as decisive, though on a crude whole-verse diff; the human ground is the single word 'murder' and the position it holds.
provenance.significance: Matthew 19:18 is the answer given to the rich young ruler when he asks 'Which?' — and Alma 22:15 has already put that same ruler's question in this king's mouth, in Matthew 19:16's own words. So the two halves of one gospel pericope are distributed across two Book of Mormon chapters and given to one man: at 22:15 he asks what he must do for eternal life and offers his kingdom, and at 23:3 he proclaims to his people the commandments Jesus answered that question with. The fourth item is the one that does not come from Matthew — 'nor to plunder' — and it is what the list has to add for a people whose sin the book has been describing since Alma 17 as robbery. Mark 10:19 ends its own version of the list with 'Defraud not', which is the KJV's nearest word for it.

links.note: 'They had not ought to murder, nor to plunder, nor to steal, nor to commit adultery, nor to commit any manner of wickedness.' A four-item decalogue, and the mediation is settled by its first word: the KJV says 'kill' everywhere in this commandment except Matthew 19:18, which says 'do no murder', and the Book of Mormon says murder. Matthew 19:18 also puts murder first, where Mark 10:19 and Luke 18:20 begin with adultery and Exodus's numbering is not a list at all. That the source should be Matthew 19:18 specifically is not incidental: Alma 22:15 borrowed Matthew 19:16, the question this verse answers. The 1830's 'had not ought to' is the first edition's; 1920 regularizes it to 'ought not to', which loses nothing of the borrowing but is worth recording as the running text's own idiom rather than the KJV's.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that when the king had sent forth this proclamation, that Aaron and his brethren went forth from city to city, and from one house of worship to another, establishing churches, and consecrating priests and teachers throughout the land among the Lamanites, to preach and to teach the word of God among them; and thus they began to have great success.

And thousands were brought to the knowledge of the Lord, yea, thousands were brought to believe in the traditions of the Nephites; and they were taught the records and the prophecies which were handed down, even to the present time;

and as sure as the Lord liveth, so sure as many as believed, or as many as were brought to the knowledge of the truth, through the preaching of Ammon and his brethren, according to the spirit of revelation and of prophecy, and the power of God, working miracles in them; yea, I say unto you, as the Lord liveth, as many of the Lamanites as believed in their preaching, and were converted unto the Lord, never did fall away,
for they became a righteous people; they did lay down the weapons of their rebellion, that they did not fight against God no more, neither against any of their brethren.—

links.text: But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.

provenance.other: “fight against God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 5:39 and Acts 23:9, and both are a Pharisee counselling a council against acting on apostles in its custody. The Book of Mormon's clause is the phrase in Gamaliel's form, negated and made a description of converts: 'they did not fight against God no more' (1830; 1920 repairs the double negative to 'any more').
provenance.significance: The whole of Acts 5:17-42 is standing behind Alma 23. Acts 5:18 is the council laying hands on the apostles and putting them in prison, which Alma 23:1-2 forbids by decree; Acts 5:38-39 is Gamaliel telling that council to refrain from these men and let them alone, because if the work is of God it cannot be overthrown and they would be found fighting against God; Acts 5:40 is the council beating them and commanding them not to preach. Alma 23 is Gamaliel's counsel actually taken — a ruler who lets the men alone, on the ground that their work is of God — and 23:3's clause that 'the word of God might have no obstruction' is Acts 5:39's 'ye cannot overthrow it' from the other side. Acts 5 has already been read into this book at Alma 2:2, where Gamaliel's Theudas supplies the shape of Amlici; the phrase itself has not been used before Alma 23:7.

links.note: 'They did lay down the weapons of their rebellion, that they did not fight against God no more, neither against any of their brethren.' 'Fight against God' is a KJV phrase of exactly two verses, both in Acts, both spoken by a Pharisee restraining a council from destroying preachers it has arrested — and Alma 23 has just described a ruler doing precisely that restraining. The converts here are not merely people who stopped fighting Nephites; the word chosen for what they stopped doing is Gamaliel's word for what a court does when it acts against apostles. Alma 2:2 has already used Gamaliel's speech for its Theudas; this is the phrase from its climax, and the chapter around it is the counsel obeyed.

pericopes.text: Now these are they which were converted unto the Lord:
The people of the Lamanites which were in the land of Ishmael,
and also of the people of the Lamanites which were in the land of Middoni,
and also of the people of the Lamanites which were in the city of Nephi,
and also of the people of the Lamanites which were in the land of Shilom, and which were in the land of Shemlon, and in the city of Lemuel, and in the city of Shimnilom;

and these are the names of the cities of the Lamanites which were converted unto the Lord; and these are they that laid down the weapons of their rebellion, yea, all their weapons of war; and they were all Lamanites.

And the Amalekites were not converted, save only one; neither was any of the Amulonites; but they did harden their hearts, and also the hearts of the Lamanites in that part of the land whithersoever they dwelt; yea, and all their villages and all their cities;
therefore we have named all the cities of the Lamanites in which they did repent and come to the knowledge of the truth, and were converted.

And now it came to pass that the king and those people which were converted, were desirous that they might have a name, that thereby they might be distinguished from their brethren; therefore the king consulted with Aaron and many of their priests, concerning the name that they should take upon them, that they might be distinguished.
And it came to pass that they called their name Anti-Nephi-Lehies; and they were called by this name, and were no more called Lamanites.

links.text: And they said unto her, There is none of thy kindred that is called by this name.

provenance.other: “called by this name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:61. “called by a new name” occurs in exactly one, Isaiah 62:2. Acts 11:26, the disciples 'called Christians first in Antioch', is the KJV's only narrative of a body of converts acquiring a distinguishing name, and it shares no wording with Alma 23:17.
provenance.significance: Luke 1:61 is an objection, and the objection is about kindred: 'There is none of thy kindred that is called by this name.' The naming of John the Baptist is the KJV's one scene in which a family's naming convention is deliberately broken, and the breaking is at God's instruction and marks the child off from his relations. Alma 23:16-17 is a people asking for a name 'that thereby they might be distinguished from their brethren', receiving one, and being 'no more called Lamanites' — a naming whose whole point is the severance from kindred that Luke 1:61 objects to. Isaiah 62:2's promised new name is the theological warrant a reader will reach for first; Luke 1:61 is where the KJV's actual words are.

links.note: 'They called their name Anti-Nephi-Lehies; and they were called by this name, and were no more called Lamanites.' The phrase 'called by this name' occurs once in the KJV, in the neighbours' protest at John's naming, and its subject there is exactly the subject here: a name that does not belong to the kindred. This is recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because four common words are all the verbal contact there is, and because the naming of a convert people has two better-known scriptural warrants — Isaiah 62:2's new name and Acts 11:26's Christians — neither of which supplies any wording.
links.whyNot: 'Called by this name' is a phrase four ordinary words long, and its being a KJV singleton may be an accident of a common construction rather than evidence of borrowing. A reader who finds Isaiah 62:2 and Acts 11:26 sufficient to explain the scene, and the wording unremarkable, is not being unreasonable.

pericopes.text: And they began to be a very industrious people; yea, and they were friendly with the Nephites; therefore they did open a correspondence with them, and the curse of God did no more follow them.

And it came to pass that the Amalekites, and the Amulonites, and the Lamanites which were in the land of Amulon, and also in the land of Helam, and which was in the land of Jerusalem, and in fine, in all the land round about, which had not been converted, and had not taken upon them the name of Anti-Nephi-Lehi, were stirred up by the Amalekites, and by the Amulonites, to anger against their brethren;

and their hatred became exceeding sore against them, even insomuch that they began to rebel against their king, insomuch that they would not that he should be their king; therefore they took up arms against the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi.

links.text: But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us.

provenance.other: “we will not have this man to reign over us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 19:14, and “would not that I should reign over them” in exactly one, Luke 19:27. The Book of Mormon's clause, 'they would not that he should be their king', is Luke 19:27's construction with 'be their king' for 'reign over them' — near enough to be recognized, not near enough to be a quotation.
provenance.significance: The parable of the pounds is the KJV's one story of subjects who refuse a king they already have: a nobleman goes into a far country to receive a kingdom, his citizens send after him to say they will not have him reign over them, and when he returns his last order is that those enemies be brought and slain before him. Alma 24 sets the same refusal in motion and then declines its ending. The rebels take up arms against a king who will not defend himself, and instead of the enemies being slain before him, his people are slain in front of them without resistance. Luke 19's outcome is the outcome the chapter is written to refuse — which is also why the parable's other half, the servant who hid what he was given in a napkin, has already been used at Mosiah 9:2 without this half.

links.note: 'They began to rebel against their king, insomuch that they would not that he should be their king.' Two KJV singletons say this and both are in the parable of the pounds, twelve verses apart: the citizens' message at Luke 19:14 and the nobleman's judgment on them at 19:27. The Book of Mormon paraphrases rather than quotes, which is why this is moderate — 'would not that he should be their king' keeps Luke's syntax and changes his verb. Mosiah 9:2 has already drawn on the same parable for a different purpose, so the passage is available to the book; what is new here is the citizens' refusal rather than the servant's excuse. The 1830 reads 'insomuch that' twice in one sentence, which the later editions leave standing.

pericopes.text: Now the king conferred the kingdom upon his son; and he called his name Anti-Nephi-Lehi.
And the king died in that self-same year that the Lamanites began to make preparation for war against the people of God.

Now when Ammon and his brethren, and all those which had come up with him, saw the preparations of the Lamanites to destroy their brethren, they came forth to the land of Midian, and there Ammon met all his brethren; and from thence they came to the land of Ishmael, that they might hold a council with Lamoni, and also with his brother Anti-Nephi-Lehi, what they should do to defend themselves against the Lamanites.

Now there was not one soul among all the people which had been converted unto the Lord, that would take up arms against their brethren; nay, they would not even make any preparations for war; yea, and also their king commanded them that they should not.

Now these are the words which he said unto the people concerning the matter: I thank my God, my beloved people, that our great God has in goodness sent these our brethren, the Nephites, unto us to preach unto us, and to convince us of the traditions of our wicked fathers.
And behold, I thank my great God that he has given us a portion of his spirit to soften our hearts, that we have opened a correspondence with these brethren, the Nephites;
and behold, I also thank my God that by opening this correspondence, we have been convinced of our sins, and of the many murders which we have committed;

and I also thank my God, yea, my great God, that he hath granted unto us that we might repent of these things, and also that he hath forgiven us of those our many sins and murders which we have committed, and took away the guilt from our hearts, through the merits of his Son.

And now behold, my brethren, since it has been all that we could do, (as we were the most lost of all mankind,) to repent of all our sins and the many murders which we have committed, and to get God to take them away from our hearts, for it was all we could do to repent sufficiently before God, that he would take away our stain.
Now my best beloved brethren, since God hath taken away our stains, and our swords have become bright, then let us stain our swords no more with the blood of our brethren.

Behold, I say unto you, Nay, let us retain our swords, that they be not stained with the blood of our brethren: for perhaps, if we should stain our swords again, they can no more be washed bright through the blood of the Son of our great God, which shall be shed for the atonement of our sins.

links.text: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

provenance.other: “washed their robes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 7:14, and “made them white in the blood” in exactly one, the same verse. 'Stain' is a rare KJV word — three verses, Job 3:5, Isaiah 23:9 and Isaiah 63:3 — and only Isaiah 63:3 stains anything with blood: 'their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment', spoken by the treader of the winepress.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:21 and 13:11 have already used Revelation 7:14 in its own terms, of garments made white in the blood of the Lamb. Alma 24:13 changes the object, and the change is the chapter's whole argument: it is not robes but swords that are washed, and not white but bright. A garment washed in blood is a paradox one can absorb as metaphor; a murder weapon washed clean in the blood of the murdered God is the same paradox made intolerable, and the speech uses it to argue that the cleaning cannot be repeated. The Isaiah 63 figure sits underneath — the one KJV passage where blood stains rather than whitens — so that the two directions blood can run in scripture are set against each other across two verses of one sermon.

links.note: 'If we should stain our swords again, they can no more be washed bright through the blood of the Son of our great God, which shall be shed for the atonement of our sins.' The washing-in-blood figure is Revelation 7:14's, a verse with two phrases that occur nowhere else in the KJV, and it has been used twice already in this book of garments (5:21, 13:11). This is not that formula recurring. The object has moved from what a convert wears to what he killed with, and the sermon's practical conclusion — bury the swords, they cannot be cleaned twice — depends entirely on the transfer. Note also the transposed adjective: Revelation's robes are made white, and these swords are made bright, which is what a sword and not a robe can be.

pericopes.text: And the great God has had mercy on us, and made these things known unto us, that we might not perish; yea, and he hath made these things known unto us beforehand, because he loveth our souls as well as he loveth our children; therefore in his mercy he doth visit us by his angels, that the plan of salvation might be made known unto us as well as unto future generations.

O how merciful is our God! And now behold, since it has been as much as we could do to get our stains taken away from us, and our swords are made bright, let us hide them away that they may be kept bright, as a testimony to our God at the last day, or at the day that we shall be brought to stand before him to be judged, that we have not stained our swords in the blood of our brethren since he imparted his word unto us, and has made us clean thereby.

And now my brethren, if our brethren seek to destroy us, behold, we will hide away our swords, yea, even we will bury them deep in the earth, that they may be kept bright, as a testimony that we have never used them, at the last day; and if our brethren destroy us, behold, we shall go to our God, and shall be saved.

And now it came to pass that when the king had made an end of these sayings, and all the people were assembled together, they took their swords, and all the weapons which were used for the shedding of man’s blood, and they did bury them up deep in the earth;

links.text: Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.

provenance.other: “man's blood” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 9:6 and Acts 5:28, and “whoso sheddeth man's blood” in exactly one, Genesis 9:6. The Book of Mormon's phrase, 'the shedding of man's blood', is Genesis 9:6's noun in Hebrews 9:22's construction — “shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22, 'without shedding of blood is no remission', which this book has adjudicated at Alma 34:13.
provenance.significance: Genesis 9:6 is the King James Bible's foundational prohibition of homicide, and its second half is the reason: 'for in the image of God made he man.' That doctrine is what Aaron read to this king's father two chapters earlier — Alma 22:12, 'how God created man after his own image' — and the covenant sworn here is the first half of the same verse. The catalogue's finding is the arc: the Lamanite conversion begins with Genesis 1:27 read to a king and ends with Genesis 9:6 enacted by his son's people, which is the order the KJV itself puts them in and the logic Genesis 9:6 itself supplies. Note what the burial does to the verse's sanction, though. Genesis 9:6 answers bloodshed with bloodshed, 'by man shall his blood be shed'; these people bury the means of the answer and then let their own blood be shed at 24:21-22 without returning it.

links.note: 'They took their swords, and all the weapons which were used for the shedding of man's blood, and they did bury them up deep in the earth.' 'Man's blood' is a KJV phrase of two verses and the shedding of it is Genesis 9:6's, the covenant with Noah that grounds the prohibition of murder in the image of God. The phrase carries through into 24:18, where the covenant is spelled out — 'that they never use weapons again for the shedding of man's blood' — so the link is adjudicated here at its first occurrence. The construction 'the shedding of' is Hebrews 9:22's rather than Genesis's, which is worth recording because 24:13 has just made the blood of the Son the thing that cleans the swords, and Hebrews 9:22 is the verse that makes shed blood the condition of remission.

pericopes.text: and this they did, it being in their view a testimony to God, and also to men, that they never use weapons again for the shedding of man’s blood; and this they did, vouching and covenanting with God, that rather than to shed the blood of their brethren, they would give up their own lives; and rather than to take away from a brother, they would give unto him; and rather than to spend their days in idleness, they would labor abundantly with theit their hands;

links.text: Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.

provenance.other: “working with his hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:28, and “to give to him that needeth” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. Paul's other statements about manual labour — 1 Corinthians 4:12, 1 Thessalonians 4:11, 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12 — have the working but not the giving, and it is the giving that Alma 24:18 has.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 4:28 is a single sentence containing a three-step exchange: stop taking, work with your hands, so that you have something to give. Alma 24:18 has the same three steps in the same order — 'rather than to take away from a brother, they would give unto him; and rather than to spend their days in idleness, they would labor abundantly with their hands' — and reproduces Paul's 'but rather' construction twice over. What the Book of Mormon adds is the step before: 'rather than to shed the blood of their brethren, they would give up their own lives.' Read Ephesians 4:28 back into the verse and the covenant is Paul's rule for a converted thief extended upward one degree, from property to life, with the same grammar carrying both. That is a strong argument for the borrowing being deliberate rather than incidental: the shape 'rather than X, they would Y' is Paul's, and the Book of Mormon runs it three times.

links.note: 'Rather than to take away from a brother, they would give unto him; and rather than to spend their days in idleness, they would labor abundantly with theit their hands.' Ephesians 4:28 is the only KJV verse that joins renounced theft, manual labour and giving to the needy, and it contributes two phrases that occur nowhere else in the Bible. The Book of Mormon's version keeps Paul's antithetical 'but rather' and his sequence while replacing his imperative with a covenant in the third person. The 1830 reading preserves a compositor's dittography, 'with theit their hands', which the later editions silently repair; the doubled word is a printing accident and carries no argument, but it is the running text.

pericopes.text: and thus we see that when these Lamanites were brought to believe and to know the truth, that they were firm, and would suffer even unto death, rather than to commit sin; and thus we see, that they buried the weapons of peace, or they buried the weapons of war, for peace.

links.text: Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.

provenance.other: The two distinctive phrases of the source are both KJV singletons — “resisted unto blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “striving against sin” occurs in exactly one, both Hebrews 12:4 — but the Book of Mormon reproduces neither of them. The contact is the proposition, not the wording: dying rather than sinning.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 12:4 is a reproach. Its readers have not yet paid for their resistance to sin with their lives, and the writer says so to shame them into endurance. Alma 24:19 reports a people who have. The reproach and the report are the two halves of one idea, and the Book of Mormon's sentence is what Hebrews 12:4 describes as not having happened yet — which is worth noticing because the verse is immediately followed in Hebrews by the discipline of sons, and Alma 24 is a chapter in which fathers' sins are what the children are being spared.

links.note: 'They were firm, and would suffer even unto death, rather than to commit sin.' Hebrews 12:4 is the King James Bible's one verse that puts resistance unto blood and striving against sin in a single clause, which is exactly the trade Alma 24:19 says these converts made. No phrase is reproduced, so this is registered as an echo and kjvSpecific is 'uncertain': 'suffer unto death' and 'commit sin' are ordinary English and Revelation 2:10's 'be thou faithful unto death' is an equally available background.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact at all beyond commonplaces. A reader may fairly say that a narrator summarizing a martyrdom would write this sentence with no New Testament verse in view, and that Hebrews 12:4 has been selected after the fact because it is memorable.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that their brethren, the Lamanites, made preparations for war, and came up to the land of Nephi, for the purpose of destroying the king, and to place another in his stead, and also of destroying the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi out of the land.

And it came to pass that when the people saw that they were coming against them, they went out to meet them, and prostrated themselves before them to the earth, and began to call on the name of the Lord; and thus they were in this attitude, when the Lamanites began to fall upon them, and began to slay them with the sword;
and thus, without meeting any resistance, they did slay a thousand and five of them; and we know that they are blessed, for they have gone to dwell with their God.

Now when the Lamanites saw that their brethren would not flee from the sword, neither would they turn aside to the right hand or to the left, but that they would lay down and perish, and praised God even in the very act of perishing under the sword;

links.text: Ye shall observe to do therefore as the LORD your God hath commanded you: ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.

provenance.other: “turn aside to the right hand or to the left” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 5:32 — ten continuous words. The KJV's other right-hand-or-left formulas differ in the joint: Deuteronomy 17:11 and 17:20 and 28:14 and Joshua 1:7 and 23:6 all read 'to the right hand, or to the left' but attach it to other verbs ('decline', 'turn not', 'depart'). Only Deuteronomy 5:32 has 'turn aside to'.
provenance.significance: The ten words are the closing sentence of the KJV's second giving of the Ten Commandments — Deuteronomy 5 ends the Decalogue with 'ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left', meaning do not deviate from what you were commanded — and the sixth of those commandments, at Deuteronomy 5:17, is the one this people has covenanted to keep. Alma 23:3 had their king proclaim that Decalogue; Alma 24:17 had them bury the means of breaking it; and here, with swords coming down on them, the KJV's idiom for exact obedience becomes a description of their bodies. They do not turn aside to the right hand or to the left because they will not move at all. That is metalepsis in Hays's sense: the phrase is dead metaphor in Deuteronomy and is reanimated by being taken literally, and the reader who recovers Deuteronomy 5 finds the commandment the whole scene is about sitting fifteen verses above it.

links.note: 'Their brethren would not flee from the sword, neither would they turn aside to the right hand or to the left, but that they would lay down and perish, and praised God even in the very act of perishing under the sword.' A ten-word run reproducing a KJV singleton exactly, and the machine stream found it — the longest run in the chapter by a wide margin. It is catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the run and of the source being identifiable beyond dispute, while falling below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and forming no part of his list. The idiom is Deuteronomy's figure for not deviating from a commandment, and it is used here of men physically refusing to dodge. The 1830's 'they would lay down and perish' is the first edition's; 1920 corrects 'lay' to 'lie', which tidies the grammar and slightly weakens the picture of men going down deliberately. 'In the very act' is John 8:4's phrase, the KJV's only occurrence, and it belongs there to a woman taken in adultery — the wording of a sin caught in progress, given here to men caught in the act of dying well.

pericopes.text: now when the Lamanites saw this, they did forbear from slaying them; and there were many whose hearts had swollen in them for those of their brethren who had fallen under the sword, for they repented of the things which they had done.

And it came to pass that they threw down their weapons of war, and they would not take them again, for they were stung for the murders which they had committed; and they came down even as their brethren, relying upon the mercies of those whose arms were lifted to slay them.

And it came to pass that the people of God were joined that day by more than the number which had been slain; and those which had been slain, were righteous people; therefore we have no reason to doubt but what they are saved.—

And there was not a wicked man slain among them; but there were more than a thousand brought to the knowledge of the truth; thus we see that the Lord worketh in many ways to the salvation of his people.
Now the greatest number of those of the Lamanites which slew so many of their brethren, were Amalekites and Amulonites, the greatest number of whom were after the order of the Nehors.
Now among those which joined the people of the Lord, there were none which were Amalekites or Amulonites, or which were of the order of Nehor, but they were actual descendants of Laman and Lemuel;

and thus we can plainly discern, that after a people has been once enlightened by the spirit of God, and hath had great knowledge of things pertaining to righteousness, and then have fallen away into sin and transgression, they become more hardened, and thus their estate becometh worse than as though they had never known these things.

links.text: For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost,

provenance.route: Hebrews 6:4-6, with 2 Peter 2:20-21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “once enlightened” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 6:4, and “fall away” occurs in exactly two, Hebrews 6:6 and Luke 8:13. The closing clause has a second source: 2 Peter 2:20-21 is the KJV's statement that for those who have known the way of righteousness and turned back, 'the latter end is worse with them than the beginning' and 'it had been better for them not to have known'. “worse than the first” occurs in three KJV verses, of which Matthew 12:45 and Luke 11:26 are the returning unclean spirit — 'the last state of that man is worse than the first'.
provenance.significance: Mormon's editorial conclusion is assembled from the two New Testament passages on apostasy, and it takes one clause from each. Hebrews 6 supplies the enlightenment and the falling away; 2 Peter 2 supplies the comparison with never having known. The reason this matters for the chapter is that the conclusion is being drawn about the Amalekites and Amulonites, who are Nephite dissenters — men who had the knowledge and left it — and set against Lamanites who never had it. That is precisely the distinction Hebrews 6:4-6 and 2 Peter 2:20-21 exist to make, and the verse borrows both of them to make it. Note the one thing it does not borrow: Hebrews 6:6's conclusion that such people are impossible to renew, which the chapter has just disproved at 24:24-27, where a thousand of the attackers repent on the spot.

links.note: 'After a people has been once enlightened by the spirit of God, and hath had great knowledge of things pertaining to righteousness, and then have fallen away into sin and transgression, they become more hardened, and thus their estate becometh worse than as though they had never known these things.' Two KJV rarities anchor it: 'once enlightened' occurs only at Hebrews 6:4, and 'fall away' in this sense only at Hebrews 6:6. The final clause moves to the other classic apostasy passage — 2 Peter 2:20-21, better not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known and turned — with the comparative of Matthew 12:45's returning spirit, 'worse than the first', behind the wording of 'worse than as though they had never known'. What makes the composite worth stating rather than assuming is that the Book of Mormon takes the diagnosis from Hebrews and declines Hebrews' verdict, which the chapter's own narrative has just contradicted.

pericopes.text: And behold, now it came to pass that those Lamanites were more angry, because they had slain their brethren; therefore they swore vengeance upon the Nephites; and they did no more attempt to slay the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi at that time;
but they took their armies and went over into the borders of the land of Zarahemla, and fell upon the people which were in the land of Ammonihah, and destroyed them.
And after that, they had many battles with the Nephites, in the which they were driven and slain;
and among the Lamanites which were slain, were almost all the seed of Amulon and his brethren, which were the priests of Noah, and they were slain by the hands of the Nephites;

and the remainder having fled into the east wilderness, and having usurped the power and authority over the Lamanites, caused that many of the Lamanites should perish by fire, because of their belief:

for many of them, after having suffered much loss and so many afflictions, they began to be stirred up in remembrance of the words which Aaron and his brethren had preached to them in their land; therefore they began to disbelieve the traditions of their fathers, and to believe in the Lord, and that he gave great power unto the Nephites; and thus there were many of them converted in the wilderness.
And it came to pass that those rulers which were the remnant of the children of Amulon, caused that they should be put to death, yea, all those that believed in these things.

Now this martyrdom caused that many of their brethren should be stirred up to anger; and there began to be contention in the wilderness; and the Lamanites began to hunt the seed of Amulon and his brethren, and began to slay them, and they fled into the east wilderness.

And behold, they are hunted at this day, by the Lamanites: thus the words of Abinadi was brought to pass, which he said concerning the seed of the priests which caused that he should suffer death by fire.
For he said unto them, What ye shall do unto me, shall be a type of things to come.
And now Abinadi was the first that suffered death by fire, because of his belief in God: now this is what he meant, that many should suffer death by fire, according as he had suffered.

And he said unto the priests of Noah, That their seed should cause many to be put to death, in the like manner as he was, and that they should be scattered abroad and slain, even as a sheep having no shepherd is driven and slain by wild beasts: and now behold, these words were verified, for they were driven by the Lamanites, and they were hunted, and they were smitten.

provenance.other: “sheep having no shepherd” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The other shepherdless-flock verses read differently — Numbers 27:17 'as sheep which have no shepherd', 1 Kings 22:17 'as sheep that have not a shepherd', 2 Chronicles 18:16 'as sheep that have no shepherd', Mark 6:34 'as sheep not having a shepherd'. Matthew 9:36 alone has the participle, and Matthew 9:36 alone puts 'scattered abroad' immediately before it. Alma 25:12 has both, in Matthew's order, separated only by 'and slain'.
provenance.significance: The point of the row is not the phrase, which Alma 5:37 has already used and which is adjudicated there. It is that this verse is quoting Abinadi, and the record of Abinadi does not read this way. Mosiah 17:18 gives his words at the stake as 'ye shall be smitten on every hand, and shall be driven and scattered to and fro, even as a WILD FLOCK is driven by wild and ferocious beasts.' Alma 25:12, reporting the same prophecy fulfilled seventy years later, keeps the driving and the beasts and replaces the wild flock with Matthew 9:36's shepherdless sheep. A prophecy delivered in one book is quoted in another with a New Testament clause it did not previously contain — and the clause imported is the KJV's one compassionate use of the figure, where the shepherdless crowd is pitied rather than condemned, set here over a seed being hunted to death.

links.note: 'They should be scattered abroad and slain, even as a sheep having no shepherd is driven and slain by wild beasts.' Two of Matthew 9:36's phrases in Matthew's order, one of them a KJV singleton. The argument for the singleton itself is at Alma 5:37; what is new here is that the sentence is presented as Abinadi's, and Mosiah 17:18 records Abinadi saying 'as a wild flock' instead. The singular 'a sheep' is the 1830 reading and stands in the current text.
links.text: But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.

provenance.other: “in the like manner” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 6:23. The KJV's ordinary form is the unarticled 'in like manner', which it uses a dozen times; the articled form is Luke's alone, and Alma 25:12 has the articled form.
provenance.significance: Recover Luke 6:23 and the clause turns out to be about exactly this: 'for in the like manner did their fathers unto the prophets.' Luke's subject is the inheritance of prophet-killing — what is done to the disciples now is what the fathers did to the prophets then — and Luke 6:26 states the converse two verses later, 'so did their fathers to the false prophets.' Alma 25:12 is a prophecy that the SEED of the men who burned Abinadi will put many to death 'in the like manner as he was', and Alma 25:9-11 spends three verses establishing that the manner is the same manner, death by fire. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's one phrase for generational repetition of the killing of prophets and used it for a generational repetition of the killing of a prophet's converts.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 23:31, 'ye are the children of them which killed the prophets', is the same doctrine without the phrase.

links.note: 'That their seed should cause many to be put to death, in the like manner as he was.' The four words are a KJV singleton and their one home is a sentence about fathers and prophets. The link is moderate rather than high because the phrase is short and unremarkable English; what argues for it is that its only KJV occurrence says what Alma 25:9-12 is saying.
links.text: Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for joy: for, behold, your reward is great in heaven: for in the like manner did their fathers unto the prophets.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when the Lamanites saw that they could not overpower the Nephites, they returned again to their own land; and many of them came over to dwell in the land of Ishmael and the land of Nephi, and did join themselves to the people of God, which was the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi;

provenance.other: “join themselves” occurs in exactly two KJV verses. Daniel 11:6 is a dynastic marriage alliance; Isaiah 56:6 is the only one about religious adhesion — 'the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD, to serve him'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 56:3-7 is the KJV's charter for the outsider who attaches himself to Israel, and its terms are the terms of Alma 25:13-15 in order: the stranger joins himself to the LORD (25:13, the Lamanites join themselves to the people of God), keeps the sabbath and takes hold of the covenant (25:14-15, they keep the commandments and the statutes and the law of Moses), and is brought to the holy mountain and accepted at the altar (which is what Alma 27 will do for them when Jershon is given). The chapter that follows Isaiah 56:6 in the Book of Mormon's own sequence — the grant of a land to a converted people — is the promise Isaiah 56:7 makes.
provenance.alternative: 1 Peter 2:10, 'which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God', supplies the sense of the clause more exactly and shares only the common phrase; it is filed in the exclusion register.

links.note: 'Many of them came over to dwell in the land of Ishmael and the land of Nephi, and did join themselves to the people of God.' The verb is Isaiah 56:6's and the situation is Isaiah 56's: foreigners attaching themselves to a covenant people, with what they must then keep spelled out immediately afterward. Moderate, because 'join themselves to' is three ordinary words and the Book of Mormon joins them to the people rather than to the LORD.
links.text: Also the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD, to serve him, and to love the name of the LORD, to be his servants, every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant;

pericopes.text: and they did also bury their weapons of war, according as their brethren had, and they began to be a righteous people; and they did walk in the ways of the Lord, and did observe to keep his commandments, and his statutes,

provenance.other: “to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 30:16, which continues 'and his statutes and his judgments'. The pair “his commandments and his statutes” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, five of them in Deuteronomy; 'observe to keep' occurs in none, though Deuteronomy 28:15's 'observe to do all his commandments and his statutes' is next to it.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 30 is the chapter of return — the covenant offered again to a people who have been scattered and have turned back — and its central verse commands walking in his ways and keeping his commandments and his statutes as the condition of life in the land. Alma 25:13-14 has a scattered people coming back to a land, joining the people of God, and doing precisely those two things in that order. The whyNot below is real, but the Deuteronomic register is not incidental here: these converts are being described in the vocabulary of covenant renewal, and the next verse puts them under the law of Moses.

links.whyNot: The formula is distributed across Deuteronomy rather than confined to one verse, and the Book of Mormon has 'walk in the ways of the Lord', which no KJV verse has, where Deuteronomy 30:16 has 'walk in his ways'. Deuteronomy 30:16 is named as the source because it alone joins the walking to the keeping of commandments and statutes in one clause, not because the wording could not have come from 30:10 or 28:15.
links.note: 'They did walk in the ways of the Lord, and did observe to keep his commandments, and his statutes.' Two Deuteronomic formulas run together, of which the second half — commandments and statutes as a pair — is almost exclusively Deuteronomy's in the KJV. Well below any quotation threshold and recorded as an allusion on the conjunction rather than the length.
links.text: In that I command thee this day to love the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments and his statutes and his judgments, that thou mayest live and multiply: and the LORD thy God shall bless thee in the land whither thou goest to possess it.

pericopes.text: yea, and they did keep the law of Moses: for it was expedient that they should keep the law of Moses as yet, for it was not all fulfilled. But notwithstanding the law of Moses, they did look forward to the coming of Christ, considering that the law of Moses was a type of his coming, and believing that they must keep those outward performances, until the time that he should be revealed unto them.

provenance.other: “keep the law of Moses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 15:5, where the believing Pharisees demand that Gentile converts be circumcised and commanded to keep it. Within the Book of Mormon the phrase is Abinadi's before it is anyone else's in this register: Mosiah 13:27 reads 'it is expedient that ye should keep the law of Moses AS YET; but … the time shall come when it shall no more be expedient to keep the law of Moses.'
provenance.significance: Alma 25:15 is Mosiah 13:27 rewritten in the third person about a different people — 'it was expedient that they should keep the law of Moses as yet' — and the proximate model is therefore the earlier Book of Mormon verse, not the KJV, which is why the mediation is not direct-NT. What makes the chain worth recording is that both ends are the same controversy. Acts 15 is the council on whether converts from outside Israel must keep the law of Moses; Alma 25:13-16 is a mass conversion from outside Israel and the ruling on exactly that question, and it answers as Acts 15 answers, that the law is kept for a season and is not what saves. The phrase 'outward performances' in the same verse comes from the same page of Abinadi: Mosiah 13:30's 'a law of performances and of ordinances'.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 5:17-18 stands behind the reason given rather than the demand: the law is kept because 'it was not all fulfilled', and 'till all be fulfilled' is Matthew 5:18's clause. Filed as a separate row.

links.note: 'It was expedient that they should keep the law of Moses as yet, for it was not all fulfilled.' The clause is a KJV singleton carried at second hand: Abinadi has it at Mosiah 13:27 with 'expedient' and 'as yet' already attached, and Alma 25:15 reproduces his sentence for the Lamanite converts. Recorded here rather than passed over as a repeat because this is a different book and a different hand — Mormon narrating, not Abinadi preaching — and because the situation, converts from outside the covenant put under the law, is Acts 15's situation and not Mosiah 13's.
links.text: But there rose up certain of the sect of the Pharisees which believed, saying, That it was needful to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.

provenance.other: “all be fulfilled” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 5:18 and Luke 21:32. Only Matthew 5:18 is about the law: 'one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.'
provenance.significance: Alma 25:15 gives a reason for keeping the law that the Book of Mormon does not usually give, and the reason is Matthew 5:18's: not that the law saves, and not that it is commanded, but that it is not yet all fulfilled. Matthew 5:17 supplies the other half — 'I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil' — and Alma 25:15's answer to why converts still sacrifice is that the fulfiller has not yet come. The verse then says the law is 'a type of his coming', which is the doctrine of Matthew 5:17 stated as typology.

links.note: 'For it was not all fulfilled.' Four words, of which three are Matthew 5:18's, and the argument they carry is the argument of Matthew 5:17-18. Filed as an echo because the contact is a single short clause and 'fulfilled' is common; what raises it above nothing is that the KJV joins 'the law' to 'all be fulfilled' in one verse only.
links.text: For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.

pericopes.text: Now they did not suppose that salvation came by the law of Moses; but the law of Moses did serve to strengthen their faith in Christ; and thus they did retain a hope through faith, unto eternal salvation, relying upon the spirit of prophecy, which spake of those things to come.

provenance.other: “by the law of Moses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse: Acts 13:39, 'by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.' The Book of Mormon's four occurrences of the phrase are Mosiah 12:31, 12:32, 13:27 and Alma 25:16, and the first three are one exchange between Abinadi and the priests of Noah.
provenance.significance: This is the verse where the catalogue's two Alma 25 chains meet. The priests of Noah answered Abinadi that salvation did come by the law of Moses (Mosiah 12:32) and he answered them out of Acts 13:39; Alma 25 has just finished narrating the destruction of those priests' seed, and it closes the episode by reporting that their victims' converts hold the position the priests denied — in the priests' own borrowed words, negated. 'They did not suppose that salvation came by the law of Moses' is Mosiah 12:32 with a negative in front of it. The Book of Mormon is not merely reusing a phrase; it is settling an argument it staged seventy years and thirteen chapters earlier.
provenance.alternative: Galatians 2:21's 'if righteousness come by the law' supplies the verb 'come' that Acts 13:39 lacks, as recorded at Mosiah 12:31.

links.note: 'Now they did not suppose that salvation came by the law of Moses; but the law of Moses did serve to strengthen their faith in Christ.' The KJV has this phrase in one verse, and the Book of Mormon has it in one earlier scene, where it is the whole point in dispute. The second clause then supplies what Acts 13:39 leaves out and Galatians 3:24 states — the law as the thing that brings a believer to Christ rather than the thing that justifies.
links.text: And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.

pericopes.text: And now behold, Ammon, and Aaron, and Omner, and Himni, and their brethren, did rejoice exceedingly, for the success which they had had among the Lamanites, seeing that the Lord had granted unto them according to their prayers, and that he had also verified his word unto them in every particular.

provenance.other: “verified” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Genesis 42:20, 1 Kings 8:26 and its parallel 2 Chronicles 6:17. It is not a common word in the Book of Mormon either: seven occurrences in the whole book, two of them in this chapter.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 8:26 is a petition inside Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple: 'let thy word, I pray thee, be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father.' Alma 25:17 is the report of that petition granted, in that petition's vocabulary: 'the Lord had granted unto them according to their prayers, and … he had also verified his word unto them in every particular.' The KJV's rare verb for a promise made good belongs to a prayer asking for it; the Book of Mormon uses it of a prayer answered. Amaleki had already used it the same way at Omni 1:6, where the full argument for the phrase's syntax is set out.

links.note: 'The Lord had granted unto them according to their prayers, and … he had also verified his word unto them in every particular.' 'Verified' is a rare KJV word and rarer still in this book, and its two royal occurrences are a prayer that a word be verified. The row is at moderate because the contact is one verb: the case rests on that verb being scarce in both corpora and on the prayer-and-answer frame it arrives inside. Alma 25:12's 'these words were verified' five verses earlier is the same usage in narration.
links.text: And now, O God of Israel, let thy word, I pray thee, be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father.

pericopes.text: And now, these are the words of Ammon to his brethren, which sayeth thus: My brothers and my brethren, behold I say unto you, how great reason have we to rejoice; for could we have supposed, when we started from the land of Zarahemla, that God would have granted unto us such great blessings?
And now I ask, What great blessings hath he bestowed upon us? Can ye tell?

Behold, I answer for you, for our brethren, the Lamanites, were in darkness, yea, even in the darkest abyss; but behold, how many of them are brought to behold the marvellous light of God! And this is the blessing which hath been bestowed upon us, that we have been made instruments in the hands of God, to bring about this great work.

provenance.other: “marvellous light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 2:9 — “who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light”. The 1830 spelling is the KJV's own and the 1920 edition modernized it to 'marvelous', so the borrowing is fractionally plainer in the running text than in the current one (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: The proximate model is not 1 Peter but Alma the Younger. Mosiah 27:29 is his own conversion sentence — 'I was in the darkest abyss; but now I behold the marvellous light of God' — and Alma 26:3 reproduces both halves of it, in order, about the Lamanites: 'were in darkness, yea, even in the darkest abyss; but behold, how many of them are brought to behold the marvellous light of God.' 'Darkest abyss' occurs in exactly two places in the Book of Mormon and they are these two. So Ammon describes a mass conversion in the private vocabulary of the one conversion the book has narrated from the inside, and the biblical phrase reaches him already carrying an interpretation: not Peter's chosen generation called out of darkness, but a particular man's memory of a particular hell.

links.note: 'Our brethren, the Lamanites, were in darkness, yea, even in the darkest abyss; but behold, how many of them are brought to behold the marvellous light of God!' The KJV singleton is 1 Peter's and it was adjudicated at Mosiah 27:29; the row is written here rather than passed over because the route matters — it comes to Ammon through Alma's conversion speech, with 'darkest abyss' attached, and that pairing is not in 1 Peter.
links.text: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light;

pericopes.text: Behold, thousands of them do rejoice, and have been brought into the fold of God.

Behold, the field was ripe, and blessed are ye, for ye did thrust in the sickle, and did reap with your mights, yea, all the day long did ye labor; and behold the number of your sheaves, and they shall be gathered into the garners, that they are not wasted;

provenance.mt: Joel 3:13 — 'Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great.'
provenance.route: Joel 3:13 → Revelation 14:15 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The two English forms differ in the verb. Joel 3:13 has 'Put ye in the sickle'; Revelation 14:15 has 'Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe.' “the harvest of the earth is ripe” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:15. Alma 26:5 has 'ye did thrust in the sickle, and did reap' — Revelation's verb, Revelation's pairing of thrusting with reaping, and Revelation's 'ripe'. `mediation-check.py` returns four decisive points, all for Revelation 14:15.
provenance.significance: A tenth-order mediation case of the kind CONVENTIONS §7 exists for, and one whose New Testament source is being used against its own grain. Revelation 14:14-20 is a judgment harvest: the sickle is thrust in and what follows is the winepress of the wrath of God, trodden until blood comes out to the horse bridles. Alma 26:5-7 keeps the sickle, the reaping and the ripeness and turns them into a harvest of converts who are gathered and kept safe from a storm. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's most violent harvest and read it as Matthew 9:37's — which is what the next two verses confirm, since 26:7's 'Lord of the harvest' is Matthew's phrase and not Revelation's.

links.note: 'Behold, the field was ripe, and blessed are ye, for ye did thrust in the sickle, and did reap with your mights.' The verb is decisive: the KJV puts a sickle in at Joel 3:13 and thrusts one in at Revelation 14:15-19, and Alma 26:5 thrusts. 'Thrust in the sickle' appears nowhere else in the Book of Mormon. The sheaves and the garners of the same verse belong to Matthew 3:12's threshing-floor instead, which is adjudicated elsewhere and registered in the exclusions.
links.text: And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to him that sat on the cloud, Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe.

pericopes.text: yea, they shall not be beaten down by the storm, at the last day; yea, neither shall they be harrowed up by the whirlwinds; but when the storm cometh, they shall be gathered together in their place, that the storm cannot penetrate to them; yea, neither shall they be driven with fierce winds, whithersoever the enemy listeth to carry them.

provenance.other: Two rarities from one verse. “fierce winds” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 3:4; 'listeth' occurs in exactly two, John 3:8 ('the wind bloweth where it listeth') and James 3:4, and only James has it in the construction 'whithersoever the governor listeth'. Alma 26:6 has 'driven with fierce winds, whithersoever the enemy listeth to carry them' — both of James's phrases, in James's order, with 'the enemy' where James has 'the governor'.
provenance.significance: James 3:4 is an image about the tongue: a great ship driven of fierce winds is turned by a very small helm wherever the steersman wants, as a small member steers a whole life. Alma 26:6 keeps the ship's grammar and changes who holds the helm. In James the governor is the one legitimately in control; in Alma the one who would carry the sheaves off wherever he listeth is 'the enemy', and the point of the sentence is that he cannot, because the harvest is in the garner and the storm cannot penetrate to it. The borrowed clause is the clause that describes being steered, and it is used to say that these people will not be.

links.note: 'Neither shall they be driven with fierce winds, whithersoever the enemy listeth to carry them.' A KJV singleton and a KJV near-singleton from the same verse, adjacent and in order, in a Book of Mormon sentence that has otherwise left the sea entirely — there is no ship in Alma 26, only sheaves in a storm. That the nautical wording survives the change of vehicle is what identifies the source.
links.text: Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth.

pericopes.text: But behold, they are in the hands of the Lord of the harvest, and they are his; and he will raise them up at the last day.

provenance.other: “Lord of the harvest” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 9:38 and Luke 10:2, which are the same saying. 'Raise them up at the last day' has no KJV verse, but 'raise him up at the last day' is John 6's refrain, four times in one chapter.
provenance.significance: Alma 25:12 borrowed Matthew 9:36's 'scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd' for the seed of the priests of Noah; two verses later in Matthew the same paragraph turns to the harvest — 'the harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few; pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest' — and Alma 26:5-7 is that harvest, with labourers who thrust in the sickle and labour all the day long. The two Alma chapters take the two halves of one Matthean paragraph in Matthew's order and apply them to the two halves of the same event: the Lamanites who were not gathered, and the Lamanites who were. Whether the writer worked from the page or from memory, the page is Matthew 9:36-38.

links.note: 'They are in the hands of the Lord of the harvest, and they are his; and he will raise them up at the last day.' The title is Matthew's and Luke's alone, and it closes a harvest allegory whose other two elements — the sickle and the garner — came from Revelation and Matthew 3. Moderate rather than high, because a harvest allegory will reach for a harvest title; what argues for the row is the Matthew 9 proximity noted above.
links.text: Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.

pericopes.text: Blessed be the name of our God; let us sing to his praise, yea, let us give thanks to his holy name, for he doth work righteousness forever.

provenance.other: “give thanks to thy holy name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “glory in thy praise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and they are the same verse: 1 Chronicles 16:35, 'Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather us together, and deliver us from the heathen, that we may give thanks to thy holy name, and glory in thy praise.' Psalm 106:47 is the same petition with 'unto thy holy name' and 'to triumph in thy praise'. 'Blessed be the name of' occurs in three KJV verses.
provenance.significance: Recover 1 Chronicles 16:35 and it is a petition to be gathered and delivered from the heathen so that thanks may be given. Alma 26:8 is that petition answered from the wrong direction: the heathen have been gathered in and are the ones being given thanks for. Ammon's psalm then supplies the verse's second singleton eight verses later — 'therefore let us glory, yea, we will glory in the Lord' at 26:16 — so the two rare phrases of 1 Chronicles 16:35 open and close the same speech. The verse sits inside David's psalm at the bringing of the ark, which is the Old Testament's model for a song of thanksgiving sung by a company rather than an individual, and Alma 26:8's 'let us sing to his praise' is exactly that form.

links.note: 'Blessed be the name of our God; let us sing to his praise, yea, let us give thanks to his holy name, for he doth work righteousness forever.' Two KJV singletons from one verse of David's thanksgiving psalm, one used here and one at 26:16. 'Work righteousness' is not itself a KJV phrase in this form; the KJV has 'worketh righteousness' at Psalm 15:2, Isaiah 64:5 and Acts 10:35, and the last of those — 'in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him' — is the Peter-and-Cornelius verse, which is the New Testament's charter for a mission outside the covenant people.
links.text: And say ye, Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather us together, and deliver us from the heathen, that we may give thanks to thy holy name, and glory in thy praise.

pericopes.text: For if we had not come up out of the land of Zarahemla, these our dearly beloved brethren, which have so dearly beloved us, would still have heen racked with hatred against us, yea, and they would also have been strangers to God.
And it came to pass that when Ammon had said these words, his brother Aaron rebuked him, saying: Ammon, I fear that thy joy doth carry thee away unto boasting.
But Ammon saith unto him, I do not boast in my own strength, or in my own wisdom; but behold, my joy is full, yea, my heart is brim with joy, and I will rejoice in my God;

yea,I know that I am nothing; as to my strength, I am weak; therefore I will not boast of myself, but I will boast of my God; for in his strength I can do all things; yea, behold, many mighty miracles we have wrought in this land, for which we will praise his name forever.

provenance.other: “I can do all things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 4:13: 'I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.' Alma 26:12 reads 'in his strength I can do all things', which keeps the clause and replaces Paul's relative clause with the noun it contains.
provenance.significance: The whole of Alma 26:11-12 is Paul's paradox in Paul's own order. 'I know that I am nothing' is 2 Corinthians 12:11's 'though I be nothing' and 1 Corinthians 13:2's 'I am nothing'; 'as to my strength, I am weak' is 2 Corinthians 12:10's 'when I am weak, then am I strong'; and the resolution — not my strength but his, and in his I can do everything — is Philippians 4:13. What makes the passage more than a chain of borrowings is its frame: Aaron has just accused Ammon of boasting (26:10), which is the charge Paul spends 2 Corinthians 10-12 answering, and Ammon answers it as Paul does, by conceding the boast and relocating its object.

links.note: 'Yea, I know that I am nothing; as to my strength, I am weak; therefore I will not boast of myself, but I will boast of my God; for in his strength I can do all things.' Five words of a KJV singleton, unaltered, at the turn of the sentence. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and catalogued as a quotation on the rarity of the clause and its exactness, not its length.
links.text: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.

pericopes.text: Behold, how many thousands of our brethren hath he loosed from the pains of hell; and they are brought to sing redeeming love; and this because of the power of his word which is in us; therefore have we not great reason to rejoice?

provenance.route: Acts 2:24 (the verb) + Psalm 116:3 (the noun) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Two KJV singletons welded. “loosed the pains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:24, where what is loosed is 'the pains of death'; “pains of hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 116:3, where they 'gat hold upon me' and are not loosed by anyone. Alma 26:13's 'loosed from the pains of hell' exists in neither, and the join is visible at the noun.
provenance.significance: The two verses the phrase is made of are on opposite sides of the same event. Psalm 116:3 is a man in the snares of death calling on the LORD; Acts 2:24 is Peter at Pentecost saying that God raised Christ 'having loosed the pains of death, because it was not possible that he should be holden of it' — the resurrection stated as a release from precisely what Psalm 116 describes. Alma 26:13 applies the resurrection verb to the psalm's hell and makes converts its object: 'how many thousands of our brethren hath he loosed from the pains of hell.' What Acts says God did once for Christ, Ammon says he has done thousands of times for Lamanites.

links.note: 'How many thousands of our brethren hath he loosed from the pains of hell; and they are brought to sing redeeming love.' Moderate, because both halves have been adjudicated separately in this book — the noun at Alma 14:6 against Psalm 116:3, the verb at Alma 11:42 against Acts 2:24 — and what is new here is only their fusion. It is recorded because the fusion is the argument: no KJV verse looses the pains of hell, and this one does.
links.text: Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it.

pericopes.text: Yea, we have reason to praise him forever, for he is the Most High God, and has loosed our brethren from the chains of hell.

Yea, they were encircled about with everlasting darkness and destruction; but behold, he hath brought them into his everlasting light, yea, into everlasting salvation; and they are encircled about with the matchless bounty of his love; yea, and we have been instruments in his hands, of doing this great and marvellous work;

therefore let us glory, yea, we will glory in the Lord; yea, we will rejoice, for our joy is full; yea, we will praise our God forever. Behold, who can glory too much in the Lord? Yea, who can say too much of his great power, and of his mercy, and of his long suffering towards the children of men? Behold I say unto you, I cannot say the smallest part which I feel.

provenance.mt: Jeremiah 9:23-24 — 'Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might … but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me.'
provenance.route: Jeremiah 9:23-24 → 1 Corinthians 1:31 / 2 Corinthians 10:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “let him glory in the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17, which are Paul quoting Jeremiah 9:24 twice. Jeremiah's own clause is 'let him that glorieth glory in THIS, that he understandeth and knoweth me' — the object is a proposition, not the LORD. The formula 'glory in the Lord' is Paul's compression and exists nowhere in the KJV Old Testament.
provenance.significance: This is a mediation case the tool cannot decide and the passage can. `mediation-check.py` on Jeremiah 9:24 against 1 Corinthians 1:31 returns no decisive divergence, because the words the Book of Mormon reproduces are words only one of the two candidates has at all. The evidence is five verses up instead: Alma 26:11-12 refuses to boast 'in my own strength, or in my own wisdom', which is Jeremiah 9:23's pair — the wise man in his wisdom, the mighty man in his might — and 26:16 then states the positive in Paul's compressed form rather than Jeremiah's expanded one. So the speech has Jeremiah's content and Paul's clause, which is exactly what a New Testament mediation looks like. Note also that 'glory in the Lord' completes 1 Chronicles 16:35's 'glory in thy praise', the other singleton of the verse quoted at 26:8.

links.note: 'Therefore let us glory, yea, we will glory in the Lord; yea, we will rejoice, for our joy is full … Behold, who can glory too much in the Lord?' The clause is Paul's, twice, and the two Corinthian verses are themselves quotations of Jeremiah 9:24 in a form Jeremiah does not have. The rhetorical question that follows — who can glory TOO MUCH in the Lord — is the Book of Mormon's own addition and it answers Aaron's rebuke at 26:10 by denying that boasting has an upper limit when its object is right.
links.text: That, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.

pericopes.text: Who could have supposed that our God would have been so merciful as to have snatched us from our awful, sinful, and polluted state?
Behold, we went forth even in wrath, with mighty threatnings to destroy his church.
O then, why did he not consign us to an awful destruction; yea, why did he not let the sword of his justice fall upon us, and doom us to eternal despair?

O my soul, almost as it were, fleeth at the thought. Behold, he did not exercise his justice upon us, but in his great mercy hath brought us over that everlasting gulf of death and misery, even to the salvation of our souls.
And now behold, my brethren, what natural man is there, that knoweth these things? I say unto you, There is none that knoweth these things, save it be the penitent;

provenance.other: “the natural man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 2:14: 'the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God … neither can he KNOW them, because they are spiritually discerned.' “mysteries of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 4:1, two chapters later in the same letter.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 3:19 has already taken 1 Corinthians 2:14's subject and given it a predicate Paul does not use — 'the natural man is an enemy to God'. Alma 26:21 takes the half of the verse Mosiah left behind: 'what natural man is there, that KNOWETH these things? … There is none that knoweth these things, save it be the penitent.' That is Paul's actual claim, that the natural man cannot know, converted into a rhetorical question and then answered with a condition Paul does not name. Paul's contrast is natural against spiritual; Alma 26:21-22's is natural against penitent, and the qualification that follows — repentance, faith, works, unceasing prayer — makes knowing the mysteries a moral achievement rather than an endowment. The row belongs in Alma as well as Mosiah because the two books divide one verse between them.

links.note: 'What natural man is there, that knoweth these things? I say unto you, There is none that knoweth these things, save it be the penitent.' A KJV singleton with the verse's own verb attached, which is what distinguishes this use from Mosiah 3:19's. The 'mysteries of God' two clauses later is 1 Corinthians 4:1's singleton, from the same letter.
links.text: But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.

pericopes.text: yea, he that repenteth and exerciseth faith, and bringeth forth good works, and prayeth continually without ceasing: unto such it is given to know the mysteries of God; yea, unto such it shall be given to reveal things which never have been revealed; yea, and it shall be given unto such, to bring thousands of souls to repentance, even as it hath been given unto us to bring these our brethren to repentance.
Now do ye remember, my brethren, that we said unto our brethren in the land of Zarahemla, We go up to the land of Nephi, to preach unto our brethren, the Lamanites, and they laughed us to scorn?

provenance.other: “laughed us to scorn” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 2:19 — 'when Sanballat the Horonite … heard it, they laughed us to scorn, and despised us'. The KJV laughs to scorn a dozen times but only here in the first person plural, which is the person Alma 26:23 is in.
provenance.significance: Two Old Testament scenes compete for this verse and the catalogue can have both. The exact wording is Nehemiah's: outsiders deriding a work undertaken at God's command, in the first person plural, by men who are told the work is impossible. But the situation is 2 Chronicles 30:10's, and that verse is nearer still — Hezekiah's posts sent from city to city to call the estranged northern tribes back to the passover, 'but they laughed them to scorn, and mocked them.' Alma 26:23-24 is a mission to estranged brethren, mocked in advance by the people who send it, and the objection quoted at 26:24 is that the Lamanites cannot be brought back. The Book of Mormon has the wording of the one and the plot of the other.
provenance.alternative: Nehemiah 4:1, 'Sanballat … mocked the Jews', continues the same derision and supplies the verb Alma 26:29 uses of the missionaries themselves.

links.note: 'We said unto our brethren in the land of Zarahemla, We go up to the land of Nephi, to preach unto our brethren, the Lamanites, and they laughed us to scorn?' The KJV has this exact four-word phrase once. Its home is the taunt against the rebuilding of Jerusalem, which Nehemiah answers with 'the God of heaven, he will prosper us' — the answer Ammon's whole speech is making.
links.text: But when Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian, heard it, they laughed us to scorn, and despised us, and said, What is this thing that ye do? will ye rebel against the king?

pericopes.text: For they said unto us, Do ye suppose that ye can bring the Lamanites to the knowledge of the truth? Do ye suppose that ye can convince the Lamanites of the incorrectness of the traditions of their fathers, as stiffnecked a people as they are; whose hearts delighteth in the shedding of blood; whose days have been spent in the grossest iniquity; whose ways have been the ways of a transgressor, from the beginning? Now my brethren, ye remember that this was their language.
And moreover, they did say, Let us take up arms against them, that we destroy them and their iniquity out of the land, lest they overrun us and destroy us.
But behold, my beloved brethren, we came into the wilderness not with the intent to destroy our brethren, but with the intent that perhaps we might save some few of their souls.

Now when our hearts were depressed, and we were about to turn back, behold, the Lord comforted us, and said, Go amongst thy brethren, the Lamanites, and bear with patience thine afflictions, and I will give unto them success.

And now behold, we have come, and been forth amongst them; and we have been patient in our sufferings, and we have suffered every privation; yea, we have travelled from house to house, relying upon the mercies of the world; not upon the mercies of the world alone, but upon the mercies of God;

provenance.other: “from house to house” occurs in exactly four KJV verses. Luke 10:7 forbids it, 1 Timothy 5:13 disparages it, Acts 2:46 uses it of breaking bread; Acts 20:20 is the only one where it describes an apostle's method of teaching — 'have taught you publickly, and from house to house'.
provenance.significance: Alma 26 belongs to a genre the King James Bible has exactly one specimen of: the missionary's retrospective defence of his own ministry, delivered to colleagues at its close. Acts 20:18-35 is Paul at Miletus, and its elements are Alma 26's — how I have been with you all this time, serving with all humility and with tears and temptations (26:27-28, the depressed hearts and the patient afflictions), teaching publicly and from house to house (26:28-29), coveting no man's silver (26:28, 'not upon the mercies of the world alone'), and a farewell that commends the converts to God. The verbal contact is one phrase; the structural contact is a whole speech, and it is what makes the phrase worth naming.
provenance.alternative: Acts 5:42, 'daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach', is the closer match for 26:29's temples and houses together, without the phrase.

links.note: 'We have travelled from house to house, relying upon the mercies of the world; not upon the mercies of the world alone, but upon the mercies of God.' Moderate: four words of ordinary English that the KJV happens to use in four places, one of which is a missionary describing exactly this practice. The row rests on the genre argument in the significance field as much as on the phrase.
links.text: And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,

pericopes.text: and we have entered into their houses and taught them, and we have taught them in their streets; yea, and we have taught them upon their hills; and we have also entered into their temples and their synagogues and taught them; and we have been cast out, and mocked, and spit upon, and smote upon our cheeks; and we have been stoned, and taken and bound with strong cords, and cast into prison; and through the power and wisdom of God, we have been delivered again;

provenance.route: Mark 10:33-34 / Luke 18:32 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Spit upon' occurs in four KJV verses; three are the mocking of Jesus (Matthew 27:30, Mark 10:34, Mark 15:19) and the fourth is a purity law about discharge (Leviticus 15:8). Mark 10:34's is the only one in a prediction rather than a narration: 'they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him.'
