Luke 18:32 gives the same prediction as 'he shall be mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on'.
provenance.significance: Ammon's catalogue of what the mission suffered runs mocked, spit upon, smitten on the cheek, stoned, bound, imprisoned. The first three are the passion predictions' sequence and the last three are Paul's — 2 Corinthians 11:25's 'thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned', and the prisons of 11:23. So the missionaries are described as suffering what the Gospels say Christ would suffer and what Paul says he did suffer, in that order, which is the New Testament's own way of arranging an apostolic catalogue. The Book of Mormon adds one item to it: 'smote upon our cheeks', which is the blow the KJV gives to the judge of Israel at Micah 5:1 and to the servant of the LORD at Lamentations 3:30, and which the Sermon on the Mount tells a disciple to invite.

links.whyNot: No phrase here is rare and none is reproduced exactly. 'Mocked', 'stoned', 'cast into prison' are all common KJV words in common KJV forms, and a list of persecutions will contain them whether or not any source is in view. The row is an argument about the shape of the list, not about its wording, and a reader who declines the shape should decline the row; `kjvSpecific` is 'uncertain' for the same reason.
links.note: 'We have been cast out, and mocked, and spit upon, and smote upon our cheeks; and we have been stoned, and taken and bound with strong cords, and cast into prison.' Recorded as a figural-leaning allusion under CONVENTIONS §0a: the individual words will not carry a source, and the sequence is the passion prediction followed by Paul's catalogue of hardships, which is a real and checkable claim about how the sentence is built.
links.text: And they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him: and the third day he shall rise again.

pericopes.text: and we have suffered all manner of afflictions, and all this, that perhaps we might be the means of saving some soul; and we supposed that our joy would be full, if perhaps we could be the means of saving some.

provenance.other: “save some” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both Paul's: Romans 11:14, 'if by any means I may provoke to emulation them which are my flesh, and might save some of them', and 1 Corinthians 9:22, 'I am made all things to all men, that I might by all MEANS save some'. Alma 26:30 has both of 1 Corinthians 9:22's words — 'that perhaps we might be the MEANS of saving some soul … if perhaps we could be the means of saving SOME' — with 'means' turned from an adverbial into the missionaries themselves.
provenance.significance: Romans 11:14 is the closer situation and 1 Corinthians 9:22 is the closer wording, and the two together are the whole of Ammon's apologia. Romans 11 is Paul hoping to save some of his own flesh, his kinsmen after the flesh, by a ministry aimed elsewhere — which is the Lamanite mission's exact case, brethren estranged and pursued for their own sake. 1 Corinthians 9 is the passage on becoming all things to all men, and it is the New Testament's defence of accommodating a mission to the people it is sent to, which is what Ammon did at the court of Lamoni and what Alma 26:28-29 is describing when it lists the houses, streets, hills, temples and synagogues taught in.

links.note: 'That perhaps we might be the means of saving some soul … if perhaps we could be the means of saving some.' Two words that occur together in one KJV verse, repeated twice in one Book of Mormon verse. The syntactic shift is worth noting: Paul's 'by all means' is adverbial and Alma's 'be the means' makes the preachers instruments, which is the figure the chapter opened with at 26:3 and returns to at 26:15.
links.text: To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.

pericopes.text: Now behold, we can look forth and see the fruits of our labors; and are they few? I say unto you, Nay, they are many; yea, and we can witness of their sincerity, because of their love towards their brethren, and also towards us.

For behold, they had rather sacrifice their lives, than even to take the life of their enemy; and they have buried their weapons of war deep in the earth, because of their love towards their brethren.
And now behold I say unto you, Has there been so great love in all the land? Behold, I say unto you, Nay, there has not even among the Nephites.

For behold, they would take up arms against their brethren; they would not suffer themselves to be slain. But behold, how many of these have laid down their lives; and we know that they have gone to their God, because of their love, and of their hatred to sin.

Now have we not reason to rejoice? Yea, I say unto you, There never was men that had so great reason to rejoice as we, since the world began; yea, and my joy is carried away, even unto boasting in my God; for he has all power, all wisdom, and all understanding; he comprehendeth all things, and he is a merciful Being, even unto salvation, to those who will repent and believe on his name.

Now if this is boasting, even so will I boast; for this is my life and my light, my joy and my salvation, and my redemption from everlasting wo. Yea, blessed is the name of my God, who hath been mindful of this people, which are a branch of the tree of Israel, and hath been lost from its body, in a strange land; yea, I say, blessed be the name of my God, who hath been mindful of us wanderers in a strange land.

Now my brethren, we see that God is mindful of every people, in whatsoever land they may be in; yea, he numbereth his people, and his bowels of mercy is over all the earth. Now this is my joy, and my great thanksgiving; yea, and I will give thanks unto my God forever. Amen.

provenance.other: Psalm 145:9 reads 'The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.' Alma 26:37 reads 'his bowels of mercy is over all the earth' — the psalm's predicate with a noun from Colossians 3:12, since “bowels of mercies” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'He numbereth his people' has no KJV verse; the nearest is Psalm 147:4, 'he telleth the number of the stars', four verses after the psalm that gathers the outcasts of Israel.
provenance.significance: This is a CONVENTIONS §8 case and a striking one, because the same anomaly appears at both ends of the book. 1 Nephi 1:20 reads in the 1830 edition 'his tender mercies … IS over all', against the KJV's 'are', and the 1920 edition corrected it to 'are'. Alma 26:37 reads in 1830 'his bowels of mercy IS over all the earth', and 1920 corrected it to 'are' as well. Two verses, six hundred pages apart, borrowing the same clause of the same psalm, both with a singular verb where the KJV has a plural, both mended in the same edition. Whatever produced the grammar produced it twice, and in the modern text neither instance is visible.

links.note: 'He numbereth his people, and his bowels of mercy is over all the earth.' Psalm 145:9's predicate with Colossians 3:12's noun, and with the psalm's 'all his works' widened to 'all the earth' — which is the sentence's point, since the clause it completes is that God is mindful of every people in whatsoever land. The 1830 singular verb is the reading of the running text and is discussed above.
links.text: The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.

pericopes.text: Now it came to pass that when those Lamanites which had gone to war against the Nephites, had found, after their many struggles for to destroy them, that it was in vain to seek their destruction, they returned again to the land of Nephi.

And it came to pass that the Amalekites, because of their loss, were exceeding angry. And when they saw that they could not seek revenge from the Nephites, they began to stir up the people in anger against their brethren, the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi; therefore they began again to destroy them.
Now this people again rufused to take their arms, and they suffered themselves to be slain according to the desires of their enemies.

Now when Ammon and his brethren saw this work of destruction among those who they so dearly beloved, and among those who had so dearly beloved them; for they were treated as though they were angels sent from God to save them from everlasting destruction; therefore, when Ammon and his brethren saw this great work of destruction, they were moved with compassion, and they said unto the king,

provenance.other: 'Moved with compassion' occurs in exactly five KJV verses. Three of them build it on a participle of seeing — Matthew 9:36 ('when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them'), Matthew 14:14 ('he saw a great multitude, and was moved with compassion toward them') and Mark 6:34 ('saw much people, and was moved with compassion toward them'). Alma 27:4 has the same construction twice over: 'when Ammon and his brethren SAW this work of destruction … they were moved with compassion'.
provenance.significance: This is the third of three consecutive chapters drawing on one paragraph of Matthew, and the catalogue can now say so. Alma 25:12 takes 'scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd' from Matthew 9:36 for the hunted seed of the priests of Noah; Alma 26:5-7 builds a harvest allegory whose title, 'the Lord of the harvest', occurs only at Matthew 9:38 and Luke 10:2; Alma 27:4 takes the clause that opens the whole Matthean paragraph, the sight that moves compassion. Matthew 9:36-38 is a single sentence-chain — Jesus sees the shepherdless crowd, pities them, and tells the disciples to pray for labourers because the harvest is plenteous — and the three Alma chapters use its three elements on the same people: the Lamanites unconverted, the Lamanites reaped, and the Lamanites seen dying. Between them Alma 25-27 reproduce a Gospel paragraph nobody in the narrative quotes.
provenance.alternative: Mark 6:34 has the same construction and the same shepherdless-sheep clause; Alma 25:12 chose Matthew's participle over Mark's, which is the reason for preferring Matthew here as well.

links.note: 'When Ammon and his brethren saw this work of destruction among those who they so dearly beloved … they were moved with compassion.' Moderate, because 'moved with compassion' is the KJV's ordinary rendering and five verses have it. The row exists for the pattern set out above, and it is checkable: if 25:12's and 26:7's sources are right, this is the remaining member of the same paragraph.
links.text: But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.

pericopes.text: Let us gather together this people of the Lord, and let us go down to the land of Zarahemla, to our brethren, the Nephites, and flee out of the hands of our enemies, that we be not destroyed.
But the king saith unto them, Behold, the Nephites will destroy us, because of the many murders and sins we have committed against them.
And Ammon saith, I will go and inquire of the Lord, and if he saith unto us, Go down unto our brethren, will ye go?

And the king saith unto him Yea; if the Lord saith unto us Go, we will go down unto our brethren, and we will be their slaves until we repair unto them the many murders and sins which we have committed against them.

But Ammon saith unto him, It is against the law of our brethren, which was established by my father, that there should be any slaves among them; therefore let us go down and rely upon the mercies of our brethren.
But the king saith unto him, Inquire of the Lord, and if he saith unto us Go, we will go; otherwise we will perish in the land.
And it came to pass that Ammon went and inquired of the Lord, and the Lord said unto him,

Get this people out of this land, that they perish not, for Satan hath great hold on the hearts of the Amalekites, which do stir up the Lamanites to anger against their brethren, to slay them; therefore get thee out of this land; and blessed art this people in this generation; for I will preserve them.

provenance.mt: Genesis 12:1 — 'Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee.'
provenance.route: Genesis 12:1 (or its citation at Acts 7:3) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “get thee out of” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 12:1 and Acts 7:3, which are the call of Abram and Stephen's quotation of it. `mediation-check.py` returns no decisive divergence between them, because the Book of Mormon reproduces only the four words the two verses share and none of the clauses where they differ ('that I will shew thee' against 'which I shall shew thee'); the mediation is therefore recorded as uncertain rather than guessed. Genesis 19:14's 'Up, get you out of this place; for the LORD will destroy this city' is the KJV's other evacuation order and is adjudicated at Alma 14:24.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon opens by putting this formula in the mouth of the Lord to Lehi (1 Nephi 2:2-4, with Hebrews 11:8 behind it) and the whole first book is the journey it starts. Alma 27:12 gives the same command to a converted Lamanite king, and the sequel completes the Abrahamic shape that 1 Nephi only half-finished: the people gather their flocks and herds and go out into the wilderness (27:14, which is Genesis 12:5's inventory), and the land they arrive at is granted 'for an inheritance' (27:22-24) — Hebrews 11:8's own phrase for what Abraham was called out to receive. What the catalogue can say here that it could not say at 1 Nephi 2 is that the formula is portable: the book applies the call of Abram to the descendants of the people it has spent twenty chapters calling apostate, and grants them the inheritance under the same terms.

links.note: 'Get this people out of this land, that they perish not … therefore get thee out of this land; and blessed art this people in this generation; for I will preserve them.' Four words shared with the KJV's two calls of Abram, followed within ten verses by a departure with flocks and herds and a grant of land for an inheritance. Moderate: the four words are ordinary and the case rests on what follows them.
links.text: Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee:

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that Ammon went and told the king all the words which the Lord had said unto him.

And it came to pass that they gathered together all their people; yea, all the people of the Lord, and did gather together all their flocks and herds, and departed out of the land, and came into the wilderness which divided the land of Nephi from the land of Zarahemla, and came over near the borders of the land.

And it came to pass that Ammon saith unto them, Behold, I and my brethren will go forth into the land of Zarahemla, and ye shall remain here until we return; and we will try the hearts of our brethren, whether they will that ye shall come into their land.
And it came to pass that as Ammon was going forth into the land, that he and his brethren met Alma, over in the place of which has been spoken; and behold, this was a joyful meeting.
Now the joy of Ammon was so great, even that he was full; yea, he was swallowed up in the joy of his God, even to the exhausting of his strength; and he fell again to the earth.

provenance.other: 'Swallowed up' occurs in fourteen KJV verses, almost all of them destructions — Aaron's rod, the earth over Dathan, the LORD swallowing up the habitations of Jacob. Only two have a person swallowed by a state rather than by a thing, and “swallowed up with” occurs in exactly one KJV verse: 2 Corinthians 2:7, 'lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.'
provenance.significance: Paul's clause is a pastoral warning: forgive the offender, or grief in excess of what a man can bear will consume him. Alma 27:17 takes the same construction and the same excess and inverts the affect — Ammon is 'swallowed up in the joy of his God, even to the exhausting of his strength', and falls to the earth. The next verse insists that this is not a defect ('was not this exceeding joy?') and the verse after concedes that his brethren's joy 'was not that to exceed their strength', which is precisely 2 Corinthians 2:7's category of an emotion beyond a man's capacity, applied to joy and treated as a distinction rather than a danger. Alma 27:28 then uses the same verb in its more familiar Pauline home — 'death was swallowed up to them by the victory of Christ over it', which is 1 Corinthians 15:54 and is adjudicated at Alma 22:14. The chapter therefore has the verb twice, once for joy overwhelming a man and once for victory overwhelming death.

links.note: 'He was swallowed up in the joy of his God, even to the exhausting of his strength; and he fell again to the earth.' The one KJV verse that swallows a person up with a feeling is 2 Corinthians 2:7, and the feeling there is sorrow. Moderate rather than high: the Book of Mormon has 'in' where Paul has 'with', and the verb is common enough in the KJV that a reader could decline the identification and treat the phrase as the book's own.
links.text: So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.

pericopes.text: Now was not this exceeding joy? Behold, this is joy which none receiveth save it be the truly penitent and humble seeker of happiness.
Now the joy of Alma in meeting his brethren was truly great, and also the joy of Aaron, of Omner, and Himni; but behold, their joy was not that to exceed their strength.

And now it came to pass that Alma conducted his brethren back to the land of Zarahemla, even to his own house. And it came to pass that they went and told the Chief Judge all the things that had happened unto them in the land of Nephi among their brethren, the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that the Chief Judge sent a proclamation throughout all the land, desiring the voice of the people concerning the admitting their brethren, which were the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi.

And it came to pass that the voice of the people came, saying, Behold, we will give up the land of Jershon, which is on the east by the sea, which joins the land Bountiful, which is on the south of the land Bountiful; and this land Jershon is the land which we will give unto our brethren, for an inheritance.

And behold, we will set our armies between the land Jershon and the land Nephi, that we may protect our brethren in the land Jershon; and this we do for our brethren, on account of their fear to take up arms against their brethren, lest they should commit sin; and this their great fear came, because of their sore repentance which they had, on account of their many murders, and their awful wickedness.

And now behold, this will we do unto our brethren, that they may inherit the land Jershon; and we will guard them from their enemies with our armies, on conditions that they will give us a portion of their substance to assist us, that we may maintain our armies.

Now it came to pass that when Ammon had heard this, he returned to the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi, and also Alma with him, into the wilderness, where they had pitched their tents, and made known unto them all these things. And Alma also related unto them his conversion with Ammon, and Aaron, and his brethren.

And it came to pass that it did cause great joy among them. And it came to pass that they went down into the land of Jershon; and took possession of the land of Jershon; and they were called by the Nephites the people of Ammon; therefore they were distinguished by that name ever after;

and they were among the people of Nephi, and also numbered among the people which were of the Church of God. And they were also distinguished for their zeal towards God, and also towards men; for they were perfectly honest and upright in all things; and they were firm in the faith of Christ, even unto the end.

provenance.other: “zealous toward God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 22:3, where Paul is describing himself to the Jerusalem mob: 'taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day.' Alma 27:27 has 'they were also distinguished for their zeal towards God, and also towards men'.
provenance.significance: The next verse of Acts is what makes the borrowing worth having. Acts 22:4: 'And I persecuted this way unto the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women.' Paul's zeal toward God is introduced in order to be identified with the killing of believers, and the speech's whole point is that the man saying it was converted out of exactly that. The people of Ammon are the Book of Mormon's case of the same thing at national scale — 27:23 calls their fear of taking up arms the fruit of 'their sore repentance … on account of their many murders' — and Alma 27:27 gives them Paul's self-description with the persecution removed and 'towards men' added in its place. The phrase that in Acts precedes a confession of murder here concludes a character of people who will not kill.
provenance.alternative: Romans 10:2, 'they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge', is Paul's other verdict on the same zeal and is the negative form of this one.

links.note: 'They were also distinguished for their zeal towards God, and also towards men; for they were perfectly honest and upright in all things; and they were firm in the faith of Christ, even unto the end.' A KJV singleton, with 'towards' for Paul's 'toward'. The verse is a formal character-summary built of three clauses, and two of the three are New Testament singletons — this one and Hebrews 3:6's, filed beside it.
links.text: I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day.

provenance.other: “firm unto the end” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 3:6: 'whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end.' Hebrews 3:14 repeats the construction with a different adjective — 'if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end' — and 'unto the end' on its own occurs in twenty-two KJV verses, so the word that identifies the source is 'firm'.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 3 is about a people who came out of Egypt and did not enter the rest because they hardened their hearts, and the 'if' of 3:6 is the condition on which a new company counts as God's house. Alma 27 has just brought a people out of a land they could not stay in, into an inheritance granted them by another nation, and 27:27 says they were firm unto the end — the clause Hebrews attaches to the possibility of failing exactly this way. It is also the last thing the chapter says about them before 27:28-29 states what the firmness cost: they would suffer death rather than take up the sword. Hebrews 3:6's 'firm' is a condition; Alma 27:27's is a verdict already delivered.

links.note: 'They were firm in the faith of Christ, even unto the end.' The adjective is what makes this a singleton rather than a commonplace — the KJV's stock phrases are 'stedfast unto the end' and 'endure unto the end', and 'firm unto the end' is Hebrews 3:6's alone. The Book of Mormon inserts 'in the faith of Christ' where Hebrews has 'the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope'.
links.text: But Christ as a son over his own house; whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end.

pericopes.text: And they did look upon shedding the blood of their brethren with the greatest abhorrence; and they never could be prevailed upon to take up arms against their brethren; and they never did look upon death with any degree of terror for their hope and views of Christ and the resurrection; therefore death was swallowed up to them by the victory of Christ over it;
therefore they would suffer death in the most aggravating and distressing manner which could be inflicted by their brethren, before they would take the sword or the cimeter to smite them.
And thus they were a zealous and beloved people, a highly favored people of the Lord.

And now it came to pass that after the people of Ammon were established in the land of Jershon, and a church also established in the land of Jershon; and the armies of the Nephites were set round about the land of Jershon; yea, in all the borders round about the land of Zarahemla; behold the armies of the Lamanites had followed their brethren into the wilderness.

And thus a tremendous battle; yea, even such an one as never had been known among all the people in the land from the time Lehi left Jerusalem; yea, and tens of thousands of the Lamanites were slain and scattered abroad.
Yea, and also there was a tremendous slaughter among the people of Nephi; nevertheless, the Lamanites were driven and scattered, and the people of Nephi returned again to their land.—
And now this was a time that there was a great mourning and lamentation heard throughout all the land, among all the people of Nephi;

links.text: The LORD was as an enemy: he hath swallowed up Israel, he hath swallowed up all her palaces: he hath destroyed his strong holds, and hath increased in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation.

provenance.other: “Mourning and lamentation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Lamentations 2:5. “Great mourning” occurs in three — Esther 4:3, Zechariah 12:11 and Matthew 2:18 — and Zechariah 12:11 is the one that also stands at the head of the family-by-family list this chapter's next verse imitates.
provenance.significance: Recover Lamentations 2:5 and the clause that produced the phrase reads “The LORD was as an enemy.” Alma 28 has just narrated a battle won by the Nephites, and it declines to call the day a victory: it calls it a sorrowful day. Borrowing the grief-word of the KJV's one poem about a city destroyed by God's own hand imports the theology of that poem — that a slaughter is a visitation before it is a military event — into a chapter whose own explicit moral, four verses later, is that the war has produced nothing but an awful scene of bloodshed.

links.note: “A great mourning and lamentation heard throughout all the land.” The compound is a KJV singleton and its home is Lamentations 2, where it is what the LORD “increased in the daughter of Judah” after breaking her strong holds. Mosiah 21:9 used the same singleton for the mourning of Limhi's people, and the recurrence is worth naming: the same editorial hand reaches for the same verse whenever a Nephite army has been cut to pieces. Written as a fresh link rather than a repeat because this is a new book and a new narrative, but the argument was first made at Mosiah 21:9.

pericopes.text: yea, the cry of widows mourning for their husbands, and also of fathers mourning for their sons, and the daughter for the brother; yea, the brother for the father: and thus the cry of mourning was heard among every one of them; mourning for their kindred which had been slain.

links.text: And the land shall mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of David apart, and their wives apart; the family of the house of Nathan apart, and their wives apart;

provenance.other: “Every family apart” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Zechariah 12:12 and 12:14, and the itemised-household form of mourning is confined to that passage. No other KJV lament breaks the grief down by relation.
provenance.alternative: National mourning enumerated by kinship is a natural way to write the scene and needs no source; the shared words are only 'mourn' and the family terms.
provenance.significance: Zechariah's family-by-family mourning is for one who was pierced — “they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son.” Alma 28 puts the form to the opposite use: the households here mourn not one death that saves but tens of thousands that accomplish nothing, and verse 11 says outright that many of the mourned are “consigned to a state of endless wo.” The KJV's one liturgy of universal household grief is being run in reverse.

links.note: “The cry of widows mourning for their husbands, and also of fathers mourning for their sons, and the daughter for the brother; yea, the brother for the father.” The verbal contact is thin — mourning, and the kinship terms — but the form is distinctive and the KJV has one instance of it: Zechariah 12:12-14, where the land mourns “every family apart,” household by household, wives apart. Recorded at moderate on form rather than wording, and paired with the Lamentations 2:5 singleton in the preceding verse, which comes from the same kind of scene and which Mosiah 21:9 had already fused with this same Zechariah passage.

pericopes.text: And now surely this was a sorrowful day; yea, a time of solemnity, and a time of much fasting and prayer:

links.text: Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.

provenance.other: “Fasting and prayer,” in that order, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 7:5. The reversed “prayer and fasting” occurs in two, Matthew 17:21 and Mark 9:29. 1 Corinthians 7:5 is also the only one of the three that sets the practice inside a bounded stretch of time — “except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer” — which is the construction Alma 28:6 has.
provenance.alternative: Fasting and prayer is one of the most ordinary pairs in devotional English and the order may carry nothing.
provenance.significance: The order is the whole of the evidence, and it is worth having for that reason: where the Book of Mormon reproduces a KJV word-pair it tends to reproduce the pair as the KJV set it, and here the sequence it has is Paul's, not the Gospels'. Recovering 1 Corinthians 7:5 supplies a small irony the chapter did not ask for — Paul's time of fasting and prayer is a season husbands and wives agree to spend apart, and the mourning this one answers is, in the previous verse, first of all the cry of widows for their husbands.

links.note: “A time of solemnity, and a time of much fasting and prayer.” A four-word run against a KJV singleton, and the only KJV verse to hold “a time” and “fasting and prayer” together. The case is entirely about word order, since the sense of 1 Corinthians 7:5 is remote; held at moderate for that reason.
links.whyNot: The sense of the source is marital continence, which has nothing to do with a nation fasting after a battle, and a writer with any KJV in his ear could produce this order without 1 Corinthians 7:5.

pericopes.text: and thus ended the fifteenth year of the regin of the Judges over the people of Nephi;

and this is the account of Ammon and his brethren, their journeyings in the land of Nephi, their sufferings in the land, their sorrows, and their afflictions, and their incomprehensible joy, and the reception and safety of the brethren in the land of Jershon. And now may the Lord, the Redeemer of all men, bless their souls forever.

links.text: Thus saith the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel, and his Holy One, to him whom man despiseth, to him whom the nation abhorreth, to a servant of rulers, Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship, because of the LORD that is faithful, and the Holy One of Israel, and he shall choose thee.

provenance.other: “The Lord, the Redeemer of …” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 49:7, where the genitive is “of Israel.” The same clause stands verbatim in the Book of Mormon's own transcription of Isaiah 49 at 1 Nephi 21:7, so the proximate model cannot be discriminated from the KJV by wording; what can be said is that the phrase was already inside the corpus and available to be altered.
provenance.alternative: Direct dependence on Isaiah 49:7 in the KJV, without the intervening Book of Mormon transcription, would explain the wording equally well.
provenance.significance: The one word changed is the argument. Isaiah's title is “the Redeemer of Israel”; Alma 28:8 makes it “the Redeemer of all men,” and does so in the sentence that closes the account of a mission to the Lamanites — the nation a Nephite reader has been taught to regard as outside. Recover Isaiah 49:7 and the rest of the verse turns out to describe precisely the missionaries being blessed: it addresses “him whom man despiseth, to him whom the nation abhorreth, to a servant of rulers,” and promises that “Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship.” Ammon and his brethren spent these chapters despised, imprisoned, servants to rulers, and watching two Lamanite kings rise and worship. The chapter's benediction is worded out of the one Isaiah verse whose contents it has just narrated.

links.note: “And now may the Lord, the Redeemer of all men, bless their souls forever.” A KJV singleton clause with one substitution: Israel becomes all men. The substitution is not decorative — it is the doctrinal conclusion of the Ammon narrative stated as a divine title, and it is made on a verse the Book of Mormon has already reproduced word for word at 1 Nephi 21:7, where it still reads “of Israel.” Mediation is given as OT-via-earlier-BoM on that ground, with the caveat in provenance that the two routes are verbally identical here.

links.text: In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren;

provenance.route: 2 Corinthians 11:26 and 6:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Journeyings” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Numbers 10:28 and 2 Corinthians 11:26; “in journeyings often” is a singleton at 2 Corinthians 11:26. “As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing” is a singleton at 2 Corinthians 6:10.
provenance.alternative: A summary colophon naturally lists what a narrative contained, and the items listed are what Alma 17-27 in fact narrated.
provenance.significance: Recover the source and what Alma 28:8 has borrowed is not a phrase but a genre: Paul's catalogue of missionary hardship, the peristasis list of 2 Corinthians 6:4-10 and 11:23-27, which is the New Testament's set form for a preacher summarising what his commission cost him. Its signature is the turn at the end — “as sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing” — and Alma 28:8 ends its list the same way, with “their incomprehensible joy.” Verse 14 then names the antithesis in the abstract, “the great reason of sorrow, and also of rejoicing,” which is 2 Corinthians 6:10 unpacked.

links.note: “Their journeyings in the land of Nephi, their sufferings in the land, their sorrows, and their afflictions, and their incomprehensible joy.” The rare word is 'journeyings', which the KJV uses twice, once of Israel's marches and once in Paul's list of what apostleship cost him; the shape of the sentence is the second. Held at moderate because the individual words are common and the case rests on the form of the list plus the sorrow-and-joy turn that closes it — but the form is not a common one, and this is a missionary colophon, which is exactly where it belongs.

pericopes.text: And this is the account of the wars and contentions among the Nephites, and also the wars between the Nephites and the Lamanites; and the fifteenth year of the reign of the Judges is ended;
and from the first year to the fifteenth, has brought to pass the destruction of many thousand lives; yea, it has brought to pass an awful scene of bloodshed;

and the bodies of many thousands are laid low in the earth, while the bodies of many thousands are mouldering in heaps upon the face of the earth; yea, and many thousands are mourning for the loss of their kindred, because they have reason to fear, according to the promises of the Lord, that they are consigned to a state of endless wo;

while many thousands of others truly mourn for the loss of their kindred, yet they rejoice and exult in the hope, and even know, according to the promises of the Lord, that they are raised to dwell at the right hand of God, in a state of never ending happiness:

links.text: If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.

provenance.other: “Right hand of God” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses — Mark 16:19, Acts 2:33, Acts 7:55, Acts 7:56, Romans 8:34, Colossians 3:1, Hebrews 10:12, 1 Peter 3:22 — and in every one of the eight the occupant of that place is Christ. No KJV verse puts anyone else there.
provenance.alternative: Romans 8:34, which the machine stream ranked first, joins 'risen again' to 'the right hand of God' as tightly as Colossians 3:1 does, and the two cannot be separated on wording.
provenance.significance: The interest of the row is not which of the eight verses is in view but that the Book of Mormon has moved the seat. The KJV reserves the right hand of God for the risen Christ; Alma 28:12 has ordinary Nephite dead “raised to dwell at the right hand of God.” The only KJV licence for that transfer is the participatory logic of Colossians 3:1 — 'if ye then be risen with Christ' — where the believer's resurrection and Christ's session are the same fact seen twice. Alma 28:12 states as the destination of the faithful dead what Colossians states as a present standing.

links.note: “They are raised to dwell at the right hand of God, in a state of never ending happiness.” “Right hand of God” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses and is too widely spread to fix a source on its own, which is why this is an echo rather than an allusion; what is not widely spread is the combination of being raised and being at that right hand, which the KJV has at Colossians 3:1 and Romans 8:34 alone, and only Colossians extends the position to anyone but Christ.
links.whyNot: Eight KJV verses carry the phrase and the wording here matches none of them beyond it; a reader may reasonably treat the expression as general Christian idiom rather than dependence on any one verse.

pericopes.text: and thus we see how great the inequality of man is because of sin and transgression, and the power of the Devil, which comes by the cunning plans which he hath devised to ensnare the hearts of men;

and thus we see the great call of diligence of men to labor in the vineyards of the Lord; and thus we see the great reason of sorrow, and also of rejoicing: sorrow because of death and destruction among men, and joy because of the light of Christ unto life.

links.text: For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard.

provenance.route: Matthew 20:1 (with Isaiah 5:7) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Labourers into his vineyard” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:1; “the vineyard of the LORD” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 5:7. Alma 28:14's “labor in the vineyards of the Lord” fuses the two and matches neither exactly. “In the vineyards of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Song of Solomon 1:14, the vineyards of Engedi, which is registered as an exclusion at this verse.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 5:7 defines whose vineyard it is — “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” — and Matthew 20:1 supplies the labourers hired into it. Put them together and the metaphor Alma 28:14 uses for missionary work carries both halves: the field being worked is Israel, which is exactly the claim Alma 17-27 has been making about the Lamanites, and the labourers are hired at every hour, which is Matthew 20's point and the point of a chapter that has just watched an enemy nation come in late.

links.note: “The great call of diligence of men to labor in the vineyards of the Lord.” Neither KJV phrase is reproduced intact, which is what keeps this at moderate; but labouring in a vineyard belonging to the Lord is a fusion of two singletons and not a free-standing image, and Jacob 5 had already built the Book of Mormon's longest allegory out of the same two sources. Written as a link rather than a recurrence because Jacob is another book and another hand.

links.text: Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.

provenance.other: “Light of life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:12. The Book of Mormon's clause “the light of Christ unto life” splits the singleton and inserts the name that John 8:12 only implies.
provenance.significance: John 8:12 is a self-identification — “I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” — and its two halves are darkness and life. Alma 28:14 sets its borrowing against exactly that pair: “sorrow because of death and destruction among men, and joy because of the light of Christ unto life.” The chapter has spent eleven verses on bodies mouldering in heaps, and it closes by naming the one KJV verse in which light and life are a single phrase and the alternative to them is walking in the dark.

links.note: “Joy because of the light of Christ unto life.” The KJV joins 'light' to 'life' in one verse only, and the Book of Mormon has that verse's phrase with Christ's name written into the middle of it — the identification John 8:12 makes in its first clause moved into the second. The antithesis of death against light-and-life in the same sentence is John 8:12's own.

pericopes.text: O that I were an angel, and could have the wish of mine heart, that I might go forth and speak with the trump of God, with a voice to shake the earth, and cry repentance unto every people;

links.text: For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:

provenance.other: “Trump of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 4:16. The KJV's other eschatological trumpet is “the last trump” at 1 Corinthians 15:52; the possessive form is Thessalonians' alone.
provenance.significance: The singleton does more than supply a phrase, because the two things Alma 29:1 wishes for stand side by side inside it. 1 Thessalonians 4:16 has the Lord descending “with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God” — an angel's voice and God's trumpet in one clause — and Alma's wish is exactly that pair: “O that I were an angel … that I might go forth and speak with the trump of God.” Recover the rest of the verse and the wish is stranger still: the trump of God in the KJV is not an instrument of preaching at all, it is the sound at which “the dead in Christ shall rise first.” Alma wants the resurrection trumpet in order to cry repentance to the living, which is why the next two verses have to take the wish back.

links.note: “That I might go forth and speak with the trump of God.” A five-word run onto a KJV singleton, and the source verse holds both halves of Alma's wish — the archangel's voice and God's trump — in a single clause. Held at high rather than certain because the borrowed phrase is short; but no other KJV verse contains it, and no other KJV verse puts an angel and that trumpet together.

links.text: For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:

provenance.other: “Wish” occurs in exactly six KJV verses: Job 33:6, Psalm 40:14, Psalm 73:7, Romans 9:3, 2 Corinthians 13:9 and 3 John 1:2. Only Romans 9:3 is a minister's wish about the salvation of his own people, and only Romans 9:3 is a wish the speaker presents as one he cannot properly make.
provenance.alternative: A preacher wishing for greater reach is an obvious thing to write and requires no source.
provenance.significance: Paul's wish — “I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” — is guarded before it is uttered (“I say the truth in Christ, I lie not”) because it is not a wish a Christian may have. Alma 29 does the same thing in the opposite order: he utters the wish in verses 1-2 and then withdraws it in verse 3, “I am a man, and do sin in my wish.” The rare word in the chapter is 'wish', the KJV's one impossible ministerial wish is Romans 9:3, and this chapter is drawing on Paul continuously — 2 Corinthians 12 at verses 9 and 16, 2 Timothy 1:9 at verse 13.

links.note: The verbal contact is one word, and 'wish' is not rare enough on its own to fix a source. What carries the row is the shape: an apostolic speaker states a desire for his people's salvation that exceeds what he is permitted to desire, and immediately marks it as improper. Recorded at moderate because the chapter's other borrowings are Pauline and clustered, so recurrence is doing real work here.
links.whyNot: Nothing is shared but 'wish', and Alma's wish (to preach to all the earth) and Paul's (to be damned for Israel) are not the same wish. A reader may decline this without losing anything else in the chapter.

pericopes.text: yea, I would declare unto every soul, as with the voice of thunder, Repentance, and the plan of redemption, that they should repent and come unto our God, that there might not be no more sorrow upon all the face of the earth.

links.text: And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

provenance.other: “No more sorrow” as a contiguous phrase occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses; Revelation 21:4 separates the words — “there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain.” It is nonetheless the only KJV verse that promises the abolition of sorrow as such.
provenance.alternative: The universal end of sorrow is a commonplace of Christian hope and can be stated without Revelation.
provenance.significance: Alma's wish is for a preached repentance so complete that sorrow ends on the earth — that is, for the missionary to accomplish now what Revelation 21 reserves for the new heaven and new earth after the former things are passed away. Read against its source the wish is not merely ambitious but eschatological, and the retraction in verse 3 is the recognition of a category error: he has asked to do the work of the last chapter of the Bible.

links.note: “That there might not be no more sorrow upon all the face of the earth.” The 1830 reading carries a double negative that the 1920 edition removed, and it is worth flagging under CONVENTIONS §8: the first edition's clumsy “not be no more” is closer to Revelation 21:4's stacked negations (“no more death, neither sorrow … neither shall there be any more pain”) than the smoothed text is, so the edition that shows the borrowing is the one the catalogue runs. Held at moderate: the phrase is not contiguous in the KJV and the idea is common.
links.whyNot: No exact run is shared; “no more sorrow” is not a KJV phrase, and the resemblance is to Revelation's picture rather than its wording.

links.text: Hast thou an arm like God? or canst thou thunder with a voice like him?

provenance.other: “Thunder” occurs in exactly 19 KJV verses, which is far too many to fix a source by the word alone. Job 40:9 is singled out on structure, not rarity: it is the KJV's one verse in which a thundering voice is named specifically as the thing a man does not have.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 14:2's “as the voice of a great thunder,” a KJV singleton, is the closest verbal parallel to Alma's simile and may be all that is behind it.
provenance.significance: Job 40:9 is God's challenge out of the whirlwind: “Hast thou an arm like God? or canst thou thunder with a voice like him?” Alma 29:1-2 asks for exactly the two things the challenge denies — the trump of God, and a declaration made “as with the voice of thunder” — and verse 3 gives Job's answer: “But behold, I am a man.” The arm returns at verse 10, where the arm that matters is not Alma's but God's, “his merciful arm which he extended towards me.” Whether or not the writer had Job open, the chapter's argument is the argument of Job 40, and the reader who recovers it gets the retraction in verse 3 as a scriptural gesture rather than a mood.

links.note: Recorded as an echo on structure rather than wording, and flagged as such. The verbal contact is 'voice' and 'thunder', both common; what is uncommon is the sequence — a man wishing to speak with God's thunder, then conceding that he is a man — which the KJV stages once, at Job 40:9 answered by Job 40:4.
links.whyNot: Two common words, no shared run, and Alma 29 nowhere names Job. The row stands on a formal resemblance a reader may decline.

pericopes.text: But behold, I am a man, and do sin in my wish; for I had ought to be content with the things which the Lord hath allotted unto me.

links.text: Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.

provenance.route: Hebrews 13:5 (with Philippians 4:11) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Content with such things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 13:5; “therewith to be content” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 4:11. “Be content” occurs in exactly seven, of which the other five (Judges 19:6, 2 Kings 5:23, 2 Kings 6:3, Job 6:28, Luke 3:14) all mean “agree” or “stop complaining” rather than the contentment of a settled mind.
provenance.significance: Both New Testament sources ground contentment in something God has already done, and Alma 29:3 supplies the same ground in its own vocabulary: “the things which the Lord hath allotted unto me.” Hebrews 13:5's reason is “for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee”; Philippians 4:11's is Paul's learning “in whatsoever state I am.” Recovering either turns Alma's line from resignation into doctrine — the allotment is not a limit imposed on him but a promise held out to him, which is why verses 4 to 8 go on to argue that God's allotting is just.

links.note: “I had ought to be content with the things which the Lord hath allotted unto me.” The KJV's two verses about contentment as a virtue are Hebrews 13:5 and Philippians 4:11, and this line has Hebrews' construction — be content with the things — with the object changed from what one has to what one has been given. Held at moderate because no run of more than three words is shared. Note the 1830 “I had ought,” an American dialect form the 1920 edition removed; it is not KJV and does not bear on the source.

pericopes.text: I had not ought to harrow up in my desires, the firm decree of a just God, for I know that he granteth unto men according to their desires, whether it be unto death or unto life; yea, I know that he allotteth unto men, yea, decreeth unto them decrees which are unalterable, according to their wills; whether it be unto salvation or unto destruction;

yea, and I know that good and evil hath come before all men; or he that knoweth not good from evil, is blameless; but he that knoweth good and evil, to him it is given according to his desires; whether he desireth good or evil, life or death, joy or remorse of conscience.
Now seeing that I know these things, why should I desire more than to perform the work to which I have been called?
Why should I desire that I was an angel, that I could speak unto all the ends of the earth?—

links.text: Thou hast increased the nation, O LORD, thou hast increased the nation: thou art glorified: thou hadst removed it far unto all the ends of the earth.

provenance.other: “Unto all the ends of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 26:15, although “the ends of the earth” without the “unto all” occurs in exactly 28. The seven-word run is therefore a genuine singleton match sitting on top of a formula.
provenance.alternative: The Book of Mormon uses “the ends of the earth” constantly and could reach this exact form by accident.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 26:15's ends of the earth are where a nation was removed to — “thou hast increased the nation … thou hadst removed it far unto all the ends of the earth” — which is the diaspora geography the Book of Mormon is written inside. Alma 29:7 turns the destination of the scattering into the destination of the preaching: the ends of the earth to which Israel was carried are the ends of the earth he wishes he could speak to. In a book whose largest argument is the gathering of scattered Israel, that is not a neutral phrase to borrow.

links.note: A seven-word exact run onto a KJV singleton. Held at moderate rather than high because the underlying formula is one of the Book of Mormon's own commonest, so a coincidental match is genuinely possible; the rarity count is what keeps the row, and the metalepsis is what makes it worth having.
links.whyNot: The senses diverge — Isaiah is describing exile, Alma is describing preaching — and the Book of Mormon's heavy independent use of “the ends of the earth” means the exact form may be reached without the source.

pericopes.text: For behold, the Lord doth grant unto all nations, of their own nation and tongue, to teach his word; yea, in wisdom, all that he seeth fit that they should have; therefore we see that the Lord doth counsel in wisdom, according to that which is just and true.

links.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

provenance.other: “Just and true” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 15:3 — “just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.” The nearest neighbours are Revelation 16:7 and 19:2, which read “true and righteous.”
provenance.significance: Revelation 15:3 is the verse this catalogue met first: 1 Nephi 1:14's “great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty” is six words of it, and it is the song the same verse identifies as “the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb.” Alma 29:8 takes the other half of the same sentence. What it takes it for is the chapter's most surprising claim — that “the Lord doth grant unto all nations, of their own nation and tongue, to teach his word” — and Revelation 15:3's next verse is “all nations shall come and worship before thee.” The Book of Mormon's warrant for revelation outside Israel is worded out of the KJV's hymn of the nations.

links.note: “According to that which is just and true.” A KJV singleton, and the second borrowing this catalogue has recorded from Revelation 15:3, the first being the flagship link at 1 Nephi 1:14. Held at moderate because the phrase is short and reads as ordinary English; what argues for dependence is that the surrounding claim — God granting his word to all nations in their own tongue — is the claim Revelation 15:3-4 makes two clauses later.

pericopes.text: I know that which the Lord hath commanded me, and I glory in it; I do not glory of myself, but I glory in that which the Lord hath commanded me; yea, and this is my glory, that perhaps I may be an instrument in the hands of God, to bring some soul to repentance; and this is my joy.

links.text: Of such an one will I glory: yet of myself I will not glory, but in mine infirmities.

provenance.other: “Will not glory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:5: “Of such an one will I glory: yet of myself I will not glory, but in mine infirmities.” “Let him glory in the Lord” occurs in exactly two, 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17, which supply the positive half of the antithesis.
provenance.significance: The whole of 2 Corinthians 10-12 is Paul's argument that a minister may boast only of what was given him, and 12:5 is its hinge. Alma 29:9 reproduces the hinge: “I do not glory of myself, but I glory in that which the Lord hath commanded me.” Recover the context and the row becomes the key to the chapter, because Paul's refusal to glory of himself is stated immediately after the vision of the third heaven — and Alma 29:16 has that vision too. The two verses of Alma that draw on 2 Corinthians 12 draw on it from either side of the same sentence.

links.note: “I glory in it; I do not glory of myself, but I glory in that which the Lord hath commanded me.” The antithesis is Paul's and the KJV states it once. Where Paul completes it with “but in mine infirmities,” Alma completes it with the commandment he was given, which is the same move made in the vocabulary of a chapter about a calling one did not choose. High rather than certain: the run is short and the Book of Mormon rewrites the second half.

pericopes.text: And behold, when I see many of my brethren truly penitent, and coming to the Lord their God, then is my soul filled with joy; then do I remember what the Lord has done for me; yea, even that he hath heard my prayer; yea, then do I remember his merciful arm which he extended towards me;

yea, and I also remember the captivity of my fathers; for I surely do know that the Lord did deliver them out of bondage, and by this did establish his church; yea, the Lord God, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, did deliver them out of bondage;

links.text: Moreover he said, I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. And Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look upon God.

provenance.other: “God of Abraham the God of Isaac” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Exodus 3:6, 3:15 and 4:5. The formula is quoted five further times in the New Testament — Matthew 22:32, Mark 12:26, Luke 20:37, Acts 3:13, Acts 7:32 — and every one of those five inserts a conjunction the Old Testament verses do not have: “the God of Abraham, AND the God of Isaac.” (Acts 3:13 goes further and drops the repeated noun: “and of Isaac, and of Jacob.”) Alma 29:11 reads “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” without the conjunction. That is the Old Testament form, exactly, and it is not the form of any of the five New Testament quotations.
provenance.significance: The mediation result is a finding in its own right, because the New Testament route is the natural one to expect here: the whole New Testament use of this formula is Christological — Jesus at Matthew 22:32 and Mark 12:26 arguing the resurrection from it, Stephen at Acts 7:32 retelling the bush — and Alma 29 is a Christian sermon. It reaches past all of that to the Exodus wording, and it reaches for the reason Exodus 3 gives it: this is the name God announces immediately before he says “I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians,” which is what Alma 29:12 says next. The chapter is not quoting a title; it is quoting the deliverance scene.

links.note: A thirteen-word run, and a mediation test that comes out cleanly. tools/mediation-check.py against Acts 7:32 reported divergences in both directions, but neither of its two decisive points holds: “fathers” is picked up from “the captivity of my fathers” earlier in Alma 29:11, and the absence of “Then Moses trembled” is not a discriminator, since Alma is not narrating the theophany at all. The real test is the conjunction, which the tool skips because it ignores single common words (ADJUDICATING §4) — all three Old Testament verses omit the “and” before Isaac and all five New Testament quotations supply it, and the Book of Mormon omits it. Direct-OT, decided on one word.

pericopes.text: yea, I have always remembered the captivity of my fathers; and that same God who delivered them out of the hands of the Egyptians, did deliver them out of bondage;

yea, and that same God did establish his church among them; yea, and that same God hath called me by a holy calling, to preach the word unto this people, and hath given me much success, in the which my joy is full;

links.text: Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,

provenance.other: “An holy calling” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 1:9. The Book of Mormon has “by a holy calling” where the KJV has “with an holy calling”; the noun phrase is otherwise untouched.
provenance.significance: 2 Timothy 1:9 defines the holy calling negatively — “not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace” — and that is precisely the point Alma 29 has been making since verse 3. He may not enlarge his commission by wanting to, because the commission was never a function of his wanting; it was allotted. The chapter states in verses 3-6 what the source verse states in a subordinate clause, and then borrows the phrase the clause belongs to.

links.note: “That same God hath called me by a holy calling, to preach the word unto this people.” A KJV singleton with the preposition and article changed, in the sentence where the chapter finally names its own subject. Its coherence with the argument is unusually tight: the source's own gloss on a holy calling — that it is not according to our works — is the doctrine Alma has spent ten verses submitting to.

pericopes.text: but I do not joy in my own success alone, but my joy is more full because of the success of my brethren, which have been up to the land of Nephi.
Behold, they have labored exceedingly, and have brought forth much fruit; and how great shall be their reward.

links.text: I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.

provenance.other: “Much fruit” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — John 12:24, John 15:5 and John 15:8 — and in no other book. “Bringeth forth much fruit” is the form at John 12:24 and 15:5; Alma 29:15 has “have brought forth much fruit.”
provenance.significance: The phrase belongs entirely to John, and to two passages about the same thing: a grain that must die before it bears, and a branch that bears nothing apart from the vine. “Without me ye can do nothing” is the clause John 15:5 ends on, and it is the doctrine Alma 29:9 has just stated in his own words — “I do not glory of myself.” The fruit-bearing at verse 15 and the refusal to glory at verse 9 are the two halves of John 15:5, and Alma 29:17 completes the figure by praying for “all those which are the fruit of their labors.”

links.note: “They have labored exceedingly, and have brought forth much fruit.” A phrase confined in the KJV to three verses of John, two of them the vine discourse. Moderate rather than high because agricultural metaphor for missionary success is available everywhere; what argues for John is that the exact collocation is his alone and that this chapter has already made John 15:5's point about doing nothing of oneself.

links.text: Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.

provenance.other: “Great is your reward” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:12; Luke 6:23's parallel inverts it to “your reward is great in heaven.” Alma 29:15 has neither exactly: “how great shall be their reward.”
provenance.alternative: A reward described as great is common enough in devotional English to need no source.
provenance.significance: Matthew 5:12's reward is promised to those who have just been reviled and persecuted, and the brethren whose reward Alma is exclaiming over are the ones who went up to the land of Nephi and were bound, spat upon and imprisoned there. The beatitude's condition is the narrative of Alma 17-26; the exclamation borrows its apodosis.

links.note: “And how great shall be their reward.” A KJV singleton reworked into an exclamation, in a sentence that has just summarised a mission of exceptional hardship — which is the setting Matthew 5:11-12 attaches the promise to. Held at moderate: the wording is rearranged and the idea is common.
links.whyNot: No contiguous run survives the rearrangement, and Luke 6:23 has an equal claim on the sense.

pericopes.text: Now when I think of the success of these my brethren, my soul is carried away, even to the separation of it from the body, as it were, so great is my joy.

links.text: I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven.

provenance.other: “Out of the body” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Job 20:25, where a sword comes out of a body, and 2 Corinthians 12:2 and 12:3, where it is Paul's formula for a rapture whose mechanics he cannot describe. “Caught up to the third heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:2.
provenance.significance: This is the row that makes the chapter legible. Alma 29:9 borrows 2 Corinthians 12:5 — “of myself I will not glory” — and Alma 29:16 borrows 12:2-3, the vision that 12:5 refuses to boast about. The two Book of Mormon verses come from either side of one sentence in Paul, and they preserve its logic: the man who will not glory of himself is the same man who was caught up out of the body, and the second fact is why the first has to be said. Alma even keeps Paul's characteristic hedge. Paul writes “whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth”; Alma writes “even to the separation of it from the body, as it were” — the same refusal to be pinned down about what happened.

links.note: “My soul is carried away, even to the separation of it from the body, as it were, so great is my joy.” Nothing longer than three words is shared, which is why this is an allusion on the conceptual axis rather than a close-verbal one; but the KJV describes an out-of-body rapture in exactly one place, and Alma 29 has already quoted the sentence three verses later in the same passage. The “as it were” is Paul's hedge in Book of Mormon dress, and it is what raises the row to high.

pericopes.text: And now may God grant unto these my brethren, that they may sit down in the Kingdom of God; yea, and also all those which are the fruit of their labors, that they may go no more out, but that they may praise him forever. And may God grant that it may be done according to my words, even as I have spoken. Amen.

links.text: And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God.

provenance.other: “Sit down in the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 13:29. Matthew's parallel at 8:11 reads “sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven” — kingdom of heaven, not of God, and with the patriarchs named. The Book of Mormon has Luke's form.
provenance.significance: Luke 13:29's diners come “from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south,” and the two verses on either side of it are the harshest in Luke: the householder shuts the door on people who ate and drank in his presence, “and ye yourselves thrust out.” It is the KJV's set-piece of outsiders seated while insiders are excluded. Alma 29:17 prays it over missionaries to the Lamanites and over “all those which are the fruit of their labors” — the converted enemy nation. The last verse of the chapter asks that Luke 13:29's reversal be granted, on behalf of the people it would be granted to.

links.note: “That they may sit down in the Kingdom of God.” A six-word run onto a KJV singleton, in Luke's wording rather than Matthew's. The mediation is settled by two words: Luke has “kingdom of God” where Matthew 8:11 has “kingdom of heaven,” and the Book of Mormon has Luke's.

links.text: Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name.

provenance.other: “Go no more out” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: 2 Samuel 21:17, where David's men swear he shall go no more out to battle, and Revelation 3:12, the promise to the church at Philadelphia. Only the second is about a permanent place before God.
provenance.significance: Revelation 3:12's promise is architectural — “him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out” — and it is followed immediately by the writing of God's name upon him. Alma 29:17 keeps both halves in order: they go no more out, and then “they may praise him forever.” The image behind the prayer is not simply staying in heaven; it is being built into the temple as a fixture, which is the strongest thing the KJV has to say about permanence.

links.note: “That they may go no more out, but that they may praise him forever.” A four-word run onto one of the KJV's two occurrences, and the only one whose sense fits. The machine stream preferred Ezekiel 14:11's “may go no more astray,” which is registered as an exclusion at this verse; the Book of Mormon has “out,” not “astray.” Held at moderate because the run is short and the phrase is ordinary English.

pericopes.text: Behold, now it came to pass that after the people of Ammon were established in the land of Jershon, yea, and also after the Lamanites were driven out of the land, and their dead were buried by the people of the land.

Now their dead were not numbered, because of the greatness of their numbers; neither were the dead of the Nephites numbered. But it came to pass that after they had buried their dead, and also after the days of fasting, and mourning, and prayer, (and it was in the sixteenth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi,) there began to be continual peace throughout all the land;

yea, and the people did observe to keep the commandments of the Lord; and they were strict in observing the ordinances of God, according to the law of Moses; for they were taught to keep the law of Moses, until it should be fulfilled;
and thus the people did have no disturbance in all the sixteenth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.
And it came to pass in the seventeenth year of the reign of the Judges, there was continual peace.

But it came to pass in the latter end of the seventeenth year, there came a man into the land of Zarahemla; and he was Anti-Christ, for he began to preach unto the people against the prophecies which had been spoken by the prophets, concerning the coming of Christ.

links.text: Little children, it is the last time: and as ye have heard that antichrist shall come, even now are there many antichrists; whereby we know that it is the last time.

provenance.other: “Antichrist” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all Johannine: 1 John 2:18, 2:22, 4:3 and 2 John 1:7. The word appears nowhere else in the Bible, and the Book of Mormon uses it here and at 30:12 only. The 1830 sets it as the hyphenated, capitalised “Anti-Christ”.
provenance.significance: The term is not a label the chapter picks up loosely; the definition follows it. 1 John 2:22 asks “Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist,” and Alma 30:12 says of Korihor exactly that: “he began to preach unto the people, that there should be no Christ.” 1 John 2:18 adds the eschatological frame — “it is the last time … even now are there many antichrists” — and Korihor is introduced as one man in a series, the third such figure in this record after Sherem and Nehor. The chapter is not calling him a villain; it is placing him in a Johannine category and then testing him against its definition.

links.note: “And he was Anti-Christ, for he began to preach unto the people against the prophecies which had been spoken by the prophets, concerning the coming of Christ.” A KJV word confined to four verses of one author, imported with its definition attached: what makes a man antichrist in 1 John is the denial that Jesus is the Christ, and that is precisely the content of Korihor's preaching as verse 12 states it.

pericopes.text: Now there was no law against a man’s belief; for it was strictly contrary to the commands of God, that there should be a law which should bring men on to unequal grounds.
For thus saith the Scripture: Choose ye this day, whom ye will serve.

links.text: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

provenance.other: “Choose you this day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 24:15, and “whom ye will serve” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon reproduces the whole clause with a single change, “choose ye” for the KJV's “choose you” — the 1830 and 1920 texts agree on it — and marks the borrowing outright: “For thus saith the Scripture.”
provenance.significance: This is one of the Book of Mormon's rare explicit citations of a biblical text as scripture, and what it cites the text for is startling. Joshua 24:15 is a covenant ultimatum: choose, and here is where my house stands. Alma 30:7-11 makes it the constitutional basis of religious liberty — there was no law against a man's belief, because Scripture says choose. Recover the source's context and the citation is doing something the source did not authorise, because Joshua's very next speech (24:19-20) tells the people they cannot serve the LORD, and that if they forsake him “he will turn and do you hurt, and consume you.” The chapter then makes Joshua's warning come true on the man whose freedom the verse has just guaranteed. The verse that protects Korihor is the verse that condemns him.

links.note: A near-verbatim eight-word quotation, flagged by the text itself as scripture, and the only place the Book of Mormon quotes Joshua. The one departure is 'ye' for 'you' in the imperative, which is the 1830's own habit and not a variant of any English Bible. 1 Nephi 7:15 was recorded as a formal echo of this verse with no shared wording; here the wording is all there.

pericopes.text: Now if a man desired to serve God, it was his privilege, or rather if he believed in God, it was his privilege to serve him; but if he did not believe in him, there was no law to punish him.

But if he murdered, he was punished unto death; and if he robbed, he was also punished; and if he stole, he was also punished; and if he committed adultery, he was also punished; yea, for all this wickedness, they were punished:

for there was a law, that men should be judged according to their crimes. Nevertheless, there was no law against a man’s belief; therefore, a man was punished only for the crimes which he had done; therefore all men were on equal grounds.

And this Anti-Christ, whose name was Korihor, and the law could have no hold upon him. And he began to preach unto the people, that there should be no Christ. And after this manner did he preach, saying:
O ye that are bound down under a foolish and a vain hope, why do ye yoke yourselves with such foolish things? Why do ye look for a Christ? For no man can know of any thing which is to come.
Behold, these things which ye call prophecies, which ye say are handed down by holy prophets, behold, they are foolish traditions of your fathers.
How do ye know of their surety? Behold, ye cannot know of things which ye do not see; therefore ye cannot know that there shall be a Christ.

links.text: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

provenance.other: “Evidence of things not seen” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:1. “Evidence” itself occurs in exactly six, five of them Jeremiah's deed of purchase at Jeremiah 32; Hebrews 11:1 is the only KJV verse in which the word means grounds for belief rather than a legal document.
provenance.significance: Korihor's case is Hebrews 11:1 read backwards, clause by clause. Hebrews defines faith as the substance of things hoped for: Korihor opens at 30:13 by calling that hope “a foolish and a vain hope.” Hebrews defines it as the evidence of things not seen: Korihor answers at 30:15, “ye cannot know of things which ye do not see.” And when Alma replies at 30:40, the word he uses is the one word of Hebrews 11:1 that the KJV uses in no other epistemological sense — “what evidence have ye that there is no God?” The debate is conducted inside a single KJV verse, with each speaker holding one of its terms. Alma 32:21 then restores the verse whole, which is why that passage reads as an answer to this one rather than a new topic.

links.note: “Ye cannot know of things which ye do not see; therefore ye cannot know that there shall be a Christ.” No long run is shared, and the row is an allusion on the conceptual axis for that reason; but the three terms Korihor and Alma contest across verses 13, 15 and 40 — hope, sight, evidence — are the three terms of Hebrews 11:1, in Hebrews' own order, and 'evidence' in this sense is peculiar to that verse in the KJV. Adjudicated here rather than at Alma 32:21, which is the same verse quoted directly and at first sight the more obvious home, because this is its first use in the book and because the later passage only makes sense as a reply to this one.

pericopes.text: Ye look forward and say, that ye see a remission of your sins. But behold, it is the effects of a phrensied mind; and this derangement of your minds comes because of the tradition of your fathers, which lead you away into a belief of things which are not so.

And many more such things did he say unto them, telling them that there could be no atonement made for the sins of men, but every man fared in this life, according to the management of the creature; therefore every man prospered according to his genius, and that every man conquered according to his strength; and whatsoever a man did, was no crime.

And thus he did preach unto them, leading away the hearts of many, causing them to lift up their heads in their wickedness; yea, leading away many women, and also men, to commit whoredoms; telling them that when a man was dead, that was the end thereof.
Now this man went over to the land of Jershon also, to preach these things among the people of Ammon, which were once the people of the Lamanites.
But behold, they were more wise than many of the Nephites; for they took him, and bound him, and carried him before Ammon, which was a High Priest over that people.

And it came to pass that he caused that he should be carried out of the land. And it came to pass that he came over into the land of Gideon, and began to preach unto them also; and here he did not have much success, for he was taken and bound, and carried before the High Priest, and also the Chief Judge over the land.

And it came to pass that the High Priest saith unto him, Why do ye go about perverting the ways of the Lord? Why do ye teach this people that there shall be no Christ, to interrupt their rejoicings? Why do ye speak against all the prophecies of the holy prophets?

links.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?
