provenance.other: “Pervert the right ways of the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:10, and “wilt thou not cease” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. “Seeking some to lead him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:11.
provenance.significance: Alma 10:28 already drew on Acts 13:10, and ADJUDICATING §4 would ordinarily make this a repeat of the book's own formula. It is not, and the reason is the reason that ruling allows for: at Alma 30 the passage the phrase came from is being enacted, not merely quoted. Acts 13:6-12 runs — a sorcerer and false prophet who withstood them (13:8); the charge, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord (13:10); the sentence, thou shalt be blind, pronounced by the apostle (13:11); the immediate affliction, and the man going about seeking some to lead him by the hand (13:11); the onlookers believing (13:12). Alma 30 runs the same sequence with one substitution — dumbness for blindness: Korihor withstood the truth (30:53), is charged with perverting the ways of the Lord (30:22, 30:60), is sentenced by Alma (30:47), is struck immediately (30:50), goes about from house to house begging (30:56), and the people are all converted (30:58). The Book of Mormon's set-piece confrontation with an unbeliever is the KJV's, with the affliction changed to fit a man whose offence was his mouth.

links.note: “Why do ye go about perverting the ways of the Lord?” The chapter opens and closes on this charge — verse 22 in the high priest's mouth, verse 60 in the narrator's — and the KJV has the phrase once, in Paul's rebuke of Elymas. What makes this a fresh link rather than a recurrence of Alma 10:28 is that the whole of Acts 13:6-12 is present here in order, which is not true anywhere else in the book; the phrase has returned to its source rather than recurring as a formula. Held at high: no single run is long, and the case rests on the sequence, which is why the subtype is type-scene.

pericopes.text: Now the High Priest’s name was Giddonah. And Korihor saith unto him, Because I do not teach the foolish traditions of your fathers, and because I do not teach this people to bind themselves down under the foolish ordinances and performances which are laid down by ancient priests, to usurp power and authority over them, to keep them in ignorance, that they may not lift up their heads, but be brought down according to thy words.

links.text: But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.

provenance.other: “Usurp authority” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 2:12. The verb 'usurp' appears nowhere else in the KJV in any form.
provenance.alternative: 'Usurp authority' had become ordinary English by 1830 and may owe nothing to the KJV.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one usurpation is a usurpation of the right to teach — “I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man” — and Korihor's charge is that the priests have usurped authority in order to teach: “laid down by ancient priests, to usurp power and authority over them, to keep them in ignorance.” Both verses treat teaching and authority as the same possession. Korihor is arguing, in the KJV's only vocabulary for the offence, that the whole priesthood stands where 1 Timothy says no one may stand.

links.note: “To usurp power and authority over them, to keep them in ignorance.” The KJV uses 'usurp' once, and the collocation with 'authority' is that verse's. Held at moderate rather than high because the phrase had independent currency in 1830 English and because only two words are shared; the rarity count is what keeps the row on the page.

pericopes.text: Ye say that this people is a free people. Behold, I say they are in bondage. Ye say that those ancient prophecies are true. Behold, I say that ye do not know that they are true.
Ye say that this people is a guilty and a fallen people, because of the transgression of a parent. Behold, I say that a child is not guilty because of its parents.

links.text: The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

provenance.route: Ezekiel 18:20 (with Deuteronomy 24:16) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “The son shall not bear” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 18:20. Deuteronomy 24:16 states the same principle judicially — “every man shall be put to death for his own sin” — and is repeated at 2 Kings 14:6 and 2 Chronicles 25:4. Alma 30:25 paraphrases rather than quotes: “a child is not guilty because of its parents.”
provenance.significance: Read alongside verse 8, this is the chapter's most easily missed structural fact: Korihor argues from the Bible, and the catalogue should say so. Twice in eighteen verses the Nephite dissenter's position rests on an Old Testament text — Joshua 24:15 licensing freedom of belief at verse 8, and Ezekiel 18's doctrine of individual guilt overturning inherited transgression here. Ezekiel 18 was itself written against a proverb about children's teeth set on edge by their fathers' grapes, which is exactly the shape of the doctrine Korihor is attacking. He is not an atheist improvising; he is quoting the prophets against the priests.

links.note: “Ye say that this people is a guilty and a fallen people, because of the transgression of a parent. Behold, I say that a child is not guilty because of its parents.” No wording is reproduced, which caps this at moderate, but the doctrine is stated in the KJV twice and only twice — Ezekiel 18:20 and the judicial rule of Deuteronomy 24:16 — and the Book of Mormon's sentence is a fair paraphrase of the first. What argues for dependence is that Korihor's other appeal, four verses earlier, is a verbatim scriptural quotation.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal survives; the objection that a child should not answer for a parent is available to anyone and needs no source.

pericopes.text: And ye also say that Christ shall come. But behold, I say that ye do not know that there shall be a Christ. And ye say also, that he shall be slain for the sins of the world;

and thus ye lead away this people after the foolish traditions of your fathers, and according to your own desires; and ye keep them down, even as it were, in bondage, that ye may glut yourselves with the labors of their hands, that they durst not look up with boldness, and that they durst not enjoy their rights and privileges;

yea, they durst not make use of that which is their own, lest they should offend their priests, which do yoke them according to their desires, and hath brought them to believe by their traditions, and their dreams, and their whims, and their visions, and their pretended mysteries, that they should, if they did not do according to their words, offend some unknown being, which they say is God; a being which never hath been seen nor known, which never was nor never will be.

links.text: For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.

provenance.other: “Unknown God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 17:23, where it is the inscription on the Athenian altar. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase twice in this chapter, at 30:28 in Korihor's accusation and at 30:53 in the devil's commission to him.
provenance.significance: Korihor's charge is the Areopagus in reverse. Paul tells the Athenians that the god they worship ignorantly is the one he now declares; Korihor tells the Nephites that the being they fear is “some unknown being, which they say is God … which never hath been seen nor known.” Alma's answer at 30:44 then follows Paul's: the God who is not seen is known from what he made — Acts 17:24-28's argument from creation and providence, which Alma states as “all things denote there is a God … even the earth, and all things that is upon the face of it, yea, and its motion; yea, and also all the planets which move in their regular form.” Both speakers of this chapter have their lines from Acts 17, and Alma has Paul's.

links.note: “That they should … offend some unknown being, which they say is God; a being which never hath been seen nor known.” A KJV singleton, put into the mouth of the objector rather than the preacher, and answered four verses later by the natural theology that answers it in Acts 17. The devil's own words at 30:53 repeat the phrase — “they have all gone astray after an unknown God” — which is what raises the row above a single verbal coincidence.

pericopes.text: Now when the High Priest and the Chief Judge saw the hardness of his heart; yea, when they saw that he would revile even against God, they would not make any reply to his words; but they caused that he should be bound; and they delivered him up into the hands of the officers, and sent him to the land of Zarahemla, that he might be brought before Alma, and the Chief Judge, which was governor over all the land.
And it came to pass that when he was brought before Alma and the Chief Judge, that he did go on in the same manner as he did in the land of Gideon; yea, he went on to blaspheme.

And he did rise up in great swelling words before Alma, and did revile against the priests and teachers, accusing them of leading away the people after the silly traditions of their fathers, for the sake of glutting in the labors of the people.—

links.text: For when they speak great swelling words of vanity, they allure through the lusts of the flesh, through much wantonness, those that were clean escaped from them who live in error.

provenance.other: “Great swelling words” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Peter 2:18 and Jude 1:16, which are parallel passages about the same subject. The Book of Mormon has the phrase exactly.
provenance.significance: The KJV's two occurrences both belong to its set descriptions of the false teacher, and 2 Peter 2 supplies the rest of Korihor's portrait in advance: teachers who bring in “damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them” (2:1), who “through covetousness … with feigned words make merchandise of you” (2:3), who “speak evil of the things that they understand not” (2:12), and who promise liberty while being “the servants of corruption” (2:19). Korihor denies the Christ, accuses the priests of merchandising, reviles, and offers a people he calls enslaved their freedom. The chapter has taken its antagonist's whole vocabulary from the epistle's chapter on antagonists — and it lets him accuse the priests of the covetousness 2 Peter 2:3 charges to him.

links.note: “And he did rise up in great swelling words before Alma, and did revile against the priests and teachers.” A three-word run confined in the KJV to two parallel verses, arriving in the sentence that formally classifies Korihor as a false teacher. Held at high because the surrounding portrait tracks 2 Peter 2 well beyond the borrowed phrase, and because the very accusation he makes is the one 2 Peter 2:3 makes against his own type.

pericopes.text: Now Alma saith unto him, Thou knowest that we do not glut ourselves upon the labors of this people; for behold, I have labored even from the commencement of the reign of the Judges, until now, with mine own hands, for my support, notwithstanding my many travels round about the land, to declare the word of God unto my people.

links.text: For ye remember, brethren, our labour and travail: for labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God.

provenance.other: The individual phrases here are not rare; what is rare is the argument's shape. 1 Thessalonians 2:5-9 is the KJV's fullest defence of a preacher against the charge of preaching for profit, and it runs: no flattering words, no cloke of covetousness, no glory sought of men, no burden laid on you, and labour night and day so as not to be chargeable. Alma 30:32-35 runs the same list in the same order. The single KJV rarity in the neighbourhood, “flattering words”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 2:5, and surfaces in this same speech at verse 47. Paul's own key word for the refusal of support, “chargeable”, occurs in exactly five KJV verses, three of them his (2 Corinthians 11:9, 1 Thessalonians 2:9, 2 Thessalonians 3:8).
provenance.significance: The accusation Korihor makes at 30:31 — that the priests preach “for the sake of glutting in the labors of the people” — is the standing ancient charge against itinerant preachers, and 1 Thessalonians 2 is the KJV's standing answer to it. Alma does not construct a defence; he gives Paul's, item by item, down to working with his own hands for his support. Recovering the source shows how completely the chapter has cast its protagonist as an apostle under attack: Korihor speaks 2 Peter 2's false teacher, Alma answers in 1 Thessalonians 2's.

links.note: “I have labored even from the commencement of the reign of the Judges, until now, with mine own hands, for my support.” Held at moderate because the wording is the Book of Mormon's own and the case rests on the order of the argument rather than on a run. Note that 1 Corinthians 4:12's 'working with our own hands' is already adjudicated in this book at Alma 1:3 and is registered as an exclusion at this verse; the row here is for the larger Thessalonian defence, of which the manual labour is one item and the refusal of flattering words at verse 47 another.

pericopes.text: And notwithstanding the many labors which I have performed in the church, I have never received so much as even one senine for my labor; neither hath any of my brethren, save it were in the judgment seat; and then we have received only according to law, for our time.

And now if we do not receive any thing for our labors in the church, what doth it profit us to labor in the church, save it were to declare the truth, that we may have rejoicings in the joy of our brethren?

Then why sayest thou that we preach unto this people to get gain, when thou of thyself knowest that we receive no gain? And now, believest thou that we deceive this people, that causeth such joy in their hearts?—
And Korihor answered him, Yea.
And then Alma saith unto him, Believest thou that there is a God?
And he answered, Nay.
Now Alma saith unto him, If ye deny again that there is a God, and also deny the Christ: for behold, I say unto you, I know there is a God, and also that Christ shall come.
And now, what evidence have ye that there is no God, or that Christ cometh not? I say unto you that ye have none, save it be your word only.

But behold, I have all things as a testimony that these things are true; and ye also have all things as a testimony unto you that they are true; and will ye deny them? Believest thou that these things are true?

Behold, I know that thou believest, but thou art possessed with a lying spirit, and ye have put off the spirit of God, that it may have no place in you; but the Devil hath power over you, and he doth carry you about, working devices, that he may destroy the children of God.

links.text: And the LORD said unto him, Wherewith? And he said, I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And he said, Thou shalt persuade him, and prevail also: go forth, and do so.

provenance.other: “Lying spirit” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — 1 Kings 22:22, 22:23 and their doublets at 2 Chronicles 18:21, 18:22 — and all four belong to a single episode, Micaiah's vision of the heavenly council before Ahab's last battle.
provenance.significance: The relocation is the finding. In the KJV the lying spirit is a member of the LORD's own court who volunteers to deceive Ahab's prophets, and the text says so twice without embarrassment: “the LORD hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets.” Alma 30:42 keeps the phrase and reassigns the agency — “thou art possessed with a lying spirit … but the Devil hath power over you” — and verse 53 completes the reassignment by having the deceiving spirit appear as an angel. The Book of Mormon takes the KJV's one term for prophetic deception and detaches it from the divine council, which is a doctrinal move made entirely by where the phrase is put.

links.note: “Thou art possessed with a lying spirit.” The KJV's only phrase for a spirit that makes a prophet speak falsely, drawn from the one episode that uses it. Alma applies to a false prophet what 1 Kings applies to the four hundred, and assigns to the devil what 1 Kings assigns to the LORD.

pericopes.text: And now Korihor saith unto Alma, If thou wilt shew me a sign, that I may be convinced that there is a God, yea, shew unto me that he hath power, and then will I be convinced of the truth of thy words.

But Alma saith unto him, Thou hast had signs enough; will ye tempt your God? Will ye say, Shew unto me a sign, when ye have the testimony of all these thy brethren, and also all the holy prophets? The Scriptures are laid before thee, yea, and all things denote there is a God; yea, even the earth, and all things that is upon the face of it, yea, and its motion; yea, and also all the planets which move in their regular form, doth witness that there is a Supreme Creator;

links.text: Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 6:16 → Matthew 4:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Tempt the Lord your God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 6:16; “tempt the Lord thy God” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 4:7 and Luke 4:12, which quote it. Alma 30:44 reads “will ye tempt your God?” — the plural possessive of the Old Testament against the singular of both New Testament quotations.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 4:7 alone, with the pronoun adjusted to Alma's plural address, would explain the line without any Deuteronomic route.
provenance.significance: The two criteria pull apart here, and that is worth recording rather than resolving away. The wording is Deuteronomy's: 'your God', not 'thy God'. The situation is Matthew's, and unmistakably so — in Matthew 4:5-7 the tempter demands a demonstration of divine power, Jesus refuses to supply it, and this is the sentence he refuses with. That is Alma 30:43-44 exactly: Korihor asks for a sign to prove God has power, and Alma answers with this line before arguing that the signs are already given. So the route runs through Matthew, and the pronoun does not follow it.

links.note: “Thou hast had signs enough; will ye tempt your God?” Recorded as OT-via-NT on the situation rather than the wording, which is the reverse of the usual test and is flagged as such. tools/mediation-check.py could not decide the case: it found no divergence between Deuteronomy 6:16 and Matthew 4:7 at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces, and the pronoun that does discriminate is a single common word of the kind the tool deliberately ignores (ADJUDICATING §4). Read by eye, the possessive is Deuteronomy's; read by scene, the borrowing is Matthew's.
links.whyNot: Only three words are shared with either candidate, and 'tempt God' is a commonplace. A reader could take the line as an unmediated recollection of Deuteronomy and drop the Matthean route entirely.

pericopes.text: and yet do ye go about, leading away the hearts of this people, testifying unto them there is no God. And yet will ye deny against all these witnesses? And he said, Yea, I will deny, except ye shall shew me a sign.
And now it came to pass that Alma said unto him, Behold, I am grieved because of the hardness of your heart; yea, that ye will still resist the spirit of the truth, that thy soul may be destroyed.

links.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: “Grieved for the hardness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5. The Book of Mormon's standing formula is 'hardness of heart' alone, which is adjudicated in this book at Alma 13:4; the element added here is the grieving, and it is the element that completes the KJV singleton.
provenance.significance: Mark 3:5 is Jesus in the synagogue looking round on his opponents “with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts” — a rare notice of what the KJV's Jesus feels in the moment before a miracle that his opponents will use against him. Alma 30:46 puts the same grief in the same position: it is the last thing said before the sign is given, and the sign destroys the man who asked for it. The borrowing carries Mark's discomfort into a passage that would otherwise read as simple judgment.

links.note: “Behold, I am grieved because of the hardness of your heart.” Written as a link rather than filed as a repeat of Alma 13:4, and the reason should be stated plainly because ADJUDICATING §4 makes the repeat the default within a book: Alma 13:4 rests on 'hardness of their hearts', which is the Book of Mormon's own formula, whereas this verse adds 'grieved', and grieving over hardness is what makes Mark 3:5 a singleton. The recurrence list points back so a reader can see both. A cautious editor could file this at Alma 13:4 instead.

pericopes.text: But behold, it is better that thy soul should be lost, than that thou shouldst be the means of bringing many souls down to destruction, by thy lying and by thy flattering words; therefore if thou shalt deny again, behold, God shall smite thee, that thou shalt become dumb, that thou shalt never open thy mouth any more, that thou shalt not deceive this people any more.

links.text: For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness:

provenance.other: “Flattering words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 2:5: “For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness.”
provenance.significance: The singleton lands on Korihor, and it lands from the passage Alma has been answering him out of since verse 32. Paul's sentence pairs flattering words with a cloke of covetousness, and Korihor's accusation against the priests was precisely covetousness — that they glut themselves on the labours of the people. Alma returns both halves of 1 Thessalonians 2:5 to their author: the covetousness he has already disclaimed at 30:33, the flattering words he now assigns to Korihor. What the source says a true preacher never uses is what the false one is destroyed for.

links.note: “By thy lying and by thy flattering words.” A KJV singleton, and the second borrowing from the same short paragraph of Paul in one speech — the self-support argument at 30:32-35 is 1 Thessalonians 2:6-9, and this is 2:5. Mosiah 11:7 adjudicated the phrase first, in another book and of Noah's people; here it is doing different work, as the charge in a sentence of judgment.

links.text: And, behold, thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed, because thou believest not my words, which shall be fulfilled in their season.

provenance.other: “Not able to speak” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:20, and “a writing table” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:63. Struck dumbness as a punishment occurs in the Bible once, in this episode.
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly one man struck dumb, and the reason given is the reason given here: “because thou believest not my words.” Korihor's offence is stated in the same terms four verses earlier — he will not believe, and demands a sign instead. What settles the borrowing is what happens next. Zacharias, unable to speak, is handed a writing table and writes (Luke 1:63); Alma 30:51-52 has the chief judge “put forth his hand and wrote unto Korihor,” and Korihor “put forth his hand, and wrote.” The whole exchange that produces Korihor's confession — the most important speech in the chapter — is conducted in the one KJV episode where dumbness forces a man to write.

links.note: “God shall smite thee, that thou shalt become dumb, that thou shalt never open thy mouth any more.” Two KJV singletons and a shared cause of judgment, followed at 30:51-52 by the writing that Luke 1:63 requires. Subtype type-scene rather than close-verbal because the strongest evidence is the sequence — sentence for unbelief, dumbness, written exchange — rather than any run of words.

pericopes.text: Now Korihor saith unto him, I do not deny the existence of a God, but I do not believe that there is a God; and I say also, that ye do not know that there is a God; and except ye shew me a sign, I will not believe.

links.text: Then said Jesus unto him, Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe.

provenance.other: “Except ye see signs” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 4:48 — “Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe.” “Seeketh after a sign” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 12:39 and 16:4, which supply the judgment on the demand rather than its form.
provenance.significance: John 4:48 is a rebuke put as a conditional, and Korihor turns it into his own confession of terms: “except ye shew me a sign, I will not believe.” He states as his position the sentence Jesus states as an indictment, which is the chapter's method throughout — Korihor speaks the New Testament's descriptions of unbelief in the first person. Recovering John 4 supplies the outcome as well: the sign is given, the nobleman believes, and his whole house with him. Alma 30:58 has the same ending with the same word — “they were all converted again unto the Lord” — except that the man who asked is not among them.

links.note: “And except ye shew me a sign, I will not believe.” The KJV states this conditional once and states it as a reproach; Korihor adopts it as a demand, changing only 'see' to 'shew' and dropping the wonders. Held at high: the run is short but the sentence is verbatim in structure, and the KJV has no other verse of this shape.

pericopes.text: Now Alma saith unto him, This will I give unto thee for a sign, that thou shalt be struck dumb, according to my words; and I say, that in the name of God, that ye shall be struck dumb, that ye shall no more have utterance.
Now when Alma had said these words, Korihor was struck dumb, that he could not have utterance, according to the words of Alma.

And now when the Chief Judge saw this, he put forth his hand and wrote unto Korihor, saying: Art thou convinced of the power of a God? In whom did ye desire that Alma should shew forth his sign? Would ye that he should afflict others, to shew unto thee a sign? Behold, he hath showed unto you a sign; and now, will ye dispute more?

And Korihor put forth his hand, and wrote, saying: I know that I am dumb, for I cannot speak; and I know that nothing, save it were the power of God, could bring this upon me; yea, and I also knew that there was a God.

But behold, the Devil hath deceived me; for he appeared unto me in the form of an angel, and said unto me, Go and reclaim this people, for they have all gone astray after an unknown God. And he saith unto me, There is no God; yea, and he taught me that which I should say. And I have taught his words; and I taught them, because they were pleasing unto the carnal mind; and I taught them, even until I had much success, insomuch that I verily believed that they were true; and for this cause, I withstood the truth, even until I have brought this great curse upon me.

links.text: And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.

provenance.other: “An angel of light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 11:14. The Book of Mormon here has “in the form of an angel” rather than the full phrase, but the proposition — that the devil appears as an angel in order to deceive — is that verse's alone in the KJV.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 11:13-15 is about false apostles “transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ,” and Paul's point is that the disguise is the method: “no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.” Korihor's confession supplies the mechanism the chapter has been withholding — he was not a cynic but a man who “verily believed” his own preaching, because the being who commissioned him looked like the being who commissions prophets. Recovering Paul's context makes the confession an argument rather than an excuse: this is exactly how, according to the KJV, false teaching gets itself believed by its own teachers.
provenance.alternative: 2 Nephi 9:9 adjudicated the phrase first and could be the proximate model, since the Book of Mormon has by now established the idea in its own words.

links.note: “For he appeared unto me in the form of an angel, and said unto me, Go and reclaim this people.” The KJV's one statement that Satan appears as an angel, applied to a commission that reads like a prophetic call. Written as a fresh link rather than a recurrence of 2 Nephi 9:9 because that is another book and another voice, and because here the claim is narrated as an event rather than asserted as doctrine.

links.text: Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.

provenance.other: “Carnal mind” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:7: “Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.”
provenance.significance: Korihor's explanation of his own success is Romans 8:7 used as a marketing analysis — “I taught them, because they were pleasing unto the carnal mind.” The source verse says why that would work: the carnal mind is not merely inclined against God but constitutionally incapable of subjection to him. Korihor has correctly identified the audience the KJV says exists, and his own final sentence, that he was deceived into believing his own doctrine, shows him to have been in it.

links.note: “And I taught them, because they were pleasing unto the carnal mind.” A KJV singleton, adjudicated first at Mosiah 16:5 in another book; the row is written here because the phrase does something new — it is the false teacher's own account of why his doctrine sold.

links.text: Now as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith.

provenance.other: “Resist the truth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 3:8. “Withstood” occurs in exactly six, of which two matter here: 2 Timothy 3:8, where Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, and Acts 13:8, where Elymas the sorcerer withstood Paul and Barnabas. Alma 30:53's “I withstood the truth” fuses the verb of the one with the object of the other — and 2 Timothy 3:8 holds both in a single sentence.
provenance.significance: 2 Timothy 3:8's comparison is to Pharaoh's magicians, the KJV's type of the sign-worker who opposes a prophet with signs of his own, and the verse's judgment on them is that they are “men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith” — deceived, not merely dishonest, which is what Korihor confesses to being. Together with the Elymas sequence catalogued at 30:22, this puts Korihor at the junction of the KJV's two named magician-opponents. The Book of Mormon's word for what he did is the word both passages use.

links.note: “And for this cause, I withstood the truth, even until I have brought this great curse upon me.” Neither KJV verse has this exact phrase; 2 Timothy 3:8 has both of its halves within one sentence, and Acts 13:8 — whose scene this chapter has been running since verse 22 — has the verb applied to a sorcerer. Held at moderate because the fusion is the Book of Mormon's own.

pericopes.text: Now when he had said this, he besought that Alma should pray unto God, that the curse might be taken from him.
But Alma said unto him, If this curse should be taken from thee, thou wouldst again lead away the hearts of this people; therefore, it shall be unto thee, even as the Lord will.
And it came to pass that the curse was not taken off of Korihor; but he was cast out, and went about from house to house, a begging for his food.

Now the knowledge of what had happened unto Korihor, was immediately published throughout all the land; yea, the proclamation was sent forth by the Chief Judge, to all the people in the land, declaring unto those who had believed in the words of Korihor, that they must speedily repent, lest the same judgments would come unto them.

And it came to pass that they were all convinced of the wickedness of Korihor; therefore they were all converted again unto the Lord; and this put an end to the iniquity after the manner of Korihor. And Korihor did go about from house to house, a begging food for his support.

And it came to pass that as he went forth among the people, yea, among a people which had separated themselves from the Nephites, and called themselves Zoramites, being led by a man whose name was Zoram; and as he went forth amongst them, behold, he was run upon, and trodden down, even until he was dead;
and thus we see the end of him who perverteth the ways of the Lord; and thus we see that the Devil will not support his children at the last day, but doth speedily drag them down to hell.

Now it came to pass that after the end of Korihor, Alma having received tidings that the Zoramites were perverting the ways of the Lord, and that Zoram, which was their leader, was leading the hearts of the people to bow down to dumb idols, &c., his heart again began to sicken, because of the iniquity of the people;

links.text: Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led.

provenance.other: 'Dumb idols' occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Habakkuk 2:18, where they are what the maker of a graven image makes, and 1 Corinthians 12:2. Only the Corinthians verse joins them to a verb of leading.
provenance.alternative: Habakkuk 2:18-19 supplies the phrase and a 'teacher of lies' who is a plausible model for Zoram; but it has no leading, and the whole of its verbal contact is the two words.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is about people who are being reminded what they used to be — Gentiles, carried away, led. Alma 31:1 puts the Zoramites in exactly that grammatical position: they are not idolaters who chose, they are people being led, and the man doing the leading is named in the same clause. The chapter that follows shows the mechanism, which is a liturgy performed once a week and never mentioned again (31:23); Paul's 'even as ye were led' is the KJV's one comment on how that happens.

links.note: 'Zoram, which was their leader, was leading the hearts of the people to bow down to dumb idols.' Two words of a KJV pair plus the verb that governs them in one of the two. The Zoramite apostasy as the chapter describes it is not in fact idolatrous — there is no image on the Rameumptom, only a creed — so the phrase is doing work the narrative does not support, which is itself the reason to think it is borrowed rather than observed. Well below any quotation threshold; the case is the collocation of 'dumb idols' with 'led'.

pericopes.text: for it was the cause of great sorrow to Alma, to know of iniquity among his people; therefore his heart was exceeding sorrowful, because of the separation of the Zoramites from the Nephites.

Now the Zoramites had gathered themselves together in a land which they called Antionum, which was east of the land of Zarahemla, which lay nearly bordering upon the seashore, which was south of the land of Jershon, which also bordered upon the wilderness south, which wilderness was full of the Lamanites.
Now the Nephites greatly feared that the Zoramites would enter into a correspondence with the Lamanites, and that it would be the means of great loss on the part of the Nephites.

And now, as the preaching of the word had a great tendency to lead the people to do that which was just; yea, it had had more powerful effect upon the minds of the people than the sword, or any thing else, which had happened unto them; therefore Alma thought it was expedient that they should try the virtue of the word of God.

links.text: For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

provenance.other: Hebrews 4:12 is the one KJV verse that measures the word of God against a sword. “than any twoedged sword” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Alma 12:7 already took the last clause of this verse — 'the thoughts and intents of the heart' — as a six-word singleton. Here the same verse is used at its other end, and the argument the book makes from it is the argument Hebrews makes: the word is more powerful than the sword. Alma has just prosecuted a war, and the sentence that sends him to Antionum with five men instead of an army is a paraphrase of the verse in which scripture says why that is the better weapon.

links.note: 'It had had more powerful effect upon the minds of the people than the sword … therefore Alma thought it was expedient that they should try the virtue of the word of God.' No run of shared words, but three of Hebrews 4:12's terms in its own relation: the word of God, powerful, and the sword it outmatches. This is a second use of a verse already adjudicated in this book at 12:7, and it is written as a link rather than a cross-reference because it draws on a different clause and makes a different argument — 12:7 borrowed the discerner of thoughts, 31:5 borrows the comparison with the sword. 'Try the virtue of' is not KJV; the KJV's 'virtue' is the power that goes out of Jesus (Mark 5:30), and the sense here is the modern one of testing an efficacy.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is a paraphrase, not a run, and the proposition that preaching works better than fighting needs no source. A reader who takes 12:7 as this book's only use of Hebrews 4:12 would decline this row.

pericopes.text: Therefore he took Ammon, and Aaron, and Omner; and Himni he did leave in the church in Zarahemla; but the former three he took with him, and also Amulek and Zeezrom, which were at Melek; and he also took two of his sons.

Now the eldest of his sons he took not with him; and his name was Helaman; but the names of those which he took with him, were Shiblon and Corianton: and these are the names of those which went with him among the Zoramites, to preach unto them the word.
Now the Zoramites were dissenters from the Nephites; therefore they had the word of God preached unto them.
But they had fell into great errors, for they would not observe to keep the commandments of God, and his statutes, according to the law of Moses;
neither would they observe the performances of the church, to continue in prayer and supplication to God daily, that they might not enter into temptation;

links.text: Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.

provenance.other: 'Enter into temptation' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 26:41 and Luke 22:40, both Gethsemane. 'Prayer and supplication' occurs in five, of which Acts 1:14 alone has it as a continuing corporate practice — 'these all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication'.
provenance.significance: The Zoramites' fault is stated as the neglect of two New Testament habits fused into one sentence: the church's continuance in prayer at Acts 1:14, and the reason for praying that Jesus gives in Gethsemane. Recover the Gethsemane context and the failure described is the disciples' own — they were told to pray that they enter not into temptation and they slept. Alma 31:10 makes the Zoramite congregation the sleeping disciples, which is a milder charge than idolatry and a more accurate description of what the chapter goes on to show: a people who pray once a week and then never speak of God again (31:23).

links.note: 'Neither would they observe the performances of the church, to continue in prayer and supplication to God daily, that they might not enter into temptation.' Two New Testament phrases in one clause. 'Continue in prayer and supplication' is Acts 1:14's description of the first church at prayer, and 'enter into temptation' belongs to two KJV verses, both of which are Jesus in Gethsemane telling his disciples why to pray. The Book of Mormon has 'that they might not enter' where Matthew has 'that ye enter not', a person-shift the new setting requires; Luke 22:40's shorter form ('Pray that ye enter not into temptation') is equally close and the two cannot be separated on this wording.

pericopes.text: yea, in fine, they did pervert the ways of the Lord in very many instances; therefore, for this cause, Alma and his brethren went into the land, to preach the word unto them.

Now when they had come into the land, behold, to their astonishment, they found that the Zoramites had built synagogues, and that they did gather themselves together on one day of the week, which day they did call the day of the Lord; and they did worship after a manner which Alma and his brethren had never beheld;
for they had a place built up in the centre of their synagogue, a place of standing, which was high above the head; and the top thereof would only admit one person.

links.text: For Solomon had made a brasen scaffold of five cubits long, and five cubits broad, and three cubits high, and had set it in the midst of the court: and upon it he stood, and kneeled down upon his knees before all the congregation of Israel, and spread forth his hands toward heaven.

provenance.other: 'Scaffold' and 'in the midst of the court' are each KJV singletons, and both are in this verse. The KJV's only other purpose-built platform for public religious speech is Ezra's 'pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose' (Nehemiah 8:4, also a singleton), which is for reading the law rather than for prayer. “scaffold” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “in the midst of the court” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are 2 Chronicles 6:13.
provenance.significance: There is exactly one raised structure in the KJV built so that one man may stand on it, in the middle of a sanctuary court, and pray with his hands spread toward heaven, and it is Solomon's at the dedication of the temple. The Rameumptom is that structure with one thing changed. Solomon 'stood, and kneeled down upon his knees before all the congregation of Israel'; the Zoramite stands and does not kneel, on a top that 'would only admit one person', which removes the congregation the scaffold was built to face. Read that way the chapter's satire is precise rather than general: the Zoramites have not invented a heathen altar, they have reproduced the furniture of the temple dedication and deleted from it the two gestures — kneeling, and standing before the people — that made Solomon's prayer intercession rather than display.

links.note: 'They had a place built up in the centre of their synagogue, a place of standing, which was high above the head; and the top thereof would only admit one person.' No run of shared words, and the strength of the row is entirely in the rarity of what is being described. Two KJV singletons, 'scaffold' and 'in the midst of the court', sit in the one verse that describes a raised standing-place set in the middle of a sanctuary, and the next verse of Alma supplies its posture: stand upon the top, stretch forth the hands toward heaven. The Book of Mormon's 'centre' for the KJV's 'midst' is the sort of substitution that hides a borrowing from an n-gram search, and this candidate appeared in no machine stream.

pericopes.text: Therefore, whosoever desired to worship, must go forth and stand upon the top thereof, and stretch forth his hands towards heaven, and cry with a loud voice, saying:

links.text: And he said, Go forth, and stand upon the mount before the LORD. And, behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake:

provenance.other: 'Go forth and stand upon' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Spread forth his hands toward heaven' is Solomon's gesture at 1 Kings 8:22 and 2 Chronicles 6:13; the Book of Mormon reads 'stretch forth', which is the KJV's verb for Moses' hand toward heaven in the plagues (Exodus 9:22, 10:21) rather than for prayer.
provenance.significance: The instruction to go forth and stand is given once in the KJV, to Elijah at Horeb, and what it introduces is the discovery that God is not in the wind, not in the earthquake and not in the fire, but in a still small voice. The Zoramite obeys the same instruction and then cries with a loud voice. Nothing in the chapter says this; the two verses put side by side say it. The Rameumptom liturgy is the exact inversion of the one KJV scene in which a man is told to stand on a height and wait for God, and the inversion is in the volume.

links.note: 'Whosoever desired to worship, must go forth and stand upon the top thereof, and stretch forth his hands towards heaven, and cry with a loud voice.' The five-word run 'go forth and stand upon' is a KJV singleton, and Alma keeps its syntax exactly, swapping Horeb's mount for the top of the stand. The candidate was in the machine stream (rarity 3.00, the highest score in the chapter) and the stream had no way to see why it mattered. The gesture in the second half of the verse is Solomon's from 2 Chronicles 6:13, which is the verse behind 31:13; so the sentence is built out of the KJV's two great scenes of a man standing raised up before God, one of them a temple dedication and one of them a theophany, with the loud voice supplied by neither.
links.whyNot: 'Go forth' and 'stand upon' are both common, and their collocation could be independent. If 31:13's link to 2 Chronicles 6:13 is declined, this row loses most of its context score with it.

pericopes.text: Holy, holy God; we believe that thou art God, and we believe that thou art holy, and that thou wast a spirit, and that thou art a spirit, and that thou wilt be a spirit forever.

links.text: And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.

provenance.other: The doubled 'holy, holy' occurs in two KJV verses, Isaiah 6:3 and Revelation 4:8, and in both it is trebled.
provenance.significance: If the Rameumptom prayer opens with the seraphic acclamation docked by one, the docking is the point: a liturgy that has lost a third of its Trisagion, addressed by men on a platform to a God they immediately deny has a Son. Isaiah 6 is also the chapter in which the prophet is sent to a people whose heart is made fat and whose ears are heavy, which is the diagnosis Alma reaches by 31:24-27 in his own words.

links.note: 'Holy, holy God; we believe that thou art God, and we believe that thou art holy.' The doubled vocative is the KJV's only formula of its kind, and it is the opening of the one prayer in this chapter we are given verbatim. Recorded at echo, not allusion: two words, a truncation of the source, and a form of address common in English devotion independently of the KJV. Worth the row because of where it sits — the first line of the liturgy the whole chapter exists to describe — and not because of its length.
links.whyNot: 'Holy' repeated in direct address to God is not distinctive enough to identify a source, and the truncation to two removes precisely what makes Isaiah 6:3 and Revelation 4:8 recognisable.

pericopes.text: Holy God, we believe that thou hast separated us from our brethren; and we do not believe in the tradition of our brethren, which was handed down to them by the childishness of their fathers; but we believe that thou hast elected us to be thy holy children; and also thou hast made it known unto us that there shall be no Christ;

but thou art the same, yesterday, to-day, and forever; and thou hast elected us, that we shall be saved, whilst all around us are elected to be cast by thy wrath down to hell; for the which holiness, O God, we thank thee; and we also thank thee that thou hast elected us, that we may not be led away after the foolish traditions of our brethren, which doth bind them down to a belief of Christ, which doth lead their hearts to wander far from thee, our God.

links.text: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.

provenance.route: Hebrews 13:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon; 'but thou art the same' from Psalm 102:27 / Hebrews 1:12
provenance.other: 'The same yesterday' and 'and to day and for ever' are each KJV singletons, both in Hebrews 13:8. 'But thou art the same' occurs in exactly two verses, Psalm 102:27 and its quotation at Hebrews 1:12. mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between those two at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces; the epistle is preferred because the clause it is welded to is Hebrews' own.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's finding. The sentence immediately before it is 'thou hast made it known unto us that there shall be no Christ' — and the sentence that follows the denial is the KJV's single most compact assertion that Christ does not change. Two Hebrews verses are fused: the opening address of Psalm 102:27, which Hebrews 1:12 applies to the Son, and the whole of Hebrews 13:8, which names him. Strip 'Jesus Christ' from Hebrews 13:8 and the remainder becomes a creed about an immutable spirit; that subtraction is exactly what the Zoramites have performed, and the words they are left with are still his. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the suppressed correspondence here is a proper name.

links.note: 'And thou hast made it known unto us that there shall be no Christ; but thou art the same, yesterday, to-day, and forever.' Seven words of Hebrews 13:8 in order, minus the subject, prefixed by the clause the KJV uses to introduce the same idea at Psalm 102:27 and Hebrews 1:12. Two KJV singletons stand in the borrowed run. The 1830 hyphenation 'to-day' preserves the KJV's two-word 'to day' more visibly than the modern text's 'today'. This is well under Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six long quotations; it is catalogued as a quotation because a complete KJV predicate is reproduced with only its subject removed, and because the removal is the argument.

pericopes.text: And again: We thank thee, O God, that we are a chosen and a holy people. Amen.

links.text: The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.

provenance.other: 'God, I thank thee' is a KJV singleton. 'A chosen generation … an holy nation' is 1 Peter 2:9, itself a singleton for 'a chosen generation'; 'an holy people' and its cognates are too widely spread in Deuteronomy to identify a source. “God I thank thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “a chosen generation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The Rameumptom prayer is Luke 18:11 with its two variables filled in. The Pharisee 'stood and prayed thus with himself' — and the Zoramite structure is named, in the text's own gloss, 'the Holy Stand', a place of standing whose top admits one person and which therefore makes praying with oneself architectural. The parable's thanksgiving turns on a comparison with a named other; the Zoramite's turns on 'while others shall perish' (31:28). What the borrowing adds to Luke is the missing publican: Alma's answer at 33:11 will be a man who cries for mercy from outside the synagogue, and Luke 18:13's publican 'standing afar off' is the shape of that answer before it is given.

links.note: 'We thank thee, O God, that we are a chosen and a holy people. Amen.' The four-word run 'God, I thank thee' is a KJV singleton, and the Book of Mormon has it in the plural with the vocative moved: 'We thank thee, O God, that…'. The clause it governs is 1 Peter 2:9's description of the church, so the prayer is Luke's Pharisee praying in Peter's vocabulary. Alma 4:12 already used this parable, from its frame at 18:9 ('trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others'); this row is written in full rather than cross-referenced because it is the parable's actual prayer rather than Luke's summary of it, and because the second use is the argument — 4:12 diagnosed the Nephite church, and 31:18 gives an entire people the Pharisee's words to say aloud once a week. Alma quotes the line back at 31:28 with 'while others shall perish' added, which is the parable's comparison restored.

pericopes.text: Now it came to pass that after Alma and his brethren, and his sons, had heard these prayers, they were astonished beyond all measure.
For behold, every man did go forth and offer up the same prayers.
Now the place was called by them Rameumptom, which being interpreted, is the Holy Stand.—

Now from this stand, they did offer up, every man, the selfsame prayer unto God, thanking their God that they were chosen of him, and that he did not lead them away after the tradition of their brethren; and that their hearts were not stolen away to believe in things to come, which they knew nothing about.

Now after the people had all offered up thanks after this manner, they returned to their homes, never speaking of their God again, until they had assembled themselves together again, to the holy stand, to offer up thanks after their manner.

Now when Alma saw this, his heart was grieved: for he saw that they were a wicked and a perverse people; yea, he saw that their hearts were set upon gold, and upon silver, and upon all manner of fine goods.
Yea, and he also saw that their hearts were lifted up unto great boasting, in their pride.

And he lifted up his voice to Heaven, and cried, saying: O how long, O Lord, wilt thou suffer that thy servants shall dwell here below in the flesh, to behold such gross wickedness among the children of men.

Behold, O God, they cry unto thee, and yet their hearts are swallowed up in their pride. Behold, O God, they cry unto thee with their mouths, while they are puffed up, even to greatness, with the vain things of the world.

links.text: Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:

provenance.route: Isaiah 29:13, or its quotation at Matthew 15:8, or its transcription at 2 Nephi 27:25 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The verse exists three ways in this project's corpus: Isaiah 29:13, Matthew 15:8 / Mark 7:6, and 2 Nephi 27:25, where the Book of Mormon transcribes the Isaiah form. mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence — Alma 31:27 reproduces nothing at a point where the versions differ — so the mediation cannot be settled from this verse.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:13's complaint has two halves, mouth and heart, and Alma 31:27 sets them against each other in the same order: 'they cry unto thee with their mouths, while … their hearts are swallowed up in their pride.' The half of Isaiah that Alma does not use is the third clause, 'their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men' — which is what the Zoramite liturgy demonstrably is, a prayer every man recites word for word (31:20, 31:22). The unquoted clause is the one that fits the chapter best.

links.note: 'They cry unto thee with their mouths, while they are puffed up.' The mouth-against-heart antithesis is Isaiah 29:13's and the sequence is his, but no run survives: Alma has 'cry' for 'draw near', a plural 'mouths' for the KJV's singular, and 'puffed up' from Paul in place of the removed heart. Recorded as an echo at moderate for that reason. The chapter's other half of the figure is at 31:17, where the Zoramites say a belief in Christ 'doth lead their hearts to wander far from thee' — Isaiah's 'removed their heart far from me' with the charge turned around, which is worth more to the case than anything in 31:27 itself.
links.whyNot: Every word Alma shares with Isaiah 29:13 is common, and the mediation check returned no decisive point. A reader could take the antithesis as an independent commonplace of prophetic rebuke.

pericopes.text: Behold, O my God, their costly apparel, and their ringlets, and their bracelets, and their ornaments of gold, and all their precious things which they are ornamented with; and behold, their hearts are set upon them, and yet they cry unto thee and say, We thank thee, O God, for we are a chosen people unto thee, while others shall perish.
Yea, and they say that thou hast made it known unto them, that there shall be no Christ.

O Lord God, how long wilt thou suffer that such wickedness and iniquity shall be among this people? O Lord, wilt thou give me strength, that I may bear with mine infirmities? for I am infirm, and such wickedness among this people doth pain my soul.

O Lord, my heart is exceeding sorrowful; wilt thou comfort my soul in Christ? O Lord, wilt thou grant unto me that I may have strength, that I may suffer with patience these afflictions which shall come upon me, because of the iniquity of this people?

O Lord, wilt thou comfort my soul, and give unto me success, and also my fellow-laborers which are with me; yea, Ammon, and Aaron, and Omner, and also Amulek, and Zeezrom, and also my two sons; yea, even all these wilt thou comfort, O Lord? Yea, wilt thou comfort their souls in Christ?
Wilt thou grant unto them that they may have strength, that they may bear their afflictions which shall come upon them, because of the iniquities of this people?
O Lord, wilt thou grant unto us that we may have success in bringing them again unto thee, in Christ?
Behold, O Lord, their souls are precious, and many of them are our near brethren, therefore, give unto us O Lord, power and wisdom, that we may bring these, our brethren, again unto thee.

Now it came to pass, that when Alma had said these words, that he clapped his hands upon all they which were with him. And behold, as he clapped his hands upon them, they were filled with the holy Spirit.
And after that, they did separate themselves one from another, taking no thought for themselves what they should eat, or what they should drink, or what they should put on.

links.text: Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?

provenance.other: 'Take no thought' occurs in five KJV verses and 'what ye shall eat' in three; the three-membered eat/drink/put on series occurs only at Matthew 6:25. mediation-check.py is decisive for Matthew over Luke 12:22: the Book of Mormon has 'or what ye shall drink', which Luke's version of the saying does not contain. “what ye shall put on” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:25 and Luke 12:22.
provenance.significance: The Sermon on the Mount's next verse is the reason the command can be obeyed — 'Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not … yet your heavenly Father feedeth them' — and Alma 31:38 supplies exactly that: 'And the Lord provided for them.' So the Book of Mormon has taken two consecutive verses of Matthew 6 and turned them into a narrative sequence, command then fulfilment, which is what a sermon cannot do and a history can. The care taken over the third member of the series is what makes the row certain rather than probable: Luke tells the same saying without the drink, and this is Matthew's.

links.note: 'Taking no thought for themselves what they should eat, or what they should drink, or what they should put on.' Fourteen words of Matthew 6:25 in order with only the pronoun and tense changed — 'they should' for 'ye shall' throughout — and with Matthew's three-part series intact. The series is the evidence: the same saying at Luke 12:22 has two members, eat and put on, and the mediation check finds the Book of Mormon on Matthew's side at the one point where the two Gospels differ. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And the Lord provided for them that they should hunger not, neither should they thirst; yea, and he also gave them strength, that they should suffer no manner of afflictions, save it were swallowed up in the joy of Christ.— Now this was according to the prayer of Alma; and this, because he prayed in faith.

links.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun smite them: for he that hath mercy on them shall lead them, even by the springs of water shall he guide them.

provenance.other: 'Shall not hunger' and 'hunger nor thirst' are each KJV singletons, both at Isaiah 49:10; 'hunger no more' is a singleton at Revelation 7:16, which quotes it. mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for the Old Testament form: Alma lacks Revelation's 'any more'. Against that, the 'neither' joining the two verbs is Revelation's and not Isaiah's, so the row is written as direct-OT with the counter-evidence named rather than suppressed. “hunger nor thirst” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “hunger no more” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 7:16 supplies the conjunction and is elsewhere a live source in this book (Alma 5:21, 13:11 both use Revelation 7:14); the promise there is made to those who came out of great tribulation, which fits missionaries sent into affliction as well as Isaiah's returning exiles do.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 49 is the chapter the Book of Mormon transcribed whole at 1 Nephi 21, so its wording is available to this book at first hand and not only through the KJV. What Isaiah 49:10 promises is safe passage to people being brought home from exile; Alma 31 applies it to five men and two sons walking into a land that has separated itself from them. The promise of the return is spent on the mission that goes the other way.

links.note: 'And the Lord provided for them that they should hunger not, neither should they thirst.' Two KJV singletons, 'shall not hunger' and 'hunger nor thirst', both belong to Isaiah 49:10, and the Book of Mormon has Isaiah's negation rather than Revelation 7:16's 'no more … any more' — which is the one point at which the mediation check can decide, and it decides for Isaiah. The verse also completes the borrowing begun at 31:37: Matthew's command not to take thought for food and drink, then Isaiah's promise that they shall have both.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they did go forth, and began to preach the word of God unto the people, entering into their synagogues, and into their houses; yea, and even they did preach the word in their streets.

And it came to pass that after much labor among them, they began to have success among the poor class of people; for behold, they were cast out of the synagogues, because of the coarseness of their apparel;

links.text: For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment;

provenance.other: “goodly apparel” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “despised the poor” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are in this passage. James 2:1-6 is the Bible's only scene of a congregation sorting its worshippers by their clothes, and the 'assembly' of 2:2 is the one place in the epistles where the KJV so renders the word it elsewhere gives as 'synagogue' — which is what Alma 32:2 calls the building the poor are put out of.
provenance.significance: James asks a congregation why the man in vile raiment is given the worse seat and answers his own question at 2:5 — 'Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith' — and at 2:6, 'But ye have despised the poor.' Alma 32 takes that indictment and runs it forward: the poor are not merely seated badly but expelled, and the sermon Alma preaches to them is the demonstration of James 2:5, that they are the ones rich in faith. The whole discourse on faith that follows is addressed to the congregation James says God chose, delivered outside the building they were thrown out of. Neither text says the other's half; put together they make one argument.

links.note: 'They were cast out of the synagogues, because of the coarseness of their apparel.' The verbal contact is three words — apparel, poor, despised (32:5) — and the case does not rest on them. It rests on the fact that the KJV contains exactly one passage in which people are sorted inside a place of worship according to what they are wearing, and this is it, down to the reversal of James's terms: his rich man is in 'goodly apparel', Alma's poor are refused for the 'coarseness' of theirs. Recorded at moderate because a reader who wants a run of shared words will not find one here.
links.whyNot: Poverty and fine clothing are the Book of Mormon's own standing preoccupation from Jacob 2 onward, and this scene could be written from that habit with no epistle in view.

pericopes.text: therefore they were not permitted to enter into their synagogues to worship God, being esteemed as filthiness; therefore they were poor; yea, they were esteemed by their brethren as dross; therefore they were poor as to things of the world; and also they were poor in heart.

Now as Alma was teaching and speaking unto the people upon the hill Onidah, there came a great multitude unto him, which were those of which we have been speaking, of which were poor in heart, because of their poverty as to the things of the world.

And they came unto Alma; and the one which was the most foremost among them, saith unto him, Behold, what shall these my brethren do, for they are despised of all men, because of their poverty; yea, and more especially by our priests; for they have cast us out of our synagogues, which we have labored abundantly to build, with our own hands; and they have cast us out because of this our exceeding poverty, that we have no place to worship our God; and behold, what shall we do?

And now when Alma heard this, he turned him about, his face immediately towards him, and he beheld, with great joy; for he beheld that their afflictions had truly humbled them, and that they were in a preparation to hear the word;
therefore he did say no more to the other multitude, but he stretched forth his hand, and cried unto those which he beheld, which were truly penitent, and saith unto them,
I behold that ye are lowly in heart; and if so, blessed are ye.

links.text: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

provenance.other: “lowly in heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “poor in spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons frame the opening of the sermon. At 32:3 the multitude are 'poor in heart', which is the first Beatitude with one word changed; at 32:8 they are 'lowly in heart', which in the KJV is what Jesus says about himself and nobody else. Alma's greeting therefore tells the expelled poor that the condition their expulsion produced is the condition of the man who invites the heavy laden to come to him. Matthew 11:29's promise — 'ye shall find rest unto your souls' — is the promise Alma will spend the chapter converting into an experiment; and the chapter ends, at 32:42, on the fourth Beatitude. The discourse opens and closes inside Matthew 5.

links.note: 'I behold that ye are lowly in heart; and if so, blessed are ye.' A three-word KJV singleton, and the singleton belongs to Christ's self-description. It arrives attached to the Beatitude formula — 'blessed are ye' — and five verses earlier the same people were called 'poor in heart', which is Matthew 5:3's 'poor in spirit' with the noun the chapter is about substituted for Matthew's. The substitution is worth noticing rather than smoothing: Alma's poor are poor in the pocket first (32:3, 'poor as to things of the world'), and 'in heart' is the term he has to add to make the Beatitude apply.

pericopes.text: Behold, thy brother hath said, What shall we do? for we are cast out of our synagogues, that we cannot worship our God.
Behold I say unto you, Do ye suppose that ye cannot worship God, save it be in your synagogues only?
And moreover, I would ask, Do ye suppose that ye must not worship God only once in a week?

I say unto you, It is well that ye are cast out of your synagogues, that ye may be humble, and that ye may learn wisdom; for it is necessary that ye should learn wisdom; for it is because that ye are cast out, that ye are despised of your brethren; because of your exceeding poverty, that ye are brought to a lowliness of heart; for ye are necessarily brought to be humble.

And now because ye are compelled to be humble, blessed are ye; for a man sometimes, if he is compelled to be humble, seeketh repentance; and now surely, whosoever repenteth, shall find mercy; and he that findeth mercy and endureth to the end, the same shall be saved.

links.text: And ye shall be hated of all men for my name’s sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.

provenance.route: Matthew 10:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with the closing clause from Matthew 24:13 / Mark 13:13
provenance.other: “endureth to the end” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 10:22; “the same shall be saved” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 24:13 and Mark 13:13, which both read 'he that shall endure unto the end'. mediation-check.py is decisive for Matthew 10:22 on the verb — the Book of Mormon has 'endureth to', not 'shall endure unto' — while the demonstrative it does not weigh belongs to the other pair.
provenance.significance: The sentence is a splice of the two KJV forms of one saying: Matthew 10:22's verb welded to Matthew 24:13's predicate, producing a clause that stands in no KJV verse but is made entirely of KJV words. What makes the join more than a curiosity is where the rest of Matthew 10:22 has gone. Its first half is 'ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake', and eight verses earlier, at 32:5, the poor man's complaint was that 'they are despised of all men, because of their poverty'. The verse Alma quotes at 32:13 to promise them salvation is the verse whose other half describes what has just happened to them — with the ground of the hatred changed from Christ's name to their poverty, which is the change the whole chapter exists to undo.

links.note: 'He that findeth mercy and endureth to the end, the same shall be saved.' Seven continuous words of the KJV, and the seven come from two verses: 'endureth to the end' is a singleton at Matthew 10:22, and 'the same shall be saved' occurs only at Matthew 24:13 and Mark 13:13, which use a different verb. The mediation check settles the verb for Matthew 10:22 and ignores 'the same' as too common to weigh, so the fusion is a judgment by eye rather than a machine result. 32:15 repeats the formula ('endureth to the end') within the same sermon and is Alma reusing his own sentence, not a second borrowing.

pericopes.text: And now as I said unto you, That because ye were compelled to be humble, ye were blessed, do ye not suppose that they are more blessed who truly humble themselves because of the word?

Yea, he that truly humbleth himself, and repenteth of his sins, and endureth to the end, the same shall be blessed; yea, much more blessed than they who art compelled to be humble, because of their exceeding poverty;

therefore blessed are they who humbleth themselves without being compelled to be humble; or rather, in other words, blessed is he that believeth in the word of God, and is baptized without stubbornness of heart; yea, without being brought to know the word, or even compelled to know, before they will believe.
Yea, there are many which do say, If thou wilt show unto us a sign from Heaven, then we shall know of a surety; then we shall believe.

links.text: The Pharisees also with the Sadducees came, and tempting desired him that he would shew them a sign from heaven.

provenance.other: “a sign from heaven” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 16:1, Mark 8:11 and Luke 11:16 — and in every one of the three the request is made by people described as tempting Jesus. Matthew's is the only one that supplies the verb 'shew … us'; the Book of Mormon's 1830 spelling is 'show', so the KJV's orthography is not preserved here and cannot be used as evidence.
provenance.significance: In all three Gospels the demand for a sign from heaven is the mark of a hostile questioner, and in Matthew 16:4 the answer is that no sign shall be given but the sign of Jonas. Alma gives the same answer in the form of an argument rather than a refusal: 'if a man knoweth a thing, he hath no cause to believe, for he knoweth it.' The chapter's whole theory of faith — that faith is not perfect knowledge, and that a sign would abolish it — is Matthew 16's refusal turned into a definition. Alma 30 has just finished a story about a man who demanded a sign and was given one, and did not believe.

links.note: 'There are many which do say, If thou wilt show unto us a sign from Heaven, then we shall know of a surety; then we shall believe.' Four words shared with a phrase the KJV uses three times, always of the same demand and always by opponents. The setting is exactly the Gospel one: a demand addressed to a preacher whose credentials are in question. The Book of Mormon 'show' for KJV 'shew' is a genuine departure and is recorded as such — the 1830 text has 'show' here, so this row does not have the orthographic evidence that CONVENTIONS §8 looks for.

pericopes.text: Now I ask, Is this faith? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; for if a man knoweth a thing, he hath no cause to believe, for he knoweth it.
And now, how much more cursed is he that knoweth the will of God and doeth it not, than he that only believeth, or only hath cause to believe, and falleth into transgression?

links.text: Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.

provenance.other: “and doeth it not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Luke 12:47 supplies the comparative measure of punishment — the servant 'which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself … shall be beaten with many stripes' — against 12:48's servant who knew not.
provenance.significance: James 4:17 defines the sin of the knowing, and Luke 12:47-48 grades it against the sin of the ignorant. Alma 32:19 asks precisely the question those two verses answer together — 'how much more cursed is he that knoweth the will of God and doeth it not, than he that only believeth' — and it asks it in order to establish something neither text says: that not knowing is an advantage, because it leaves room for faith. The New Testament's harder judgment on the knowing becomes, three verses later, the reason a sign from heaven would be a misfortune.
provenance.alternative: The proposition that knowledge aggravates guilt is a commonplace of Christian moral theology and reaches the 1820s through catechism as readily as through either verse.

links.note: 'How much more cursed is he that knoweth the will of God and doeth it not.' The four-word run 'and doeth it not' is a KJV singleton, and the clause it completes in James — 'to him that knoweth to do good' — is what Alma has, with 'the will of God' for 'to do good'. That substitution is Luke's: Luke 12:47's servant 'knew his lord's will'. So the sentence takes its structure from James and its object from the parable that supplies the comparative the sentence needs. This is the pivot of the chapter's argument: it converts ignorance from a deficiency into the space where faith is possible.

pericopes.text: Now of this thing, ye must judge. Behold, I say unto you, That it is on the one hand, even as it is on the other; and it shall be unto every man according to his work.
And now as I said concerning faith: Faith, is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith, ye hope for things which is not seen, which are true.

links.text: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

provenance.other: “things hoped for” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “things not seen” occurs in exactly two, Hebrews 11:1 and Hebrews 11:7, both in the same chapter. Hebrews 11 is a source elsewhere in this corpus in its own order — 11:8, 11:9, 11:13 and 11:29 across 1 Nephi 2-5.
provenance.significance: Alma 32:21 is the KJV's definition of faith with its two abstract nouns removed. Hebrews says faith is the substance and the evidence; Alma says what faith is not — 'not to have a perfect knowledge of things' — and then gives the positive half as an action rather than a property: 'ye hope for things which is not seen, which are true.' The added clause is the whole of the chapter's originality. Hebrews' 'things not seen' are unseen; Alma's are unseen and true, and the rest of the chapter is a procedure for finding out which unseen things those are. The seed experiment exists because the definition was amended by three words.

links.note: 'Faith, is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith, ye hope for things which is not seen, which are true.' Both of Hebrews 11:1's distinctive phrases are present, one of them a KJV singleton, and they are present in the source's order — hoped for, then not seen. The 1830 reading is 'things which is not seen', a singular verb the 1920 edition corrected to 'are'; the KJV supplies no verb at all ('the evidence of things not seen'), so the correction moves the sentence away from the source's construction rather than back toward it, which is the opposite of the usual direction (CONVENTIONS §8). Catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the two phrases despite the recasting; it is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And now, behold, I say unto you: and I would that ye should remember that God is merciful unto all who believe on his name; therefore he desireth, in the first place, that ye should believe, yea, even on his word.

And now, he imparteth his word by angels, unto men; yea, not only men, but women also. Now this is not all: little children doth have words given unto them many times, which doth confound the wise and the learned.

links.text: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;

provenance.other: “confound the wise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Matthew 11:25 and its parallel at Luke 10:21 are the two verses in which what is hidden from 'the wise and prudent' is revealed 'unto babes'.
provenance.significance: Two New Testament sources are needed to make this sentence and each supplies what the other lacks. Paul gives the verb and its object — the foolish confounding the wise — but his instrument is a class of things, not a class of people. Matthew 11:25 gives the people: babes, to whom what the wise cannot have is revealed. Alma's 'little children doth have words given unto them many times, which doth confound the wise and the learned' is those two verses held together, and the addition is 'and the learned', which is not in either. The chapter is preached to people the priests have expelled, and the sentence tells them that the traffic in revelation runs the other way.
