links.note: 'Little children doth have words given unto them many times, which doth confound the wise and the learned.' A three-word KJV singleton carrying Paul's verb, with Matthew 11:25's babes supplying the subject Paul does not have. 'The wise and the learned' extends the KJV's pair; compare 2 Nephi 27:15-20, where the learned man who cannot read the book is the Book of Mormon's own development of the same idea, and which is the more likely proximate model for the added word.

pericopes.text: And now, my beloved brethren, as ye have desired to know of me what ye shall do because ye are afflicted and cast out: now I do not desire that ye should suppose that I mean to judge you only according to that which is true;

for I do not mean that ye all of you have been compelled to humble yourselves; for I verily believe there are some among you which would humble themselves, let them be in whatsoever circumstances they might.
Now as I said concerning faith—that it was not a perfect knowledge, even so it is with my words. Ye cannot know of their surety at first, unto perfection, any more than faith is a perfect knowledge.

But behold, if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith; yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you, even until ye believe in a manner that ye can give place for a portion of my words.

Now we will compare the word unto a seed. Now if ye give place, that a seed may be planted in your heart, behold, if it be a true seed, or a good seed, if ye do not cast it out by your unbelief, that ye will resist the spirit of the Lord, behold it will begin to swell within your breasts; and when you feel these swelling motions, ye will begin to say within yourselves, It must needs be that this is a good seed, or that the word is good, for it beginneth to enlarge my soul; yea, it beginneth to enlighten my understanding; yea, and it beginneth to be delicious to me.

links.text: Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.

provenance.other: “the seed is the word” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Mark 4:14's form is 'The sower soweth the word', and Matthew 13:19 has 'the word of the kingdom' without the equation.
provenance.significance: Luke 8:11 is Jesus explaining a parable he has already told; Alma 32:28 announces the equation before telling anything, and then builds the parable out of it in front of the congregation — 'Now we will compare the word unto a seed.' The reversal matters. In Luke the seed is a figure whose meaning has to be disclosed; in Alma it is a stipulated term in an experiment, and the hearer is not the ground but the experimenter who decides whether to give the seed place. That shift from parable to procedure is what the chapter is for, and it starts by taking Luke's identification as its premise instead of its conclusion.

links.note: 'Now we will compare the word unto a seed.' Five words of a KJV singleton stand behind the equation, and the whole of the following allegory presupposes it. Alma 16:17 has already used this parable in the book, from Luke 8:13 ('receive the word with joy'); this row is written in full because it is the parable's premise rather than one of its soils, and because 32:28-43 is the Book of Mormon's most sustained rewriting of it.

pericopes.text: Now behold, would not this increase your faith? I say unto you, yea; nevertheless it hath not grown up to a perfect knowledge.
But behold, as the seed swelleth, and sprouteth, and beginneth to grow, and then ye must needs say, That the seed is good; for behold it swelleth, and sprouteth, and beginneth to grow.
And now behold, are ye sure that this is a good seed? I say unto you, Yea; for every seed bringeth forth unto its own likeness;
therefore, if a seed groweth, it is good, but if it groweth not, behold, it is not good; therefore it is cast away.
And now behold, because ye have tried the experiment, and planted the seed, and it swelleth, and sprouteth, and beginneth to grow, ye must needs know that the seed is good.

And now behold, is your knowledge perfect? Yea, your knowledge is perfect in that thing, and your faith is dormant; and this because you know; for ye know that the word hath swelled your souls; and ye also know that it hath sprouted up, that your understanding doth begin to be enlightened, and your mind doth begin to expand.

O then, is not this real? I say unto you, yea; because it is light; and whatsoever is light, is good, because it is discernible; therefore ye must know that it is good. And now behold, after ye have tasted this light, is your knowledge perfect?
Behold, I say unto you, Nay; neither must ye lay aside your faith, for ye have only exercised your faith to plant the seed, that ye might try the experiment, to know if the seed was good.

And behold, as the tree beginneth to grow, ye will say, Let us nourish it with great care, that it may get root, that it may grow up and bring forth fruit unto us. And now behold, if ye nourish it with much care, it will get root, and grow up, and bring forth fruit.

But if ye neglect the tree, and take no thought for its nourishment, behold, it will not get any root; and when the heat of the sun cometh and scorcheth it, and because it hath no root, it withereth away, and ye pluck it up and cast it out.

links.text: And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.

provenance.route: Matthew 13:6 or Mark 4:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “no root” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all four of them in this parable or its explanation (Matthew 13:6, Mark 4:6, Mark 4:17, Luke 8:13). Luke's sowing has no sun in it — his seed withers 'because it lacked moisture' — so the scorching narrows the source to Matthew and Mark. mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between those two.
provenance.significance: The clause 'because it hath no root, it withereth away' is one of the KJV's tightest causal sentences and Alma reproduces its logic exactly, but he has moved the fault. In the parable the seed on stony ground has no root because of the ground; in Alma the tree has no root because 'ye neglect the tree, and take no thought for its nourishment', and 32:39 says so outright — 'this is not because the seed was not good … it is because your ground is barren, and ye will not nourish the tree.' The parable's soils are conditions a hearer is in; Alma's are conditions a hearer maintains. That is the single doctrinal change the whole allegory is built to make, and it is made by keeping the KJV's sentence and changing who is responsible for the root.

links.note: 'When the heat of the sun cometh and scorcheth it, and because it hath no root, it withereth away.' Seven words of the KJV in order, with the tense moved to the present. The singular pronoun matches Mark 4:6 against Matthew 13:6's plural, but Alma has been speaking of one tree since 32:37, so the singular is forced by his own grammar and is not evidence of Mark — the mediation check, which ignores 'it' and 'they' as too common, is right to decline the point. The 1830 'withereth away' preserves the KJV's morphology where the 1920 text reads 'withers'; the borrowing is plainer in the first edition. Note also that 'take no thought' in this verse is the phrase quoted from Matthew 6:25 at Alma 31:37, reused here in the opposite sense — there a command to trust, here a name for neglect.

pericopes.text: Now this is not because the seed was not good; neither is it because the fruit thereof would not be desirable. But it is because your ground is barren, and ye will not nourish the tree; therefore ye cannot have the fruit thereof.
And thus if ye will not nourish the word, looking forward with an eye of faith to the fruit thereof, ye can never pluck of the fruit of the tree of life.

But if ye will nourish the word, yea, nourish the tree as it beginneth to grow, by your faith, with great diligence, and with patience, looking forward to the fruit thereof, and it shall take root; and behold, it shall be a tree springing up unto everlasting life;

links.text: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.

provenance.other: “springing up into everlasting life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the Book of Mormon reads 'springing up unto everlasting life', one preposition away.
provenance.significance: The KJV grows exactly one thing up into everlasting life, and it is not a tree but a well. Alma takes the phrase and gives it to the tree instead, which is the more obvious figure and the one the source declined; and John's promise that the drinker 'shall never thirst' turns up one verse later in Alma, at 32:42, where those who feast on the fruit 'hunger not, neither shall ye thirst'. So both halves of John 4:14 are used, the second detached from the first and given to the end of the allegory. What the chapter takes from John is the grammar of a thing that keeps rising by itself once it is in you — which is precisely the property Alma needs to distinguish a living faith from a completed knowledge.

links.note: 'It shall be a tree springing up unto everlasting life.' Five words of a KJV singleton with one preposition changed, and the phrase is welded onto the wrong plant: John's is a well of water, and the whole of his figure is liquid. That the Book of Mormon transplants it to a tree is what makes the row worth writing rather than assuming — a writer working from memory of John 4:14 would produce exactly this, the memorable tail of the sentence attached to whatever image is in hand.

pericopes.text: and because of your diligence, and your faith, and your patience with the word, in nourishing it, that it may take root in you, behold, by and by, ye shall pluck the fruit thereof, which is most precious, which is sweet above all that is sweet, and which is white above all that is white; yea, and pure above all that is pure; and ye shall feast upon this fruit, even until ye are filled, that ye hunger not, neither shall ye thirst.

links.text: Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.

provenance.route: Matthew 5:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the negated form of the promise from Isaiah 49:10, adjudicated at Alma 31:38
provenance.other: “hunger and thirst” occurs in exactly three KJV verses and “they shall be filled” in exactly two, of which Matthew 5:6 is the only verse containing both. The negative form — 'hunger not, neither shall ye thirst' — is the wording adjudicated at Alma 31:38 against Isaiah 49:10, whose “hunger nor thirst” is a KJV singleton.
provenance.significance: The chapter that opened by calling the expelled poor 'lowly in heart' and 'blessed are ye' closes on the Beatitude that answers hunger, and closes it in the perfect tense: Matthew's blessed are those who hunger and thirst, for they shall be filled; Alma's have eaten, and are filled, and therefore hunger not. The fourth Beatitude is given as already kept. Underneath it sits Isaiah 49:10, the promise of safe passage to exiles being brought home, which supplied the same clause seven verses earlier at 31:38 for the missionaries entering Antionum. Alma spends it here on the people they were sent to.

links.note: 'Ye shall feast upon this fruit, even until ye are filled, that ye hunger not, neither shall ye thirst.' Three of Matthew 5:6's terms — hunger, thirst, filled — in its own order, with the Beatitude's promise converted from future to accomplished. The negated pair is the formula already argued at Alma 31:38 from Isaiah 49:10, so this row records what the second use adds rather than restating the first: Isaiah's clause alone does not account for 'filled', which is Matthew's, and the pairing of the two is the Book of Mormon's. Recorded at moderate; no run survives, and 'hunger' and 'thirst' are common enough that only the third term makes the Beatitude visible.
links.whyNot: 'Filled' after feasting is the natural word regardless of any source, and a reader could take the whole clause as Alma reusing his own sentence from 31:38 with nothing of Matthew in it.

pericopes.text: Then my brethren ye shall reap the rewards of your faith, and your diligence, and patience, and long suffering, waiting for the tree to bring forth fruit unto you.

Now after Alma had spoken these words, they sent forth unto him desiring to know whether they should believe in one God, that they might obtain this fruit of which he had spoken, or how they should plant the seed, or the word, of which he had spoken, which he said must be planted in their hearts; or in what manner they should begin to exercise their faith.

And Alma saith unto them, Behold, ye have said that ye could not worship your God, because ye are cast out of your synagogues. But behold, I say unto you, If ye suppose that ye cannot worship God, ye do greatly err, and ye had ought to search the Scriptures; for if ye suppose that they have taught you this, ye do not understand them.

links.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.

provenance.other: “search the scriptures” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The phrase had become detached devotional English well before 1830, which is why Alma 14:1's use of it is held at moderate; this row is stronger because of what follows it, not because of the words.
provenance.significance: John 5:39 gives a reason for searching the scriptures — 'they are they which testify of me' — and Alma 33 is that reason executed at length. From 33:3 to 33:19 the chapter does nothing but produce witnesses: Zenos, then Zenock, then Moses, each introduced as having spoken of the Son of God, with 33:14 asking outright 'if ye have read the Scriptures? If ye have, how can ye disbelieve on the Son of God?' That is John 5:39's clause turned into a syllogism. Compare Hays on metalepsis: what the borrowed imperative suppresses is the ground of the imperative, and Alma spends seventeen verses supplying it.

links.note: 'Ye do greatly err, and ye had ought to search the Scriptures.' Three words of a KJV singleton, in its imperative sense rather than Alma 14:1's narrative one ('began … to search the Scriptures'). The row is written in full rather than cross-referenced back to 14:1 because the second use is the argument: John 5:39 says the scriptures testify of Christ, and Alma 33:3-19 is a catalogue of scriptures testifying of Christ, ending at 33:14 with the inference John's clause licenses.

links.text: He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living: ye therefore do greatly err.

provenance.other: “do greatly err” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 12:27, which closes the exchange that Mark 12:24 opens: 'Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?'
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons stand in this one sentence and they come from two different arguments about scripture. What Mark supplies is the diagnosis Alma needs and the shape of it: erring, and erring specifically from not knowing the scriptures. Recover the context and the Sadducees are being answered on the resurrection — they had constructed an absurdity out of the law to prove the resurrection false, and Jesus tells them the fault is in their reading. Alma's hearers have constructed an absurdity out of a building to prove they cannot worship, and get the same answer. The parallel extends to the remedy: Mark 12:26 begins 'have ye not read in the book of Moses', and Alma 33:19 ends with Moses.

links.note: 'If ye suppose that ye cannot worship God, ye do greatly err, and ye had ought to search the Scriptures; for if ye suppose that they have taught you this, ye do not understand them.' The three-word run is a KJV singleton, and the clause it belongs to in Mark is 'ye know not the scriptures' — which is the second half of Alma's sentence, given as 'ye do not understand them'. Mark 12:24 and 12:27 are the bookends of a single reply and the Book of Mormon has both ends of it in one verse, in Mark's own order: err, then scriptures, then a charge of not understanding.

pericopes.text: Do ye remember to have read what Zenos, the prophet of old, hath said concerning prayer or worship?

for he saith, Thou art merciful O God, for thou hast heard my prayer, even when I was in the wilderness; yea, thou wast merciful when I prayed concerning those which were mine enemies, and thou didst turn them to me;
yea, O God, and thou wast merciful unto me when I did cry unto thee in my field; when I did cry unto thee in my prayer, and thou didst hear me.
And again, O God, when I did turn to my house thou didst hear me in my prayer.
And when I did turn unto my closet, O Lord, and prayed unto thee, thou didst hear me;

links.text: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.

provenance.other: “into thy closet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “seen of men” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 6:5 and Matthew 23:5, both of them indictments of display. The KJV's 'closet' elsewhere is Joel 2:16's bridal chamber, which has nothing to do with prayer.
provenance.significance: This is the answer to Alma 31, and it is Matthew's. The Zoramites pray standing on a platform in a synagogue, once a week, in a voice loud enough for a crowd; Matthew 6:5 describes hypocrites who 'love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men'; and Matthew 6:6 gives the alternative, which is the closet with the door shut. The prophecy Alma produces to prove that the expelled poor can still worship is a prayer whose sequence runs wilderness, field, house, closet — four places, none of them a synagogue, and the last of them the KJV's one word for private prayer. Two chapters of narrative set up a problem that a pair of consecutive Sermon on the Mount verses solves, with the Sermon's own vocabulary and without naming it.

links.note: 'And when I did turn unto my closet, O Lord, and prayed unto thee, thou didst hear me.' Three words of a KJV singleton attached to the KJV's own verb of praying, inside a text the chapter attributes to a prophet of old. The next verse completes the pair: 'when they cry unto thee to be heard of thee, and not of men' inverts Matthew 6:5's 'that they may be seen of men' — Alma keeps the construction and changes the sense from sight to hearing, which is the change the whole Zenos prayer is built on, since every stanza of it turns on 'thou didst hear me'. The Zenos text has no biblical original and is not extant outside the Book of Mormon; what can be said is that its distinctive vocabulary at this point is Matthew's.

pericopes.text: yea, thou art merciful unto thy children, when they cry unto thee to be heard of thee, and not of men; and thou wilt hear them;
yea, O God, thou hast been merciful unto me, and heard my cries in the midst of thy congregations;

yea, and thou hast also heard me when I have been cast out, and have been despised by mine enemies; yea, thou didst hear my cries, and wast angry with mine enemies, and thou didst visit them in thine anger, with speedy destruction;

and thou didst hear me because of mine afflictions and my sincerity; and it is because of thy Son that thou hast been thus merciful unto me; therefore I will cry unto thee in all mine afflictions; for in thee is my joy; for thou hast turned thy judgments away from me, because of thy Son.

links.text: The LORD hath taken away thy judgments, he hath cast out thine enemy: the king of Israel, even the LORD, is in the midst of thee: thou shalt not see evil any more.

provenance.other: “taken away thy judgments” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the only place in the KJV where God's judgments are removed from a person rather than executed. The Book of Mormon reads 'turned thy judgments away from me', which keeps the noun and the removal and changes the verb.
provenance.significance: Zephaniah 3:15 puts two things in one sentence — the judgments taken away, and the enemy cast out — and Alma 33:10-11 has both in the same order, with the casting out reassigned: 'thou hast also heard me when I have been cast out, and have been despised by mine enemies … thou hast turned thy judgments away from me.' In the prophet it is the enemy who is cast out; in Zenos it is the speaker, by his enemies. That reassignment is the whole point of quoting Zenos to this congregation, since the men Alma is preaching to have just been cast out of their synagogue (33:2), and the verse tells them that the one whose judgments were turned away was the one who was thrown out. Alma repeats the clause at 33:13 as the single thing his hearers must believe, and attaches to it the reason Zephaniah does not give: 'because of thy Son'.

links.note: 'Thou hast turned thy judgments away from me, because of thy Son.' The KJV removes judgments from a person exactly once, at Zephaniah 3:15, and that verse also supplies the casting out of an enemy which stands one verse earlier in Alma. No run survives — 'turned … away' for 'taken away' is a real departure, and 'turned away' by itself is formulaic across twenty-four KJV verses — so the row rests on the collocation rather than on the wording. Recorded at moderate.
links.whyNot: Judgments turned away is ordinary prophetic English (compare Isaiah 12:1's 'thine anger is turned away'), and the Zenos prayer is a composed text whose phrases may be assembled from the Book of Mormon's own idiom rather than from any one verse.

pericopes.text: And now Alma saith unto them, Do ye believe those Scriptures which have been written by them of old?
Behold, if ye do, ye must believe what Zenos saith; for behold, he saith, Thou hast turned away thy judgments, because of thy Son.—
Now behold, my brethren, I would ask, if ye have read the Scriptures? If ye have, how can ye disbelieve on the Son of God?
For it is not written that Zenos alone spake of these things, but Zenock also spake of these things;
for behold, he saith, Thou art angry, O Lord, with this people, because they will not understand of thy mercies which thou hast bestowed upon them, because of thy Son.
And now my brethren, ye see that a second prophet of old has testified of the Son of God; and because the people would not understand his words, they stoned him to death.
But behold, this is not all; these are not the only ones which have spoken concerning the Son of God.
Behold, he was spoken of by Moses; yea, and behold, a type was raised up in the wilderness, that whosoever would look upon it might live. And many did look and live.

links.text: And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.

provenance.route: Numbers 21:8-9 read through John 3:14-15 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Numbers 21:8 supplies the looking and the living — 'when he looketh upon it, shall live' — and John 3:14-15 supplies the frame: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness … That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.' mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence, because the two texts do not compete at any point: the Book of Mormon has parts of both. The call is therefore made by eye, on two words. 'In the wilderness' stands in John and not in Numbers, whose setting is the wilderness but whose sentence does not say so; and 'whosoever' is John's, where Numbers has 'every one that is bitten'. Alma's own verb, 'raised up', is in neither — it is Deuteronomy 18's word for the prophet, and it is the seam between this row and the next. “looketh upon it” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Numbers 21:8 and Isaiah 28:4, and only the first has anyone live by it; “serpent in the wilderness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 3:14.
provenance.alternative: Numbers 21:8-9 alone accounts for the looking and the living, and the Book of Mormon could reach the christological reading through its own earlier use of the type rather than through John.
provenance.significance: Alma does not mention a serpent. He says 'a type was raised up in the wilderness, that whosoever would look upon it might live' — which presupposes that his hearers know what was raised up, and simultaneously presupposes John's reading of it, since Numbers offers no ground for calling the pole a type of anything. What the verse borrows from John is not wording but permission: John 3:14 is the text that makes Numbers 21 available as a prophecy of the Son of God, and Alma 33:19 uses it as such while quoting the Old Testament. The chapter then does something John does not: 33:20-21 asks why anyone would refuse to look, and answers that they did not believe it would heal them — which converts the type from a promise into a diagnosis of unbelief, and hands Alma the transition back to his seed.

links.note: 'A type was raised up in the wilderness, that whosoever would look upon it might live. And many did look and live.' The looking and the living are Numbers 21:8's, in Numbers' order; the wilderness and the 'whosoever' are John 3:14-15's. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Numbers 21:4-9 at 33:20, the verse in which the refusal to look is explained; the wording is at 33:19 and the link is filed there, with 33:20-21 carried in the recurrence list — see the exclusion register at 33:20. Mediation is recorded as OT-via-NT on a judgment rather than on a machine result, and the two words carrying it are named above so the call can be disputed.

links.text: The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken;

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 18:15-18, or its quotation at Acts 3:22-23 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: mediation-check.py was run twice on this verse and returned no decisive divergence either time — Deuteronomy 18:15 against Acts 3:22, and Deuteronomy 18:19 against Acts 3:23 — because Alma 33:19-20 reproduces nothing at any point where the two differ. The one word held in common with both is 'raise up' / 'raised up', and it is common to both, so it discriminates nothing. Contrast 1 Nephi 22:20, where twenty-six continuous words settle the same question decisively for Acts.
provenance.significance: The claim 'he was spoken of by Moses' is not a quotation; it is a title deed, and Deuteronomy 18:15-18 is the deed. It is the one place in the Pentateuch where Moses is made to speak of a coming figure, and Acts 3:22 is the New Testament's own citation of it, introduced with a formula Alma's clause resembles in substance — 'For Moses truly said unto the fathers.' What is worth recording is the difference between this verse and 1 Nephi 22:20. Nephi quotes the prophecy; Alma asserts it and moves immediately to the brazen serpent, a passage in which Moses does not speak of anyone. Alma 33:19 uses Deuteronomy 18 as a warrant rather than as a text, and that is a different relation to scripture from the one the same book displays at its opening.

links.note: Filed to discharge a Hardy cross-reference (PLAN §7.2) that has been checked against the printed page and confirmed correctly keyed: the footnote sits on 'he was spoken of by Moses' in this verse, and the row is not a parser artifact. Our own reading is that there is no verbal borrowing here, so the link is figural and the confidence is moderate — the reference is right about what Alma is claiming and cannot be shown from the wording. Not to be read as a second instance of the 1 Nephi 22:20 quotation; the recurrence list points there so that a reader can see what the same source looks like when the Book of Mormon does quote it.
links.whyNot: There is no shared wording at all beyond 'raise up', which stands in both candidates and in hundreds of other KJV verses. Alma 33:19 names Moses and then quotes Numbers, not Deuteronomy. If the Hardy row were withdrawn, nothing in the verse would generate this link on its own evidence, and it should be withdrawn if the brazen serpent is judged to exhaust the reference to Moses.

pericopes.text: But few understood the meaning of those things, and this because of the hardness of their hearts. But there were many which were so hardened that they would not look; therefore they perished. Now the reason that they would not look, is because they did not believe that it would heal them.

O my brethren, if ye could be healed by merely casting about your eyes, that ye might be healed, would ye not behold quickly, or would ye rather harden your hearts in unbelief, and be slothful, that ye would not cast about your eyes, that ye might perish?

If so, wo shall come upon you; but if not so, then cast about your eyes, and begin to believe in the Son of God, that he will come to redeem his people, and that he shall suffer and die to atone for their sins; and that he shall rise again from the dead, which shall bring to pass the resurrection, that all men shall stand before him, to be judged, at the last and judgment day, according to their works.

And now my brethren, I desire that ye should plant this word in your hearts, and as it beginneth to swell, even so nourish it by your faith. And behold, it will become a tree, springing up in you unto everlasting life. And then may God grant unto you that your burdens may be light, through the joy of his Son. And even all this can ye do, if ye will. Amen.

links.text: For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

provenance.other: “burden is light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “lowly in heart” — used at Alma 32:8 — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the verse immediately before it.
provenance.significance: The sermon is bracketed by two consecutive verses of Matthew 11. Alma opened at 32:8 by telling the expelled poor 'I behold that ye are lowly in heart', which is Matthew 11:29's description of Christ himself; he closes here by praying 'that your burdens may be light', which is Matthew 11:30's promise about what following that Christ costs. Between them stands the whole seed allegory. Recover the source's context and the invitation the two verses complete is 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' — addressed, in Alma, to people who have just told him they have nowhere to worship and no one to hear them. The bracket is not stated by either text and is not likely to be accidental: the two KJV singletons involved sit next to each other in Matthew and at the two ends of one sermon in Alma.

links.note: 'And then may God grant unto you that your burdens may be light, through the joy of his Son.' Three words of a KJV singleton, in the same figurative sense, closing the discourse whose opening greeting came from the preceding verse of the same Matthean saying. Alma adds the agent Matthew leaves implicit — the burden is light 'through the joy of his Son' — which is the chapter's governing addition to everything it borrows, since 33:11 and 33:13 make 'because of thy Son' the clause Zenos's prayer turns on as well.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that after Alma had spoken these words unto them, he sat down upon the ground, and Amulek arose and began to teach them, saying:

My brethren, I think that it is impossible that ye should be ignorant of the things which have been spoken concerning the coming of Christ, who is taught by us to be the Son of God; yea, I know that these things were taught unto you, bountifully, before your dissention from among us.

And as ye have desired of my beloved brother, that he should make known unto you what ye should do, because of your afflictions; and he hath spoken somewhat unto you to prepare your minds; yea, and he hath exhorted you unto faith, and to patience;
yea, even that ye would have so much faith as even to plant the word in your hearts, that ye may try the experiment of its goodness;
and we have beheld that the great question which is in your minds, is whether the word be in the Son of God, or whether there shall be no Christ.
And ye also beheld that my brother hath proven unto you, in many instances, that the word is in Christ, unto salvation.

My brother hath called upon the words of Zenos, that redemption cometh through the Son of God, and also upon the words of Zenock; and also he hath appealed unto Moses, to prove that these things are true.

And now behold, I will testify unto you of myself, that these things are true.— Behold, I say unto you, that I do know that Christ shall come among the children of men, to take upon him the transgressions of his people, and that he shall atone for the sins of the world; for the Lord God hath spoken it;

for it is expedient that an atonement should be made; for according to the great plan of the Eternal God, there must be an atonement made, or else all mankind must unavoidably perish; yea, all are hardened; yea, all are fallen, and are lost, and must perish, except it be through the atonement which it is expedient should be made;

for it is expedient that there should be a great and last sacrifice; yea, not a sacrifice of man, neither of beast, neither of any manner of fowl; for it shall not be a human sacrifice; but it must be an Infinite and an Eternal sacrifice.

Now there is not any man that can sacrifice his own blood, which will atone for the sins of another. Now if a man murdereth, behold, will our law, which is just, take the life of his brother? I say unto you Nay.

links.text: None of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him:

provenance.other: “redeem his brother” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 49:7, as does “a ransom for him”. The Book of Mormon does not reproduce either phrase; what it reproduces is the sentence's logic and its universal negative.
provenance.significance: Psalm 49:7-8 is the KJV's one flat denial that a human being can buy another's life — 'for the redemption of their soul is precious, and it ceaseth for ever'. Amulek's argument at 34:11-12 is that denial turned into an argument for the atonement: because no man's blood can atone for another's sins, the sacrifice that does must be infinite. The Psalm states the impossibility and stops; Alma states it in order to say who overcomes it.
provenance.alternative: The thought is also Pauline (Romans 5:6-8) and could be reached without the Psalm.

links.note: 'Now there is not any man that can sacrifice his own blood, which will atone for the sins of another.' The proposition is Psalm 49:7's: no man can redeem his brother or give God a ransom for him. Alma's vocabulary is sacrificial where the Psalm's is commercial — 'sacrifice his own blood' for 'give to God a ransom' — which is why this is an allusion rather than a quotation, but the shape of the sentence, a universal negative about one man's power to buy another out, is the Psalm's and is nowhere else in the KJV so baldly stated.

links.text: And, behold, the whole family is risen against thine handmaid, and they said, Deliver him that smote his brother, that we may kill him, for the life of his brother whom he slew; and we will destroy the heir also: and so they shall quench my coal which is left, and shall not leave to my husband neither name nor remainder upon the earth.

provenance.other: “the life of his brother” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 14:7. The n-gram stream ranked it here and was, for once, pointing at something.
provenance.significance: The KJV's only sentence about a law taking 'the life of his brother' is the widow of Tekoa's parable, which exists to make David suspend the law of blood for the sake of a survivor — and it is a fiction told to bring Absalom home. Amulek is asking the same question of the same law and answering it the same way: 'will our law, which is just, take the life of his brother? I say unto you, Nay.' Both passages get a just law to stop short of a second death, and in both the stopping is not a defect in the law but the opening through which mercy is argued.

links.note: 'Now if a man murdereth, behold, will our law, which is just, take the life of his brother? I say unto you, Nay.' The one KJV verse containing 'the life of his brother' is also a case of fratricide argued before a judge, which is a coincidence worth recording even though the roles do not line up.
links.whyNot: In 2 Samuel the life demanded is the killer's own, exacted for the brother he slew; in Alma the life is an innocent brother's, offered as a substitute. The phrase is identical and the legal question adjacent, but the referent of 'his brother' is not the same, and a reader who wanted only a singleton and no argument could take this for coincidence.

pericopes.text: But the law requireth the life of him who hath murdered; therefore there can nothing, which is short of an Infinite atonement, which will suffice for the sins of the world;

therefore it is expedient that there should be a great and last sacrifice; and then shall there be, or it is expedient there should be, a stop to the shedding of blood; then shall the law of Moses be fulfilled; yea, it shall all be fulfilled; every jot and tittle, and none shall have passed away.

links.text: For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.

provenance.other: “jot” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “tittle” in exactly two, Matthew 5:18 and Luke 16:17; only Matthew has both words, and only Matthew has 'till all be fulfilled'. Luke 16:17 is therefore excluded by the pairing itself.
provenance.significance: Matthew 5:18 is the verse in which Jesus refuses to abolish the law: not one jot passes 'till all be fulfilled', which in Matthew is a promise that the law stands. Alma 34:13 keeps every word of the guarantee and reverses its use. Where Matthew's clause holds the law open, Alma's closes it — 'then shall the law of Moses be fulfilled; yea, it shall all be fulfilled; every jot and tittle, and none shall have passed away' — so the fulfilment that Matthew defers indefinitely is dated here to the great and last sacrifice, and the jot and tittle that Matthew says will not pass are said not to have passed precisely because they have all been kept.

links.note: 'Then shall the law of Moses be fulfilled; yea, it shall all be fulfilled; every jot and tittle, and none shall have passed away.' Two words that occur almost nowhere in the KJV, taken from the one verse that has both, and taken with the clause they belong to — 'till all be fulfilled' becomes 'it shall all be fulfilled'. The 1830 reading is 'it shall all be fulfilled'; 1920 transposed it to 'it shall be all fulfilled', moving away from the KJV's word order, so the first edition shows the borrowing a shade more plainly than the current text does. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations.

links.text: And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.

provenance.other: “shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22. Hebrews 9:26's 'once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself' is the KJV's nearest thing to Alma's repeated 'great and last sacrifice', a phrase that occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 9 is the argument Alma 34:8-14 is running: the law's sacrifices are repeated because none of them is final, and the one that is final is offered once. Recovering the context sharpens Alma's odd formulation. Hebrews says there is no remission WITHOUT shedding of blood; Alma says the great and last sacrifice brings 'a stop to the shedding of blood'. The same three words carry the argument in both, and Alma has moved them from the condition of forgiveness to the thing forgiveness ends.

links.note: 'And then shall there be, or it is expedient there should be, a stop to the shedding of blood.' The KJV uses 'shedding of blood' once, in the chapter of the New Testament that argues most closely what Alma 34 argues — a last sacrifice that makes the law's repeated ones unnecessary. Recorded at moderate because the three shared words are the whole of the verbal contact; what raises it above an echo is that the surrounding argument is Hebrews' argument, in Hebrews' order: many sacrifices, insufficient; one sacrifice, infinite; the law thereby fulfilled.

pericopes.text: And behold, this is the whole meaning of the law; every whit a pointing to that great and last sacrifice; and that great and last sacrifice will be the Son of God; yea, Infinite and Eternal;

and thus he shall bring salvation to all those who shall believe on his name; this being the intent of this last sacrifice, to bring about the bowels of mercy, which overpowereth justice and bringeth about means unto men that they may have faith unto repentance.

And thus mercy can satisfy the demands of justice, and encircles them in the arms of safety, while he that exerciseth no faith unto repentance, is exposed to the whole law of the demands of justice; therefore, only unto him that hath faith unto repentance, is brought about the great and Eternal plan of redemption;
therefore may God grant unto you, my brethren, that ye might begin to exercise your faith unto repentance, that ye begin to call upon his holy name, that he would have mercy upon you;
yea, cry unto him for mercy; for he is mighty to save;

links.text: Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.

provenance.other: “mighty to save” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 63:1. Zephaniah 3:17's 'he will save' and Isaiah 59:1's 'his hand is not shortened, that it cannot save' are the nearest competitors and share no phrase.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 63:1-3 is the winepress: the figure who answers 'mighty to save' is the one whose garments are dyed red because he has trodden the peoples in his anger, and 'their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments'. Amulek offers the title as pure reassurance — 'cry unto him for mercy; for he is mighty to save' — but the chapter it comes from makes salvation and bloodstained clothing the same picture, which is where Alma 34 is going: 34:36 ends with garments made white through the blood of the Lamb. The KJV's one 'mighty to save' and the passage's closing garment both belong to the same Isaianic image, running in opposite directions.

links.note: 'Yea, cry unto him for mercy; for he is mighty to save.' Four words from the only KJV verse that has them, dropped into the middle of the prayer exhortation as a title needing no explanation. The phrase does no work Isaiah's context would predict, which is what makes it a borrowing rather than a citation: it has become a standing epithet.

pericopes.text: yea, humble yourselves, and continue in prayer unto him;
cry unto him when ye are in your fields; yea, over all your flocks;
cry unto him in your houses, yea, over all your household, both morning, mid-day, and evening;
yea, cry unto him against the power of your enemies;
yea, cry unto him against the Devil, which is an enemy to all righteousness.
Cry unto him over the crops of your fields, that ye may prosper in them;
cry over the flocks of your fields, that they may increase.
But this is not all: ye must pour out your souls in your closets, and your secret places, and in your wilderness;

links.text: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.

provenance.other: “closet” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Joel 2:16 and Matthew 6:6, and only Matthew's is a place to pray in; “shut thy door” is a KJV singleton in the same verse. “poured out my soul” is a KJV singleton at 1 Samuel 1:15, Hannah's answer to the charge of drunkenness at the sanctuary.
provenance.significance: Matthew 6:5-6 is the KJV's one instruction about where to pray, and it works by contrast: not in the synagogues and street corners like the hypocrites, but in a closet with the door shut. Alma 34:19-28 has just spent nine verses commanding prayer in fields, over flocks, in houses, morning and evening — the most public and agricultural prayer imaginable — and then says 'but this is not all', and sends the hearer to the closet. The Sermon's private-versus-public opposition is kept but re-sequenced into an ascent, and the hypocrites of Matthew 6:5 duly arrive two verses later at 34:28, in Matthew's own word.

links.note: 'Ye must pour out your souls in your closets, and your secret places, and in your wilderness.' The KJV has one prayer-closet and it comes with a shut door and a Father who 'seeth in secret'; Alma has the closet and the secret place and adds a wilderness the Sermon does not have. Note that the Zoramites' complaint at 33:2 was that they had no place to worship, which is what makes this instruction the answer to the chapter's own problem: the poor who are cast out of the synagogue are given the one place of prayer the Sermon on the Mount actually recommends.

pericopes.text: yea, and when you do not cry unto the Lord, let your hearts be full, drawn out in prayer unto him continually for your welfare, and also for the welfare of those which are around you.

And now behold, my beloved brethren, I say unto you, Do not suppose that this is all; for after ye have done all these things, if ye turn away the needy, and the naked, and visit not the sick and afflicted, and impart of your substance, if ye have, to those which stand in need; I say unto you, if ye do not any of these things, behold, your prayer is vain, and availeth you nothing, and ye are as hypocrites which do deny the faith;

links.text: I was a stranger, and ye took me not in: naked, and ye clothed me not: sick, and in prison, and ye visited me not.

provenance.route: Matthew 25:41-45, with Matthew 6:5 and James 5:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sick and ye visited me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:36, and its negative counterpart at 25:43 is the form Alma has. “as the hypocrites” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 6:2, 6:5 and 6:16, of which 6:5 is the one about prayer. James 5:16 is the KJV's only verse joining prayer to availing: 'the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.'
provenance.significance: Alma 34:28 is built from the negative half of the sheep and the goats. Matthew 25:43 is the sentence passed on those who did not visit or clothe, and Alma reproduces its list in Matthew's order — naked, sick, visited not — and adds the verdict Matthew's parable withholds until 25:46. What Matthew's judgment scene does not do is connect the failure to prayer; that is Alma's own move, and he makes it in James's vocabulary turned inside out. James says a righteous man's prayer availeth much; Alma says an uncharitable man's prayer 'availeth you nothing'. The one KJV verse that measures the efficacy of prayer is being used to set its floor at zero.

links.note: 'If ye turn away the needy, and the naked, and visit not the sick and afflicted, and impart of your substance, if ye have, to those which stand in need … your prayer is vain, and availeth you nothing, and ye are as hypocrites which do deny the faith.' Three New Testament passages meet in one sentence: Matthew 25's list of the uncared-for in its negative form, James 5:16's availing prayer negated, and the hypocrite of Matthew 6:5 — who in the Sermon is precisely a man whose prayer is worthless. Given that 34:26 has just quoted Matthew 6:6, the hypocrite here is almost certainly Matthew's and not a generic one. The 1830 'which do deny the faith' was modernized to 'who' in 1920.

links.text: But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.

provenance.other: “denied the faith” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 5:8; the phrase 'deny the faith' occurs in no KJV verse at all, so Alma's present-tense form is a small conjugational shift off a singleton rather than an independent idiom.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one man who has 'denied the faith' has denied it by failing to provide materially for dependents — the same failure, and only that failure, that Alma 34:28 says makes a man's prayer vain. 1 Timothy 5 is a chapter about the church's register of widows and who is obliged to support them; Alma 34:28 is addressed to people who have just been told that their own poverty is not an excuse for withholding (34:40). Recovering the context turns Alma's clause from an insult into a citation of the New Testament's most concrete definition of apostasy.

links.note: 'And ye are as hypocrites which do deny the faith.' The KJV never says 'deny the faith' and says 'denied the faith' once, of a man who will not provide for his own household — which is exactly the offence Alma has just described. The interest of the row is that Alma has generalised a household duty into a general one: 1 Timothy's provision is for 'his own', Alma's is for 'those which stand in need'.

pericopes.text: therefore, if ye do not remember to be charitable, ye are as dross, which the refiners do cast out, (it being of no worth,) and is trodden under foot of men.

links.text: Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.

provenance.other: “trodden under foot of men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:13. Luke 14:34-35, the other savourless-salt saying, ends 'men cast it out' and has no treading, so the mediation is decided by the tread.
provenance.significance: Matthew 5:13's structure survives intact and only its substance is swapped: a thing that has lost the property that made it valuable, judged 'good for nothing', cast out, trodden under foot of men. Alma exchanges salt for dross and supplies the parenthesis Matthew leaves implicit — '(it being of no worth,)' for 'good for nothing'. What the substitution costs is the paradox: Matthew's salt was good and became useless, whereas dross was never anything else, so the warning that an uncharitable man is dross is harsher than the one it is made from.

links.note: 'If ye do not remember to be charitable, ye are as dross, which the refiners do cast out, (it being of no worth,) and is trodden under foot of men.' Four of the KJV's words in their KJV order, from the one verse that has them, with the three elements of Matthew 5:13's ending kept in Matthew's sequence — worthless, cast out, trodden under foot of men. The refiner is Alma's own addition and points at Malachi 3:2-3 rather than Matthew, which is what makes the sentence a fusion and not a quotation.

pericopes.text: And now, my brethren, I would that after ye have received so many witnesses, seeing that the Holy Scriptures testify of these things, come forth and bring fruit unto repentance;

yea, I would that ye would come forth and harden not your hearts any longer; for behold, now is the time, and the day of your salvation; and therefore, if ye will repent and harden not your hearts, immediately shall the great plan of redemption be brought about unto you.
For behold, this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God; yea, behold, the day of this life is the day for men to perform their labors.

And now as I said unto you before, as ye have had so many witnesses, therefore I beseech of you, that ye do not procrastinate the day of your repentance until the end; for after this day of life, which is given us to prepare for eternity, behold, if we do not improve our time while in this life, then cometh the night of darkness, wherein there can be no labor performed.

links.text: I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.

provenance.other: “the night cometh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 9:4. Its companion in Alma — 'the day of this life is the day for men to perform their labors' at 34:32 — answers to John's 'while it is day', so the two verses take the two halves of one sentence in order.
provenance.significance: John 9:4 stands immediately before the healing of the man born blind, and the day and night in it are the length of Jesus's own ministry, not a human lifetime; the works to be done before dark are his. Alma 34:32-33 transfers the sentence to the hearer and makes the night death — 'then cometh the night of darkness, wherein there can be no labor performed' — so a saying about the shortness of the Son's opportunity becomes the KJV's sharpest statement of the shortness of everyone's. The transfer is what the passage's famous line depends on: 'this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God' is John 9:4 with the speaker changed.

links.note: 'Then cometh the night of darkness, wherein there can be no labor performed.' John's is the only KJV verse in which the night comes, and it comes in the same clause-shape and with the same consequence, that work stops. Alma 34:32 has already supplied the daylight half — the day of this life is the day for men to perform their labors — so the borrowing spans two verses and keeps John's order. 'Night of darkness' is the Book of Mormon's own intensification and occurs in no KJV verse.

pericopes.text: Ye cannot say, when ye are brought to that awful crisis, that I will repent, that I will return to my God. Nay, ye cannot say this; for that same spirit which doth possess your bodies at the time that ye go out of this life, that same spirit will have power to possess your body in that eternal world.

For behold, if ye have procrastinated the day of your repentance, even until death, behold, ye have become subjected to the spirit of the Devil, and he doth seal you his; therefore the spirit of the Lord hath withdrawn from you, and hath no place in you, and the Devil hath all power over you: and this is the final state of the wicked.

links.text: I know that ye are Abraham’s seed; but ye seek to kill me, because my word hath no place in you.

provenance.other: “hath no place in you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:37.
provenance.significance: John 8:37 diagnoses hearers who are Abraham's seed and murderous anyway: the descent is intact and the word has nowhere to lodge. That is the diagnosis Alma 34:35 gives the Zoramites, who have a synagogue, a genealogy and a weekly confession of election, and in whom the spirit of the Lord now 'hath no place'. In John the thing with no place is the word; in Alma it is the Spirit, and the substitution is the difference between a hearing that fails and a person who has been vacated and filled by something else.

links.note: 'Therefore the spirit of the Lord hath withdrawn from you, and hath no place in you, and the Devil hath all power over you.' A five-word run from the KJV's only verse containing it. Recorded at moderate rather than high because the phrase is ordinary English and could be arrived at independently; what argues for the borrowing is that both sentences describe the same condition — a hearer in whom something divine cannot lodge — and that neither is about physical room.

pericopes.text: And this I know, because the Lord hath said, he dwelleth not in unholy temples, but in the hearts of the righteous doth he dwell; yea, and he hath also said, that the righteous should sit down in his kingdom, to go no more out; but their garments should be made white, through the blood of the Lamb.

links.text: Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name.

provenance.other: “go no more out” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Samuel 21:17 (David's men forbidding him the battlefield) and Revelation 3:12. Only Revelation's is a promise, and only Revelation's stands in a temple. The verse's other three clauses are re-used rather than fresh: 'dwelleth not in unholy temples' is adjudicated at Alma 7:21 against Acts 7:48, the seating with the patriarchs at Alma 5:24 against Luke 13:28-29 and Matthew 8:11-12, and the garments made white at Alma 5:21 and 13:11 against Revelation 7:14. The exclusion register carries all three cross-references from this verse.
provenance.significance: This is the one clause of 34:36 with no earlier adjudication in Alma, and it is the clause that binds the verse together. Amulek's sentence opens with a temple God will not dwell in and closes with a permanence — 'sit down in his kingdom, to go no more out' — and Revelation 3:12 is the single KJV verse that joins those two things: the overcomer is made a pillar IN the temple of God and therefore goes no more out. Recover it and Amulek's two halves stop being a pair of unrelated sayings and become one image: the man who is himself no unholy temple is built into the holy one, and the going-no-more-out is not a promise of rest but of fixture. It also explains the odd verb 'sit down … to go no more out', which reads as a mixture until Revelation supplies the pillar that cannot leave.

links.note: 'The righteous should sit down in his kingdom, to go no more out.' Amulek attributes the whole verse to what 'the Lord hath said', and it is in fact four sayings spliced: Acts 7:48's temple, Luke 13:28-29's seating, Revelation 3:12's permanence and Revelation 7:14's whitened garments. Three of the four have been adjudicated earlier in Alma and are registered as cross-references here rather than argued again; Revelation 3:12 is new, and it is the join. The 1830 'the righteous should sit down' was changed to 'shall' in 1920, which moves the clause away from Revelation's future promise and toward a general rule.

pericopes.text: And now my beloved brethren, I desire that ye should remember these things, and that ye should work out your salvation with fear before God, and that ye should no more deny the coming of Christ;

links.text: Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.

provenance.other: “work out your own salvation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 2:12, and “name which is above every name” in exactly one, Philippians 2:9. Alma drops 'own' and replaces 'and trembling' with 'before God'.
provenance.significance: The next verse is the reason to name Philippians 2:9 as well. Alma 34:37-38 asks for three things in sequence — work out your salvation with fear, take upon you the name of Christ, humble yourselves even to the dust — and Philippians 2:8-12 has the same three in reverse: Christ humbled himself, God gave him a name above every name, therefore work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. Read together, Amulek's exhortation is the Christ-hymn run backwards through the hearer: the name that was given because of the humbling is now taken by people who are told to humble themselves after taking it.

links.note: 'That ye should work out your salvation with fear before God.' A KJV singleton with one deletion and one substitution, and the substitution is the argument: Paul's 'fear and trembling' is an inward posture, Amulek's 'fear before God' names the one it is felt in front of — which is where 34:32's 'prepare to meet God' has been heading all along. The 'own' that Alma drops is the word doing Paul's work against boasting; without it the phrase becomes an instruction rather than a warning.

pericopes.text: that ye contend no more against the Holy Ghost, but that ye receive it, and take upon you the name of Christ; that ye humble yourselves even to the dust, and worship God in whatsoever place ye may be in, in spirit and in truth; and that ye live in thanksgiving daily, for the many mercies and blessings which he doth bestow upon you;

links.text: God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.

provenance.other: “in spirit and in truth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 4:23 and 4:24, and nowhere else; “worship the Father” likewise occurs only at John 4:21 and 4:23. Both of Alma's clauses come from the same four verses of one discourse.
provenance.significance: John 4:21-24 is the KJV's one argument that worship has been detached from a place: not this mountain, not Jerusalem, but spirit and truth. Amulek gives both halves — 'worship God in whatsoever place ye may be in, in spirit and in truth' — and the placelessness is the point of the sermon, since his hearers are the Zoramite poor who have been shut out of the synagogue they built. Two verses earlier he denied that God dwells in unholy temples; here he supplies the replacement, and it is the replacement Jesus offers a Samaritan whose temple was also the wrong one. The whole Zoramite episode is a synagogue-exclusion story answered out of John 4.

links.note: 'Worship God in whatsoever place ye may be in, in spirit and in truth.' The closing phrase belongs to John 4 and to no other KJV chapter, and the clause before it paraphrases John 4:21's refusal of the two rival sites. The pairing is the finding rather than either phrase alone: Alma has compressed a discourse into a sentence and kept its logic — no place, therefore spirit and truth.

pericopes.text: yea, and I also exhort you, my brethren, that ye be watchful unto prayer continually, that ye may not be led away by the temptation of the Devil, that he may not overpower you, that ye may not become his subjects at the last day: for behold, he rewardeth you no good thing.

links.text: But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.

provenance.route: 1 Peter 4:7 with 1 Peter 5:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sober and watch” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 4:7; “watch unto prayer” is the same singleton. Alma's 'watchful unto prayer' is the adjectival form of it and occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter puts the watching and the devil in two places that belong together — 'watch unto prayer' at 4:7 because the end of all things is at hand, and at 5:8 'be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour'. Alma 34:39 joins them into a single sentence: be watchful unto prayer continually, that ye may not be led away by the temptation of the Devil, that he may not overpower you. The devouring lion becomes 'overpower', and the eschatological urgency of 4:7 becomes 'at the last day' — so the letter's two halves are read as one instruction, which is how a preacher rather than an editor uses a text.

links.note: 'Yea, and I also exhort you, my brethren, that ye be watchful unto prayer continually, that ye may not be led away by the temptation of the Devil.' The KJV joins watching and prayer in one verse only, and Peter's second warning about the devil supplies the danger the watching is against. Moderate rather than high: the collocation is common in devotional English and could have reached the passage without either verse, but the singleton status of Peter's phrase is worth the row.

pericopes.text: And now my beloved brethren, I would exhort you to have patience, and that ye bear with all manner of afflictions; that ye do not revile against those who do cast you out because of your exceeding poverty, lest ye become sinners like unto them;
but that ye have patience, and bear with those afflictions, with a firm hope that ye shall one day rest from all your afflictions.
Now it came to pass that after Amulek had made an end of these words, they withdrew themselves from the multitude, and came over into the land of Jershon;
yea, and the rest of the brethren, after they had preached the word unto the Zoramites, also came over into the land of Jershon.

And it came to pass that after the more popular part of the Zoramites had consulted together, concerning the words which had been preached unto them, they were angry because of the word, for it did destroy their craft; therefore they would not hearken unto the words.

links.text: So that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought; but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth.

provenance.other: “craft” occurs in six KJV verses; in only two, Acts 19:25 and 19:27, does it mean a trade, and those two are the only place in the KJV where preaching endangers one. “our craft is in danger” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 19:27. 'Destroy their craft' occurs in no KJV verse — Alma has fused Demetrius's 'craft is in danger' with the same speech's fear that Diana's magnificence 'should be destroyed'.
provenance.significance: Acts 19 is the KJV's one riot caused by a sermon's effect on revenue, and it runs in the order Alma 35:3-6 runs: the trade is threatened, the interested party calls the workmen together, the whole city is gathered and consulted, and the outcome is expulsion rather than argument. The metalepsis is in what Demetrius's craft actually was — silver shrines for a temple. The Zoramites' craft is the Rameumptom: a built holy place, a scripted weekly worship, and a class of people who profit by administering it. Recover Acts 19 and the accusation Alma 35:3 makes in four words becomes specific — what the preaching destroyed was not their belief but their business in it, and the Book of Mormon's word for that, 'priestcraft', is Acts 19's word with the trade named.
provenance.alternative: The angry-tradesmen motif could be independent narrative invention; 'craft' in the sense of trade is ordinary English.

links.note: 'They were angry because of the word, for it did destroy their craft; therefore they would not hearken unto the words.' The KJV's only trade destroyed by preaching is Demetrius's at Ephesus, and Alma 35:3-4 reproduces the episode's mechanism rather than its wording: the injured party will not argue with the preaching, he organises against it. Recorded at moderate because a single content word carries the verbal contact; what earns the row is the sequence — anger, refusal to hear, a gathering of the whole population convened privately by the interested party, and expulsion of those persuaded.

pericopes.text: And they sent and gathered together throughout all the land, all the people, and consulted with them concerning the words which had been spoken.
Now their rulers, and their priests, and their teachers, did not let the people know concerning their desires; therefore they found out privily the minds of all the people.

And it came to pass that after they had found out the minds of all the people, those which were in favor of the words which had been spoken by Alma and his brethren, were cast out of the land; and they were many; and they came over also into the land of Jershon.
And it came to pass that Alma and his brethren did minister unto them.

Now the people of the Zoramites were angry with the people of Ammon which were in Jershon, and the chief ruler of the Zoramites being a very wicked man, sent over unto the people of Ammon desiring them that they should cast out of their land all those which came over from them into their land.

And he breathed out many threatnings against them. And now the people of Ammon did not fear their words, therefore they did not cast them out, but they did receive all the poor of the Zoramites that came over unto them; and they did nourish them, and did clothe them, and did give unto them lands for their inheritance; and they did administer unto them according to their wants.

links.text: And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,

provenance.route: Acts 9:1, with Acts 4:29 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “breathing out threatenings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 9:1, and the noun 'threatenings' occurs in only one other, Acts 4:29 — 'Lord, behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word.' Both are Luke's, and Alma 35:9 has the breathing from one and the not-fearing from the other. The 1830 spells it 'threatnings'; 1920 normalised the spelling to the KJV's 'threatenings', so here the later edition moves toward the source rather than away from it (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: Acts 9:1 is the last sentence of Saul's persecution and the first of his conversion — the breathing out of threatenings is what he is doing on the road when the light stops him. Alma 35 gives the sentence to the chief ruler of the Zoramites and lets it run to its other possible end: he is not stopped, and the threatenings become the war of Alma 43. The pairing with Acts 4:29 sharpens it further. There the church prays not to be delivered from threatenings but to speak boldly in spite of them, and Alma's people of Ammon do precisely that — 'did not fear their words, therefore they did not cast them out' — so Luke's two threatening-verses supply both the persecutor and the answer to him.

links.note: 'And he breathed out many threatnings against them. And now the people of Ammon did not fear their words.' A KJV singleton with one word inserted: Saul breathes out threatenings and slaughter, the chief ruler breathes out many threatenings, and the object in both is a body of disciples in a named place. What Alma adds is the recipients' reaction, and it comes from the KJV's only other threatenings-verse. Note that the chief ruler's demand is precisely Saul's errand — authority from elsewhere to expel believers from a city that is not his own.

pericopes.text: Now this did stir up the Zoramites to anger against the people of Ammon, and they began to mix with the Lamanites, and to stir them up also to anger against them:
and thus the Zoramites and the Lamanites began to make preparations for war against the people of Ammon, and also against the Nephites.
And thus ended the seventeenth year of the reign of the Judges, over the people of Nephi.

And the people of Ammon departed out of the land of Jershon, and came over into the land of Melek, and gave place in the land of Jershon for the armies of the Nephites, that they might contend with the armies of the Lamanites, and the armies of the Zoramites; and thus commenced a war betwixt the Lamanites and the Nephites, in the eighteenth year of the reign of the Judges; and an account shall be given of their wars hereafter.

And Alma, and Ammon, and their brethren, and also the two sons of Alma, returned to the land of Zarahemla, after having been instruments in the hands of God of bringing many of the Zoramites to repentance; and as many as were brought to repentance, were driven out of their land; but they have lands for their inheritance in the land of Jershon, and they have taken up arms to defend themselves, and their wives, and their children, and their lands.

Now Alma, being grieved for the iniquity of his people, yea for the wars, and the bloodsheds, and the contentions which were among them; and having been to declare the word, or sent to declare the word, among all the people in every city; and seeing that the hearts of the people began to wax hard, and that they began to be offended because of the strictness of the word, his heart was exceeding sorrowful;

links.text: Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.

provenance.other: “because of the word” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 21:4 and Matthew 13:21, and only Matthew's is about hearers. mediation-check.py was run on Matthew 13:21 against Mark 4:17 and returns one decisive point: the Book of Mormon has Matthew's 'because of the word … he is offended' and not Mark's 'for the word's sake … they are offended', which is a KJV singleton Alma does not have. Luke 8:13, the third form, has no 'offended' at all. The same chapter's 'this people's heart is waxed gross' (Matthew 13:15, from Isaiah 6:10) stands behind Alma's 'hearts of the people began to wax hard', though the adjective differs and the hardened heart is the Book of Mormon's own standing formula.
provenance.significance: This is the sentence that closes the Zoramite mission, and it closes it with the sower's own account of failure. Alma 32 built an entire sermon on a seed planted in the heart, swelling, taking root and growing — and Matthew 13:21 is the KJV verse that says what happens to a hearer who has no root: when trouble arises because of the word, by and by he is offended. So the narrative frame reports the outcome of Alma's parable in the vocabulary of the parable Alma's is modelled on, and it reports it as the second soil, not the fourth. The 'strictness of the word' is Alma's own gloss on Matthew's tribulation, and it names something Matthew leaves general: what these hearers could not bear was not persecution from outside but the demand the preaching made.

links.note: 'Seeing that the hearts of the people began to wax hard, and that they began to be offended because of the strictness of the word.' Matthew's clause with one word inserted. The insertion is the argument — Matthew's hearer is offended because of the word, Alma's because of its strictness — and the mediation against Mark and Luke is decided by the phrase itself, since Mark's is 'for the word's sake' and Luke's has no offence in it. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his quotations.

links.text: Then saith he unto them, My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me.

provenance.other: “exceeding sorrowful” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 26:22, Matthew 26:38 and Mark 14:34 — all three inside the Passion narrative, two of them Gethsemane and the third the disciples at the last supper. The phrase has no Old Testament occurrence. Matthew and Mark's Gethsemane forms are identical in the shared words, so the mediation between them is not decidable here.
provenance.significance: The KJV reserves this adjective for one night. Alma's grief in 35:15 is over 'the wars, and the bloodsheds, and the contentions which were among them' and over hearers who will not bear the word, and the sentence that reports it is the sentence Jesus speaks to three disciples he is about to leave in order to pray alone. What Alma does next is exactly that: he gathers his sons and gives each his charge separately, and the first charge, Alma 36, is a conversion narrative told as a descent into 'the pains of a damned soul'. The Gethsemane phrase at 35:15 is the hinge into that.

links.note: 'His heart was exceeding sorrowful.' Two words the KJV uses only of Christ and his disciples in Passion week, applied to a prophet grieving over a failed mission. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because the phrase is short and its English is unremarkable; what argues for the borrowing is its distribution — the KJV never says this of anyone else, anywhere — and the placement, immediately before the charges to Alma's sons.
links.whyNot: 'Exceeding sorrowful' is ordinary enough English that a writer could reach it without Matthew, and Alma's heart is sorrowful where Christ's soul is; if the phrase entered the Book of Mormon's idiom generally rather than from this verse, the row is coincidence.

pericopes.text: therefore, he caused that his sons should be gathered together, that he might give unto them every one his charge, separately, concerning the things pertaining unto righteousness. And we have an account of his commandments, which he gave unto them according to his own record.
My son, give ear to my words; for I swear unto you, that inasmuch as ye shall keep the commandments of God, ye shall prosper in the land.

links.text: Give ear to my words, O LORD, consider my meditation.

provenance.other: “give ear to my words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 5:1. The nearest competitors are Job 34:2's 'give ear unto me' and Acts 2:14's 'hearken to my words', neither of which has the phrase.
provenance.significance: The direction is reversed, and that is the interest of the row. Psalm 5:1 is a man asking God to give ear; Alma 36:1 is a father asking his son to. The chapter that follows is Alma's account of being heard when he cried out of torment, so the opening sentence borrows a supplicant's formula from the one who is now in a position to be obeyed — and the whole chiasm turns on the middle verse where he does the psalmist's thing and cries within his heart.

links.note: 'My son, give ear to my words.' A KJV singleton used as an exordium. Low context score because the Psalm's setting contributes nothing beyond the formula; the row is here on rarity and on the fact that this is the first line of the most carefully built chapter in the book.

pericopes.text: I would that ye should do as I have done, in remembering the captivity of our fathers; for they were in bondage, and none could deliver them, except it was the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; and he surely did deliver them in their afflictions.—

links.text: Saying, I am the God of thy fathers, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Then Moses trembled, and durst not behold.

provenance.route: Exodus 3:6-8 → Acts 7:32-36 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The formula stands in three Old Testament verses (Exodus 3:6, 3:15, 4:5) and is quoted five times in the New (Matthew 22:32, Mark 12:26, Luke 20:37, Acts 3:13, Acts 7:32). Every Old Testament verse reads 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'; every New Testament quotation inserts a conjunction — 'the God of Abraham, AND the God of Isaac'. Alma 36:2 has the conjunction. (“and the God of Isaac” occurs in exactly 5 KJV verses — the five New Testament quotations, and no Old Testament verse.) That is the same one-word test by which Alma 29:11 was decided direct-OT, applied to the same book and the same speaker, and here it comes out the other way.
provenance.significance: Two verses of this book quote one formula in two different KJV forms, and the catalogue's business is to say so. Alma 29:11 reaches past the New Testament to Exodus 3:6; Alma 36:2 takes the New Testament's conjunction, and the rest of the sentence says which New Testament verse. Of the five quotations only Stephen's is embedded in a recital of the bondage and the deliverance: Acts 7:34 gives 'I have seen the affliction of my people which is in Egypt … and am come down to deliver them', which is Alma's 'they were in bondage, and none could deliver them … and he surely did deliver them in their afflictions', and Acts 7:36 gives the Red sea that Alma 36:28 comes back to at the far end of the chiasm. Recover Acts 7 and the frame of Alma 36 is Stephen's speech — the last sermon Saul of Tarsus heard before the road to Damascus, and the chapter's other great source is that road.

links.note: 'None could deliver them, except it was the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; and he surely did deliver them in their afflictions.' A fourteen-word run, and the conjunction settles the mediation.
