This is not the recurrence of Alma 29:11's borrowing but a different one: the same prophet, quoting the same formula twenty-five pages later, in the New Testament's wording rather than the Old Testament's, and with the affliction-and-deliverance clause that only Stephen's version of the bush supplies.

pericopes.text: And now, O my son Helaman, behold, thou art in thy youth, and therefore I beseech of thee that thou wilt hear my words, and learn of me; for I do know that whomsoever shall put his trust in God, shall be supported in their trials, and their troubles, and their afflictions, and shall be lifted up at the last day;

links.text: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

provenance.other: “learn of me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 11:29, and the clause that follows it in Alma keeps Matthew's syntax: 'learn of me; for I …'. It was the highest-scoring candidate in the chapter's n-gram stream.
provenance.significance: Matthew 11:28-30 is addressed to all that labour and are heavy laden and promises rest to the soul; Alma 36:3 borrows its invitation and substitutes a promise that whoever trusts God 'shall be supported in their trials, and their troubles, and their afflictions, and shall be lifted up at the last day'. Support under affliction is what Matthew's easy yoke amounts to, so the substitution is a paraphrase rather than a change of subject. What the metalepsis exposes is who is speaking: in the KJV this sentence has exactly one speaker, and here it is a dying father talking to his son.

links.note: 'I beseech of thee that thou wilt hear my words, and learn of me; for I do know that whomsoever shall put his trust in God, shall be supported in their trials.' A KJV singleton in its KJV construction. Moderate rather than high because 'learn of me' is unremarkable English and Alma supplies his own content after the semicolon; what argues for the borrowing is that the promise he supplies is Matthew's promise in other words. The 1830 'whomsoever' was corrected to 'whosoever' in 1920.

pericopes.text: and I would not that ye think that I know of myself, not of the temporal, but of the spiritual; not of the carnal mind, but of God.

Now behold I say unto you, If I had not been born of God, I should not have known these things; but God hath, by the mouth of his holy angel, made these things known unto me, not of any worthiness of myself,
for I went about with the sons of Mosiah, seeking to destroy the church of God; but behold, God sent his holy angel to stop us by the way.—

links.text: For ye have heard of my conversation in time past in the Jews’ religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the church of God, and wasted it:

provenance.other: “persecuted the church of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Galatians 1:13 and 1 Corinthians 15:9, and 'the church of God' in eight; 'destroy' as the verb for that persecution is Galatians 1:23's ('the faith which once he destroyed') and Acts 9:21's. No single KJV verse joins the verb to the object as Alma does.
provenance.significance: The first adjudication of this formula is at Mosiah 27:10, where the narrator uses it of Alma and where the whole Galatians 1 sequence follows — destroyer, revelation, preacher of the faith he destroyed. A new book gets its own row (ADJUDICATING §4), and what is new here is that Alma is now quoting it himself, twice more as the angel's own words at 36:9 and 36:11. The phrase has moved from a narrator's description to the sentence the convert remembers being said to him, which is what Galatians 1 does too: Paul's persecution formula reaches us only in his own retelling.

links.note: 'I went about with the sons of Mosiah, seeking to destroy the church of God.' The argument for the borrowing was made at Mosiah 27:10 and is not restated. What this verse adds is repetition under quotation: the same words come back at 36:9 and 36:11 in the angel's mouth — 'seek no more to destroy the church of God' — so Alma 36 makes Paul's autobiographical formula into the hinge of its chiasm.

pericopes.text: And behold, he spake unto us, as it were the voice of thunder, and the whole earth did tremble beneath our feet, and we all fell to the earth, for the fear of the Lord came upon us.

links.text: And when we were all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice speaking unto me, and saying in the Hebrew tongue, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.

provenance.route: Acts 26:14, with Acts 9:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “fell to the earth” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which only Acts 9:4 has a voice with it; “fallen to the earth” occurs in exactly two, of which only Acts 26:14 does. The KJV's three Damascus accounts differ on who falls: at Acts 9:4 Saul alone falls and at 9:7 the men stand speechless; at 26:14 'we were all fallen to the earth'. Alma 36:7 has 'we all fell to the earth' — Acts 9:4's verb with Acts 26:14's subject.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 27:12-13 told this event from Acts 9, and the falling there is the companions' at 27:12 with the voice to Alma at 27:13. Alma 36:7 retells it from Acts 26, Paul's third and last account, given before Agrippa — the version in which nobody is left standing. The shift matters because Acts 26 is the version Paul tells as a defence of his own life to a king, at the end of it, which is the genre of Alma 36 exactly: an old man giving an account of himself to his heir. The Book of Mormon's two narrations of one conversion follow the New Testament's two narrations of the other, and follow them in the same order — the third-person report first, the apologia last.

links.note: 'He spake unto us, as it were the voice of thunder, and the whole earth did tremble beneath our feet, and we all fell to the earth, for the fear of the Lord came upon us.' The KJV tells this story three times and disagrees with itself about who fell; Alma 36:7 takes the answer given at Acts 26:14, which is the one Mosiah 27 did not take. The trembling earth is neither account's and belongs to the Book of Mormon's theophany vocabulary.

links.text: And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.

provenance.other: “as it were the voice” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 19:6 — which is also the KJV verse that pairs the construction with thunder, 'as the voice of mighty thunderings'. 'Voice of thunder' occurs in no KJV verse at all; the KJV's thunder is a 'voice of thunderings' (Revelation 19:6) or God thundering with his voice (Job 37:4-5, Psalm 18:13).
provenance.significance: Revelation 19:6 is the acclamation of the reign — the multitude crying Alleluia because the Lord God omnipotent reigneth. Alma's angel speaks 'as it were the voice of thunder' and what he says is a sentence about sovereignty over a man's destruction. The borrowing is of a simile, not of a message, which is why it stays an echo; but it is worth noticing that the KJV's one place for this construction is a place where a voice like thunder announces that God has taken his power.

links.note: 'He spake unto us, as it were the voice of thunder.' A five-word run from the KJV's only verse with the construction, and it is the Book of Mormon's standing formula for angelic speech: Mosiah 27:11 has 'he spake as it were with a voice of thunder' of this same event, in a different book and therefore with its own row. Recorded at moderate because the formula may have entered the corpus's idiom before this verse and 'voice of thunder' is what an English reader would say unprompted.
links.whyNot: The simile is generic enough that Revelation may be an accident of it: any writer wanting a loud supernatural voice writes 'as it were the voice of thunder', and the KJV singleton status attaches to the frame ('as it were the voice') rather than to the image.

pericopes.text: But behold, the voice said unto me, Arise. And I arose and stood up, and beheld the angel.

links.text: And I said, What shall I do, LORD? And the Lord said unto me, Arise, and go into Damascus; and there it shall be told thee of all things which are appointed for thee to do.

provenance.route: Acts 22:10 and 26:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The three accounts word the command differently: Acts 9:6 'Arise, and go into the city', Acts 22:10 'the Lord said unto me, Arise, and go into Damascus', Acts 26:16 'But rise, and stand upon thy feet'. Alma 36:8 has the first-person report-formula of 22:10 ('the voice said unto me, Arise') and the standing-up of 26:16, and neither of the destinations.
provenance.significance: The two verses Alma splices are the two first-person accounts — the one Paul gives to a Jerusalem mob and the one he gives to Agrippa — not the narrator's account at Acts 9. Alma 36 is first-person throughout, and the source it draws on shifts accordingly. The stripped command is also the chapter's economy at work: the KJV's voice tells Saul where to go, Alma's tells him only to get up, because in the chiastic structure the standing up at 36:8 is answered by the standing up at 36:23 and nothing may intervene.

links.note: 'But behold, the voice said unto me, Arise. And I arose and stood up, and beheld the angel.' Five words from Acts 22:10 in Acts 22:10's grammatical person, completed by the action Acts 26:16 commands. Moderate: the words are common and the case rests on the fact that this verse sits inside a sustained rewriting of the same three chapters of Acts.

pericopes.text: And he said unto me, If thou wilt of thyself be destroyed, seek no more to destroy the church of God.
And it came to pass that I fell to the earth; and it was for the space of three days and three nights, that I could not open my mouth; neither had I the use of my limbs.

links.text: For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.

provenance.route: Matthew 12:40, over Acts 9:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “three days and three nights” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Samuel 30:12, Jonah 1:17 and Matthew 12:40; only Matthew's is a figure for death and rising. The Damascus source has a different measure — Acts 9:9's Saul 'was three days without sight, and neither did eat nor drink' — with no nights in it.
provenance.significance: This is where the Damascus narrative and the sign of Jonas cross. Everything else in Alma 36:6-11 comes from Acts, and Acts gives three days; the nights are Matthew's, and Matthew's three days and three nights are the one KJV measure of a burial. Alma 36:16 then names the interval 'the pains of a damned soul', 36:23 has his limbs receive their strength and his standing on his feet, and 36:24 has him going out to preach — a death, a term in the heart of the earth, and a rising. The added word 'nights' is what converts a convalescence into a resurrection, and it is a KJV borrowing.
provenance.alternative: Jonah 1:17 alone; but Jonah's three days and three nights are not a type of anything until Matthew makes them one.

links.note: 'It was for the space of three days and three nights, that I could not open my mouth; neither had I the use of my limbs.' The Book of Mormon's other account of this event does not have the nights, and neither does the Acts narrative behind it. Recorded at moderate because the phrase is a natural way to say 'three days' and the writer may simply have doubled it; what argues for Matthew is that the chapter goes on to use the interval exactly as Matthew 12:40 uses it.

pericopes.text: And the angel spake more things unto me, which were heard by my brethren, but I did not hear them; for when I heard the words, If thou wilt be destroyed of thyself, seek no more to destroy the church of God, I was struck with such great fear and amazement, lest perhaps that I should be destroyed, that I fell to the earth, and I did hear no more;

links.text: And the men which journeyed with him stood speechless, hearing a voice, but seeing no man.

provenance.route: Acts 9:7 against Acts 22:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV's best-known internal contradiction, and both halves of it are singletons — “hearing a voice” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “heard not the voice” in exactly one: Acts 9:7 says the companions stood 'hearing a voice', Acts 22:9 says 'they heard not the voice of him that spake to me'. Mosiah 27:12 resolved it the standard harmonizing way, by making the companions fall and 'understand not the words' — Acts 9:4's falling with Acts 22:9's failure, and 'understood' substituted for 'heard'. Alma 36:11 resolves it the other way and does not harmonize at all.
provenance.significance: This is the finding of the chapter. The two Book of Mormon accounts of one conversion divide along the same seam as the KJV's two accounts of the other, and they divide in opposite directions. Mosiah 27 gives the companions Acts 22:9's not-hearing; Alma 36:11 gives them Acts 9:7's hearing — 'the angel spake more things unto me, which were heard by my brethren' — and then transfers the deafness to the convert himself: 'but I did not hear them.' Neither Acts verse says that. The move is what the chapter needs, because Alma 36 is a chiasm whose centre is a man who cannot hear, speak or move, and it produces the only version of the scene in which the man at its centre is the one who misses what is said. Whether the writer noticed that he was standing on the crux of Acts 9 and 22 is unanswerable; that the two Book of Mormon accounts between them occupy both sides of it is a fact about the text.

links.note: 'The angel spake more things unto me, which were heard by my brethren, but I did not hear them.' A sentence with no single KJV source and an unmistakable KJV problem behind it. Acts 9:7 has the companions hearing; Acts 22:9 has them not hearing; the Book of Mormon has used one at Mosiah 27:12 and uses the other here, of the same episode, and inverts it so that the failure to hear belongs to Alma. The reason given for the failure is his own — 'I was struck with such great fear and amazement' — which is Acts 9's 'trembling and astonished' at 9:6 in the received text.

pericopes.text: but I was racked with eternal torment, for my soul was harrowed up to the greatest degree, and racked with all my sins.
Yea, I did remember all my sins and iniquities, for which I was tormented with the pains of hell; yea, I saw that I had rebelled against my God, and that I had not kept his holy commandments;

yea, and I had murdered many of his children, or rather led them away unto destruction; yea, and in fine, so great had been my iniquities, that the very thoughts of coming into the presence of my God, did rack my soul with inexpressible horror.
O, thought I, that I could be banished and become extinct both soul and body, that I might not be brought to stand in the presence of my God, to be judged of my deeds.
And now, for three days and for three nights was I racked, even with the pains of a damned soul.

And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my many sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophecy unto the people, concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world.

Now as my mind caught hold upon this thought, I cried within my heart, O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who art in the gall of bitterness, and art encircled about by the everlasting chains of death.

links.text: For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity.

provenance.other: “gall of bitterness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:23, and 'the bond of iniquity' with it. The 1830 reading is the evidence here: 'have mercy on me, who ART in the gall of bitterness, and ART encircled about by the everlasting chains of death'. The second person is Peter's — 'thou art in the gall of bitterness' — retained in a sentence whose subject is the speaker himself, and 1920 corrected both verbs to 'am'. CONVENTIONS §8's case in its sharpest form: the first edition carries the source's grammar as a fingerprint, and the modern text has cleaned it off.
provenance.significance: Adjudicated at Mosiah 27:29, where the point made is that Alma's self-description reaches past his own Saul-shaped conversion to Simon Magus. Alma 36:18 adds the fingerprint. In Acts 8:23 the words are an accusation spoken TO a man by an apostle; in the 1830 they are still in the second person while being said BY the man of himself, so the first edition preserves the moment of borrowing rather than the finished sentence. Alma is quoting a rebuke, in the grammar it was delivered in, as a self-diagnosis — and the substitution of 'everlasting chains of death' for 'the bond of iniquity' turns Peter's second clause into the phrase Alma 5:7-10 had already made his own.

links.note: 'O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who art in the gall of bitterness, and art encircled about by the everlasting chains of death.' Two clauses of a KJV singleton, in order, and the argument for the borrowing was made at Mosiah 27:29. What is new is the 1830 grammar: twice 'art' where the sentence requires 'am', which is Acts 8:23's own verb form surviving into a first-person sentence and then being edited away in 1920. A borrowing is rarely this visible in the mechanics of the text.

links.text: And, behold, they cried out, saying, What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time?

provenance.route: Matthew 8:29, with Mark 10:47 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Jesus thou Son of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 8:29 and Luke 8:28 ('Jesus, thou Son of God most high'), and both are cries from men possessed by devils. The petition attached to it is Bartimaeus's: 'Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me' (Mark 10:47, Luke 18:38). Alma's cry is the demoniac's vocative with the blind man's request.
provenance.significance: The KJV never lets anyone address Jesus as 'thou Son of God' except a legion of devils, and what they say next is 'art thou come hither to torment us before the time?' Alma 36:12-17 has just used 'torment' or 'racked' six times of himself, and 36:16 names his state 'the pains of a damned soul'. So the words he cries are the words the KJV assigns to the damned in torment — and he attaches to them the one thing the demoniacs never ask for. The composite is the whole argument: the address of the possessed, the petition of the beggar, and the difference between them is mercy.

links.note: 'I cried within my heart, O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me.' The vocative belongs, in the KJV, to devils; the petition belongs to a blind man on the Jericho road. Moderate rather than high because 'have mercy on me' occurs in six KJV verses and the title is a natural Christian address — but the title in this exact form is not, and its two occurrences are both cries out of torment, which is precisely where Alma is when he makes it.

pericopes.text: And now behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more.
And O, what joy, and what marvellous light I did behold; yea, my soul was filled with joy as exceeding as was my pain;

links.text: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light;

provenance.other: “marvellous light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 2:9, and the 1830 spells it with the KJV's double l — 'what marvellous light I did behold' — where 1920 has 'marvelous'. CONVENTIONS §8: the first edition preserves an orthography the modern text has erased.
provenance.significance: Argued at Mosiah 27:29, where the same singleton appears in the same author's other account. The new thing here is its position. Alma 36 is a chiasm and 36:20 is one step out from the centre, answering 36:16's three days and nights of the pains of a damned soul; 1 Peter 2:9's light is what one is called out of darkness INTO, and Alma has placed it exactly where the chapter turns from darkness to light. The verse it comes from is also about a people being made a people — 'which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God' — which is what Alma 36:24-26 says happened next.

links.note: 'And O, what joy, and what marvellous light I did behold.' A KJV singleton whose 1830 spelling is the KJV's own. The argument was made at Mosiah 27:29 and is not restated; the row is here because a new book gets its own row (ADJUDICATING §4) and because this occurrence is structurally placed in a way the Mosiah one is not.

pericopes.text: yea, I say unto you, my son, that there could be nothing so exquisite and so bitter, as was my pains. Yea, and again I say unto you, my son, that on the other hand, there can be nothing so exquisite and sweet as was my joy;

yea, and methought I saw even as our father Lehi saw, God sitting upon his throne, surrounded with numberless concourses of angels, in the attitude of singing and praising their God; yea, and my soul did long to be there.

links.text: And he said, Hear thou therefore the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.

provenance.other: The divine-council formula — one seated on a throne with the heavenly host about him — stands at 1 Kings 22:19, 2 Chronicles 18:18, Isaiah 6:1, Daniel 7:9-10 and Revelation 4:2-4. The link at 1 Nephi 1:8 adjudicates it against 1 Kings 22:19; Alma 36:22 does not reach for any of them independently.
provenance.significance: This is the clearest case in the book for the OT-via-earlier-BoM route, because the text says so itself: 'methought I saw even as our father Lehi saw'. The proximate model is not 1 Kings but 1 Nephi 1:8, and the sentence is built to be recognised as a quotation of it — the throne, the numberless concourses, the attitude of singing and praising. What Alma adds is the wish, 'my soul did long to be there', which is nowhere in Lehi and nowhere in 1 Kings; the vision is inherited and the longing is his.

links.note: 'Methought I saw even as our father Lehi saw, God sitting upon his throne, surrounded with numberless concourses of angels, in the attitude of singing and praising their God.' The Book of Mormon marks its own borrowing here, and the thing borrowed is a Book of Mormon verse rather than a biblical one; the biblical source stands behind 1 Nephi 1:8, where it is argued. Recorded so that a reader of Alma is not left to suppose there is no scriptural background, and so that the route is visible.

pericopes.text: But behold, my limbs did receive their strength again, and I stood upon my feet, and did manifest unto the people that I had been born of God;

yea, and from that time, even until now, I have labored without ceasing, that I might bring souls unto repentance; that I might bring them to taste of the exceeding joy of which I did taste; that they might also be born of God, and be filled with the Holy Ghost.
Yea, and now behold, O my son, the Lord doth give me exceeding great joy in the fruit of my labors;

for because of the word which he hath imparted unto me, behold, many hath been born of God, and hath tasted as I have tasted, and hath seen eye to eye, as I have seen; therefore they do know of these things of which I have spoken, as I do know; and the knowledge which I have is of God.

links.text: Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye, when the LORD shall bring again Zion.

provenance.other: “eye to eye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:8. (Numbers 14:14's 'eye to eye' reads 'thou LORD art seen face to face' in the KJV and does not contain the phrase.)
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:8 is about agreement in sight — watchmen who see the same thing at the same moment and therefore sing with one voice — and Alma 36:26 is making exactly that claim about converts: 'many hath been born of God, and hath tasted as I have tasted, and hath seen eye to eye, as I have seen.' What the source adds is corporate. In Isaiah the seeing eye to eye is the sign that the LORD is bringing again Zion; Alma offers his converts' agreement with his own vision as the same kind of evidence, which is the argument the whole chapter has been making from 36:4 — that his knowledge is not of himself.

links.note: 'Many hath been born of God, and hath tasted as I have tasted, and hath seen eye to eye, as I have seen.' A KJV singleton used for the corroboration of a testimony by others' experience. Moderate: three words, and the English idiom 'to see eye to eye' was current by 1830 in something close to its modern sense of agreement, so the writer may have it from ordinary speech — but the ordinary sense derives from this verse, and Alma's use is the biblical one, about seeing rather than agreeing.

pericopes.text: And I have been supported under trials and troubles of every kind, yea, and in all manner of afflictions; yea, God hath delivered me from prison, and from bonds, and from death; yea, and I do put my trust in him, and he will still deliver me;

links.text: Who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us;

provenance.other: The KJV's three-tense deliverance formula — delivered / in whom we trust / will yet deliver — occurs in one verse, 2 Corinthians 1:10, whose closing clause “he will yet deliver us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Alma 36:27 has all three members in the same order: 'God hath delivered me from prison, and from bonds, and from death; yea, and I do put my trust in him, and he will still deliver me.' 'Still' for 'yet' is the only substitution in the frame.
provenance.significance: The paragraph the verse comes from is Paul's own list of afflictions — 'we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life' — and it turns on 2 Corinthians 1:9: 'we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead.' Alma 36:27 gives the deliverance formula and Alma 36:28 gives the reason Paul gives for it: 'I know that he will raise me up at the last day.' Two verses of Alma reproduce two verses of Paul in Paul's order, and the second is the ground of the first in both. It is also the reason the catalogue reads 36:27's 'prison, and bonds, and death' as more than a list — in 2 Corinthians 1 the deliverances being counted are from a death sentence actually expected.

links.note: 'God hath delivered me from prison, and from bonds, and from death; yea, and I do put my trust in him, and he will still deliver me.' Paul's three tenses of deliverance with the trust between them, in Paul's order. The n-gram stream proposed Hebrews 2:13 here on 'put my trust in him', a KJV singleton — but that verse is a quotation of Isaiah 8:17 with no deliverance around it, and it cannot account for the tense sequence that makes Alma's sentence what it is.

pericopes.text: and I know that he will raise me up at the last day, to dwell with him in glory; yea, and I will praise him forever, for he hath brought our fathers out of Egypt, and he hath swallowed up the Egyptians in the red sea; and he led them by his power into the promised land; yea, and he hath delivered them out of bondage and captivity, from time to time;

links.text: No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.

provenance.other: “raise him up at the last day” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, John 6:40, 6:44 and 6:54, and 'at the last day' in only five, of which four are in John 6. The phrase is effectively one chapter's property.
provenance.significance: In John 6 the promise is always Christ's about a believer — 'I will raise him up at the last day' — and Alma converts it to the first person as a thing known about himself: 'I know that he will raise me up at the last day.' The chapter's use of the phrase has been building since 36:3, where the same promise was offered to Helaman ('shall be lifted up at the last day'), so the borrowing frames the chiasm's outer members. What John supplies that Alma keeps is the pairing of resurrection with eating and tasting — John 6:54's raising is promised to whoever eats — and Alma 36:24-26 has just spent three verses on tasting.

links.note: 'I know that he will raise me up at the last day, to dwell with him in glory.' A phrase that in the KJV belongs almost entirely to one discourse, moved from Christ's mouth to a man's and from the third person to the first. Moderate: the resurrection formula is one the Book of Mormon uses constantly, so this may be its own idiom by Alma 36 rather than a fresh borrowing; the John 6 wording is nevertheless where the idiom comes from.

links.text: Thou stretchedst out thy right hand, the earth swallowed them.

provenance.route: Exodus 15:4-12, with Exodus 14:27-28 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Exodus 14:26-28 at this verse, and the narrative it points to is certainly the one Alma is reciting — but the wording is not there. Exodus 14:27-28 has the LORD overthrowing the Egyptians and the waters returning and covering them; nothing in chapter 14 is swallowed. The verb is the Song of the Sea's: “the earth swallowed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 15:12, of these same Egyptians, and “drowned in the Red sea” occurs in exactly one, Exodus 15:4. Alma 36:28's 'he hath swallowed up the Egyptians in the red sea' takes the verb from 15:12 and the location from 15:4, both from the poem rather than the prose. CONVENTIONS §6a: the link is placed where the wording is, and the cross-reference is recorded.
provenance.significance: The recital is the chiasm's outer answer to 36:2, and it is worth seeing which Exodus it uses. Exodus 14 is a report; Exodus 15 is a song of praise sung after deliverance, and Alma 36:28 is introduced by 'I will praise him forever, for …'. The form of Alma's sentence is the form of the Song of the Sea — a first-person vow of praise, followed by what God did to the Egyptians — so the verse is not merely alluding to the event but adopting the genre in which Israel remembered it. Acts 7:36's 'wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, and in the Red sea' stands behind the summary shape, and completes the frame begun at 36:2 from Acts 7:32-34.

links.note: 'He hath brought our fathers out of Egypt, and he hath swallowed up the Egyptians in the red sea; and he led them by his power into the promised land.' Hardy cross-references Exodus 14:26-28 here; the event is right and the words come from the chapter after it. Recorded at moderate because a recital of the exodus can be assembled from any of a dozen KJV passages, and Alma's summary is compressed enough that no one of them is demonstrable — but 'swallowed' is a choice, and the KJV makes it in exactly one verse about exactly these people.

pericopes.text: yea, and he hath also brought our fathers out of the land of Jerusalem; and he hath also, by his everlasting power, delivered them out of bondage and captivity, from time to time, even down to the present day; and I have always retained in remembrance their captivity; yea, and ye also had ought to retain in remembrance, as I have done, their captivity.—

But behold, my son, this is not all: for ye had ought to know, as I do know, that inasmuch as ye shall keep the commandments of God, ye shall prosper in the land; and ye had ought to know also, that inasmuch as ye will not keep the commandments of God, ye shall be cut off from his presence. Now this is according to his word.
And now my son Helaman, I command you that ye take the records which have been entrusted with me;

and I also command you that ye shall keep a record of this people, according as I have done, upon the plates of Nephi, and keep all these things sacred which I have kept, even as I have kept them: for it is for a wise purpose that they are kept;
and these plates of brass which contain these engravings, which have the records of the Holy Scriptures upon them, which have the genealogy of our forefathers, even from the beginning.

And behold, it hath been prophesied by our fathers, that they should be kept and handed down from one generation to another, and be kept and preserved by the hand of the Lord, until they should go forth unto every nation, kindred, tongue and people, that they shall know of the mysteries contained thereon.

links.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

provenance.other: “nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:6, and “the everlasting gospel” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The fourfold list is Revelation's signature — 5:9, 7:9, 11:9, 13:7, 14:6 — but only at 14:6 does it stand in the Book of Mormon's order and syntax, governed by a verb of going forth. Daniel 3:4 and 7:14 have a threefold 'people, nations, and languages' with no kindreds.
provenance.significance: The angel of Revelation 14:6 does not carry a message; he carries a book — 'the everlasting gospel', a KJV singleton — and flies with it to the four categories of the earth. Alma 37:4 has the plates of brass 'kept and preserved by the hand of the Lord, until they should go forth unto every nation, kindred, tongue and people'. The Book of Mormon has given the angel's itinerary to an object, and to an object which its own nineteenth-century readers would meet as a book brought by an angel. The metalepsis runs the right way: recover Revelation 14:6 and the record Alma is handing his son is already, in the source, airborne.

links.note: The catalogue adjudicates this formula first at 1 Nephi 5:18, where the plates of brass are likewise its subject; the argument is made there and is not restated. It is given as a link rather than a recurrence because Alma is a new book and a new hand (CONVENTIONS/ADJUDICATING §4, ratified 2026-09-05), and because Alma 37:4 restores the 1 Nephi 5:18 setting exactly — the same plates, the same going forth, the same four categories — after thirty-five chapters in which the formula has drifted into general use. The 1830 'nation, kindred, tongue and people' is singular throughout, as Revelation 14:6 is; the plural 'kindreds, and tongues' of Revelation 7:9 is not what is being copied.

pericopes.text: And now behold, if they are kept, they must retain their brightness; yea, and they will retain their brightness; yea, and also shall all the plates which do contain that which is Holy Writ.

Now ye may suppose that this is foolishness in me; but behold I say unto you, That by small and simple things, are great things brought to pass; and small means, in many instances, doth confound the wise.

links.text: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;

provenance.other: “confound the wise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 1:27, which is also the only KJV verse with 'the foolish things of the world' and 'the weak things of the world'.
provenance.significance: The catalogue has met 'confound the wise' before, at Alma 32:23, where three words were borrowed and the argument around them was Alma's own. Here the argument is Paul's as well. 1 Corinthians 1:18-27 runs: the preaching of the cross is foolishness to them that perish; it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe; the weakness of God is stronger than men; God hath chosen the foolish and the weak things of the world to confound the wise and the mighty. Alma 37:6-7 runs: you may suppose this is foolishness in me; by small and simple things are great things brought to pass; small means doth confound the wise; and by very small means the Lord bringeth about the salvation of many souls. Paul's four moves in Paul's order, with 'small' substituted throughout for 'foolish' and 'weak'. The substitution is the finding: Alma is defending an object — a set of plates that looks trivial — where Paul was defending a message that sounded absurd, and 'small' is the term that transfers the argument from a proposition to a thing.

links.note: 'Now ye may suppose that this is foolishness in me; but behold I say unto you, That by small and simple things, are great things brought to pass; and small means, in many instances, doth confound the wise.' The KJV singleton is the hinge, and the sentence that precedes it names foolishness while the sentence that follows it names the salvation of souls — which is 1 Corinthians 1:21's 'by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe'. The whole borrowing falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his passages; it is a compressed argument, not a quotation. Filed at 37:6 with 37:7 in recurrence because 37:7 repeats 'confound the wise' with the substituted term ('very small means') made explicit.

pericopes.text: And the Lord God doth work by means to bring about his great and eternal purposes; and by very small means the Lord doth confound the wise, and bringeth about the salvation of many souls.

And now, it hath hitherto been wisdom in God, that these things should be preserved: for behold, they have enlarged the memory of this people, yea, and convinced many of the error of their ways, and brought them to the knowledge of their God, unto the salvation of their souls.

links.text: Let him know, that he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins.

provenance.other: “the error of his way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “save a soul from death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are James 5:20, in the same clause. 'Salvation of souls' occurs in no KJV verse at all — the Book of Mormon's noun phrase is a nominalisation of James's verb.
provenance.significance: James 5:19-20 is the last sentence of the epistle and its subject is the one office Alma is handing over: not preaching to the world but turning back a brother who has erred. Recover it and the promise attached is startling for the setting — the converter saves a soul from death 'and shall hide a multitude of sins'. Alma is describing what the records have already done to the Lamanites (37:9) and what he expects them to do to 'our stiffnecked brethren, the Nephites' (37:10), who are precisely the erring insiders James has in view. The plates are being cast as the agent of James's final imperative.

links.note: 'They have enlarged the memory of this people, yea, and convinced many of the error of their ways, and brought them to the knowledge of their God, unto the salvation of their souls.' Two KJV singletons from one verse, in that verse's order — convincing a man of the error of his way, and the saving of the soul — with James's singular pronouns pluralised to fit a people. The clause between them, 'brought them to the knowledge of their God', is the Book of Mormon's own; James has 'converteth', which Alma reserves for the parallel sentence at 37:9 ('brought them unto repentance; that is, they brought them to the knowledge of the Lord their God'). The verse was invisible to the n-gram stream, which proposed nothing at all here.

pericopes.text: Yea, I say unto you, were it not for these things that these records do contain, which are on these plates, Ammon and his brethren could not have convinced so many thousand of the Lamanites, of the incorrect tradition of their fathers; yea, these records and their words, brought them unto repentance; that is, they brought them to the knowledge of the Lord their God, and to rejoice in Jesus Christ, their Redeemer.

And who knoweth but what they will be the means of bringing many thousands of them, yea, and also many thousands of our stiffnecked brethren, the Nephites, which are now hardening their hearts in sin and iniquities, to the knowledge of their Redeemer?—
Now these mysteries are not yet fully made known unto me; therefore I shall forbear.

And it may suffice, if I only say, they are preserved for a wise purpose, which purpose is known unto God: for he doth counsel in wisdom over all his works, and his paths are straight, and his course is one eternal round.

O remember, remember, my son Helaman, how strict are the commandments of God. And he saith, If ye will keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land; but if ye keep not his commandments, ye shall be cut off from his presence.

And now remember, my son, that God hath entrusted you with these things, which are sacred, which he hath kept sacred, and also which he will keep and preserve for a wise purpose in him, that he may shew forth his power unto future generations.

And now behold, I tell you by the spirit of prophecy, that if ye transgress the commandments of God, behold, these things which are sacred, shall be taken away from you by the power of God, and ye shall be delivered up unto satan, that he may sift you as chaff before the wind;

links.text: And the Lord said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat:

provenance.route: Luke 22:31 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Psalm 35:5 supplying the substituted object
provenance.other: “sift you as” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 22:31, and “as chaff before the wind” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 35:5. 'Delivered up unto Satan' answers to 1 Corinthians 5:5, 'to deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh' — the KJV's only handing of a person over to Satan as a disciplinary act.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the whole finding. Luke 22:31 is spoken to Peter on the night of the betrayal and its threat is survivable by design: sifting wheat is what separates wheat from chaff, and Christ's next words are 'I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not; and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren'. Alma keeps Luke's clause word for word and replaces its object with the Psalter's — 'sift you as chaff before the wind', where Psalm 35:5 asks that the wicked be chased away by the angel of the LORD, and Psalm 1:4 makes chaff the figure of the ungodly. The sifted man in Luke is the one who survives sifting; the sifted man in Alma is the residue that blows away. Alma is warning a son who is about to receive the records, and he has taken the Bible's one consoling sentence about Satanic sifting and removed the consolation from it by changing one noun.

links.note: 'Ye shall be delivered up unto satan, that he may sift you as chaff before the wind.' Six words are Luke 22:31's and are found nowhere else in the KJV; the four that follow are Psalm 35:5's and are found nowhere else in the KJV. The construction is Luke's exactly — 'that he may sift you as' — so the fusion happens at the last word, which is where the sense turns. The preceding clause, 'ye shall be delivered up unto satan', is 1 Corinthians 5:5's disciplinary formula, so all three of the sentence's elements are borrowed and each from a different testament. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the reader who does not recover Luke 22:31 loses the fact that a promise has been converted into a threat.

pericopes.text: but if ye keep the commandments of God, and do with these things which are sacred, according to that which the Lord doth command you, (for you must appeal unto the Lord for all things whatsoever ye must do with them,) behold, no power of earth or hell can take them from you, for God is powerful to the fulfilling of all his words:
for he will fulfil all his promises which he shall make unto you, for he hath fulfilled his promise which he hath made unto our fathers.
For he promised unto them that he would reserve these things for a wise purpose in him, that he might shew forth his power unto future generations.

And now behold, one purpose hath he fulfilled, even to the restoration of many thousands of the Lamanites to the knowledge of the truth; and he hath shewn forth his power in them, and he will also still shew forth his power in them, unto future generations; therefore they shall be preserved;
therefore I command you, my son Helaman, that ye be diligent in fulfilling all my words, and that ye be diligent in keeping the commandments of God, as they are written.

And now, I will speak unto you concerning those twenty-four plates, that ye keep them, that the mysteries and the works of darkness, and their secret works, or the secret works of those people, which have been destroyed, may be made manifest unto this people; yea, all their murders, and robbings, and their plunderings, and all their wickedness, and abominations, may be made manifest unto this people; yea, and that ye preserve these directors.

links.text: And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.

provenance.other: “works of darkness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ephesians 5:11 and Romans 13:12. Romans has it in an armour-and-daylight figure with nothing secret about it; Ephesians has it in a passage about secrecy and disclosure. 'Made manifest' is common (nineteen verses) and carries no weight on its own.
provenance.alternative: Luke 8:17, 'nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest', is the tighter match for the two words 'secret' and 'manifest' considered alone, and a reader who wants a single verse rather than a window should take it.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:11-13 is the New Testament's one sustained treatment of the problem Alma 37:21-29 is actually facing: what to do with a record of secret wickedness. Paul's three moves are reprove the works of darkness (11), do not so much as speak of the things done in secret (12), and let the light make them manifest (13). Alma's are make the murders and abominations manifest to this people (21, 29), retain their oaths and covenants and signs so that the people never learn them (27), and let the Lord's stone bring the secret works out of darkness into light (23-25). He has taken all three of Paul's moves and separated what Paul left joined — the wickedness is published, the method is suppressed. That distinction is not in Ephesians, and it is the chapter's own contribution.

links.note: 'That the mysteries and the works of darkness, and their secret works, or the secret works of those people, which have been destroyed, may be made manifest unto this people.' No single phrase here is decisive, which is why this is filed as an echo at moderate; what argues for it is that a three-verse window in Ephesians supplies all three of the verse's terms in the verse's order, and that the same window governs Alma's next eight verses. Note the 1830 'directors' at the end of the verse, changed to 'interpreters' in 1920 — the object under discussion is renamed between editions, though nothing in the biblical contact depends on it.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is one two-verse phrase ('works of darkness') plus two common words. If the Book of Mormon simply inherited 'works of darkness' as ordinary religious English — which by 1830 it plainly was — the Ephesians window explains nothing that the Romans 13:12 phrase does not.

pericopes.text: For behold, the Lord saw that his people began to work in darkness, yea, work secret murders and abominations; therefore the Lord said, If they did not repent, they should be destroyed from off the face of the earth.

And the Lord said, I will prepare unto my servant Gazelem, a stone, which shall shine forth in darkness unto light, that I may discover unto my people which serve me, that I may discover unto them the works of their brethren; yea, their secret works, their works of darkness, and their wickedness and abominations.

links.text: He discovereth deep things out of darkness, and bringeth out to light the shadow of death.

provenance.other: “discovereth deep things out of darkness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 12:22, which is also the KJV's only pairing of the verb 'discover' in its old sense — uncover, disclose — with a movement from darkness to light.
provenance.significance: Job 12:13-25 is Job's ironic hymn to a wisdom that undoes governments: God 'leadeth counsellors away spoiled', 'looseth the bond of kings', 'poureth contempt upon princes', 'taketh away the heart of the chief of the people of the earth' — and, at 12:22, discovers deep things out of darkness. Alma is describing a stone given so that a secret conspiracy inside a nation can be exposed and, in the event, so that the nation destroyed by it can be catalogued. The passage he has reached for is the Bible's one description of God as the discoverer of what political darkness conceals, and Job's list of what that discovery does to rulers is the fate of the people whose record the stone reads.

links.note: 'I will prepare unto my servant Gazelem, a stone, which shall shine forth in darkness unto light, that I may discover unto my people which serve me, that I may discover unto them the works of their brethren; yea, their secret works, their works of darkness.' 'Discover' is used twice and in the KJV's obsolete transitive sense, which by 1829 was archaic English and is the mark of the borrowing; the darkness-to-light movement attached to it is Job 12:22's, in Job 12:22's order. Held at moderate because the shared content words are two and the construction is not reproduced. The link is filed here rather than at 37:25 because 'discover' is the word only Job supplies; 37:25 repeats the darkness-to-light clause and is adjudicated separately to 1 Corinthians 4:5, which supplies what Job does not.

pericopes.text: And now my son, these directors were prepared, that the word of God might be fulfilled, which he spake, saying:

I will bring forth out of darkness unto light, all their secret works and their abominations; and except they repent, I will destroy them from off the face of the earth; and I will bring to light all their secrets and abominations, unto every nation that shall hereafter possess the land.

links.text: Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God.

provenance.other: “bring to light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “hidden things of darkness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are 1 Corinthians 4:5, where they stand in the order Alma 37:25 uses them.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is an instruction to withhold judgment: judge nothing before the time, because the Lord's coming is what will bring the hidden things of darkness to light. Alma 37:25 is the divine speech that the Jaredite record fulfils, and 37:26 reports the fulfilment — 'thus far the word of God hath been fulfilled; yea, their secret abominations have been brought out of darkness'. The Book of Mormon has taken the eschatological clause out of Paul's prohibition and made it a completed act of publication inside history, discharged by a translated record rather than by the Lord's coming. What Paul defers, Alma reports as done; and what Alma has in hand is the book his own reader is holding.

links.note: 'I will bring forth out of darkness unto light, all their secret works and their abominations … and I will bring to light all their secrets and abominations, unto every nation that shall hereafter possess the land.' Two KJV singletons from a single verse, in that verse's sequence, and the surrounding vocabulary of 37:21-26 — 'made manifest', the works of darkness, the secret things — is 1 Corinthians 4:5's remaining clause ('will make manifest the counsels of the hearts') distributed across the passage. The closing phrase 'unto every nation that shall hereafter possess the land' returns the divine speech to the going-forth of 37:4, so the two ends of the chapter's argument about records are both worded out of the New Testament's language for eschatological disclosure.

pericopes.text: And now my son, we see that they did not repent; therefore they have been destroyed, and thus far the word of God hath been fulfilled; yea, their secret abominations have been brought out of darkness, and made known unto us.

And now my son, I command you that ye retain all their oaths, and their covenants, and their agreements in their secret abominations; yea, and all their signs and their wonders ye shall retain from this people, that they know them not, lest peradventure they should fall into darkness also, and be destroyed.

For behold, there is a curse upon all this land, that destruction shall come upon all those workers of darkness, according to the power of God, when they are fully ripe; therefore I desire that this people might not be destroyed.—

links.text: And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe.

provenance.other: “fully ripe” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:18; Joel 3:13, the verse Revelation is reworking, reads 'for the harvest is ripe' without the adverb.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:18-20 is the vintage of wrath: the grapes are gathered when fully ripe and cast into the winepress, and blood comes out of the press to the horses' bridles. Alma's clause is a timing rule for national destruction — the curse falls on the workers of darkness 'when they are fully ripe', and 37:31 repeats it as the condition that can still be escaped, 'except they repent before they are fully ripe'. What the Book of Mormon takes from Revelation is not the imagery, which it drops entirely, but the adverb: ripeness that is not yet full is the interval in which repentance is possible, and that interval exists in the source only as the moment before the sickle is thrust in.
provenance.alternative: By Alma the phrase is a Book of Mormon formula in its own right (2 Nephi 28:16, and forward to Alma 45:16 and Ether), so the proximate model may be internal rather than biblical.

links.note: The catalogue adjudicates the phrase first at 2 Nephi 28:16 and the argument for the KJV singleton is made there. The row is given here rather than passed over because Alma is a different book and a different hand (ADJUDICATING §4), and because Alma 37:28-31 does something 2 Nephi 28:16 does not: it turns the adverb into a condition with an escape clause, twice, and makes it the ground of a request ('therefore I desire that this people might not be destroyed'). Moderate rather than high because the verbal contact is two words and by this point in the corpus the phrase is plainly internal currency.

pericopes.text: Therefore, ye shall keep these secret plans of their oaths and their covenants from this people, and only their wickedness, and their murders, and their abominations, shall ye make known unto them; and ye shall teach them to abhor such wickedness, and abominations, and murders; and ye shall also teach them, that these people were destroyed on account of their wickedness, and abominations, and their murders.

For behold, they murdered all the prophets of the Lord which came among them, to declare unto them concerning their iniquities; and the blood of those which they murdered, did cry unto the Lord their God, for vengeance upon those which were their murderers; and thus the judgments of God did come upon these workers of darkness and secret combinations;
yea, and cursed be the land forever and ever unto those workers of darkness and secret combinations, even unto destruction, except they repent before they are fully ripe.
And now my son, remember the words which I have spoken unto you: trust not those secret plans unto this people, but teach them an everlasting hatred against sin and iniquity;

preach unto them repentance, and faith on the Lord Jesus Christ; teach them to humble themselves, and to be meek and lowly in heart; teach them to withstand every temptation of the Devil, with their faith on the Lord Jesus Christ;
teach them to never be weary of good works, but to be meek and lowly in heart: for such shall find rest to their souls.

links.text: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

provenance.other: “meek and lowly in heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “rest unto your souls” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Matthew 11:29. Jeremiah 6:16, which Matthew is reworking, has 'ye shall find rest for your souls'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 11:28-30 is an invitation issued by Christ in the first person — come unto me, take my yoke, learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart. Alma converts every first person in it to a third: teach them to be meek and lowly in heart, for such shall find rest to their souls. The self-description becomes a curriculum, and the promise that in Matthew is attached to a person ('rest unto your souls' follows 'learn of me') is here attached to a disposition. That is a considerable theological move made entirely by changing pronouns, and it is the third time in six chapters that Alma has taken a piece of this verse — 'lowly in heart' at 32:8, 'learn of me' at 36:3, the yoke's ease at 33:23 — without ever quoting it whole. Here he quotes it whole.

links.note: 'Teach them to never be weary of good works, but to be meek and lowly in heart: for such shall find rest to their souls.' Two KJV singletons in Matthew's own order and with Matthew's own connective ('for'), which is what lifts this above the partial borrowings the catalogue has already filed at Alma 32:8, 33:23 and 36:3 and is why it is a fresh link rather than a recurrence of them (ADJUDICATING §4). Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages. `mediation-check.py` on Jeremiah 6:16 against Matthew 11:29 returns two decisive points for Matthew and none for Jeremiah — Alma has the meekness and lowliness that only Matthew supplies, and none of Jeremiah's old paths — so the route is the Gospel, not the prophet. One departure is worth recording: Alma reads 'rest TO their souls' where Matthew has 'unto your souls' and Jeremiah has 'for your souls', a third preposition belonging to neither.

pericopes.text: O remember my son, and learn wisdom in thy youth; yea, learn in thy youth to keep the commandments of God;

links.text: Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.

provenance.other: “in thy youth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ecclesiastes 11:9, which also carries the near variant 'in the days of thy youth' — repeated at 12:1. 'Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth' (12:1) and 'Fear God, and keep his commandments' (12:13) are the epilogue's opening and closing imperatives.
provenance.significance: Read Alma 37:35-36 against Ecclesiastes 11:9 and it is a rebuttal, clause by clause. Qoheleth: rejoice in thy youth, let thy heart cheer thee, walk in the ways of thine heart and in the sight of thine eyes — but know that God will bring thee into judgment. Alma: learn wisdom in thy youth, learn in thy youth to keep the commandments, let thy thoughts be directed unto the Lord, let the affections of thy heart be placed upon the Lord forever. The two verses share the singleton, the address to a young man, and the heart as the thing that must be pointed somewhere; they differ on where. Alma has kept Qoheleth's warning and deleted the permission that precedes it, and he has done to Ecclesiastes 11:9 what Ecclesiastes 12:1 already does to it — which is to say he has read the source's own self-correction and finished it.

links.note: 'O remember my son, and learn wisdom in thy youth; yea, learn in thy youth to keep the commandments of God.' The KJV singleton twice in one verse, opened by 'remember' (Ecclesiastes 12:1's imperative) and closed by 'keep the commandments' (12:13's). Three points of the Preacher's epilogue in eleven words, and the epilogue is the KJV's one address by an old teacher to a young man about what to do with his youth — which is the situation of Alma 37 exactly. The n-gram stream proposed Deuteronomy 10:13 here on 'keep the commandments of', which is boilerplate; the actual source shares only three content words and is invisible to a contiguous window (CONVENTIONS §9).

pericopes.text: yea, and cry unto God for all thy support; yea, let all thy doings be unto the Lord, and whithersoever thou goest, let it be in the Lord; yea, let thy thoughts be directed unto the Lord; yea, let the affections of thy heart be placed upon the Lord forever;

counsel the Lord in all thy doings, and he will direct thee for good; yea, when thou liest down at night, lie down unto the Lord, that he may watch over you in your sleep; and when thou risest in the morning, let thy heart be full of thanks unto God; and if ye do these things, ye shall be lifted up at the last day.

links.text: In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.

provenance.other: “he shall direct thy paths” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 3:6. “when thou liest down” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Deuteronomy 6:7, Deuteronomy 11:19 and Proverbs 3:24 — and 'and when thou risest' in two of them, so the whole of Alma's day-and-night frame is drawn from those three verses and no others.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 3 is the KJV's model of the speech Alma 37 is: a father to a son, 'My son, forget not my law; but let thine heart keep my commandments' (3:1). Alma has used two widely separated verses of it in one sentence. Proverbs 3:6 supplies the conditional — acknowledge him in all thy ways and he will direct you — and Proverbs 3:24 supplies what happens at night: 'When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet.' Between them the borrowing picks up Deuteronomy 6:7's Shema formula, 'when thou liest down, and when thou risest up', which is the KJV's phrase for the whole of a day's obedience. So the sentence that tells Helaman what to do with his waking and sleeping hours is assembled from the Bible's two places for saying it, the wisdom text and the covenant text, and the substitution of 'doings' for 'ways' is Alma's only word of his own in the frame.

links.note: 'Counsel the Lord in all thy doings, and he will direct thee for good; yea, when thou liest down at night, lie down unto the Lord, that he may watch over you in your sleep; and when thou risest in the morning, let thy heart be full of thanks unto God.' Proverbs 3:6's construction is kept intact — imperative, 'in all thy [x]', 'and he will direct thee' — with the object of the verb changed from the paths to the person, and 'ways' changed to 'doings'. Note that 37:36 has already used 'let all thy doings be unto the Lord', so the substituted noun is established a verse earlier; and note the reversal in the imperative itself, 'counsel the Lord' where Proverbs has the man acknowledging God. The 1830 reads 'watch over you in your sleep' with no preposition before 'sleep' in the following clause where 1920 supplies 'with'; nothing in the borrowing turns on it.

links.text: Wherefore the rather, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall:

provenance.other: “if ye do these things, ye shall” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 1:10 — a seven-word run found nowhere else in the Bible.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 1:5-10 is a ladder of virtues to be added one to another — faith, virtue, knowledge, temperance, patience, godliness, brotherly kindness, charity — closed by the promise that whoever does these things shall never fall. Alma 37:33-37 is a list of the same shape and length, delivered as instructions to a son: preach repentance and faith, teach humility, teach meekness, never be weary of good works, learn wisdom, cry unto God, let thy doings be unto the Lord, counsel the Lord, lie down unto the Lord, rise with thanks. The seven-word run arrives at the end of it, exactly where 2 Peter's does, and the promise it introduces is changed from a negative to a positive: not 'ye shall never fall' but 'ye shall be lifted up at the last day'. The suppressed correspondence is that the source's guarantee is against falling, and the Book of Mormon's is about resurrection.

links.note: 'And if ye do these things, ye shall be lifted up at the last day.' The longest exact run in the chapter and a KJV singleton at seven words, closing a catalogue of virtues in the position 2 Peter closes one. Held at moderate rather than high because the run is entirely made of common words and could be arrived at independently; what argues against coincidence is its placement — it is the clause that discharges a list, in both texts. The n-gram stream ranked this highest in the chapter (rarity 3.50) and for once the ranking is right.

pericopes.text: And now my son, I have somewhat to say concerning the thing which our fathers call a ball, or director; or our fathers called it liahona, which is, being interpreted, a compass; and the Lord prepared it.
And behold, there cannot any man work after the manner of so curious a workmanship. And behold, it was prepared to shew unto our fathers the course which they should travel in the wilderness;

and it did work for them according to their faith in God; therefore if they had faith to believe that God could cause that those spindles should point the way they should go, behold, it was done; therefore they had this miracle, and also many other miracles wrought by the power of God, day by day;

nevertheless, because those miracles were worked by small means, nevertheless it did shew unto them marvellous works. They were slothful, and forgot to exercise their faith and diligence, and then those marvellous works ceased, and they did not progress in their journey;
therefore they tarried in the wilderness, or did not travel a direct course, and were afflicted with hunger and thirst, because of their transgressions.

And now my son, I would that ye should understand that these things are not without a shadow; for as our fathers were slothful to give heed to this compass, (now these things were temporal,) they did not prosper; even so it is with things which are spiritual.

For behold, it is as easy to give heed to the word of Christ, which will point to you a straight course to eternal bliss, as it was for our fathers to give heed to this compass, which would point unto them a straight course to the promised land.

And now I say, Is there not a type in this thing? For just as suredly as this director did bring our fathers, by following its course, to the promised land, shall the words of Christ, if we follow its course, carry us beyond this vale of sorrow, into a far better land of promise.

O my son, do not let us be slothful, because of the easiness of the way; for so was it with our fathers; for so was it prepared for them, that if they would look, they might live; even so it is with us. The way is prepared, and if we will look, we may live forever.
And now my son, see that ye take care of these sacred things; yea, see that ye look to God and live. Go unto this people, and declare the word, and be sober.— My son, farewell.

My son, give ear to my words: for I say unto you, even as I said unto Helaman, That inasmuch as ye shall keep the commandments of God, ye shall prosper in the land; and inasmuch as ye will not keep the commandments of God, ye shall be cast off from his presence.

And now my son, I trust that I shall have great joy in you, because of your steadiness and your faithfulness unto God; for as you have commenced in your youth, to look to the Lord your God, even so I hope that you will continue in keeping his commandments: for blessed is he that endureth to the end.
I say unto you my son, that I have had great joy in thee already, because of thy faithfulness, and thy diligence, and thy patience, and thy long suffering among the people of the Zoramites.

For I knew that thou wast in bonds; yea, and I also knew that thou wast stoned for the word’s sake; and thou didst bear all these things with patience, because the Lord was with thee: and now thou knowest that the Lord did deliver thee.

links.text: Persecutions, afflictions, which came unto me at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra; what persecutions I endured: but out of them all the Lord delivered me.

provenance.other: “the Lord delivered me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 3:11, and “out of them all” occurs in exactly two, of which this is one. The catalogue of virtues immediately before it — 2 Timothy 3:10, 'my doctrine, manner of life, purpose, faith, longsuffering, charity, patience' — is the KJV's only list that pairs longsuffering with patience as things one man has observed in another.
provenance.significance: 2 Timothy is an old apostle's last letter to a younger man he has trained, and 3:10-11 is the point where he appeals to what that young man has personally watched him endure. Alma 38:3-5 reverses the direction and keeps everything else: it is the old man telling the young one what HE has endured, and it runs the same list — patience and longsuffering (3:10), persecutions and afflictions culminating in a stoning (3:11), and deliverance out of them all. The stoning is what makes the correspondence hard to put down. 2 Timothy 3:11 names Lystra, and the one thing the reader of Acts knows about Lystra is Acts 14:19, 'having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead.' Alma 38:4's 'thou wast stoned' has no other biblical model in which stoning is survived and the survivor is afterwards addressed about it.

links.note: 'For I knew that thou wast in bonds; yea, and I also knew that thou wast stoned for the word's sake; and thou didst bear all these things with patience, because the Lord was with thee: and now thou knowest that the Lord did deliver thee.' Four elements in 2 Timothy's order — patience and longsuffering listed at 38:3, imprisonment, a stoning, and 'the Lord delivered me' — with the persons exchanged. The verbal contact is a KJV singleton in the last clause and nothing longer elsewhere, which is why this is filed as an allusion rather than a quotation; what carries it is the sequence. The n-gram stream proposed Genesis 26:28 and 1 Kings 2:15 here and could not see this, because the agreement is distributed across three Book of Mormon verses and two source verses (CONVENTIONS §9).

links.text: And have no root in themselves, and so endure but for a time: afterward, when affliction or persecution ariseth for the word’s sake, immediately they are offended.

provenance.other: “for the word's sake” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 4:17. The apostrophe is the reason to run the tool rather than grep: `kjv-rarity.py` normalizes the KJV's curly form, which a naive search misses.
provenance.significance: Mark 4:17 is the stony ground of the parable of the sower: the hearers who receive the word with gladness, have no root in themselves, and are offended when 'affliction or persecution ariseth for the word's sake'. Alma is commending a son who did the opposite — he was stoned for the word's sake and 'didst bear all these things with patience'. The suppressed correspondence is a good one: the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase names the persecution that makes shallow converts fall away, and Alma applies it to the one man in his family who did not.

links.note: 'Thou wast stoned for the word's sake.' A four-word KJV singleton, and it lands in a chapter that has just been about the Zoramites, whose defect in Alma 31-35 is precisely rootlessness under pressure. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is short and unremarkable as English; what argues for the borrowing is that it is nevertheless unique in the KJV, and that the 1830 keeps the possessive singular ('the word's sake') that Mark has, rather than the plural or the generic 'for my sake'.

pericopes.text: And now my son Shiblon, I would that ye should remember that as much as ye shall put your trust in God, even so much ye shall be delivered out of your trials, and your troubles, and your afflictions; and ye shall be lifted up at the last day.

Now my son, I would not that ye should think that I know these things of myself, but it is the spirit of God which is in me, which maketh these things known unto me: for if I had not been born of God, I should not have known these things.

But behold, the Lord in his great mercy sent his angel to declare unto me, that I must stop the work of destruction among his people; yea, and I have seen an angel face to face; and he spake with me, and his voice was as thunder, and it shook the whole earth.

And it came to pass that I was three days and three nights in the most bitter pain and anguish of soul; and never, until I did cry out unto the Lord Jesus Christ for mercy, did I receive a remission of my sins. But behold, I did cry unto him, and I did find peace to my soul.

And now my son, I have told you this, that ye may learn wisdom, that ye may learn of me that there is no other way nor means whereby man can be saved, only in and through Christ. Behold, he is the life and the light of the world. Behold, he is the word of truth and righteousness.

links.text: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.

provenance.other: “whereby we must be saved” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “none other name under heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Acts 4:12.
provenance.significance: Peter says this to the Sanhedrin, under arrest, in answer to the question 'by what power, or by what name, have ye done this?' It is a courtroom answer about the source of a healing. The Book of Mormon has made it a father's answer to a son about the source of his own knowledge — 38:6 has just insisted 'I know these things of myself' is exactly what Alma does NOT claim — so Peter's exclusive clause arrives as the content of a private testimony rather than a public defence. The first person plural of 'whereby WE must be saved' is preserved in effect by Alma's 'whereby man can be saved', which generalises rather than narrows it.

links.note: 'There is no other way nor means whereby man can be saved, only in and through Christ.' The catalogue adjudicates this formula first at 2 Nephi 25:20 and again at Mosiah 3:17; the argument for the KJV singletons is made there and is not restated. The row is given here rather than passed over because Alma is a new book and this is its first use of the formula (ADJUDICATING §4). What Alma 38:9 adds is the doubling 'no other way nor means', which imports the chapter's own vocabulary — 'means' is Alma 37:6-7's word for the small things by which God works — so the exclusivity claim and the chapter before it are stitched together at this verse.

pericopes.text: And now, as ye have begun to teach the word, even so I would that ye should continue to teach; and I would that ye would be diligent and temperate in all things.

links.text: And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.

provenance.other: “temperate in all things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 9:25. The adjective is rare in the KJV altogether: elsewhere only in the qualifications for bishops and elders at 1 Timothy 3:2 (as 'sober') and Titus 1:8, 2:2.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 9:24-27 is Paul's athletic figure: they which run in a race run all, every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things, they for a corruptible crown and we for an incorruptible, and so 'I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.' The passage is about a preacher's self-discipline as the condition of his own salvation, which is exactly what Alma 38:10-12 is: continue to teach, be temperate, do not be lifted up, bridle your passions, refrain from idleness. Two verses later Alma reaches for James 3:2's bridling, which is the New Testament's other figure for keeping the body under, so the whole counsel to Shiblon is assembled from the Bible's two passages about a teacher restraining himself.

links.note: 'And I would that ye would be diligent and temperate in all things.' A four-word KJV singleton, given as an instruction where Paul gives it as an observation about athletes, and paired with 'diligent' — which is the word Alma has used twice to Helaman (37:20) and which is not Paul's. The 1830 and 1920 agree here. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his passages.

pericopes.text: See that ye are not lifted up unto pride; yea, see that ye do not boast in your own wisdom, nor of your much strength;

links.text: Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches:

provenance.other: “glory in his wisdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the mighty man glory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Jeremiah 9:23 — but the Book of Mormon reproduces neither phrase, only the pair of nouns and the prohibition around them.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17 quote Jeremiah, but they quote 9:24 ('he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord') and drop the triad entirely, so neither can be the route for a sentence whose content is the triad's first two members.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 9:23 forbids three boasts in a fixed order — wisdom, might, riches — and Alma forbids the first two in that order and omits the third. The omission is legible: Shiblon is a missionary among the Zoramites, and riches are the sin Alma has just spent four chapters assigning to them (Alma 31:24-28, 32:2), not to his son. Compare Hays on thematic coherence: the borrowing has been trimmed to the person addressed.
provenance.mt: The Hebrew triad is the same; nothing in the judgment turns on the versions.

links.note: 'See that ye are not lifted up unto pride; yea, see that ye do not boast in your own wisdom, nor of your much strength.' A prohibition of boasting in wisdom followed immediately by a prohibition of boasting in strength is Jeremiah 9:23's structure and, so far as the KJV goes, only Jeremiah 9:23's. `mediation-check.py` against 1 Corinthians 1:31 returns no decisive divergence, because the Book of Mormon reproduces none of the words the two candidates differ over; the mediation is argued instead from the content, since Paul never carries the wisdom-and-might pair across. The phrase returns at Alma 39:2, where Alma tells the other son 'thou didst go on unto boasting in thy strength, and thy wisdom' — the same pair in reverse order, and a rebuke where 38:11 was a caution; the register cross-references it there rather than adjudicating it twice.
