variants: 1830 'had became as God' → 1920 'had become as God'

provenance.other: “put forth his hand and take also” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:22, and the sixteen-word run from 'lest he should put forth his hand' to 'live forever' departs from it in one word. “as one of us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon's 'as God' occurs there in no form; the nearest KJV phrasing is Genesis 3:5's 'ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil', which supplies the plural the Book of Mormon has made singular.
provenance.significance: The one substitution in an otherwise verbatim sentence is a theological correction, and it is made in the direction the Book of Mormon consistently goes. Genesis 3:22 has the LORD say 'the man is become as ONE OF US' — the KJV's plural of divine deliberation, a verse the whole history of Christian exegesis has had to manage. Alma writes 'the man had became as God', which removes the plurality and with it the exegetical problem. Note that he does not simply take the serpent's version either: Genesis 3:5's promise is 'ye shall be as GODS, knowing good and evil', plural again, and the Book of Mormon's singular matches neither verse. What it does match is the Book of Mormon's own settled reading of Genesis 3, made twice before — Mosiah 16:3 and Alma 12:31, both of which say 'knowing good and evil' with a singular divine referent. So the fall's outcome is reported in Genesis's exact words with Genesis's one grammatical embarrassment quietly removed.

links.note: Sixteen consecutive words of Genesis 3:22, and the departure is the interesting part: 'as one of us' becomes 'as God'. Alma had made the same argument publicly at 12:23 and 12:31 without quoting the verse this closely; here, writing to his son, he lays the whole text out. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 3:22-24 at this verse. 1830 reads 'had became', which 1920 corrected to 'had become' — the KJV's own participle, so the later edition moved toward the source, unlike the repair it made in the previous verse.

pericopes.text: and thus we see, that there was a time granted unto man, to repent, yea, a probationary time, a time to repent and serve God.

For behold, if Adam had put forth his hand immediately, and partook of the tree of life, he would have lived forever, according to the word of God, having no space for repentance; yea, and also the word of God would have been void, and the great plan of salvation would have been frustrated.

links.text: And I gave her space to repent of her fornication; and she repented not.

provenance.other: “space to repent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 2:21, and it is the KJV's only use of 'space' to mean an interval granted for repentance. The Book of Mormon nominalizes it — 'having no space for repentance' — a form that occurs in no KJV verse. Alma 12:24 has the same idea in looser words, 'a space granted unto man, in which he might repent', and was not adjudicated to this source there.
provenance.significance: In Revelation the space to repent is given to Jezebel of Thyatira and refused; here it is the whole point of the expulsion from Eden, which Alma is arguing was a mercy. The recovered context sharpens the argument he is making to a son who has sinned and not yet repented: 2:21's sentence continues 'and she repented not', and 2:22 is what follows for those who do not. Alma 42's case is that the interval exists at all — that Adam was prevented from eating precisely so that there would be a space — and the KJV's one phrase for such an interval carries with it a story about someone who was given one and wasted it. The letter's last word to Corianton, at 42:29-30, is that he should let his sins trouble him now.

links.note: 'Having no space for repentance.' The KJV grants a 'space to repent' exactly once, at Revelation 2:21, and Alma's clause is that phrase turned into a noun. Held at moderate rather than higher because only two words are shared and 'space' in the sense of an interval of time is ordinary English; but the collocation of space with repentance is not ordinary in the KJV, it occurs in one verse only, and Alma builds a doctrine on it — the probationary time of 42:4 is that space, given a name.

pericopes.text: But behold, it was appointed unto man to die; therefore as they were cut off from the tree of life, therefore they should be cut off from the face of the earth; and man became lost forever; yea, they became fallen man.
And now we see by this, that our first parents were cut off, both temporally and spiritually, from the presence of the Lord; and thus we see they became subjects to follow after their own will.
Now behold, it was not expedient that man should be reclaimed from this temporal death, for that would destroy the great plan of happiness;

therefore, as the soul could never die, and the fall had brought upon all mankind a spiritual death as well as a temporal; that is, they were cut off from the presence of the Lord; therefore it was expedient that mankind should be reclaimed from this spiritual death;
therefore as they had become carnal, sensual and devilish, by nature, this probationary state became a state for them to prepare: it became a preparatory state.

links.text: This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.

provenance.other: “sensual, devilish” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 3:15, which is also the KJV's only occurrence of 'sensual' in this list-form (Jude 1:19 has 'sensual, having not the Spirit'). Mosiah 16:3, the Book of Mormon's earlier use, reads 'carnal and devlish' in 1830 without 'sensual'; Alma 42:10 is the first place in the book where the full triad appears.
provenance.significance: James's three adjectives describe a WISDOM — 'this wisdom descendeth not from above' — and they are a judgment on a way of knowing, made in a passage about bitter envying and strife among teachers. Alma applies them to a nature rather than a wisdom, and swaps the first: 'earthly' becomes 'carnal'. The substitution is doing theological work, because 'earthly' locates the fault in a place and 'carnal' locates it in the flesh, which is what a doctrine of the Fall needs. The argument for the borrowing, as against the Book of Mormon simply having a stock phrase, is that Mosiah 16:3 has the pair without the middle term and this verse has all three in James's order; the formula is filling out toward its source rather than wearing down away from it.

links.note: 'As they had become carnal, sensual and devilish, by nature.' The last two words are a KJV singleton pair belonging to James 3:15, in James's order, with 'earthly' exchanged for 'carnal'. The link was made across the book boundary at Mosiah 16:3, but the 1830 text there reads only 'carnal and devlish' — this is the first appearance of the complete triad, and 'sensual' is the word that makes James unavoidable, since it appears nowhere else in the Book of Mormon's fall vocabulary and only twice in the KJV.

pericopes.text: And now remember, my son, if it were not for the plan of redemption, (laying it aside,) as soon as they were dead, their souls were miserable, being cut off from the presence of the Lord.
And now there was no means to reclaim men from this fallen state which man had brought upon himself, because of his own disobedience;

therefore, according to justice, the plan of redemption could not be brought about, only, on conditions of repentance of men in this probationary state; yea, this preparatory state; for except it were for these conditions, mercy could not take effect except it should destroy the work of justice. Now the work of justice could not be destroyed: if so, God would cease to be God.
And thus we see that all mankind were fallen, and they were in the grasp of justice; yea, the justice of God, which consigned them forever to be cut off from his presence.

And now the plan of mercy could not be brought about, except an atonement should be made; therefore God himself atoneth for the sins of the world, to bring about the plan of mercy, to appease the demands of justice, that God might be a perfect, just God, and a merciful God. Also,

links.text: Tell ye, and bring them near; yea, let them take counsel together: who hath declared this from ancient time? who hath told it from that time? have not I the LORD? and there is no God else beside me; a just God and a Saviour; there is none beside me.

provenance.other: “just God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 45:21, and so does the construction “a just God and a —”. The KJV has 'a just man' and 'the just God of Israel' nowhere in this form; the pairing of justice with a second divine title in one breath is unique to this verse.
provenance.significance: This is the metalepsis the chapter is built to need. Isaiah 45:21 completes the phrase one way — 'a just God AND A SAVIOUR' — and Alma 42:15 completes it the other: 'that God might be a perfect, just God, and a merciful God'. Everything between 42:13 and 42:25 is an argument that those two completions are the same completion, that the God who cannot let justice be destroyed is the God who saves, and that the atonement is what makes the conjunction possible rather than a contradiction. The KJV's one verse holding the two words together is the verse Alma's whole argument is a commentary on, and the next line of Isaiah is 'Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth'. Held at moderate because the shared run is four words and could be reached without Isaiah; but four words that occur in one KJV verse, in a sentence whose subject is precisely the compatibility of those words, is not nothing.

links.note: 'That God might be a perfect, just God, and a merciful God.' The KJV says 'a just God and a' exactly once, at Isaiah 45:21, where the second term is 'Saviour'. Alma substitutes 'merciful' and spends the surrounding fifteen verses arguing that the substitution is not one — that mercy and justice meet in the atonement, so that the God who is just is thereby the one who saves. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is short and 'just God' is a natural English collocation; what argues for the link is that it is not a natural KJV one.

pericopes.text: now repentance could not come unto men, except there were a punishment, which also was as eternal as the life of the soul should be, affixed opposite to the plan of happiness, which was as eternal also as the life of the soul.—
Now, how could a man repent, except he should sin? How could he sin, if there was no law? How could there be a law, save there was a punishment?
Now there was a punishment affixed, and a just law given, which brought remorse of conscience unto man.
Now if there was no law given, if a man murdered he should die, would he be afraid he should die if he should murder?
And also, if there was no law given against sin, men would not be afraid to sin.
And if there was no law given if men sinned, what could justice do, or mercy either, for they would have no claim upon the creature?

But there is a law given, and a punishment affixed, and repentance granted; which repentance, mercy claimeth; otherwise, justice claimeth the creature, and executeth the law, and the law inflicteth the punishment; if not so, the works of justice would be destroyed, and God would cease to be God.

But God ceaseth not to be God, and mercy claimeth the penitent, and mercy cometh because of the atonement; and the atonement bringeth to pass the resurrection of the dead; and the resurrection of the dead bringeth back men into the presence of God; and thus they are restored into his presence, to be judged according to their works; according to the law and justice;
for behold, justice exerciseth all his demands, and also mercy claimeth all which is her own; and thus, none but the truly penitent are saved.
What, do ye suppose that mercy can rob justice? I say unto you, Nay; not one whit. If so, God would cease to be God.

And thus God bringeth about his great and eternal purposes, which was prepared from the foundation of the world. And thus cometh about the salvation and the redemption of men, and also their destruction and misery;

therefore, O my son, whosoever will come, may come, and partake of the waters of life freely; and whosoever will not come, the same is not compelled to come; but in the last day, it shall be restored unto him, according to his deeds.

links.text: And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.

provenance.other: “water of life freely” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 21:6 and 22:17, and only 22:17 has 'whosoever will' attached to it. The Book of Mormon reads 'waters' plural, which is in neither.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:34 already had 'the waters of life freely', and this catalogue adjudicated it there; but 5:34 has only the phrase, and 42:27 has the sentence. Revelation 22:17's structure is an invitation repeated three times and then made universal — Come, Come, let him that is athirst come, and whosoever will, let him take — and Alma reproduces both halves of that structure and then adds the half Revelation leaves unspoken: 'and whosoever will not come, the same is not compelled to come.' That negative clause is the reason the verse is here rather than in the register as a recurrence of 5:34. The whole chapter has been arguing that the sinner is not the victim of a sentence but the author of one, and the last thing it does with the Bible's most open invitation is to spell out its converse, which the Bible does not. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the meaning is in what the borrowing declines to leave suppressed.

links.note: 'Whosoever will come, may come, and partake of the waters of life freely; and whosoever will not come, the same is not compelled to come.' Revelation 22:17 is the only KJV verse that joins 'whosoever will' to the water of life freely given, and Alma 5:34 — where this catalogue placed the link for the phrase alone — has neither the 'whosoever' nor the repeated 'come'. This is the verse where the source's sentence is reproduced, so it gets a row rather than a register entry, and what it adds is the express negative: the invitation is unconditional and so is the freedom to refuse it.

links.text: Who will render to every man according to his deeds:

provenance.other: “according to his deeds” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 2:6. The KJV's other renderings of the same principle read 'according to their works' (Revelation 20:12-13, adjudicated in this book at Alma 3:26, 11:41 and 40:21) or 'according to his ways' (Jeremiah 17:10, Ezekiel 33:20); 'deeds' in this construction is Paul's alone.
provenance.significance: Alma has used the 'according to their works' formula throughout — three chapters earlier at 40:21, and again five verses before this one at 42:23 — and here, at the closing of the argument, he changes the noun. Romans 2 is the chapter where the change matters: 2:5 has the impenitent heart 'treasuring up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath', and 2:6 is the verse that follows it. That is the sentence Alma 42:28 goes on to write in his own words — 'if he hath desired to do evil, and hath not repented in his days, behold, evil shall be done unto him' — and the point of Romans 2 is that the judgment is not an imposition but the sinner's own store, opened. Which is Alma 41-42's entire doctrine of restoration.

links.note: 'In the last day, it shall be restored unto him, according to his deeds.' A KJV singleton, and a deliberate-looking departure from the 'according to their works' formula this letter has used twice already. Held at moderate because four words is a short run and the shift from 'works' to 'deeds' could be stylistic; what argues for Romans is that the verse immediately before it, on wrath treasured up by an impenitent heart, is what Alma 42:28 says next.

pericopes.text: If he hath desired to do evil, and hath not repented in his days, behold, evil shall be done unto him, according to the restoration of God.
And now my son, I desire that ye should let these things trouble you no more, and only let your sins trouble you, with that trouble which shall bring you down unto repentance.

O my son, I desire that ye should deny the justice of God no more. Do not endeavor to excuse yourself in the least point, because of your sins, by denying the justice of God, but do you let the justice of God, and his mercy, and his long suffering, have full sway in your heart; but let it bring you down to the dust, in humility.

And now, O my son, ye are called of God to preach the word unto this people. And now, my son, go thy way, declare the word with truth and soberness, that thou mayest bring souls unto repentance, that the great plan of mercy may have claim upon them.— And may God grant unto you even according to my words.— Amen.

links.text: But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.

provenance.other: “truth and soberness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:25. Every Book of Mormon occurrence — Jacob 6:5, Mosiah 4:15, Alma 42:31 and 53:21 — reproduces the pair exactly, and Alma 42:31 keeps Paul's verb of utterance as well: 'declare the word with truth and soberness' against 'speak forth the words of truth and soberness'.
provenance.significance: Paul says it to Festus, who has just shouted that Paul is mad — 'much learning doth make thee mad' — and it is a defence of the sanity of preaching resurrection to a hostile court. Alma is commissioning a son to go and preach after a letter that has spent three chapters on the resurrection and the justice of God, and the two words he chooses are the two Paul used when the doctrine was called insane. The recovered context supplies the anxiety the commission does not state: Corianton has already failed once at this work (Alma 39:3), and the charge is not merely to preach but to be credible. 'Soberness' is the KJV's word for that, and it exists there in one verse.

links.note: 'Go thy way, declare the word with truth and soberness.' A KJV singleton, and this is its fourth appearance in the Book of Mormon; the argument for the pair as a borrowing was made at Mosiah 4:15 and it is a different narrator's voice here, so ADJUDICATING §4's across-a-book rule gives the row rather than a register entry. What Alma 42:31 adds is the verb: Paul 'speaks forth the words of truth and soberness' and Alma tells his son to 'declare the word with truth and soberness', which is nearer to Acts than the Jacob and Mosiah occurrences, both of which use the pair as a quality of persons or of a path rather than of speech.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass, that the sons of Alma did go forth among the people, to declare the word unto them. And Alma also, himself, could not rest, and he also went forth.—

Now we shall say no more concerning their preaching, except that they preached the word, and the truth, according to the spirit of prophecy and revelation; and they preached after the holy order of God, by which they were called.
And now I return to an account of the wars between the Nephites and the Lamanites, in the eighteenth year of the reign of the Judges.

For behold, it came to pass that the Zoramites became Lamanites; therefore, in the commencement of the eighteenth year, the people of the Nephites saw that the Lamanites were coming upon them; therefore they made preparations for war; yea, they gathered together their armies in the land of Jershon.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites came with their thousands; and they came into the land of Antionam, which was the land of the Zoramites; and a man by the name of Zerahemnah was their leader.

And now as the Amalekites were of a more wicked and a murderous disposition than the Lamanites were, in and of themselves, therefore Zerahemnah appointed Chief Captains over the Lamanites, and they were all the Amalekites and the Zoramites.
Now this he done, that he might preserve their hatred towards the Nephites; that he might bring them into subjection, to the accomplishment of his designs;

for hehold behold, his designs were to stir up the Lamanites to anger against the Nephites; this he done that he might usurp great power over them; and also that he might gain power over the Nephites, by bringing them into bondage, &c.

And now the design of the Nephites were to support their lands, and their houses, and their wives, and their children, that they might preserve them from the hands of their enemies, and also, that they might preserve their rights and their privileges; yea, and also their liberty, that they might worship God according to their desires;
for they knew that if they should fall into the hands of the Lamanites, that whosoever should worship God, in spirit and in truth, the true and the living God, the Lamanites would destroy;

yea, and they also knew the extreme hatred of the Lamanites towards their brethren, which were the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi; which were called the people of Ammon; and they would not take up arms; yea, they had entered into a covenant, and they would not break it; therefore, if they should fall into the hands of the Lamanites, they would be destroyed.
And the Nephites would not suffer that they should be destroyed; therefore they gave them lands for their inheritance.

And the people of Ammon did give unto the Nephites a large portion of their substance, to support their armies; and thus the Nephites were compelled, alone, to withstand against the Lamanites, which were a compound of Laman and Lemuel, and the sons of Ishmael, and all those which had dissented from the Nephites, which were Amalekites, and Zoramites, and the descendants of the priests of Noah.
Now those descendants were as numerous, nearly, as were the Nephites; and thus the Nephites were obliged to contend with their brethren, even unto bloodshed.
And it came to pass, as the armies of the Lamanites had gathered together in the land of Antionum, behold, the armies of the Nephites were prepared to meet them in the land of Jershon.

Now the leader of the Nephites, or the man which had been appointed to be the Chief Captain over the Nephites: Now the Chief Captain took the command of all the armies of the Nephites; and his name was Moroni;
and Moroni took all the command, and the governments of their wars.— And he was only twenty and five years old when he was appointed Chief Commander over the armies of the Nephites.

links.text: He was twenty and five years old when he began to reign, and reigned twenty and nine years in Jerusalem. And his mother’s name was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem.

provenance.route: the KJV regnal accession formula (2 Kings 14:2 and parallels) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Twenty and five years old' occurs in exactly seven KJV verses. One is the Levite service age (Numbers 8:24); the other six are the accession notices of four kings of Judah — Amaziah (2 Kings 14:2, 2 Chronicles 25:1), Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:2), Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:36, 2 Chronicles 36:5) and Jotham (2 Chronicles 27:1). The longer shape 'X years old when he began to reign' runs to thirty-five verses and is the KJV's standard coronation formula. Modern versions read 'twenty-five'; the compound numeral is the KJV's idiom.
provenance.alternative: The number may simply be the number, and the sentence a chronicler's ordinary way of giving an age.
provenance.significance: The one biblical sentence-shape the KJV reserves for a man's age at accession is here spent on a man's age at *appointment* — 'he was only twenty and five years old when he was appointed Chief Commander' — in a polity that abolished kingship forty years earlier (Mosiah 29) and in a chapter that will insist, at 43:45, that these men 'were not fighting for monarchy nor power'. If the formula is heard, Moroni is introduced in the cadence of a Judahite coronation and then explicitly denied the thing the cadence announces. The 1830's 'Chief Commander' was changed to 'chief captain' in 1920, which flattens the singularity of the office the sentence is conferring.

links.note: 'He was only twenty and five years old when he was appointed Chief Commander over the armies of the Nephites.' No clause is reproduced, but the syntax is the KJV's accession notice — age, then the verb of taking office, then the extent of the rule — and twenty-and-five is specifically the accession age of four kings of Judah and of nobody else in the Bible outside the Levite service law. The 'only' is the tell: it is an authorial gloss on a formula the sentence expects the reader to recognise, and the thing it apologises for is youth at a throne.
links.whyNot: Regnal formulae are the commonest narrative furniture in Kings and Chronicles, and any writer imitating biblical English would produce this shape without meaning anything by it. Twenty-five is also a plausible age to invent for a young commander on its own.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he met the Lamanites in the borders of Jershon, and his people were armed with swords, and with cimeters, and all manner of weapons of war.

And it came to pass, that when the armies of the Lamanites saw that the people of Nephi, or that Moroni had prepared his people with breast-plates, and with arm-shields; yea, and also shields to defend their heads; and also they were dressed with thick clothing.

Now the army of Zerahemnah was not prepared with any such thing. They had only their swords, and their cimeters, their bows and their arrows, their stones and their slings; but they were naked, save it were a skin which was girded about their loins; yea, all were naked, save it were the Zoramites and the Amalekites.

links.text: And Uzziah prepared for them throughout all the host shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones.

provenance.other: 2 Chronicles 26:14 is the KJV's only armoury inventory. 'Slings to cast stones' occurs in exactly one verse; so does 'bows and slings'; so does 'helmets and habergeons'. 'Shields and spears' occurs in two, both in Chronicles (11:12 and 26:14). Nothing else in the Bible lists defensive and missile equipment together in one breath — Goliath's arming in 1 Samuel 17:5-7 describes one man, and Ephesians 6:13-17 is allegory.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon takes the KJV's single equipment list and splits it between the two armies. Moroni's people get the protective half — 'breast-plates, and with arm-shields; yea, and also shields to defend their heads' (43:19), the last being a periphrasis for the helmets the list names — and Zerahemnah's get the missile half, 'their bows and their arrows, their stones and their slings.' Recover the source and the division is not neutral: 2 Chronicles 26:14 is what Uzziah prepared 'throughout all the host', and the next verse says he was 'marvellously helped, till he was strong. But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction.' The KJV's one story of a king who out-equipped his enemies is a story about what winning by equipment does to the winner, and Alma 43 hands that equipment to the Nephites twenty-five verses before it starts explaining why their cause is better than their armour.

links.note: 'They had only their swords, and their cimeters, their bows and their arrows, their stones and their slings.' Three of the four distinctive strings in 2 Chronicles 26:14 are KJV singletons, and Alma 43:18-21 reproduces the whole inventory across four verses, distributed between the two armies rather than assigned to one. The order survives the distribution: shields and body armour first (43:19), then bows, then stones-and-slings (43:20), which is 2 Chronicles 26:14's order exactly. The link is filed here because 43:20 carries the rarest element, the slings and the stones together; 43:18-19 and 43:21 are the same borrowing continued.

pericopes.text: But they were not armed with breast-plates, nor shields; therefore they were exceeding afraid of the armies of the Nephites, because of their armour, notwithstanding their number being so much greater than the Nephites.

Behold, now it came to pass, that they durst not come against the Nephites in the borders of Jershon; therefore they departed out of the land of Antionum, into the wilderness, and took their journey round about in the wilderness, away by the head of the river Sidon, that they might come into the land of Manti, and take possession of the land; for they did not suppose that the armies of Moroni would know whither they had gone.

But it came to pass, as soon as they had departed into the wilderness, Moroni sent spies into the wilderness, to watch their camp; and Moroni, also, knowing of the prophecies of Alma, sent certain men unto him, desiring him that he should inquire of the Lord whither the armies of the Nephites should go, to defend themselves against the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that the word of the Lord came unto Alma; and Alma informed the messengers of Moroni that the armies of the Lamanites were marching round about in the wilderness, that they might come over into the land of Manti, that they might commence an attack upon the more weak part of the people. And those messengers went and delivered the message unto Moroni.

Now Moroni, leaving a part of his army in the land of Jershon, lest by any means, a part of the Lamanites should come into that land and take possession of the city; and Moroni took the remainder part of his army and marched over into the land of Manti.

And he caused that all the people in that quarter of the land, should gather themselves together to battle, against the Lamanites, to defend their lands and their country, their rights and their liberties; therefore they were prepared against the time of the coming of the Lamanites.
And it came to pass, that Moroni caused that his army should be secreted in the valley which was near the bank of the river Sidon, which was on the west of the river Sidon, in the wilderness.
And Moroni placed spies round about, that he might know when the camp of the Lamanites should come.

And now as Moroni knew the intention of the Lamanites, that it was their intention to destroy their brethren, or to subject them and bring them into bondage, that they might establish a kingdom unto themselves, over all the land;

and he also knowing that it was the only desire of the Nephites to preserve their lands and their liberty, and their church, therefore he thought it no sin that he should defend them by stratagem; therefore he found, by his spies, which course the Lamanites were to take.

links.text: And thou shalt do to Ai and her king as thou didst unto Jericho and her king: only the spoil thereof, and the cattle thereof, shall ye take for a prey unto yourselves: lay thee an ambush for the city behind it.

provenance.other: There is almost no shared wording, and what there is is generic — 'on the west of the' is shared with Joshua 8:13 and is a compass direction. The Book of Mormon does not use 'ambush', 'ambushment' or 'liers in wait' anywhere in this chapter; it says 'secreted', 'concealed' and 'stratagem'. The case is structural.
provenance.alternative: Judges 20:29-38 (the liers in wait at Gibeah) and 2 Samuel 5:23 ('fetch a compass behind them') are the KJV's other ambush narratives and could stand behind the same scene.
provenance.significance: The theological problem the verse raises — is a concealed attack lawful? — has one biblical answer, and Joshua 8 is it: the LORD himself gives the order, 'lay thee an ambush for the city behind it.' Mormon writes 'he thought it no sin that he should defend them by stratagem' as though the thought needed defending, and the defence is available in the one place in scripture where the ambush is divinely commanded. The staging then follows Joshua 8 step for step: the army divided (8:3-4 / 43:31-32), one part concealed and one part visible, the enemy drawn past the concealed part (8:14-15 / 43:34-35), and the enemy taken 'in the midst' with Israel on both sides (8:22 / 43:52, 'the armies of Moroni encircled them about; yea, even on both sides'). Even the compass points are worked: at Ai the host is on the north of the city and the liers in wait on the west; at Riplah the Lamanites come up on the north of the hill and the remainder of Moroni's army is concealed in the west valley.

links.note: 'He thought it no sin that he should defend them by stratagem.' Filed as figural because there is no wording to test, and filed at 43:30 rather than at the ambush itself because 43:30 is where the argument is: Mormon pauses the narrative to license a tactic, and Joshua 8 is the licence. The whole of 43:27-52 then runs the Ai sequence — divide, conceal, let the enemy pass, close from behind, surround — with the river Sidon doing the work Ai's gate does. The strongest evidence is the sequence score; the vocabulary score is honestly low and the row should be read as a proposal in the sense of CONVENTIONS §0a.
links.whyNot: Ambush is a universal military manoeuvre and needs no literary source, and the chapter's own terms ('secreted', 'stratagem') are the ones Joshua 8 does not use. A reader who wants shared words will not find them here.

pericopes.text: Therefore he divided his army, and brought a part over into the valley, and concealed them on the east, and on the south of the hill Riplah;
and the remainder he concealed in the west valley, on the west of the river Sidon, and so down into the borders of the land Manti.
And thus having placed his army according to his desire, he was prepared to meet them.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites came up on the north of the hill where a part of the army of Moroni was concealed.

And it came to pass that as the Lamanites had passed the hill Riplah, and came into the valley, and began to cross the river Sidon, the army which was concealed on the south of the hill, who was led by a man whose name was Lehi; and he led his army forth and encircled the Lamanites about, on the east, in their rear.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites, when they saw the Nephites coming upon them in their rear, turned them about, and began to contend with the army of Lehi;

and the work of death commenced, on both sides; but it was more dreadful on the part of the Lamanites; for their nakedness was exposed to the heavy blows of the Nephites, with their swords and their cimeters, which brought death almost at every stroke;

while on the other hand, there was now and then a man fell among the Nephites, by their swords, and the loss of blood; they being shielded from the more vital parts of the body, or the more vital parts of the body being shielded from the strokes of the Lamanites, by their breast-plates, and their arm-shields, and their head-plates; and thus the Nephites did carry on the work of death among the Lamanites.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites became frightened, because of the great destruction among them, even until they began to flee towards the river Sidon.

And they were pursued by Lehi and his men, and they were driven by Lehi into the waters of Sidon; and they crossed the waters of Sidon. And Lehi retained his armies upon the bank of the river Sidon, that they should not cross.

And it came to pass that Moroni and his army met the Lamanites in the valley, on the other side of the river Sidon.— And it came to pass that Moroni and his army began to fall upon them, and to slay them.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites did flee again before them, towards the land of Manti; and they were met again by the armies of Moroni.—
Now in this case, the Lamanites did fight exceedingly; yea, never had the Lamanites been known to have fought with such exceeding great strength and courage; no, not even from the beginning;

and they were inspired by the Zoramites, and the Amalekites, which were their Chief Captains and leaders, and by Zerahemnah, who was their Chief Captain, or their chief leader and commander; yea, they did fight like dragons; and many of the Nephites were slain by their hands; yea, for they did smite in two many of their head-plates; and they did pierce many of their breast-plates; and they did smite off many of their arms; and thus the Lamanites did smite in their fierce anger.

Nevertheless, the Nephites were inspired by a better cause; for they were not fighting for monarchy nor power; but they were fighting for their homes, and their liberties, their wives, and their children, and their all; yea, for their rites of worship, and their church;

links.text: And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the LORD, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.

provenance.other: 'Fight for your brethren' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and 'your wives and your houses' in the same one. The third-person string the Book of Mormon actually has, 'their wives, and their children', is itself a KJV singleton at 2 Chronicles 20:13 — so the wording is closest to Chronicles and the rhetorical act is Nehemiah's. Both are recorded here.
provenance.alternative: 2 Chronicles 20:13, whose 'their wives, and their children' is the exact string, though it describes people standing before the LORD rather than fighting for anybody.
provenance.significance: Nehemiah 4:14 is the Bible's one sentence in which a leader names the things his people are fighting for, in a list, to men who are about to give way. Everything around it fits Alma 43 better than the string-match does: Nehemiah's people build with a weapon in the other hand (4:17), they are outnumbered, and they are defending a place rather than taking one. Alma 43 supplies its list three times — 'their lands, and their houses, and their wives, and their children' (43:9), 'their lands and their country, their rights and their liberties' (43:26), 'their homes, and their liberties, their wives, and their children, and their all' (43:45) — and then, at 43:48, gives Moroni Nehemiah's own moment: the men 'were about to shrink and flee from them', and the commander speaks to their hearts and turns them. What the Book of Mormon adds to the list is the two items Nehemiah has no word for, 'their liberties' and 'their rites of worship'.

links.note: 'They were fighting for their homes, and their liberties, their wives, and their children, and their all; yea, for their rites of worship, and their church.' The list is the argument, and the KJV has one list like it. Two of Nehemiah 4:14's phrases are singletons and both of them are list-items of the same kind the verse is enumerating; the Book of Mormon's version keeps the shape, converts the pronouns to third person (where 2 Chronicles 20:13 supplies the exact string), and extends the list past what a fifth-century wall-builder could have said into liberty and worship. Filed at 43:45 because that is where the list is fullest and where it is explicitly a *reason for fighting*; 43:9, 43:26 and 43:47 are the same borrowing at lower resolution.

pericopes.text: and they were doing that which they felt it was the duty which they owed to their God; for the Lord had said unto them, and also unto their fathers, That inasmuch as ye are not guilty of the first offence, neither the second, ye shall not suffer yourselves to be slain by the hands of your enemies.

And again: The Lord hath said That ye shall defend your families, even unto bloodshed; therefore, for this cause were the Nephites contending with the Lamanites, to defend themselves, and their families, and their lands, their country, and their rights, and their religion.

And it came to pass that when the men of Moroni saw the fierceness and the anger of the Lamanites, they were about to shrink and flee from them. And Moroni, perceiving their intent, sent forth and inspired their hearts with these thoughts; yea, the thoughts of their lands, their liberty, yea, their freedom from bondage.
And it came to pass that they turned upon the Lamanites, and they cried with one voice unto the Lord their God, for their liberty, and their freedom from bondage.

links.text: And Moses came and told the people all the words of the LORD, and all the judgments: and all the people answered with one voice, and said, All the words which the LORD hath said will we do.

provenance.other: 'With one voice' occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Exodus 24:3, where Israel ratifies the covenant, and Acts 19:34, where the Ephesian mob shouts for Diana for two hours. 'Answered with one voice' is a singleton at Exodus 24:3. The phrase enters the Book of Mormon at Mosiah 4:2, where it is adjudicated against the same verse; this is its first use in Alma.
provenance.alternative: Acts 19:34 — a crowd crying out in one voice, which is closer to what an army does than to what a congregation does.
provenance.significance: The covenant reading is available here in a way it is not everywhere the phrase recurs, because Mormon has just, three verses earlier, quoted the terms: 'the Lord had said unto them, and also unto their fathers, That inasmuch as ye are not guilty of the first offence, neither the second, ye shall not suffer yourselves to be slain' (43:46), and 'The Lord hath said That ye shall defend your families' (43:47). That is the structure of Exodus 24:3 — the words of the LORD recited, then the people answering with one voice — with the answer converted from assent into a battle-cry. What Israel says at Sinai is 'all the words which the LORD hath said will we do'; what Moroni's army says is nothing, it simply cries 'for their liberty, and their freedom from bondage', and the doing is the fighting.

links.note: 'They cried with one voice unto the Lord their God, for their liberty, and their freedom from bondage.' The phrase is adjudicated at Mosiah 4:2 and the argument for Exodus 24:3 over Acts 19:34 is made there; it is given again here because this is its first appearance in Alma and because the immediate setting supplies something Mosiah's did not — a recitation of the LORD's words at 43:46-47 immediately before the one-voiced answer, which is Exodus 24:3's own sequence and not merely its phrase.

pericopes.text: And they began to stand against the Lamanites with power; and in that self-same hour that they cried unto the Lord for their freedom, the Lamanites began to flee before them; and they fled even to the waters of Sidon.

links.text: And Jesus said unto the centurion, Go thy way; and as thou hast believed, so be it done unto thee. And his servant was healed in the selfsame hour.

provenance.other: 'Selfsame hour' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Selfsame' itself occurs in fifteen, and every other one of them is 'selfsame day' — the circumcision of Abraham, the exodus, the feast days, the day Moses is told to climb Nebo. The hour is Matthew 8:13's alone. The phrase occurs once in the whole Book of Mormon, here; the 1830 hyphenates it, 'self-same hour', and 1920 closed it up to the KJV's spelling.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the KJV's one 'selfsame hour' is the hour in which a centurion's servant is healed at a distance, without the healer going to the house, because the centurion has argued from military command to divine command — 'I say to this man, Go, and he goeth' — and been told that no such faith has been found in Israel. Alma 43:50 is the answer to that verse from the other side of the transaction: here it is the soldiers, not the officer, who ask; the effect is again instantaneous and again at a distance from the one who grants it; and what turns in the selfsame hour is a battle. The Book of Mormon's one use of the New Testament's timestamp for faith answered without delay is spent on an army that cries out and is not touched, only relieved.

links.note: 'In that self-same hour that they cried unto the Lord for their freedom, the Lamanites began to flee before them.' A two-word borrowing from a KJV singleton, used once in the Book of Mormon, and used to do exactly what it does in Matthew — mark the coincidence of a petition and its effect, with nothing in between. The clause is also the chapter's theological hinge: 43:44-48 has just conceded that the Lamanites fought better and that the Nephites were about to break, so the reversal cannot be attributed to arms, and the phrase that attributes it instead is the Gospel's phrase for a cure granted on a soldier's word.

pericopes.text: Now the Lamanites were more numerous; yea, by more than double the number of the Nephites; nevertheless, they were driven insomuch that they were gathered together in one body, in the valley, upon the bank, by the river Sidon;
therefore the armies of Moroni encircled them about; yea, even on both sides of the river; for behold, on the east, were the men of Lehi;

therefore when Zerahemnah saw the men of Lehi on the east of the river Sidon, and the armies of Moroni on the west of the river Sidon, that they were encircled about by the Nephites, they were struck with terror.
Now Moroni, when he saw their terror, he commanded his men that they should stop shedding their blood.

And it came to pass that they did stop, and withdrew a pace from them. And Moroni said unto Zerahemnah, Behold, Zerahemnah, that we do not desire to be men of blood. Ye know that ye are in our hands, yet we do not desire to slay you.

links.text: Behold, this day thine eyes have seen how that the LORD had delivered thee to day into mine hand in the cave: and some bade me kill thee: but mine eye spared thee; and I said, I will not put forth mine hand against my lord; for he is the LORD’s anointed.

provenance.other: 'Delivered thee to day into mine hand' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The speech-closing formula the chapter uses eight verses later — 'when Zerahemnah had made an end of speaking these words' (44:10) — reproduces 1 Samuel 24:16 ('when David had made an end of speaking these words unto Saul'), which is also a KJV singleton and is adjudicated in this catalogue at Jacob 3:14 and again at Alma 12:19. Two singletons from the same short chapter, sixteen verses apart in the source and nine apart here.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 24 is the Bible's set piece on holding an enemy's life and declining to take it: David has Saul in the cave, his men quote him an oracle telling him to strike, he cuts a token instead, and then argues the case aloud to the man he spared. Alma 44:1-11 is that scene with the arithmetic reversed — the spared party here is the aggressor, not the anointed king, and the argument does not work. Moroni makes David's speech ('ye are in our hands, yet we do not desire to slay you'), receives Zerahemnah's refusal rather than Saul's tears, and has to make the offer twice. The chapter closes the frame in the negative: where 1 Samuel 24 ends with an enemy weeping and swearing, Alma 44 ends with an enemy 'exceeding wroth' and a slaughter resumed.

links.note: 'Ye know that ye are in our hands, yet we do not desire to slay you.' No clause is reproduced at 44:1 itself, but the situation is 1 Samuel 24's exactly — enemy in hand, killing declined, the declining then made into a speech — and the chapter carries two of that chapter's KJV singletons, 24:10's 'delivered … into mine hand' construction and 24:16's speech-closing formula at 44:10. The interest of the row is what the Book of Mormon does with the scene rather than that it uses it: David's mercy converts Saul, Moroni's does not convert Zerahemnah, and 44:17-18 is what the source has no room for.

pericopes.text: Behold, we have not come out to battle against you, that we might shed your blood, for power; neither do we desire to bring any one to the yoke of bondage. But this is the very cause for which ye have come against us; yea, and ye are angry with us because of our religion.

links.text: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.

provenance.other: 'Yoke of bondage' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon uses it five times; the first is Mosiah 21:13, where it is adjudicated, and Mosiah 23:13 takes the other half of the same verse ('stand fast in this liberty wherewith ye have been made free'). This is its first appearance in Alma.
provenance.significance: The row is worth writing again in a new book because Alma 43-44 is the one place in the Book of Mormon that puts both halves of Galatians 5:1 into a single argument and makes them the terms of a war. The liberty half runs through 43:26, 43:45, 43:48-50 ('their liberty, yea, their freedom from bondage') and returns at 44:5 as 'that liberty which binds us to our lands and our country'; the yoke half is 44:2, where Moroni denies wanting to impose it and immediately charges the Lamanites with wanting exactly that. Paul's antithesis is between the freedom of the gospel and the law's servitude — a purely religious opposition with no political content whatever — and Alma 44 spends it on a treaty negotiation, then hands it back to religion in the same breath: 'ye are angry with us because of our religion.' The 1830's 'liberty' has not been touched by any later edition, so the Pauline pair stands in every printing.

links.note: 'Neither do we desire to bring any one to the yoke of bondage. But this is the very cause for which ye have come against us.' A KJV singleton reproduced entire. Recorded across the book boundary under ADJUDICATING §4 rather than restating the argument made at Mosiah 21:13; what is new here is that the verse's other half is running simultaneously through the surrounding chapter, so that Moroni's terms of peace are Galatians 5:1 taken apart and used as a political vocabulary.

pericopes.text: But now ye behold that the Lord is with us; and ye behold that he hath delivered you into our hands. And now I would that ye should understand that this is done unto us because of our religion and our faith in Christ. And now ye see that ye cannot destroy this our faith.

links.text: And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD’s, and he will give you into our hands.

provenance.other: 'Into our hands' occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Deuteronomy 3:3, Joshua 2:24, Judges 16:24, 1 Samuel 17:47); only 1 Samuel 17:47 is spoken to the enemy's face before the fighting. 'The battle is the Lord's' is a KJV singleton in the same verse. Two verses earlier, 'in the name of the LORD of hosts' (17:45) occurs in two KJV verses, and Alma 44:5 opens 'I command you, in the name of that all-powerful God'.
provenance.significance: David's speech to Goliath is the Bible's only pre-combat address delivered by the victor to the loser on the field, and it has three moves: I come in the name of God, God has delivered you, and the point of it is that the assembly may know the Lord saves without weapons. Alma 44:2-7 makes all three, in order, at greater length — 44:3 'the Lord is with us … he hath delivered you into our hands', 44:5 'I command you, in the name of that all-powerful God', 44:4 'ye see that this is the true faith of God'. What the Book of Mormon adds is a reply. Goliath is given no answer in 1 Samuel; Zerahemnah is given 44:9, and he answers the one clause David rests on, that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear.

links.note: 'Ye behold that the Lord is with us; and ye behold that he hath delivered you into our hands.' The chapter's frame is the champion-speech of 1 Samuel 17:45-47 — the KJV's single instance of a warrior telling a defeated enemy, in advance, why he lost — and the two rarest strings in that speech, 'into our hands' and 'in the name of the LORD of hosts', both surface in Moroni's version within three verses. Adjudicated here because 44:3 carries the verbal contact; 44:5, 44:7 and 44:11 continue it, and 44:9 answers it.

pericopes.text: Now ye see that this is the true faith of God; yea, ye see that God will support, and keep, and preserve us, so long as we are faithful unto him, and unto our faith, and our religion; and never will the Lord suffer that we shall be destroyed, except we should fall into transgression, and deny our faith.

And now, Zerahemnah, I command you, in the name of that all-powerful God, who hath strengthened our arms, that we have gained power over you by our faith, by our religion, and by our rites of worship, and by our church, and by the sacred support which we owe to our wives and our children, by that liberty which binds us to our lands and our country; yea, and also by the maintenance of the sacred word of God, to which we owe all our happiness; and by all that is most dear unto us;

yea, and this is not all; I command you by all the desires which ye have for life, that ye deliver up your weapons of war unto us, and we will seek not your blood, but we will spare your lives, if ye will go your way, and come not again to war against us.—

And now if ye do not this, behold, ye are in our hands, and I will command my men that they shall fall upon you, and inflict the wounds of death in your bodies, that ye may become extinct; and then we will see who shall have power over this people; yea, we will see who shall be brought into bondage.

And now it came to pass that when Zerahemnah had heard these sayings, he came forth and delivered up his sword and his cimeter, and his bow, into the hands of Moroni, and saith unto him, Behold, here is our weapons of war; we will deliver them up unto you, and we will not suffer ourselves to take an oath unto you, which we know that we shall break, and also our children; but take our weapons of war, and suffer that we may depart into the wilderness; otherwise we will retain our swords, and we will perish or conquer.

Behold, we are not of your faith; we do not believe that it is God that hath delivered us into your hands; but we believe that it is your cunning that hath preserved you from our swords. Behold, it is your breast-plates, and your shields that hath preserved you.

links.text: And he had an helmet of brass upon his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of brass.

provenance.other: 'Coat of mail' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Samuel 17:5 and 17:38 — Goliath wearing it and Saul putting it on David. Goliath's kit is a helmet, a coat of mail, a spear and a shield-bearer; the two items Zerahemnah names here, breastplates and shields, are the two of Goliath's the Book of Mormon has vocabulary for. No word is reproduced; the case rests on the argument, not the string.
provenance.significance: This is the inversion the catalogue exists to record. In 1 Samuel the armour belongs to the enemy of God: Goliath is described by his equipment for three verses, David refuses Saul's borrowed version of it because he has not proved it, and the whole point of 17:47 is that 'the LORD saveth not with sword and spear'. Alma 43-44 puts the armour on the covenant side. Moroni's men have the breastplates, the arm-shields and the head-shields; the Lamanites are naked with slings and stones, which is David's equipment (17:40, 17:50); and it is the losing side that makes David's argument. Zerahemnah's 'we do not believe that it is God that hath delivered us into your hands; but we believe that it is your cunning that hath preserved you … it is your breast-plates, and your shields that hath preserved you' is 1 Samuel 17:47 stated as an accusation, and 44:18's 'their naked skins, and their bare heads, were exposed to the sharp swords' concedes that he is factually right about the mechanism. The Book of Mormon's answer is not to deny the armour but to relocate the argument to 44:4-5: it is faith that supplies the armour, so the armour is what God's deliverance looks like.

links.note: 'We believe that it is your cunning that hath preserved you from our swords. Behold, it is your breast-plates, and your shields that hath preserved you.' A conceptual allusion with almost no shared wording, filed high because the argument, not the vocabulary, is the evidence: the KJV has exactly one debate about whether armour or God wins a battle, it is 1 Samuel 17:45-47, and Alma 44 stages both sides of it with the equipment swapped and the losing champion given the winning champion's line. The naming of breastplates and shields — two of Goliath's four items and the two Alma 43:19-21 has been listing for a chapter — is what ties the argument to that passage rather than to armour in general.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal connects the two passages. Breastplates and shields are the obvious things a defeated soldier would blame, and the theological argument about arms versus divine help is common enough in the Old Testament (Psalm 20:7, Psalm 33:16-17) that no single source need be in view.

pericopes.text: And now when Zerahemnah had made an end of speaking these words, Moroni returned the sword, and the weapons of war which he had received, unto Zerahemnah, saying, Behold, we will end the conflict.

Now I cannot retain the words which I have spoken; therefore, as the Lord liveth, ye shall not depart, except ye depart with an oath, that ye will not return again against us to war. Now as ye are in our hands, we will spill your blood upon the ground, or ye shall submit to the conditions to which I have proposed.

And now when Moroni had said these words, Zerahemnah retained his sword, and he was angry with Moroni, and he rushed forward that he might slay Moroni; but as he raised his sword, behold, one of Moroni’s soldiers smote it even to the earth; and it broke by the hilt; and he also smote Zerahemnah, that he took off his scalp, and it fell to the earth. And Zerahemnah withdrew from before them, into the midst of his soldiers.

And it came to pass that the soldier which stood by, which smote off the scalp of Zerahemnah, took up the scalp from off the ground, by the hair, and laid it upon the point of his sword, and stretched it forth unto them, saying unto them with a loud voice, saying:

links.text: Therefore David ran, and stood upon the Philistine, and took his sword, and drew it out of the sheath thereof, and slew him, and cut off his head therewith. And when the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled.

provenance.other: No string is reproduced. The elements are: a commander's own weapon turned against him (17:51 / 44:12, where Zerahemnah's raised sword is struck down and breaks by the hilt), a part of his head taken off (17:51 / 44:12), that part then taken up and carried in the hand or on the weapon as a display (17:54, 17:57 / 44:13), and the enemy army's collapse at the sight (17:51, 'when the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled' / 44:15, 'when they heard these words, and saw the scalp which was upon the sword, they were struck with fear').
provenance.significance: The catalogue has already recorded the Book of Mormon's fullest use of this passage at 1 Nephi 4:18, where Nephi takes Laban by the hair of the head and smites off his head with Laban's own sword. Alma 44:12-15 is the same source run through a filter: the commander is not killed, the thing taken off is a scalp rather than a head, and the display is made not by the general but by an anonymous soldier who turns it into a prophecy — 'Even as this scalp hath fallen to the earth … so shall ye fall to the earth, except ye will deliver up your weapons of war.' The nearest biblical thing to that speech is not 1 Samuel 17 but 1 Samuel 24:11, where David holds up the cut skirt of Saul's robe and argues from it; here the token argues for surrender rather than for innocence. And 44:18's 'even as the soldier of Moroni had prophesied' is the narrator conceding that the sign-act worked, which is what makes the row worth having: the Book of Mormon has converted a trophy into a prophetic sign.

links.note: 'Took up the scalp from off the ground, by the hair, and laid it upon the point of his sword, and stretched it forth unto them.' A conceptual allusion; the wording is the Book of Mormon's own throughout. The sequence is what carries it — sword broken, head-part struck off, part raised as a display, army breaks — and that sequence has one home in the KJV. Confidence held at moderate rather than high because the Book of Mormon has used this passage before, at 1 Nephi 4:18, and a writer with that scene already in his repertoire may be repeating himself rather than returning to Samuel. Note also 'by the hair', which 1 Nephi 4:18 has and 1 Samuel 17:51 does not.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal. Displaying an enemy's head to break the enemy's morale is a commonplace of ancient warfare and appears in the KJV at 1 Samuel 31:9, Judges 7:25 and 2 Kings 10:7-8 as well, none of which the Book of Mormon is closer to than to 1 Samuel 17.

pericopes.text: Even as this scalp hath fallen to the earth, which is the scalp of your Chief, so shall ye fall to the earth, except ye will deliver up your weapons of war, and depart, with a covenant of peace.

links.text: Wherefore say, Behold, I give unto him my covenant of peace:

provenance.other: 'Covenant of peace' occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Numbers 25:12, Ezekiel 34:25 and Ezekiel 37:26 — and in exactly two Book of Mormon verses, Alma 44:14 and 44:15, both in this scene and nowhere else in the book.
provenance.alternative: Ezekiel 34:25 or 37:26, where the covenant of peace is God's own promise to a restored Israel; the machine ranked Ezekiel 34:25 here on the five-word run.
provenance.significance: All three KJV owners of the phrase use it for a covenant God makes; the Book of Mormon uses it for terms an army dictates to a defeated enemy at swordpoint, which is a genuine semantic move and not a slip. Numbers 25:12 is proposed over the Ezekiel verses because of what it is given for: Phinehas receives the covenant of peace as the reward for a javelin-thrust through two bodies, an act of violence that stops a plague — 'so the plague was stayed from the children of Israel'. Alma 44's covenant of peace is likewise offered from behind a raised weapon, by a man holding the evidence of a head-wound, and likewise stops a slaughter: 44:15's covenanters are 'suffered to depart' and 44:20 has Moroni cause 'that the work of death should cease again'. The KJV's oddest covenant of peace and the Book of Mormon's oddest are odd in the same direction.

links.note: 'Except ye will deliver up your weapons of war, and depart, with a covenant of peace.' A three-verse KJV phrase, used twice in this chapter and nowhere else in the Book of Mormon, and used for something none of the three KJV verses uses it for. The Ezekiel alternative is recorded and is the machine's proposal; Numbers 25:12 is preferred because its covenant of peace is also granted at the end of a killing that stops a killing, which is the shape of the whole scene from 44:12 to 44:20. Proposed in the sense of CONVENTIONS §0a — the phrase alone would not settle which of the three verses is in view.
links.whyNot: Two words, and the Book of Mormon's sense matches none of the three candidates exactly, so the choice among them rests on situational fit rather than on wording.

pericopes.text: Now there were many, when they heard these words, and saw the scalp which was upon the sword, they were struck with fear, and many came forth and threw down their weapons of war, at the feet of Moroni, and entered into a covenant of peace. And as many as entered into a covenant, they suffered to depart into the wilderness.
Now it came to pass that Zerahemnah was exceeding wroth, and he did stir up the remainder of his soldiers to anger, to contend more powerfully against the Nephites.

And now Moroni was angry, because of the stubbornness of the Lamanites; therefore he commanded his people that they should fall upon them and slay them. And it came to pass that they began to slay them; yea, and the Lamanites did contend with their swords and their mights.

But behold, their naked skins, and their bare heads, were exposed to the sharp swords of the Nephites; yea, behold, they were pierced and smitten; yea, and did fall exceeding fast before the swords of the Nephites; and they began to be swept down, even as the soldier of Moroni had prophesied.

Now Zerahemnah, when he saw that they were all about to be destroyed, he cried mightily unto Moroni, promising that he would covenant, and also his people, with them, if they would spare the remainder of their lives, that they never would come to war again against them.

And it came to pass that Moroni caused that the work of death should cease again among the people. And it came to pass, that he took the weapons of war from the Lamanites; and after they had entered into a covenant with him of peace, they were suffered to depart into the wilderness.
Now the number of their dead were not numbered, because of the greatness of the number; yea, the number of their dead were exceeding great, both on the Nephites, and on the Lamanites.—
And it came to pass that they did cast their dead into the waters of Sidon; and they have gone forth, and are buried in the depths of the sea.
And the armies of the Nephites, or of Moroni, returned, and came to their houses, and their lands.
And thus ended the eighteenth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi. And thus ended the record of Alma, which was wrote upon the plates of Nephi.

Behold, now it came to pass that the people of Nephi were exceedingly rejoiced, because the Lord had again delivered them out of the hands of their enemies; therefore they gave thanks unto the Lord their God; yea, and they did fast much and pray much, and they did worship God with exceeding great joy.

And it came to pass in the nineteenth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, that Alma came unto his son Helaman, and saith unto him, Believest thou the words which I spake unto thee concerning those records which have been kept?
And Helaman saith unto him, Yea, I believe.—
And Alma saith again, Believest thou in Jesus Christ, which shall come?
And he saith, Yea, I believe all the words which thou hast spoken.
And Alma saith unto him again, Will ye keep my commandments?
And he said, Yea, I will keep thy commandments with all my heart.
Then Alma saith unto him, Blessed art thou; and the Lord shall prosper thee in this land.

links.text: And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.

provenance.other: 'Blessed art thou' occurs in five KJV verses, which alone would not identify a source; but 'unto him, Blessed art thou' occurs in exactly one, Matthew 16:17, and Alma 45:8 reads 'Then Alma saith unto him, Blessed art thou'. The phrase appears fourteen times in the Book of Mormon and three times earlier in Alma (8:15, 19:10, 19:12); none of those follows a confession of Christ, and this one does.
provenance.significance: The evidence is the sequence, not the salutation. Matthew 16 runs: a question put to a disciple ('But whom say ye that I am?'), the disciple's confession ('Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God'), and then the blessing addressed to him by name. Alma 45:2-8 runs the same three steps twice over — 'Believest thou the words which I spake unto thee concerning those records?' / 'Yea, I believe'; 'Believest thou in Jesus Christ, which shall come?' / 'Yea, I believe all the words which thou hast spoken' — and closes with 'Then Alma saith unto him, Blessed art thou.' Recover Matthew's context and the blessing is followed immediately by the commission of a successor: 'thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church … I will give unto thee the keys.' Alma 45 does exactly that, and does it in the same order: blessing at 45:8, prophecy entrusted at 45:9 with an instruction to write and to withhold, and at 45:20-22 Helaman going out to establish the church in every city and appoint priests and teachers. The Book of Mormon has used this passage for a succession before — at 1 Nephi 2:1 and Mosiah 26:15 — but this is the place where it takes the whole shape of Matthew 16:15-19 and not merely the greeting.

links.note: 'Then Alma saith unto him, Blessed art thou; and the Lord shall prosper thee in this land.' Filed at 45:8 rather than at the phrase's first appearance in the book because what carries the row is the catechism in front of it: five verses of question-and-confession culminating in a named blessing, which is Matthew 16:15-17's structure and not a formula the Book of Mormon repeats elsewhere. The four-word run 'unto him, Blessed art thou' is a KJV singleton and belongs to that verse. The 1830 reads 'saith' where 1920 reads 'said', which keeps the historic present the KJV uses at this kind of turn.

pericopes.text: But behold, I have somewhat to prophesy unto thee; but what I prophesy unto thee, ye shall not make known; yea, what I prophesy unto thee shall not be made known, even until the prophecy is fulfilled; therefore write the words which I shall say.

And these are the words: Behold, I perceive that this very people, the Nephites, according to the spirit of revelation which is in me, in four hundred years from the time that Jesus Christ shall manifest himself unto them, shall dwindle in unbelief;
yea, and then shall they see wars and pestilences, yea, famines and bloodshed, even until the people of Nephi shall become extinct;

links.text: For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places.

provenance.other: 'Famines and pestilences' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:7 and Luke 21:11, and nowhere else; 'wars and rumours of wars' in exactly two, Matthew 24:6 and Mark 13:7. Alma 45:11 is the only verse in Alma that uses 'famines' at all. The Book of Mormon inverts the pair — 'wars and pestilences, yea, famines and bloodshed' — where both synoptic verses read famines first.
provenance.significance: The Olivet discourse is a prediction of the destruction of Jerusalem which the Book of Mormon has been mining since 1 Nephi 12:2 for predictions of the destruction of the Nephites, and Alma 45:10-14 is the fullest of them: four hundred years from Christ's appearance, dwindling in unbelief, wars and pestilences and famines, a generation that shall not all pass away before the iniquity comes, and a remnant that survives by being absorbed into the enemy. Every one of those is a move Matthew 24 makes — including 'this generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled' (24:34), which Alma 45:12's 'the fourth generation shall not all pass away' answers by lengthening the interval and keeping the idiom. What the Book of Mormon does that the source cannot is give the prophecy a date and then narrate its fulfilment, which is the burden of the four books after this one.

links.note: 'Then shall they see wars and pestilences, yea, famines and bloodshed, even until the people of Nephi shall become extinct.' The pair 'famines and pestilences' is a two-verse KJV rarity and the surrounding sentence keeps the Olivet frame — a prophecy delivered privately, at a request to know when, running from wars through famine to a generation-count. Recorded across the book boundary under ADJUDICATING §4; the argument for Matthew 24 as the Book of Mormon's apocalyptic vocabulary is made at 1 Nephi 12:2 and 2 Nephi 10:6. What is new here is that the borrowing is put into the mouth of Alma as a private prophecy to a single son, with an instruction that it not be published until fulfilled (45:9) — which is not how Matthew 24 is delivered and is how apocalyptic literature says it was.

pericopes.text: yea, and this because they shall dwindle in unbelief, and fall into the works of darkness and lasciviousness, and all manner of iniquities; yea, I say unto you, that because they shall sin against so great light and knowledge; yea, I say unto you, that from that day, even the fourth generation shall not all pass away, before this great iniquity shall come;

and when that great day cometh, behold, the time very soon cometh that those which are now, or the seed of those which are now numbered among the people of Nephi, shall no more be numbered among the people of Nephi;

but whosoever remaineth, and is not destroyed in that great and dreadful day, shall be numbered among the Lamanites, and shall become like unto them all, save it be a few, which shall be called the disciples of the Lord; and them shall the Lamanites pursue, even until they shall become extinct. And now, because of iniquity, this prophecy shall be fulfilled.

links.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD:

provenance.other: 'Great and dreadful day' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Joel 2:31 and Joel 3:14's nearest equivalents read 'the great and the terrible day of the LORD' and 'the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision'; the adjective 'dreadful' in this phrase is Malachi's alone. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase twice: here, and at 3 Nephi 25:5, which is inside the transcribed Malachi 3-4 block. Alma 45:14 is therefore the only free-standing use in the book, and it precedes the transcription by four books.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and Malachi 4:5 is not a threat but a provision: before the great and dreadful day the LORD undertakes to send Elijah, so that the earth is not smitten with a curse. Alma 45 takes the day and drops the provision — the great and dreadful day at 45:14 is the one on which the Nephites are wiped out, and the very next verse has Alma blessing the earth 'for the righteous' sake' and then, at 45:16, pronouncing exactly the curse Malachi 4:6 says Elijah's coming exists to prevent. And then, four verses on, a prophet leaves the land, is never heard of again, and is said to have been taken up. The chapter has the Malachi sequence in it — the dreadful day, the curse on the land, a prophet who does not die where anyone can find him — with the sending reversed into a departure.

links.note: 'Whosoever remaineth, and is not destroyed in that great and dreadful day.' A KJV singleton reproduced entire, used here for the destruction of a people rather than for the day of the LORD, and used four books before the Book of Mormon transcribes the chapter it comes from. Filed high on rarity. The reading offered in `significance` — that 45:14-19 runs the whole of Malachi 4 in altered order — is a proposal in the sense of CONVENTIONS §0a and rests on the sequence, not on further wording.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that after Alma had said these things to Helaman, he blessed him, and also his other sons; and he also blessed the earth, for the righteous’ sake.

And he said, Thus saith the Lord God: Cursed shall be the land, yea, this land, unto every nation, kindred, tongue, and people, unto destruction, which do wickedly, when they are fully ripe; and as I have said, so shall it be: for this is the cursing and the blessing of God upon the land, for the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance.

links.text: Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?

provenance.other: 'Canst not look on iniquity' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does 'purer eyes' — the same verse, Habakkuk 1:13. The Book of Mormon's rendering — 'the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance' — is a hapax in the Book of Mormon: 'least degree of allowance' occurs at Alma 45:16 and nowhere else in the book, though the sentence became one of the most quoted in it. The catalogue's earlier row at 1 Nephi 10:21 pairs Psalm 5:4 with Habakkuk 1:13 for 'no unclean thing can dwell with God'; this is the first place the Book of Mormon renders Habakkuk's clause itself.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis here is unusually sharp, because Habakkuk 1:13 is not a doctrinal statement at all — it is the opening of a complaint. The prophet says God cannot look on iniquity precisely in order to ask why he is doing so: 'wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?' The clause is a premise in an accusation about divine inaction while an invading army destroys the righteous. Alma 45:16 lifts it out of the complaint and makes it the ground of a curse — the reason the land will be destroyed when its people are fully ripe — in a chapter that has just come through a war and is predicting the extinction of the righteous nation. Habakkuk's question, in other words, is the question Alma 45:10-14 has just answered in advance: the wicked will devour the more righteous, and it will be allowed. The Book of Mormon uses the premise and declines the protest.

links.note: 'For the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance.' No clause is reproduced, but the proposition and its shape are Habakkuk 1:13's, and Habakkuk 1:13 is the only KJV verse that states it — the two strings that carry it, 'purer eyes' and 'canst not look on iniquity', are both singletons there. What the Book of Mormon adds is the quantifier: 'with the least degree of allowance' is not biblical English and not Book of Mormon English elsewhere either, and it turns Habakkuk's absolute into a scale, which is what a doctrine of degrees of accountability needs. Filed as paraphrase rather than allusion for that reason.

pericopes.text: And now, when Alma had said these words, he blessed the church, yea, all those which should stand fast in the faith, from that time henceforth;

and when Alma had done this, he departed out of the land of Zarahemla, as if to go into the land of Melek.— And it came to pass that he was never heard of more; as to his death or his burial, we know not of.

Behold, this we know, that he was a righteous man; and the saying went abroad in the church, that he was taken up by the spirit, or buried by the hand of the Lord, even as Moses. But behold, the Scripture saith the Lord took Moses unto himself; and we suppose that he hath also received Alma in the spirit, unto himself; therefore, for this cause, we know nothing concerning his death and burial.

links.text: And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 34:5-6, with the assumption tradition that stands behind Jude 1:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Moses is named outright, so the source is not in doubt; the question the verse raises is which claim about Moses it is making. Deuteronomy 34:5-6 says Moses died and that the LORD buried him — 'he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab … but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day' — which is the second of the two options Alma 45:19 offers ('buried by the hand of the Lord'). No KJV verse says the first. The clause 'God took him' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and its subject is Enoch (Genesis 5:24, glossed at Hebrews 11:5 as translation 'that he should not see death'); Elijah's going up by a whirlwind is 2 Kings 2:11. Jude 1:9 is the only verse in the Bible that touches an afterlife for the body of Moses at all, and it does so at second hand, reporting a dispute between Michael and the devil over it — the fragment of the extra-canonical Assumption of Moses that survived into the New Testament canon.
