provenance.alternative: Read strictly, 45:19 may intend only Deuteronomy 34:6 — 'the Lord took Moses unto himself' as a loose paraphrase of God burying him where nobody can find the grave — in which case the verse is not appealing to an assumption tradition at all and the Jude connection is ours, not the text's.
provenance.significance: Alma 45:19 makes an explicit appeal to a text: 'But behold, the Scripture saith the Lord took Moses unto himself.' No scripture says it. Deuteronomy 34:5 says the opposite in as many words — 'So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab' — and 34:6 supplies a burial and a lost grave, which is why the verse has to offer the reader both options before choosing. The only biblical hint that Moses did not simply stay buried is Jude 1:9, and Jude gets it from a book that is not in the canon. So this verse is doing something the rest of the catalogue rarely catches: it is citing, as scripture, a tradition the King James Bible transmits only as the residue of a lost apocryphon, and it is using it to license a matching claim about its own prophet. The apparatus of the sentence is the tell — 'the saying went abroad in the church', 'the Scripture saith', 'we suppose', 'we know nothing' — a narrator reasoning from a disputed proof-text to a conclusion he marks as inference. And the two figures the KJV actually does take up, Enoch and Elijah, are the two the verse does not name, though Genesis 5:24's 'God took him' is the sentence its 'the Lord took Moses unto himself' is built out of.

links.note: 'He was taken up by the spirit, or buried by the hand of the Lord, even as Moses. But behold, the Scripture saith the Lord took Moses unto himself.' The second half of Alma's disappearance is Deuteronomy 34:5-6 — a prophet who leaves, dies out of sight, is buried by God, and whose sepulchre no man knows — and the chapter reproduces that verse's effect exactly at 45:18, 'as to his death or his burial, we know not of'. The first half is not in the Bible. The narrator's own citation formula is what makes the row valuable: he says the Scripture says a thing the Scripture does not say, and the nearest the canon comes to saying it is Jude 1:9's report of a quarrel over Moses's body, itself a quotation from outside the canon. Confidence is certain as to dependence on Deuteronomy 34 (Moses is named and the burial is the point); the Jude element is recorded as the tradition the verse's claim requires, not as a verbal borrowing. `mediation` is left uncertain because tools/mediation-check.py finds no point at which the OT and NT candidates differ and the Book of Mormon follows one of them — the two texts are not parallel versions of one saying, so the verse cannot settle its own route.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Alma 45.19 (cross-references Deuteronomy 34:5-6 and Jude 1:9)

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass in the commencement of the nineteenth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, that Helaman went forth among the people to declare the word unto them:

for behold, because of their wars with the Lamanites, and the many little dissentions and disturbances which had been among the people, it became expedient that the word of God should be declared among them; yea, and that a regulation should be made throughout the church;

therefore Helaman and his brethren went forth to establish the church again in all the land, yea, in every city throughout all the land which was possessed by the people of Nephi. And it came to pass that they did appoint priests and teachers throughout all the land, over all the churches.

And now it came to pass that after Helaman and his brethren had appointed priests and teachers over the churches, that there arose a dissention among them, and they would not give heed to the words of Helaman and his brethren;

but they grew proud, being lifted up in their hearts, because of their exceeding great riches; therefore they grew rich in their own eyes, and would not give heed to their words, to walk uprightly before God.
And it came to pass that as many as would not hearken to the words of Helaman and his brethren, were gathered together against their brethren.
And now behold, they were exceeding wroth, insomuch that they were determined to slay them.
Now the leader of those which were wroth against their brethren, was a large and a strong man; and his name was Amalickiah.

And Amalickiah was desirous to be a king; and those people which were wroth, were also desirous that he should be their king; and they were the greater part of them the lower Judges of the land; and they were seeking for power.
And they had been led by the flatteries of Amalickiah, that if they would support him, and establish him to be their king, that he would make them rulers over the people.

Thus they were led away by Amalickiah, to dissentions, notwithstanding the preaching of Helaman and his brethren; yea, notwithstanding their exceeding great care over the church, for they were High Priests over the church.

And there were many in the church which believed in the flattering words of Amalickiah; therefore they dissented even from the church; and thus were the affairs of the people of Nephi exceeding precarious and dangerous, notwithstanding their great victory which they had had over the Lamanites, and their great rejoicings which they had had, because of their deliverance by the hands of the Lord.
Thus we see how quick the children of men doth forget the Lord their God; yea, how quick to do iniquity, and to be led away by the evil one;
yea, and we also see the great wickedness one very wicked man can cause to take place among the children of men;

yea, we see that Amalickiah, because he was a man of cunning devices, and a man of many flattering words, that he led away the hearts of many people to do wickedly; yea, and to seek to destroy the church of God, and to destroy the foundation of liberty which God had granted unto them, or which blessing God had sent upon the face of the land, for the righteous’ sake.
And now it came to pass that when Moroni, which was the chief commander of the armies of the Nephites, had heard of these dissentions, he was angry with Amalickiah.

And it came to pass that he rent his coat; and he took a piece thereof, and wrote upon it, In memory of our God, our religion, and freedom, and our peace, our wives, and our children; and he fastened it upon the end of a pole thereof.

links.text: And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the LORD, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.

provenance.other: “Fight for your brethren” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 4:14, and the list that follows it — “your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses” — is likewise unique to that verse. The Book of Mormon's list is shorter and the pronouns are first-person plural: “our God, our religion, and freedom, and our peace, our wives, and our children.”
provenance.alternative: “Our wives and our children” with the Book of Mormon's own pronoun occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 14:3 — but there the phrase belongs to the wilderness generation arguing for surrender, which is the opposite of a muster cry. See the exclusion register at this verse.
provenance.significance: Nehemiah 4 is the King James Bible's one scene of a civil population arming itself around a leader who has just rallied it by naming what it stands to lose, and it is the chapter in which the workers build with a weapon in one hand and a trumpeter beside the leader (4:17-20). Moroni's rent coat on a pole is that trumpet: an improvised signal raised over a people who must be told, in a list, what they are defending. Recover Nehemiah's context and the borrowing supplies what Alma 46 never says outright — that the title of liberty is a wall-building banner, defensive and domestic, not a conquest standard. Nehemiah's rally ends “our God shall fight for us” (4:20); Moroni's ends with a prayer that God will favour the cause.

links.note: The writing on the rent coat is a list of goods in the possessive plural — God, religion, freedom, peace, wives, children — and the KJV has one such list on the lips of one such leader, at Nehemiah 4:14, where it is likewise preceded by a call to remember. Moroni writes “In memory of our God”; Nehemiah says “remember the LORD.” No clause is reproduced, and the case rests on the shape of the sentence and the identity of the scene rather than on shared wording; catalogued as an allusion at moderate confidence for that reason. It falls far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is in no sense a quotation.
links.whyNot: Every content word in Moroni's list is ordinary, the pronouns differ from Nehemiah's, and the last two items in the KJV list (daughters, houses) are absent. A leader listing wives and children as what an army defends is not a literary borrowing on its own; only Nehemiah 4's whole situation makes the case.

links.text: And Ahijah caught the new garment that was on him, and rent it in twelve pieces:

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 15:27-28 and 1 Kings 11:30-31 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Hath rent the kingdom” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Samuel 15:28 and 28:17, both of Saul; 1 Kings 11:31 has the cognate “I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon.” These are the Bible's two rent-garment political signs.
provenance.significance: The Bible tears a garment twice as an act of state, and both times the tearing announces that a kingdom is being taken away from a man who wanted to keep it: Samuel's mantle rent as Saul clutches it, Ahijah's new garment rent into twelve pieces for Jeroboam. Alma 46 inverts the figure precisely. Amalickiah is a man who wants to be king (46:4), and the garment torn against him is torn not by a prophet but by a commander, and not into a kingdom's portions but into a single banner. The type-scene's grammar is preserved and its outcome reversed: the rending here does not transfer a monarchy, it abolishes the claim to one.

links.note: Moroni rends his coat, takes a piece of it, and raises it on a pole as a public sign against a would-be king. There is almost no shared wording — the case is entirely at the level of the scene — and it is catalogued as figural for that reason. What makes it more than a coincidence of gesture is 46:21, where the covenant reads the sign the way 1 Samuel 15:28 reads Samuel's mantle: the tearing is a declaration of what God will do to the tearer's own party if it transgresses. Compare Hays on the recovery of a precursor's context; the argument here is that the Book of Mormon has borrowed the biblical logic of the torn garment rather than any biblical sentence.
links.whyNot: Rending a garment is the commonest gesture of grief and outrage in the KJV — “rent his clothes” alone occurs in fifteen verses — and Moroni's tearing may be nothing but that. Neither 1 Samuel 15 nor 1 Kings 11 supplies a phrase, and a reader who declines the type-scene is left with no evidence at all.

pericopes.text: And he fastened on his head-plate, and his breast-plate, and his shields, and girded on his armour about his loins; and he took the pole, which had on the end thereof his rent coat, (and he called it the title of liberty,) and he bowed himself to the earth, and he prayed mightily unto his God for the blessings of liberty to rest upon his brethren so long as there should a band of Christians remain to possess the land:

links.text: Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness;

provenance.other: “The whole armour” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ephesians 6:11 and 6:13; “girt about” in exactly two, Ephesians 6:14 and Revelation 1:13. The 1830 spells the noun “armour” with the KJV's u, which 1920 Americanized to “armor” — the borrowing is plainer in the first edition than in the modern text.
provenance.significance: Paul's panoply is the King James Bible's one catalogue of armour piece by piece, and it is a catalogue of things that are not armour: truth, righteousness, faith, salvation. Alma 46:13 re-literalizes it. Moroni puts on the helmet, the breastplate, the shield and the girded loins as actual metal, and then does with them what Ephesians 6:18 tells the armoured man to do next — “praying always” — bowing to the earth and praying mightily. The chapter then completes the circuit at 46:21, where the people come with their armours girded about their loins to enter a covenant. A figure Paul made spiritual has been made military again, and the prayer that follows the arming is the seam where the two readings meet.

links.note: Head-plate, breast-plate, shields, and armour girded about the loins: four pieces, and the same four Ephesians 6 names, in a book whose prophets elsewhere quote that passage's fiery darts. The wording is not Paul's — “head-plate” is not the KJV's helmet and no clause is reproduced — so this is an allusion at moderate confidence, resting on the closed set of items plus the immediate turn to prayer. Below Skousen's threshold by a wide margin.
links.whyNot: A soldier arming himself will put on a helmet, a breastplate and a shield whatever his author has read, and 1 Samuel 17:5-6 arms Goliath from the same inventory without any Pauline help. The girded loins are the only item that is more natural as a borrowing than as observation.

pericopes.text: for thus were all the true believers of Christ, which belonged to the church of God, called, by those which did not belong to the church; and those who did belong to the church,

and those who did belong to the church, were faithful; yea, all those who were true believers in Christ, took upon them, gladly, the name of Christ, or Christians, as they were called, because of their belief in Christ, which should come;

links.text: And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.

provenance.other: “Christians” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 11:26. The singular “Christian” occurs in two more, Acts 26:28 and 1 Peter 4:16 — three verses in the whole Bible, and Alma 46 draws on all three within nine verses (46:13, 46:15, 46:18, 46:21).
provenance.significance: Acts 11:26 does not say the disciples took the name; it says they were called it, by outsiders, in a city where they were a minority. Alma 46:14-15 reproduces that exact structure and then adds the move Acts leaves out: “called, by those which did not belong to the church … took upon them, gladly, the name of Christ, or Christians, as they were called.” The nickname is accepted. Recover Acts 26:28 — “Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian,” Agrippa's sneer — and 1 Peter 4:16 — “if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed” — and the whole biblical career of the word is a name given from outside and worn under contempt. That is precisely Moroni's argument at 46:18: “we, who are despised because we take upon us the name of Christ.”

links.note: The word itself is the evidence. “Christians” is a New Testament coinage that occurs in one KJV verse, and Alma 46:15 uses it in that verse's own frame: a body of believers named by people outside it, the name then owned. The catalogue's exclusion at Alma 23:16 declined Acts 11:26 there because that passage shares nothing but the idea of a distinguishing name; the objection does not apply here, where the shared item is the singular noun. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not a quotation, but the rarity is absolute.

pericopes.text: and therefore, at this time, Moroni prayed that the cause of the Christians, and the freedom of the land, might be favored.—

And it came to pass that when he had poured out his soul to God, he gave all the land which was south of the land Desolation; yea, and in fine, all the land, both on the north and on the south, a chosen land, and the land of liberty.—

links.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

provenance.other: “Poured out his soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 53:12. Luke 22:37 quotes the neighbouring clause of that verse and not this one; mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for the Isaiah form, so the route is direct-OT and the New Testament is not in play.
provenance.significance: The one biblical soul poured out is the servant's, and it is poured out unto death, as the price of interceding for transgressors. Alma 46:17 pours out a soul in prayer for a people about to go to war, and the sentence it opens ends by naming the land “a chosen land, and the land of liberty.” The suppressed correspondence is the cost: in Isaiah the pouring out buys a portion divided with the great, and here it precedes a chapter of executions (46:35) for those who will not covenant. The catalogue does not claim the writer meant the servant song; it records that the phrase available to him for total self-expenditure in prayer was a phrase the KJV uses once, of a death.

links.note: “When he had poured out his soul to God.” A four-word KJV singleton, and the Book of Mormon uses it of prayer where Isaiah uses it of dying. That semantic shift is why this is an echo and not an allusion: nothing else in 46:17 touches Isaiah 53, and the phrase may simply have entered the writer's English as a devotional idiom. It is recorded because the idiom has exactly one biblical home.
links.whyNot: “Pour out the soul” is close to 1 Samuel 1:15's “poured out my soul before the LORD,” which is prayer and not death and which would make the Book of Mormon's usage unremarkable; the exact string is Isaiah's alone, but the idea is Hannah's.

pericopes.text: And he saith, Surely God shall not suffer that we, who are despised because we take upon us the name of Christ, shall be trodden down and destroyed, until we bring it upon us, by our own transgressions.

And when Moroni had said these words, he went forth among the people, waving the rent of his garment in the air, that all might see the writing which he had wrote upon the rent, and crying with a loud voice, saying:

Behold, whosoever will maintain this title upon the land, let them come forth in the strength of the Lord, and enter into a covenant that they will maintain their rights, and their religion, that the Lord God may bless them.

links.text: I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.

provenance.other: “In the strength of the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 71:16 and Micah 5:4. Psalm 71:16 has the verb of motion the Book of Mormon uses (“I will GO in the strength of the Lord GOD”); Micah 5:4's is a verb of standing and feeding.
provenance.significance: The catalogue adjudicated this phrase at Mosiah 9:17, where Zeniff's people go out to battle in it; the link is written afresh here because Alma is a new book with a new narrator's voice and the reader of Alma 46 should not be shown silence. What is new here is the imperative. Psalm 71 is a single old man's confidence — “I will go” — and Moroni turns it into a summons to a nation: “let them come forth in the strength of the Lord.” The Psalm's first person becomes a muster.

links.note: “Let them come forth in the strength of the Lord, and enter into a covenant.” Two KJV verses have the phrase and one of them has the Book of Mormon's verb of going. The wording is short enough that a reader could call it common English piety, so it is an echo at moderate confidence; the argument is the same one made at Mosiah 9:17, and is not restated here at length.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Moroni had proclaimed these words, behold, the people came running together, with their armours girded about their loins, rending their garments in token, or as a covenant, that they would not forsake the Lord their God; or, in other words, if they should transgress the commandments of God, or fall into transgression, and be ashamed to take upon them the name of Christ, the Lord should rend them even as they had rent their garments.

links.text: Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf.

provenance.other: “Suffer as a Christian” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 4:16, and it is the only place in the Bible where the noun “Christian” and the verb “ashamed” stand together. Alma 46:21 has “be ashamed to take upon them the name of Christ”; 46:18 has “despised because we take upon us the name of Christ.”
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 4:16 is the New Testament's one instruction about how to hold the name under pressure, and it holds it two ways at once: do not be ashamed, and glorify God. Alma 46 splits the verse across its covenant. The people rend their garments as a token that if they are ever “ashamed to take upon them the name of Christ,” the Lord should rend them likewise — Peter's shame clause turned into a self-imprecation. And 46:16, where Moroni prays that the cause of the Christians might be favoured, is Peter's second clause: the name is glorified rather than concealed. The suppressed term is persecution. Peter's Christians suffer from outside; Moroni's covenant makes the danger internal, and the thing to be ashamed of is one's own transgression.

links.note: The chapter's three uses of the Christian name (46:15, 46:18, 46:21) exhaust the KJV's three verses containing that noun, and this one takes the rarest pairing in them: shame and the name together, which the King James Bible puts in one verse only. The covenant clause “be ashamed to take upon them the name of Christ” is 1 Peter 4:16's “let him not be ashamed” restated as the condition of a curse. No clause is reproduced verbatim, so this is an allusion, not a quotation, and it is far below Skousen's threshold.

links.text: When Jesus saw that the people came running together, he rebuked the foul spirit, saying unto him, Thou dumb and deaf spirit, I charge thee, come out of him, and enter no more into him.

provenance.other: “The people came running together” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 9:25. The five words are reproduced in order and without change.
provenance.significance: Mark 9:25 is a crowd forming around a leader who then acts decisively in front of it, and the King James translators used this phrase nowhere else. Alma 46:21 has the identical five words in the identical function — Moroni proclaims, and the people come running together — but Mark's crowd is a spectacle drawn by a failed exorcism, and Moroni's is a covenant assembly. If the borrowing is real it is a borrowing of narrative furniture rather than of meaning, which is itself worth recording: this catalogue's other Markan links (1 Nephi 7:11's “how great things”) are of the same kind, phrases taken for their usefulness and not their theology.

links.note: Five consecutive words, exactly as the KJV has them, from the only verse in the Bible that contains them. Against that, there is no thematic contact whatever with Mark 9 and no other Markan wording in the chapter, so the possibility that two writers independently reached for the natural English of a gathering crowd cannot be dismissed — hence echo at moderate rather than allusion. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold.
links.whyNot: “The people came running together” is unremarkable English and the KJV's single occurrence may be an accident of how rarely the KJV describes crowds forming. Nothing else in Alma 46 touches Mark's exorcism, and no argument improves by importing it.

pericopes.text: Now this was the covenant which they made; and they cast their garments at the feet of Moroni, saying: We covenant with our God, that we shall be destroyed, even as our brethren in the land northward, if we shall fall into transgression; yea, he may cast us at the feet of our enemies, even as we have cast our garments at thy feet, to be trodden under foot, if we shall fall into transgression.

links.text: And they brought him to Jesus: and they cast their garments upon the colt, and they set Jesus thereon.

provenance.other: “Cast their garments” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 11:7 and Luke 19:35, both of the triumphal entry; Matthew 21:8 has “spread their garments in the way,” and Luke 19:36 adds “they spread their clothes in the way.” 2 Kings 9:13 is the Old Testament analogue — “they hasted, and took every man his garment, and put it under him on the top of the stairs” — where garments cast down proclaim a king.
provenance.significance: In the King James Bible, casting garments before a man is an act of acclamation and it makes him a king: Jehu on the stairs, Jesus on the colt, in both cases with a crowd shouting. Alma 46:22 stages the gesture and cancels its meaning. The people cast their garments at Moroni's feet, but not to enthrone him — the words spoken over the casting are a curse on themselves, and the garments are cast down “to be trodden under foot” rather than ridden over. The chapter's whole quarrel is with a man who wants to be king (46:4), and this is the one moment where its crowd performs the biblical coronation gesture toward someone who is not going to accept it.

links.note: The exact phrase belongs to two verses of the triumphal entry and to no others, and it arrives here in a chapter already dense with New Testament rarities. The sense, however, is inverted: acclamation in Mark and Luke, self-abasement here. Catalogued as an echo because the inversion is complete and three words is a thin base; it is recorded rather than excluded because the inversion is legible as an argument, not as a mismatch.
links.whyNot: “Cast their garments” may be nothing more than the ordinary English for the action Alma 46:22 describes, which really does involve garments being thrown down; the two KJV occurrences agree with it in wording and disagree with it in everything else. A reader who requires shared sense as well as shared words should decline this row.

pericopes.text: Moroni saith unto them, Behold, we are a remnant of the seed of Jacob; yea, we are a remnant of the seed of Joseph, whose coat was rent by his brethren, into many pieces; yea, and now behold, let us remember to keep the commandments of God, or our garments shall be rent by our brethren, and we be cast into prison, or be sold, or be slain;

links.text: And he knew it, and said, It is my son’s coat; an evil beast hath devoured him; Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces.

provenance.other: “Rent in pieces” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 37:33 — Jacob's cry over the bloodied coat. Alma 46:23 has “whose coat was rent by his brethren, into many pieces.” Note that the Book of Mormon has moved the tearing: in Genesis the brothers dip the coat in blood and do not tear it, and it is Joseph, not the coat, whom Jacob supposes to be rent in pieces.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's hinge, and its interest is in what it gets wrong. Moroni identifies his people as the remnant of Joseph and grounds the identification in a torn coat — but the coat of Genesis 37 was not torn. Jacob's words “rent in pieces” are an inference about his son's body from a garment that has only been bloodied, and Alma 46:23 collapses the inference into the object, so that the brothers tear the coat because Jacob said Joseph was torn. Whether that is a misreading of Genesis or a deliberate fusion of the coat with the extra-biblical remnant tradition Moroni then quotes at 46:24, it is the same operation the chapter has been performing since 46:12: a garment torn by kinsmen becomes a sign that a people can be preserved in pieces. The rest of Moroni's speech — prison, sold, slain (46:23) — is Joseph's biography in three verbs, and the KJV supplies all three in Genesis 37 and 39.
provenance.alternative: Alma 46:24's prophecy of Jacob about the preserved remnant of the coat is not in the King James Bible at all; no source can be assigned to it here, and it is registered as an exclusion rather than forced onto Genesis 37.

links.note: Hardy's study edition cross-references Genesis 37:31-33 at this verse, and the wording bears it out: “rent in pieces” is a KJV singleton, and it belongs to the moment Jacob is shown the coat. Moroni's sentence reproduces the two decisive elements — Joseph's coat, and its being rent into pieces — while relocating the tearing from the father's imagination of his son's body to the brothers' hands. The remaining verbs of 46:23, “cast into prison, or be sold, or be slain,” run the rest of the Joseph story forward. It is not a quotation and falls below Skousen's threshold; as an allusion its rarity is absolute.

pericopes.text: yea, let us preserve our liberty, as a remnant of Joseph; yea, let us remember the words of Jacob, before his death; for behold, he saw that a part of the remnant of the coat of Joseph was preserved, and had not decayed. And he saith, Even as this remnant of garment of my sons hath been preserved, so shall a remnant of the seed of my son be preserved by the hand of God, and be taken unto himself, while the remainder of the seed of Joseph shall perish, even as the remnant of his garment.
Now behold, this giveth my soul sorrow; nevertheless, my soul hath joy in my son, because that part of his seed which shall be taken unto God.
Now behold, this was the language of Jacob.

And now who knoweth but what the remnant of the seed of Joseph, which shall perish as his garment, are those which have dissented from us; yea, and even it shall be us, if we do not stand fast in the faith of Christ.

And now it came to pass that when Moroni had said these words, he went forth, and also sent forth in all the parts of the land where there were dissentions, and gathered together all the people which were desirous to maintain their liberty, to stand against Amalickiah, and those which had dissented, which were called Amalickiahites.

And it came to pass that when Amalickiah saw that the people of Moroni were more numerous than the Amalickiahites; and he also saw that his people were doubtful concerning the justice of the cause in which they had undertaken; therefore, fearing that he should not gain the point, he took those of his people which would, and departed into the land of Nephi.

Now Moroni thought it was not expedient that the Lamanites should have any more strength; therefore he thought to cut off the people of Amalickiah, or to take them and bring them back, and put Amalickiah to death; yea, for he knew that they would stir up the Lamanites to anger against them, and cause them to come to battle against them; and this he knew that Amalickiah would do, that he might obtain his purposes;

therefore Moroni thought it was expedient that he should take his armies, which had gathered themselves together, and armed themselves, and entered into a covenant to keep the peace:— And it came to pass that he took his army, and marched out into the wilderness, to cut off the course of Amalickiah in the wilderness.
And it came to pass that he did according to his desires, and marched forth into the wilderness, and headed the armies of Amalickiah.
And it came to pass that Amalickiah fled with a small number of his men, and the remainder were delivered up into the hands of Moroni, and were taken back into the land of Zarahemla.

Now Moroni being a man which was appointed by the Chief Judges and the voice of the people, therefore he had power according to his will, with the armies of the Nephites, to establish and to exercise authority over them.

And it came to pass that whomsoever of the Amalickiahites that would not enter into a covenant to support the cause of freedom, that they might maintain a free government, he caused to be put to death; and there was but few which denied the covenant of freedom.

links.text: And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul;

provenance.other: “Entered into a covenant” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 15:12 and Ezekiel 16:8, and only the first has the Book of Mormon's construction with an infinitive of purpose (“to seek the LORD” / “to support the cause of freedom,” “to keep the peace” at 46:31). “Whosoever would not” occurs in exactly two, 2 Chronicles 15:13 and Ezra 10:8, and only the first attaches death to the refusal. The 1830 reads “there was but few which denied the covenant of freedom”, which 1920 corrected to “were … who”.
provenance.significance: Asa's covenant at Jerusalem is the King James Bible's one national oath enforced by execution, and Alma 46 rebuilds it clause by clause. Both begin with a purge of dissenters and a gathering (2 Chronicles 15:8-10 / Alma 46:28); both have a people entering into a covenant with a stated object; both provide that whosoever would not enter it should be put to death (15:13 / 46:35); both swear it with a loud voice and shouting (15:14 / Alma 46:19-21); and both end in rest and peace given to the land (15:15, “the LORD gave them rest round about” / Alma 46:37, “they began to have peace again in the land”). Recover the Chronicler's context and the most uncomfortable sentence in Alma 46 stops being an outlier: Moroni executing the men who would not covenant is Asa's covenant clause carried out, and the Book of Mormon has kept the biblical penalty while changing what is sworn to from the God of Israel to a free government. The substitution is the finding. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the suppressed term here is that in Chronicles the covenant is religious and the death penalty is for apostasy, and Alma 46 has transposed both onto a constitution.

links.note: “Whomsoever of the Amalickiahites that would not enter into a covenant to support the cause of freedom, that they might maintain a free government, he caused to be put to death.” Two rare KJV constructions meet in this sentence — the covenant entered into with an infinitive of purpose, and the “whosoever would not” whose penalty is death — and both belong to one biblical passage, Asa's covenant assembly in 2 Chronicles 15:12-13. The correspondence extends past the wording to the sequence of the whole chapter, which is why this is catalogued as structural. No clause is reproduced verbatim and it falls below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; the evidence is the co-occurrence of two two-verse rarities in the same syntactic frame.
links.whyNot: “Enter into a covenant” is one of the Book of Mormon's own standing formulas and appears four times in this chapter alone, so its KJV rarity may reflect the King James translators' idiom rather than a borrowing; and a leader executing men who refuse an oath is a situation that can be invented without a model. The structural argument is what carries the row, and structural arguments are the easiest to construct after the fact.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass also, that he caused the title of liberty to be hoisted upon every tower which was in all the land, which was possessed by the Nephites; and thus Moroni planted the standard of liberty among the Nephites.
And they began to have peace again in the land; and thus they did maintain peace in the land, until nearly the end of the nineteenth year of the reign of the Judges.
And Helaman and the High Priests did also maintain order in the church; yea, even for the space of four years, did they have much peace and rejoicing in the church.
And it came to pass that there were many who died, firmly believing that their souls were redeemed by the Lord Jesus Christ; thus they went out of the world rejoicing.

And there were some who died with fevers, which at some seasons of the year, was very frequent in the land; but not so much so with fevers, because of the excellent qualities of the many plants and roots which God had prepared, to remove the cause of diseases which was subsequent to man, by the nature of the climate.
But there were many who died with old age; and those who died in the faith of Christ, are happy in him, as we must needs suppose.

Now we will return in our record, to Amalickiah, and those which had fled with him into the wilderness: for behold, he had taken those which went with him, and went up into the land of Nephi, among the Lamanites, and did stir up the Lamanites to anger, against the people of Nephi, insomuch that the king of the Lamanites sent a proclamation throughout all his land, among all his people, that they should gather themselves together again, to go to battle against the Nephites.

And it came to pass that when the proclamation had gone forth among them, they were exceeding fraid; yea, they feared to displease the king, and they also feared to go to battle against the Nephites, lest they should lose their lives. And it came to pass that they would not, or the more part of them would not obey the commandments of the king.

And now it came to pass that the king was wroth, because of their disobedience; therefore he gave Amalickiah the command of that part of his army which was obedient unto his commands, and commanded him that he should go forth and compel them to arms.
Now behold, this was the desire of Amalickiah: for he being a very subtle man to do evil, therefore he laid the plan in his heart to dethrone the king of the Lamanites.

provenance.other: “A very subtil man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 13:3, of Jonadab. The King James spelling is “subtil”, which the 1830 already modernizes to “subtle” — the spelling is the one place where this borrowing is less visible in the first edition than the rest of the chapter's are, and it is recorded rather than smoothed over. The adjective itself is rare: “subtil” stands in only three KJV verses, Genesis 3:1, 2 Samuel 13:3 and Proverbs 7:10.
provenance.significance: Jonadab is the King James Bible's one named schemer, introduced by this exact epithet and by nothing else — he has no acts of his own, only a plan he puts into another man's head, and the plan detonates the whole succession crisis of 2 Samuel 13-18: Amnon's rape of Tamar, Absalom's revenge, Absalom's coup. Alma 47:4 gives Amalickiah Jonadab's epithet and then makes him his own Absalom: “he laid the plan in his heart to dethrone the king.” Recover 2 Samuel 13 and the chapter that follows in the Book of Mormon is legible as a compressed rerun of the Absalom cycle — the schemer's epithet here, Absalom's twice-refused summons at 47:11, and Absalom's stolen hearts at 47:30, three verses from three consecutive chapters of one biblical narrative inside thirty verses of one Book of Mormon chapter. That concentration is the chapter's finding, and it is exactly Hays's criterion of recurrence: it is the repeated resort to one stretch of scripture, not any single phrase, that makes the dependence hard to decline.

links.note: “He being a very subtle man to do evil.” Four words reproducing a KJV singleton, and the four words are a character label rather than a piece of narrative furniture — the King James Bible applies them to exactly one person. The Book of Mormon adds “to do evil”, which the KJV does not, and modernizes the spelling. This catalogue already carries 2 Samuel 13:3 as a composite at Alma 12:4, where the subject is the devil's subtlety and no string is reproduced; here the string is reproduced and the subject is a man, so the row is written in full.
links.text: But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah David’s brother: and Jonadab was a very subtil man.

pericopes.text: And now he had got the command of those parts of the Lamanites which were in favor of the king; and he sought to gain favor of those which were not obedient; therefore he went forward to the place which was called Onidah, for thither had all the Lamanites fled; for they discovered the army coming, and supposing that they were coming to destroy them, therefore they fled to Onidah, to the place of arms.—
And they had appointed a man to be a king and a leader over them, being fixed in their minds with a determined resolution that they would not be subjected to go against the Nephites.
And it came to pass that they had gathered themselves together upon the top of the mount which was called Antipas, in preparation to battle.

Now it was not Amalickiah’s intention to give them battle, according to the commandments of the king; but behold, it was his intention to gain favor with the armies of the Lamanites, that he might place himself at their head, and dethrone the king, and take possession of the kingdom.
And behold, it came to pass that he caused his army to pitch their tents in the valley which was near the mount Antipas.

And it came to pass that when it was night, he sent a secret embassy into the mount Antipas, desiring that the leader of those which were upon the mount, whose name was Lehonti, that he should come down to the foot of the mount, for he desired to speak with him.

And it came to pass that when Lehonti received the message, he durst not go down to the foot of the mount. And it came to pass that Amalickiah sent again the second time, desiring him to come down. And it came to pass that Lehonti would not; and he sent again the third time.

provenance.other: “Sent again the second time” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 14:29, and the Book of Mormon has it word for word: “Amalickiah sent again the second time.” The KJV verse continues “he would not come”; Alma 47:11 continues “Lehonti would not”. The longer “again the second time” without the verb is spread over six verses and would prove nothing; the auxiliary is what closes the count.
provenance.significance: 2 Samuel 14:29 is Absalom, home from exile and beginning his campaign, unable to get the army's commander to come to him. He sends twice, is twice refused, and escalates — in 14:30 by setting Joab's barley field on fire, which finally brings Joab down. Alma 47:10-13 runs the identical sequence with the identical arithmetic and one change: Amalickiah sends four times rather than two, and instead of forcing his man down he climbs the mount himself. Recover Absalom's context and the shape of what follows is already given — a commander drawn into a usurper's confidence is a commander who has agreed to serve a coup. Joab survives it; Lehonti is poisoned by degrees. The Old Testament's other man on a mountain top who is repeatedly ordered to come down is Elijah in 2 Kings 1:9-13, where three companies are sent and the third captain's plea is what brings the prophet down safely; that scene supplies the mount and the escalating count, and this catalogue uses its opening verse at 1 Nephi 4:1. Alma 47 fuses the two and reverses both outcomes: the man who comes down off the mount is the one who dies.

links.note: Five consecutive words from the only KJV verse that contains them, followed in both texts by the same refusal (“he would not come” / “Lehonti would not”), inside a scene that reproduces the biblical situation — a usurper summoning a soldier who will not come to him, and escalating when refused. The chapter's other Absalom contacts at 47:4 and 47:30 are what raise this from a coincidence of five words to a sustained borrowing. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and not a quotation. The register's entry at this verse explains why Nehemiah 6:2-4, which a reader will also think of, is not the source.
links.text: Therefore Absalom sent for Joab, to have sent him to the king; but he would not come to him: and when he sent again the second time, he would not come.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Amalickiah found that he could not get Lehonti to come down off from the mount, he went up into the mount, nearly to Lehonti’s camp; and he sent again the fourth time, his message unto Lehonti, desiring that he would come down, and that he would bring his guards with him.

And it came to pass that when Lehonti had come down with his guards to Amalickiah, that Amalickiah desired him to come down with his army in the night time, and surround those men in their camps, over whom the king had gave him command, and that he would deliver them up into Lehonti’s hands, if he would make him, (Amalickiah,) a second leader over the whole army.
And it came to pass that Lehonti came down with his men, and surrounded the men of Amalickiah, so that before they awoke at the dawn of the day, they were surrounded by the armies of Lehonti.

And it came to pass that when they saw that they were surrounded, they plead with Amalickiah that he would suffer them to fall in with their brethren, that they might not be destroyed. Now this was the very thing which Amalickiah desired.
And it came to pass that he delivered his men, contrary to the commands of the king. Now this was the thing that Amalickiah desired, that he might accomplish his designs in dethroning the king.
Now it was the custom among the Lamanites, if their chief leader was killed, to appoint the second leader to be their chief leader.
And it came to pass that Amalickiah caused that one of his servants should administer poison, by degrees, to Lehonti, that he died.
Now when Lehonti was dead, the Lamanites appointed Amalickiah to be their leader and their chief commander.
And it came to pass that Amalickiah marched with his armies (for he had gained his desires) to the land of Nephi, to the city of Nephi, which was the chief city.

And the king came out to meet him, with his guards: for he supposed that Amalickiah had fulfilled his commands, and that Amalickiah had gathered together so great an army for to go against the Nephites to battle.

But behold, as the king came out to meet him, Amalickiah caused that his servants should go forth to meet the king. And they went and bowed themselves before the king, as if to reverence him, because of his greatness.—
And it came to pass that the king put forth his hand to raise them, as was the custom with the Lamanites, and a token of peace, which custom they had taken from the Nephites.
And it came to pass that when he had raised the first from the ground, behold, he stabbed the king to the heart; and he fell to the earth.

provenance.other: The Book of Mormon's verb is not the King James Bible's. “Stabbed” occurs in no KJV verse at all, and “gore” as a noun in none — the KJV's verb “gore” at Exodus 21:28 is what an ox does. The KJV's formula for exactly this act is “smote him under the fifth rib”, in four verses (2 Samuel 2:23, 3:27, 4:6, 20:10), and every one of them is a political assassination. Alma 47:24 has the scene and declines the formula, which is a fact about this row worth as much as the resemblance.
provenance.significance: Joab greets Amasa with his right hand out, asks after his health, and kills him with the other hand before the greeting is finished. Alma 47:23-24 builds the same trap out of a different courtesy: the king extends his hand to raise a bowing servant, in what the text stops to explain is “a token of peace”, and the raised man drives in the knife. In both, the gesture that guarantees safety is the gesture that delivers the victim, and in both the killer is a subordinate manoeuvring for the command. What Alma 47 adds is the explanation of the custom — the narrator tells the reader what the raised hand means before showing it betrayed, which is how the scene works on a reader who does not know Joab. Compare Hays on metalepsis: this is the case where the precursor is doing structural work the surface has deliberately made unnecessary.

links.note: The killing of the Lamanite king is the KJV's treacherous-greeting assassination — Joab and Amasa, and behind it Ehud in the summer parlour — with the weapon concealed inside a ceremony of peace. It is figural, not verbal: no phrase is shared, the Book of Mormon's “stabbed … to the heart” is not King James English, and “he fell to the earth” is the only string with any KJV pedigree, and it stands in two verses, one of them Paul on the Damascus road, which has nothing to do with this. Held at moderate because the type-scene is specific and the chapter's other borrowings all come from the same run of 2 Samuel, and no higher because a treacherous greeting is a thing that happens as well as a thing that is written.
links.whyNot: There is no shared wording, and Alma 47:24 pointedly does not use the one KJV idiom that would have settled the question. A reader who requires verbal contact for anything but an avowed type-scene should decline this row and read the assassination as invented narrative.
links.text: And Joab said to Amasa, Art thou in health, my brother? And Joab took Amasa by the beard with the right hand to kiss him.

pericopes.text: Now the servants of the king fled; and the servants of Amalickiah raised a cry, saying:
Behold, the servants of the king have stabbed him to the heart, and he has fell, and they have fled; behold, come and see.

And it came to pass that Amalickiah commanded that his armies should march forth, and see what had happened to the king; and when they had come to the spot, and found the king lying in his gore, Amalickiah pretended to be wroth, and said, Whosoever loved the king, let him go forth and pursue his servants, that they may be slain.
And it came to pass that when all they who loved the king, when they heard these words, came forth and pursued after the servants of the king.
Now when the servants of the king saw an army pursuing after them, they were frightened again, and fled into the wilderness, and came over into the land of Zarahemla, and joined the people of Ammon;
and the army which pursued after them, returned, having pursued after them in vain: and thus Amalickiah, by his fraud, gained the hearts of the people.

provenance.other: “Stole the hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 15:6 — “so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.” “The hearts of the men” occurs in exactly two, 15:6 and 15:13, both of Absalom's coup. Alma 47:30 has “thus Amalickiah, by his fraud, gained the hearts of the people”; the noun phrase and the summarizing “so/thus” are the KJV's, the verb is not.
provenance.significance: This catalogue adjudicated the phrase at Alma 17:29, where Ammon hopes to “win the hearts of these my fellow servants … that I may lead them to believe in my words” — a missionary borrowing a usurper's sentence and meaning it well. Alma 47:30 is not that formula recurring. It is the sentence going home. Amalickiah does with the hearts of the Lamanites exactly what Absalom did with the hearts of Israel: takes a throne by winning a people away from its king, by fraud, having first arranged that the king's own servants be blamed for his death. ADJUDICATING §4 ratified this case in 2026-09-07 at Mosiah 29:2 — a phrase's second use can be the argument when the passage it first translated is the passage now being enacted — and this is the same shape. Ammon steals hearts for God; Amalickiah steals them for himself, which is what the words meant in the first place.

links.note: “Thus Amalickiah, by his fraud, gained the hearts of the people.” The King James Bible has one heart-stealing sentence and it belongs to the Bible's chief usurper, in the chapter that begins his coup. The full row is written here rather than cross-referenced to Alma 17:29 because this is the third contact with 2 Samuel 13-15 in one chapter (13:3 at 47:4, 14:29 at 47:11) and because, unlike at 17:29, the borrower is doing what Absalom did. The verb is changed — “gained” for “stole” — which is Amalickiah's own euphemism and the one word a reader should notice.
links.text: And on this manner did Absalom to all Israel that came to the king for judgment: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass on the morrow, he entered the city Nephi, with his armies, and took possession of the city.

And now it came to pass that the queen, when she had heard that the king was slain: for Amalickiah had sent an embassy to the queen, informing her that the king had been slain by his servants; that he had pursued them with his army, but it was in vain, and they had made their escape:

Therefore when the queen had received this message, she sent unto Amalickiah, desiring him that he would spare the people of the city; and she also desired him that he should come in unto her; and she also desired him that he should bring witnesses with him, to testify concerning the death of the king.

And it came to pass that Amalickiah took the same servant that slew the king, and also they which were with him, and went in unto the queen, unto the place where she sat; and they all testified unto her that the king was slain by his own servants; and they said, also, They have fled: Does not this testify against them? And thus they satisfied the queen concerning the death of the king.

And it came to pass that Amalickiah sought the favor of the queen, and took her unto him to wife; and thus by his fraud, and by the assistance of his cunning servants, he obtained the kingdom; yea, he was acknowledged king throughout all the land, among all the people of the Lamanites, which was composed of the Lamanites, and the Lemuelites, and the Ishmaelites, and all the dissenters of the Nephites, from the reign of Nephi down to the present time.

provenance.route: 1 Kings 2:22 (with 2 Samuel 3:7 and 16:21) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: No wording is shared. “Took her to wife” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 20:30, where it belongs to the Sadducees' levirate riddle and has nothing to do with a throne; it is registered as an exclusion at this verse rather than counted as evidence.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible states the rule this verse depends on, and states it in one sentence: “ask for him the kingdom also.” Solomon says it of Adonijah's request for Abishag, his father's last companion, and he says it as though the inference were too obvious to argue — a claim on the dead king's woman is a claim on the dead king's throne, which is why Abner's taking of Rizpah is treated as treason in 2 Samuel 3:7 and why Ahithophel's advice to Absalom in 16:21 is to go in to his father's concubines publicly. Alma 47:35 draws the same inference in the same breath: “took her unto him to wife; and thus by his fraud … he obtained the kingdom.” The Book of Mormon does not explain the connection between the marriage and the crown any more than 1 Kings 2:22 does, which is the mark of a convention taken over whole rather than reasoned out.

links.note: Amalickiah's last act is to marry the widow of the king he had killed, and the sentence puts the marriage and the kingdom in one clause without connecting them. That silence is the evidence: the equation is a biblical one, stated outright at 1 Kings 2:22 and assumed at 2 Samuel 3:7 and 16:21, and a writer with the KJV in his ear would not need to explain it. Figural, and honestly so — there is no shared wording at all, and the row rests entirely on a convention plus the chapter's demonstrated appetite for 2 Samuel.
links.whyNot: Marrying a dead king's widow to legitimate a usurpation is a commonplace of monarchy and of historical fiction about monarchy, available to any nineteenth-century reader of Shakespeare as readily as of Kings. Nothing in the wording points anywhere, and a reader may reasonably hold that the catalogue is here recording a shared institution rather than a shared text.
links.text: And king Solomon answered and said unto his mother, And why dost thou ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? ask for him the kingdom also; for he is mine elder brother; even for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab the son of Zeruiah.

pericopes.text: Now these dissenters, having the same instruction and the same information of the Nephites; yea, having been instructed in the same knowledge of the Lord; nevertheless, it is strange to relate, not long after their dissentions, they became more hardened and impenitent, and more wild, wicked and ferocious, than the Lamanites; drinking in with the traditions of the Lamanites; giving way to indolence, and all manner of lasciviousness; yea, entirely forgetting the Lord their God.

provenance.other: “Forgat the LORD their God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 3:7 and 1 Samuel 12:9. Alma 47:36 has “entirely forgetting the Lord their God”, with the participle for the preterite and an adverb the KJV does not supply.
provenance.significance: Judges 3:7 is the first sentence of the Judges cycle proper — Israel does evil, forgets the LORD, serves Baalim, and is sold into a foreign hand — and 1 Samuel 12:9 is Samuel's summary of the same cycle at the moment Israel asks for a king. Alma 47:36 uses the formula for Nephite dissenters who have gone over to the Lamanites and become worse than their hosts, and the chapter it closes has just installed a foreign king over them. The Deuteronomistic diagnosis has been transferred from a people who forget God in prosperity to a people who forget him in defection, and the Book of Mormon keeps the diagnosis's terms while inverting its direction of travel: in Judges the forgetting brings the foreign power in, here it is the consequence of having gone out.

links.note: “Drinking in with the traditions of the Lamanites; giving way to indolence, and all manner of lasciviousness; yea, entirely forgetting the Lord their God.” The closing phrase is the King James Bible's apostasy formula, which stands in exactly two verses and marks the opening and the summary of the same historical cycle. It is an echo rather than an allusion because the Book of Mormon changes the tense and inserts an adverb, and because this is the kind of pious clause a writer steeped in the KJV would produce without reaching for a verse.
links.text: And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, and forgat the LORD their God, and served Baalim and the groves.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that as soon as Amalickiah had obtained the kingdom, he began to inspire the hearts of the Lamanites against the people of Nephi; yea, he did appoint men to speak unto the Lamanites from their towers, against the Nephites;

and thus he did inspire their hearts against the Nephites, insomuch, that in the latter end of the nineteenth year of the reign of the Judges, he having accomplished his designs thus far; yea, having been made king over the Lamanites, he sought also to reign over all the land; yea, and all the people which were in the land; the Nephites as well as the Lamanites;

therefore he had accomplished his design: for he had hardened the hearts of the Lamanites, and blinded their minds, and stirred them up to anger, insomuch that he had gathered together a numerous host, to go to battle against the Nephites.
For he was determined, because of the greatness of the number of his people, to overpower the Nephites, and to bring them into bondage:

and thus he did appoint Chief Captains of the Zoramites, they being the most acquainted with the strength of the Nephites, and their places of resort, and the weakest parts of their cities; therefore he appointed them to be Chief Captains over his armies.
And it came to pass that they took their camp, and moved forth towards the land of Zarahemla, in the wilderness.

Now it came to pass that while Amalickiah had thus been obtaining power by fraud and deceit, Moroni, on the other hand, had been a preparing the minds of the people to be faithful unto the Lord their God;

yea, he had been strengthening the armies of the Nephites, and erecting small forts, or places of resort; throwing up banks of earth round about, to enclose his armies, and also building walls of stone to encircle them about, round about their cities, and the borders of their lands;
yea, all round about the land; and in their weakest fortifications, he did place the greater number of men; and thus he did fortify and strengthen the land which was possessed by the Nephites.

And thus he was preparing to support their liberty, their lands, their wives, and their children, and their peace, and that they might live unto the Lord their God, and that they might maintain that which was called by their enemies the cause of Christians.

And Moroni was a strong and a mighty man; he was a man of a perfect understanding; yea, a man that did not delight in bloodshed; a man whose soul did joy in the liberty and the freedom of his country, and his brethren from bondage and slavery;

provenance.other: “Perfect understanding” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:3. The Book of Mormon adds an indefinite article — “a man of a perfect understanding” — and the fuller string “a perfect understanding” occurs in no KJV verse, so the borrowing is of the collocation and not of a clause.
provenance.significance: Luke 1:3 is the King James Bible's one sentence in which a writer explains his qualifications for compiling a record: having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, he will write in order for Theophilus. The phrase belongs to a historian's preface, not to a soldier. Alma 48 is the Book of Mormon's most conspicuous compiler's intrusion — Mormon stopping his narrative to say what kind of man Moroni was, and, seven verses later, to say what would have happened to the powers of hell if all men had been like him — and the compliment he reaches for is the phrase the KJV gives to the evangelist introducing his own abridgment. The suppressed correspondence is between the two abridgers rather than between Moroni and Luke: the one place the King James Bible praises a man for perfect understanding is the place a writer is vouching for the reliability of what follows.

links.note: “He was a man of a perfect understanding.” Two words, one KJV verse, and a wholly different register in each: a Gospel preface against a general's obituary. It is an allusion rather than an echo because the collocation is genuinely distinctive — the KJV pairs “perfect” with “understanding” nowhere else — and moderate rather than high because two words plus an added article is a slender base and the phrase is unremarkable English on its own. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold.
links.whyNot: “Perfect understanding” is an ordinary compliment in nineteenth-century English and needs no biblical model; the KJV's single occurrence may say more about how rarely the King James translators used the word “perfect” of an intellect than about where Alma 48:11 got its phrase.
links.text: It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,

provenance.other: “Delight in war” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 68:30 — “scatter thou the people that delight in war.” The Book of Mormon's object is different: “did not delight in bloodshed” here, “not in the shedding of blood” at 48:16, “they did not delight in the shedding of blood” at 48:23. That last is the psalm's verb married to the noun phrase of Hebrews 9:22, which this catalogue adjudicates at Alma 34:13 and carries as a composite at Alma 24:17.
provenance.significance: Psalm 68:30 is a prayer that God scatter the warlike, and it is the King James Bible's only use of “delight” with war as its object. Alma 48 states the negative of it three times in fifteen verses, of the man who is at that moment fortifying every city in the land. The chapter's whole difficulty — a book praising a general for not being warlike — is the psalm's category being invoked in order to be denied, and the denial is what licenses everything Moroni then does. Recover the psalm's context and the prayer is for the scattering of the nations that come against Israel, which is precisely the position Moroni's enemies occupy and precisely the position he is at pains not to occupy himself.

links.note: “A man that did not delight in bloodshed”, and again at 48:16 and 48:23. The collocation the Book of Mormon is negating stands in one KJV verse, and its object there is war rather than blood; the Book of Mormon substitutes the noun phrase of Hebrews 9:22. Held at echo because neither element is reproduced intact and the sentiment is available without a source, and at moderate because the triple repetition inside one chapter is the shape of a writer working from a phrase rather than reaching a thought twice.
links.whyNot: Nobody needs Psalm 68 to say that a good man does not enjoy killing. The row rests on a single verb-plus-object collocation whose KJV rarity may be an accident of the psalter's vocabulary, and a reader who declines it loses nothing from the chapter.
links.text: Rebuke the company of spearmen, the multitude of the bulls, with the calves of the people, till every one submit himself with pieces of silver: scatter thou the people that delight in war.

pericopes.text: yea, a man whose heart did swell with thanksgiving to his God, for the many privileges and blessings which he bestowed upon his people; a man who did labor exceedingly for the welfare and safety of his people;
yea, and he was a man who was firm in the faith of Christ, and he had sworn with an oath, to defend his people, his rights, and his country, and his religion, even to the loss of his blood.

provenance.other: “Sworn with an oath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:30, and the Book of Mormon reproduces the four words without change: “he had sworn with an oath, to defend his people.” The phrase returns at Alma 49:17 of the Lamanite chief captains, which is the same book and the same narrator's formula.
provenance.significance: In Acts 2:30 the swearer is God and the oath is the Davidic promise — Peter at Pentecost, arguing from Psalm 132 that God bound himself by oath to set Christ on David's throne. It is the King James Bible's one solemn-oath formula, and it belongs to a promise about a king. Alma 48:13 puts it in the mouth of the man who has just prevented one: Moroni swears, in his own person, to defend “his people, his rights, and his country, and his religion, even to the loss of his blood”, in the chapter after a usurper took a throne by fraud. The oath that in Acts establishes a monarchy here underwrites a republic. Note also what the borrowing does to 49:17, where the Lamanite captains swear with the same oath to take a city: the formula is applied to both sides, and the Book of Mormon does not mark the difference — the difference is in what is sworn to.

links.note: Four consecutive words reproducing the King James Bible's only oath-formula of this shape, in the chapter's most formal sentence. The catalogue's row for the second Alma occurrence is at 49:17; this is the first use in the book and carries the argument. Not a quotation and well below Skousen's threshold, but the string is exact and the source is unique.
links.text: Therefore being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne;

pericopes.text: Now the Nephites were taught to defend themselves against their enemies, even to the shedding of blood, if it were necessary; yea, and they were also taught never to give an offence; yea, and never to raise the sword, except it were against an enemy, except it were to preserve their lives:

provenance.other: “Give none offence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 10:32 — “Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God.” Alma 48:14 has “they were also taught never to give an offence”, with the KJV's verb and its object and a negative adverb for the KJV's negative determiner. This catalogue already carries 1 Corinthians 10:32 as a composite at Alma 4:10, where the shared material is Paul's stumblingblock argument rather than this phrase.
provenance.significance: Paul's rule is about the table and the conscience of a watching outsider: do not let your liberty be the thing that trips a Jew, a Gentile, or the church. Alma 48:14 makes it a rule of war. “Never to give an offence; yea, and never to raise the sword, except it were against an enemy” — the second clause glosses the first, so that giving offence now means striking first. Recover Paul's context and the transposition is doing real work: the Nephite doctrine of the defensive war is grounded in an apostolic rule about not being a stumblingblock, which is why the chapter can insist in the same breath that Moroni fortified every city and that his people never gave offence. The word “offence” carries its Pauline sense of an occasion of stumbling into a sentence about who may draw a sword first.

links.note: A KJV singleton, reproduced with the verb and object intact, in the sentence that states the Book of Mormon's doctrine of defensive war. The catalogue's earlier row at Alma 4:10 uses this verse for its stumblingblock clause; the phrase itself is borrowed here, and the two uses are different enough that the row is written rather than cross-referenced. Moderate rather than high because three words is a slender base and “give offence” had long since passed into ordinary English independent of Paul.
links.whyNot: “Give offence” is common English and the KJV's single occurrence of the imperative may be incidental; the Book of Mormon's sentence would read the same if no biblical rule stood behind it, and its own following clause about the sword supplies all the sense the passage needs.
links.text: Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God:

pericopes.text: and this was their faith, that by so doing, God would prosper them in the land; or in other words, if they were faithful in keeping the commandments of God, that he would prosper them in the land; yea, warn them to flee, or to prepare for war, according to their danger;

and also, that God would make it known unto them, whither they should go to defend themselves against their enemies; and by so doing, the Lord would deliver them: and this was the faith of Moroni; and his heart did glory in it; not in the shedding of blood, but in doing good, in preserving his people; yea, in keeping the commandments of God; yea, and resisting iniquity.

Yea, verily, verily I say unto you, If all men had been, and were, and ever would be, like unto Moroni, behold, the very powers of hell would have been shaken forever; yea, the Devil would never have no power over the hearts of the children of men.
Behold, he was a man like unto Ammon, the son of Mosiah, yea, and even the other sons of Mosiah; yea, and also Alma and his sons: for they were all men of God.

Now behold, Helaman and his brethren were no less serviceable unto the people, than was Moroni; for they did preach the word of God, and they did baptize unto repentance, all men whosoever would hearken unto their words.

And thus they went forth, and the people did humble themselves because of their words, insomuch that they were highly favored of the Lord; and thus they were free from wars and contentions among themselves; yea, even for the space of four years.
But as I have said in the latter end of the nineteenth; yea, notwithstanding their peace amongst themselves, they were compelled reluctantly to contend with their brethren, the Lamanites;
yea, and in fine, their wars never did cease for the space of many years with the Lamanites, notwithstanding their much reluctance.

Now they were sorry to take up arms against the Lamanites, because they did not delight in the shedding of blood; yea, and this was not all; they were sorry to be the means of sending so many of their brethren out of this world into an eternal world, unprepared to meet their God;

nevertheless, they could not suffer to lay down their lives, that their wives and their children should be massacred by the barbarous cruelty of those who was once their brethren, yea, and had dissented from their church, and had left them, and had gone to destroy them, by joining the Lamanites;

links.text: Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.

provenance.other: “Lay down our lives” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 3:16 — “we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” — and it is the King James Bible's only plural of the idiom; the singular “lay down his life” is likewise a singleton, at John 15:13. Alma 48:24 has “they could not suffer to lay down their lives”, which is the plural with a third-person pronoun and a negative. “Lay down their lives” with that pronoun occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: 1 John 3:16 states the duty in the plural and names its beneficiaries: we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren. Alma 48:24 refuses it, and refuses it on a ground the epistle does not consider — “they could not suffer to lay down their lives, that their wives and their children should be massacred by the barbarous cruelty of those who was once their brethren.” The word “brethren” is in both sentences and it has changed sides: in the epistle the brethren are whom you die for, and in Alma 48:24 the brethren are the dissenters who would do the killing. That is the chapter's whole moral problem in one clause, and the borrowing is what makes it visible. Compare Hays on metalepsis — the suppressed term is the epistle's next verse, on shutting up one's bowels of compassion from a brother in need, which is exactly the charge the Nephites are anticipating against themselves for taking up arms.

links.note: “They could not suffer to lay down their lives, that their wives and their children should be massacred.” The King James Bible forms this plural once, and it forms it as a command; Alma 48:24 forms it as an impossibility. Held at moderate rather than high because the idiom had long been ordinary English and the negative construction is the Book of Mormon's own, but the plural and the shared noun “brethren” are more than the singular Johannine tag would give. The catalogue's other row for this verse is at Alma 53:17, where the pledge is made rather than declined; this is the first use in the book and carries the argument.
links.whyNot: “Lay down one's life” is thoroughly naturalized English and no writer needs 1 John to reach it, and Alma 48:24's sentence is a negation, which is the weakest kind of verbal contact. A reader may hold that the catalogue has found a common idiom and read an inversion into an accident.

pericopes.text: yea, they could not bear that their brethren should rejoice over the blood of the Nephites, so long as there were any who should keep the commandments of God: for the promise of the Lord were, If they should keep his commandments, they should prosper in the land.
And now it came to pass, in the eleventh month of the nineteenth year, on the tenth day of the month, the armies of the Lamanites were seen approaching towards the land of Ammonihah.

And behold, the city had been re-built, and Moroni had stationed an army by the borders of the city, and they had cast up dirt round about, to shield them from the arrows and the stones of the Lamanites; for behold, they fought with stones, and with arrows.

links.text: Therefore thus saith the LORD concerning the king of Assyria, He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shield, nor cast a bank against it.

provenance.route: 2 Kings 19:32 (= Isaiah 37:33) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Cast a bank' occurs in two KJV verses, 2 Kings 19:32 and its Isaiah 37:33 doublet; 'cast up a bank' in exactly one, 2 Samuel 20:15, where it is the besieger who casts it. The two candidate verses differ by a single letter — 2 Kings has 'with shield', Isaiah 'with shields' — and Alma 49:2's 'shield' is a verb, not the noun, so the doublet cannot be decided from this verse. Alma 49:6's 'shields' is plural, which would favour Isaiah if it were the same clause. It is not.
provenance.significance: The oracle against Sennacherib promises Jerusalem four things her enemy will not do: come into the city, shoot an arrow there, come before it with shield, cast a bank against it. Alma 49 grants the Lamanites three of the four and takes the fourth away from them — they shoot arrows, they come with shields, they cannot enter, and the bank is already there because the defenders cast it up first. Read the source's context back into the borrowing and the rest of the chapter falls into place: the foreign king does not come down himself (49:10-11), his host is destroyed without a single defender lost (49:23), he blasphemes the God of the city he could not take (49:27), and he returns to his own land to be killed in his tent (51:34). That is the shape of 2 Kings 18-19 from the Rabshakeh's boast to Sennacherib's murder at Nineveh, run once through a Nephite war chapter.

links.note: The chapter's siege vocabulary is the KJV's, redistributed. Alma 49:2 has the Nephites 'cast up dirt round about, to shield them from the arrows and the stones'; 49:18 has 'the highness of the bank which had been thrown up, and the depth of the ditch'; 49:22 has the Lamanites trying to 'dig down their banks of earth'. In the KJV a bank is what an army casts up against a city (2 Samuel 20:15) or is forbidden to (2 Kings 19:32), never what a city casts up around itself, and Moroni's innovation is exactly that reversal — which is why the Lamanite captains are 'astonished exceedingly' at a technique 'which never had been known' (49:5, 49:8). The link is placed at 49:2 because that is where the earthwork, the arrows and the shielding stand in one sentence; the elements are distributed across the chapter and each word of them is ordinary siege English, which is what holds the confidence at moderate.
links.whyNot: No clause is reproduced. 'Bank', 'ditch', 'arrows' and 'shield' are the common stock of any English siege narrative, and a writer describing fortifications in KJV idiom would reach for them without a source. The argument rests on the distribution — four of the oracle's elements in the right relation, plus the Sennacherib outcome — not on any one phrase.

pericopes.text: Behold, I said that the city of Ammonihah had been re-built. I say unto you, yea, that it was in part re-built, and because the Lamanites had destroyed it once because of the iniquity of the people, they supposed that it would again become an easy prey for them.

But behold, how great was their disappointment; for behold, the Nephites had dug up a ridge of earth round about them, which was so high that the Lamanites could not cast their stones and their arrows at them, that they might take effect; neither could they come upon them, save it was by their place of entrance.
Now at this time, the Chief Captains of the Lamanites were astonished exceedingly, because of the wisdom of the Nephites in preparing their places of security.

Now the leaders of the Lamanites had supposed, because of the greatness of their numbers; yea, they supposed that they should be privileged to come upon them as they had hitherto done; yea, and they had also prepared themselves with shields, and with breast-plates; and they had also prepared themselves with garments of skins; yea, very thick garments, to cover their nakedness.

links.text: And thou shalt make them linen breeches to cover their nakedness; from the loins even unto the thighs they shall reach:

provenance.route: Exodus 28:42 + Genesis 3:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
