provenance.other: 'To cover their nakedness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 28:42, of the linen breeches made for Aaron and his sons. 'Coats of skins' occurs in exactly one, Genesis 3:21. 'Garments of skins' occurs in none: the Book of Mormon has the substance of Genesis 3:21 in words that are not quite its own, and the priestly formula verbatim.
provenance.significance: Both KJV singletons behind this armour are garments God gives, not armour men make. Genesis 3:21 clothes the newly ashamed; Exodus 28:42 clothes the priest so that he may approach the altar and 'not bear iniquity, and die' (28:43). The Lamanites put on the two garments of covered nakedness in order to approach a fortification, and die anyway. The narrative has already told us why the covering is needed: nakedness has been the Lamanites' mark since 2 Nephi 5:24 and Enos 1:20, so the verse quietly reports that the Lamanites have taken the remedy Genesis and Exodus supply and turned it into equipment for a massacre (49:7).

links.note: 'They had also prepared themselves with shields, and with breast-plates; and they had also prepared themselves with garments of skins; yea, very thick garments, to cover their nakedness.' The four-word run 'to cover their nakedness' is a KJV singleton and the sentence it comes from is the last item of the priestly wardrobe in Exodus 28. Skins and the covering of nakedness together are Genesis 3:21's provision, and the two rare phrases arrive in one clause. Held at moderate because the sentence is describing armour and the borrowing may be no more than the readiest English for what armour does; that it reaches for the priestly phrase rather than 'to cover them' is the reason for recording it.

pericopes.text: And being thus prepared, they supposed that they should easily overpower and subject their brethren to the yoke of bondage, or slay and massacre them according to their pleasure.

But behold, to their uttermost astonishment, they were prepared for them, in a manner which never had been known among all the children of Lehi. Now they were prepared for the Lamanites, to battle, after the manner of the instructions of Moroni.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites, or the Amalickiahites, were exceedingly astonished at their manner of preparation for war.

Now if king Amalickiah had come down out of the land of Nephi, at the head of his army, perhaps he would have caused the Lamanites to have attacked the Nephites at the city of Ammonihah; for behold, he did care not for the blood of his people.

But behold, Amalickiah did not come down himself, to battle. And behold, his Chief Captains durst not attack the Nephites at the city of Ammonihah, for Moroni had altered the management of affairs among the Nephites, insomuch that the Lamanites were disappointed in their places of retreat, and they could not come upon them;
therefore they retreated into the wilderness, and took their camp, and marched towards the land of Noah, supposing that to be the next best place for them to come against the Nephites;

for they knew not that Moroni had fortified or had built forts of security for every city in all the land round about; therefore they marched forward to the land of Noah, with a firm determination; yea, their Chief Captains came forward, and took an oath that they would destroy the people of that city.
But behold, to their astonishment, the city of Noah, which had hitherto been a weak place, had now, by the means of Moroni, become strong; yea, even to exceed the strength of the city Ammonihah.

And now behold, this was wisdom in Moroni; for he had supposed that they would be frightened at the city Ammonihah; and as the city of Noah had hitherto been the weakest part of the land, therefore they would march thither to battle; and thus it was, according to his desires.
And behold, Moroni had appointed Lehi to be Chief Captain over the men of that city; and it was that same Lehi which fought with the Lamanites in the valley, on the east of the river Sidon.

And now behold, it came to pass, that when the Lamanites had found that Lehi commanded the city, they were again disappointed, for they feared Lehi exceedingly; nevertheless, their Chief Captains had sworn with an oath, to attack the city; therefore they brought up their armies.

links.text: Therefore being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne;

provenance.other: 'Sworn with an oath' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:30. The Old Testament's cognate formula is 'sware with an oath' (Numbers 30:10 has 'bound her soul by a bond with an oath'); the perfect participle is Peter's.
provenance.significance: The one KJV oath sworn with an oath is God's to David, that of the fruit of his loins he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne — Peter's proof text at Pentecost that a promise sworn this way cannot fail. Alma 49 puts the phrase in the mouths of captains who swear to take a city, and the next six verses kill every one of them (49:23). The catalogue's interest is in the pairing: the formula the New Testament reserves for the one oath that holds is here used for an oath that is broken by the death of everyone who swore it, and the chapter says twice that they swore (49:13, 49:17) before it says that they all fell.

links.note: 'Their Chief Captains had sworn with an oath, to attack the city.' A six-word run against the only KJV verse that contains it, and the fear of Lehi in the same sentence is what makes the oath rather than the tactics decide their movement. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation, and catalogued as an allusion accordingly. The confidence is moderate rather than high because 'sworn with an oath' is unremarkable English and the context in Acts is remote from a Lamanite war council; the rarity count, not the setting, is the evidence.

pericopes.text: Now behold, the Lamanites could not get into their forts of security, by any other way save by the entrance, because of the highness of the bank which had been thrown up, and the depth of the ditch which had been dug round about, save it were by the entrance.
And thus were the Nephites prepared to destroy all such as should attempt to climb up to enter the fort, by any other way, by casting over stones and arrows at them.

Thus they were prepared; yea, a body of their most strong men, with their swords and their slings, to smite down all who should attempt to come into their place of security, by the place of entrance; and thus were they prepared to defend themselves against the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that the Captains of the Lamanites brought up their armies before the place of entrance, and began to contend with the Nephites, to get into their place of security; but behold, they were driven back from time to time, insomuch that they were slain, with an immense slaughter.

Now when they found that they could not obtain power over the Nephites by the pass, they began to dig down their banks of earth, that they might obtain a pass to their armies, that they might have an equal chance to fight; but behold, in these attempts, they were swept off by the stones and the arrows which were thrown at them; and instead of filling up their ditches by pulling down the banks of earth, they were filled up in a measure, with their dead and wounded bodies.

Thus the Nephites had all power over their enemies; and thus the Lamanites did attempt to destroy the Nephites, until their Chief Captains were all slain; yea, and more than a thousand of the Lamanites were slain; while on the other hand, there was not a single soul of the Nephites which were slain.

There were about fifty which were wounded, which had been exposed to the arrows of the Lamanites through the pass; but they were shielded by their shields, and their breast-plates, and their head-plates, insomuch thattheir wounds were upon their legs; many of which were very severe.

And it came to pass, that when the Lamanites saw that their Chief Captains were all slain, they fled into the wilderness. And it came to pass that they returned to the land of Nephi, to inform their King, Amalickiah, who was a Nephite by birth, concerning their great loss.
And it came to pass that he was exceeding angry with his people, because he had not obtained his desire over the Nephites; he had not subjected them to the yoke of bondage;

yea, he was exceeding wroth, and he did curse God, and also Moroni, and swearing with an oath that he would drink his blood; and this because Moroni had kept the commandments of God in preparing for the safety of his people.

links.text: Then said his wife unto him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die.

provenance.other: 'Curse God' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 2:9. Job 1:5 and 1:11 and 2:5 use 'curse thee' and 'curse thee to thy face' of the same act; the bare imperative with God as its object is the wife's alone.
provenance.significance: Job's wife names two things in one breath: the integrity a man retains, and the cursing of God that would end him. Alma 49:27 names the same two and assigns them to different men. Amalickiah curses God, 'and this because Moroni had kept the commandments of God in preparing for the safety of his people' — that is, another man's retained integrity is given as the cause of the cursing, which is the exact relation Job 2:9 sets up and then leaves unresolved. The Book of Mormon resolves it by splitting the verse between two characters, and by carrying the consequence Job's wife attaches to the cursing ('and die') forward to Amalickiah's own death two chapters later.

links.note: 'He was exceeding wroth, and he did curse God, and also Moroni.' The KJV has exactly one verse in which anyone is told to curse God, and it is the verse that also asks 'Dost thou still retain thine integrity?' — the two halves that Alma 49:27 holds together, the cursing and the other man's kept commandments. The 1830's 'exceeding wroth' (1920 'exceedingly') keeps the KJV's adverbial 'exceeding' here, as at 49:26. Note that the Book of Mormon uses the phrase of a man doing it, where Job 2:9 has it as advice refused; the borrowing takes the act his wife proposed and gives it to someone who performs it.

links.text: Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.

provenance.other: 'Drink his blood' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 6:53. The other four KJV verses that drink blood name what is drunk — the blood of the slain (Numbers 23:24), of these men (1 Chronicles 11:19), of goats (Psalm 50:13), of the princes of the earth (Ezekiel 39:18). Only John has the pronoun, and only John makes the drinking a condition of life.
provenance.significance: The one man in the King James Bible whose blood anyone is invited to drink is the Son of man, and the invitation is that without it 'ye have no life in you'. Amalickiah swears in the same three words to drink the blood of the one man in the chapter who has kept the commandments of God, and the oath is the thing that kills him: 'his promise which he made, was rash' (51:10), and the javelin goes into his heart while he sleeps (51:34). Standing beside the cursing of God in the same sentence, the borrowing reads as a deliberate inversion — the eucharistic condition of life sworn as a threat of death, by a man who has just blasphemed.

links.note: 'Swearing with an oath that he would drink his blood.' The three words are a KJV singleton and they arrive in the same clause as a second singleton, 'curse God' (Job 2:9), which is the argument for taking the coincidence seriously: one rare phrase in a verse is chance, two rare phrases from two testaments in one sentence is a habit of composition. The oath recurs at 51:9 in the form 'drink the blood of Moroni' and is answered at 51:34. Held at moderate, and kjvSpecific left uncertain, because an oath to drink an enemy's blood is a stock threat in English independent of any Bible.
links.whyNot: 'Drink his blood' as a vow of vengeance is ordinary nineteenth-century English and needs no scriptural source; the KJV singleton may be an accident of how seldom the Bible attaches that pronoun to that verb. The link rests on the company it keeps in 49:27, not on the phrase alone.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass, that on the other hand, the people of Nephi did thank the Lord their God, because of his matchless power in delivering them from the hands of their enemies.
And thus ended the nineteenth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi;

yea, and there was continual peace among them, and exceeding great prosperity in the church, because of their heed and diligence which they gave unto the word of God, which was declared unto them by Helaman, and Shiblon, and Corianton, and Ammon, and his brethren, &c.; yea, and by all those which had been ordained by the holy order of God, being baptised unto repentance, and sent forth to preach among the people, &c.

And now it came to pass that Moroni did not stop making preparations for war, or to defend themselves against the Lamanites; for he caused that his armies should commence in the commencement of the twentieth year of the reign of the Judges, that they should commence in digging up heaps of earth round about all the cities, throughout all the land which was possessed by the Nephites;
and upon the top of these ridges of earth, he caused that there should be timbers; yea, works of timbers built up to the height of a man, round about the cities.
And he caused that upon those works of timbers, that there should be a frame of pickets built upon the timbers, round about; and they were strong and high;

and he caused towers to be erected that overlooked those works of pickets; and he caused places of security to be built upon those towers, that the stones and the arrows of the Lamanites could not hurt them.

links.text: And he made in Jerusalem engines, invented by cunning men, to be on the towers and upon the bulwarks, to shoot arrows and great stones withal. And his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong.

provenance.other: 'Built towers' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 26:9 and 26:10, both of Uzziah. 'Arrows and great stones' occurs in exactly one, 2 Chronicles 26:15, and it is the only verse in the Bible that puts towers, arrows and stones in a single engineering sentence. The Book of Mormon does not reproduce either phrase — it has 'towers' and 'the stones and the arrows' in the reversed order — which is what holds this at moderate.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 26 is the KJV's one sustained account of a king who fortifies his way to safety, and it does not end well: 'his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong. But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction' (26:15-16). Alma 50 follows the same curve inside twenty verses. The fortifications go up (50:1-6), the people 'did prosper exceedingly, and they became exceeding rich; yea, and they did multiply, and were strong in the land' (50:18), and the narrator then explains at once that what destroys this people is 'their quarrellings, and their contentions; yea, their murderings, and their plunderings, their idolatry, their whoredoms' (50:21) — Uzziah's transgression at the moment of his strength, distributed across a nation. The link is worth having for that reason and not for its wording: recover 26:16 and Alma 50:18's prosperity notice stops being a happy ending.

links.note: 'He caused towers to be erected that overlooked those works of pickets; and he caused places of security to be built upon those towers, that the stones and the arrows of the Lamanites could not hurt them.' The King James Bible has two fortification set pieces, Uzziah's in 2 Chronicles 26:9-15 and Hezekiah's in 32:5, and Alma 50:1-6 is built from the elements of both — towers, walls raised, engines on the towers against arrows and stones, strongholds round about every city. Uzziah is the closer of the two because his towers carry the shooting engines and because his account supplies the moral the chapter goes on to draw. Held at moderate: nothing is quoted, and a writer describing earthworks, timbers, pickets and towers is describing a real technology, not necessarily a text.
links.whyNot: The vocabulary is technical and common. Towers, walls, stones and arrows appear in every KJV siege, and the strongest single count here — 'arrows and great stones' at 2 Chronicles 26:15 — is a phrase the Book of Mormon does not use. The case is the sequence (fortify, prosper, grow strong, be destroyed by what strength permits) rather than the words.

pericopes.text: And they were prepared, that they could cast stones from the top thereof, according to their pleasure and their strength, and slay him which should attempt to approach near the walls of the city.
Thus Moroni did prepare strong holds against the coming of their enemies, round about every city in all the land.

And it came to pass that Moroni caused that his armies should go forth into the east wilderness; yea, and they went forth, and drove all the Lamanites which were in the east wilderness into their own lands, which were south of the land of Zarahemla;
and the land of Nephi did run in a straight course from the East Sea to the West.

And it came to pass that when Moroni had driven all the Lamanites out of the east wilderness, which was north of the lands of their own possessions, he caused that the inhabitants which were in the land of Zarahemla, and in the land round about, should go forth into the east wilderness, even to the borders, by the seashore, and possess the land.

And he also placed armies on the south, in the borders of their possessions, and caused them to erect fortifications, that they might secure their armies and their people from the hands of their enemies.

And thus he cut off all the strong holds of the Lamanites, in the east wilderness; yea, and also on the west, fortifying the line between the Nephites and the Lamanites, between the land of Zarahemla and the land of Nephi; from the West Sea, running by the head of the river Sidon; the Nephites possessing all the land northward; yea, even all the land which was northward of the land Bountiful, according to their pleasure.

Thus Moroni, with his armies, which did increase daily, because of the assurance of protection which his works did bring forth unto them; therefore they did seek to cut off the strength and the power of the Lamanites, from off the lands of their possessions, that they should have no power upon the lands of their possession.

And it came to pass that the Nephites began the foundation of a city; and they called the name of the city Moroni; and it was by the East Sea; and it was on the south by the line of the possessions of the Lamanites.
And they also began a foundation for a city, between the city of Moroni and the city of Aaron, joining the borders of Aaron and Moroni; and they called the name of the city, or the land, Nephihah.
And they also began, in that same year, to build many cities on the north; one in a particular manner, which they called Lehi, which was in the north, by the borders of the seashore.
And thus ended the twentieth year.
And in these prosperous circumstances were the people of Nephi, in the commencement of the twenty and first year of the reign of the Judges, over the people of Nephi.
And they did prosper exceedingly, and they became exceeding rich; yea, and they did multiply, and were strong in the land.

And thus we see how merciful and just are all the dealings of the Lord, to the fulfilling of all his words unto the children of men; yea, we can behold that his words are verified, even at this time, which he spake unto Lehi, saying:

links.text: And now, O God of Israel, let thy word, I pray thee, be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father.

provenance.route: 1 Kings 8:26 (doublet at 2 Chronicles 6:17) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Verified' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Genesis 42:20, where Joseph tests his brothers, and 1 Kings 8:26 with its Chronicles doublet 2 Chronicles 6:17, which are the same sentence of Solomon's dedication prayer. The doublet cannot be decided here — mediation-check.py finds no divergence the Book of Mormon reproduces — though Alma's simple preterite 'he spake unto Lehi' sits nearer 1 Kings's 'thou spakest' than 2 Chronicles's 'thou hast spoken'.
provenance.alternative: 2 Chronicles 6:17, verbally indistinguishable at every point Alma 50:19 touches.
provenance.significance: Solomon asks that a promise made to a named father be verified, at the dedication of the temple, and the promise is the conditional dynastic covenant: keep my commandments and thy children shall not fail. Alma 50:19-21 declares that the promise made to a named father has been verified, and then quotes it — and the promise quoted at 50:20 is the conditional prosperity clause of 1 Nephi 2:20-21, whose biblical shape is the same Kings covenant, down to the threat at 1 Kings 9:6-7 of being cut off out of the land. So the narrator does not merely borrow a rare word; he takes over Solomon's whole speech act. The difference is the tense. Solomon prays that the word may be verified; the Nephite historian reports that it has been, 'even at this time'.

links.note: 'His words are verified, even at this time, which he spake unto Lehi, saying.' 'Verified' is one of the rarer words in the KJV and two of its three occurrences are one sentence — Solomon's 'let thy word be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father'. The Book of Mormon reproduces its frame exactly: word(s) + verified + relative clause + 'spake unto' + the named patriarch. Alma 50:21 then repeats it ('these promises have been verified'), which is what a writer does with a formula he has just picked up rather than a word he happened to use. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and catalogued as an allusion.

pericopes.text: Blessed art thou, and thy children; and they shall be blessed, inasmuch as they shall keep my commandments; they shall prosper in the land. But remember, inasmuch as they will not keep my commandments, they shall be cut off from the presence of the Lord.

And we see that these promises have been verified to the people of Nephi; for it has been their quarrellings, and their contentions; yea, their murderings, and their plunderings, their idolatry, their whoredoms, and their abominations, which were among themselves, which brought upon them their wars and their destructions.

And those who were faithful in keeping the commandments of the Lord, were delivered at all times, whilst thousands of their wicked brethren have been consigned to bondage, or to perish by the sword, or to dwindle in unbelief, and mingle with the Lamanites.

links.text: But if they obey not, they shall perish by the sword, and they shall die without knowledge.

provenance.other: 'Perish by the sword' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 36:12. The KJV's ordinary idioms are 'fall by the sword' (some thirty verses) and 'die by the sword'; 'perish' with 'by the sword' is Elihu's alone.
provenance.significance: Elihu's couplet is a two-branch conditional: 'If they obey and serve him, they shall spend their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasures. But if they obey not, they shall perish by the sword, and they shall die without knowledge.' Alma 50:22 is that couplet with both branches intact and the second one expanded — the faithful 'were delivered at all times', the wicked are 'consigned to bondage, or to perish by the sword, or to dwindle in unbelief'. The third term is the finding: 'dwindle in unbelief' is the Book of Mormon's standing phrase, and here it stands in Job's slot for 'die without knowledge'. Recovering Elihu's context shows the Nephite historian using a wisdom text, not a covenant text, to explain his own nation's history — and Elihu is the speaker God does not answer, which the narrator either does not know or does not mind.

links.note: 'And those who were faithful in keeping the commandments of the Lord, were delivered at all times, whilst thousands of their wicked brethren have been consigned to bondage, or to perish by the sword, or to dwindle in unbelief, and mingle with the Lamanites.' The sentence is Job 36:11-12's two-branch conditional in the same order, and its one distinctive phrase is a KJV singleton. Preceding verses supply the prosperity half in Elihu's own terms ('they did prosper exceedingly', 50:18). The n-gram stream did not propose this: it is split across a clause boundary in the way CONVENTIONS §9 describes.

pericopes.text: But behold, there never was a happier time among the people of Nephi, since the days of Nephi, than in the days of Moroni; yea, even at this time, in the twenty and first year of the reign of the Judges.
And it came to pass that the twenty and seeond year of the reign of the Judges, also ended in peace; yea, and also the twenty and third year.

And it came to pass that in the commencement of the twenty and fourth year of the reign of the Judges, there would also have been peace among the people of Nephi, had it not been for a contention which took place among them concerning the land of Lehi, and the land of Morianton, which joined upon the borders of Lehi; both of which were on the borders, by the sea shore.

For behold, the people which possessed the land of Morianton, did claim a part of the land of Lehi; therefore there began to be a warm contention between them, insomuch that the people of Morianton took up armss against their brethren, and they were determined, by the sword to slay them.
But behold, the people which possessed the land of Lehi, fled to the camp of Moroni, and appealed unto him for assistance; for behold, they were not in the wrong.

And it came to pass that when the people of Morianton, which were led by a man whose name was Morianton, found that the people of Lehi had fled to the camp of Moroni, they were exceeding fearful, lest the army of Moroni should come upon them, and destroy them;
therefore, Morianton put it into their hearts that they should flee to the land which was northward, which was covered with large bodies of water, and take possession of the land which was northward.

And behold, they would have carried this plan into an effect, (which would have been a cause to have been lamented,) but behold, Morianton, being a man of much passion, therefore he was angry with one of his maidservants, and he fell upon her, and beat her much.
And it came to pass that she fled, and came over to the camp of Moroni, and told Moroni all things concerning the matter; and also concerning their intentions to flee into the land northward.

Now behold, the people which were in the land Bountiful, or rather Moroni, feared that they would hearken to the words of Morianton, and unite with his people, and thus he would obtain possession of those parts of the land, which would lay a foundation for serious consequences among the people of Nephi; yea, which consequences would lead to the overthrow of their liberty;
therefore Moroni sent an army, with their camp, to head the people of Morianton, to stop their flight into the land northward.

And it came to pass that they did not head them, until they had come to the borders of the land Desolation; and there they did head them, by the narrow pass which led by the sea into the land northward; yea, by the sea, on the west, and on the east.

And it came to pass that the army which was sent by Moroni, which was led by a man whose name was Teancum, did meet the people of Morianton; and so stubborn were the people of Morianton, (being inspired by his wickedness and his flattering words,) that a battle commenced between them, in the which Teancum did slay Morianton, and defeat his army, and took them prisoners, and returned to the camp of Moroni. And thus ended the twenty and fourth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.

And thus was the people of Morianton brought back. And upon their covenanting to keep the peace, they were restored to the land of Morianton, and a union took place between them and the people of Lehi; and they were also restored to their lands.

And it came to pass that in the same year that the people of Nephi had peace restored unto them, that Nephihah, the second Chief Judge, died, having filled the judgement seat with perfect uprightness before God;

nevertheless, he had refused Alma to take possession of those records and those things which were esteemed by Alma and his fathers to be most sacred; therefore Alma had conferred them upon his son Helaman.

Behold, it came to pass that the son of Nephihah was appointed to fill the judgement seat, in the stead of his father; yea, he was appointed Chief Judge, and Governor over the people, with an oath, and sacred ordinance to judge righteously, and to keep the peace, and the freedom of the people, and to grant unto them their sacred privileges to worship the Lord their God; yea, to support and maintain the cause of God all his days, and to bring the wicked to justice, according to their crime.

links.text: And I charged your judges at that time, saying, Hear the causes between your brethren, and judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger that is with him.

provenance.other: 'Judge righteously' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 1:16 and Proverbs 31:9. Deuteronomy 1:16 is the charge Moses gives the judges he has just appointed; Proverbs 31:9 is a mother's advice to a king about the poor and needy. The Nephite judgeship is a bench, not a throne, which is what puts Deuteronomy first.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 29 built the Nephite judgeship out of Deuteronomy 1: the qualification of the judges at 29:11 comes from 1:13, the warning not to respect persons at 29:28 from 1:17. Deuteronomy 1:16 — 'Hear the causes between your brethren, and judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger that is with him' — is the verse of that charge Mosiah's account left unused, and it surfaces here, in the oath sworn by the first man to inherit the office rather than be elected to it. The judgeship's founding charter is being recited at the point where it becomes hereditary, which is the anxiety Alma 51 will act on.

links.note: 'He was appointed Chief Judge, and Governor over the people, with an oath, and sacred ordinance to judge righteously, and to keep the peace, and the freedom of the people.' Pahoran's oath of office uses one of the KJV's two occurrences of 'judge righteously', and uses it in Deuteronomy 1:16's setting — a charge to a judge over brethren. The preceding verse's 'perfect uprightness before God' (50:37) is in no KJV verse, but 'uprightness' is what the KJV pairs with righteous judging (Psalm 9:8), so the two verses together read as the language of the biblical bench rather than of a nineteenth-century one. Moderate rather than high: two words, and the second of the two KJV verses cannot be ruled out.

pericopes.text: Now behold, his name was Pahoran. And Pahoran did fill the seat of his father, and did commence his reign in the end of the twenty and fourth year, over the people of Nephi.

And now it came to pass, in the commencement of the twenty and fifth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, they having established peace between the people of Lehi and the people of Morianton concerning their lands, and having commenced the twenty and fifth year in peace;

nevertheless, they did not long maintain an entire peace in the land, for there began to be a contention among the people concerning the Chief Judge, Pahoran; for behold, there were a part of the people which desired that a few particular points of the law should be altered.
But behold, Pahoran would not alter, nor suffer the law to be altered; therefore he did not hearken to those who had sent in their voices with their petitions, concerning the altering of the law;

therefore those which were desirous that the law should be altered, were angry with him, and desired that he should no longer be Chief Judge over the land; therefore there arose a warm dispute concerning the matter; but not unto bloodshed.

And it came to pass that those who were desirous that Pahoran should be dethroned from the judgement seat, were called king-men, for they were desirous that the law should be altered in a manner to overthrow the free government, and to establish a king over the land.

And those who were desirous that Pahoran should remain Chief Judge over the land, took upon them the name of freemen; and thus was the division among them: for the freemen had sworn or covenanted to maintain their rights, and the privileges of their religion, by a free government.

links.text: For he that is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord’s freeman: likewise also he that is called, being free, is Christ’s servant.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 7:22 (+ Galatians 5:1) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Freeman' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 7:22; 'free men' in none. The other half of the chapter's political vocabulary — liberty, being made free, the yoke of bondage — is Galatians 5:1, itself a KJV singleton for 'yoke of bondage' and adjudicated at Mosiah 21:13 and 23:13.
provenance.significance: The two Pauline verses behind the word are both about a freedom that is not political. Paul's freeman is a slave who has been called in the Lord; Paul's liberty is the liberty wherewith Christ made us free, and the yoke to avoid is circumcision. Alma 51 takes both and makes them a party register: men 'took upon them the name of freemen', they had 'sworn or covenanted to maintain their rights, and the privileges of their religion, by a free government', and by 51:21 the beaten king-men are made 'to fight valiantly for their freedom from bondage'. Recover the sources and the chapter's politics turn out to be spoken in the vocabulary of Christian manumission — which is exactly the register in which the Book of Mormon's freemen understand a constitutional dispute about the office of chief judge.

links.note: 'Those who were desirous that Pahoran should remain Chief Judge over the land, took upon them the name of freemen.' The naming of a party is a deliberate act in the narrative and the word chosen has one occurrence in the King James Bible. Set beside the chapter's other half — the king-men, and the freedom-from-bondage of 51:21 — the pair of party names is built out of the KJV's two Pauline statements about liberty and servitude. Recorded at 51:6, where the name is conferred; the vocabulary runs through the chapter and is listed in recurrenceRefs.
links.whyNot: 'Freeman' is ordinary English in 1829 and carried a specific American political sense — a qualified voter — that fits Alma 51 better than 1 Corinthians 7:22 does. The KJV singleton may therefore be a coincidence of the KJV's own vocabulary rather than evidence of borrowing, and the confidence is moderate for that reason. What keeps the row is the company: the same chapter's liberty-and-bondage antithesis is Galatians 5:1's, and the two Pauline verses stand together.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that this matter of their contention was settled, by the voice of the people. And it came to pass that the voice of the people came in the favor of the freemen, and Pahoran retained the judgement seat, which caused much rejoicing among the brethren of Pahoran, and also many of the people of liberty; which also put the king-men to silence, that they durst not oppose, but were obliged to maintain the cause of freedom.
Now those which were in favor of kings, were those of high birth; and they sought to be kings; and they were supported by those which sought power and authority over the people.

But behold, this was a critical time for such contentions to be among the people of Nephi; for behold, Amalickiah had again stirred up the hearts of the people of the Lamanites, against the people of the Nephites, and he was gathering together soldiers, from all parts of his land, and arming them, and preparing for war, with all diligence; for he had sworn to drink the blood of Moroni.
But behold, we shall see that his promise which he made, was rash; nevertheless, he did prepare himself and his armies, to come to battle against the Nephites.

Now his armies were not so great as they had hitherto been, because of the many thousands which had been slain by the hand of the Nephites; but notwithstanding their great loss, Amalickiah had gathered together a wonderful great army, insomuch that he feared not to come down to the land of Zarahemla.

Yea, even Amalickiah did himself come down, at the head of the Lamanites. And it was in the twenty and fifth year of the reign of the Judges; and it was at the same time that they had began to settle the affairs of their contentions concerning the Chief Judge, Pahoran.

And it came to pass that when the men which were called king-men, had heard that the Lamanites were coming down to battle against them, they were glad in their hearts, and they refused to take up arms; for they were so wroth with the Chief Judge, and also with the people of liberty, that they would not take up arms to defend their country.

And it came to pass that when Moroni saw this, and also saw that the Lamanites were coming into the borders of the land, he was exceeding wroth, because of the stubbornness of those people, of whom he had labored with so much diligence to preserve; yea, he was exceeding wroth; his soul was filled with anger against them.

And it came to pass that he sent a petition, with the voice of the people, unto the Governor of the land, desiring that he should read it, and give him, (Moroni,) power to compel those dissenters to defend their country, or to put them to death;

for it was his first care to put an end to such contentions, and dissentions among the people; for behold, this had been hitherto a cause of all their destruction.—And it came to pass that it was granted, according to the voice of the people.

And it came to pass that Moroni commanded that his army should go against those king-men, to pull down their pride and their nobility, and level them with the earth, or they should take up arms and support the cause of liberty.

And it came to pass that the armies did march forth against them; and they did pull down their pride and their nobility, insomuch, that as they did lift their weapons of war to fight against the men of Moroni, they were hewn down, and levelled to the earth.

links.text: Behold, the Lord, the LORD of hosts, shall lop the bough with terror: and the high ones of stature shall be hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled.

provenance.other: ‘High ones of stature’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 10:33, and ‘the haughty shall be humbled’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one — two absolute rarities in a single line. The verb they frame, ‘hewn down’, occurs in five verses (Isaiah 10:33, Isaiah 33:9, Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19, Luke 3:9). mediation-check.py finds no divergence between Isaiah 10:33 and Matthew 3:10 that Alma 51:18 reproduces, because the two words the Book of Mormon takes are the two words the candidates share. The context decides instead: Matthew’s axe, tree, fruit and fire are all absent here, and Isaiah’s stature, haughtiness and humbling are all present in the surrounding verses.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 3:10, which supplies the same two words and is the source adjudicated at Alma 5:52. The same phrase routes to different sources at different points of this book, and the discriminator is the company it keeps.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 10:33-34 is the felling of Assyria under the figure of a forest: the LORD of hosts lops the bough, the high ones of stature are hewn down, the haughty are humbled, and Lebanon falls by a mighty one. Alma 51 does the whole figure in prose and drops the trees. What Moroni pulls down is 'their pride and their nobility'; what falls is people 'which professed the blood of nobility'; and what happens to the survivors is that they are 'brought down to humble themselves' (51:21) — Isaiah's three terms, high stature, hewing down, humbling of the haughty, in Isaiah's order. The suppressed half of the borrowing is the agent. In Isaiah it is the LORD of hosts who lops the bough, and the passage is about a foreign empire; in Alma it is a Nephite general with an army, against four thousand of his own countrymen. The verse that makes the humbling divine is the verse Alma 51:18 does not quote.

links.note: 'They did pull down their pride and their nobility, insomuch, that as they did lift their weapons of war to fight against the men of Moroni, they were hewn down, and levelled to the earth.' 'Hewn down' is the Book of Mormon's borrowed verb elsewhere too, but at Alma 5:52 it arrives inside Matthew 3:10's axe-and-tree sentence and here it arrives inside Isaiah 10:33's, with 'high birth' at 51:8 for the high ones of stature and 'brought down to humble themselves' at 51:21 for the haughty humbled. Neither singleton is reproduced word for word — this is not a quotation and falls far below Skousen's threshold — but the three elements of the Isaiah line are all present within four verses and in its sequence, which is what carries the confidence.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there were four thousand of those dissenters, which were hewn down by the sword; and those of their leaders which were not slain in battle, were taken and cast into prison, for there was no time for their trials at this period;

and the remainder of those dissenters, rather than to be smote down to the earth by the sword, yielded to the standard of liberty, and were compelled to hoist the title of liberty upon their towers, and in their cities, and to take up arms in defence of their country.

And thus Moroni put an end to those king-men, that there were not any known by the appellation of king-men; and thus he put an end to the stubbornness, and the pride of those people which professed the blood of nobility; but they were brought down to humble themselves like unto their brethren, and to fight valiantly for their freedom from bondage.

Behold, it came to pass that while Moroni was thus breaking down the wars and contentions among his own people, and subjecting them to peace and civilization, and making regulations to prepare for war against the Lamanites, behold, the Lamanites had come into the land of Moroni, which was in the borders by the seashore.

And it came to pass that the Nephites were not sufficiently strong in the city of Moroni; therefore Amalickiah did drive them, slaying many. And it came to pass that Amalickiah took possession of the city; yea, possession of all their fortifications.

And those which fled out of the city of Moroni, came to the city of Nephihah; and also the people of the city of Lehi gathered themselves together, and made preparations, and were ready to receive the Lamanites to battle.

But it came to pass that Amalickiah would not suffer the Lamanites to go against the city of Nephihah to battle, but kept them down by the seashore, leaving men in every city to maintain and defend it;

and thus he went on, taking possession of many cities: the city of Nephihah, and the city of Lehi, and the city of Morianton, and the city of Omner, and the city of Gid, and the city of Mulek, all of which were on the east borders, by the seashore.

And thus had the Lamanites obtained, by the cunning of Amalickiah, so many cities, by their numberless hosts, all of which were strongly fortified, after the manner of the fortifications of Moroni; all of which afforded strong holds for the Lamanites.
And it came to pass that they marched to the borders of the land Bountiful, driving the Nephites before them, and slaying many.
But it came to pass that they were met by Teancum, who had slain Morianton, and had headed his people in his flight.
And it came to pass that he headed Amalickiah also, as he was marching forth with his numerous army, that he might take possession of the land Bountiful, and also the land northward.

But behold, he met with a disappointment, by being repulsed by Teancum and his men, for they were great warriors: for every man of Teancum did exceed the Lamanites in their strength, and in their skill of war, insomuch that they did gain advantage over the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that they did harrass them, insomuch that they did slay them even until it was dark. And it came to pass that Teancum and his men did pitch their tents in the borders of the land Bountiful; and Amalickiah did pitch his tents in the borders on the beach by the seashore: and after this manner were they driven.

And it came to pass that when the night had come, Teancum and his servant stole forth and went out by night, and went into the camp of Amalickiah; and behold, sleep had overpowered them, because of their much fatigue, which was caused by the labors and heat of the day.

links.text: So David and Abishai came to the people by night: and, behold, Saul lay sleeping within the trench, and his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster: but Abner and the people lay round about him.

provenance.other: 'Went out by night' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 2:13, which is a night inspection of broken walls and not this scene; the singleton is recorded and set aside. 'Heat of the day' occurs in four, of which 2 Samuel 4:5 is the assassination of a sleeping king by two men. 1 Samuel 26 supplies no distinctive phrase at all — its evidence is that every element of Alma 51:33-36 is in it, in order.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 26 is the Bible's one night raid on a sleeping enemy camp, and it is famous for the killing that does not happen. David and one companion go by night into the camp; the king lies asleep with his spear beside him; Abishai asks leave to smite him with the spear even to the earth at once; David forbids it, takes the spear away, and 'no man saw it, nor knew it, neither awaked'. Alma 51 runs the episode with the restraint removed: Teancum and one servant go by night into the camp, the king is asleep, the weapon goes into him, and still 'he did not awake his servants'. The suppressed point of correspondence is David's reason for staying his hand — 'who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD's anointed, and be guiltless?' Amalickiah is a Nephite dissenter wearing a Lamanite crown, and the book has just spent fifty verses arguing that no one in this land should be anointed at all.

links.note: 'Teancum and his servant stole forth and went out by night, and went into the camp of Amalickiah; and behold, sleep had overpowered them, because of their much fatigue.' The scene is assembled rather than quoted. Two men entering a hostile camp at night, one of them a servant, is 1 Samuel 26:7 and Judges 7:11 (Gideon with Phurah his servant); a whole army so asleep that the intruders come and go unnoticed is 1 Samuel 26:12's deep sleep from the LORD, here given a naturalistic cause; and the heat of the day that makes a king sleep through his own murder is 2 Samuel 4:5. There is no shared clause, and 'kjvSpecific' is left uncertain accordingly — the case is the sequence, which 51:35-36 completes by having Teancum return and wake his own men, as David returns and calls across the valley. The 1 Samuel restraint material is live in this part of the book — Alma 44:1 borrows from 1 Samuel 24:10, the other episode in which David has Saul in his hand and lets him go — which is context for reading Teancum’s night raid as the same scene with the opposite ending.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Teancum stole privily into the tent of the king, and put a javelin to his heart; and he did cause the death of the king immediately, that he did not awake his servants.

links.text: Then Jael Heber’s wife took a nail of the tent, and took an hammer in her hand, and went softly unto him, and smote the nail into his temples, and fastened it into the ground: for he was fast asleep and weary. So he died.

provenance.other: 'Went softly' and 'fast asleep' each occur in exactly two KJV verses, and Judges 4:21 is one of the two in both cases — it is the only verse in the Bible that holds a tent, a sleeper, a weapon driven through the body and a silent approach together. The Book of Mormon reproduces none of the words: 'stole privily' for 'went softly', 'sleep had overpowered them' for 'fast asleep and weary'. 'Javelin' occurs in six KJV verses, five of them Saul's, and Saul's javelin is thrown at David and misses every time.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible has three tent-and-chamber assassinations of an enemy commander by one person: Ehud and Eglon, Jael and Sisera, Rechab and Baanah with Ishbosheth. Jael's is the one the Book of Mormon is closest to, and the reason is the weariness — Sisera is killed because he has fled far and is 'fast asleep and weary', which is precisely the explanation Alma 51:33 gives for why the Lamanite camp cannot be roused. Recover Judges 4 and the borrowing acquires an argument the Book of Mormon does not make out loud: Sisera's death is sung in Judges 5 as the deliverance of Israel, and the weapon is the domestic tool of the person the story treats as least likely to be holding it. Teancum's javelin, by contrast, is the weapon Saul kept in his hand to throw at David — the KJV's javelin is a king's weapon, used badly — and here it is carried into a king's tent by a man who is not a king, and used once.

links.note: 'Teancum stole privily into the tent of the king, and put a javelin to his heart; and he did cause the death of the king immediately, that he did not awake his servants.' Judges 4:21 is the model for the scene and no word of it is reproduced; the case rests on the four elements arriving together — the tent, the silent approach, the sleeper who cannot be woken, the single fatal thrust — and on the weariness that Judges 4:21 and Alma 51:33 both supply as the reason the sleep is that deep. Abishai's 'let me smite him with the spear even to the earth at once, and I will not smite him the second time' (1 Samuel 26:8) is the closest the KJV comes to the Book of Mormon's insistence that one blow did it. Left kjvSpecific uncertain: a figural link of this kind has no wording to test, and what is being followed is a narrative shape rather than an English translation.

pericopes.text: And he returned again privily to his own camp, and behold, his men were asleep; and he awoke them, and told them all the things that he had done.
And he caused that his armies should stand in readiness, lest the Lamanites had awoke, and should come upon them.
And thus ended the twenty and fifth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi; and thus ended the days of Amalickiah.

And now it came to pass in the twenty and sixth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, behold, when the Lamanites awoke on the first morning of the first month, behold, they found Amalickiah was dead, in his own tent; and they also saw that Teancum was ready to give them battle on that day.

links.text: And, behold, as Barak pursued Sisera, Jael came out to meet him, and said unto him, Come, and I will shew thee the man whom thou seekest. And when he came into her tent, behold, Sisera lay dead, and the nail was in his temples.

provenance.route: Judges 4:21-22 (the discovery in the tent) + 2 Kings 19:35-36 (the morning after, and the abandoned campaign) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “lay dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 4:22, and it is the discovery of a dead enemy commander inside a tent — the KJV's only such scene. Alma 52:1 does not reproduce the phrase; it reproduces the situation. Separately, “dead corpses” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Kings 19:35 and its doublet Isaiah 37:36, both reading 'and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses'.
provenance.alternative: An army waking to find its general dead is a situation a writer could reach without a source; nothing in the verse is verbally distinctive.
provenance.significance: The killing at Alma 51:34 — a javelin driven into a sleeping commander in his own tent, by night, by a single assailant who then withdraws — is Jael's; this verse is Barak's half of that story, the morning arrival of the men who came for Sisera and find the work already done. What the Book of Mormon adds is the Assyrian ending. In Judges the discovery is a victory scene; in 2 Kings 19:35-36 the enemy wakes to death in the camp and Sennacherib simply 'departed, and went and returned' — the campaign is over without a battle. Alma 52:1-2 has both movements in order: the body found at first light, and then an army that abandons its design of marching into the land northward and retreats. Teancum has done to Amalickiah what Jael did to Sisera and got what the angel got at Jerusalem.

links.note: 'When the Lamanites awoke on the first morning of the first month, behold, they found Amalickiah was dead, in his own tent.' No clause is borrowed, and the link is offered as a type-scene rather than a verbal one. What carries it is that the KJV has exactly one scene of an enemy commander found dead inside a tent and exactly one of an enemy army waking to find its dead, and Alma 52:1-2 executes them consecutively — the second supplying what the first does not, namely the invading army's withdrawal. Recorded at moderate because the situation is generic enough to have been invented, and because the assassination itself belongs to Alma 51:34, where the Jael allusion is at its strongest.
links.whyNot: There is no reproduced wording at all. 'Awoke', 'first morning' and 'found ... dead' are ordinary English, and an army discovering a murdered general has one natural way of being narrated.

pericopes.text: And now when the Lamanites saw this, they were affrighted; and they abandoned their design in marching into the land northward, and retreated with all their army into the city of Mulek, and sought protection in their fortifications.—

And it came to pass that the brother of Amalickiah was appointed king over the people; and his name was Ammoron: thus king Ammoron, the brother of king Amalickiah, was appointed to reign in his stead.
And it came to pass that he did command that his people should maintain those cities which they had taken by the shedding of blood; for they had not taken any cities, save they had lost much blood.

links.text: And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.

provenance.other: “shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22. This catalogue has twice declined the same singleton on sense — at Mosiah 20:22 and Mosiah 29:40, both registered in data/exclusions.json — and has accepted it once, at Alma 34:13, where Hebrews 9's whole argument is in view.
provenance.alternative: The phrase is the natural English for the thing and needs no source; a war narrative will say 'shedding of blood' whether or not it has read Hebrews.
provenance.significance: The two Mosiah refusals turned on the same point: Hebrews makes blood-shedding the condition of obtaining something, and those verses make it a regrettable cost to be stopped. Alma 52:4 does not do that. Ammoron's decree is 'maintain those cities which they had taken by the shedding of blood', and the reason given is 'for they had not taken any cities, save they had lost much blood' — that is Hebrews' logic exactly, in a military key: without shedding of blood, no acquisition. The clause is a purchase argument, and it is the KJV's one purchase-by-blood verse that supplies its words.

links.note: Proposed under CONVENTIONS §0a and kept at `low` on purpose. The rarity is absolute and the argument-shape agrees with the source where the register's two earlier refusals of this phrase disagreed with it — Ammoron reasons that what cost blood must be held, which is the form of 'without shedding of blood is no remission'. Nothing else in the verse touches Hebrews 9, so the row is a proposal, not a finding, and it is flagged as one.
links.whyNot: Three words, and a war chapter has every reason to use them without borrowing. The catalogue has declined this singleton at Mosiah 20:22 and Mosiah 29:40 for wrong sense; a reader who thinks the sense-agreement argued above is a coincidence should decline it here too, and the row is written so that it can be withdrawn on that ground alone.

pericopes.text: And now Teancum saw that the Lamanites were determined to maintain those cities which they had taken, and those parts of the land which they had obtained possession of; and also seeing the enormity of their number, Teancum thought it was not expedient that he should attempt to attack them in their forts;
but he kept his men round about, as if making preparations for war; yea, and truly he was preparing to defend himself against them, by casting up walls round about, and preparing places of resort.
And it came to pass that he kept thus preparing for war, until Moroni had sent a large number of men to strengthen his army;

and Moroni also sent orders unto him, that he should retain all the prisoners which fell into his hands; for as the Lamanites had taken many prisoners, that he should retain all the prisoners of the Lamanites, as a ransom for those which the Lamanites had taken.

And he also sent orders unto him, that he should fortify the land Bountiful, and secure the narrow pass which led into the land northward, lest the Lamanites should obtain that point, and should have power to harrass them on every side.

And Moroni also sent unto him, desiring him that he would be faithful in maintaining that quarter of the land, and that he would seek every opportunity to scourge the Lamanites in that quarter, as much as was in his power, that perhaps he might take again, by stratagem or some other way, those cities which had been taken out of their hands; and that he also would fortify and strengthen the cities round about, which had not fallen into the hands of the Lamanites.

links.text: And certain of the chief of Asia, which were his friends, sent unto him, desiring him that he would not adventure himself into the theatre.

provenance.other: “sent unto him desiring him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 19:31; the shorter “desiring him that he would” occurs in exactly two, Acts 19:31 and Acts 9:38, and “desiring him” in the same two. The construction is therefore not merely rare in the KJV, it is Lukan and confined to Acts.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing acquires an argument the Book of Mormon then uses twice, in opposite directions. Acts 19:31 is the Ephesian riot: Paul's friends among the chief of Asia send to him desiring that he would NOT go out into the theatre, the public arena where the crowd is waiting. Alma 52:10 uses the formula for Moroni's message to Teancum, and Alma 52:20 uses it again for the embassy sent to the Zoramite Jacob 'desiring him that he would come out with his armies to meet them upon the plains' — a request to enter exactly the open arena Acts 19:31's message was sent to prevent. Jacob refuses, and by refusing does what Paul's friends wanted Paul to do. The KJV's one verse for an embassy carrying a request is the verse in which the right answer was to stay inside the walls. The formula returns a third time at Alma 54:1, where it is Ammoron who 'sent unto Moroni, desiring that he would exchange prisoners' — so all three of the chapter-block's negotiations, in both directions, are carried by the KJV's one verse for a message asking somebody to do something.

links.note: 'And Moroni also sent unto him, desiring him that he would be faithful in maintaining that quarter of the land.' Eight consecutive words of Acts 19:31, from the only KJV verse that has them, in a chapter whose plot turns on messages sent between commanders. The n-gram stream ranked it first for the verse and it is one of the rare cases where that stream is right: the run is not connective tissue but a whole verbal frame — sent unto him, desiring him that he would, plus infinitive — and the Book of Mormon reuses the frame ten verses later for the embassy to Jacob. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his 36.

links.text: And Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again out of the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael the cities, which he had taken out of the hand of Jehoahaz his father by war. Three times did Joash beat him, and recovered the cities of Israel.

provenance.other: “taken out of the hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Kings 13:25, and “recovered the cities” in exactly one, the same verse. Alma 52:10 has the plural, 'taken out of their hands', so the singleton string is not literally reproduced; what is reproduced is the whole sentence-shape — take again + the cities + taken out of the hand(s) — from the KJV's single verse about a king recovering cities an enemy king had taken from his predecessor.
provenance.alternative: The n-gram stream also offered 2 Chronicles 15:8 on 'the cities which he had taken', where Asa's captured cities are the setting for a religious reform; the verbal overlap is real but the situation is not this one.
provenance.significance: 2 Kings 13:25 is the KJV's one verse of exactly this military problem, and the correspondence extends past the words. Jehoash recovers cities lost in his father's reign to Benhadad, son of Hazael — a dynastic aggressor whose successor is fought by a successor. Alma 52 is Moroni's campaign to retake cities lost to Amalickiah, against Amalickiah's brother and successor Ammoron, who has been installed in this chapter seven verses earlier. The Book of Mormon has taken its formula for recovering lost cities from the Bible's only account of it, and it has taken it into a war that has the same two-generation shape.

links.note: 'That perhaps he might take again, by stratagem or some other way, those cities which had been taken out of their hands.' Three of the source's distinctive elements arrive together — 'take again', 'the cities', 'taken out of the hand(s)' — and the source is a KJV singleton on two of them. The chapter then runs the programme the verse announces: retake Mulek (52:16), 'take again the city of Mulek' (52:19), and the possession obtained at 52:26.

pericopes.text: And he also said unto him, I would come unto you, but behold, the Lamanites are upon us in the borders of the land by the West Sea; and behold, I go against them, therefore I cannot come unto you.

Now the king (Ammoron,) had departed out of the land of Zarahemla, and had made known unto the queen concerning the death of his brother, and had gathered together a large number of men, and had marched forth against the Nephites, on the borders by the West Sea;

and thus he was endeavoring to harrass the Nephites, and to draw away a part of their forces to that part of the land, while he had commanded those which he had left to possess the cities which he had taken, that they should also harrass the Nephites on the borders by the East Sea; and should take possession of their lands as much as it were in their power, according to the power of their armies.
And thus were the Nephites in those dangerous circumstances, in the ending of the twenty and sixth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.

But behold, it came to pass in the twenty and seventh year of the reign of the Judges, that Teancum, by the command of Moroni, who had established armies to protect the south and the west borders of the land, had began his march towards the land Bountiful, that he might assist Teancum with his men, in retaking the cities which they had lost.
And it came to pass that Teancum had received orders to make an attack upon the city of Mulek, and retake it if it were possible.

And it came to pass that Teancum made preparations to make an attack upon the city of Mulek, and march forth with his army against the Lamanites; but he saw that it was impossible that he could overpower them while they were in their fortifications; therefore he abandoned his designs, and returned again to the city Bountiful, to wait for the coming of Moroni, that he might receive strength to his army.
And it came to pass that Moroni did arrive with his army to the land of Bountiful, in the latter end of the twenty and seventh year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.

And in the commencement of the twenty and eighth year, Moroni and Teancum, and many of the Chief Captains, held a council of war, what they should do to cause the Lamanites to come out against them to battle; or that they might by some means, flatter them out of their strong holds, that they might gain advantage over them, and take again the city of Mulek.

And it came to pass that they sent embassies to the army of the Lamanites, which protected the city of Mulek, to their leader, whose name was Jacob, desiring him that he would come out with his armies to meet them upon the plains, between the two cities. But behold, Jacob, which was a Zoramite, would not come out with his army to meet them upon the plains.
And it came to pass that Moroni, having no hopes of meeting them upon fair grounds, therefore he resolved upon a plan that he might decoy the Lamanites out of their strong holds.

Therefore he caused that Teancum should take a small number of men, and march down near the seashore; and Moroni and his army, by night, marched into the wilderness, on the west of the city Mulek; and thus, on the morrow, when the guards of the Lamanites had discovered Teancum, they ran and told it unto Jacob, their leader.

links.text: And when they had set the people, even all the host that was on the north of the city, and their liers in wait on the west of the city, Joshua went that night into the midst of the valley.

provenance.other: “on the west of the city” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 8:13, and the shorter “west of the city” in exactly one, the same verse. Joshua 8:16's “drawn away from the city” occurs in exactly two, Joshua 8:16 and Judges 20:31 — the two biblical decoy-ambushes, of which Judges 20 is modelled on Joshua 8.
provenance.significance: Joshua 8 is the Bible's set-piece on the tactic Alma 52:19-31 executes, and Alma has it verse by verse: an ambush force set on the west of the city and moving by night (8:13); a small force shown to the defenders in the morning (8:14-15); a feigned flight that draws the garrison out and away (8:15-16); the ambush entering and taking the emptied city (8:19); and the fleeing force turning back on its pursuers (8:20-21). What makes the borrowing verbal rather than merely typological is that the one element with no tactical necessity — the compass point — is the one Alma reproduces, from the only KJV verse where it stands. There is no military reason the wilderness Moroni marches into must be west of Mulek; there is a textual reason.

links.note: 'Moroni and his army, by night, marched into the wilderness, on the west of the city Mulek.' Three of Joshua 8:13's elements in one clause — the ambush position west of the city, the night march, and (from 8:15) the wilderness the decoy uses — and 'on the west of the city' is a KJV singleton. Moroni's plan at 52:21 is called a decoy in the text's own word, and the chapter then follows Joshua 8's sequence to the end, which is why this row carries recurrence references to 52:24, 52:31 and 52:36 rather than repeating the argument there.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the armies of the Lamanites did march forth against Teancum, supposing by their numbers to overpower Teancum, because of the smallness of his numbers. And as Teancum saw the armies of the Lamanites coming out against him, he began to retreat down by the seashore, northward.

And it came to pass that when the Lamanites saw that he began to flee, they took courage and pursued them with vigor. And while Teancum was thus leading away the Lamanites which were pursuing them in vain, behold, Moroni commanded that a part of his army which were with him, should march forth into the city, and take possession of it.
And thus they did, and slew all those who had been left to protect the city; yea, all those who would not yield up their weapons of war.
And thus Moroni had obtained a possession of the city Mulek, with a part of his army, while he marched with the remainder to meet the Lamanites, when they should return from the pursuit of Teancum.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites did pursue Teancum until they came near the city Bountiful, and then they were met by Lehi, and a small army, which had been left to protect the city Bountiful.

And now behold, when the Chief Captains of the Lamanites had beheld Lehi, with his army, coming against them, they fled in much confusion, lest perhaps they should not obtain the city Mulek, before Lehi should overtake them; for they were wearied because of their march; and the men of Lehi were fresh.
Now the Lamanites did not know that Moroni had been in their rear with his army; and all they feared, was Lehi and his men.
Now Lehi was not desirous to overtake them, till they should meet Moroni and his army.

And it came to pass that before the Lamanites had retreated far, they were surrounded by the Nephites; by the men of Moroni on one hand, and the men of Lehi on the other, all of whom were fresh and full of strength; but the Lamanites were wearied, because of their long march.

links.text: And the other issued out of the city against them; so they were in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side: and they smote them, so that they let none of them remain or escape.

provenance.other: “some on this side” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 8:22. Alma 52:31 does not reproduce it — the Book of Mormon reads 'by the men of Moroni on one hand, and the men of Lehi on the other' — so this row rests on structure and position within the borrowed sequence, not on a shared string.
provenance.significance: Joshua 8:22 is the moment the two Israelite forces close, and the KJV's phrase for it is 'in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side'. Alma 52:31 is the same moment with the same two-force geometry and a different English idiom for it, and it arrives at exactly the point in the sequence where Joshua puts it: after the flight, after the taking of the city, before the surrender. Where Joshua's closure is total — 'they let none of them remain or escape' — Moroni's ends in the surrender of 52:37-39 and a body of prisoners larger than the body of dead. The Book of Mormon has followed the Ai script to its last verse and then declined its ending.

links.note: 'They were surrounded by the Nephites; by the men of Moroni on one hand, and the men of Lehi on the other.' The wording is not Joshua's; the position is. This is the payoff of the ambush adjudicated at 52:22, and it is recorded separately because a reader arriving at 52:31 should be told which biblical battle the pincer belongs to. Moderate, and the absent verbal contact is stated rather than argued around.
links.whyNot: 'On one hand and on the other' is ordinary English and shares no phrase with Joshua 8:22. If the Joshua 8:13 link at 52:22 is declined, nothing here stands on its own.

pericopes.text: And Moroni commanded his men that they should fall upon them, until they had given up their weapons of war.
And it came to pass that Jacob, being their leader, being also a Zoramite, and having an unconquerable spirit, he led the Lamanites forth to battle, with exceeding fury against Moroni.

Moroni being in their course of march, therefore Jacob was determined to slay them, and cut his way through to the city of Mulek. But behold, Moroni and his men were more powerful; therefore they did not give way before the Lamanites.
And it came to pass that they fought on both hands with exceeding fury; and there were many slain on both sides; yea, and Moroni was wounded, and Jacob was killed.

And Lehi pressed upon their rear with such fury, with his strong men, that the Lamanites in the rear delivered up their weapons of war; and the remainder of them, being much confused, knew not whether to go or to strike.

links.text: And when the men of Ai looked behind them, they saw, and, behold, the smoke of the city ascended up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that way: and the people that fled to the wilderness turned back upon the pursuers.

provenance.other: “this way or that way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 8:20, and “no power to flee” in exactly one, the same verse. Alma 52:36's 'knew not whether to go or to strike' is a paraphrase of that idea, not a reproduction of the phrase.
provenance.significance: Joshua 8:20 describes a very particular military condition: a force caught between an ambush and a turned pursuit, which has not been beaten but has ceased to be able to choose. The KJV renders it as having 'no power to flee this way or that way'; Alma 52:36 renders the same condition as being 'much confused' and knowing 'not whether to go or to strike'. Alma's version supplies the alternative Joshua's leaves out — fight, not merely flight — which is what the verse needs, since Lehi is pressing on the rear and the front rank has already surrendered its weapons.

links.note: 'The remainder of them, being much confused, knew not whether to go or to strike.' The clause is one of the more distinctive sentences in the Book of Mormon's war narrative and it has no KJV wording behind it, but it stands at the precise point of Joshua 8 where the KJV supplies its own one-off formula for the same paralysis. Recorded as an echo, at moderate, on the strength of the sequence adjudicated at 52:22 rather than on the words.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal is shared. Read on its own the sentence is the Book of Mormon's own idiom, and the row depends entirely on the Joshua 8 sequence being granted at 52:22.

pericopes.text: Now Moroni seeing their confusion, he said unto them, If ye will bring forth your weapons of war, and deliver them up, behold we will forbear shedding your blood.

And it came to pass that when the Lamanites had heard these words, their Chief Captains, all those which were not slain, came forth and threw down their weapons of war at the feet of Moroni, and also commanded their men that they should do the same;

but behold, there were many that would not; and those who would not deliver up their swords, were taken and bound, and their weapons of war were taken from them, and they were compelled to march with their brethren forth into the land Bountiful.
And now the number of prisoners which were taken, exceeded more than the number of those which had been slain; yea, more than those which had been slain on both sides.

And it came to pass that they did set guards over the prisoners of the Lamanites, and did compel them to go forth and bury their dead; yea, and also the dead of the Nephites which were slain; and Moroni placed men over them to guard them while they should perform their labors.

And Moroni went to the city of Mulek with Lehi, and took command of the city, and gave it unto Lehi. Now behold this Lehi was a man who had been with Moroni in the more part of all his battles; and he was a man like unto Moroni; and they rejoiced in each other’s safety; yea, they were beloved by each other, and also beloved by all the people of Nephi.

links.text: And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.

provenance.other: “knit with the soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 18:1, and “loved him as his own soul” in exactly two, 1 Samuel 18:1 and 18:3 — the same episode. Alma 53:2 reproduces none of this; its words are 'they rejoiced in each other's safety; yea, they were beloved by each other'. The row is filed on the situation and on the company it keeps in this chapter, not on a string.
provenance.alternative: Two commanders fond of one another is not a scene that needs a source, and the Book of Mormon's language for it is its own.
provenance.significance: The KJV has one friendship between fighting men that it troubles to describe as love, and it describes it in the chapter immediately after the giant is killed — Jonathan's soul knit to David's, a covenant made, and the elder man handing over his own equipment. Alma 53:2 gives Lehi the same standing beside Moroni: 'he was a man like unto Moroni', with him in the more part of his battles, and the transfer that occasions the sentence is Moroni taking the city and giving it to Lehi. Read with the rest of the chapter the reading firms up considerably: 53:20 gives the young men Saul's charge to David ('be thou valiant for me'), and 53:22 calls them by the one word the KJV uses for David himself. Alma 53 is working the David material of 1 Samuel 17-18, and this verse is its Jonathan.

links.note: 'He was a man like unto Moroni; and they rejoiced in each other's safety; yea, they were beloved by each other.' No wording is shared, and the row is offered as a type-scene under CONVENTIONS §0a. What lifts it above a guess is recurrence rather than volume: the same twenty verses of 1 Samuel supply the chapter's 'valiant for' at 53:20 and its KJV-singleton 'stripling' at 53:22, so a Jonathan figure at 53:2 is the reading the chapter's own field of allusion predicts.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal at all. If the 1 Samuel 17-18 field claimed for the chapter is declined, this row has no independent support, and 'beloved by each other' is ordinary Book of Mormon diction.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after the Lamanites had finished burying their dead, and also the dead of the Nephites, they were marched back into the land Bountiful; and Teancum, by the orders of Moroni, caused that they should commence in laboring in digging a ditch round about the land, or the city Bountiful;

and he caused that they should build a breastwork of timbers upon the inner bank of the ditch; and they cast up dirt out of the ditch against the breastwork of timbers; and thus they did cause the Lamanites to labor, until they had encircled the city of Bountiful round about with a strong wall of timbers and earth, to an exceeding height.

And this city became an exceeding strong hold ever after; and in this city they did guard the prisoners of the Lamanites; yea, even within a wall, which they had caused them to build with their own hands. Now Moroni was compelled to cause the Lamanites to labor, because it were easy to guard them while at their labor; and he desired all his forces, when he should make an attack upon the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that Moroni had thus gained a victory over one of the greatest of the armies of the Lamanites, and had obtained possession of the city Mulek, which was one of the strongest holds of the Lamanites in the land of Nephi; and thus he had also built a strong hold to retain his prisoners.

And it came to pass that he did no more attempt a battle with the Lamanites in that year, but he did employ his men in preparing for war; yea, and in making fortifications to guard against the Lamanites; yea, and also delivering their women and their children from famine and affliction, and providing food for their armies.
