And now it came to pass that the armies of the Lamanites, on the West Sea, south, while in the absence of Moroni, on account of some intrigue amongst the Nephites, which caused dissensions amongst them, had gained some ground over the Nephites, yea, insomuch that they had obtained possession of a number of their cities in that part of the land;
and thus because of iniquity amongst themselves, yea, because of dissensions and intrigue among themselves, they were placed in the most dangerous circumstances.

And now behold, I have somewhat to say concerning the people of Ammon, which, in the beginning, were Lamanites; but by Ammon and his brethren, or rather by the power and word of God, they had been converted unto the Lord; and they had been brought down into the land of Zarahemla, and had ever since been protected by the Nephites;

and because of their oath, they had been kept from taking up arms against their brethren: for they had taken an oath, that they never would shed blood more; and according to their oath, they would have perished; yea, they would have suffered themselves to have fallen into the hands of their brethren, had it not been for the pity and the exceeding love which Ammon and his brethren had had for them;
and for this cause, they were brought down into the land of Zarahemla; and they ever had been protected by the Nephites.

But it came to pass that when they saw the danger, and the many afflictions and tribulations which the Nephites bore for them, they were moved with compassion, and were desirous to take up arms in the defence of their country.
But behold, as they were about to take their weapons of war, they were overpowered by the persuasions of Helaman and his brethren, for they were about to break the oath which they had made;

and Helaman feared lest by so doing, they should lose their souls; therefore all those which had entered into this covenant, were compelled to behold their brethren wade through their afflictions, in their dangerous circumstances, at this time.

But behold, it came to pass they had many sons, which had not entered into a covenant that they would not take their weapons of war to defend themselves against their enemies; therefore they did assemble themselves together at this time, as many as were able to take up arms; and they called themselves Nephites;

and they entered into a covenant, to fight for the liberty of the Nephites; yea, to protect the land unto the laying down of their lives; yea, even they covenanted that they never would give up their liberty, but they would fight in all cases to protect the Nephites and themselves from bondage.

links.text: Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.

provenance.route: 1 John 3:16, with John 15:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “lay down our lives” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 3:16, and “laid down his life” in exactly one, the same verse; “lay down his life” occurs in exactly one, John 15:13. The idiom is confined to the Johannine books. Alma 53:17 nominalizes it — 'unto the laying down of their lives' — and “laying down” occurs in no KJV verse at all, which is what keeps this at moderate rather than high.
provenance.significance: 1 John 3:16 is the KJV's one verse that makes laying down one's life a duty owed by the many to the many: Christ laid down his, 'and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.' That is precisely the covenant of Alma 53:17, and the covenanters are the ones for whom it should be hardest. Their fathers swore never to shed blood and were prepared to be slaughtered on that oath (53:11); the sons swear the opposite-looking oath and reach the same place, since 'to protect the land unto the laying down of their lives' is a promise to die rather than to kill. The Johannine verse holds both halves of what the chapter has separated — the fathers' willingness to be killed and the sons' willingness to fight — under one word, and the word is 'brethren', which is what the Lamanites are to the people of Ammon throughout 53:11-13.

links.note: 'They entered into a covenant, to fight for the liberty of the Nephites; yea, to protect the land unto the laying down of their lives.' The KJV's only idiom for pledging one's death on another's behalf is the Johannine one, and Alma 53:17 has it in a noun phrase the KJV never forms. Recorded at moderate because the borrowing is of a construction rather than a clause; what makes it worth having is the metalepsis, since 1 John 3:16 supplies exactly the logic that reconciles the sons' covenant with their fathers'. The covenant formula itself ('they entered into a covenant' plus an infinitive of purpose) is 2 Chronicles 15:12's and is adjudicated at Alma 46:35; see the register at this verse.
links.whyNot: The shared material is a verbal noun and a possessive, not a clause, and 'laying down of their lives' could be reached from the King James idiom by any nineteenth-century writer steeped in it without a particular verse in mind.

pericopes.text: Now behold, there were two thousand of those young men which entered into this covenant, and took their weapons of war to defend their country.

And now behold, as they never had hitherto been a disadvantage to the Nephites, they became now at this period of time also a great support; for they took their weapons of war, and they would that Helaman should be their leader.

And they were all young men, and they were exceeding valiant for courage, and also for strength and activity; but behold, this was not all: they were men which were true at all times in whatsoever thing they were entrusted;
yea, they were men of truth and soberness, for they had been taught to keep the commandments of God, and to walk uprightly before him.

links.text: Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens:

provenance.route: Exodus 18:21 (the character list) fused with Acts 26:25 (the phrase) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “men of truth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 18:21. “truth and soberness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:25, and “soberness” itself in exactly one, the same verse. Alma 53:21's 'they were men of truth and soberness' is the two singletons welded at the shared word.
provenance.significance: Both halves of the weld carry their context in. Exodus 18:21 is Jethro's specification for the men Moses is to set over Israel — able men, God-fearing, men of truth, not covetous — the Bible's one checklist for choosing officers, and Alma 53:20-21 is a checklist for choosing soldiers in exactly that form: valiant, strong and active, true at all times in whatsoever they were entrusted, men of truth and soberness, taught to keep the commandments. Acts 26:25 supplies the other word from the least military scene imaginable: Paul on trial before Agrippa, accused by Festus of being mad, answering that he speaks 'the words of truth and soberness'. Two thousand adolescents going to war are commended in the phrase a prisoner used to prove he was not raving — and 'soberness', a word the KJV uses once in its whole extent, is what the Book of Mormon chooses for teenagers. The book has taken the Bible's standard for magistrates and applied it to children.

links.note: 'Yea, they were men of truth and soberness, for they had been taught to keep the commandments of God, and to walk uprightly before him.' Two KJV singletons meet in five words, and neither is decorative: Exodus 18:21 governs the shape of the surrounding list (53:20-21 is a qualifications catalogue, which is what Exodus 18:21 is) and Acts 26:25 governs its wording. The n-gram stream found the Acts half and missed the Exodus half, which is the split-agreement blindness CONVENTIONS §9 describes — 'men of truth' and 'truth and soberness' overlap on one word and no contiguous window sees both.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that Helaman did march at the head of his two thousand stripling soldiers, to the support of the people in the borders of the land on the south, by the West Sea.

links.text: And the king said, Enquire thou whose son the stripling is.

provenance.other: “stripling” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 17:56 — the whole of it being 'And the king said, Enquire thou whose son the stripling is.' The word appears nowhere else in the King James Bible in any form. Separately, “valiant for” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, one of which is 1 Samuel 18:17, Saul's 'only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD's battles', said to the same young man twenty verses later; Alma 53:20 reads 'they were exceeding valiant for courage'.
provenance.significance: This is metalepsis of the cleanest kind, because the KJV's single 'stripling' sits inside a question about parentage. Saul, having watched a boy kill a giant, does not ask the boy's name; he asks whose son he is, and 17:58 makes David answer with his father — 'I am the son of thy servant Jesse the Bethlehemite.' Whose sons these two thousand are is the entire content of Alma 53:10-18. They exist in the narrative only as the sons of the people of Ammon; the covenant they can make is defined by the covenant their fathers made and they did not; the book will call them by their fathers for the rest of the war. The one KJV verse containing the word Alma uses for them is the verse in which a king demands to know a young soldier's father — and the answer, in 1 Samuel as in Alma, is the point of the story.

links.note: 'Helaman did march at the head of his two thousand stripling soldiers.' A KJV singleton, and one of the most conspicuous single words in the Book of Mormon; 'stripling' is not ordinary nineteenth-century American English for a soldier and the King James Bible uses it once. The chapter has been in this field throughout — Jonathan's love at 53:2, Saul's 'valiant for' at 53:20 — so the borrowing is not an isolated flourish but the naming of a David typology the chapter has already built. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his 36; the case here rests entirely on the rarity of one word and the aptness of the verse it comes from.

pericopes.text: And thus ended the twenty and eigth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, &c.
And now it came to pass in the twenty and ninth year of the Judges, that Ammoron sent unto Moroni, desiring that he would exchange prisoners.

And it came to pass that Moroni felt to rejoice exceedingly at this request, for he desired the provisions which was imparted for the support of the Lamanite prisoners, for the support of his own people; and he also desired his own people for the strengthening of his army.—

Now the Lamanites had taken many women and children; and there was not a woman nor a child among all the prisoners of Moroni, or the prisoners which Moroni had taken; therefore Moroni resolved upon a stratagem, to obtain as many prisoners of the Nephites from the Lamanites, as it were possible;
therefore he wrote an epistle, and sent it by the servant of Ammoron, the same who had brought an epistle to Moroni. Now these are the words which he wrote unto Ammoron, saying:

links.text: And it came to pass in the morning, that David wrote a letter to Joab, and sent it by the hand of Uriah.

provenance.other: “and sent it by” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 11:14, and “sent it by the hand” in exactly one, the same verse. “wrote a letter” occurs in exactly four (2 Samuel 11:14, 2 Kings 10:6, Ezra 4:8, Acts 23:25), and 2 Samuel 11:14 is the only one of them that also has the sending clause.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one letter sent by a named bearer is the letter David wrote to Joab and sent by the hand of Uriah — a document carried by the man it condemns to death, who cannot read it. Alma 54:4 sends its epistle 'by the servant of Ammoron, the same who had brought an epistle to Moroni', and the epistle it carries is a refusal to trade prisoners except at a price its bearer's master will not pay, closing with the sentence that he is a child of hell. The correspondence in this chapter runs on messengers who carry threats against their own side, and the wording comes from the Bible's one instance of the practice at its worst. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the borrowed clause is unremarkable until the recovered context supplies what the Book of Mormon does not say, namely that a letter of this kind is a way of killing a man by the hand that holds it.

links.note: 'Therefore he wrote an epistle, and sent it by the servant of Ammoron, the same who had brought an epistle to Moroni.' A KJV singleton on four words, and the surrounding sentence reproduces the source's whole action — wrote, and sent it by, plus a named bearer belonging to the other party. The n-gram stream ranked it first for the verse and was right. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his 36.

pericopes.text: Behold, Ammoron, I have wrote unto you somewhat concerning this war which ye have waged against my people, or rather which thy brother hath waged against them, and which ye are still determined to carry on after his death.

Behold, I would tell you something concerning the justice of God, and the sword of his Almighty wrath, which doth hang over you: Except ye repent and withdraw your armies into your own lands, or the lands of your possessions, which is the land of Nephi;

yea, I would tell you these things, if ye were capable of hearkening unto them; yea, I would tell you concerning that awful hell that awaits to receive such murderers as thou and thy brother hath been, except ye repent and withdraw your murderous purposes, and return with your armies to your own lands;
but as ye have rejected these things, and have fought against the people of the Lord, even so I may expect you will do it again.

And now behold, we are prepared to receive you; yea, and except you withdraw your purposes, behold, ye will pull down the wrath of that God whom you have rejected, upon you, even to your utter destruction;

but as the Lord liveth, our armies shall come upon you, except ye withdraw, and ye shall soon be visited with death, for we will retain our cities and our lands; yea, and we will maintain our religion and the cause of our God.

But behold, it supposeth me that I talk to you concerning these things in vain; or it supposeth me that thou art a child of hell; therefore I will close my epistle, by telling you that I will not exchange prisoners, save it be on conditions that ye will deliver up a man, and his wife, and his children, for one prisoner; if this be the case that ye will do it, I will exchange.

links.text: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.

provenance.other: “child of hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 23:15. The catalogue adjudicates the borrowing at Alma 11:23, where Amulek says 'O thou child of Hell' to Zeezrom and the 1830 capitalizes the noun; the argument for the dependence is made there and is not repeated here.
provenance.significance: This is not the Alma 11 formula recurring — it is the other half of the same verse being used. At 11:23 what mattered was the speaker: the phrase is Jesus's, from the week of the Jerusalem confrontation, and Amulek takes it up in a confrontation of the same shape. Here what matters is the syntax of Matthew's insult, which is about manufacture. A child of hell in Matthew 23:15 is not born but made — 'ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves' — and Ammoron is the Book of Mormon's most exact instance of the type. He is a Nephite by descent who says so himself twelve verses later ('I am Ammoron, and a descendant of Zoram'), converted into a Lamanite king by his brother's proselytizing, and more violent in the office than the people who made him. Moroni calls him what Jesus calls a convert who has outdone his converters.

links.note: 'It supposeth me that thou art a child of hell.' A KJV singleton, and its second use in this book. It is written as a link rather than registered as a repeat because the second use turns on a feature of the source the first did not touch: Matthew's child of hell is a made proselyte, and Ammoron's whole identity in this chapter is that he was made into what he is and has exceeded his makers, which he half-admits at 54:23-24. CONVENTIONS §4's default sends a within-book repeat to the register; the exception for a phrase that goes back to work on its source is what is claimed here.

links.text: Then answered all the wicked men and men of Belial, of those that went with David, and said, Because they went not with us, we will not give them ought of the spoil that we have recovered, save to every man his wife and his children, that they may lead them away, and depart.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 30:22 (with 1 Samuel 30:1-3, 18-19) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “his wife and his children” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 30:22. The catalogue's usual caution about a family formula does not apply: the KJV's ordinary phrasings are 'his wives and his children', 'their wives and their children', 'thy sons and thy daughters', and the exact singular-plus-plural string Alma 54:11 uses stands in one verse only.
provenance.significance: The verse the phrase comes from is the Bible's one negotiation about returning captured non-combatants. At Ziklag the Amalekites carry off the wives and children and burn the city; David recovers everything, 'and David rescued his two wives'; and then the men of Belial in his own force propose that those who did not fight should get nothing back of the spoil 'save to every man his wife and his children' — that is, that a wife and children are the minimum a man is owed and everything else is negotiable. Alma 54:11 sets the identical unit and inverts the arithmetic: 'ye will deliver up a man, and his wife, and his children, for one prisoner.' Moroni prices a whole family against a single soldier because the Lamanites hold Nephite women and children and he holds none (54:3), which is exactly the asymmetry 1 Samuel 30 is about. The chapter's harshest sentence is built out of the KJV's one verse on the recovery of captive families, and it is spoken by the party the source assigns to the men of Belial.

links.note: 'Save it be on conditions that ye will deliver up a man, and his wife, and his children, for one prisoner.' A KJV singleton whose verse is not merely rare but situationally identical — captured wives and children, a recovery, and a hard bargain over what the non-combatants are worth. The machine ranked 1 Samuel 30:22 second for this verse on the shared words and had no way to see the situational agreement, which is what raises the row to high.

pericopes.text: And behold, if ye do not this, I will come against you with my armies; yea, even I will arm my women and my children, and I will come against you, and I will follow you even into your own land, which is the land of our first inheritance; yea, and it shall be blood for blood; yea, life for life; and I will give you battle, even until you are destroyed from off the face of the earth.

links.text: And if any mischief follow, then thou shalt give life for life,

provenance.other: “life for life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 21:23. Deuteronomy 19:21 has 'life shall go for life' and Leviticus 24:18 'beast for beast', so the bare formula is Exodus's alone. “blood for blood” occurs in no KJV verse at all — the Book of Mormon has coined a member for the series that the Bible does not have. The Sermon on the Mount quotes the talionic list at Matthew 5:38 and drops the life clause entirely, keeping only 'An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth'; `mediation-check.py` returns two decisive points for Exodus 21:23 over Matthew 5:38 on that ground, so the mediation is direct-OT.
provenance.alternative: 1 Kings 20:42 is the other candidate and is worth naming: 'thy life shall go for his life, and thy people for his people', said to Ahab for sparing a captured enemy king, and the same verse contains 'utter destruction', which Alma 54:9 has used three verses earlier. But the string Alma reproduces is Exodus's, not 1 Kings's.
provenance.significance: Moroni is writing about a prisoner exchange, which is the one context in which the lex talionis becomes an exchange rate rather than a punishment. Exodus 21:23 sets the price of a life at a life in a case of accidental injury to a pregnant woman — the KJV's most domestic application of the principle — and Moroni applies it to a war in which he has just demanded a man, his wife and his children for one soldier. The added 'blood for blood', which no KJV verse says, is the tell: he wants the Mosaic formula and then wants more than it gives, and the extra term is placed first.

links.note: 'Yea, and it shall be blood for blood; yea, life for life.' Three words from the KJV's only verse containing them, in the sentence of Moroni's epistle that states his terms. Catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the absolute rarity and the fact that the clause is reproduced whole, though it is three words and far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; it is not one of his 36. The mediation is a clean result rather than a default — the Gospel form of the talion has no life clause to borrow.

pericopes.text: Behold, I am in my anger, and also my people; ye have sought to murder us, and we have only sought to defend ourselves. But behold, if ye seek to destroy us more, we will seek to destroy you; yea, and we will seek our land, the lands of our first inheritance.
Now I close my epistle. I am Moroni; I am a leader of the people of the Nephites.
Now it came to pass that Ammoron, when he had received this epistle, he was angry, and he wrote another epistle unto Moroni; and these are the words which he wrote, saying:

I am Ammoron, the king of the Lamanites; I am the brother of Amalickiah, whom ye have murdered. Behold, I will avenge his blood upon you; yea, and I will come upon you with my armies, for I fear not your threatnings.
For behold, your fathers did wrong their brethren, insomuch that they did rob them of their right to the government, when it rightly belonged unto them.

And now behold, if ye will lay down your arms, and subject yourselves to be governed by those to whom the government doth rightly belong, then will I cause that my people shall lay down their weapons, and shall be at war no more.
Behold, ye have breathed out many threatnings against me and my people; but behold, we fear not your threatnings;

links.text: And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,

provenance.route: Acts 9:1, with Acts 4:29 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “breathing out threatenings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 9:1, and “threatenings” in exactly two, Acts 9:1 and Acts 4:29. The noun is confined to Acts. The 1830 spells it 'threatnings' at all three occurrences in this chapter (54:16 twice at 54:19), which is the same syncopated spelling the first edition uses at 1 Nephi 18:17; 1920 restored the KJV's 'threatenings'. The catalogue adjudicates the borrowing at 1 Nephi 18:17, and this row is written rather than registered because Alma is a different book and a different hand (CONVENTIONS §4, ratified 2026-09-05).
provenance.significance: Both Acts verses are in play and they belong to the two sides of this exchange. Ammoron accuses Moroni of the thing Saul of Tarsus is doing on the road to Damascus — 'ye have breathed out many threatnings against me and my people' — and answers it, twice, with the words of the disciples who were on the receiving end of exactly those threatenings: Acts 4:29's prayer is 'behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word', and Ammoron says 'we fear not your threatnings' at 54:16 and again at 54:19. So a Lamanite king denying that God exists is given the persecuted church's line, and the man he calls a persecutor is Moroni. Recover Acts 9 a verse or two further and the borrowing carries what neither correspondent wants: the KJV's one breather-out of threatenings is stopped on the road and becomes an apostle, which is what the whole epistolary exchange of Alma 54 refuses to imagine for anyone in it.

links.note: 'Behold, ye have breathed out many threatnings against me and my people; but behold, we fear not your threatnings.' A KJV singleton and a two-verse noun, both from Acts, in one sentence of Ammoron's reply. The argument for dependence was made at 1 Nephi 18:17, where Laman and Lemuel breathe out threatenings; it is given again here because Alma is a new book and a reader of this chapter shown nothing would be told there is no borrowing. What is new is the pairing with Acts 4:29 — the accusation and the retort come from the two sides of the same persecution — and the 1830 spelling, which preserves the KJV contact more plainly than the modern text does.

pericopes.text: nevertheless, I will grant to exchange prisoners according to your request, gladly, that I may preserve my food for my men of war; and we will wage a war which shall be eternal, either to the subjecting the Nephites to our authority, or to their eternal extinction.

And as concerning that God whom ye say we have rejected, behold, we know not such a being; neither do ye; but if it so be that there is such a being, we know not but that he hath made us as well as you;

links.text: But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these?

provenance.route: Job 12:3 (the retort) + Acts 13:34 (the opening formula) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “as well as you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 12:3. “as concerning that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:34. Alma 54:21 opens with the second and closes with the first, and both were proposed independently by the n-gram stream for this verse.
provenance.significance: Job 12:3 is the Bible's sharpest sentence of a man refusing to be lectured about God — 'I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these?' — spoken by Job to friends who have been explaining the deity to him. Ammoron's reply is the same speech-act by a man who has just been sent a lecture on the justice of God and the sword of his Almighty wrath, and it lands on the same words: 'we know not such a being; neither do ye … we know not but that he hath made us as well as you.' The difference is the one that makes the borrowing interesting. Job's retort is a believer's; he is claiming equal standing in a dispute about a God he does not doubt. Ammoron takes the same posture and empties it, arguing not that he knows God as well as Moroni does but that neither of them knows anything. The KJV formula that carries the opening is Acts 13:34's, the only 'as concerning that' in the Bible, and it introduces the resurrection — 'as concerning that he raised him up from the dead'. Ammoron's introduces his denial of a hereafter, which he completes at 54:22.

links.note: 'And as concerning that God whom ye say we have rejected, behold, we know not such a being; neither do ye; but if it so be that there is such a being, we know not but that he hath made us as well as you.' Two KJV singletons bracket the verse, one at each end, and neither is doing decorative work: the Acts formula frames a proposition about God's action and the Job formula asserts parity in a quarrel about God. Held at moderate rather than high because each singleton is short and the two come from unrelated books, so a reader may prefer to treat the coincidence as the ordinary King James colouring of the whole epistle.
links.whyNot: Four words and three words, from an OT wisdom dialogue and a Pauline sermon that have nothing to do with each other or with a war. 'As well as you' and 'as concerning that' are rare in the KJV largely because the KJV rarely needs them, not because they are marked phrases.

pericopes.text: and if it so be that there is a Devil and a hell, behold, will he not send you there, to dwell with my brother, which ye have murdered, which ye have hinted that he hath gone to such a place? But behold, these things mattereth not.
I am Ammoron, and a descendant of Zoram, whom your fathers pressed and brought out of Jerusalem.
And behold, now, I am a bold Lamanite. Behold, this war hath been waged, to avenge their wrongs, and to maintain, and to obtain their rights to the government; and I close my epistle to Moroni.

Now it came to pass that when Moroni had received this epistle, he was more angry, because he knew that Ammoron had a perfect knowledge of his fraud; yea, he knew that Ammoron knew that it was not a just cause that had caused him to wage a war against the people of Nephi.

And he said, Behold, I will not exchange prisoners with Ammoron, save he will withdraw his purpose, as I have stated in my epistle; for I will not grant unto him that he shall have any more power than what he hath got.

Behold, I know the place where the Lamanites doth guard my people, which they have taken prisoners; and as Ammoron would not grant unto me mine epistle, behold, I will give unto him according to my words; yea, I will seek death among them, until they shall sue for peace.
And now it came to pass that when Moroni had said these words, he caused that a search should be made among his men, that perhaps he might find a man which was a descendant of Laman among them.
And it came to pass that they found one, whose name was Laman; and he was one of the servants of the king which was murdered by Amalickiah.
Now Moroni caused that Laman and a small number of his men, should go forth unto the guards which were over the Nephites.
Now the Nephites were guarded in the city of Gid; therefore Moroni caused that Laman and a small number of men which was appointed to go with him.

And it came to pass that when it was evening, Laman went to the guards which were over the Nephites, and behold, they saw him coming, and they hailed him. But he saith unto them, Fear not. Behold, I am a Lamanite. Behold, we have escaped from the Nephites, and they sleepeth; and behold, we have took of their wine, and brought with us.

Now when the Lamanites heard these words, they received him with joy.— And they said unto him, Give us of your wine, that we may drink; we are glad that ye have thus taken wine with you, for we are weary.

links.text: Wherefore the people did chide with Moses, and said, Give us water that we may drink. And Moses said unto them, Why chide ye with me? wherefore do ye tempt the LORD?

provenance.other: “that we may drink” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 17:2, and “give us water” occurs in exactly one KJV verse as well — the same one. The whole KJV has one sentence of the form 'give us <drink> that we may drink', and it is Israel's at Rephidim.
provenance.significance: The verse Alma 55:9 is worded out of is the verse that names Massah and Meribah — 'because they tempted the LORD, saying, Is the LORD among us, or not?' (Exodus 17:7). Recover that context and the guards' demand becomes the archetypal demand for drink that is really a test of God, and the answer to it, in Exodus, is water struck from a rock by the man they were chiding. Here the answer is wine deliberately prepared in its strength, and the men who insist on it lose the city in their sleep. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's one formula for demanding drink and put it in the mouths of the people it is about to destroy with drink.

links.note: 'Give us of your wine, that we may drink.' The four-word clause is a KJV singleton and its source is Israel demanding water of Moses. The structural parallel is exact and easy to miss: in both places a demand for drink is made of a man who resists it (Moses answers 'why chide ye with me?'; Laman answers 'let us keep of our wine till we go against the Nephites to battle'), and in both places the resistance only sharpens the demand — Alma 55:10's 'this saying only made them more desirous to drink of the wine' is the narrative equivalent of Exodus 17:3's 'and the people thirsted there for water, and the people murmured'. The machine stream found the string; what it could not see is that the two refusals match as well as the two demands.

pericopes.text: But Laman saith unto them, Let us keep of our wine till we go against the Nephites to battle. But this saying only made them more desirous to drink of the wine.—
For, said they, We are weary; therefore let us take of the wine, and by and by we shall receive wine for our rations, which will strengthen us to go against the Nephites.
And Laman saith unto them, You may do according to your desires.
And it came to pass that they did take of the wine freely, and it was pleasant to their taste; therefore they took of it more freely; and it was strong, having been prepared in its strength.

links.text: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.

provenance.other: “it was pleasant to” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:6, and “pleasant to the” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which two are Eden (Genesis 2:9, 3:6). The KJV's other 'pleasant' constructions are 'pleasant land', 'pleasant vessels', 'pleasant plant' — attributive, not this predicate-plus-sense idiom.
provenance.significance: Genesis 3:6 supplies not one phrase but a sequence, and Alma 55:13 has the sequence: a thing perceived as pleasant to a sense, and then taken. 'It was pleasant to the eyes ... she took of the fruit thereof' becomes 'it was pleasant to their taste; therefore they took of it more freely'. The metalepsis is that the reader who recovers Genesis 3 recovers the outcome as well: the pleasantness is the bait, the taking is the fall, and the sentence immediately after the taking is 'and the eyes of them both were opened'. Alma 55:22's Lamanites likewise wake to find out what they have done — 'when the Lamanites awoke in the morning, they beheld that they were surrounded'. A military stratagem is being narrated in the grammar of the first temptation, and the wine, like the fruit, is not poisoned. It only has to be pleasant.

links.note: 'They did take of the wine freely, and it was pleasant to their taste; therefore they took of it more freely.' Two elements of Genesis 3:6 in Genesis's own order, one of them a KJV singleton, and the substitution of taste for eyes is precisely what the new object requires. The n-gram stream did propose Genesis 3:6 here, on the four words alone; the argument is the second half of the verse, 'she took of', which the window could not reach across the intervening clause. Note that the source is already at work elsewhere in this book — Alma 12:22 stands on Genesis 3 as a whole — but there the reference is doctrinal and stated, and here it is verbal and silent, which is the more interesting of the two.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass they did drink and were merry, and by and by they were all drunken.

links.text: And he took and sent messes unto them from before him: but Benjamin’s mess was five times so much as any of theirs. And they drank, and were merry with him.

provenance.other: “drank and were merry” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 43:34, and “were merry” occurs in exactly two, that verse and Judges 16:25. The Book of Mormon's own auxiliary idiom supplies “did drink,” which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Zechariah 7:6, so the underlying agreement is with the KJV's three-word run.
provenance.significance: Genesis 43:34 is the drinking-scene of a man whose identity the drinkers do not know. Joseph seats his brothers, sends them portions from his own table, and they drink and are merry with him while he is still the Egyptian to them; the recognition comes two chapters later. Alma 55:8-14 is the same scene with the same concealment and the opposite motive: Laman is a Nephite in Lamanite mouth, he tells them what they want to hear ('behold, I am a Lamanite'), he presses the drink on them by pretending to withhold it, and they drink and are merry with a man who is not who he says he is. The Book of Mormon has borrowed the KJV's one phrase for a merry drinking-party and attached it to the KJV's own story of a host in disguise.

links.note: 'They did drink and were merry, and by and by they were all drunken.' Three words, but they are the KJV's only occurrence of the collocation and the narrative frame around them matches at the point that matters — a party drinking with a host who is not what he appears. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold by a wide margin and not one of his quotations; the case rests on rarity and on the disguise, not on length.
links.whyNot: The agreement is three ordinary words and the Book of Mormon's own 'did drink' breaks even that. 'Merry' with drink is a natural English collocation and a reader could reasonably hold that no source is needed.

links.text: And it came to pass, when their hearts were merry, that they said, Call for Samson, that he may make us sport. And they called for Samson out of the prison house; and he made them sport: and they set him between the pillars.

provenance.other: “were merry” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 43:34 and Judges 16:25. The second is the only one where the merriment is a garrison's and the man they are making merry over is their prisoner.
provenance.significance: This is the shape of the whole chapter, not one phrase of it. Judges 16:25 is the last hour of the Philistine lords: their hearts are merry, they send to the prison house for the captive they have disarmed, and the captive brings the building down on them. Alma 55 runs the same reversal in slow motion — the guards drink until they are merry, the prisoners inside the wall are armed while they sleep, and the captors wake surrounded by the men they were holding. Where the Book of Mormon departs from Judges is where the argument is: Samson kills more at his death than in his life, and Moroni, given the identical opening at 55:18, refuses it — 'he did not delight in murder or bloodshed'. The chapter borrows the Philistine feast and then declines the Philistine ending.

links.note: 'They did drink and were merry, and by and by they were all drunken' — and by 55:22 the prisoners are armed and the drinkers are surrounded. The verbal contact is two words in a KJV pair, which on its own would be an echo at best; what carries the link is that Judges 16:25 is the Bible's one scene of drunken captors and an armed captive, and that Alma 55 reproduces it element for element and then withholds the massacre. Recorded as an allusion rather than figural because the two-word contact is with the rarer half of a two-verse set, and because 55:16-17's arming of prisoners 'even to their women, and all those of their children' is the Judges scene's crowd (16:27, 'and there were upon the roof about three thousand men and women') on the other side of the wall.
links.whyNot: Two words of contact, and 'merry' is unavoidable English for a drunken company. A reader who declines typological argument will see nothing here but a coincidence of adjective.

pericopes.text: And now when Laman and his men saw that they were all drunken, and were in a deep sleep, they returned to Moroni, and told him all the things that had happened.

And now this was according to the design of Moroni. And Moroni had prepared his men with weapons of war; and he went to the city Gid, while the Lamanites were in a deep sleep, and drunken, and cast in the weapons of war in unto the prisoners, insomuch that they were all armed;

yea, even to their women, and all those of their children, as many as were able to use a weapon of war; when Moroni had armed all those prisoners. And all those things were done in a profound silence.
But had they awoke the Lamanites, behold they were drunken, and the Nephites could have slain them.

But behold this was not the desire of Moroni. He did not delight in murder or bloodshed; but he delighted in the saving of his people from destruction; and for this cause he might not bring upon him injustice, he would not fall upon the Lamanites and destroy them in their drunkennes.

links.text: By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house; by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith.

provenance.other: “the saving of his” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:7. The KJV's ordinary noun for the thing is 'salvation' or 'deliverance'; the verbal noun 'saving' governing a possessive is Hebrews' construction and nobody else's in the canon.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:7 is the verse in which a man who has been warned prepares something in advance, and the preparing is credited as the saving of the people belonging to him while the world outside is condemned. Alma 55 has the same two motions in the same order and three verses apart: 'Moroni had prepared his men with weapons of war' (55:16), and 'he delighted in the saving of his people from destruction' (55:19). What the recovered context adds is the clause between them — 'by the which he condemned the world'. Moroni's refusal at 55:18-19 is exactly a refusal to condemn: he has the drunken army at his mercy and does not take it, and the sentence in which he declines is worded out of the KJV's one verse about being saved while others drown.

links.note: 'He delighted in the saving of his people from destruction.' Four words, but 'the saving of his' is a KJV singleton and it sits in a chapter whose central action is a preparation made in secret that preserves one household of people from a destruction the preparer could have inflicted. Hebrews 11 is a demonstrated working index for this corpus — the 1 Nephi pass found it used in its own order across four chapters — which raises the prior for a phrase of it turning up as the description of a deliverance.
links.whyNot: The phrase is a natural English construction and the shared words are all function words but one; the link rests almost entirely on the singleton count and on Hebrews 11's track record elsewhere in the corpus rather than on anything distinctive in Alma 55:19 itself.

pericopes.text: But he had obtained his desires; for he had armed those prisoners of the Nephites which were within the wall of the city, and had gave them power to gain possession of those parts which were within the walls;
and then he caused the men which were with him, to withdraw a pace from them, and surround the armies of the Lamanites.

Now behold, this was done in the night time, so that when the Lamanites awoke in the morning, they beheld that they were surrounded by the Nephites without, and that their prisoners were armed within.

And thus they saw that the Nephites had power over them; and in these circumstances they found that it was not expedient that they should fight with the Nephites; therefore their Chief Captains demanded their weapons of war, and they brought them forth, and cast them at the feet of the Nephites, pleading for mercy.

Now behold, this was the desire of Moroni. He took them prisoners of war, and took possesion of the city, and caused that all the prisoners should be liberated, which were Nephites; and they did join the army of Moroni, and were a great strength to his army.
And it came to pass that he did cause the Lamanites which he had taken prisoners, that they should commence a labor in strengthening the fortifications round about the city Gid.

And it came to pass that when he had fortified the city Gid, according to his desires, he caused that his prisoners should be taken to the city Bountiful. And he also guarded that city with an exceeding strong force.

And it came to pass that they did, notwithstanding all the intrigues of the Lamanites, keep and protect all the prisoners which they had taken, and also maintain all the ground and the advantage which they had retaken.
And it came to pass that the Nephites began again to be victorious, and to reclaim their rights and their privileges.
Many times did the Lamanites attempt to encircle them about by night, but in these attempts they did lose many prisoners.—
And many times did they atempt to administer of their wine to the Nephites, that they might destroy them with poison or with drunkenness.

links.text: Their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps.

provenance.other: “poison” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses and “wine is the poison” occurs in exactly one. Deuteronomy 32:33 is the only place in the whole Bible where wine and poison stand in the same sentence; the other seven poison verses are all about serpents' venom or the tongue (Job 6:4, Job 20:16, Psalm 58:4, Psalm 140:3, Romans 3:13, James 3:8) or about beasts sent in judgement (Deuteronomy 32:24). tools/mediation-check.py, run against Romans 3:13 — the New Testament's one poison verse, which quotes Psalm 140:3 rather than Deuteronomy 32 — returns one decisive point for Deuteronomy: the Book of Mormon has 'wine', which is Deuteronomy 32:33's noun, and not 'throat', which is Romans 3:13's. The route is direct-OT.
provenance.significance: The possessive is what makes this worth recording. Deuteronomy 32:32-33 is the Song of Moses on the enemy: *their* vine is of the vine of Sodom, *their* grapes are grapes of gall, *their* wine is the poison of dragons. Alma 55:30-32 is a paragraph of exactly that possessive — 'their wine', four times in three verses, always the enemy's and always suspected of being poison — and it ends by making the Song's metaphor literal and testable: 'if their wine would poison a Lamanite, it would also poison a Nephite; and thus they did try all their liquors'. The Book of Mormon has taken the one KJV verse that calls an enemy's wine poison and turned it into a field protocol.

links.note: 'Many times did they attempt to administer of their wine to the Nephites, that they might destroy them with poison or with drunkenness.' Two content words, but they are two the KJV joins once, and the chapter has already spent seventeen verses making the enemy's wine the instrument of destruction. Deuteronomy 32:33's alternative to poison is drunkenness in the next breath of the same Song (32:42's 'I will make mine arrows drunk with blood'), and Alma 55:30 names both together as the two things the wine might do.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is 'wine' and 'poison' and nothing else — no shared phrase, no shared syntax. A reader may hold that a besieged army suspecting the enemy's drink of being poisoned needs no source at all, and that the coincidence with Deuteronomy 32:33 is an artifact of how rarely the KJV mentions poison.

pericopes.text: But behold, the Nephites were not slow to remember the Lord their God, in this their times of affliction. They could not be taken in their snares; yea, they would not partake of their wine; yea, they would not take of wine, save they had firstly given to some of the Lamanite prisoners.
And they were thus cautious, that no poison should be administered among them; for if their wine would poison a Lamanite, it would also poison a Nephite; and thus they did try all their liquors.

And now it came to pass that it was expedient for Moroni to make preparations to attack the city Morianton.—For behold, the Lamanites had, by their labors, fortified the city Morionton until it had become an exceeding strong hold;
and they were continually bringing new forces into that city, and also new supplies of provisions.
And thus ended the twenty and ninth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.

And now it came to pass in the commencement of the thirtieth year of the reign of the Judges, in the second day, on the first month, Moroni received an epistle from Helaman, stating the affairs of the people in that quarter of the land.

And these are the words which he wrote, saying: My dearly beloved brother, Moroni, as well in the Lord as in the tribulations of our warfare; behold, my beloved brother, I have somewhat to tell you concerning our warfare in this part of the land.

links.text: (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)

provenance.other: “our warfare” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 10:4. The noun itself is rare — “warfare” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — and in the possessive it is Paul's alone. “strong holds” is commoner (nineteen KJV verses), so it carries nothing by itself; what is worth noting is that Alma 56 uses both of 2 Corinthians 10:4's two distinctive nouns, at 56:2 and again at 56:21 ('we were not desirous to make an attack upon them in their strong holds').
provenance.significance: Helaman's letter opens in the register of a Pauline epistle — a named addressee, 'my dearly beloved brother', the pairing 'as well in the Lord as in the tribulations of our warfare' — and the phrase it reaches for is from the one Pauline passage that insists the warfare in question is not the kind fought with weapons. 2 Corinthians 10:3-4 says 'though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh: for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal'. Alma 56 then spends fifty-five verses on weapons that emphatically are carnal, and ends by saying that the young men who carried them 'fought as if with the strength of God' and that not one of them fell. The letter borrows Paul's phrase for a spiritual campaign and applies it to an actual one, and the chapter's own explanation of the outcome — strength that is not the soldiers' own — is Paul's 'mighty through God' arriving by a different road.

links.note: 'My dearly beloved brother, Moroni, as well in the Lord as in the tribulations of our warfare.' 'Our warfare' is a KJV singleton and it belongs to 2 Corinthians 10:4; the epistolary frame around it is Pauline in shape, and 'strong holds', the other distinctive noun of that verse, returns at 56:21. Recorded at moderate because a first-person plural possessive on a common noun is easy to generate independently, and because the two words are nineteen verses apart in the Book of Mormon rather than adjacent as they are in Paul.
links.whyNot: Two words, one of them a pronoun. 'Warfare' is ordinary English and 'our warfare' would be produced by anyone writing a war letter in the first person plural; the KJV singleton may be an accident of how seldom the KJV uses the noun at all.

pericopes.text: Behold, two thousand of the sons of those men which Ammon brought down out of the land of Nephi: Now ye have known that these were a descendant of Laman, which was the eldest son of our father Lehi.
Now I need not rehearse unto you concerning their traditions or their unbelief, for thou knowest concerning all these things;
therefore it supposeth me that I tell you that two thousand of these young men hath taken their weapons of war, and would that I should be their leader; and we have come forth to defend our country.
And now ye also know concerning the covenant which their fathers made, that they would not take up their weapons of war against their brethren, to shed blood.

But in the twenty and sixth year, when they saw our afflictions and our tribulations for them, they were about to break the covenant which they had made, and take up their weapons of war in our defence.

But I would not suffer them that they should break this covenant which they had made, supposing that God would strengthen us, insomuch that we should not suffer more because of the fulfilling the oath which they had taken.

But behold, here is one thing in which we may have great joy. For behold, in the twenty and sixth year, I Helaman, did march at the head of these two thousand young men, to the city of Judea, to assist Antipus, whom ye had appointed a leader over the people of that part of the land.

And I did join my two thousand sons, (for they are worthy to be called sons,) to the army of Antipus; in the which strength Antipus did rejoice exceedingly; for behold, his army had been reduced by the Lamanites because of the numerority of their forces having slain a vast number of our men; for which cause we have to mourn.
Nevertheless, we may console ourselves in this point: that they have died in the cause of their country and of their God; yea, and they are happy.

And the Lamanites had also retained many prisoners, all of whom are Chief Captains; for none other have they spared alive. And we suppose that they are now at this time in the land of Nephi; it is so if they are not slain.
And now these are the cities which the Lamanites have obtained possession, by the shedding of the blood of so many of our valiant men:
The land of Manti, or the city of Manti, and the city of Zeezrom, and the city of Cumeni, and the city of Antiparah.
And these are the cities which they possessed when I arrived at the city of Judea; and I found Antipus and his men toiling with their mights to fortify the city;

yea, and they were depressed in body as well as in spirit; for they had fought valiantly by day, and toiled by night, to maintain their cities; and thus they had suffered great afflictions of every kind.

And now they were determined to conquer in this place, or die; therefore you may well suppose that this little force which I brought with me; yea, those sons of mine, gave them great hopes and much joy.

And now it came to pass that when the Lamanites saw that Antipus had received a greater strength to his army, they were compelled, by the orders of Ammoron, to not come against the city of Judea, or against us, to battle.
And thus were we favored of the Lord: for had they come upon us in this our weakness, they might have perhaps destroyed our little army; but thus were we preserved.

They were commanded by Ammoron to maintain those cities which they had taken. And thus ended the twenty and sixth year. And in the commencement of the twenty and seventh year, we had prepared our city and ourselves for defence.
Now we were desirous that the Lamanites should come upon us; for we were not desirous to make an attack upon them in their strong holds.

And it came to pass that we kept spies out round about, to watch the movements of the Lamanites, that they might not pass us by night, nor by day, to make an attack upon our other cities, which were on the northward;

for we knew in those cities they were not sufficiently strong to meet them; therefore we were desirous, if they should pass by us, to fall upon them in their rear, and thus bring them up in the rear, at the same time they were met in the front. We supposed that we could overpower them; but behold, we were disappointed in this our desire.
They durst not pass by us with their whole army; neither durst they with a part, lest they should not be sufficiently strong, and they should fall.
Neither durst they march down against the city of Zarahemla; neither durst they cross the head of Sidon, over to the city of Nephihah.
And thus, with their forces, they were determined to maintain those cities which they had taken.
And now it came to pass, in the second month of this year, there was brought unto us many provisions, from the fathers of those my two thousand sons.
And also there was sent two thousand men unto us, from the land of Zarahemla. And thus we were prepared with ten thousand men, and provisions for them, and also for their wives, and their children.

And the Lamanites, thus seeing our forces increase daily, and provisions arrive for our support, they began to be fearful, and began to sally forth, if it were possible, to put an end to our receiving provisions and strength.

Now when we saw that the Lamanites began to grow uneasy on this wise, we were desirous to bring a stratagem into an effect upon them; therefore Antipus ordered that I should march forth with my little sons, to a neighboring city, as if we were carrying provisions to a neighboring city.
And we were to march near the city Antiparah, as if we were going to the city beyond, in the borders, by the seashore.
And it came to pass that we did march forth, as if with our provisions, to go to that city.

And it came to pass that Antipus did march forth, with a part of his army, leaving the remainder to maintain the city. But he did not march forth, until I had gone forth with my little army, and came near the city Antiparah.
And now in the city Antiparah, were stationed the strongest army of the Lamanites; yea, the most numerous.
And it came to pass that when they had been informed by their spies, they came forth with their army, and marched against us.
And it came to pass that we did flee before them, northward. And thus we did lead away the most powerful army of the Lamanites;

yea, even to a considerable distance, insomuch that when they saw the army of Antipus pursuing them, with their mights, they did not turn to the right nor to the left, but pursued their march in a straight course after us; and, as we supposed, it was their intent to slay us before Antipus should overtake them, and this that they might not be surrounded by our people.

links.text: And Asahel pursued after Abner; and in going he turned not to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner.

provenance.other: “turned not to the right hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 2:19. The fuller formula “to the right hand nor to the left” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, and the other four are all about conduct rather than pursuit: two are requests to pass peaceably through a country (Numbers 20:17, Deuteronomy 2:27), one is obedience to a judicial sentence (Deuteronomy 17:11), one is Proverbs 4:27 on moral straightness, and 2 Chronicles 34:2 is Josiah's walk. 2 Samuel 2:19 is the only KJV verse in which the phrase describes a man chasing another man.
provenance.significance: The recovered context is the whole point and it is grim. Asahel's refusal to turn to the right hand or the left is not praised in 2 Samuel 2; it is the reason he dies. Abner turns and warns him twice — 'turn thee aside to thy right hand or to thy left' (2:21), 'wherefore should I smite thee to the ground?' (2:22) — and Asahel will not, and Abner kills him with the hinder end of the spear. Alma 56:37 gives the phrase to the Lamanite army pursuing Helaman, and gives it in the same posture: the pursuer who will not deviate, running down a smaller force, with a second army closing behind. Helaman even names the danger Abner named — 'it was their intent to slay us before Antipus should overtake them, and this that they might not be surrounded by our people' — and the outcome is the one 2 Samuel 2 predicts for the man who does not turn aside. At 56:40 the phrase is turned around and applied to Helaman himself, so both parties in the chase are Asahel, and neither can afford to be.

links.note: 'They did not turn to the right nor to the left, but pursued their march in a straight course after us.' The KJV's one pursuit-verse using this formula, and the Book of Mormon has it in a pursuit. The one departure is the dropped noun: every KJV instance reads 'right hand', and Alma 56:37 and 56:40 both read 'right' alone, which is the phrase compressed rather than a different phrase. Note that 56:40 uses it twice more in three lines, once of the Lamanites and once of Helaman — a doubling that reads as a writer working a borrowed formula rather than reaching for an idiom of his own.

pericopes.text: And now Antipus, beholding our danger, did speed the march of his army. But behold, it was night; therefore they did not overtake us, neither did Antipus overtake them; therefore we did camp for the night.

And it came to pass that before the dawn of the morning, behold, the Lamanites were pursuing us. Now we were not sufficiently strong to contend with them; yea, I would not suffer that my little sons should fall into their hands; therefore we did continue our march; and we took our march into the wilderness.

Now they durst not turn to the right nor to the left, lest they should be surrounded; neither would I turn to the right or to the left, lest they should overtake me, and we could not stand against them, but be slain, and they would make their escape; and thus we did flee all that day into the wilderness, even until it was dark.
And it came to pass that again when the light of the morning came, we saw the Lamanites upon us, and we did flee before them.
But it came to pass that they did not pursue us far, before they halted; and it was in the morning of the third day, on the seventh month.

And now whether they were overtaken by Antipus, we knew not; but I said unto my men, Behold, we know not but they have halted for the purpose that we should come against them, that they might catch us in their snare;
therefore, what say ye, my sons, will ye go against them to battle?
And now I say unto you, my beloved brother Moroni, That never had I seen so great courage, nay, not amongst all the Nephites.

For as I had ever called them my sons, (for they were all of them very young,) even so they said unto me, Father, behold, our God is with us, and he will not suffer that we shall fall; then let us go forth; we would not slay our brethren, if they would let us alone; therefore let us go, lest they should overpower the army of Antipus.

links.text: Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us.

provenance.other: “God is with us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 8:10 — the translation of Immanuel worked into the oracle itself. Matthew 1:23 has the interpretation without the verb ('Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us'), so the finite clause the Book of Mormon uses is Isaiah's and not the Gospel's.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 8:9-10 is a war oracle addressed to armies, and the sons of the stripling warriors answer their commander with its last clause. Recover the context and the whole of what Helaman's young men are claiming becomes visible: 'Associate yourselves, O ye people, and ye shall be broken in pieces … Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us.' That is a promise that an enemy's confederacy and an enemy's plan will fail, which is exactly the news of Alma 56 — Ammoron's orders at 56:18 and 56:20 keep his armies from attacking, the pursuit at 56:37 is a plan that comes to nought, and the chapter closes with the pursuers surrendering. The young men say four words and the source supplies the argument for them. Note also that the KJV's sole occurrence of the clause sits between the two Immanuel verses (Isaiah 7:14, 8:8), so the phrase these sons of a converted people use of themselves is the name given to a promised child.

links.note: 'Father, behold, our God is with us, and he will not suffer that we shall fall.' A KJV singleton, and the one place in the Bible where the clause is a finite sentence rather than a gloss on a name. The interpolated possessive ('our God is with us') is the Book of Mormon making the clause the speakers' own, and it fits the chapter's insistence that this faith was taught to them and not inherited from the fathers, who had buried their weapons. The second half of the young men's answer, 'he will not suffer that we shall fall', is then cashed out at 56:56, where not one of them has fallen.

pericopes.text: Now they never had fought, yet they did not fear death; and they did think more upon the liberty of their fathers, than they did upon their lives; yea, they had been taught by their mothers, that if they did not doubt, that God would deliver them.

links.text: Jesus answered and said unto them, Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith, and doubt not, ye shall not only do this which is done to the fig tree, but also if ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; it shall be done.

provenance.other: “doubt not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 21:21. The word appears in thirteen KJV verses altogether, but in nine of them it is the adverbial 'no doubt' or the noun; the only two places where doubting is negated as a condition of a promise are Matthew 21:21 and its Markan double, Mark 11:23's 'shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe'.
provenance.significance: The mothers' teaching is given in the grammar of the KJV's mountain-moving saying: a negated doubt as the condition, and a guaranteed outcome as the apodosis. What the Book of Mormon changes is who holds the condition. In Matthew the promise is to the one who does not doubt; in Alma 56:47-48 the young men do not doubt because their mothers did not, and the sentence they actually say is about someone else's certainty — 'we do not doubt our mothers knew it'. That is a displacement worth naming: the faith that moves the mountain has been made hereditary and second-hand, and the chapter treats that as a strength rather than a defect.
provenance.alternative: James 1:6's 'ask in faith, nothing wavering' is the same doctrine in different words and could stand behind the sentiment without any of Matthew's wording.

links.note: 'They had been taught by their mothers, that if they did not doubt, that God would deliver them.' The conditional is the KJV's and so is the negated verb, though the Book of Mormon inflects it ('did not doubt', 'do not doubt') rather than reproducing Matthew's imperative form 'doubt not'. Filed as an echo, not an allusion, because the only shared content word is 'doubt' and the shape of the sentence is doing most of the work.
links.whyNot: One content word. Doubt is the natural antonym for the faith the passage is about, and a writer describing a taught confidence would arrive at the negation without any source. The rarity count is real but it measures the KJV's vocabulary, not this verse's dependence.

pericopes.text: And they rehearsed unto me the words of their mothers, saying: We do not doubt our mothers knew it.

And it came to pass that I did return with my two thousand, against these Lamanites which had pursued us. And now behold, the armies of Antipus had overtaken them, and a terrible battle had commenced.

The army of Antipus being weary, because of their long march in so short a space of time, were about to fall into the hands of the Lamanites; and had I not returned with my two thousand, they would have obtained their purpose:

for Antipus had fallen by the sword, and many of his leaders, because of their weariness, which was occasioned by the speed of their march; therefore the men of Antipus being confused, because of the fall of their leaders, began to give way before the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that the Lamanites took courage, and began to pursue them; and thus were the Lamanites pursuing them with great vigor, when Helaman came upon their rear with his two thousand, and began to slay them exceedingly, insomuch that the whole army of the Lamanites halted, and turned upon Helaman.
Now when the people of Antipus saw that the Lamanites had turned them about, they gathered together their men, and came again upon the rear of the Lamanites.

And now it came to pass that we, the people of Nephi, the people of Antipus, and I with my two thousand, did surround the Lamanites, and did slay them; yea, insomuch that they were compelled to deliver up their weapons of war, and also themselves as prisoners of war.
And now it came to pass that when they had surrendered themselves up unto us, behold, I numbered those young men which had fought with me, fearing lest there were many of them slain.

But behold, to my great joy, there had not one soul of them fallen to the earth; yea, and they had fought as if with the strength of God; yea, never was men known to have fought with such miraculous strength; and with such mighty power did they fall upon the Lamanites, that they did frighten them; and for this cause did the Lamanites deliver themselves up as prisoners of war.

links.text: Then said she, I pray thee, let the king remember the LORD thy God, that thou wouldest not suffer the revengers of blood to destroy any more, lest they destroy my son. And he said, As the LORD liveth, there shall not one hair of thy son fall to the earth.

provenance.other: “one hair of thy son” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 14:11, and “not one hair” in exactly two, that verse and 1 Samuel 14:45. The verb phrase “fall to the earth” occurs in exactly three KJV verses; taking earth and ground together, the KJV's fixed formula 'there shall not one hair … fall to the earth/ground' occurs at 1 Samuel 14:45, 2 Samuel 14:11 and 1 Kings 1:52 and nowhere else. Alma 56:56 has the formula with 'earth', which is 2 Samuel 14:11's and 1 Kings 1:52's word, and with 'soul' substituted for 'hair'.
provenance.significance: All three KJV verses carrying this formula are guarantees that a particular young man under sentence of death will be spared: Jonathan, whom the people rescue from his father's oath after he alone attacked a garrison and wrought a great salvation; the widow of Tekoah's surviving son, spared from the avengers of blood; and Adonijah, spared on condition. Two of the three are pleas made by a parent or on a son's behalf, and 2 Samuel 14:11 is the mother's. Alma 56:56 reports the outcome of a battle fought by two thousand sons whose commander calls them his own and whose mothers' faith is the chapter's stated cause of their survival, and it reports it in the formula the KJV reserves for a threatened son who is spared. 1 Samuel 14:45 sharpens it further: Jonathan is the KJV's one young man who attacks a superior garrison on the conviction that 'there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few', which is the doctrine Helaman's letter exists to demonstrate.

links.note: 'There had not one soul of them fallen to the earth.' The KJV has one way of saying that a young man in danger will not be lost, and this is it, with 'soul' for 'hair' because two thousand men and not one man is the quantity in view. The substitution is the Book of Mormon's, and it is not a weakening: 'not one hair' is a figure for total preservation and 'not one soul' makes the same claim literally. The 1830 reading is unchanged here, so nothing in the transmission is doing the work.

links.text: And they said unto Moses, Thy servants have taken the sum of the men of war which are under our charge, and there lacketh not one man of us.

provenance.other: “there lacketh not one man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and so does “taken the sum of the men of war”; both are Numbers 31:49. There is no verbal contact with Alma 56:55-56 at all — the Book of Mormon numbers rather than takes the sum, and its men are souls rather than men — so the count is recorded to show that the scene is a KJV singleton, not to claim the wording.
provenance.significance: This catalogue declined Numbers 31:49 once already, at Alma 49:23, on the ground that not one word is shared and the Book of Mormon's 'not a single soul' is in no KJV verse. That reasoning was right there and it does not reach here, because Alma 56:55 supplies what 49:23 lacked: the muster itself. Numbers 31:48-49 is a scene, not a phrase — subordinate officers come to the commander after a battle, report that they have counted the men under their charge, and report that none is missing — and Alma 56:55-56 is that scene entire, with the added detail that Helaman counts 'fearing lest there were many of them slain' and that the report reaches Moroni as a letter, which is the only form a subordinate's post-battle census can take at this distance. The KJV has exactly one such scene. That the Book of Mormon reproduces it without reproducing a word of it is the finding.

links.note: 'I numbered those young men which had fought with me, fearing lest there were many of them slain. But behold, to my great joy, there had not one soul of them fallen to the earth.' Filed as figural under CONVENTIONS §2 because the link is at the level of the scene and there is no shared wording to test; kjvSpecific is 'no' for the same reason, and no claim about the King James English is being made. The verbal case at this verse is carried by the separate row on 2 Samuel 14:11. Compare the exclusion at Alma 49:23, which sent the same source away for want of exactly what 56:55 provides.
links.whyNot: Zero verbal contact, and a commander counting his men after a battle is a natural thing to narrate. If Numbers 31:49 is the only KJV instance, that may say more about how rarely the KJV narrates a muster than about where Alma 56:55 came from — and a reader who applied the Alma 49:23 reasoning consistently would decline this row too.

pericopes.text: And as we had no place for our prisoners, that we could guard them to keep them from the armies of the Lamanites, therefore we sent them to the land of Zarahemla, and a part of those men which were not slain of Antipus, with them; and the remainder I took and joined them to my stripling Ammonites, and took our march back to the city of Judea.

And now it came to pass that I received an epistle from Ammoron, the king, stating that if I would deliver up those prisoners of war which we had taken, that he would deliver up the city of Antiparah unto us.

But I sent an epistle unto the king, That we were sure our forces were sufficient to take the city of Antiparah by our force; and by delivering up the prisoners for that city, we should suppose ourselves unwise, and that we would only deliver up our prisoners on exchange.
And Ammoron refused mine epistle, for he would not exchange prisoners; therefore we began to make preparations to go against the city of Antiparah.
But the people of Antiparah did leave the city, and fled to their other cities which they had possession of, to fortify them; and thus the city of Antiparah fell into our hands.
And thus ended the twenty and eighth year of the reign of the Judges.

And it came to pass that in the commencement of the twenty and ninth year, we received a supply of provisions, and also an addition to our army, from the land of Zarahemla, and from the land round about, to the number of six thousand men, besides sixty of the sons of the Ammonites, which had come to join their brethren, my little band of two thousand. And now behold, we were strong; yea, and we had also a plenty of provisions brought unto us.
And it came to pass that it was our desire to wage a battle with the army which was placed to protect the city Cumeni.

And now behold, I will shew unto you that we soon accomplished our desire; yea, with our strong force, or with a part of our strong force, we did surround, by night, the city Cumeni, a little before they were to receive a supply of provisons.

And it came to pass that we did camp round about the city for many nights; but we did sleep upon our swords, and keep guards, that the Lamanites could not come upon us by night, and slay us, which they attempted many times; but as many times as they attempted this, their blood was spilt.
At length their provisions did arrive, and they were about to enter the city by night. And we, instead of being Lamanites, were Nephites; therefore, we did take them and their provisions.—

And notwithstanding the Lamanites being cut off from their support after this manner, they were still determined to maintain the city; therefore it became expedient that we should take those provisions and send them to Judea and our prisoners to the land of Zarahemla.

And it came to pass that not many days had passed away, before the Lamanites began to lose all hopes of succor; therefore they yielded up the city into our hands; and thus we had accomplished our designs, in obtaining the city Cumeni.
But it came to pass that our prisoners were so numerous, that notwithstanding the enormity of our numbers, we were obliged to employ all our force to keep them, or to put them to death.

For behold, they would break out in great numbers, and would fight with stones, and with clubs, or whatsoever things they could get into their hands, insomuch that we did slay upwards of two thousand of them, after they had surrendered themselves prisoners of war;

therefore it became expedient for us, that we should put an end to their lives, or guard them, sword in hand, down to the land of Zarahemla; and also our provisions were not any more than sufficient for our own people, notwithstanding that which we had taken from the Lamanites.

And now, in those critical circumstances, it became a very serious matter to determine concerning these prisoners of war; nevertheless, we did resolve to send them down to the land of Zarahemla; therefore we selected a part of our men, and gave them charge over our prisoners, to go down to the land of Zarahemla.

But it came to pass that on the morrow, they did return.— And now behold, we did not inquire of them concerning the prisoners; for behold, the Lamanites were upon us, and they returned in season to save us from falling into their hands.— For behold, Ammoron had sent to their support a new supply of provisions, and also a numerous army of men.
And it came to pass that those men which we sent with the prisoners, did arrive in season to check them, as they were about to overpower us.
But behold, my little band of two thousand and sixty, fought most desperately; yea, they were firm before the Lamanites, and did administer death unto all those who opposed them;
and as the remainder of our army were about to give way before the Lamanites, behold, those two thousand and sixty were firm and undaunted;

yea, and they did obey and observe to perform every word of command with exactness; yea, and even according to their faith, it was done unto them; and I did remember the words which they said unto me that their mothers had taught them.

links.text: Then touched he their eyes, saying, According to your faith be it unto you.

provenance.route: Matthew 9:29 + Matthew 8:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “according to your faith” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “be it unto you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are Matthew 9:29, which is the whole of the sentence. “be it done unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 8:13's 'as thou hast believed, so be it done unto thee'. “according to thy faith” occurs in no KJV verse at all, so the possessive the Book of Mormon inflects is the one the KJV actually has.
provenance.significance: Every KJV verse standing behind this sentence is a healing. Matthew 9:29 is said to two blind men who have just answered 'Yea, Lord' to 'Believe ye that I am able to do this?'; Matthew 8:13 is said to the centurion whose servant is healed in the selfsame hour; Matthew 15:28, the third of the family, restores a daughter. Alma 57:21 puts the formula on a battlefield, and the payoff is four verses later: two hundred of the two thousand and sixty have fainted from loss of blood, 'there was not one soul of them which did perish', and not one of them is unwounded. The metalepsis is exact and it is the chapter's argument — these young men are not preserved from wounds, they are preserved through them, which is what a healing is. Note also what the tense does.
