Matthew's clause is an optative said before the outcome; the Book of Mormon's is an indicative said after it, and 57:21 immediately adds 'and I did remember the words which they said unto me that their mothers had taught them', so the report of the fulfilment is joined to the memory of the promise at 56:47-48.

links.note: 'Yea, and even according to their faith, it was done unto them.' The clause is Matthew 9:29's entire saying with the person changed from second to third and the verb realized as a past indicative, and its two halves are separately KJV singletons. The realized verb is not Matthew 9:29's own — 'be it done unto' is Matthew 8:13's — so the sentence fuses the two healing formulas of Matthew 8-9, which stand nineteen verses apart in one stretch of miracle narratives. Catalogued as a quotation on the completeness of the reproduction and the double singleton, not on length: at six words it is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and it is not one of his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And now behold, it was these, my sons, and those men which had been selected to convey the prisoners, to whom we owe this great victory; for it was they who did beat the Lamanites; therefore they were driven back to the city of Manti.
And we retained our city Cumeni, and were not all destroyed by the sword; nevertheless, we had suffered great loss.

And it came to pass that after the Lamanites had fled, I immediately gave orders that my men which had been wounded, should be taken from among the dead, and caused that their wounds should be dressed.

And it came to pass that there were two hundred, out of my two thousand and sixty, which had fainted because of the loss of blood; nevertheless, according to the goodness of God, and to our great astonishment, and also the foes of our whole army, there was not one soul of them which did perish; yea, and neither was there one soul among them which had not received many wounds.

And now, their preservation was astonishing to our whole army; yea, that they should be spared, while there was a thousand of our brethren which were slain. And we do justly ascribe it to the miraculous power of God, because of their exceeding faith in that which they had been taught to believe, that there was a just God; and whosoever did not doubt, that they should be preserved by his marvellous power.
Now this was the faith of these of which I have spoken; they are young, and their minds are firm; and they do put their trust in God continually.

links.text: And they were helped against them, and the Hagarites were delivered into their hand, and all that were with them: for they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him.

provenance.other: “they put their trust in him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Chronicles 5:20. The wider phrase “put their trust in” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, and the other five are all devotional rather than narrative — Psalm 2:12, 5:11, 9:10, 17:7 and Proverbs 30:5, where trusting God is praised in the abstract. 1 Chronicles 5:20 is the only place in the King James Bible where putting one's trust in God is given as the recorded cause of winning a particular battle.
provenance.significance: 1 Chronicles 5:18-22 is the KJV's one battle report constructed as an argument from faith rather than from numbers. It counts the men of war exactly (forty-four thousand seven hundred and threescore, 'valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword'), states the enemy's losses, and then gives the cause: they cried to God in the battle, he was intreated of them, because they put their trust in him. Alma 57:25-27 is that report in the same order — the exact count of two thousand and sixty and the two hundred who fainted, the thousand slain brethren set against them, and then the cause: 'we do justly ascribe it to the miraculous power of God, because of their exceeding faith … they do put their trust in God continually.' Helaman is writing the one kind of war dispatch the King James Bible contains, and he is using its concluding formula for his own conclusion.

links.note: 'They are young, and their minds are firm; and they do put their trust in God continually.' The phrase is a KJV singleton in the one KJV battle narrative that ends by ascribing the victory to it, and Alma 57:26-27 is doing precisely that ascription. Held at moderate rather than high because 'put their trust in' is a live devotional idiom across the Psalms and the Book of Mormon could have taken it from there; what argues for Chronicles is not the words alone but the fact that the words arrive at the same point in the same kind of document.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that after we had thus taken care of our wounded men, and had buried our dead, and also the dead of the Lamanites, which were many, behold, we did inquire of Gid concerning the prisoners which they had started to go down to the land of Zarahemla with.
Now Gid was the Chief Captain over the band which was appointed to guard them down to the land.

And now, these are the words which Gid said unto me: Behold, we did start to go down to the land of Zarahemla, with our prisoners. And it came to pass that we did meet the spies of our armies, which had been sent out to watch the camp of the Lamanites.
And they cried unto us, saying: Behold, the armies of the Lamanites are a marching towards the city of Cumeni; and behold, they will fall upon them, yea, and will destroy our people.
And it came to pass that our prisoners did hear their cries, which caused them to take courage; and they did rise up in rebellion against us.

And it came to pass because of their rebellion, we did cause that our swords should come upon them. And it came to pass that they did, in a body, run upon our swords, in the which, the greater number of them were slain; and the remainder of them broke through and fled from us.

And behold, when they had fled, and we could not overtake them, we took our march with speed towards the city Cumeni; and behold, we did arrive in time that we might assist our brethren in preserving the city.
And behold, we are again delivered out of the hands of our enemies. And blessed is the name of our God: for behold, it is he that hath delivered us; yea, that hath done this great thing for us.

Now it came to pass that when I, Helaman, had heard these words of Gid, I was filled with exceeding joy, because of the goodness of God in preserving us, that we might not all perish; yea, and I trust that the souls of them which has been slain, have entered into the rest of their God.

And behold, now it came to pass that our next object was to obtain the city of Manti; but behold, there was no way that we could lead them out of the city, by our small bands. For behold, they remembered that which we had hitherto done; therefore we could not decoy them away from their strong holds;
and they were so exceeding more numerous than was our army, that we durst not go forth and attack them in their strong holds.

Yea, and it became expedient that we should employ our men, to the maintaining those parts of the land, of the which we had retained of our possessions; therefore it became expedient that we should wait, that we might receive more strength from the land of Zarahemla, and also a new supply of provisions.

And it came to pass that I thus did send an embassy to the governor of our land, to acquaint him concerning the affairs of our people. And it came to pass that we did wait to receive provisions and strength, from the land of Zarahemla.
But behold, this did not profit us but little: for the Lamanites were also receiving great strength, from day to day, and also many provisions; and thus were our circumstances at this period of time.

And the Lamanitas were sallying forth against us, from time to time, resolving by stratagem, to destroy us; nevertheless, we could not come to battle with them, because of their retreats and their strong holds.
And it came to pass that we did wait in these difficult circumstances, for the space of many months, even until we were about to perish for the want of food.

But it came to pass that we did receive food, which was guarded to us by an army of two thousand men, to our assistance; and this is all the assistance which we did receive, to defend ourselves and our country from falling into the hands of our enemies; yea, to contend with an enemy which was innumerable.

And now the cause of these our embarrassments, or the cause why they did not send more strength unto us, we knew not; therefore we were grieved, and also filled with fear, lest by any means the judgements of God should come upon our land, to our overthrow and utter destruction;

therefore we did pour out our souls in prayer to God, that he would strengthen us and deliver us out of the hands of our enemies; yea, and also give us strength, that we might retain our cities, and our lands, and our possessions, for the support of our people.

links.text: And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God.

provenance.other: 'In prayer to God' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 6:12. The other half of the clause is the pour-out-the-soul idiom, which the KJV has twice and in two grammatical forms: Psalm 42:4's present 'I pour out my soul in me' and 1 Samuel 1:15's past 'I have poured out my soul before the LORD'. Alma 58:10 has the present, which is the Psalm's; 'pour out our' occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.alternative: That the four words are an unremarkable English construction anyone could compose independently. The count says otherwise about the KJV, but not about 1829.
provenance.significance: Recover Luke 6:12 and the phrase turns out to belong, in the King James Bible, to one man on one night: it is the vigil Jesus keeps alone on a mountain, and it is the only all-night prayer the Gospels give him. What Alma 58 does with it is hand it to an army. A body of starving soldiers in a fortified camp prays in the words the KJV reserves for Christ's solitary vigil, and the next verse answers them the way Luke's vigil is answered — with a naming and a sending. Luke's morning produces the twelve; Helaman's produces the assurance, the peace, and the two thousand who do not die.

links.note: 'Therefore we did pour out our souls in prayer to God, that he would strengthen us and deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.' Two KJV idioms meet in one clause and neither is the war-narrative language the chapter has been running for nine verses. The pouring out of the soul is the Psalter's and Hannah's — private, distressed, and answered; 'in prayer to God' is a Lukan singleton. Held at moderate because the second is only four words long and the shared vocabulary with the first is two; what argues for the row is that a chapter otherwise built out of provisions, spies and strong holds changes register entirely for one sentence, and changes into scripture's register.

pericopes.text: Yea, and it came to pass that the Lord our God did visit us with assurances, that he would deliver us; yea, insomuch that he did speak peace to our souls, and did grant unto us as great faith, and did cause us that we should hope for our deliverance in him;

links.text: I will hear what God the LORD will speak: for he will speak peace unto his people, and to his saints: but let them not turn again to folly.

provenance.other: 'Speak peace' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 28:3, Psalm 85:8 and Zechariah 9:10. Only one of the three has God as the speaker and a people as the hearer, and that is Psalm 85:8. The preposition is the awkward datum — 'speak peace to' with 'to' rather than 'unto' is itself a KJV singleton, and it belongs to Psalm 28:3, where the workers of iniquity 'speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts'. Alma 58:11 has Psalm 28's preposition and Psalm 85's sense.
provenance.significance: Psalm 85 is not a psalm of private consolation; it is a national one, addressed to a land God has already once turned back from captivity and asking him to do it again — 'Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?' The verse the Book of Mormon borrows is the psalm's hinge, the moment the speaker stops petitioning and listens for the answer, and what follows it is 'Surely his salvation is nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land'. Helaman's epistle is a report on whether glory will dwell in the land, written by a man who has just told the chief judge he fears the judgments of God on it. The psalm supplies not only the phrase but the shape of the paragraph: petition (58:10), a pause to hear (58:11), and an answer about the land.

links.note: 'Insomuch that he did speak peace to our souls, and did grant unto us as great faith, and did cause us that we should hope for our deliverance in him.' The answer to the prayer of 58:10 is given in the words of the one KJV verse in which God speaks peace to a people, and the sentence keeps the psalm's sequence — the speaking, then the hope. Held at moderate because the object is changed from 'his people' to 'our souls', which is the Book of Mormon's own idiom rather than the psalm's; the 1830's 'as great faith', flattened to 'great faith' in 1920, preserves a comparative whose second term the sentence never supplies.

pericopes.text: and we did take courage with our small force which we had received, and were fixed with a determination to conquer our enemies, and to maintain our lands, and our possessions, and our wives, and our children, and the cause of our liberty.
And thus we did go forth with all our might against the Lamanites, which were in the city of Manti; and we did pitch our tents by the wilderness side, which was near to the city.

And it came to pass that on the morrow, that when the Lamanites saw that we were in the borders by the wilderness which was near the city, that they sent out their spies round about us, that they might discover the number and the strength of our army.

And it came to pass that when they saw that we were not strong, according to our numhers, and fearing that we should cut them off from their support, except they should come out to battle against us, and kill us, and also supposing that they could easily destroy us with their numerous hosts, therefore they began to make preparations to come out against us to battle.

And when we saw that they were making preparations to come out against us, behold, I caused that Gid, with a small number of men, should secrete himself in the wilderness, and also that Teomner should, with a small number of men, secrete themselves also in the wilderness.

Now Gid and his men was on the right, and the others on the left; and when they had thus secreted themselves, behold, I remained with the remainder of my army, in that same place where we had first pitched our tents, against the time that the Lamanites should come out to battle.

And it came to pass that the Lamanites did come out with their numerous army against us. And when they had come, and were about to fall upon us with the sword, I caused that my men, those which were with me, should retreat into the wilderness.

And it came to pass that the Lamanites did follow after us with great speed, for they were exceedingly desirous to overtake us, that they might slay us; therefore they did follow us into the wilderness; and we did pass by in the midst of Gid and Teomner, insomuch that they were not discovered by the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that when the Lamanites had passed by, or when the army had passed by, Gid and Teomner did rise up from their secret places, and did cut off the spies of the Lamanites, that they should not return to the city.

And it came to pass that when they had cut them off, they ran to the city, and fell upon the guards which were left to guard the city, insomuch that they did destroy them, and did take possession of the city.
Now this was done, because the Lamanites did suffer their whole army, save a few guards only, to be led away into the wilderness.

And it came to pass that Gid and Teomner, by this means, had obtained possession of their strong holds. And it came to pass that we took our course, after having travelled much in the wilderness, towards the land of Zarahemla.

And when the Lamanites saw that they were marching towards the land of Zarahemla, they were exceeding fraid, lest there was a plan laid to lead them on to destruction; therefore they began to retreat into the wilderness again, yea, even back by the same way which they had came.

And behold, it was night, and they did pitch their tents; for the Chief Captains of the Lamanites had supposed that the Nephites were weary, because of their march; and supposing that they had driven their whole army, therefore they took no thought concerning the city of Manti.
Now it came to pass that when it was night, that I caused that my men should not sleep, but that they should march forward, by another way, towards the land of Manti.
And because of this our march in the night time, behold, on the morrow, we were beyond the Lamanites, insomuch that we did arrive before them to the city of Manti.
And thus it came to pass, that by this stratagem, we did take possession of the city of Manti, without the shedding of blood.

And it came to pass that when the armies of the Lamanites did arrive near the city, and saw that we were prepared to meet them, they were astonished exceedingly, and struck with great fear, insomuch that they did flee into the wilderness.—
Yea, and it came to pass that the armies of the Lamanites did flee out of all this quarter of the land. But behold, they have carried with them many women and children out of the land.

And those cities which had been taken by the Lamanites, all of them are at this period of time, in our possession; and our fathers, and our women, and our children, are returning to their homes, all save it be those which have been taken prisoners and carried off by the Lamanites.
But behold, our armies are small, to maintain so great a number of cities, and so great possessions.
But behold, we trust that our God, who hath given us victory over those lands, insomuch that we have obtained those cities and those lands, which were our own.
Now we do not know the cause that the government does not grant us more strength; neither does those men which came up unto us, know why we have not received greater strength.
Behold, we do not know but what ye are unsuccessful, and ye have drawn away the forces into that quarter of the land; if so, we do not desire to murmur.

And if it is not so, behold, we fear that there is some faction in the government, that they do not send more men to our assistance; for we know that they are more numerous than that which they have sent.
But behold, it mattereth not; we trust God will deliver us, notwithstanding the weakness of our armies, yea, and deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.—
Behold, this is the twenty and ninth year, in the latter end, and we are in the possessson of our lands; and the Lamanites have fled to the land of Nephi.

And those sons of the people of Ammon, of which I have so highly spoken, are with me in the city of Manti; and the Lord hath supported them, yea, and kept them from falling by the sword, insomuch that even one soul hath not been slain.

But behold, they have received many wounds; nevertheless they stand fast in that liberty wherewith God hath made them free; and they are strict to remember the Lord their God, from day to day; yea, they do observe to keep his statutes, and his judgements, and his commandments continually; and their faith is strong in the prophecies concerning that which is to come.

links.text: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.

provenance.other: 'Liberty wherewith' is a KJV singleton, and so is the whole run 'wherewith Christ hath made us free'. 'Stand fast' occurs in nine KJV verses and is Pauline in seven of them; the Book of Mormon has taken the one where it governs liberty. 'Made them free' occurs in no KJV verse, which is the mark of the substitution: the phrase had to be re-pronouned to fit.
provenance.significance: The book of Alma has been quarrying Galatians 5:1 for fifteen chapters, and always from the back end. Moroni throws the yoke of bondage at Zerahemnah (44:2); the narrator uses it twice of Amalickiah (49:7, 49:26); the whole political vocabulary of the war chapters — liberty, freedom, bondage — is the vocabulary of that one verse. What happens at 58:40 is that the front half finally arrives, and it arrives attached to the two thousand young men. The verse's substitution is the argument: Paul writes 'the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free' of a freedom from the law, and Helaman writes 'that liberty wherewith God hath made them free' of soldiers who have received many wounds and lost no one. Read Galatians back into it and the sentence claims that the political liberty these chapters have spent twenty pages defending with swords is the same liberty Paul tells the Galatians not to trade for a yoke — and the clause is picked up and repeated word for word three chapters later, when Pahoran closes his reply to Moroni by blessing 'all those who stand fast in that liberty wherewith God hath made them free' (61:21). Whatever else divides the two epistles, they end in the same borrowed sentence.

links.note: 'Nevertheless they stand fast in that liberty wherewith God hath made them free.' The clause reproduces Galatians 5:1's opening entire, with two changes and no others: 'therefore in the' becomes 'in that', and 'Christ hath made us free' becomes 'God hath made them free'. 'Liberty wherewith' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. This falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six, but it is a complete clause taken from a verse the chapter can be shown to know at both ends — 58:41 immediately returns to it, 'the Lord our God who hath redeemed us and made us free' — and the argument for its earlier half was made at Alma 44:2. The 1830's 'hath' was modernized to 'has' in 1920, so the first edition preserves the KJV's verb form as well as its words.

pericopes.text: And now my beloved brother Moroni, that the Lord our God who hath redeemed us and made us free, may keep you continnally in his presence; yea, and that he may favor this people, even that ye may have success in obtaining the possession of all that which the Lamanites hath taken from us, which was for our support. And now behold, I close mine epistle. I am Helaman, the son of Alma.

Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, after Moroni had received and had read Helaman’s epistle, he was exceedingly rejoiced because of the welfare, yea, the exceeding success which Helaman had had, in obtaining those lands which were lost;
yea, and he did make it known unto all his people in all the land round about in that part where he was, that they might rejoice also.

And it came to pass that he immediately sent an epistle to Pahoran, desiring that he should cause men to be gathered together, to strengthen Helaman, or the armies of Helaman, insomuch that he might with ease maintain that part of the land which he had been so miraculously prospered in retaining.—

And it came to pass when Moroni had sent this epistle to the land of Zarahemla, he began again to lay a plan, that he might obtain the remainder of those possessions and cities which the Lamanites had taken from them.

And it came to pass that while Moroni was thus making preparations to go against the Lamanites to battle, behold, the people of Nephihah which were gathered together from the city of Moroni, and the city of Lehi, and the city of Morianton, were attacked by the Lamanites;
yea, even those which had been compelled to flee from the land of Manti, and from the land round about, had come over and joined the Lamanites in this part of the land;

and thus being exceeding numerous, yea, and receiving strength from day to day, by the command of Ammoron, they came forth against the people of Nephihah, and they did begin to slay them with an exceeding great slaughter.
And their armies were so numerous, that the remainder of the people of Nephihah were obliged to flee before them; and they came even and joined the army of Moroni.—

And now as Moroni had supposed that there should be men sent to the city of Nephihah, to the assistance of the people to maintain that city, and knowing that it was easier to keep the city from falling into the hands of the Lamanites, than to retake it from them, he supposed that they would easily maintain that city;
therefore he retained all his force to maintain those places whieh he had recovered.

And now when Moroni saw that the city of Nephihah was lost, he was exceeding sorrowful, and began to doubt, because of the wickedness of the people, whether they should not fall into the hands of their brethren.

links.text: And they were exceeding sorrowful, and began every one of them to say unto him, Lord, is it I?

provenance.other: 'Exceeding sorrowful' occurs in three KJV verses and all three are Passion-week verses: Matthew 26:22, Matthew 26:38 and Mark 14:34. The corpus has used the phrase once before, at Alma 35:15, where the source is the Gethsemane pair. Here the phrase runs one word further — 'exceeding sorrowful and began' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, and it belongs not to Gethsemane but to the table.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 26:38 / Mark 14:34, the Gethsemane form, which is the source of the corpus's other use at Alma 35:15. It is ruled out by the continuation: neither Gethsemane verse has 'and began', and both put the sorrow in a soul rather than in a company.
provenance.significance: Recover Matthew 26:22 and it is the one moment in the Gospels when a body of loyal men is told that one of their own has betrayed them, and answers not with denial but with self-suspicion — 'Lord, is it I?' Alma 59 is the Book of Mormon's version of that table. Moroni has just learned that a city was lost for want of the reinforcements he asked for, he is exceeding sorrowful and he begins to doubt; 59:12 immediately extends the doubt to every one of his chief captains, which is Matthew's 'every one of them'; and 59:13 names what he thinks the cause is — a government indifferent to the freedom of its country. The chapter is thirteen verses long and its whole function is to move a commander from grief to the suspicion of treachery, which is Matthew 26:22's function exactly. What the borrowing supplies, and what Alma 59 never says, is the answer to the question. The disciples ask 'Lord, is it I?'; Moroni does not ask it, and Alma 60 is what he writes instead. Pahoran's reply at 61:9 — 'I am not angry, but do rejoice in the greatness of your heart' — is a correction of an accusation that Matthew's disciples were careful not to make.

links.note: 'He was exceeding sorrowful, and began to doubt, because of the wickedness of the people.' The four words 'exceeding sorrowful, and began' occur in exactly one KJV verse, and the sentence they open in Alma has the same shape as the one they open in Matthew: a sorrow that turns immediately into a suspicion about the company. The n-gram stream ranked this fifth among the candidates at this verse and behind two chronological formulas, which is §9's point about the recall floor. The 1830 and 1920 agree on the wording here; what carries the row is the collocation, not any variant.

pericopes.text: Now this was the case with all his Chief Captains. They doubted and marvelled also, because of the wickedness of the people; and this because of the success of the Lamanites over them.
And it came to pass that Moroni was angry with the government, because of their indifference concerning the freedom of their country.

And it came to pass that he wrote again to the governor of the land, which was Pahoran, and these are the words which he wrote, saying, Behold, I direct mine epistle to Pahoran, in the city of Zarahemla, which is the Chief Judge and the governor over the land, and also to all those who hath been chosen by this people to govern and manage the affairs of this war;

for behold, I have somewhat to say unto them by the way of condemnation; for behold, ye yourselves know that ye have been appointed to gather together men, and arm them with swords, and with cimeters, and all manner of weapons of war, of every kind, and send forth against the Lamanites, in whatsoever parts they should come into our land.

And now behold, I say unto you, That myself, and also my men, and also Helaman and his men, have suffered exceeding great sufferings; yea, even hunger, thirst, and fatigue, and all manner of afflictions of every kind.
But behold, were this all we had suffered, we would not murmur nor complain;

but behold, great has been the slaughter among our people; yea, thousands have fallen by the sword, while it might have otherwise been, if ye had rendered unto our armies sufficient strength and succor for them. Yea, great has been your neglect towards us.
And now behold, we desire to know the cause of this exceeding great neglect; yea, we desire to know the cause of your thoughtless state.
Can you think to sit upon your thrones, in a state of thoughtless stupor, while your enemies are spreading the work of death around you? Yea, while they are murdering thousands of your brethren;

yea, even they which have looked up to you for protection, yea, have placed you in a situation that ye might have succored them; yea, ye might have sent armies unto them, to have strengthened them, and have saved thousands of them from falling by the sword?

But behold, this is not all: Ye have withheld your provisions from them, insomuch that many have fought and bled out their lives because of their great desires which they had for the welfare of this people; yea, and this they have done, when they were about to perish with hunger, because of your exceeding great neglect towards them.

links.text: And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!

provenance.other: 'Perish with hunger' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Luke 15:17. Moroni uses it twice in this one epistle, at 60:9 of his own men and at 60:35 of what God will not allow; the corpus has it at 2 Nephi 1:24 and Mosiah 21:17, and both of those are adjudicated to the same source. The Book of Mormon has no competing idiom for starvation of its own: 'famish', the KJV's other word for it, appears once in the whole corpus and only inside the transcribed Isaiah of 2 Nephi 15:13.
provenance.significance: The prodigal's line is not a description of hunger but a comparison: he perishes with hunger while his father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, and the sentence exists to make the contrast unbearable. That is precisely the rhetorical work Alma 60:9 needs. Moroni is not reporting a famine; he is contrasting men who 'bled out their lives' at the front with a government sitting in the heart of the country 'surrounded by security' (60:19), and the comparison is his whole argument. Recover Luke 15 and the borrowing carries the parable's next move with it — the starving son's remedy is to go home and confront the household that has bread — which is exactly what Moroni threatens at 60:30 and 60:35: 'I come unto you even into the land of Zarahemla', 'he will give unto us of your food, even if it must be by the sword'. The parable's return is a repentance; Moroni's is an invasion.

links.note: 'When they were about to perish with hunger, because of your exceeding great neglect towards them.' Three words, but a KJV singleton, and the same three words close the epistle at 60:35 with the argument reversed — there it is God who 'will not suffer that we should perish with hunger'. The corpus has used the phrase twice before and this is its first appearance in Alma; the row is written here rather than carried from Mosiah 21:17 because a new book is a new hand (ADJUDICATING §4) and because Moroni does something with it neither earlier user does, which is to make a starving army's complaint into an accusation against the people who have the bread.

pericopes.text: And now, my beloved brethren; for ye had ought to be beloved; yea, and ye had ought to have stirred yourselves more diligently for the welfare and the freedom of this people: but behold, ye have neglected them, insomuch that the blood of thousands shall come upon your heads for vengeance; yea, for known unto God were all their cries, and all their sufferings.

links.text: Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.

provenance.other: 'Known unto God are all' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Acts 15:18. The only other KJV verse with 'known unto God' at all is Philippians 4:6, where the direction is reversed — requests made known unto God. Alma 60:10 has the Acts word order intact and changes one word: 'known unto God were all their cries, and all their sufferings.'
provenance.significance: Acts 15:18 is the closing line of James's speech at the Jerusalem council, and its function there is jurisdictional: it settles a dispute between two parties about what may be required of a body of believers by asserting that God has already seen the whole matter. Moroni's sentence does the same work in a fight between a general and a government about what may be required of soldiers. But the substitution is where the row earns its place. James says God knows all his works; Moroni says God knew all their cries and all their sufferings — the object is changed from the divine acts to the human casualties, and the tense from the timeless present to a completed past. Recover Acts and the borrowing quietly claims that the dead of the Nephite garrisons stand in the record where God's own works stand in James's. That is the ground of the sentence's first half, 'the blood of thousands shall come upon your heads for vengeance'.

links.note: 'Yea, for known unto God were all their cries, and all their sufferings.' Five words of a KJV singleton in their KJV order, with the verb moved to the past and the object replaced. The corpus reaches Acts 15:18 twice before, at 1 Nephi 9:6 and Words of Mormon 1:7, and in both places for the doctrinal claim that the Lord knows all things; this is the first use of the verse's actual wording, and it is put to a forensic purpose rather than a doctrinal one. The 1830 and 1920 agree here.

pericopes.text: Behold, could ye suppose that ye could sit upon your thrones, and because of the exceeding goodness of God, ye could do nothing, and he would deliver you? Behold, if ye have supposed this, ye have supposed in vain.

Do ye suppose that, because so many of your brethren have been killed, because of their wickedness? I say unto you, if ye have supposed this, ye have supposed in vain: for I say unto you, there are many which have fallen by the sword; and behold, it is to your condemnation;

for the Lord suffereth the righteous to be slain, that his justice and judgement may come upon the wicked; therefore ye need not suppose that the righteous are lost because they are slain; but behold, they do enter into the rest of the Lord their God.

And now behold, I say unto you, I fear exceedingly that the judgements of God will come upon this people, because of their exceeding slothfulness; yea, even the slothfulness of our government, and their exceeding great neglect towards their brethren, yea towards those which have been slain:
For were it not for the wickedness which first commenced at our head, we could have withstood our enemies, that they could have gained no power over us;

yea, had it not been for the war which broke out among ourselves; yea, were it not for these king-men, which caused so much bloodshed among ourselves; yea, at the time we were contending among ourselves, if we had united our strength, as we hitherto have done; yea, had it not been for the desire of power and authority which those king-men had over us; had they been true to the cause of our freedom, and united with us, and gone forth against our enemies, instead of taking up their swords against us, which was the cause of so much bloodshed among ourselves; yea if we had gone forth against them, in the strength of the Lord, we should have dispersed our enemies; for it would have been done according to the fulfilling of his word.

But behold, now the Lamanites are coming upon us, and they are murdering our people with the sword; yea, our women and our children; taking possession of our lands, and also carrying them away captive; causing them that they should suffer all manner of afflictions; and this because of the great wickedness of those who are seeking for power and authority; yea, even those king-men.
But why should I say much concerning this matter, for we know not but what ye yourselves are seeking for authority? We know not but what ye are also traitors to your country?
Or is it that ye have neglected us because ye are in the heart of our country, and ye are surrounded by security, that ye do not cause food to be sent unto us, and also men to strengthen our armies?
Have ye forgot the commandments of the Lord your God? Yea, have ye forgot the captivity of our fathers? Have ye forgot the many times we have been delivered out of the hands of our enemies?
Or do ye suppose that the Lord will still deliver us, while we sit upon our thrones, and do not make use of the means which the Lord hath provided for us?

Yea, will ye sit in idleness, while ye are surrounded with thousands of those, yea, and tens of thousands, which do also sit in idleness, while there are thousands round about in the borders of the land, which are falling by the sword, yea, wounded and bleeding?

Do ye suppose that God will look upon you as guiltless, while ye sit still and behold these things? Behold I say unto you, Nay. Now I would that ye should remember that God hath said that The inward vessel shall be cleansed first, and then shall the outer vessel be cleansed also.

links.text: Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also.

provenance.route: Matthew 23:26, with Luke 11:39 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Two of the saying's three moving parts are KJV singletons and both belong to Matthew 23:26: 'cleanse first' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, and so does 'clean also'. The third, 'inward', is Luke's — Matthew 23:26 reads 'that which is within', while Luke 11:39 has 'your inward part'. Neither Gospel has 'vessel'; both have 'the cup and the platter'. tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for each Gospel and reports the divergences as pointing both ways, which is the finding: the Book of Mormon's saying is neither evangelist's wording but a fusion of the two.
provenance.alternative: Luke 11:39-41 alone, which supplies 'inward' and the Pharisees but neither of the two singletons and not the first/also structure that gives the saying its shape.
provenance.significance: Moroni does not quote this as a saying of Jesus. He introduces it with 'God hath said', as a standing word of scripture, and then applies it to a civil government — 'it will be expedient that we contend no more with the Lamanites until we have first cleansed our inward vessel; yea, even the great head of our government' (60:24). Recover Matthew 23 and the context is the chapter of woes against men who 'sit in Moses' seat' (23:2), and the whole indictment is that they are diligent about what is visible and negligent about what is not. Moroni has been building that charge for twenty-two verses in exactly Matthew's terms: three times he accuses Pahoran of sitting — 'sit upon your thrones' (60:7, 60:11), 'sit in idleness' (60:22) — and three times of neglect. The cup saying arrives as the seal on that argument, and it converts a private-purity image into a constitutional one: the vessel to be cleansed first is the head of state. Whether the appropriation is deliberate or not, the effect is that the Book of Mormon's one use of Jesus's Pharisee-woe is aimed at a legislature.

links.note: 'Now I would that ye should remember that God hath said that The inward vessel shall be cleansed first, and then shall the outer vessel be cleansed also.' Marked in the text as a citation — 'God hath said' — but not reproduced as one: the wording is a paraphrase, and the two phrases that pin it are Matthew 23:26's 'cleanse first' and 'clean also', each a KJV singleton, while the adjective 'inward' comes from Luke 11:39's parallel. 'Outer' is the Book of Mormon's own supply; the KJV's word in both Gospels is 'outside', and its four uses of 'outer' are Ezekiel's court and Matthew's darkness. Hardy's study edition cross-references Matthew 23:25-26 at this verse. Recorded as an allusion rather than a quotation because no clause survives intact, and at high rather than certain because a saying this compressed could in principle be independent — but two singletons from one verse, in that verse's order, is not the shape of independence.

pericopes.text: And now except ye do repent of that which ye have done, and begin to be up and doing, and send forth food and men unto us, and also unto Helaman, that he may support those parts of our country which he hath retained, and that we may also recover the remainder of our possessions in these parts, behold it will be expedient that we contend no more with the Lamanites until we have first cleansed our inward vessel; yea, even the great head of our government;

and except ye grant mine epistle, and come out and shew unto me a true spirit of freedom, and strive to strengthen and fortify our armies, and grant unto them food for their support, behold I will leave a part of my freemen to maintain this part of our land, and I will leave the strength and the blessings of God upon them, that none other power can operate against them;
and this because of their exceeding faith and their patience in their tribulations;

and I will come unto you, and if there be any among you that hath a desire for freedom, yea, if there be even a spark of freedom remaining, behold I will stir up insurrections among you, even until those who hath desires to usurp power and authority, shall become extinct;

links.text: Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it.

provenance.route: Isaiah 13:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon, or Isaiah 13:17 → 2 Nephi 23:17 → Book of Mormon; see below
provenance.other: 'I will stir up' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Isaiah 13:17, and the Book of Mormon has the four-word opening 'Behold, I will stir up' twice: here, and at 2 Nephi 23:17, which is the corpus's own transcription of Isaiah 13. The transcription departs from the KJV in its second half ('which shall not regard silver and gold, nor they shall not delight in it') but reproduces the opening exactly, so the two routes are verbally indistinguishable at the only words Alma 60:27 shares. Mediation is recorded as uncertain for that reason, and the reason is the whole of it — this is not a default.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 13 is the burden of Babylon, and 13:17 is the verse in which God announces the instrument of its fall: a people stirred up against a capital that is 'the glory of kingdoms' (13:19). Moroni's charge against Pahoran three verses later is 'your love of glory, and the vain things of the world' (60:32). What he says at 60:27 is 'behold I will stir up insurrections among you, even until those who hath desires to usurp power and authority, shall become extinct' — the sentence in which a general announces that he will raise a rising inside his own nation's capital. He speaks it in the grammar of Isaiah 13:17, which is God's grammar, in the first person, about a city his book calls Zarahemla and Isaiah calls Babylon. It is the most theologically reckless sentence in the epistle and the borrowing is what makes it so.

links.note: 'Behold I will stir up insurrections among you.' Four words of a KJV singleton, kept in order and in the first person, with the object changed from a foreign army to a domestic rising. Held at moderate rather than high because the run is short and 'stir up' is ordinary English, and because the corpus already contains the source verse verbatim at 2 Nephi 23:17, so the borrowing cannot be shown to reach here from the KJV rather than from the Nephite record's own Isaiah. What argues for the row is the company the phrase keeps: Isaiah 13's charge against Babylon is glory and vain magnificence, and Alma 60:32's charge against the government is 'your love of glory, and the vain things of the world'.
links.whyNot: Four words is thin, and a general threatening to raise an insurrection has an obvious reason to say 'I will stir up' without any source at all. The row rests on the count plus the Isaiah 13:19 / Alma 60:32 pairing, and a reader who declines the second will rightly decline the first.

pericopes.text: yea, behold I do not fear your power nor your authority, but it is my God whom I fear, and it is according to his commandments that I do take my sword to defend the cause of my country, and it is because of your iniquity that we have suffered so much loss.

Behold it is time, yea, the time is now at hand, that except ye do bestir yourselves in the defence of your country and your little ones, the sword of justice doth hang over you; yea, and it shall fall upon you and visit you even to your utter destruction.

links.text: And let it be, when thou hearest the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees, that then thou shalt bestir thyself: for then shall the LORD go out before thee, to smite the host of the Philistines.

provenance.other: 'Bestir' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 2 Samuel 5:24, and in exactly one Book of Mormon verse, Alma 60:29. It is a word neither book uses twice.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one use of the word is a divine order to a king about the timing of an attack: David is to wait for the sound in the mulberry trees and then bestir himself, because at that moment the LORD goes out before him to smite the Philistines. It is the Bible's clearest statement that there is a right moment to move an army and that failing to move at it forfeits a battle God had already given. Alma 60:29 is that verse turned into an accusation — 'Behold it is time, yea, the time is now at hand, that except ye do bestir yourselves in the defence of your country and your little ones, the sword of justice doth hang over you.' Moroni's sentence begins by announcing the moment and ends by naming the penalty for missing it, which is 2 Samuel 5:24's structure with the promise removed and a threat put in its place. The whole epistle argues that the government has heard the sound and not moved.

links.note: A one-word row, and the word is a KJV singleton in a book that reuses very little. 'Bestir' is not ordinary nineteenth-century English either; where it survives it survives as a biblicism, and the verse it comes from is about the exact subject of Alma 60 — a commander waiting for a government that will not move at the appointed time. Held at moderate because a single word cannot carry syntax or sequence, and the note is the argument (CONVENTIONS §3a): what makes the row worth having is that 2 Samuel 5:24's sense arrives with its word.

pericopes.text: Behold, I wait for assistance from you, and except ye do administer unto our relief, behold I come unto you even into the land of Zarahemla, and smite you with the sword, insomuch that ye can have no more power to impede the progress of this people in the cause of our freedom;
for behold the Lord will not suffer that ye shall live and wax strong in your iniquities, to destroy his righteous people.

Behold, can you suppose that the Lord will spare you and come out in judgement against the Lamanites, when it is the tradition of their fathers that hath caused their hatred; yea, and it hath been redoubled by those which have dissented from us, while your iniquity is for the cause of your love of glory, and the vain things of the world?

Ye know that ye do transgress the laws of God, and ye do know that ye do trample them under your feet. Behold, the Lord saith unto me, If those whom ye have appointed your governors, do not repent of their sins and iniquities, ye shall go up to battle against them.

links.text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.

provenance.other: 'Trample them under' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Matthew 7:6, and Alma 60:33 reproduces it with one pronoun changed: 'ye do trample them under your feet' for 'lest they trample them under their feet'. The KJV's usual verb for this action is 'tread' or 'trodden'; 'trample' occurs in only three KJV verses altogether. Alma 5:53 has the verb with a divine object and is adjudicated to Hebrews 10:29 with Matthew 7:6 as a composite; this is the corpus's closest reproduction of Matthew's actual run.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:6 is about entrusting holy things to keepers who will not keep them, and its second half is what the trampling leads to: the swine 'turn again and rend you'. Alma 60:33 has both halves in two sentences. The first names the trampling and its object — 'ye do transgress the laws of God, and ye do know that ye do trample them under your feet' — and the second is the rending: 'Behold, the Lord saith unto me, If those whom ye have appointed your governors, do not repent of their sins and iniquities, ye shall go up to battle against them.' Recover Matthew and the verse supplies the premise Moroni never states, which is that the laws of God were a holy thing given into the keeping of men who proved to be the wrong keepers. The corpus will later transcribe Matthew 7:6 entire at 3 Nephi 14:6; here it is being used before it is quoted.

links.note: Five words of a KJV singleton with one pronoun changed, in a verse whose second sentence supplies Matthew's own consequence. Written here rather than carried from Alma 5:53 because 5:53's phrase is 'trample the holy one under your feet', which is why that row's primary source is Hebrews 10:29; the KJV run that Matthew 7:6 actually contains appears in Alma only at 60:33.

links.text: And Micaiah said, As the LORD liveth, what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak.

provenance.other: 'The LORD saith unto me' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 1 Kings 22:14. The bare 'saith unto me' occurs in six, four of them in Revelation, where the speaker is an angel and not the Lord.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 22 is the King James Bible's set piece on a prophet, a king and a war council. Two kings are about to go up to Ramoth-gilead; four hundred prophets tell them to go and prosper; Micaiah alone says he will speak only what the LORD saith unto him, and what he then says is that Israel will be scattered on the hills as sheep that have not a shepherd, because 'these have no master' (22:17). Moroni's clause introduces the one moment in his epistle when he stops arguing and claims a word: 'Behold, the Lord saith unto me, If those whom ye have appointed your governors, do not repent of their sins and iniquities, ye shall go up to battle against them.' He is in Micaiah's position and says so in Micaiah's words — the lone voice against a body of men who govern a war — and the word he brings is Micaiah's word inverted. Micaiah forbids a battle a king wants; Moroni commands one nobody wants, and against the governors themselves.

links.note: 'Behold, the Lord saith unto me' is a five-word KJV singleton and the machine found it on a six-word run. Held at moderate because the words are the plainest possible way in English to introduce a divine communication, so the count is a fact about the KJV rather than proof of borrowing; what raises it is that the KJV's one instance is the scene Alma 60 has been re-enacting since verse 1 — a war council, a governing body committed to a course, and one man claiming the only word from God in the room.

pericopes.text: And now behold, I Moroni am constrained, according to the covenant which I have made to keep the commandments of my God; therefore I would that ye should adhear to the word of God, and send speedily unto me of your provisions and of your men, and also to Helaman.

links.text: Depart from me, ye evildoers: for I will keep the commandments of my God.

provenance.other: 'Keep the commandments of my God' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Psalm 119:115, and so does the shorter 'the commandments of my God'. The Book of Mormon's usual form of this formula is second or third person — 'keep the commandments of God', 'his commandments' — and 'commandments of my God' occurs in exactly one Book of Mormon verse, this one. Both the KJV and the corpus use the first-person possessive once each.
provenance.significance: Psalm 119:115 is a verse of separation, and it is the only one in the psalm that addresses anyone but God: 'Depart from me, ye evildoers: for I will keep the commandments of my God.' The keeping of the commandments is given there as the reason for the break — the psalmist dismisses the company because he intends to obey. Moroni's use is identical in function and unstated in its first half. He writes 'I Moroni am constrained, according to the covenant which I have made to keep the commandments of my God' at the point in the epistle where he has just been told nothing and is about to march on Zarahemla, and the covenant he invokes is the ground of a separation from the men he is writing to. Recover the psalm and the sentence's missing clause is supplied: depart from me, ye evildoers. Two verses later he tells them he is coming.

links.note: Six words reproduced exactly from a verse in which they occur once in the whole King James Bible. This falls below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not among his thirty-six, but the clause is complete and the possessive is distinctive: 'commandments of my God' occurs once in the King James Bible and once in the Book of Mormon. Catalogued as a quotation on CONVENTIONS §2's ground that length does not decide the category — a complete clause from a KJV singleton is a quotation whatever its length.

pericopes.text: And behold if ye will not do this, I come unto you speedily; for behold, God will not suffer that we should perish with hunger; therefore he will give unto us of your food, even if it must be by the sword. Now see that ye fulfil the word of God.

Behold, I am Moroni, your Chief Captain. I seek not for power but to pull it down. I seek not for honor of the world, but for the glory of my God, and the freedom and welfare of my country. And thus I close mine epistle.
Behold, now it came to pass that soon after Moroni had sent his epistle unto the Chief Governor, he received an epistle from Pahoran, the Chief Governor. And these are the words which he received:

I, Pahoran, which art the Chief Governor of this land, do send these words unto Moroni, the Chief Captain over the army: Behold I say unto you, Moroni, That I do not joy in your great afflictions; yea, it grieves my soul.

But behold, there are those who do joy in your afflictions; yea, insomuch that they have risen up in rebellion against me, and also those of my people which are free men; yea, and those which have risen up, are exceeding numerous.

And it is those who have sought to take away the judgement seat from me, that have been the cause of this great iniquity; for they have used great flattery; and they have led away the hearts of many people, which will be the cause of sore affliction among us; they have withheld our provisions, and have daunted our freemen, that they have not come unto you.

links.text: And on this manner did Absalom to all Israel that came to the king for judgment: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

provenance.other: 'Stole the hearts' is a KJV singleton at 2 Samuel 15:6; the Book of Mormon has 'led away the hearts', which is its own idiom (Alma 46:10) and not the KJV's verb. The catalogue adjudicates the verbal borrowing of that idiom at Mosiah 27:9 and Alma 17:29; this row is not about the words.
provenance.alternative: Daniel 11:21 and 11:32 give the KJV its political 'flatteries', and a reader who wants a source for Pahoran's 'great flattery' alone would take it there rather than to Absalom.
provenance.significance: The sequence, not the vocabulary, is the argument. 2 Samuel 15 is the KJV's one full account of a coup mounted from the judgment seat: Absalom stations himself where 'any man that had a controversy came to the king for judgment' and wishes aloud that he 'were made judge in the land' (15:4); he steals the hearts of Israel (15:6); he is proclaimed king in Hebron (15:10); and the lawful ruler flees the capital rather than fight for it (15:14). Alma 61:4-8 runs the same four beats in the same order — rebels who 'have sought to take away the judgement seat', hearts led away, a king appointed over them in the captured capital, and Pahoran driven out to Gideon. Nothing in the epistle names Absalom, which is what makes it worth recording: if the pattern is borrowed, it is borrowed whole and silently, and it supplies the one thing Pahoran's letter needs and never argues for — that a chief judge who abandons his capital is not thereby a coward.

links.note: 'It is those who have sought to take away the judgement seat from me … they have used great flattery; and they have led away the hearts of many people.' A figural row, filed under CONVENTIONS §0a with its thinness stated. The verbal contact is one displaced idiom, and the catalogue has already adjudicated that idiom against 2 Samuel 15:6 twice, so nothing here rests on it. What rests on this row is the shape of verses 4 through 8, which reproduces the Absalom rebellion's distinctive order — judgment seat, hearts, usurped kingship, flight of the rightful ruler — a sequence the KJV tells once. Moroni's epistle in Alma 60 had accused Pahoran of sitting 'upon a thoughtless stupor' in the seat of government; the reply's first move is to describe the loss of that seat in the terms of the Bible's one story where losing it is the innocent party's fate.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact worth the name. 'Led away the hearts' is the Book of Mormon's own phrase, used of Amalickiah at Alma 46:10 before Pahoran uses it here, and a rebellion that captures a capital and crowns a king will resemble Absalom's whether or not anyone was reading 2 Samuel. The row stands or falls on whether the ordering of four common elements is evidence, and a reasonable reader can say it is not.

pericopes.text: And behold, they have driven me out before them, and I have fled to the land of Gideon, with as many men as it were possible that I could get.

links.text: Now therefore, I pray thee, let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If the LORD have stirred thee up against me, let him accept an offering: but if they be the children of men, cursed be they before the LORD; for they have driven me out this day from abiding in the inheritance of the LORD, saying, Go, serve other gods.

provenance.other: 'Have driven me out' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The longer 'they have driven me' likewise resolves to 1 Samuel 26:19 alone.
provenance.significance: The KJV has one man who says that they have driven him out, and it is David, complaining to Saul from the far side of a hill about being expelled from 'the inheritance of the LORD'. Pahoran, writing from the land of Gideon after the loss of Zarahemla, uses the same sentence. Taken with the row at 61:4 the two halves of David's career are doing the same work in four verses: the exile of 1 Samuel and the coup of 2 Samuel, both of them stories in which the legitimate ruler is out of his capital and is not thereby illegitimate. That is precisely the charge Alma 60 laid against Pahoran and precisely what this letter has to answer.

links.note: 'They have driven me out before them, and I have fled to the land of Gideon.' Four words, but they are a KJV singleton and they are spoken in the Bible by the anointed king in flight. The machine stream proposed the verse on the string alone; what makes it more than a string is that the situation matches — a rightful ruler displaced by his own people, protesting his legitimacy from outside the seat of power — and that the surrounding verses are running the Absalom sequence catalogued at 61:4. Held at moderate: the phrase is ordinary English and could be reinvented by anyone describing an expulsion.

pericopes.text: And behold, I have sent a proclamation throughout this part of the land; and behold, they are flocking to us daily, to their arms, in the defence of their country, and their freedom, and to avenge our wrongs.
And they have come unto us, insomuch that those which have rose up in rebellion against us, are set at defiance; yea, insomuch that they do fear us, and durst not come out against us to battle.

They have got possession of the land, or the city of Zarahemla; they have appointed a king over them, and he hath written unto the king of the Lamanites, in the which he hath joined an alliance with him; in the which alliance, he hath agreed to maintain the city of Zarahemla, in the which maintenance, he supposeth will enable the Lamanites to conquer the remainder of the land, and he shall be placed king over this people, when they shall be conquered under the Lamanites.

And now, in your epistle, ye hath censured me; but it mattereth not, I am not angry, but do rejoice in the greatness of your heart. I, Pahoran, do not seek for power, save only to retain my judgement seat, that I may preserve the rights and the liberty of my people. My soul standeth fast in that liberty, in the which God hath made us free.
And now behold we will resist wickedness even unto bloodshed. We would not shed the blood of the Lamanites, if they would stay in their own land.

links.text: Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.

provenance.other: Hebrews 12:4 is seven words long and two of its three phrases are KJV singletons: “resisted unto blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “striving against sin” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Resist' in any form occurs in only ten KJV verses, nine of them in the New Testament; Alma 61 uses the word five times in five verses.
provenance.significance: 'Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin' is a reproach in Hebrews: the readers' struggle against sin has not yet cost them anything, and the writer means martyrdom, not war. Pahoran answers the reproach in the affirmative and in the literal sense — 'we will resist wickedness even unto bloodshed' — and the sentence that follows makes the blood other people's, not his own: 'we would not shed the blood of the Lamanites, if they would stay in their own land'. The metalepsis is the whole point. Recover Hebrews 12's context and the resistance unto blood is Christ's, 'who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross'; Alma 61:10-14 converts the passive endurance of the epistle into a doctrine of just war, and does it with the epistle's own vocabulary. This is the pivot of Pahoran's ethics and it is built out of a seven-word verse.

links.note: 'And now behold we will resist wickedness even unto bloodshed.' Four content words, and three of them — resist, unto, blood — are Hebrews 12:4's, in Hebrews 12:4's order, with 'wickedness' standing where the KJV has 'sin'. The remaining KJV occurrence of 'unto blood' is Ezekiel 35:6, where blood pursues the guilty and no one resists anything, so the phrase resolves to Hebrews without ambiguity. Taken with the Matthew 5:39 row at 61:14, the epistle's argument for fighting is assembled from the two KJV verses about resistance that most obviously forbid it.

pericopes.text: We would not shed the blood of our brethren, if they would not rise up in rebellion and take the sword against us.
We would subject ourselves to the yoke of bondage, if it were requisite with the justice of God, or if he should command us so to do.
But behold he doth not command us that we shall subject ourselves to our enemies, but that we should put our trust in him, and he will deliver us.

links.text: If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.

provenance.other: 'He will deliver us' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 3:17, and in exactly one Book of Mormon verse, this one. The companion phrase from the same verse, 'able to deliver us', is likewise a KJV singleton and is adjudicated at 1 Nephi 4:3; the two halves of Daniel 3:17 therefore enter the Book of Mormon at its first chapter of narrative and at its last epistle, and nowhere in between.
provenance.significance: Daniel 3:17-18 is the KJV's model of principled refusal: our God is able to deliver us and he will deliver us, but if not, we still will not serve. Alma 61:12-13 puts the same two clauses in the same order and inverts the condition — 'we would subject ourselves to the yoke of bondage, if it were requisite with the justice of God … but behold he doth not command us that we shall subject ourselves to our enemies, but that we should put our trust in him, and he will deliver us'. Where the three young men submit to the furnace because God has not promised rescue, Pahoran declines submission because God has not commanded it. The borrowed sentence is the hinge on which the reversal turns, and the reversal is what licenses the war: obedience in Daniel means going into the fire, and here it means going to Zarahemla.

links.note: 'That we should put our trust in him, and he will deliver us.' A KJV singleton reproduced verbatim, in a two-verse structure that reproduces Daniel 3:17-18's conditional as well as its wording. The catalogue takes the phrase's other half at 1 Nephi 4:3, where Nephi cites the deliverance of the fathers from the Egyptians; this row is a fresh borrowing rather than a recurrence, because it is a different clause of the verse, in a different book, doing the opposite work — Nephi invokes Daniel's confidence to justify a killing, Pahoran invokes it to decline a surrender.

pericopes.text: Therefore my beloved brother Moroni, let us resist evil; and whatsoever evil we cannot resist with our words, yea, such as rebellions and dissensions, let us resist them with our swords, that we may retain our freedom, that we may rejoice in the great privilege of our church and in the cause of our Redeemer and our God.

links.text: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.

provenance.other: 'Resist not evil' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reproduces that verse without the negative at 3 Nephi 12:39, in its own Sermon; 'resist evil' as a positive imperative occurs in the Book of Mormon only here.
provenance.significance: Two Book of Mormon verses contain the phrase. One is 3 Nephi 12:39, where the risen Christ quotes Matthew 5:39 as it stands — 'resist not evil'. The other is this one, where a chief governor writes 'let us resist evil … let us resist them with our swords'. The catalogue cannot say which was composed first, but a reader of the finished book meets Pahoran's sentence four hundred pages before the Sermon that contradicts it, and then meets the contradiction. Metalepsis here works by suppression: Matthew 5:39's next clause is 'whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also', and Pahoran's next clause is the sword. The one verse of the KJV that forbids resistance supplies the words with which resistance is urged.

links.note: 'Let us resist evil; and whatsoever evil we cannot resist with our words … let us resist them with our swords.' The verbal contact is two words, and they are not rare words; what is rare is their pairing, which the KJV makes once and makes negative. Held at moderate rather than high because a writer wanting a positive imperative to resist evil could reach it without Matthew — James 4:7's 'resist the devil' is close by, and 'resist' is scattered across nine other New Testament verses. What tips it is the company: the same paragraph has already taken Hebrews 12:4 (61:10) and Daniel 3:17 (61:13), so the chapter is demonstrably assembling its war ethic out of the KJV's resistance vocabulary, and Matthew 5:39 is the verse that vocabulary is most conspicuously borrowed against.
links.whyNot: Two common words, and the Book of Mormon reverses the polarity of the only thing that makes them rare. A reader could hold that the resemblance to Matthew 5:39 is an accident of the English verb, and that the sentence's real background is the general New Testament exhortation to resist (James 4:7, 1 Peter 5:9) with no particular verse in view.

pericopes.text: Therefore come unto me speedily, with a few of your men, and leave the remainder in the charge of Lehi and Teancum; give unto them power to conduct the war in that part of the land, according to the spirit of God, which is also the spirit of freedom which is in them.

links.text: Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.

provenance.other: 'There is liberty' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Spirit of the Lord is' occurs in two, Luke 4:18 and 2 Corinthians 3:17; only the second predicates liberty of the Spirit. The Book of Mormon's word here is 'freedom', not 'liberty', which is why this is filed as an echo — though the same chapter uses 'liberty' for the same thing at 61:9 and 61:21.
provenance.significance: 'The spirit of God, which is also the spirit of freedom which is in them' is an identification, not a description, and the KJV makes that identification once: 'Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.' Paul is contrasting the veiled reading of Moses with the unveiled reading of Christ; the liberty is hermeneutical and interior. Pahoran gives Lehi and Teancum a commission to conduct a war 'according to the spirit of God, which is also the spirit of freedom'. If 2 Corinthians 3:17 is behind it, the sentence completes what Galatians 5:1 began three verses earlier: the chapter has taken Paul's two great statements about Christian liberty and made them the charter of a standing army. That is the reading; the wording alone will not compel it.

links.note: Proposed under CONVENTIONS §0a. There is no shared string — the Book of Mormon has 'freedom' where Paul has 'liberty' — so this is an echo on the strength of the proposition rather than the words: the equation of God's Spirit with freedom is Pauline and, in the KJV, is made in one verse. It is offered because the chapter's other borrowings make the Pauline liberty vocabulary demonstrably present (61:9, 61:12, 61:21 = Galatians 5:1), and because a reader who has been sent from 61:9 to the Galatians 5:1 row at Alma 58:40 should also be shown where that verse's companion would fall.
links.whyNot: No verbal contact at all. 'Spirit of freedom' is the Book of Mormon's own phrase, coined at Alma 51:6-7 with the freemen and used here without any sign of a source; a writer who had already made liberty the theme of a letter needs no epistle of Paul to call the impulse behind it a spirit.

pericopes.text: Behold I have sent a few provisions unto them, that they may not perish until ye can come unto me.
Gather together whatsoever force ye can upon your march hither, and we will go speedily against those dissenters, in the strength of our God, according to the faith which is in us.

And we will take possession of the city of Zarahemla, that we may obtain more food to send forth unto Lehi and Teancum; yea, we will go forth against them in the strength of the Lord, and we will put an end to this great iniquity.
And now, Moroni, I do joy in receiving your epistle; for I was somewhat worried concerning what we should do, whether it should be just in us to go against our brethren.
But ye have said, Except they repent, the Lord hath commanded you that ye should go against them.

See that ye strengthen Lehi and Teancum in the Lord; tell them to fear not, for God will deliver them; yea, and also all those who stand fast in that liberty wherewith God hath made them free. And now I close mine epistle to my beloved brother Moroni.

And now it came to pass that when Moroni had received this epistle, his heart did take courage, and was filled with exceeding great joy, becaus of the faithfulness of Paharon, that he was not also a traitor to the freedom and cause of his country.

But he did also mourn exceedingly, because of the iniquity of those who had driven Paharon from the judgement seat; yea, in fine, because of those who had rebelled against their country and also their God.

And it came to pass that Moroni took a small number of men, according to the desire of Paharon, and gave Lehi and Teancum command over the remainder of his army, and took his march towards the land of Gideon.
And he did raise the standard of liberty in whatsoever place he did enter, and gained whatsoever force he could in all his march towards the land of Gideon.
And it came to pass that thousands did flock unto his standard, and did take up their swords in the defence of their freedom, that they might not come into bondage.

And thus when Moroni had gathered together whatsoever men he could in all his march, he came to the land of Gideon; and uniting his forces with that of Pahoran, they became exceeding strong, even stronger than the men of Pachus, which was the king of those dissenters which had driven out the freemen out of the land of Zarahemla, and had taken possession of the land.

And it came to pass that Moroni and Pahoran went down with their armies into the land of Zarahemla, and went forth against the city, and did meet the men of Pachus, insomuch that they did come to battle.
And behold, Pachus was slain, and his men were taken prisoners; and Pahoran was restored to his judgement seat.

And the men of Pachus received their trial, according to the law, and also those king-men which had been taken and cast into prison; and they were executed according to the law; yea, those men of Pachus, and those king-men, whosoever would not take up arms in the defence of their country, but would fight against it, were put to death.—

And thus it became expedient that this law should be strictly observed, for the safety of their country; yea, and whosoever was found denying their freedom, was speedily executed according to the law.

And thus ended the thirtieth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi: Moroni and Pahoran having restored peace to the land of Zarahemla, among their own people, having inflicted death upon all those who were not true to the cause of freedom.

And it came to pass in the commencement of the thirty and first year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, Moroni immediately caused that provisions should be sent, and also an army of six thousand men, should be sent unto Helaman, to assist him in preserving that part of the land;

and he also caused that an army of six thousand men, with a sufficient quantity of food, should be sent to the armies of Lehi and Teancum. And it came to pass that this was done, to fortify the land against the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that Moroni and Pahoran, leaving a large body of men in the land of Zarahemla, took their march with a large body of men towards the land of Nephihah, being determined to overthrow the Lamanites in that city.
And it came to pass that as they were marching towards the land, they took a large body of men of the Lamanites, and slew many of them, and took their provisions, and their weapons of war.
And it came to pass after they had took them, they caused them to enter into a covenant, that they would no more take up their weapons of war against the Nephites.
And when they had entered into this covenant, they sent them to dwell with the people of Ammon; and they were in number about four thousand, which had not been slain.

And it came to pass that when they had sent them away, they pursued their march towards the land of Nephihah. And it came to pass that when they had come to the city Nephihah, they did pitch their tents in the plains of Nephihah, which is near the city Nephihah.

Now Moroni was desirous that the Lamanites should come out to battle against them, upon the plains; but the Lamanites knowing of their exceeding great courage, and beholding the greatness of their numbers, therefore they durst not come out against them; therefore they did not come to battle in that day.
And when the night came, Moroni went forth in the darkness of the night, and came upon the top of the wall to spy out in what part of the city the Lamanites did camp with their army.

And it came to pass that they were on the east, by the entrance; and they were all asleep. And now Moroni returned to his army, and caused that they should prepare in haste strong cords and ladders, to be let down from the top of the wall into the inner part of the wall.

links.text: Then she let them down by a cord through the window: for her house was upon the town wall, and she dwelt upon the wall.

provenance.other: “by a cord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 2:15, and that verse is also the KJV's one instance of a cord, a wall and a letting-down in a single sentence. The New Testament has the manoeuvre twice more, both of Paul at Damascus: “let down by the wall” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 11:33, and Acts 9:25 has “let him down by the wall in a basket”. Neither of those has a cord. In the Book of Mormon “let down” occurs only at Alma 62:21 and 62:23, and “with a cord” only at 62:36 — three verses of one chapter, and nowhere else in the volume.
provenance.significance: Every biblical descent by cord over a city wall is an escape: Rahab's spies get out of Jericho, Michal's David gets out of the house, Paul gets out of Damascus. Alma 62 reverses the vector twice in seventeen verses. Moroni's men go down the wall to get *into* Nephihah, and Teancum goes down a wall on a cord to get into the Lamanite camp. The reversal is what makes the borrowing legible as more than a coincidence of siegecraft, and it is thematically exact: the manoeuvre that in scripture preserves a life is used here to take a city and, at 62:36, to kill a king and lose the killer. Note too what precedes it. Moroni goes up the wall by night “to spy out in what part of the city the Lamanites did camp”, which is Joshua 2:1's errand — men sent by night to spy out a walled city — and the cord follows the spying in Joshua as it follows it here. The city is taken “without the loss of one soul” (62:26), which is Jericho's outcome for Rahab's household and not for anyone else in it.

links.note: “They should prepare in haste strong cords and ladders, to be let down from the top of the wall into the inner part of the wall.” The nouns are ordinary and the combination is not: cord, wall, and a body let down over it is one KJV verse in the Old Testament and two in the New, and the Book of Mormon confines the whole vocabulary to this chapter. Filed as an allusion at moderate rather than high because siege narrative will independently produce ropes and walls, and because the Book of Mormon adds ladders, which no source has.
